title: Alaska Senate’s coalition majority shrinks to bare minimum as three Republicans leave
description: The coalition majority in the 20-person Alaska Senate will be a bare-minimum 11 people after the departure of three Republican lawmakers. On Thursday, Sen. Jesse Bjorkman, R-Nikiski and a former member of the majority, said he will be minority leader of a newly expanded nine-person, all-Republican Senate minority. Sen. Robert Yundt, R-Wasilla, will be the […[...]
text:
Sen. Jesse Bjorkman, R-Nikiski, expresses frustration at a March 19, 2024, news conference the day after the legislature failed by one vote to override Gov. Mike Dunleavy's education-funding veto. Next to him is Sen. Bert Stedman, R-Sitka, a co-chair of the finance committee. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)The coalition majority in the 20-person Alaska Senate will be a bare-minimum 11 people after the departure of three Republican lawmakers.
On Thursday, Sen. Jesse Bjorkman, R-Nikiski and a former member of the majority, said he will be minority leader of a newly expanded nine-person, all-Republican Senate minority.
Sen. Robert Yundt, R-Wasilla, will be the Minority Whip, effectively the No. 2-ranked member of the minority.
The change means the Senate’s majority will be predominantly Democratic, which could mean an easier working relationship with the predominantly Democratic coalition in the state House and with Democratic Governor-elect Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins. It also means that the absence of a single member — due to illness, travel or family issues — could halt work in the Senate.
From 2025 through this year, the Senate Majority had 14 members — nine Democrats and five Republicans. As well as Bjorkman, its Republican membership included Sens. Kelly Merrick, R-Eagle River; Cathy Giessel, R-Anchorage; Gary Stevens, R-Kodiak; and Bert Stedman, R-Sitka.
Stevens retired and is on course to be replaced by Rep. Louise Stutes, R-Kodiak, who was leading a three-way race as of Friday.
Giessel will replace Stevens as Senate President. Stedman and Merrick are joining Bjorkman in the minority. 
According to a news release from the new Senate minority, Stedman will serve as the lead member of the minority on the Senate Finance Committee. 
Sen. Cathy Tilton, R-Wasilla, is on course to lose her election campaign to fellow Republican Ryan Berry. By phone, Berry said he will take Tilton’s spot in the minority and will not seek to join the majority.

name: WyoFile
title: Pragmatist Republicans tapped to lead Wyoming Legislature following Freedom Caucus’ electoral defeat
description:
Lawmakers nominated Cheyenne Sen. Tara Nethercott and Lander Rep. Lloyd Larsen respectively to serve as Senate President and House Speaker. 
The post Pragmatist Republicans tapped to lead Wyoming Legislature following Freedom Caucus’ electoral defeat appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
When the Wyoming Legislature convenes in January, they’ll likely be led by two Republicans known more for their traditionalist, pragmatic approach than the ideological conservatism of their predecessors.
Senate Republicans selected Cheyenne Sen. Tara Nethercott as the next president while House GOP members chose Lander Rep. Lloyd Larsen as incoming speaker, several legislators told WyoFile. 
Leadership positions hold significant power in both chambers, particularly the speaker and the president. They decide the makeup and head of each committee as well as what legislation goes to which committees, and in what order. Leadership also has the tools to kill legislation before it’s even considered by the larger body. 
While the GOP has controlled both chambers in the Wyoming Legislature for decades, its supermajority split in recent years between more traditional  Republicans and those aligned with the Wyoming Freedom Caucus. For the last two years, Freedom Caucus members have held all of the majority leadership positions in the House. During their tenure, the Legislature did away with most of the state’s gun-free zones, adopted a string of changes to the state’s election system and created a private-school waiver program with no income limits.
However, the caucus lost its House majority in this year’s primary election, and no longer has enough allies to form a voting bloc big enough to do much. Speaker of the House and Freedom Caucus member Chip Neiman, R-Hulette, lost his seat in the August primary, as did House Majority Floor Leader Scott Heiner, R-Green River, and House Majority Whip Ocean Andrew, R-Laramie. The caucus’s allies also backslid in the Senate. 
As a result, most legislative leadership races this weekend came down to contests between traditional Republicans with similar policy positions. 
Nethercott, who is now majority floor leader in the Senate, ran unopposed for president while Larsen competed against Casper Rep. Art Washut for speaker.
Larsen, who voters first elected in 2013, has become one of the House’s healthcare policy wonks and has spent much of his tenure trying to improve public health services. He also has eight years worth of experience serving on the Joint Appropriations Committee — a powerful panel of lawmakers responsible for crafting the initial budget bill. Larsen was also a vocal opponent of many of the budget cuts called for by the Freedom Caucus in the most recent session. 
Nethercott, an attorney, has largely focused her legislative career on economic development, higher education and judicial issues, including a term as chair of the Senate Judiciary Committee. In the most recent term, Nethercott worked as part of a coalition in the Senate to improve decorum and efficiency in the upper chamber.
“Wyoming deserves leadership that is steady in its principles, disciplined in its decisions, and focused on the future,” Nethercott said in a statement. “Our responsibility is to strengthen the foundations of our state, protect the opportunities that make Wyoming exceptional, and ensure the decisions we make today serve generations to come.”
Selections for some positions are only nominations at this point, since the entire body — Democrats included — must vote to affirm them. That includes the position of Senate president and vice president as well as House speaker and speaker pro tempore. However, with just two Democrats in the Senate and seven in the House, the nominations will likely win approval when the session begins in January in Cheyenne. 
If the chamber backs her next year, Nethercott would be just the second woman in Wyoming history to serve as president of the Senate, according to Legislative Service Office records. The first was Sen. April Brimmer-Kunz, also a Laramie County Republican, who served as president from 2003 to 2004. 
Lawmakers chose Evanston Sen. Wendy Schuler, who ran unopposed, to serve as Senate majority floor leader, a position that comes with the responsibility of deciding the order of bills lawmakers work through on the floor, among other things. 
For Senate vice president, Ten Sleep Sen. Ed Cooper bested Lander Sen. Cale Case for the second-in-command post.
In the House, Lusk Rep. JD Williams won majority floor leader over Wheatland Rep. Jeremy Haroldson, one of the few Freedom Caucus members who won their reelection bid. 
Jackson Rep. Andrew Byron beat Cheyenne Rep. Clarence Styvar for speaker pro tempore while Rock Springs Rep. Cody Wylie bested Worland Rep. Martha Lawley for majority whip. 
The Legislature’s democratic members also met Saturday in Casper to decide leadership positions, such as minority floor leader and whip in each chamber. Their meeting had not concluded by publishing time. 
This is a breaking news story and may be updated.

title: Colorado Senate Republicans pick Lisa Frizell as minority leader
description: Colorado Senate Republicans unanimously selected Sen. Lisa Frizell of Castle Rock as their new minority leader on Saturday morning. The vote came after Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, a Democrat, named former Senate Minority Leader Cleave Simpson as his nominee for Commissioner of Agriculture. Frizell arrived to the Senate in 2025 after one term in the House […]
text:
Colorado state Sen. Lisa Frizell, a Castle Rock Republican, listens to opening day proceedings on the first day of the 2025 session of the Colorado Legislature on Jan. 8, 2025, at the Colorado Capitol. (Lindsey Toomer/Colorado Newsline)Colorado Senate Republicans unanimously selected Sen. Lisa Frizell of Castle Rock as their new minority leader on Saturday morning.
The vote came after Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, a Democrat, named former Senate Minority Leader Cleave Simpson as his nominee for Commissioner of Agriculture.
Frizell arrived to the Senate in 2025 after one term in the House of Representatives and a career in the Douglas County Assessor’s Office. Before Saturday, she was the assistant minority leader for the caucus. When the new legislative session starts in January, she will lead the 11 Republicans in the chamber against a 24-member Democratic supermajority.
“It is forever my honor to serve this caucus, serve the people of Colorado and serve with this caucus, because we are a team and we are in this together,” she said. “I look forward to the opportunities in front of us — not the adversity — but the opportunities. They are there and we will make the most of them.”
Senate Republicans also unanimously chose Sen. Byron Pelton of Sterling as assistant minority leader, Sen. Scott Bright of Platteville as caucus chair and Sen. Janice Rich of Grand Junction as caucus whip. Sen. Barbara Kirkmeyer of Weld County will continue serving on the Joint Budget Committee.
In the Colorado House, Republicans earlier this month reelected Rep. Jarvis Caldwell as minority leader, a post he has served in since September 2025.
The legislative session will begin on Jan. 11, 2027.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Commentary: Washington needs to keep pushing for youth safety on social media
description: Existing at the forefront of any new technological frontier comes with advantages and drawbacks, and that is especially true for our digital lives. Organizing, connecting, and communicating has never been quite as seamless as it is today, and social media has progressed far beyond just entertainment. It’s granted us an awesome ability to foster community […]
text:
Washington's attorney general will not push a sweeping bill to limit social media for youths following a court settlement with Meta. (Photo Illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)Existing at the forefront of any new technological frontier comes with advantages and drawbacks, and that is especially true for our digital lives. Organizing, connecting, and communicating has never been quite as seamless as it is today, and social media has progressed far beyond just entertainment.
It’s granted us an awesome ability to foster community amongst those of us who would otherwise remain disconnected. But at the same time, the power to connect with virtually anyone and anything can be all-consuming. And in an era where it feels like many adults aren’t equipped to engage with social media, how on earth can we expect that of children?
It’s time we stand up to the big-tech giants that design our children’s digital lives who have left parents with little to no say in the matter. I have spoken with families across Washington who do their very best to stay up-to-date with the latest that social media has to offer, both in terms of parental control options and social/educational opportunities for their kids. But in a reality where most kids are juggling multiple apps with multiple profiles, parents simply can’t keep up.
Washington Attorney General Nick Brown took a stand on their behalf. He and other attorneys general across the country secured a settlement deal with Meta that will bring safeguards to its platforms to help parents do their job. These new features will roll out over the next couple of months and include time limits, notification blockers at night/during school hours, and options to switch off auto-play features. These types of settings will help kids manage a healthier relationship with technology so they can best succeed at home and in the classroom. The fight, however, is not over yet.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
I laud AG Brown for his work, as I’m sure most parents do across Washington state, but we know that the movement to keep kids safe does not stop at just Instagram and Facebook. Any form of social media that engages kids the way Meta’s platforms do should be held to the same standard. YouTube and TikTok both offer the same style of short-form, auto-playing content that exists on Instagram, but neither is bound by the agreement. This is meaningful because part of the agreement states that if the other major platforms adopt the same standards, Meta will release more money to states. In Washington, that means jumping from $237 million to nearly $339 million over the next decade. That’s roughly $100 million more that could help fund the youth mental health programs so many students in our communities rely on.
Surveys show that YouTube is the most widely used social media platform amongst American teens, so there is an even greater urgency for the platform to adopt these common-sense standards. YouTube is trying to evade responsibility by claiming it isn’t social media, which won’t fool anyone who has used the app recently.
I’ve seen firsthand how beneficial social media platforms have been for teens in the LGBTQ community. Finding peers and mentors with similar lived experience can be transformative, and in many cases, life-saving. I want to make sure these platforms are being used the right way, and AG Brown deserves great credit for heading that mission. We are so close to a huge breakthrough in the mission to keep kids safe online. I sincerely hope YouTube and TikTok step up so we get to see it through.
Sheila Stickel is a renowned family advocate throughout the Pacific Northwest. She has worked for 20 years advocating for human rights, including managing Washington State’s history making same-sex marriage campaign in 2012.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts led twice on health care. It’s time for a third major reform – this one focused on keeping people well.
description: Finding people whose risk is rising, before they become patients, is what makes prevention pay.
text:
GOV. HEALEY won her second term promising, among other things, to lower health care costs and expand access to primary, mental, and maternal health care. She takes up that challenge in the 20th anniversary year of the law that made Massachusetts the national model for health coverage. 
Twice, the Commonwealth has led the country on health care. If Healey wants affordable access to last, it will have to lead a third time, by building a system that pays to keep people well. 
The first wave was coverage. The 2006 reform, signed by a Republican governor, Mitt Romney, and written with a Democratic Legislature, made near-universal insurance a state guarantee and a template for the Affordable Care Act. It worked: 97.9 percent of residents are insured, against about 92 percent nationally. 
The second wave was cost. In 2012, Chapter 224 made Massachusetts the first state to set a target for health care spending growth, and created the Health Policy Commission to monitor it. For a while, it worked. Spending per resident grew an average of 3.5 percent a year from 2012 to 2019. 
Since then, the benchmark has been left behind. Growth has averaged 5.3 percent a year since 2019. In 2024, the state spent $83.3 billion on health care, or $11,663 per resident, an increase of 5.7 percent against a 3.6 percent target, the fourth year in a row it was missed. 
Two in five residents report trouble affording care. Family premiums for employer coverage reached $28,151, the highest in the country, and with out-of-pocket costs, a family’s health care cost $32,469. At recent growth rates, family premiums would reach a staggering $50,000 by 2032, according to Health Policy Commission projections presented last week.  
Coverage is also under strain. Federal Medicaid changes are expected to double the state’s uninsured rate. Expanding access is the right goal. But access built on a cost curve like this one will not hold. 
The benchmark measures what the system spends without changing what it buys. Meanwhile, primary care’s share of spending is shrinking, even though it is where most prevention happens: From 2019 to 2023, primary care spending grew 13.6 percent, against 20.6 percent for other medical care. 
I have seen this problem from the inside. For eight years, I built and scaled an integrated health care platform across the US and Canada under the two basic ways care is paid for. Under global payment contracts, we were responsible for a population’s total cost of care, so a visit that kept a patient out of the hospital saved money.  
Under fee-for-service, we were paid for each service delivered, so the same visit, by the same patient to the same clinician, earned only a modest fee, and keeping that patient out of the hospital earned us nothing at all. The contract, not the medicine, decided what got done. 
Massachusetts sits between those two models. It pioneered global budgets, and MassHealth now pays for 92 percent of members in its accountable care and managed care plans that way.  
But in commercial insurance, only about 35 percent of members’ care was under such arrangements in 2024, down from 39 percent two years earlier; the rest is still paid service by service.  
And even global contracts are settled year by year against spending targets, rewarding savings that appear quickly rather than those that arrive a decade later. For most residents, the system still works the way fee-for-service always has. I call it find it, fix it. Wait for disease to appear, then pay to treat it. Coverage brought more people into that model, and the benchmark tried to make it cheaper, but neither changed it.  
The third wave should finish what global payment began, and build a system to predict illness and prevent it. 
Prevention is not a blank check. Screening everyone for everything costs money. The Congressional Budget Office found that about 80 percent of the preventive services it studied raised total spending.  



What pays is prevention aimed at the right people. In the national Diabetes Prevention Program, an intensive lifestyle program cut new cases of type 2 diabetes by 58 percent among high-risk adults. And the opportunity for big gains with the right targets is huge: Only about one in four Americans with high blood pressure has it under control. That is why prediction comes first. Finding people whose risk is rising, before they become patients, is what makes prevention pay. 
Massachusetts already owns most of the tools. Five moves would lay the foundation for a system built to predict disease and prevent it: 
1. Measure health, not just spending. Alongside the cost growth benchmark, the Health Policy Commission should publish a yearly prevention scorecard for every major insurer and provider system. This should show the share of patients with blood pressure and blood sugar under control, and the hospital admissions that good primary care should have prevented.
2.  Use the data the state already has. The state’s all-payer claims database already tracks claims across most of the state’s insurers. Used with strong privacy protections, it can show where residents’ risk is rising before a diagnosis, so prevention can be targeted. 
3.  Protect primary care’s share. The Legislature is close: the House and Senate have each passed bills requiring at least 15 percent of health care spending to go to primary care, more than double today’s share, and a conference committee is now reconciling them. Lawmakers should finish the job before the year ends, and keep the new primary care payment models both bills include, so that practices are paid for keeping patients well rather than for the number of visits they log. 
4.  Pay for results, starting with the state’s own plans. MassHealth and the Group Insurance Commission, which covers state and municipal employees, should tie a meaningful share of payments to those control rates and avoided admissions. The state is a long-term payer. It should act like one. 
5.  Give prevention time to pay. The same two plans should also offer multiyear global contracts that credit providers for prevention savings measured over five years or more, and the Health Policy Commission should judge prevention investments over the same horizon when it assesses performance against the benchmark. 
None of this requires choosing between Democrats and Republicans. Romney, a Republican, signed the first wave into law with a Democratic Legislature. Gov. Deval Patrick, a Democrat, signed the second. Healey now has the chance to build the third. The Health Policy Commission has urged that Massachusetts “once again be the national leader in reimagining our health care system.” 
Twenty years ago, the question was who would be covered. Fourteen years ago, it was how much the system should cost. The question now is what all that money buys. Massachusetts answered the first two questions for the country. It should answer the third by laying the foundation for a health system that is paid to predict illness and prevent it. 
M. Vaman Rao is a Boston-based scientist, serial entrepreneur, innovator, and investor. He built and scaled an integrated health care platform across the US and Canada.

title: Tower Hill Field Hockey Crowned State Champions for First Time in nearly Two Decades
description: The Tower Hill Hillers defeated the Caravel Buccaneers, 3-1, in the 2026 DIAA Division Two State Championship, earning the program’s 19th state title.   FREDERICA, Del. — Tower Hill junior Molly Gallagher stepped to the penalty spot with her team tied, 1-1, under a minute to play in the third quarter. Gallagher placed the ball down and readied to take ... Re[...]
text:
The 2026 Tower Hill Field Hockey team poses for a picture after winning the 2026 DIAA Division Two Field Hockey State Championship game. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Tower Hill Hillers defeated the Caravel Buccaneers, 3-1, in the 2026 DIAA Division Two State Championship, earning the program’s 19th state title.
 
FREDERICA, Del. — Tower Hill junior Molly Gallagher stepped to the penalty spot with her team tied, 1-1, under a minute to play in the third quarter. Gallagher placed the ball down and readied to take her shot. The whistle blew and Gallagher didn’t waste a second. 
Gallagher fired a quick shot toward the right of the cage. Caravel goalkeeper, Hartley Haynes, moved quickly and got in front of the shot. Haynes seemed to have stopped the shot with the pad on her left hand, but the ball deflected off the pad backwards and right behind her to the back of the cage.
Gallagher scored on a second penalty stroke opportunity in the fourth quarter helping Tower Hill defeat Caravel, 3-1, and earn the 2026 DIAA Division Two State title.
“It’s just such an amazing feeling. We’ve been working so hard all season,” Gallagher said postgame. “This was such like a team effort, it wasn’t just one person. We like, we passed so well, we moved the ball, we stuck to the gameplan. This is just like an unreal feeling.”   
The Hillers and Buccaneers played a close game through frigid temperatures and strong winds, Friday night. The two teams battled for possession through most of the first quarter with only a pair of Caravel penalty corners presenting possible scoring chances. Midway through the second quarter the Hillers broke through.
The game’s opening goal was scored by Tower Hill senior Hailey Allen on the right of the cage. The play was initiated by Gallagher who dribbled through a pair of Buccaneer defenders at the top of the circle to create a bit of space for a pass to Charlotte Vanni a few yards away from the goal. Vanni quickly fired a backhand shot that was deflected by a Caravel defender, but landed right in front of Allen to knock in.    
Tower Hill’s defense withstood three Caravel penalty corner attempts in the final five minutes of the quarter and closed out the half with a 1-0 lead.
The midfield battle continued into the second half until Caravel worked the ball into its offensive zone with just under six minutes to play in the third quarter. The Buccaneers breached the circle and fired a pair of shots at the goal to no avail. One of the shot attempts drew a foul call on the Hiller defense and resulted in a penalty stroke opportunity for Buccaneer sophomore, Allie Sweeney. Sweeney fired a low shot to the left of the cage to tie the game, 1-1.
Gallagher’s first penalty stroke followed about four minutes later and her success returned the advantage back to the Hillers before the fourth quarter. 
Caravel’s offense put together a couple strong attempts at an equalizer, but the Hillers’ defense stood strong and didn’t allow another score. Gallagher added a second goal to her ledger with a score on a second penalty stroke opportunity and Tower Hill protected the lead until the final buzzer rang out. Gallagher finished the game with two goals on two successful penalty stroke attempts.
“It’s such an honor, like, it’s so much pressure but I know they believe in me and that just gives me the strength to keep going,” Gallagher said about being the one to take the penalty shots while a group of Tower Hill fans shouted MVP chants in the background. 
The 2026 Hiller team finished the season with a 17-1 overall record and the program’s first state championship since 2008. Tower Hill head coach Lindsay Goeller graduated from the school a year before that title but won three before that as a player under former Hiller head coach Robin Adair. Adair led the Hillers to ten state championship victories over her career, winning four straight titles multiple times.
Goeller said her staff is filled with alumni that span across three decades of Hiller field hockey and that passion and investment for the school and program make this state championship special.
“As a staff we’re so invested in this program, in Tower Hill, in the culture of field hockey and its so special to bring a state championship back to Tower Hill,” Goeller said. “We’re so proud and you can feel the tradition, you can feel what it means to our program to have the trophy back.” 
Caravel finished the season with a 13-5 overall record and the program’s first state championship appearance since 2020.

title: State librarian seeks funding, Capitol campus return amid budget cuts
description: This article was first published by TVW. Washington’s new state librarian wants $4.2 million to stabilize services and restore public access to historic collections while advancing a long-delayed plan to return the State Library and Archives to the Capitol campus. On Thursday, the Joint State Capitol Committee and Capitol Campus Design Advisory Committee vot[...]
text:
This article was first published by TVW.
Washington’s new state librarian wants $4.2 million to stabilize services and restore public access to historic collections while advancing a long-delayed plan to return the State Library and Archives to the Capitol campus.
On Thursday, the Joint State Capitol Committee and Capitol Campus Design Advisory Committee voted to recommend a new library and archives building to the Legislature to be built on the site of the former General Administration building on the campus.
Melody Sky Weaver told Inside Olympia host Austin Jenkins that persistent budget cuts have left the state’s oldest cultural institution struggling to maintain services.
State Librarian Melody Sky Weaver appears on TVW’s “Inside Olympia.” (Photo courtesy of TVW)
Twelve employees received layoff notices in 2025 after revenue from real estate recording fees fell short of projections. The state library in Tumwater is now open by appointment only, on Thursdays from 1 to 4 p.m.
“The level of access they had before has been crippled by these budget cuts,” Weaver said.
The library’s approximately $12.7 million biennial budget supports historic collections, institutional libraries in prisons and other facilities, and the Washington Talking Book and Braille Library.
Even before Weaver began as state librarian on October 1, she made news by advocating for the return of the library to the Capitol campus, which it left following the 2001 Nisqually earthquake.
The proposed Library and Archives Building (LAB) would replace aging and inadequate facilities with collection storage, exhibition space, meeting rooms and other public amenities.
Weaver sees the project as an opportunity to make the library more accessible to lawmakers, researchers and visitors. A self-described “extroverted loud librarian,” Weaver says advocacy is essential to reversing years of cuts and raising the institution’s profile.
Her larger goal is to make the State Library indispensable, rather than one of Washington’s best-kept secrets. “I feel like libraries are very sexy, but of course I’m biased,” she said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: ‘The auditor owns a used car dealership. His landlord is a friend he signed deeds for.’
description: The relationship that led to calls for investigation and resignation by state lawmakers between state Auditor Mark Hunt and Charleston attorney Robert L. Johns goes beyond property deeds and state office work.
text:
After Hours Used Auto was a by-appointment car dealership owned and operated by state Auditor Mark Hunt and high ranking officials in his administration. The owner of the property is Robert L. Johns, an attorney Hunt signed tax deeds for in a move some lawmakers say may have violated the law. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)The relationship that led to calls for investigation and resignation by state lawmakers between state Auditor Mark Hunt and Charleston attorney Robert L. Johns goes beyond property deeds and state office work. 
During Hunt’s term as auditor he has sold cars at After Hours Used Auto, a by-appointment car dealership less than a mile from the state Capitol in Charleston, West Virginia, that sits on land owned by Johns. 
The lot holds five cars — including a black 2013 Ford Expedition, with dents in the hatch door and a silver sedan with a flat tire — and a small shack with a sign telling customers to call to book an appointment to see a car. 
A silver sedan with a flat tire sits on the lot of After Hours Used Auto, a dealership owned and operated by the state Auditor and high ranking officials in his administration. (Photo by Lori Kersey/West Virginia Watch)
Hunt established the business in July 2024, roughly four months before he would be elected state auditor. When reached by phone Friday at his private law practice, Hunt stressed that no cars were sold during state government working hours.  
“It was a hobby. That’s the reason, you know it’s kind of funny, the name was After Hours,” he said. 
The owner of the property is NAJ, a limited liability company owned by Johns, who has accumulated $38 million in tax delinquent land across the state. A West Virginia Watch investigation revealed that Hunt, as auditor, has signed nine tax deeds for Johns, even though state law says that’s a duty of the deputy land commissioner. 
Hunt acknowledged Johns had been a “friend for years.” Johns, a bankruptcy attorney, was also hired by the Auditor’s Office after Hunt took office to act as a receiver in the event that McDowell County declared insolvency. 
Johns was paid $14,000 for his work in 2025, according to the State Checkbook, an online repository detailing West Virginia’s finances. 
Hunt said the fact that Johns owns the land the lot sits on is a coincidence. 
“(There’s) not a ghost behind every door. It’s just coincidental,” Hunt said. “He happens to have all of these vacant lots, and most of this property is scrub property. It’s hillsides, it’s vacant lots, it’s right-of-ways, and he just happened to own this.” 
The revelations about the tax deeds led to outcry from public officials, both Republican and Democrat. The Democratic caucuses in the House of Delegates and the state Senate also sent letters to Attorney General JB McCuskey to request an opinion on the legality of the situation. 
Del. Tristan Leavitt, R-Kanawha, has been a leading Republican voice in the tax deed controversy, taking to social media to call for the auditor’s resignation. The car dealership has added fuel to that fire, he said. 
“This new information raises significant additional questions about Hunt’s relationship with Johns,” he said. “Is Hunt’s car dealership paying market price for rent on the lot owned by Johns’ company, or did Hunt illegally sign his landlord’s deeds as payback for a sweetheart lease? Regardless, this business relationship further underscores Hunt’s cronyism and why he should resign as auditor immediately for signing those deeds.” 
Hunt said that he paid fair market rent to Johns for the lot. But he doesn’t know how much. 
“I’m not saying that like I’m hiding it,” Hunt said. “I don’t know how much we were paying. I didn’t do that part of it. OK. So all I did was cut the grass.” 
The “we” Hunt referred to are people he calls “the boys” — his co-deputy chiefs of staff Caleb Hanna and David Cole. 
Hanna is a former state delegate who ran for auditor during the 2024 Republican Primary. Cole worked at Hunt’s law office for 17 years as an operations and marketing manager. 
Hanna sold a 2012 Lincoln MKZ Hybrid to Amber Blankenship, of Huntington, on a Saturday in October 2025. 
“It was for my then-19-year-old son,” she said. 
Blankeship said she did not visit the lot on a Friday evening in October. Instead, Blankenship met the state auditor at his private law office, she recalled. 
“The main office that I walked in was, they asked what I was there for, and I said, ‘Well, I’m supposed to be meeting somebody here about a car,’ and they called him (Hunt) and told him to bring it over,” Blankenship said.
The sign on the door at After Hours Auto Sales explains that it is appointment only, and includes a phone number to call. (Photo by Henry Culvyhouse/West Virginia Watch)
Blankenship said after taking it for a test drive, she was ready to buy. Hanna filled out the paperwork and Cole helped handle the payment. Cole asked her to send the money via an app, but the sale price was over the limit allowed by the app. Instead, she came back the following day and paid for it with her savings from the bank. 
Hunt said he never sold cars personally on the lot, but in this case the Lincoln was his personal, daily driver. 
“Yeah, I sold my car like anybody else does. I bought another car and I sold that one. I mean that that’s all it was,” Hunt said. “A deal between two parties is a deal.” 
Blankenship sued Hanna and After Hours Used Auto after the car broke down just nine days after purchase, according to Kanawha County court records. 
She accused the dealership of selling a lemon, court records show. 
Hunt himself entered an appearance in the case on a Tuesday in February 2026. A magistrate court judge dismissed the case after finding Blankenship had agreed to buy the car “as is.” 
Blankenship said she later sold the car for “basically scrap.” 
Hunt said the dealership from the beginning was a money losing proposition and in recent months has shuttered its doors. He said he, Cole and Hanna haven’t gotten around to clearing the cars off the lot. 
“After we lost about $40,000, I convinced the boys that we need to quit doing this. There’s no more to it or less to it than that,” Hunt said. 
Lori Kersey contributed to this report.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Scammers stole his image to lure the lovesick. Then the lovesick came looking for him
description: A portrait of Hunter Bigham and screenshots of fake social media profiles from scammers using Bigham's images are captured in this single long exposure photograph, Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026, in Tupelo, Miss.
text:
TUPELO — The peace of the Palm Springs evening was shattered by the woman’s scream, as piercing as if she’d seen a ghost.
Her shriek tore across the sidewalk, startling Hunter Bigham, who’d been waiting with his husband to cross the street. Glancing over his shoulder, he tried to work out who the woman — now beelining toward him — could possibly be screaming at.
“I told her you weren’t real!” she shouted, eyes locked on Hunter. “I told her you weren’t real!”
It was then that Hunter knew: He was the ghost, the cause of the chaos. And he knew why.
The woman’s story was, by this point, grimly familiar to him: Her friend had fallen in love with a stranger online who was using Hunter’s photos as his own. The woman had been trying to persuade her friend that the romance — and Hunter’s supposed online persona as her romancer — were not real.
Hunter assured the woman that he didn’t know her friend, that he was a happily married gay man, and that he, too, was a victim of romance scammers: not as their financial target, but as their unwilling bait.
For more than eight years, romance scammers have stolen Hunter’s photos to create hundreds of fake online profiles that have been used to trick lovesick men and women out of their money. When many victims realize they’ve been duped, they dig — eventually finding Hunter. The losses he’s tallied just from victims who have contacted him have reached roughly $1.4 million.
As the face of scammers’ schemes, people like Hunter are highly visible. As victims of identity theft, they are virtually unseen, left to handle the fallout alone.
Some victims, wrongly believing that Hunter is the scammer, threaten to hurt him, his family and themselves, injecting a thread of dread into his daily life. One victim furiously cursed at Hunter, said he knew where he lived and vowed to destroy his son’s career.
A mural of Elvis Presley decorates a downtown building in his hometown of Tupelo, Miss., as a resident places American flags along West Main Street for the Labor Day holiday, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026. Credit: David Goldman/Associated Press
At its peak, Hunter says, up to 15 victims a day contacted him. They have come from the United States, Spain, Venezuela, Hong Kong. They have been cancer survivors, a retired cop, a CEO. They knew him not as Hunter, but as Vince, Roberto, and — perhaps most prolifically — Henry Clerk. Under that name alone (sometimes spelled Clark), The Associated Press found 177 accounts on Facebook using Hunter’s photos as their profile pictures.
The scammers have claimed he is a widowed petroleum geologist in Houston. A Spanish secret agent named John. Frequently — and conveniently — they claim he is an oil rig worker, stuck at sea while the landlocked lovelorn pine for him … or, rather, the person they think is him.
The real Hunter Bigham is a father of three who lives with his husband, Johnny, in Elvis Presley’s hometown of Tupelo, Mississippi. He spends his time not on oil rigs, but on the phone as a sales executive for a furniture manufacturer. He also spends his time on social media posting photos of himself and his family — and promoting his side hustle, as he calls it, in the adult entertainment industry.
In the days after the Palm Springs incident, the enormity of the fraud associated with his face began to sink in, as did the futility of his attempts to stop it. His requests to internet platforms to remove the fake profiles have been largely rejected, and his complaints to the FBI have gotten him nowhere.
For a gay man in the American South who fought to live his true identity, the theft of it has been particularly agonizing — as has the suggestion that he try to stop the scammers by erasing himself from the internet.
“I worked so hard to get where I am and to accept myself for who I am,” he says, his voice breaking. “It nearly killed me. And I just — I just can’t go back there again.”
—
The rainbow flag adorning the back porch of Hunter and Johnny’s home flaps in a breeze that’s losing its battle against Mississippi’s sticky summer heat. The couple put it there as a symbol of gay pride.
The steeple of a church is seen through the window of the Bigham family home next to a rainbow flag, Thursday, Sept. 3, 2026, in Tupelo, Miss.  Credit: David Goldman/Associated Press
That pride was hard-won after Hunter’s long struggle to shed the shame he felt over being gay. Those feelings of shame have resurfaced amid the knowledge that his image is being used to con the vulnerable.
“People just don’t understand the depth of it and the breadth of it,” he says. “It goes really, really deep, but it also goes really wide because it takes in so many people’s lives.”
Few in the Western world are untouched by scams. Ninety-eight percent of Americans suspect they have been targeted with scam messages, according to a poll by The Associated Press-NORC Center for Public Affairs Research.
Little is known about those whose images make such scams possible. But Hunter’s experience is not unique, says Bryan Denny, a retired U.S. Army colonel whose pictures have been used by romance scammers for the past decade.
His life, too, has been upended by victims who have harassed him and his family. In response, he co-founded the group Advocating Against Romance Scammers, which he says has reported more than 3,000 fraudulent profiles of Denny to Facebook. The group backed a recently enacted law that requires dating apps to warn users when they are talking to someone who has been banned for suspected fraud.
Denny, who believes there are thousands of people used as scammers’ bait, understands Hunter’s guilt: It is his image, Denny says, being used to defraud people. Beyond guilt is anger.
“I spent 26 years in a uniform to fight bullies, to fight people who took advantage of other people — only at the end of that to have my pictures in my uniform used to do the very thing that I detested,” he says.
Bryan Denny, a retired Army colonel and founder of the group Advocating Against Romance Scammers, poses for a portrait with one of the many fake online profiles using his photos, Monday, Sept. 28, 2026, at his home in Williamsburg, Va.  Credit: Allen G. Breed/Associated Press
Not even those who investigate scammers are safe. Rebecca Keithley, who retired in July from her role as an assistant section chief in the FBI’s Financial Crimes Section, says she was impersonated twice online this year, on Instagram and Facebook. Though the Facebook account used her name and photos, Keithley says Meta repeatedly determined the account did not violate its community standards; it was removed only after FBI leadership contacted the company.
Around a week later, the same fraudulent account was restored. Meta again initially declined to remove it, she says, and it took another intervention to get it taken down.
“I’m at a loss for what to do,” Keithley says. “I have no confidence in Meta’s security’s ability to do anything.”
While such scams also plague other platforms, Meta, which owns Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp, is the largest social media company in the world. In a statement to the AP, Meta said in the first half of 2026, it removed over 179 million accounts, pages and groups for misrepresenting identity — the vast majority before anyone reported them. It also said new AI tests cut reports of the most impersonated celebrities by over 80%.
“We fight impersonation on our platforms because it’s not good for us or the people and businesses that rely on our services,” a Meta spokesperson said.
In Keithley’s case, Meta said its systems initially detected and disabled the impostor account but it was reinstated in error. As for Denny, Meta said it is continually improving detection and enforcement with fake accounts.
LinkedIn — another platform used by Hunter’s impersonators — told the AP that 99.7% of the fake accounts it removes are shut down before a report is made.
Hunter has some compassion for the scammers; he recognizes that many are trafficking victims forced to work in prisonlike compounds. But he has no patience for internet platforms like Meta, which he says could prevent fraudulent profiles by requiring people to provide identification. (Meta told the AP it aims to limit the amount of sensitive information it collects.)
Hunter Bigham, right, who for more than eight years has had his photos stolen by romance scammers to create hundreds of fake online profiles, sits to eat at a barbecue restaurant with his husband, Johnny, left, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026, in Starkville, Miss.  Credit: David Goldman/Associated Press
“I hold the most responsibility for the platforms,” Hunter says. “They could stop this today.”
But they haven’t. And so Hunter became committed to dealing with it himself — one victim at a time.
—
The chaos began in 2018, with the arrival of a string of mysterious online messages: Was he in London? Berlin? Sydney? the strangers asked. He wasn’t. But accounts featuring his face were posting from far-flung locations.
Hunter was initially flattered, assuming the impersonators thought he was handsome and were emulating him to gain followers.
But soon, the people contacting him said they were losing money. He realized this was something more sinister: He was being used by scammers. And he suspected they were using him for reasons far less flattering than he first thought.
“I realized it’s not because I’m so good looking,” he says. “It’s just because I am so average that I look attainable.”
Indeed, while some victims said they’d been drawn to Hunter’s looks, many were drawn more to the attention the posers provided.
“Hunter, I fell in love. And I was a fool. You are now the only one who knows the extent of it,” wrote one woman in 2019, a cancer survivor who lost $75,000 to a scammer who had insisted he was Hunter’s (nonexistent) identical twin. “I am retired and have no way to replenish this money.”
His agony is clear in his response: “I’m just at a complete loss. … My heart is just breaking. I wish I could help somehow,” he wrote. “I feel partly responsible.”
That responsibility compelled him to reply to every victim. He reassured the heartbroken that they were worthy of love.
He felt kinship in their longing for real love; for so long, it had seemed unattainable. Raised as a Southern Baptist to believe that homosexuality is a sin, he’d spent decades denying who he was. He married his childhood sweetheart, and they had three children. When she found out about his sexuality, she was crushed. He wondered whether it would be easier on his family if he was dead.
Hunter Bigham, left, embraces his father, Ernest, at the start of a Mississippi State college football game, Saturday, Sept. 5, 2026, in Starkville, Miss.  Credit: David Goldman/Associated Press
At her urging, he met with staff at a “conversion therapy” program; the discredited practice attempts to suppress a person’s sexuality and has been widely condemned as dangerous by mainstream medical associations.
Unnerved, he saw a Christian counselor instead, then spent six weeks in a treatment facility for sex addiction.
When it became clear therapy couldn’t turn him straight, he and his wife divorced. He let go of his self-hatred, dabbled in modeling and moved across the street from his ex to be near his children.
He knew who Johnny was long before they met online. At the time, Johnny was one of the most prominent adult film actors in the industry. Like Hunter, he had once been married to a woman. His first gay relationship was with his divorce attorney – and the attorney’s boyfriend – as part of a throuple.
Hunter knew within 30 minutes of meeting Johnny in person that he was the one. Johnny moved in with him three months later.
The duo started producing adult content together. Shirtless photos of Hunter became a staple of his social media, along with more typical proud dad posts about his kids.
Hunter Bigham, right, and his husband, Johnny, are photographed in their home, Monday, Sept. 7, 2026, in Tupelo, Miss. (AP Photo/David Goldman)
The scammers seemed to favor him fully clothed, using photos of him on business trips and alongside his children. “The gayer my posts got, the less they used of it,” he says. So he minimized photos featuring his family and maximized those featuring his flexed abs.
But the victims kept rolling in, some of whom found the humor in their situations.
After realizing the face — and body — of the man she loved belonged to an adult film actor, one great-grandmother congratulated Hunter on his nude physique.
“Not as notable as my first husband,” she wrote, “but deserves an applause.”
Others, though, were devastated by all they had lost.
“I am not beautiful and I felt you were out of my league,” one woman wrote. “Just for a short time I felt like Cinderella and your photo was my Prince, midnight is past and I will treasure my memories of being loved.”
His response is gentle. “You seem to have a kind, trusting heart, so I hope that doesn’t change despite bad people taking advantage of you,” he wrote. “You are indeed beautiful!”
Yet alongside his sympathy was a burgeoning unease. One woman told Hunter that he was coincidentally near her home on a business trip when she realized she was being scammed. She would have fainted if she’d bumped into him, she wrote.
“I think it’s going to happen one day,” he told her. “That I cross paths with a victim who thinks I should know them or that somebody is going to unload a gun through my window.”
At the heart of his anxiety were the victims who refused to believe he was a pawn rather than a perpetrator. His stomach knotted at the arrival of each new message, some of which snowballed into weekslong exchanges in which he tried to persuade the victim he was not the enemy.
He wondered how far this could possibly go.
—
Hunter Bigham, who has a side job in the adult entertainment industry and started lifting weights around the time he came out, flexes in front of a mirror during a gym workout, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Tupelo, Miss.  Credit: David Goldman/Associated Press
As the losses deepened, of money and of hope, Hunter grew desperate to shut it all down.
He reported the fake profiles to Facebook, he said, but the platform repeatedly told him they didn’t violate community standards and removed only a handful. (Meta told the AP it removed four accounts Hunter recently reported and is investigating his case.)
He tried watermarking his photos; the scammers stripped them off.
He asked victims for the scammers’ phone numbers and tried tracking them down. After Hunter posed as a potential victim, one scammer, “Kyle,” promised to pay off his debt if Hunter sent him credit card details.
He baited Kyle by asking: “What do you look like?” Kyle responded with a series of photos – of Hunter.
Enraged, Hunter filed a report with the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center and called the local FBI office. But apart from advising him to share the agency’s contact details with victims, he says, the FBI staffer told him there was little they could do. (The FBI told the AP it couldn’t comment on individual complaints.)
He debated whether to shutter his social media accounts. But then the scammers could just keep using the photos they already had, and victims would have virtually no way of finding the real Hunter.
He acknowledges a less benevolent motivation: He uses social media to promote his work in the adult content industry. Beyond that, he says, vanishing from public view felt like being forced back into the closet.
“It’s the shame, or the resistance of it, that has kept me from disappearing off of social media,” he says, voice cracking as he begins to cry. “Because if I disappear, then it’s admitting the shame.”
By 2020, the scammers had become more sophisticated. Victims told Hunter they’d had video calls with people who looked like him. They sent him pictures of passports bearing his image but strangers’ names.
The scammers’ net grew so wide that seven people Hunter knew told him they’d been approached online by his impersonators.
One day, his boss at the furniture manufacturer told him that someone had contacted the company insisting that Hunter owed them money. Worried the job he loved was at risk, Hunter explained that the person was a scam victim.
Hunter Bigham, who for more than eight years has had his photos stolen by romance scammers to create hundreds of fake online profiles, works in his home office, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, in Tupelo, Miss. (AP Photo/David Goldman)
He stopped talking about it much, even to Johnny. In a rare moment, one victim acknowledged Hunter’s suffering alongside her own.
“I feel as bad for you guys having your identity stolen as I do for all of us having our hearts and money stolen,” she wrote.
His message-checking became a protective mechanism against aggressive victims he sought to calm before things escalated. Vicious or depressing messages could tank his mood for the day.
Johnny absorbed his partner’s emotional shrapnel. Soft-spoken and nurturing, he is a worrier who became even more so amid his husband’s fixation on the pain of strangers.
Those worries escalated sharply when, in 2022, Hunter came to him with a request: A victim in Switzerland had asked to meet him in France during their upcoming family vacation. Was that OK with Johnny?
It was not. This has gone too far, Johnny replied.
But Hunter assured him the meeting would be quick. And maybe it could answer some of his questions — about who these victims really were, and why they kept falling for his image over and over again.
—
She was waiting for Hunter in the dark, standing outside the holiday apartment he’d rented in Nice, France.
Hunter, flanked by his 25-year-old daughter, her three friends and Johnny, was carrying a cup of gelato as he approached — a deliberate choice to make the meeting appear more casual, less consequential.
For a year, the woman had believed Hunter’s face belonged to the man she loved. For another year, she’d tried to reconcile the two versions through her correspondence with the real Hunter.
Hunter’s nerves calmed, too. “She’s not crazy,” he thought as he looked at her. “She’s just sad.”
Hunter Bigham, left, and his husband, Johnny, make breakfast, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, at their home in Tupelo, Miss.  Credit: David Goldman/Associated Press
But as soon as she saw Hunter’s smile, her anxiety melted. “This beautiful man really does exist,” she thought.
He invited the woman up to their apartment. Johnny rolled his eyes; The couple had agreed beforehand that the meeting would happen in public.
But the woman seemed harmless, and Hunter didn’t want to have an emotional conversation on the street. So they gathered in the living room. She gave them chocolates from her village and shared her story.
She was a mother of two in a rocky marriage when she was approached on LinkedIn by a geologist from Florida named Bryce Kane. Staring at his photo, she was struck by the warmth in his eyes — Hunter’s eyes.
“It all felt kind of like a fairy tale,” she told the AP on the condition that her name be withheld to protect her children’s privacy. She fell in love.
“I’m so ashamed of it,” she says now. “But that’s how it was.”
She is a finance professional who has taken courses on internet fraud and warned her own clients against making questionable payments. But Bryce seemed genuine. He sent her a picture of his passport, and had a video call with her. She received a call from a woman who said she was Bryce’s daughter, urging her to help her father.
Bryce said he was leaving for Venezuela to work aboard a ship. He needed money to pay his employees’ wages. She was eventually drained of 48,000 euros ($54,000).
It unraveled when she noticed Bryce was also communicating with another woman online. She began digging and found three more profiles bearing Bryce’s photos. “Bryce” eventually admitted he was a scammer from Nigeria.
In the French apartment, Hunter sought to assuage her shame. “You’re not alone in this,” he told her.
Next to him, Johnny’s worries had given way to empathy and a sense of the surreal. How odd, he thought, to be talking to someone who once believed she was in love with my husband.
Their meeting ended in an embrace. She walked away in tears, relieved.
“They’re both so great,” she says now of Hunter and Johnny. “I love them to pieces.”
Hunter, too, was relieved. He felt like he finally understood the who and the why behind the strangers who contacted him. But he had no desire to meet any others.
“I’m not the person they fell in love with,” he says. “And I don’t want to be.”
—
Yet where there has been love, there has also been hate.
The first venomous messages from the American man arrived as Hunter was preparing to depart for France. He’d lost $600,000 to a scammer who had groomed him for more than three years. And he was certain that scammer was Hunter.
The man assailed him with insults and threatened to turn him into the FBI. He mentioned Hunter’s oldest son by name and said he was going to ruin the young man’s career. He sent a photo of Hunter and his son that had been altered to align with the scammer’s backstory. Hunter sent him the original image, explained that the photo had been manipulated. Yet the man continued to rage before dissolving into despair.
“I (fell) in love with you,” he wrote. “Now I want to kill my self.”
Despite the abuse, Hunter’s reply was sympathetic. “I’m sorry for that. I can put you in contact with plenty of others in your situation. You’re not alone in this.”
The man again threatened suicide. Hunter suggested a paper trail might help investigators track the money.
“It all went by bitcoin,” the man wrote. “Goodbye”
One day, while on a business trip, Hunter noticed he had a voicemail. He pressed play.
“After what you put me through … you don’t think I’m gonna let this slide?” the man’s voice sneered into his ear. “There’s no way in hell I’m gonna let this slide.”
For three minutes the man ranted, threatening to report Hunter to his boss and issuing expletives about Hunter’s sexuality.
“You, my funny friend, better come up with the 600,000, and get it to me, in cash,” he said, voice rising into a shout: “You got it? YOU GOT IT?”
Hunter felt panic swelling. He was away from home. Was his family safe?
He sent the voicemail to a lawyer. But the man’s messages continued to poison his inbox.
“I’m contacting your work place,” he warned. “do they know your a scammer”
Hunter begged him to contact the FBI and to save all his conversations and documents. The man’s reply chilled him.
“Does the police know where you live in MS,” he wrote. “I do.”
Hunter blocked the man’s number and profiles, preventing further contact.
Everything felt like it had gotten out of control. His sleep was plagued by nightmares.
Not wanting to frighten his children, he kept the threats to himself. He acknowledges his silence was also self-preserving: He didn’t want his kids to hate him for posting photos of them that had been used to hurt others.
When his youngest daughter was 4, he nearly lost her in a car crash that killed his mother. Though she is now 25, he still refers to her as “the baby” and remains fiercely protective. And yet he admits his posts have exposed her to possible harm.
One recent morning, Hunter sends her a photo of the two of them that scammers have altered to make her look pregnant. She laughs. “That’s actually insane,” she replies. “My boobs look good though!”
She frequently laughs over the absurdity of it all. But behind her laughter is genuine concern. Unlike her father, she is deeply private and spoke on the condition that her name not be used.
“I don’t know them — or what they’re capable of,” she says of the victims. “The threat is very real.”
She is torn over her father’s presence online, though would prefer that he not post photos of her.
“He has a family and I understand he wants to share that,” she says. “But it is kind of a double-edged sword.”
—
Hunter Bigham messages a scammer he suspects is using his social media post to phish for victims, Friday, Sept. 4, 2026, part of his morning routine before getting out of bed at his home in Tupelo, Miss.  Credit: David Goldman/Associated Press
It is just after dawn and the glow from Hunter’s phone has woken Johnny, as it does every morning. Next to him in bed, Hunter is immersed in his ritualistic message checking, though until today Johnny didn’t realize what was really happening inside his husband’s mind.
What’s happening is this: Are any of the victims about to kill themselves? Are any coming after my family? How can I defuse the ticking time bombs in my inbox?
“I honestly didn’t know the extent of it until today,” Johnny says, voice trembling. “He keeps a lot in.”
Hunter pats his partner’s arm.
“I’m OK,” Hunter tries to assure him. “I’m just kind of numb to it at this point.”
Johnny wipes away tears and clasps his husband’s hand. He used to love listening to Hunter laugh in his sleep. He hasn’t laughed in a long time.
“I’d just like it to be over,” Hunter says.
The next night, sitting amid thousands of fans at a Mississippi State football game, thoughts about the scammers invade Hunter’s mind, cutting through the chaos of the crowd’s clanging cowbells, the Dolly Parton tributes, the thumping of the marching band’s bass drums. He tries to check his messages, but the network is overloaded.
After temporarily defaulting to auto-replies, he has returned to responding fully to many victims. He recently consoled a Canadian woman battling cancer who lost 265,000 Canadian dollars ($190,000).
He knows he can’t continue like this. Not long ago, his boss told him that they needed the old Hunter back.
Over plates of pasta, Hunter and Johnny ponder their options.
“I’ve got to do something to make it stop for the kids because now it’s starting to really affect them,” he says. “They don’t like it and I don’t blame them.”
If he goes offline, at least it wouldn’t be in his face. But, Johnny tells him gently, it would still be in his thoughts.
The only thing that will stop it, Hunter says, is if the internet platforms change their policies. But both he and Johnny admit that’s unlikely.
“I don’t know what else to do because I’m a dude in Mississippi with no power,” Hunter says.
He lets out a rueful laugh.
“I think we’re faced with this for a very, very long time,” he says.
“Probably forever,” Johnny replies.
“Probably forever,” Hunter agrees.
The pasta is eaten, the plates are cleared, and Hunter is back on his phone, his thumb returning to its relentless, rhythmic swiping of the screen, waiting with dread for the arrival of another victim’s pain.
Associated Press journalist Allen G. Breed in Williamsburg, Va., contributed to this report.
