name: California
title: Tax the rich — sometimes. California voters sent mixed signals with ballot measures
description: California voters shot down a tax on billionaires' assets but said yes to a high-income tax. They were just two of the five tax questions on the ballot.
text:
In summary
California voters shot down a tax on billionaires’ assets but said yes to a high-income tax. They were just two of the five tax questions on the ballot.


California voters faced big questions about money in this election, and the results sent mixed signals about how the electorate feels about taxation.
They want to tax the rich — but only sometimes. They want the money counters at the Franchise Tax Board to stay far away from personal assets, but are leaving the door open for future taxes or taxes on other people.
On Election Day, voters: 

Rejected Proposition 40, an effort to levy a first-of-its-kind wealth tax on billionaires
Rejected Proposition 41, a taxation transparency measure 
Approved Proposition 42, a ban on wealth taxes and retroactive taxes 
Rejected Proposition 43, an attempt to make it more difficult for local governments to raise taxes
Approved Proposition 3, a proposal to make permanent a tax on high-income earners

Voters also approved several high-profile local taxes, including two measures to fund the Bay Area’s regional transit systems, including Muni and BART, and a half-cent sales tax to fund firefighting in the city of Los Angeles.
The mixed outcome, experts say, shows that California voters are embracing tax hikes — but only when they can ensure the money is funding tangible services they support.
“Voters are willing to open up their wallet if they believe it’s for a good cause … and that it’s actually going to that place,” said Brandon Castillo, a prominent ballot measure strategist in California.
It also demonstrates voters’ willingness to support taxes that likely won’t affect their own pocketbook, said Mark Baldassare, survey director of the nonpartisan Public Policy Institute of California.
“We are a very progressive state where voters, particularly today when affordability weighs on them, have a tendency to say somebody else will be paying taxes, not me.”
Still, that “not me” attitude didn’t stretch as far as the state’s contentious billionaire tax, which faced opposition from business interests, Democrats and deep-pocketed Silicon Valley executives alike.
Why did the billionaire tax fail?
The failure of the billionaire tax represents the most stunning defeat of Election Day for progressive Democrats who tried unsuccessfully to capitalize on souring sentiment toward the ultra-wealthy amid high gas prices and worsening inflation for average Californians. How could the most progressive measure in the most progressive state fail during a “blue wave” election?
“California voters are sometimes more conservative on ballot propositions than they are on voting for candidates,” said Christian Grose, a political science and public policy professor at USC.
In recent years, voters through ballot measures got tougher on crime, shot down a minimum wage increase and rejected efforts to make it easier to pass local bonds. In fact, voters upheld the death penalty the last time it appeared on the ballot even though the state has not executed anyone since 2006. In a historic decision, Gov. Gavin Newsom also earlier this month commuted all death row sentences to life without parole. 
Rob Stutzman, a Republican political consultant, said this trend likely holds true because ballot initiatives — including taxation questions — generally ask voters to consider one issue at a time and are presented in a nonpartisan manner. In contrast, voting for a liberal or conservative candidate requires voters to weigh multiple aspects of a person’s record, character or values.
“They just have the policy question, and voters sort it out for themselves,” Stutzman said.
Those centrist tendencies helped push Prop. 42, one of two measures put on the ballot by billionaires trying to protect their wealth, across the finish line. That measure bans taxes on personal property, business interests and financial investments. The Associated Press confirmed its passage by 51.3% Friday.
Anti-tax and union supporters touted it as a way to protect retirement savings and pensions potentially targeted by the billionaire tax, though billionaire tax proponents countered that their measure never targeted ordinary retirement accounts in the first place.
Experts say voter confusion and a $378 million opposition warchest donated primarily by Silicon Valley tech billionaires doomed the billionaire tax.
Props. 41 and 42 were designed specifically to kill Prop. 40 if it had passed, creating a chaotic array of choices. The billionaire tax also amassed a coalition of diverse and vocal opponents, including Gov. Gavin Newsom, Planned Parenthood, medical clinics and the state’s largest teachers union, despite the California Democratic Party and California Labor Federation supporting it.
Polling showed support for the measure dropped 6 points in the last two months before the election, taking it from a narrow lead to a crushing defeat. 
“The campaign against the billionaire tax was a success,” Grose said.
Other taxes succeeded
But few view the results on Prop. 40 as a referendum on the state’s progressive tax system. Instead, many analysts said it was simply bad policy that splintered California’s Democratic base.
Prop. 40 aimed to focus almost all the revenue in healthcare while cutting out other areas of state spending, which would lose funding if billionaires left the state and stopped paying income taxes, said Thad Kousser, a political science professor at UC San Diego. That, he said, was “an unforced error.” 
“It made it a David and Goliath fight, but it didn’t need to be,” he said. “You don’t pass a landmark progressive tax increase that is sort of a change to how America has historically done anything by dividing up the progressive coalition.”
At the same time, Prop. 42’s anti-taxation sentiment was also somewhat tempered by the defeat of Prop. 43, which would have made increasing taxes for local public services more difficult, and the success of Prop. 3, which sticks a higher tax bracket on high-income earners to help fund schools.
Prop. 43 would have required a two-thirds vote to pass any local tax dedicated to specific services. Kousser said voters are concerned the measure would allow for “minority rule,” where just a third of voters would be able to block essential funding for local services.
“Voters don’t like to put in place these rules that seem to be tilted in one direction,” he said.
David Goldberg, president of the California Teachers Association, said Prop. 3’s passage sent a “resounding message of support for taxing the wealthy.” That measure passed with nearly 59% of the vote and sets a higher tax bracket on individually earned income above $360,000.
People in that income bracket have been paying that extra tax since 2012 as a temporary state budget fix; Prop. 3 made it permanent.
Why could voters distinguish between the income tax Prop. 3 and the wealth tax in Prop. 40? Partly because Prop. 3 had no opposition among Democrats, Kousser noted. It also extended an existing tax, whereas Prop. 40 opponents ran ads claiming that state lawmakers could come after average Californians’ personal savings.
Ballot box tempting for revenue seekers
Dustin Corcoran, chief executive of the California Medical Association, which opposed the billionaire tax, said he also does not view its defeat “as an endorsement of wealth inequality or the status quo.”
The state still needs to find a way to securely finance healthcare, education and other core services, Corcoran said, and the medical association is exploring future ballot initiative options to generate revenue. 
Not even Prop. 40’s supporters view its defeat as a reason to stop trying to tax the ultra-wealthy in California. Dave Regan, president of Service Employees International Union-United Healthcare Workers West, the primary proponents of the billionaire tax, vowed to come back in 2028 with another billionaire tax initiative.
Regan also pushed back on the notion that Democrats were divided on wealth taxes, arguing that polling showed between 60% to 70% of Democrats supported the measure and only Democratic leaders such as Newsom and Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra opposed it. 
“At the very highest levels of state officials there’s actually, you know, a different point of view, but that’s out of step with where regular people are at,” Regan said. 
Still, fiscal conservatives, the state’s non-partisan budget analyst, and even some moderate Democrats say taxation cannot be the only solution to California’s budget woes. The state has faced four consecutive deficit years and spending that outpaces revenue despite the budget as a whole growing. The current state budget calls for $351.7 billion in total spending — a 64% increase over the $214.8 billion Newsom signed in his first year as governor seven years ago.
“California’s budget is structurally overextended despite booming and near-record revenues,” the Legislative Analyst’s Office wrote in a new budget assessment. “This overextended budget reflects a higher ongoing spending base; diminished reserves; an already accumulated wall of debt; and annual, out-year operating deficits of $8 billion to $10 billion.”

name: South Dakota Searchlight
title: Commentary: South Dakota floats toward moderation, even without a wave
description: “The Blue Wave Washed Across Much of America,” said a recent headline in The New York Times, “But Not Here.” It was a reference to South Dakota, and it missed some nuance. There was in fact a political shift that washed across the state this year. But it was less like a wave crashing on […]
text:
Sioux Falls residents vote in South Dakota's general election on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)“The Blue Wave Washed Across Much of America,” said a recent headline in The New York Times, “But Not Here.”
It was a reference to South Dakota, and it missed some nuance.
There was in fact a political shift that washed across the state this year. But it was less like a wave crashing on the shore, and more like a flood creeping over the land.
The shift was toward moderation — or South Dakota’s version of it, anyway — and was best exemplified by four developments: the fall of Kristi Noem, the rise of less-absolutist Republican legislators, the trouncing of a MAGA millionaire in the race for governor, and the first Democratic gains in 18 years.
Noem’s bad year
Department of Homeland Security Secretary Kristi Noem speaks at a Nashville press conference on July 18, 2025, to discuss arrests during Immigration and Customs Enforcement sweeps. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
Officers working for the federal Department of Homeland Security — which Noem led as secretary — shot and killed American citizens Renee Good and Alex Pretti during January immigration enforcement operations in Minneapolis. Public and congressional outrage forced President Donald Trump to demote Noem by early March. A tabloid reported a titillating story about Noem’s husband a few weeks later, and by September, they began divorce proceedings.
All of that turmoil is perhaps what kept Noem, who formerly served as governor and in the U.S. House, from challenging Republican U.S. Sen. Mike Rounds in the June primary election. While neither of them can be counted on to moderate Trump’s excesses, Rounds, who won reelection, spends a lot of time on bipartisan efforts like supporting the military, improving the Postal Service and incentivizing grassland conservation. Noem would use a Senate seat mostly to pad her social media following and chase higher office.
The fight for the Legislature
The back-and-forth battle among Republican legislative factions continued this year, resulting in 16 lawmakers losing to fellow Republicans, after 14 such losses in 2024.
The Republicans who rose to power two years ago effectively blocked a controversial carbon-capture pipeline proposal as one of their first orders of business. They were responding to property-rights concerns that contributed to incumbent losses in the low-turnout 2024 primary election.
But the property-rights crusaders weren’t the only faction empowered by the 2024 primary. Republican lawmakers hoping to relitigate the pandemic, push Trump’s false election fraud claims and wage culture wars also found themselves newly empowered.
Many of those bills ultimately failed, and in this year’s June primary election, so did many of the lawmakers who sponsored them. The Republicans who seized power in this year’s higher-turnout primary are led by lawmakers who opposed some of the more extreme ideas from their soon-to-be-former colleagues.
Rise and fall of a MAGA millionaire
Republican candidate for governor Toby Doeden gives a speech to a room full of supporters in Sioux Falls, South Dakota, on June 2, 2026. (Photo by Joshua Haiar/South Dakota Searchlight)
Aberdeen businessman Toby Doeden finished first in June’s four-way primary race for the Republican nomination for governor, but lost the top-two runoff by 42 points in July despite spending $5.3 million of his own money on the campaign.
What’s instructive about Doeden is how he aligned himself with the politics and persona of Trump, and how little it helped. Doeden played up his business prowess and wealth, much like Trump, and featured Trump in campaign ads. Doeden also had his version of a big, beautiful idea: eliminating property taxes, which fund South Dakota schools and counties.
The candidate who beat Doeden and won the general election, Gov. Larry Rhoden, agrees with Trump on a lot of issues but disagrees with him on some, and is about as un-Trump-like in his personality as it’s possible to be. Instead of repealing property taxes, he has signed bills reducing them for homeowners with revenue from higher sales taxes.
First Democratic gains in years
It may seem silly to find significance in Democrats’ meager rise from eight to 12 seats in the 105-member Legislature. But that slight upward tick is imbued with outsized importance when weighed against the state party’s prior trajectory.
South Dakota Democrats had not gained any legislative seats since 2008 and still have not won a race for statewide office since 2008, all while suffering a roughly 70,000-person decline in registered voters. The wins by Democratic legislative candidates in this year’s general election aren’t much, but they’re a baby step away from one-party rule.
Taken together, Noem’s political demise, the rise of more pragmatic Republican lawmakers, the rejection of a Trump wannabe, and a tiny advance by Democrats all reflect South Dakotans floating a little closer to the center, or at least a little further from the edge.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: Missouri Republicans, voters didn’t leave conservatism. We did.
description: Missouri Republicans learned this month what happens when a party trades its principles for a personality. Ann Wagner represented the 2nd Congressional District since 2013. She entered the summer with roughly $4.2 million in the bank against her opponent’s $242,000. She lost by nearly five percentage points to Fred Wellman, who will be the first […]
text:
President Donald Trump speaks during an Oct. 19, 2026, rally at the Heartland Credit Union Arena in Park City, Kansas (Sherman Smith/Kansas Reflector).Missouri Republicans learned this month what happens when a party trades its principles for a personality. Ann Wagner represented the 2nd Congressional District since 2013. She entered the summer with roughly $4.2 million in the bank against her opponent’s $242,000.
She lost by nearly five percentage points to Fred Wellman, who will be the first Democrat to hold the seat since the early 1990s. In Jefferson City, Democrats broke the Republican supermajorities in both the House and the Senate.
There will be excuses about a “national blue wave” or a court ruling that kept the 2022 district lines in place. Both mattered, but neither fully explains what went wrong. The blue wave was built on millions of individual votes and verdicts, and Republicans should pay attention to the concerns behind them: what groceries cost, what gas costs, and whether Washington is making their lives more secure or less.
The good news is that the Republican Party already has answers.
They are our own. Our Republican Legacy, co-founded by former Missouri Sen. John Danforth, rests on five principles: the Constitution, unity, fiscal responsibility, free enterprise and peace through strength. Three of them speak directly to the concerns voters expressed at the ballot box.
Start with free enterprise. Soybeans are Missouri’s most valuable crop, worth roughly $2.9 billion in 2025. China, once the largest buyer, sharply curtailed purchases of American soybeans during the trade war. Even after a deal, its tariff on our soybeans stood at 13 percent at the start of this year, versus 3 percent on beans from Brazil and Argentina. Washington picked a fight, and Missouri farmers got the bill.
Tariffs are taxes, and Americans bear the costs. When the government imposes tariffs that hurt farmers and then writes them relief checks, that is not conservatism. It is the crony capitalism Republicans once spent careers opposing, with political favors picking winners and losers instead of markets.
The same goes for peace through strength. Reagan’s phrase never meant reaching for force first, and it never meant walking away from friends. It meant being strong and reliable enough that adversaries think twice and allies sleep well.
Today, our allies, from Kyiv to Seoul, have reason to wonder whether America’s word still holds. Whatever one thinks of the war with Iran, Missourians are paying for it at the pump, and Wagner’s challenger made her support for it a campaign issue.
Peace through strength is the opposite of drift and bluster: steady alliances, credible deterrence and the patience to keep wars from starting in the first place.
Then there is unity, and Missouri voters sent a message Republicans should heed. Wellman held 13 town halls, campaigned in every corner of the district and talked about restoring faith in government rather than demonizing the other side.
In St. Charles County, where Wagner won by about 16,000 votes in 2024, her margin shrank to roughly 4,000. That shift should force Republicans to consider whether voters are growing tired of politics built on division. Even Wagner’s concession pointed the way: she called Wellman late Tuesday night, and he described her as gracious. Unity used to be something Republicans did better than anyone. It can be again.
Republicans do not need to become Democrats to win again. We need to remember who we are. Missouri does not have to look far for an example. Jack Danforth served three terms in the U.S. Senate and later represented our country at the United Nations. He believed in a strong defense and open markets, and he saw public service as earning the trust of people who did not always agree with him.
That is the Republican Party many Missourians still recognize, and the one I believe they could support again.
Rebuilding will not happen in one election cycle. It starts with recruiting candidates willing to be honest with farmers about what trade wars cost them, who will stand with our allies even when it isn’t popular, and who understand that elected office means answering to the people back home, not to the powerful.
It requires county committees that welcome back the Republicans who drifted away rather than purging them. And it demands accepting the voters’ verdict instead of looking for someone else to blame.
Missouri voters did not abandon conservatism on Tuesday. They abandoned a party that had stopped practicing it. The way to win them back is simple, if not easy: start practicing it again.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: OPPD’s energy future is region’s economic future
description: Major economic development projects increasingly turn on a few critical infrastructure questions: how much power a facility will require, when that power must be available and whether the system can support future growth. Those answers increasingly shape where major investments happen. For many major projects competing for investment today — including advanc[...]
text:
(Getty Images)Major economic development projects increasingly turn on a few critical infrastructure questions: how much power a facility will require, when that power must be available and whether the system can support future growth.
Those answers increasingly shape where major investments happen. For many major projects competing for investment today — including advanced manufacturers, technology companies, and agricultural processors — reliable electricity is now economic development infrastructure. A region that can answer the power question with confidence is prepared to compete for projects that can create jobs and generate investment for decades.
That is why the Omaha Public Power District’s 2026 Integrated System Plan deserves attention well beyond the utility industry. It belongs in the broader regional conversation about growth.
Every five years, OPPD develops a long-range plan for meeting future demand. This year’s process reaches across generation, transmission, distribution and customer solutions through 2050. OPPD’s planning materials include a base case with moderate large-customer growth and a high-growth case with extensive large-customer growth. The utility has also said it expects roughly 100 megawatts of load growth annually for the foreseeable future.
Those are utility planning assumptions. From our vantage point at the Greater Omaha Chamber, they also describe economic opportunity.
Our economic development team works every day with companies considering major investments, expansions, and relocations. We see the scale of projects moving through the market and the speed at which their energy needs are growing. Major projects often make location and infrastructure decisions years before the first employee reports to work. They need confidence that a community can deliver the power they need on the timeline their investment requires.
Greater Omaha should plan for that level of success.
A growth mindset does not require predicting every company, technology or megawatt that will arrive over the next 15 years. It means preserving our ability to say yes when opportunity comes. Electric infrastructure takes years to plan, permit, procure, connect and build. The capacity our region may need in 2035 must be contemplated long before 2035.
OPPD is now entering the initial-results phase of this process. The decisions that follow should treat strong growth as a central planning case and build enough runway for the region through 2040 and beyond.
The same mindset should guide the generation portfolio.
Every energy resource runs on a different clock. Some can help meet nearer-term needs. Others require years of study, permitting, equipment procurement and construction. An all-of-the-above strategy allows OPPD to advance those clocks at the same time.
Battery storage, demand-response programs, natural gas generation, renewable resources and emerging technologies can each contribute to a reliable and resilient system. Longer-lead options, including advanced nuclear, deserve serious study now because the work started today determines which options are available a decade from now.
This also matters for reliability. Utilities must maintain generation capacity above forecast demand to help ensure they can continue serving customers during peak conditions, extreme weather, unexpected outages, and other stresses. That cushion is known as a planning reserve margin. Those requirements are becoming more stringent across the Southwest Power Pool even as OPPD’s customer demand grows. OPPD says it has continued to meet those requirements.
The Integrated System Plan is an opportunity to align our energy infrastructure with the economic ambitions greater Omaha is already pursuing.
The companies making location and expansion decisions today are planning facilities that may operate for generations. Our energy planning should carry the same horizon.
The goal is straightforward: build the capacity for the growth we intend to achieve.
Done well, power becomes one of greater Omaha’s strongest competitive advantages and a foundation for the jobs, investment and prosperity our region can create for the next generation.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: Ibach, Kauth detail runs for 2027-28 speaker of the Nebraska Legislature
description: LINCOLN — As Nebraska lawmakers prepare for the 2027 legislative session, where the state budget and property taxes will again be priorities, the race for the chamber’s next leader is on. Two senators so far have said they are seeking at least 25 votes to be the next speaker of the Nebraska Legislature: state Sens. Teresa […]
text:
State Sens. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, left, and Teresa Ibach of Sumner, right, are vying for speaker of the Nebraska Legislature in the 2027-28 legislative cycle. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — As Nebraska lawmakers prepare for the 2027 legislative session, where the state budget and property taxes will again be priorities, the race for the chamber’s next leader is on.
Two senators so far have said they are seeking at least 25 votes to be the next speaker of the Nebraska Legislature: state Sens. Teresa Ibach of Sumner and Kathleen Kauth of Omaha. More senators could run by the first day of the 2027-28 biennium on Jan. 6. Speaker John Arch of La Vista, who is finishing his fourth year as top dog of the one-house body, is term-limited.
State Sens. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, left, and Teresa Ibach of Sumner, right, are vying for speaker of the Nebraska Legislature in the 2027-28 legislative cycle. (Photos by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In a Nov. 8 letter to all of her colleagues announcing her run for speaker, Ibach said her service has been the “honor” of her life and that the institution “deserves our respect and protection.” She is currently vice chair of the top internal legislative committee, the Executive Board.
“If elected speaker, I will work every day to foster an environment built on trust, open communication and mutual respect among my colleagues,” Ibach wrote.
Kauth, chair of the Legislature’s Business and Labor Committee, sent a letter to fellow conservatives in July confirming she would seek the speakership. She described her tenure as “among some of the most difficult moments in our history.”
“The speaker is routinely criticized, attacked on the floor and blamed for bills not advancing,” Kauth wrote. “As a frequent target of the leftists’ attacks, I am uniquely suited to ignore those attacks at the speaker level. Dealing with conflict is part of the job — the speaker cannot be more concerned about being nice than being effective and fair. I pledge to do just that.”
Lawmakers prepare to count secret ballots for the Business and Labor Committee chairship on Jan. 8, 2025, for the first day of the Nebraska Legislature’s 2025 session in Lincoln, Nebraska. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Legislative leadership is selected by secret ballot. In 2027, Republicans will hold 30 seats, Democrats 18. There will be one registered nonpartisan. The chamber is officially nonpartisan, meaning candidates’ parties don’t appear on the ballot, and lawmakers don’t caucus by party. Ibach and Kauth are both Republicans.
Nebraska has never elected a female speaker in the state’s nearly 160 years of existence. Kauth is term-limited after 2029. Ibach was just reelected to another four-year term through 2030.
A different type of leader
Nebraska’s speaker is different from those in other states. They set the daily agenda, decide debate timing limits and help keep a procedural flow in the lawmaking machine. In other states, a speaker might appoint committee chairs or have a heavier hand in policy.
In addition to the speaker, the chair of the Legislature’s Exec Board runs day-to-day operations of the legislative branch, including human resources. State Sen. Ben Hansen of Blair, the current chair, is term-limited. The board’s vice chair is the only one selected by the full Legislature.
Speaker John Arch of La Vista greets his colleagues after a tribute speech on his eight years of legislative service, including four as speaker of the Legislature, from State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte. April 10, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
State Sen. Brad von Gillern of Elkhorn, who had been seen as a front-runner for speaker, did not win reelection this fall. State Sen. Mike Jacobson of North Platte, who wants to succeed von Gillern as Revenue Committee chair, had said he would run for speaker if von Gillern lost. However, Jacobson endorsed Ibach after she agreed to run.
Kauth told the Nebraska Examiner that she didn’t like how Arch had “essentially anointed” von Gillern and that the Legislature shouldn’t have someone who won’t be returning influencing the speaker decision. She had telegraphed her desire to run for speaker in the spring.
“If I don’t get to 25, that’s fine — I will try for Business and Labor (chair) — but I do think I bring a lot to the role,” Kauth said.
Arch, who describes a good speaker as looking toward “process over policy,” said he had heard from other lawmakers who viewed von Gillern as the “most logical” next speaker.
“I wouldn’t call that ‘anointed,’” Arch said. “Everybody knows term limits are a reality and nothing lasts forever, and so people start to look to the future. And his name came up many times.”
Ibach said the upcoming session would “undoubtedly bring challenges.” This includes a projected $1.2 billion deficit to the state budget and continued desire to reform property taxes.
“However, with effective leadership, I believe we can accomplish great things for the citizens of Nebraska,” Ibach wrote.
Managing lawmakers’ personalities
Ibach said the role of speaker has two “essential functions.” One is facilitating the consideration of bills and resolutions. The other is the “opportunity to positively influence the culture of the Legislature by promoting productive debate and thoughtful decision-making.”
State Sen. Teresa Ibach of Sumner. March 3, 2023. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska News Service)
“These responsibilities are fundamental to the success of our institution, and I strongly believe I have the experience, judgment and commitment necessary to fulfill them,” Ibach said.
Kauth said the idea that the Legislature must protect minority voices is “completely invalid” in a unicameral system. She views it as 49 independent individuals each vying to pass legislation, and she said the speaker shouldn’t view appeasement as a solution.
“It’s not something where we’re going to give extra chances to people who are considered to be in a minority party,” Kauth said. “Again, we don’t have parties, so that’s No. 1 — treat everybody individually and as equals.”
Structuring debate
Kauth has already outlined three key ways she would be different from Arch:

Filibusters: Under Arch, prolonged debate on legislation could end after eight hours in first-round debate (general file), four hours in the second round (select file) and two hours on final reading. Kauth wants to halve the limits. She suggested some bills could face different limits, as needed, and she said she would outline the limits ahead of time.


Agenda setting: Lawmakers would begin debate on legislation quickly each day, and Kauth said there would never be a day when the agenda is “over.” She said, “Everything needs to be on the agenda so that we don’t waste the people’s time.”


Priority bills: Each lawmaker, plus each committee, can increase the chances of legislation being heard by designating a bill as a “priority bill.” There are more than 100 priority bills each year among 700-800 bills introduced. Kauth said each priority would be heard on the floor, in part aided by changes to filibusters and agendas. The speaker can select 25 priority bills, which have traditionally been noncontroversial.

“I will work with you where I can, do battle where I must and always treat you with the respect you deserve,” Kauth said of a personal leadership motto.
State Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha, left, talks with State Sen. Carolyn Bosn of Lincoln. Feb. 2, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Kauth told conservative senators she would consult with each senator about their bill and expected opposition, seek a vote card of anticipated support and opposition if known, invite committee chairs to a weekly meeting to discuss pending legislation and recommend scheduling, and always be available to discuss strategy or provide mentoring. She tapped a conservative think tank to provide training to conservatives 
“When we have filibustering talking about recipes,” Kauth said, “that’s literally just wasting time. It’s not adding to the discussion.”
That’s a nod to 2023, Kauth’s first full session as a lawmaker, when she led legislation to prohibit certain gender-related medical treatments and surgeries for youths with gender dysphoria. State Sen. Machaela Cavanaugh of Omaha, who is now term-limited, led days-long filibusters on unrelated bills protesting Kauth. Kauth’s bill still passed.
Ibach has not yet said how she’ll approach filibusters or scheduling. Multiple lawmakers said they would be waiting to hear Ibach’s approach and meet with her before deciding their vote.
A pitch to conservatives
Kauth has passed laws to define “sex” and require K-12 and collegiate sports teams to be designated as “male,” “female” or “coed.” She’s pledged to keep pushing for similar definitions for public bathrooms, which have so far not passed.
Kauth rejected a sentiment she’s heard that lawmakers shouldn’t bring difficult bills because they might make people “feel bad.” She said how someone feels about legislation is “their responsibility to manage their feelings.” She said she does bring difficult topics but works people through them and has never lost her composure on the floor. 
“Whenever I hear people say, ‘Well, you’re too divisive,’ I’m not divisive,” Kauth said. “I am willing to engage in hard decisions and hard discussions. That’s not divisive. That’s leadership.”
State Sen. Kathleen Kauth of Omaha. April 10, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In 2026, Kauth introduced kill motions and placeholder amendments on nearly every bill as a way to get around filibusters often led by Democratic senators, a counter to Cavanaugh. If needed, Kauth said, that option could remain available in 2027.
Kauth told her conservative colleagues in July that she would “need” their vote and proposed that all conservatives meet ahead of the session to cast straw votes for all leadership positions. She acknowledged challenges Republicans would have to maintain their 33-vote supermajority in the November election, the minimum to overcome a filibuster. 
Republicans lost three seats this election. It takes 30 votes to change rules or override a veto.
“Only by maintaining a unified front will we be able to enact conservative legislation,” Kauth wrote in July.
‘Free from bias or favoritism’
Ibach told the Examiner that she wouldn’t compare her approach to Kauth’s but would highlight her own skills. She added that, with the recent election, “it’s going to be important to find compromise in order to be effective for the citizens of NE.”
“We have two major priorities,” she said in a text, “balancing the budget (constitutionally required) and delivering meaningful property tax relief for the citizens of Nebraska.”
State Sen. Teresa Ibach of Sumner, center, talks with State Sens. Tony Vargas of Omaha and Carol Blood of Bellevue. July 25, 2024. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
In her first two years, Ibach served as vice chair of the Agriculture, Business and Labor and Nebraska Retirement Systems committees. In the past two years, she was again vice chair of the Ag Committee and vice chair of the Exec Board. She said she’s witnessed different approaches to addressing issues, the importance of fiscal responsibility and the value of listening to diverse perspectives.
In her letter, Ibach told her colleagues that Nebraskans elected each “for one fundamental purpose: to make the lives of Nebraskans better.” 
“I will approach every issue with an open mind, free from bias or favoritism and work to ensure full and fair debate,” Ibach wrote. “I firmly believe we can accomplish great things when we work together in a healthy, respectful and productive manner.”

title: Offshore wind offered a ‘limitless’ future for CT. Trump scuttled the plan.
description: This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License.  On a tour a few years ago through the North Sea coast of the United Kingdom, Michael Passero, the mayor of New London, Connecticut, caught a glimpse of what a resurgence of manufacturing might look like […]
text:
Staging for offshore wind projects at New London State Pier in Connecticut is shown  on Sept. 18, 2026. (Photo by Sarah Gordon/CT Mirror)This article first appeared on CT Mirror and is republished here under a Creative Commons Attribution-NoDerivatives 4.0 International License. 
On a tour a few years ago through the North Sea coast of the United Kingdom, Michael Passero, the mayor of New London, Connecticut, caught a glimpse of what a resurgence of manufacturing might look like back home.
At a factory in Hartlepool, he watched workers assemble underwater cables that deliver power from the country’s numerous offshore wind farms to shore. To the south, he visited a workforce development center run by the shipping giant Maersk, where workers received specialized training to work at sea on gigantic turbines.
There was even a lab developing submersible robots capable of completing jobs in rough seas that are too dangerous for humans, Passero recalled.
In the port of Blythe — which, like New London, had seen its maritime trades wither due to decades of deindustrialization — the harbor had been repurposed as a staging area for the U.K.’s surging offshore wind industry, one of the world’s largest.
“I think the future just looked limitless,” Passero said. “You could almost look to Europe and really see the future here, see everything that can be done. And we have some of the best wind in the world right off the Northeast here, so the industry really looked good there for a while.
“Until Donald Trump got reelected,” he said.
New London Mayor Michael Passero poses for a portrait along New London Waterfront Park with New London State Pier in the background on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. New York’s Sunrise Wind, an Ørsted project, is currently being staged at the pier but beyond that there are no projects planned.
Before last year’s efforts by the Trump administration to grind America’s offshore wind industry to a halt, New London was poised to become a regional hub for developers looking to take advantage of the Atlantic’s abundant winds.
The state of Connecticut, through the use of public borrowing, invested more than $211 million to expand a state-owned pier in the city to handle the loading and offloading of parts onto specialized installation vessels. The Danish energy developer Ørsted, partnering with local utility company Eversource, signed on to launch its first three U.S. offshore wind projects from New London, kicking in another $100 million toward the redevelopment of the State Pier.
In addition to employing thousands of workers during construction, the wind projects were billed as a way to wean the region off its historic dependence on oil and natural gas to meet its growing energy needs.
Revolution Wind, the second of the three Ørsted projects launched from New London, is contracted to sell 704 megawatts of electricity — enough to power 350,000 homes — to customers in Connecticut and Rhode Island. The other two projects, South Fork and Sunrise Wind, are connected to New York through underwater cables.
As those connections get up and running, much of the work will dry up. If the Trump administration succeeds in its ongoing efforts to end future offshore wind development in the United States — which by recent accounts is likely — it will eliminate thousands of current and future jobs on America’s waterfronts from Massachusetts to Virginia. Many of these jobs are located in struggling seaports like New Bedford, Massachusetts, and New London, where states invested hundreds of millions of dollars in port infrastructure and workforce training to court giant offshore wind companies.
The resulting uncertainty has led international wind developers to redirect investment towards other countries or even sell back their leases. Workers who have undergone specialized training or pinned their futures on the promise of steady offshore wind construction could find themselves unable to continue working in the industry. Meanwhile, the states that invested heavily in offshore wind infrastructure are at risk of seeing their purpose-built piers sitting empty, as is the case in New Bedford.
Today, the State Pier in New London remains a bustling hive of activity. Turbine blades that stretch the length of a football field are stacked on the heavy-lift platform, ready to be transported out to sea on the specialized installation vessel Wind Scylla — named for one of the mythic sea monsters from Homer’s “Odyssey.”
That initial run of offshore wind projects is only scheduled to last through 2027. Officials are searching for a future tenant that can take over Ørsted’s position at the pier, but no contracts have been announced.
Just a few years ago, however, the investment in wind was touted by local leaders as a long-term vision for New London’s waterfront.
“This is going to be a major facility for decades and decades to come,” Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont triumphantly declared during a visit to the then-active construction site in 2022.
Elements of wind turbine towers for offshore wind projects are staged at New London State Pier is seen on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026.
 A new purpose for the port

New London is an old port city of irregular streets and 19th-Century buildings squeezed into a 10-square-mile strip of land where the Thames River meets Long Island Sound. Like New Bedford, the city was once home to a large whaling fleet but struggled to compete with larger trading ports like New York and Boston after that industry declined.
Across the river, in Groton, the waterfront is dominated by the Navy’s primary East Coast submarine base and General Dynamics Electric Boat’s sprawling shipyard.
But prior to the launch of the offshore wind industry, New London’s maritime trade had mostly dwindled to a few ferries shuttling passengers to and from Long Island alongside the underutilized State Pier, which had been used to import wood pulp, road salt and other products.
All that seemed destined to change by the time Passero joined a delegation of state and local officials on a tour of the U.K.’s offshore wind industry in 2024.
Between community host agreements, docking fees and crews coming ashore to spend money in the bars and restaurants along Bank Street, Passero said he estimated the economic benefit would amount to around $1 million a year for the city — a modest sum that would nonetheless provide a boost to Passero’s efforts to reinvigorate the city’s struggling downtown.
“You’re not going to fit much in New London, but we got the pier,” Passero said.
Passero was thinking beyond the city’s borders, too. North of New London, the Thames River once powered textile mills that served as one of the birthplaces of the Industrial Revolution.
“We’d get our share of what was appropriate to put in New London, but then the whole area — think of this whole river, all the empty factories along the river — I had visions of these factories being repurposed, you know to be able to, provide some of the materials and equipment that’s needed for this industry,” he said.
Before entering politics, Passero worked as a union laborer on several area projects, including the redevelopment of an old railroad bridge and erecting a new laboratory building at Pfizer’s research campus across the harbor in Groton.
“It was good money,” he said. “My BA wasn’t going to get me anything.”
Passero’s son, Thomas Passero, followed his father into the building trades and wound up working on both the redevelopment of the State Pier and the subsequent staging of offshore wind projects through Laborers Local 547.
With the exception of a short diversion to work on an unrelated highway project, the younger Passero said the activity at the State Pier has provided him with a steady stream of income for more than five years, a rarity in the industry. Even when the Trump administration ordered its halt to the work taking place miles offshore, he said workers at the pier never experienced even a single-day layoff.
“As a New London man, I’ve never seen it so busy,” the younger Passero said. “And it’s not just the pier, you go down to Ocean Beach and see the cargo ships — cargo ships! It’s pretty cool.”
Staging for Sunrise Wind, an Ørsted project, is seen at New London State Pier on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026.
 30 gigawatts by 2030

By all accounts, the revitalization Mayor Passero imagined on that trip to the U.K. had hit a few bumps before Trump took office the following January.
Ørsted, the developer behind the three New London-based projects, pulled out of two similar projects off the coast of New Jersey in 2023, citing rising interest rates and supply chain issues that plagued much of the industry during the COVID-19 pandemic. Elsewhere cost overruns, project delays and technical challenges threatened to slow the progress toward reaching President Joe Biden’s goal of deploying 30 gigawatts of offshore wind power by 2030.
Still, work was moving forward on projects off the coast of Massachusetts, Rhode Island, New York and Virginia.
The first of those projects, Ørsted’s South Fork Wind, began sending power to the electric grid in 2023. It was followed over the last year by Revolution Wind, Dominion’s Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind and Avangrid’s Vineyard Wind. The final two projects under construction, Ørsted’s Sunrise Wind and Equinor’s Empire Wind, are scheduled to reach commercial operation sometime next year.
Trump’s unsuccessful efforts to halt each of those projects have scuttled the long-term outlook for U.S. offshore wind. The completed projects are slated to supply a total of 6 gigawatts to the grid by the end of next year, far from the 30-gigawatt goal established by Trump’s predecessor.

Instead of planning new projects in American waters once its current work in New London is complete, Ørsted announced last year that it would instead shift its focus to “core markets” in Europe and Asia. During an earnings call with the investors in February, Ørsted chief executive Rasmus Errboe delivered a blunt assessment of his company’s future in the U.S.
“We have no expectations whatsoever to increase our exposure to offshore wind in the U.S.,” he said.
Worker Thomas Passero speaks to reporters at the Connecticut State Pier in New London on Aug. 25, 2025.
 Standing on the sidelines

Thomas Passero, the mayor’s son who works at the pier, said he wasn’t too anxious about the future of offshore wind construction. “Being in the trade unions… it’s kind of beaten into us that we’re gonna just build ourselves out of a job and go to another one anyway,” Passero said. “So how permanent is anything, you know?”
Still, he said it was hard to find a job site like the one he had — with consistent hours, years of work, and all only a 10 minute drive from his home and two young children.
“I hope it stays busy forever. I hope they keep building windmills or something that we can participate in here.”
Speaking at Yale University in May, Eversource’s president of transmission Bill Quinlan said the industry had been severely weakened by macroeconomic forces and “nonconstructive federal policy.” (Eversource exited the offshore wind industry in 2024, selling its stake in two projects for $745 million.)
While the current slate of projects is likely to be completed, he said, it would could some time before any new projects are announced.
“I would set that aside for the time being, I don’t see [wind] making a significant comeback in the near term in this country,” Quinlan said.
“I think developers — the international developers who have the expertise — are probably going to stand on the sidelines for a period of time here in the U.S.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: State leaders vow new multiyear approach to mounting budget gaps
description: Maryland's governor and legislative leaders said Friday they have agreed on a new multiyear approach to setting the state budget as the state prepares to grepple next spring with another in a string of looming budget gaps.
text:
Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City), House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) and Gov. Wes Moore (D) during a bill signing in April. (File photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)Maryland’s governor and legislative leaders said Friday they have agreed on a new multiyear approach on the state budget as they look to resolve a series of looming budget gaps.
Gov. Wes Moore (D) and lawmakers will return in January facing a nearly $3 billion projected structural budget gap for fiscal 2028. Larger gaps are projected for the following three years.
Moore, Senate President Bill Ferguson (D-Baltimore City) and House Speaker Joseline Peña-Melnyk (D-Prince George’s and Anne Arundel) said in a joint statement that addressing the deficits one year at a time “cannot continue.”
“Today, we agreed to work together to develop a four-year plan that addresses the state’s ongoing budget shortfalls and puts our finances on a more sustainable path,” the trio of Democrats said in their statement. “A more predictable state budget will be a stronger foundation for diversifying our economy and supporting the most vulnerable in our communities.”
Much of Maryland’s fiscal problem is self inflicted, as lawmakers approve aspirational but expensive programs not moored to adequate sustainable funding. Lawmakers have long been told that mandated spending grows by nearly 5% while projected revenues increase by 3.5%.
Traditionally, the gaps were addressed in one-year fixes. More recently, state fiscal leaders have had to address structural gaps to varying degrees — some small enough to be considered rounding errors. Others, like those projected in each of the next four years, are big enough to become cause for concern.
Budget officials ask agencies to tighten belts, including a 10% cut scenario

A pandemic, a business climate seen by many as unfavorable and national pressures exacerbated the problem.
“Trump administration cuts and economic uncertainty have added to the financial pressures facing Maryland,” the trio said in their statement. “But we cannot wait for Washington to change course. We have a responsibility to address the challenges within our control.”
There is also pressure on the state to get its fiscal house in better order. The state’s “sizable and growing out-year budget gaps” were cited by bond rating agency Standard & Poor’s in May when it downgraded the outlook on the state’s debt.
“It is our understanding that, ahead of the January 2027 fiscal 2028 budget introduction, the state intends to establish a consensus budget framework that will meaningfully address these gaps through structural adjustments that better align revenues with spending, which will be critical, in our view, to maintain the state rating,” S&P wrote.
Maryland’s current $71 billion total budget includes just under $30 billion in general funds — money collected directly by the state through sources including personal and corporate income taxes and sales taxes.
The Department of Legislative Services in June projected a nearly $2.6 billion structural gap in the fiscal 2028 budget — about $150 million lower than a December estimate. The Department of Budget and Management in an email to agencies earlier this year pegged that gap at closer to $3 billion.”
Fiscal 2028 is also the first year in which costs of the Blueprint for Maryland’s Future, the decade-long education reform plan, will exceed dedicated revenues. To cover the balance, the state will have to dip into the general fund, as a first-in-the-nation digital ad tax meant to help pay for the Blueprint remains in legal limbo.
The Blueprint is seen as a driver of the structural budget gap projections for the coming four years. Lawmakers may be asked to trim back the program or extend implementation over a longer period of time to better absorb costs.
In a September interview, Budget Secretary Yaakov “Jake” Weissmann acknowledged the urgency of the budget problem. He said “tough decisions” would need to be made.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“There will be difficult decisions ahead,” Moore, Ferguson and Peña-Melnyk said in their statement. “We know those decisions affect people’s lives, and we are committed to making them together, being straightforward with Marylanders about the choices we face, and protecting the services and investments that matter most to our state’s future.”
Over the last four years, Moore and his team have addressed budget gaps with the shifting of one-time funds, taxes and some cuts.
“Developing this joint four-year plan will require a careful review of state spending, a commitment to making government more efficient, and an honest assessment of which investments are delivering results and where changes are needed.”
Over the summer, state agencies were asked to submit budget requests for the coming year that included roughly 3% reductions. Two dozen Cabinet-level agencies were asked to also prepare budgets with 10% in cuts — an amount roughly equal to the structural gap projected for fiscal 2028.
Weissmann said in September that the goal would be to put the state budget on better footing for the next two decades rather than battling annual budget gaps.
Weissman said “all options are on the table.”
One of those options is likely to be cuts coupled with a tax increase. The easiest of those to implement — though not a popular option — would be an increased sales tax.
Maryland has not raised its sales tax since 2008, when it went from 5% to 6%. Going from 6% to 7% — a penny on the dollar — could generate an additional $1.2 billion a year.
Another option could include expanding the sales tax to services — an option considered in 2020 and 2024.
But sales taxes are seen as regressive, as they hit lower-income families harder, proportionally, than higher-income taxpayers.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Blue wave meets blue line in Frederick, as sheriff’s race just one of Democrats’ wins
description: After losing three times to Frederick County Sheriff Chuck Jenkins, Democratic challenger Karl Bickel swamped the veteran sheriff at the polls this year -- the clearest evidence that the blue wave that swept the county last week also washed over Frederick County.
text:
Frederick County Sheriff Chuck Jenkins speaks at a press conference this spring, with Maryland Senate Republicans, in support of the 287(g) program. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)In the end, it wasn’t even close.
After three consecutive losses to longtime Frederick County Sheriff Chuck Jenkins (R), by sometimes sizeable margins, Democratic challenger Karl Bickel swamped the 20-year veteran sheriff. As of Friday returns, Bickel had 67,164 votes to Jenkins’ 45,939, a 59% to 41% margin.
It was the clearest evidence that the blue wave that swept the county last week also washed over Frederick County, a once-solidly red county that has steadily been turning purple.
It is comfortably purple after last week, if not outright blue now: Except for Del. Jesse Pippy, the House minority leader, and State’s Attorney Charlie Smith, who was running unopposed, the only Republicans to win in Frederick where those whose districts also included parts of neighboring counties.
Jenkins said in a Friday interview he wasn’t totally surprised at the Democratic victories across the county, but he was surprised by the margins.
“Democrats came out because they were angry. Democrats came out in larger numbers,” he said. “I don’t think it was particularly me as much as it was the Republicans in general.”
Sheriffs make plea for restraint, as House, Senate weigh more immigration enforcement limits

With the effort he put into campaigning and speaking with county residents, Jenkins said he was disappointed in the result and concerned about his successor. When asked if he thought the county would be less safe with Bickel taking the lead, Jenkins responded with, “Two words: Hell yes.”
“The election was just a week ago, I don’t know what the future is going to be for me. I’m still a county resident now, I still care,” Jenkins said. “As much as [Bickel] criticized me over the past how many years, you can bet your ass I’ll be on the sideline criticizing him.”
Before this year, Bickel lost to Jenkins by 20,085 votes in 2014; 4,137 in 2018; and 2,950 votes in 2022, a 2.8% margin. Yet, throughout their campaigns this year, Jenkins out-raised Bickel.
Bickel was not available for comment on the race, after repeated requests over the course of the week. But other advocates were more than happy to talk about Jenkins’ loss.
Jenkins reputation was, to a large degree, wrapped around his stance on immigration enforcement and his defense of 287(g) propgrams, which let local police cooperate with federal immigration authorities. That ran up against a Frederick County population that was 11.8% Latino in 2020, according to the U.S. Census Bureau. By 2025, it said, 15.6% of the population was foreign-born and 43.4% of that population were not U.S. citizens.
Ninfa Amador-Hernandez, We Are CASA Maryland’s policy manager, said she feels voters, especially immigrants, were “tired of living under that pressure” of Jenkins’ support for Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
“Sheriff Jenkins ran that department with terror and fear,” she said Tuesday. “He did not build trust with working class Black, Latine immigrant communities.”
Progressive Maryland spokesperson Christianne Marguerite said last week that Frederick County voters are beginning to be more perceptive of ICE’s “violence.” She said Progressive Maryland, a nonprofit advocacy organization promoting racial and social justice, first endorsed Bickel in his third run for sheriff, in 2022, and has been doing grassroots organizing for his campaign since.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Frederick County became almost a symbol of the kind of local collaboration with ICE that immigrant communities have been fighting against for years under Jenkins, and I think that people started to see that,” Marguerite said. “This victory really represents an opportunity for big changes in how the Frederick County sheriff’s office approaches working with the community.”
Under Jenkins, the Frederick County Sheriff’s Department had been in a partnership with ICE since 2008. When the General Assembly this year succeeded in banning 287(g) agreements, Jenkins became one of the main voices in opposition.
Jenkins said it isn’t accurate to paint him as “MAGA conservative,” as he’s been making the same decisions and holding the same ideals since before President Donald Trump’s campaign made MAGA a movement. He said he will always stand by his belief that the county’s partnership with ICE was an effective way of improving the county’s safety, and doesn’t regret expressing it, even if that opinion is what could’ve cost him reelection. 
“I am who I am in this county, and people know that,” said Jenkins, a county native.
Jenkins had other issues to deal with in this latest election. He faced a federal indictment in 2023, along with 2026 GOP lieutenant governor nominee Rob Krop, on five counts for conspiracy and making false statements to acquire machine guns on behalf of a county shooting range, The Machine Gun Nest. Krop was acquitted on all charges in October 2024, and federal prosectors dropped all charges against Jenkins just a few weeks later.
Federal prosecutors drop gun conspiracy charges against Frederick County sheriff

Amador-Hernandez believes this race’s outcome is a local example of the winning streak of Democrats across the nation this fall. But she noted the race result was also a product of advocacy efforts from various organizations sparked by Jenkins’ immigration stance.
We are CASA doesn’t endorse candidates, but Amador-Hernandez said it continues to show opposition for any police department’s partnership with ICE. 
“This particular race just shows that voters are ready for a politic of love, a politic of community, and leaders that build trust, particularly when it comes to public safety,” Amador-Hernandez said. 
Marguerite said the win doesn’t end the work. Progressive Maryland and those who supported Bickel’s campaign will continue holding him to his promises to combat ICE collaborations and operations in the county. 
Still, the vote signifies a broader shift in how county voters feel about their elected officials, she said.
“Beyond Frederick County, this also makes a statement for our state and how people want to see leadership that aligns with their community values,” Marguerite said. “Hopefully, Bickel holds to that with the outcomes of his work in the sheriff’s office, and we’ll set a good example for transparency and community-focused solutions.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Baltimore priest heads to the Vatican with a message on working with the homeless
description: To the Rev. Brendan Fitzgerald of Baltimore, it seems that both religious and lay efforts to support homeless people can neglect a “hidden suffering” – a lack of connection to others. He and others hope to take that message to the pope next week.
text:
A tent being used by an unhoused person on Oct. 18, 2025, outside of the Baltimore Basilica. (Photo by Danielle J. Brown/Maryland Matters)To the Rev. Brendan Fitzgerald, it seems that both religious and lay efforts to support homeless people can neglect a “hidden suffering” – a lack of connection to others.
That vital but often forgotten need — what Fitzgerald calls “relational ministry” — is the message he and 19 other Catholic leaders from across the United States hope to take to Pope Leo XIV, as they head to Rome this weekend as the Vatican gears up for the 10th World Day of the Poor on Sunday.
“Social services are just as important and vital. We need to try to provide housing and food and shelter and job training and drug rehabilitation,” Fitzgerald said Friday ahead of his eight-hour flight to Italy. “But the human relationship can get lost, and that’s the gift we’re trying to give.”
Those comments came ahead of Friday’s nationwide ground stop ordered by the Federal Aviation Administration due to a communication issue at regional air traffic control centers — which Fitzgerald avoided because his was leaving Newark, New Jersey, and headed across the ocean.
Once in Rome, he hopes to promote the work at Baltimore-based mission to help homeless individuals form connections and feel less alone.
Father Brendan Fitzgerald says that the human connection can often get overlooked when religious leaders and state officials support homeless people. (Photo courtesy Brendan Fitzgerald)
Fitzgerald, the rector at the Basilica of the Assumption in downtown Baltimore, is also executive director of Source of All Hope. Twice a week, missionaries in the program walk the streets of Baltimore and meet with the homeless individuals they run into.
While they come with bottles of water and socks for those without, their goal is to simply talk to and make friends with the people struggling with homelessness, who Fitzgerald refers to as “our friends on the street.”
Whether it’s talking about the challenges they face day-to-day or just chatting about the Baltimore Orioles, Fitzgerald says that conversations with homeless people are “not too different” from conversations with anyone else. But building those connections not only helps the homeless individual feel less alone, it’s fulfilling for the Fitzgerald and the 11 missionaries who participate.
“I really don’t start those conversations off too differently from how I would talk to any parishioner or a visitor to our basilica,” he said. “Usually I start with, ‘Where are you from? Are you from Baltimore? What part of Baltimore? How long have you been around?’
“You come to understand that there’s something in common between the two of you that runs deeper – shared life histories, shared values, shared experiences,” he said, “What we offer is friendship, real relationships.”
Homelessness has been an ongoing challenge in Baltimore, and Catholic organizations often lead housing initiatives, job opportunities and meal assistance to help some of the roughly 1,600 people experiencing homelessness on a given night, according to the most recent “Point-in-Time Count” of the number of homeless people on a single January night.
But efforts specifically to connect with homeless individuals on a personal and social level are less common, which is why Source of All Hope began in 2019 to develop relationships with those experiencing homelessness.
“I always thought of poverty as a problem to be solved – and it is, we don’t want anyone to be poor – but there’s people there. People you can talk to … people you can care for through relationships,” Fitzgerald said.
21% of poverty in Maryland driven by high housing costs, report says

The trip to the Vatican is part of a collaboration with nine similar programs in other states, called Authentic Response, to promote the importance of human connection in supporting the homeless population. Each of the 10 organizations is sending two representatives.
The director of mission for Source of All Hope, Emma Zanotelli, is traveling with Fitzgerald to Rome for World Day for the Poor on Sunday. The following week, Catholic churches and organizations around the world will offer additional aid to those in need, including food drives, medical assistance and other charitable work.
Fitzgerald said that the organizations with Authentic Response will participate in a general audience with the pope on Wednesday, fresh off his return to Rome after a tour of South America.
“We’ll see the Holy Father, we’ll introduce ourselves and tell him a little bit about some of the work we’re doing,” he said. “We’ll also be over there to pray and learn and we’ll see what good can come from it.”
Fitzgerald said he hopes to thank the pope for his first exhortation, a letter to the church issued in October 2025 that focused on the church’s relationship to those living in poverty.
“It was a letter on the reality of poverty, encouraging the church to care for and love the poor, and challenge the church to think differently about poverty,” Fitzgerald said.
“If I just get the moment to shake the Holy Father’s hand, I want to tell him thank you for that letter – let him know that it changed my heart and my mind,” he said. “That I’m grateful for it and that here in our little corner of Baltimore, we’re doing what we can to support the mission.”

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Opinion: Voters rejected AI data centers in dozens of communities as 2026 blue wave crested
description: Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections. A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development. The centers also may have played a role in several […]
text:
Jay Vehige and Haley Radford prepare to circulate a petition to ban data centers in Emporia, Kansas, on June 23, 2026. Both were named defendants by a city commissioner who is suing them to block a separate recall petition alleging official misconduct. (Photo by Max McCoy/Kansas Reflector)Data centers were on the ballot, both directly and indirectly, in the 2026 midterm elections.
A total of 41 local ballot initiatives concerning data centers in 10 states were up for a vote. All but one resulted in measures to restrict or limit their development.
The centers also may have played a role in several high-profile contests. In Ohio’s race for a U.S. Senate seat, Democratic challenger Sherrod Brown hammered incumbent Jon Husted for his past support of data centers. In Texas, Gina Hinojosa made Republican Gov. Greg Abbott’s track record of supporting tax breaks for data centers a focal point of her winning campaign. Her victory marked a historic break with decades of Republican control in the state. As governor-elect, she immediately reaffirmed her campaign pledge to pursue legislation protecting Texans from data centers.
According to NBC exit poll data, 56% of voters felt that data centers were a major or even a crucial factor in influencing their congressional vote. For Black voters, the share was even higher, at 68%.
Data centers are key components in artificial intelligence infrastructure, housing the computing resources used to train AI models. These massive facilities guzzle energy and water and are very noisy. Many Americans argue that their costs, in terms of land use, higher utility bills and environmental degradation, outweigh the benefits.
I’m a professor of political science who studies political parties, electoral politics and technology. My forthcoming book, “Democratic Intelligence: Navigating Electoral Politics in an AI World,” examines how the adoption of this technology is reshaping established practices and power dynamics in campaigns.
Before the midterms, it had already appeared to be disrupting some partisan alignments. Following those historic elections, which have thoroughly shaken up America’s political geography, the widespread pushback against data centers is now part of the narrative explaining the dramatic results of the 2026 midterms.
 
Disrupting political polarization
In contrast to many other issues, concern about data centers is relatively bipartisan. The Annenberg Public Policy Center asked Americans in mid-2026 whether they support or oppose having data centers in their communities. Opposition was stronger among Democrats, at 69%, than Republicans, at 54%, but it crossed party lines.
Local ballot measures restricting data centers also cut across traditional political alignments. Communities as disparate as deeply red Edgewater, Florida, and solidly blue Alhambra, California, voted to prohibit them. The margins for the restrictions were large, averaging 49 percentage points.
The one restrictive local measure that failed to pass was in Harwood, North Dakota, population around 800. With a data center project already in progress, political and economic leaders prevailed in arguing that restrictions would cut into local revenue and stifle economic development more generally.
 
Allies and adversaries
Exit polls taken during the midterm elections also detected a degree of bipartisanship. Of the 56% of voters who said data centers played a “major” or “crucial” role in their vote, approximately two-thirds were Democrats and one-third Republicans. Exit polls, however, should be interpreted with care, given their methodological limitations.
These responses hint at why the narrative that opposition to data centers helped fuel the Democrats’ historic midterm victory emerged right away.
The seeds of this argument were in place before the election, picking up on unusual alliances that marked the data center opposition. In cities and counties, zoning fights are drawing a diverse kind of resistance: environmentalists, voters reeling under high electricity costs, local-control advocates and farmers concerned that data centers eat up land. They unite in opposition to projects backed by powerful corporate interests.
Some of the bipartisanship around this issue has even seeped into Congress. Several weeks before Election Day, the House passed the Ratepayer Protection Act by a 417-3 vote. The bill would require states to consider adopting a policy that data centers pay for the upgrades necessary to meet their high electricity needs. The three nay House votes were from progressives who felt the bill’s measures, which would be voluntary, didn’t go far enough to protect consumers.
Similar concerns killed the Senate version, a reminder that even allies sometimes follow different strategic paths. Some proponents of tighter regulation will accept incremental progress, while others push for more sweeping change.
Brookings Institution scholars anticipate that the newly elected Congress will take up the issue again, this time with a directive to states to establish mandatory, not voluntary, requirements.
 
Politics as usual
As the midterm elections approached, candidates up and down the ballot blanketed the airwaves and digital platforms with ads against data centers. President Donald Trump pushed back, suggesting that data center opponents want their communities to be “backwards and poor.”
Some Republican candidates walked a fine line between responding to voters’ concerns and not alienating the president.
It matters little whether the data center electoral narrative is accurate, and so far, the reported evidence is limited. We need to know where losing candidates stood on data centers, not just the winners. That voters considered data centers important says nothing about which direction they leaned. And despite a 98% success rate across the 41 local ballot measures, it’s hard to gauge how much resistance there is to the more than 600 proposed data centers that are slated to be built.
What does matter is that many people apparently are accepting the narrative because that alone will affect politics and the economy. Consider Elon Musk’s post on Nov. 4 on X, his social media platform: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now,” and the sell-off of data center-related stocks the next day.
As the 2028 presidential primaries come into focus, I believe we should expect to see many Democratic and Republican hopefuls emphasizing their support for data center restrictions and bans as they throw their hats into the ring.
