Barbara A. Trish is a professor of political science, with a Ph.D. from The Ohio State University. Through its opinion section, Kansas Reflector works to amplify the voices of people who are affected by public policies or excluded from public debate. Find information, including how to submit your own commentary, here.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Naming names for a transition, an addition and a delegation, in political notes
description: Montgomery County Executive-elect Will Jawando builds out his transition team, the county's House delegation gets new leadership and the Maryland Farm Bureau adds some homegrown talent, in political notes.
text:
Montgomery County Executive-elect Will Jawando adds to his transition team ahead of his Dec. 7 swearing-in. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)A week after naming a transition  steering committee of former White House and current state and local officials, Montgomery County Executive-elect Will Jawando (D) identified the folks who will serve on the 11 policy committees for the transition, which he’s calling “Our Moment Montgomery.”
Some of the members include former Del. Alfred Carr Jr., who served in the House from December 2007 until 2023, when a failed bid for county couuncil cost him his House seat. He will serve on the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee, which will be co-chaired by Shawn Eum, chief of staff with the Maryland Motor Vehicle Administration; and Ken O’Connell, president of O’Connell and Lawrence Inc., an engineering and consulting firm.
Joanne Antoine, executive director of Common Cause Maryland, will serve on “A Government That Works for All” committee, co-chaired by Del. Jheanelle Wilkins (D-Montgomery) and Michelle Whittaker, the executive director of Ranked Choice Voting Maryland.
Each committee is slated to provide recommendations for Jawando’s first 100 days in office and beyond. A committee kickoff was held Wednesday, with community workshops throughout the county set to begin the week of Nov. 30. Jawando will be sworn in as executive Dec. 7.
“Montgomery County’s greatest strength is its people, and these committees look like the county we love,” Jawando said in a statement. “There’s a young person at every table, next to faith leaders, union members, small business owners, teachers and advocates. I asked them to tell us the truth and help us build a government that works for everyone.”
Montgomery delegation shuffle
The Montgomery County House delegation will have a new chair leading its 26 members: Del. Ryan Spiegel.
Del. Ryan Spiegel (D-Montgomery)
Spiegel, who was appointed to the House in 2023 to replace former Del. Kumar Barve, was unanimously chosen to lead the all-Democratic delegation during a post-election delegation meeting Thursday.
“I intend to focus on advocating for, and delivering on, the priorities of Montgomery County; providing leadership development opportunities for our members; and debating and moving local legislation with fair and transparent processes,” Spiegel, who serves on the House Appropriations Committee, said in a statement.
He replaces Del. Julie Palakovich Carr, who was term-limited in her position as chair for four years.
The delegation also unanimously chose Del. Sarah Wolek as vice chair in place of Del. Emily Shetty, who was also term limited.
Dels. Bernice Mireku-North and Aaron Kaufman were chosen as the new co-chairs of the county’s House Democratic Caucus. They replace Wolek and Del. Lorig Charkoudian. The delegation is the largest in the House, representing 18% of the 141-member House chamber.
Halfway there
When a number of progressive organizations announced earlier this week that they were going to hold a rally in Baltimore on Saturday, the goal was to get Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for the job of Democratic leader of the Senate.
Check.
After being prodded by progressives, including some incoming senators elected in this fall’s blue wave of Democratic victories, Van Hollen announced Thursday that he would run for leader in the next Congress, when Democrats will be in the majority. Most analysts say Van Hollen has his work cut out for him against Schumer, the Senate Democrats’ leader since 2017, who is getting some of the credit for the stunning gain of at least eight Senate seats in this year’s elections.
The grassroots groups – Baltimore Rapid Response Network, Charm City Indivisible, Allies for Democracy and IfNotNow Baltimore – will still rally in support of Van Hollen at 2 p.m. Saturday outside the senator’s Baltimore office, but expect more anti-Schumer than pro-Van Hollen.
Another group, Progressive Maryland, is behind a change.org petition urging Van Hollen to run for majority leader. The petition, which had more than 4,000 signatures Friday, doesn’t name Schumer, but says that “if the caucus defaults to the leadership that has run it since 2017, this [blue] wave will fade into business as usual.”
Home-grown farm lobbying talent
The Maryland Farm Bureau has tapped a fifth-generation farmer as its next lobbyist.
Sydnie Grossnickle, director of government relations for the Maryland Farm Bureau. (Photo courtesy Maryland Farm Bureau)
The bureau announced Thursday that Sydnie Grossnickle will serve as director of government relations where she will “lead MDFB’s advocacy efforts in Annapolis and Washington, D.C., as well as heading up grassroots policy development between MDFB’s 23 county farm bureaus.” It said her experience coming from a farm family “will give her great insight as she advocates for MDFB’s over 6,000 members.”
She had served as government affairs coordinator for the Delaware Farm Bureau.
Grossnickle said she was honored to join the Maryland Farm Bureau and to “advocate for farmers and ag communities that helped shape my passion for the industry.” Farm Bureau Executive Director Parker Welch welcomed Grossnickle.
“With her years of advocacy work with the Delaware Farm Bureau and having been raised on her family farm in Frederick County, she will be a huge asset to our team when working with members and elected officials,” Welch said in the announcement.
Grossnickle starts at the bureau is gearing up for the 2027 General Assembly. But as director of government relations, she will direct the bureau’s public policy program year-round, including “the planning, organization, and implementation of legislative and regulatory goals within the boundaries of member-driven grassroots policy, budget, and Board of Directors direction.” She can be reached at sgrossnickle@marylandfb.org.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Commentary: Wisconsin Democrats have their work cut out for them
description: There are a lot of big things Democrats in Wisconsin can do with their new, trifecta control of state government. Reinvesting in public schools — and shifting the burden for keeping schools afloat off local property taxpayers — would be a great start. So would overturning Act 10 (unless the state Supreme Court beats them […]
text:
Scaffolding on the State Capitol of Wisconsin | Photo by Greg AndersonThere are a lot of big things Democrats in Wisconsin can do with their new, trifecta control of state government. Reinvesting in public schools — and shifting the burden for keeping schools afloat off local property taxpayers — would be a great start. So would overturning Act 10 (unless the state Supreme Court beats them to it), restoring the prevailing wage law and getting rid of so-called right-to-work legislation, thus reversing the largest decline in union representation in any state over the last 40 years. Add to that getting rid of PFAS, preserving public land, creating a nonpartisan redistricting process that ends gerrymandering once and for all. All of these things are possible when the new governor and Legislature get to work. 
While state officials can’t reverse federal policies that are driving up the cost of living, let alone end the disastrous Iran war, they can do a lot to improve the material wellbeing of state residents just by turning the page on 15 years of austerity.
Wisconsin is sitting on a state budget surplus that mostly represents the money the state no longer pays to support schools. For more than a decade, Wisconsin has let its education historic system degrade while hoarding that money. 
At the same time, local property taxpayers are overextended and grouchy from years of reaching into their own pockets to make up for the state’s failure to support schools.
Former Wisconsin Gov. Scott Walker’s assault on unions hurt teachers and other public employees directly, but it also created a much harsher, leaner environment for working people across Wisconsin and their families. 
A recent report by the Illinois Economic Policy Institute highlights the ways anti-union policies in Wisconsin have harmed the middle class, degraded a once-great public school system and made life more expensive and less secure for working families. 
This was not what Walker and his allies advertised when they pioneered the divide-and-conquer politics that pushed down union membership, wages and labor force participation for both union and non-union workers. 
Supposedly, busting teachers’ unions was going to give schools the budget flexibility to do more with less, and slashing state funding for education would mean lower taxes. Instead, schools went into a long financial slide, accompanied by cuts to programs, increasing class sizes and declining test scores, while property tax rates soared. 
Walker and the Republicans talked a lot about making Wisconsin “open for business” and ushering in a new era of prosperity. But the promised 250,000 new private sector jobs never materialized, and wages, job growth and GDP languished compared to our neighboring Great Lakes states, as “data wonk” Bruce Thompson wrote in an analysis for Urban Milwaukee of the effects of Act 10.
All of this, plus Republicans’ stubborn refusal to accept the federal Medicaid expansion for years before President Donald Trump’s massive assault on healthcare, contributed to Wisconsinites’ particular struggles with affordability — the issue that drove the blue tsunami across the country in the 2026 midterms.
Voters in the last election expressed serious doubt about some of the core tenets of Republican economic policy, including the idea that tax breaks for the very rich will make us all more prosperous, and spending on schools and other basic social goods is a burdensome waste. 
In the Republican radio address this week, incoming Republican Senate minority leader Julian Bradley acknowledged the stunning midterm rebuke to his party, saying “folks who are struggling to get by want to know that there’s a path to get ahead.”
“We hear you,” he said on behalf of his fellow members of Wisconsin’s severely diminished Republican caucus. Then he doubled down on the philosophy that got them where they are today: “If the new Democrat majority wants to focus on affordability, then we should be talking about meaningful tax cuts, returning the surplus to the families who earned it and clearing away the red tape that makes it harder to build a home or hire a worker.”
If voters wanted more of the same Republican tax cuts and deregulation Bradley is pushing, and which reached a new peak with Trump’s massive “One Big Beautiful” transfer of wealth from the many to the few, the election wouldn’t have gone the way it did.
According to Bradley, Democrats are talking about “higher taxes, more spending, redrawing maps” and “not a single one of these ideas will lower your grocery bills.”
It’s true that ending Trump’s tariffs and the war in Iran that is driving record-high diesel prices would be the fastest route to cheaper groceries. But state Democrats can do a lot to improve Wisconsinites’ economic wellbeing by bringing back middle class jobs and union protections that raise wages. Using state money to support schools will lower property taxes. Investing in healthcare, child care, mass transit, environmental protection and clean energy will improve the economy and the future of our state.
Wisconsinites are eager to see government get to work to get those things done.

name: Maryland Matters
title: University of Maryland, Eastern Shore backers sue for 136 years of underfunding
description: Since its founding in 1890, the University of Maryland, Eastern Shore has been underfunded and systemically shortchanged by the state and the university system, say supporters of the historically Black university, who are suing to do something about it.
text:
The University of Maryland, Eastern Shore is one of 19 historically Black universities in the U.S. that were established as land-grant universities under the Second Morrill Act of 1890. (Photo courtesy the Governor's Office)Since its founding in 1890, the University of Maryland, Eastern Shore has been underfunded and systemically shortchanged by the state and the university system, say supporters of the historically Black university, who are suing to do something about it.
The group called ForUMES, comprised of students, faculty, alumni and prospective applicants, is seeking billions of dollars in relief for the Princess Anne school in the complaint it filed Oct. 26 in U.S. District Court in Maryland. The suit claims the state has “deliberately underfunded” UMES since it became a land-grant institution in 1890.
The suit names Gov. Wes Moore (D) and several higher education officials with the University System of Maryland and Maryland Higher Education Commission as defendants.
A news conference has been scheduled in Baltimore Tuesday to discuss the laswsuit, and an alumnus of the school declined to comment on the suit Friday.
UMES officials, on the other hand, were happy to talk about their relationship with the state. UMES spokesperson Rudy Williams said Friday the school has a “great relations with the state.”
UMES President Heidi M. Anderson speaks about the school Sept. 23 at the J. Millard Tawes Crab & Clam Bake at Crisfield. (Photo by William J. Ford/Maryland Matters)
“We are happy with the support that we’ve gotten from the state,” he said. “We’re looking forward to continued support and good relations with the [Moore] administration and with the state.”
There’s a reason why.
State funding for a full-time equivalent student increased from $19,640 in fiscal 2022 to more than $26,000 in each of the next three fiscal years.
In April, the University System Board of Regents approved nearly $15 million toward renovations and new construction of the Eastern Shore campus’ new School of Veterinary Medicine. The school, which began accepting applications last week for a June 2027 opening, will be the state’s first veterinary school and the first one at a public historically Black college and university in the nation.
But the lawsuit filed by ForUMES looks to the history of the school. Founded in 1886 as the Delaware Conference Academy, the school became a land-grant institution in 1890 to account for the fact that the state’s first land-grant institution was the University of Maryland, College Park, which opened in 1865, did not admit Black students.
“UMES was supposed to be a separate but equal Land-grant college. Instead, UMES was and continues to be a woefully underfunded stepchild of the University System of Maryland,” says the suit. “Maryland deliberately underfunded UMES…. This lawsuit aims to right this horrible wrong.”
The Lower Shore school is one of just 19 historically Black colleges and universities in the nation designated as land-grant institutions. Under the Civil War-era Morrill Act, states were given federal land that they were expected to sell it and use the proceeds to fund an agricultural college. The land was often taken from Indigenous tribes. In total, nearly 11 million acres were taken from more than 250 tribes, according to a project published in High Country News.
Because Black Americans were excluded from those institutions, the Second Morrill Act of 1890 was signed into law and established land-grant institutions for Black students.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
Part of UMES’ mission, according to the suit, is “fostering research including innovative public impact research, such that UMES research improves lives and has a significant impact on economic development and growth throughout Maryland.”
The school’s supporters have several attorneys representing them including prominent Baltimore attorney William “Billy” Murphy. A representative from his office didn’t return a phone call or email for comment Friday.
A spokesperson for the governor said that while the office “cannot comment on active litigation, the Moore-Miller administration’s dedication to supporting University of Maryland, Eastern Shore is unwavering.” Moore attended the UMES  commencement in May 2025.
“In the wake of an inherited structural budget deficit, the Moore-Miller administration has kept its commitment to our state’s HBCUs – investing record funding for UMES as an 1890 Land Grant University,” said Rhyan Lake, the spokeperson, in an email Friday afternoon. “UMES is a shining example of one of our state’s prize institutions for molding the next generation of minds, and the State will continue to invest in UMES to ensure it has the resources it needs to continue that legacy.”
In an email, University System of Maryland spokesperson Michael Sandler declined comment in an email because of the pending litigation.

name: Delaware
title: Cape Henlopen Field Hockey wins Eighth Championship since 2017 with Victory over Milford
description: The Cape Henlopen Vikings defeated the Milford Buccaneers, 7-0, earning the program’s 15th championship title.   FREDERICA, Del. — The Cape Henlopen field hockey program and the DIAA Division One Field Hockey State Championship game have become synonymous over the past nine seasons. The Vikings have won or played in every state championship game since the sp[...]
text:
The 2026 Cape Henlopen Field Hockey team poses for a team photo following their win in the 2026 DIAA Division One Field Hockey State Championship game. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Cape Henlopen Vikings defeated the Milford Buccaneers, 7-0, earning the program’s 15th championship title.
 
FREDERICA, Del. — The Cape Henlopen field hockey program and the DIAA Division One Field Hockey State Championship game have become synonymous over the past nine seasons. The Vikings have won or played in every state championship game since the sport was split into two divisions and have won seven of those games.
Friday night at DE Turf the Vikings increased that championship tally to eight. 
Cape Henlopen field hockey defeated Milford, 7-0, in the DIAA Division One Field Hockey State Championship on November 13, earning the program’s 15th state title.
The Vikings started the championship game with strong play in the midfield that allowed them to get out on a breakaway opportunity early in the game. The scoring chance was broken up by the Milford defense, but the play forced a penalty corner opportunity. One of ten the Vikings generated throughout the game. 
“In our midfield, we know that the opposite team had a really strong center forward [Molly Matsen] so our gameplan was to use the outside thirds and really focus on our one on one defense,” Atia Sabbagh said postgame. 
The initial corner didn’t reap any results, but kept the possession on their offensive end. A minute later the Vikings turned the offensive pressure into a point. 
Sabbagh wound up for a shot while standing just within the circle near the right of the cage. Sabbagh fired a strong shot toward the Milford goalkeeper and the Milford goalie, Sophia Daniels, stuck her right foot out to deflect the shot. The ball grazed Daniels’ foot and hit the stick of Teagan Baker who lunged her stick out just in time to deflect the ball into the air and to the back of the cage.
Kailey McMahon scored the Vikings’ other two goals in the first half starting with a short shot in front of an empty cage. Freshman Brynn Evick drew out the Milford goalkeeper and delivered a tough pass for McMahon to tap in and earned an assist for her effort. Senior Emily Wells assisted on McMahon’s second goal delivering a pass between two Milford defenders for McMahon to finish with a backhand shot to the back right of the cage. 
McMahon’s goal gave the Vikings a 3-0 lead at halftime. The lead doubled in the first seven minutes of the third quarter.
Two of the Vikings’ three third quarter goals were scored on a pair of penalty corner conversions by Baker and senior Mairead Rishko. Rishko scored the first penalty corner less than two minutes into the half on a pass from Baker that Rishko redirected to the far left of the cage. Baker scored her penalty corner after the initial inbound pass from senior Grace Heers, sending a strong shot through the legs of Daniels in goal. The scores bookended a solo effort by Wells where the senior dribbled the ball through the circle and to the front right of the cage for a backhand shot that hit the back of the goal.
Wells added a second goal to her total in the fourth quarter which completed Cape Henlopen’s scoring. The Vikings’ seven goals are the most by a division one winner since the two division system was introduced before the 2017 season. It’s the most goals scored in a championship game since Delmar won the division two title, 7-1, in 2022.   
“I feel like what was working the best was hitting the ball into space and then moving the defense,” Wells said about Cape Henlopen’s offensive attack. “We really had to work on that big pull right where we pulled back and then around because the pull left wasn’t there and they were doubling us. So, just getting there before the double and shooting.”
Cape Henlopen’s win is the program’s eighth state championship win over the past ten seasons and the 11th for head coach Kate Austin. Austin’s 2026 team finished the year 19-0 and allowed just a single goal all season.
“Just how light they’re able to keep it while playing at a high level. I mean I haven’t seen anything like it before,” Austin said about the traits that made this iteration of Cape Henlopen field hockey special. “It’s just impressive and to be able to play at a high level while having fun and while enjoying what you’re doing. And that’s what we preach.”
“It feels amazing,” Wells said postgame about being state champions. “I got my best friends from this team and I’ll probably be best friends [with] them for the rest of my life and we have a great coaching staff. Everyday I come to practice with a smile.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: Gov. Evers grants first Wisconsin commutations in decades
description: Gov. Tony Evers has granted commutations to 14 of the 24 people who came before his Commutation Advisory Board in August and September, his office announced Friday. They are the first commutations since the administration of former Gov. Tommy Thompson in 1995. That doesn’t mean 14 people will be immediately released from prison. A commutation […]
text:
Wisconsin Gov. Tony Evers announced he is commuting the sentences of 14 people, the first commutations in Wisconsin since 1995.(Photo by Caspar Benson/Getty Images)Gov. Tony Evers has granted commutations to 14 of the 24 people who came before his Commutation Advisory Board in August and September, his office announced Friday. They are the first commutations since the administration of former Gov. Tommy Thompson in 1995.
That doesn’t mean 14 people will be immediately released from prison. A commutation doesn’t necessarily mean a person will be released or have their sentence shortened, the governor’s office said. 
For one of the 14, Amanda Weaver, the commutation will allow for immediate release from confinement; she will have two years of extended supervision in the community. 
In 2008, Weaver was sentenced to 30 years of incarceration and 20 years of extended supervision in the community, the Examiner reported in August. She had been convicted of five counts of burglary. At Weaver’s sentencing hearing, the prosecution and defense recommended jointly that she receive five years of confinement and 12 years of extended supervision, according to the governor’s office. The others involved in the burglaries were sentenced to no more than three years of confinement, the governor’s office said. 
The rest of the 14 will not be immediately released, but they may see release sooner than they would have without a commutation. For example, Touissant Harley’s sentence was reduced “to reflect a mandatory transition to parole” by June 1, 2027.
Not all incarcerated people are eligible for parole. Under Wisconsin’s Truth-in-Sentencing laws, if a person committed a felony offense on or after Dec. 31, 1999 and is sentenced to at least a year in prison, the person will not be eligible for parole.
Some legislators are criticizing the commutations, with Sen. Eric Wimberger (R-Gillett) stating that Evers “is releasing 10 murderers, a burglar, an arsonist and a drug dealer — who all deserve their punishments,” and that this puts “our communities in physical danger.” Sen. Julian Bradley (R-New Berlin), who was recently elected to be the next Senate Minority Leader, also voiced opposition to the news. 
“So there’s no confusion, Tony Evers is commuting the sentences of 10 convicted murderers and he’s releasing it on a Friday afternoon, hoping nobody notices,” Bradley said in a Facebook post.
The ACLU of Wisconsin praised the commutations in a statement.
“Voters across the political spectrum support the use of commutations to end or shorten unjust prison sentences so that people can rejoin their communities and get a fair chance at life. Granting clemency is the right thing to do — and it’s also the popular thing to do,” the ACLU said. “We urge the governor to continue commuting sentences before he leaves office, and we hope Governor-elect Crowley builds on this by expanding the commutations process and making it a routine part of his administration, just like it is for many Republican and Democratic governors across the country. Wisconsin’s prison population is at record highs. This is a start, but so much more needs to be done.”
Who are the people receiving commutations? 
Mighty Howell, 50, who has served 33 years of a life sentence for first-degree intentional homicide, had his parole eligibility moved up from 2038 to September 2027.
Howell was 17 years old when convicted and sentenced in 1993 for the May 27, 1993 death of Roger Bucholz in Milwaukee during an attempted robbery.
He had applied for a commutation under the Juvenile Life Sentence Commutation because he was at least 19 at the time of his conviction.
In Evers’s announcement, it was noted that Howell had worked on rehabilitating himself and helping others, maintained continuous employment, and received 20 letters of support from family members and a retired correctional officer he had worked with in prison.
Michael Maldonado, 47, having served 31 years of a life sentence, had his sentence shortened to four more years of incarceration followed by parole.
Maldonado was sentenced in 1995 for first-degree intentional homicide (use of a dangerous weapon and party to a crime), for his part in the 1994 killing of Ruben Borchardt of Jefferson County when Maldonado was 15.
His first eligible parole hearing was set in the year 2044, but after an accomplice who had been given a shorter sentence took responsibility for the actual shooting, noting Maldonado had only supplied the weapon, Maldonado had his sentence modified in 2025, making him currently eligible for release from prison and parole by the Wisconsin Parole Commission.
As part of the commutation, Maldonado was recognized for his “rehabilitation efforts while incarcerated,” noting his educational achievements, including an associate’s degree in business and certifications, along with his extensive work history and volunteering efforts.
He also received several letters of support from family members and others who offered housing and support upon his release.
Daniel Cerney, 43, was sentenced with two concurrent life sentences for the 1999 shooting deaths of Wiliam Leis, 51 and his 85-year-old mother, Evelyn Leis, when Cerney was 16, and also sentenced for burglary-armed with a dangerous weapon and theft of movable property He had his parole eligibility moved from the year 2044 to 2030.
After serving 26 years in prison, it was noted that Cerney had participated in several rehabilitation programs, developed job skills, and worked productively for Badger State Industries in several capacities.
He also had several letters of support, including one from the victims’  family who had consistently visited Cerney in prison.
Sabir Wilcher, 46, having served 31 years of a life sentence given in 1995 when he was 15 years of age for the killing of Elvis Anderson, 20, in Milwaukee, had his sentence commuted to three more years of incarceration before he will be placed on parole.
Wilcher has been eligible for parole since 2025, and depending on a decision by the Wisconsin Parole Commission, he could be released earlier than the commutation release date.
Wilcher had obtained a bachelor’s degree and other certifications and also participated in several programs for rehabilitative development, and worked in several capacities, including as a certified peer specialist, helping other incarcerated people.
The victim’s son spoke on Wilcher’s behalf, and the prosecuting district attorney also supported Wilcher’s commutation.
Wazir El-Amin, formerly Wade A. Curtis, 55, having served 36 years of confinement for a life sentence given on November 21, 1990, for first-degree intentional homicide with a dangerous weapon in Racine County, was made immediately eligible for parole, with the parole commission to hold a hearing as soon as possible.
Previously, El-Amin had been eligible for parole in 2028.
Besides significant educational achievements and programs he had completed, he had also participated in a childhood trauma group and had spoken to at-risk youth.
In El-Amin’s application, it was noted that he had secured work with a construction company upon his release, and that he would also volunteer in a non-profit he had started with his wife to work with those who had been recently released from prison.
DeQuelvin Douglas, 47, who was convicted of first-degree intentional homicide and attempted first-degree intentional homicide in Kenosha County at age 15 and sentenced to life imprisonment when he was 16, resulting in 31 years in prison, had his parole eligibility commuted from the year 2056 to 2029.
Rep. Amanda Nedweski (R-Pleasant Prairie) criticized the commutation of Douglas, citing “significant opposition from the Kenosha County District Attorney’s Office.”
Douglas had received a letter of support from a former Department of Corrections sergeant who said, “of all the individuals I supervised, he stands out as someone who truly deserves a second chance.” 
Dawn Dobbs, 59, who has been incarcerated for 32 years, convicted of first-degree intentional homicide (party to a crime) in Milwaukee County and sentenced July 1, 1994, to life imprisonment for the killing of her life partner and father of their two sons, had the date of her parole eligibility changed from 2035 to November 2026.
In 2010, she helped the DOC make a suicide prevention video that is still being used, and she also has served as a peer mentor and volunteered to make masks during the COVID pandemic.  
The district attorney and her son each supported a commutation.
The other 10 people heard at the August and September hearings of the Commutation Advisory Board have been denied commutation, the governor’s office said. 
What’s next for commutations? 
Evers may issue more commutations before leaving office. The Commutation Advisory Board heard from other applicants seeking a commutation in October and November. The board also has hearings scheduled for Nov. 20 and Dec. 11.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: JKT tops 50% of first-choice votes for Alaska governor, Republican opponents concede
description: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, is declaring victory in Alaska’s gubernatorial election. In results posted Thursday night by the Alaska Division of Elections, Kreiss-Tomkins had more than 50% of the first-choice votes for governor in this year’s election, putting him above the threshold for a ranked choice runoff. CNN declared him the winner against thr[...]
text:
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins speaks with a reporter before voting on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the University of Alaska Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, is declaring victory in Alaska’s gubernatorial election.
In results posted Thursday night by the Alaska Division of Elections, Kreiss-Tomkins had more than 50% of the first-choice votes for governor in this year’s election, putting him above the threshold for a ranked choice runoff.
CNN declared him the winner against three Republican challengers on Thursday night. The Associated Press has not yet called the race, and the Alaska Division of Elections is not scheduled to certify the result until Nov. 25. Preliminary final results are expected Nov. 18.
“It was a team effort every step of the way, and we always believed we could (win),” Kreiss-Tomkins said on Monday. “So it’s really really gratifying to have that official race call, or whatever CNN calls it, to kind of put some punctuation on the sentence.”
Kreiss-Tomkins was the lone Democrat in a field of four candidates seeking to replace Republican Gov. Mike Dunleavy, who is term-limited and was unable to run for re-election this year. Dunleavy could run again in four years.



SIDEBAR: How Alaska elections work
In Alaska, all candidates for an office run together in an August primary election, and voters pick their favorite candidate. The top four vote-getters advance to the November general election.
If there are four or fewer candidates, all advance to November.
In November, voters rank the four candidates in order of preference. If one candidate has more than 50% of the first-choice votes, they win. If none have 50%, the person with the fewest first-choice votes is eliminated, and their votes are redistributed to their voters’ second choices.
Eliminations and redistributions continue until two candidates are left. The person with the most votes wins.



Even before Thursday, preliminary results indicated Kreiss-Tomkins would win the race even if it went to a ranked choice runoff. 
Kreiss-Tomkins’ closest opponent in the election was Republican Bernadette Wilson, who had 28.7% of the 256,823 first-choice votes counted by the end of the day Thursday. 
Republican candidate Dave Bronson was third, with 13.7% and Republican candidate Treg Taylor was fourth with 7.3%. 
“Congratulations to Governor-elect Kreiss-Tomkins on winning the Alaska governor’s race with a majority of the vote,” Bronson said in a statement posted on his campaign Facebook page. “Alaskans have made their choice, and I respect their decision. It was a pleasure campaigning against him. I wish him all the success.”
By phone on Friday morning, Wilson said that while she was disappointed in the result and hoped for a different outcome as more ballots were counted, the trajectory since Election Day wasn’t a surprise. 
“JKT was on top on election night, on top in the first round. He’s gonna be your governor,” she said. 
Wilson and Kreiss-Tomkins were both born in Alaska, and Wilson said that while they disagree on policy, she is happy that someone from the state will be leading it.
“I know that he genuinely cares about the state. We disagree very strongly on what (caring for the state) looks like and how we get there, but I don’t look at him and think, ‘Oh my gosh, you’re some outsider guy who just moved here 10 years ago and now thinks you should be the governor.’ And so he’ll be just the third governor that was born here,” Wilson said.
Kreiss-Tomkins, 37, also will be the youngest governor in state history and the first Democrat since 2002, when Tony Knowles left office after an eight-year term. 
Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins gets a hug from his mother, Connie Kreiss, at an election night party Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 at the Broken Blender in downtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
No announcements on transition plan yet
Kreiss-Tomkins said he expects to announce the members of his transition team — the people who will help organize Alaska’s new government — early next week.
“Next week there will start to be a pretty steady cadence of updates and announcements from us,” he said.
Alaska’s constitution requires the new governor to be sworn into office at noon Dec. 7. Kreiss-Tomkins said he hasn’t yet decided a location for that event. He declined to say whether he’s thinking of Anchorage, Juneau, or Sitka, his hometown. 
Dec. 15 is the statutory deadline for the new governor to present a draft budget. In 2018, when Dunleavy took over from former Gov. Bill Walker, he introduced a slightly modified version of a Walker proposal, then unveiled a major fiscal austerity plan in February, the deadline for the governor to submit amendments to the budget.
“There’s a lot to do, and we’re excited to get to work with an obsessive, problem-solving energy,” Kreiss-Tomkins said on Friday.
“We’re thinking about the budget next year, we’re thinking about building an administration and we’re thinking about a governing agenda, and each of those three things are big things, and taking them all apace now that there’s a little bit more clarity,” he said.
Kreiss-Tomkins will work with predominantly Democratic coalitions in the state House and Senate. The House coalition will have at least 24 members and could have as many as 27, depending on the result of close races where ballot counting is continuing.
The Senate coalition is expected to have a bare-minimum 11 members, including 8 Democrats, 2 Republicans and 1 independent.
Bernadette Wilson, Republican candidate for governor, waves signs on Election Day, Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026 in Midtown Anchorage. (Photo by Loren Holmes/Alaska Beacon)
Wilson explains her thoughts on why Republicans lost the election
Seventeen candidates registered for the primary election, including two Democrats, three independents and 12 Republicans.
In the primary, Kreiss-Tomkins finished with the most votes, followed by fellow Democrat Tom Begich, Wilson and Bronson.
Begich withdrew from the race in order to consolidate support behind Kreiss-Tomkins, which promoted fifth-place finisher Treg Taylor into the top four.
Lt. Gov. Nancy Dahlstrom disqualified Taylor, citing his failure to properly complete a financial disclosure form on time, but she reversed her decision days later.
The brief disqualification saw Taylor’s wife replace him on the ballot; she was removed once his candidacy was restored.
Wilson had the highest vote total among Republicans in the primary election. Before the primary, she had said that in order to consolidate support, she would quit the race if she wasn’t the top vote-getter. 
Other Republicans made similar pledges, but Bronson and Taylor stayed in the race, pointing out that even if they withdrew, they would have simply been replaced by other Republicans who finished lower in the primary result.
With three Republicans on the ballot, the Alaska Republican Party and top Republican officials — including Dunleavy — generally declined to endorse one candidate or another and instead urged Republican candidates to “rank the red” by choosing Wilson, Taylor and Bronson in any order.
Wilson, by phone on Friday, said that wasn’t an effective strategy. 
“The reality is, the Republican Party, the donors, you know, all of the conservative groups, they had the ability to suck the oxygen out of the room, even if other candidates do not want to withdraw,” Wilson said. 
With three options to choose from, Republican donors stayed away or limited their financial help, Wilson said. Independent expenditure groups didn’t participate in the election to the degree that they did in 2022 or 2018, either.
While Kreiss-Tomkins is on track to win a majority of the first-choice votes for governor, Wilson believes that could have been different with more financial support and organization from Republicans.
“That’s why I say, even if JKT takes it on the first round, there’s no doubt in my mind that this is a very direct result of not being able to consolidate and collaborate, and that’s something that on the conservative side — we really got to look at ourselves in the mirror and figure out what we’re going to do here,” she said.
Wilson said she intends to stay active in Alaska politics — she has campaigned for conservative causes for almost two decades — but isn’t yet sure about her next steps.
At a statewide level, she urged Alaska conservatives to start immediately thinking about 2028, when incumbent Sen. Lisa Murkowski, R-Alaska, faces re-election.
According to historic primary election results, most registered Alaska Republicans oppose Murkowski and prefer a more conservative Republican, but Murkowski has been able to stay in office with the support of Democrats, moderate Republicans and independents.
Wilson, who opposes Murkowski, said that unless Republican organizations — including the state party — organize and back a single candidate in 2028, they risk a repeat of the vote dilution that happened this year.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Lawsuit over Arctic offshore oil prospect says resurrection of leases was illegal
description: Environmental and Alaska Native groups have sued the Trump administration over a U.S. Department of the Interior decision to revive oil leases that were terminated in 2024 for lack of progress in bringing a long-languishing offshore Arctic prospect into production. The Center for Biological Diversity and Sovereign Iñupiat for a Living Arctic filed the lawsui[...]
text:
The Beaufort Sea is seen on Aug. 23, 2018, from East Dock on the North Slope. The site of the Liberty prospect, which has yet to be developed into a producing field decades after oil was discovered there in the the 1990s, is located about 20 miles east of here. A new lawsuit is challening the Trump administration's actions that revived the three federal leases comprising the Liberty Unit. (Photo by Yereth Rosen/Alaska Beacon)Environmental and Alaska Native groups have sued the Trump administration over a U.S. Department of the Interior decision to revive oil leases that were terminated in 2024 for lack of progress in bringing a long-languishing offshore Arctic prospect into production.
The Center for Biological Diversity and Sovereign Iñupiat for a Living Arctic filed the lawsuit, which concerns the Liberty prospect in the Beaufort Sea. The Liberty field, with approximately 150 million barrels of oil, was discovered by BP Exploration (Alaska) Inc. in the 1990s. If developed, it would be the first producing oil field located entirely in federal offshore waters off Alaska’s coast.
Various plans to develop Liberty were offered over the years by BP and subsequently Hilcorp, the field’s current operator, but were not carried out.
The three leases that made up the Liberty field and the Liberty Unit itself cannot be resurrected, the groups said in their lawsuit, which was filed Thursday in U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia.
“These leases expired because Hilcorp could not meet the basic requirements, including a workable plan for an oil spill in waters covered by sea ice much of the year, the consequences of which could be devastating to our people,” Nauriaq Simmonds, executive director of Sovereign Iñupiat for a Living Arctic, said in a statement. 
“Bringing them back under the name of an emergency is Donald’s administration setting the law aside for industry. We are asking the court to hold the government to the rules that are meant to protect all of us.”
The Department of the Interior declined to comment on the lawsuit, citing policies concerning pending litigation.
The lawsuit concerns a “suspension of production” authorization denied to Hilcorp in the last weeks of the Biden administration’s Bureau of Safety and Environmental Enforcement. That authorization was later granted to the company by the same agency in April of 2025, early in the second Trump administration.
A suspension of production authorization stops the regulatory deadlines for leaseholders to make progress on bringing projects into production. BP and Hilcorp received several such suspensions in the past, based on the companies’ arguments that they needed more time to refine development plans.
The denied suspension was the 12th requested for Liberty.
In their lawsuit, the plaintiffs argue that the BSEE’s reversal was unlawful.
 

The image on the cover of the final environmental impact statment issued in 2018 by the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management shows how the Liberty project would be built. The EIS evaluated what was the third development and production plan submitted over the project’s lifetime. Plans have veered between an artificial island concept, as shown in this map, and a concept involving ultra-extended-reach drilling from existing land. (Image provided by Bureau of Ocean Energy Management)
 

	“The Liberty Unit leases had an initial period of 10 years and never produced oil or gas. When BSEE denied Hilcorp’s August 2024 request for a suspension of production, the Liberty Unit leases expired and the Liberty Unit terminated. BSEE lacked the legal authority to rescind the December 2024 decision denying Hilcorp’s SOP because the Liberty Unit leases were expired and the Unit had terminated,” the lawsuit said.
The reversal and revival of the leases was also unlawful because BSEE never explained the reason for its reversal from the 2024 decision, the groups argue in the lawsuit. Additionally, they said, the agency has failed to consider recent information about risks that Liberty development would pose to the environment from oil spills, noise and light pollution and other impacts.
Plans for Liberty, as proposed by both BP and Hilcorp, have alternated between proposals for an artificial island to serve as the drill site and an alternative that would use ultra-extended-reach wells to drill the prospect from existing land. Each company has proposed both types of development over the years.
Despite sporadic exploration programs over the past decades, offshore Arctic oil development has proved too difficult, hazardous and expensive for companies to pursue. A multibillion-dollar program mounted by Shell in the Chukchi was abandoned in 2015.
The Trump administration’s revival of the Liberty leases came amid a broad push for more oil development in federal waters off Arctic Alaska and elsewhere. The administration is proposing several lease sales in U.S. Arctic territorial waters, most of which were put off-limits to oil development by the Biden and Obama administrations. The Trump administration, in its proposed leasing plan released a year ago, has also tentatively planned a lease sale in a region it calls the “High Arctic,” where U.S. territorial claims have not won international recognition.
The Trump administration is also seeking to relax safety and environmental rules for offshore Arctic drilling that it has deemed burdensome to industry.
Earlier this year, the Department of the Interior reorganized BSEE and the Bureau of Ocean Energy Management, reuniting the agencies into what is now called the Marine Minerals Administration.
The two agencies had been split apart during the Obama administration after the Deepwater Horizon disaster of 2010. The Obama administration reorganized what was then the U.S. Minerals Management Service to reduce what its officials perceived as conflicts of interest within the agency. The reorganization separated the revenue-generating functions, which were assigned to BOEM, from the environmental regulation functions, which were assigned to BSEE.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: State education superintendent Cade Brumley chosen to lead UL System
description: The University of Louisiana System Board of Sipervisors said Friday it will replace President Rick Gallot with state education Superintendent Cade Brumley, an ally of Gov. Jeff Landry. Gallot’s resignation will take effect Dec. 1. The Louisiana Board of Elementary and Secondary Education will have to hire someone to take Brumley’s position, but the timeline [...]
text:
The University of Louisiana System announced it will hire state education superintendent Cade Brumley, left, to replace Rick Gallot as its president. (Photos by Allison Alsop/Louisiana, UL System)The University of Louisiana System Board of Sipervisors said Friday it will replace President Rick Gallot with state education Superintendent Cade Brumley, an ally of Gov. Jeff Landry. 

Gallot’s resignation will take effect Dec. 1. The Louisiana Board of Elementary and Secondary Education will have to hire someone to take Brumley’s position, but the timeline for doing so hasn’t been announced. 
Gallot’s ousting came the day after The Times-Picayune reported he owes $350,000 in back taxes and has a federal tax lien filed against him in East Baton Rouge Parish. Gallot did not return a call or text message Friday afternoon. The report indicates he blames a former accountant for failing to file his tax return. 
Brumley’s selection for the UL System job took K-12 school advocates by surprise, even though rumors have circulated for over a year that he was looking to leave his current position. His name had been floated as a possibility for jobs in the Trump administration, Florida state government and, more recently, as Louisiana Tech’s new president. 

The UL System is the largest four-year school system in Louisiana, with eight universities. Brumley is likely to make far more money in the new job than he did as state superintendent. 
As UL System president, Gallot had an annual salary of $522,000 for the current academic year on top of a $54,000 housing allowance and $24,000 car allowance. Brumley was being paid $323,939 as superintendent for the current fiscal year. He has a $24,000 car allowance but no housing benefits, according to state budget documents. 
Brumley could not be reached for comment Friday afternoon. 

Gallot leaves the UL System position about six weeks after former Louisiana Tech president Jim Henderson stepped down. The UL Board of Supervisors offered the two men their jobs on the same day in October 2023, shortly after Landry was elected governor. 
At the time of the Gallot and Henderson hires, UL board members were all appointees of then Gov. John Bel Edwards, a Democrat. 

In an unusual move, Gallot, who was Grambling State University president at the time, and Henderson, who was serving as the UL System president, were the only people considered for those respective jobs, and its board did not interview any other candidates. 

Landry also held up the hiring of Gallot for weeks while he was governor-elect. He wanted to meet with Gallot, a Democrat who served in the Louisiana Legislature for several years, before agreeing to Gallot’s contract, Landry said at the time. 
Gallot’s position was eventually finalized in the last week of 2023, less than two weeks before Landry’s inauguration. 

Since he came into office in 2024, Landry has made several changes to higher education leadership. His preferred candidates have been hired at LSU, McNeese State, Northwestern State, University of Louisiana-Lafayette and the Louisiana Community and Technical College System.  
Brumley was hired to oversee the state education department in 2020 when Edwards was still governor. Under his leadership, Louisiana has greatly improved its test scores and education ranking among states. 
Prior to his role in state government, Brumley ran the public school systems in DeSoto and Jefferson parishes. 
Over the past two years, Brumley has been an advocate for many of Landry’s education policy initiatives, including a statewide voucher program called LA GATOR that would direct tens of millions of public dollars to private education. 

So far, legislators haven’t been willing to expand the voucher program like Landry and Brumley have requested.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho election officials will audit two counties that underreported votes
description: Election results in two Idaho counties that initially underreported ballots in last week’s election will be audited by state officials. But the audits aren’t targeted.  Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf on Friday plucked numbered tiles representing Latah and Bannock counties out of a bingo-style tumbler as state officials randomly drew counties to undergo[...]
text:
Twin Falls County elections director Sabrina Harrison (left), Kathryn Goemmer (center), and Claudia Harvey (right) sort through early voter forms in the Twin Falls County West building in Twin Falls, Idaho, on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Eakin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Election results in two Idaho counties that initially underreported ballots in last week’s election will be audited by state officials.
But the audits aren’t targeted. 
Idaho State Controller Brandon Woolf on Friday plucked numbered tiles representing Latah and Bannock counties out of a bingo-style tumbler as state officials randomly drew counties to undergo audits. The audits, required by a 2022 state law, are meant to verify the accuracy of election results reported by counties, which run elections locally. 
But the unusual news out of Latah and Bannock counties — reported nearly a week after the election — was on the mind of state officials who serve on the Idaho State Board of Canvassers, a panel that is preparing to certify the state election results. 
After North Idaho’s Latah County found 2,300 of unreported ballots, recount shows no races changed

Before the random draw, Secretary of State Phil McGrane addressed the unreported ballots in those two counties, which are separated by a full days’ drive.
“Both counties are eligible today to be drawn again. … They will have a chip in the thing,” he said, referring to a golden cage, just before the draw started. “They may be prepared for more counting in each respective county.”
The first to be drawn was eastern Idaho’s Bannock County, where officials on Tuesday found 333 ballots that hadn’t been counted. Soon enough, Latah County in North Idaho, joined the list. There, officials recounted all ballots as a cautionary measure after they found more than 2,300 ballots from early voting had not been reported on Election Day. 
In both counties, officials said the late ballots left race outcomes unchanged. But they left voters with questions that state officials are still grappling with.
Here’s the full list of Idaho counties that are being audited over the next week:

Adams County
Bannock County
Benewah County
Caribou County
Gem County
Latah County
Oneida County
Washington County

 How did Latah, Bannock counties underreport votes?

On Sunday, McGrane got the first news about the unreported ballots in Latah County, he said in a Friday interview.  
Idaho Secretary of State Phil McGrane, a Republican, takes questions from an Idaho News 6 reporter at a GOP election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, in Downtown Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
The more than 2,300 ballots in question were counted. They sat on a specialized hard drive in a voting machine, which has no internet access, he said. But that memory device — which can’t be read by a typical computer — wasn’t plugged into the system that loads up results on elections, he said.
“I think it was just a misstep, just human error,” McGrane said.
By Monday, when McGrane met with Latah County Clerk Julie Fry, a local elected Republican, she was already aiming for a full recount. Five members of McGrane’s team flew out to oversee it. 
“It was like Election Day 2.0,” McGrane said at the meeting.
Local officials discovered the issue by crunching numbers. They saw that the voter turnout system showed more voters had cast ballots in the area than the number of votes they had actually reported, McGrane said.
In Bannock County, McGrane said the cause was different. 
The 333 uncounted ballots had been found in a poll volunteer’s pickup truck, the local newspaper, the Idaho State Journal, reported.
McGrane said his team got a call from Bannock County that they were missing materials. 
Then local officials asked the chief judge, who runs the local precinct, if they had them, McGrane said. 
The ballot box they found was still closed with a unique seal, so officials knew it hadn’t been tampered with, he said. But since the races there weren’t close enough to where those ballots could’ve changed an outcome, McGrane said a full recount wasn’t needed. 
“There are some lessons learned about safeguards. … Now we’re looking at ‘What are other ways we could take additional steps to ensure that this doesn’t happen again in a future election,’” McGrane said.
It’s not immediately clear if state election officials will audit the ballots that initially went unreported in Latah and Bannock counties. 
The precinct in Bannock that had unreported votes wasn’t randomly selected for audits. In Latah, the unreported votes were from early votes. It’s unclear if any batches of early votes selected to be audited include the once-unreported ballots there.
 How the audits work

As part of the audits, officials with the Idaho Secretary of State’s Office will hand count a random selection of thousands of ballots in each county to compare that to results publicly reported by county clerks. 
In the counties selected, officials are slated to audit at least 2,100 ballots, or 5% of precincts from a selection of Election Day votes and early and absentee ballots.
The audits will be for individual races in each county, such as for federal congressional offices, statewide offices such as the governor, or state legislative seats. McGrane gets to decide which races will be audited.
McGrane said his office will soon announce the dates of each audit. The audits are open to the public to observe.
Idaho election officials didn’t include in the random draw counties that were audited in recent elections, or counties that are likely to receive a recount because of close races.
The results from last week’s election remain unofficial until they are certified by the State Board of Canvassers on Nov. 24.

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Proposed restrictions on ‘sexually explicit’ library materials revised, reopened for feedback
description: The Arkansas State Library Board has again revised proposed rules hingeing public library funding on children’s access to “sexually explicit” materials after librarians and parents on Friday said the rules could restrict educational materials. The new draft rules will be available for a third round of public feedback on the Arkansas Department of Education w[...]
text:
Abbigail Getty (left) of Cabot holds up a copy of "The Immortal Life of Henrietta Lacks" by Rebecca Skloot, a book she said proposed library funding rules would keep away from children under 16 without parental consent, at the Arkansas State Library Board meeting on Nov. 13, 2026. At right is Arkansas Education Department attorney Daniel Shults. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)The Arkansas State Library Board has again revised proposed rules hingeing public library funding on children’s access to “sexually explicit” materials after librarians and parents on Friday said the rules could restrict educational materials.
The new draft rules will be available for a third round of public feedback on the Arkansas Department of Education website until Dec. 13.
The proposed restrictions come as librarians have raised questions about how to enforce a 2023 law that would impose criminal penalties for providing “harmful” materials to minors. A federal appeals court lifted the injunction on the law in July.
Arkansas librarians grapple with enforcing book restriction law after court ruling

Early in the board’s quarterly meeting Friday, members voted to approve the draft they proposed in August. The proposal would have required libraries to “take all reasonable steps” for the “appropriate placement” of materials that depict or describe sexual contact and behavior, and to prevent patrons under 16 years old from checking them out.
The board later expunged the vote by a 3-2 margin and agreed to add language specifying that libraries don’t need to keep “encyclopedias and fine art” away from patrons under 16.
Board member Jack Fortner, a former state lawmaker from Yellville, opposed expunging the vote, changing the proposed rules and reopening them for public comment. He said the changes will be “too vague to enforce,” and that public comment on the broad proposal “will be unbelievably interesting.”
A previous draft of the rules drew opposition from dozens of Arkansans who opposed limiting minors’ access to books.
Allie Gosselink, executive director of the Calhoun County Library, reiterated Friday that her library system does not have the space to segregate books some adults might consider inappropriate for children.
PEN America, a national freedom-to-read advocacy group, issued a statement Friday after the board meeting, expressing concern about the amended rules.

Executive directors Allie Gosselink of the Calhoun County Library and Clare Graham of the Mid-Ark Regional Library System express opposition to the Arkansas State Library Board’s proposed funding rules that they said would restrict children’s access to age-appropriate books about human reproduction on Nov. 13, 2026. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

“This policy sends a fundamental message to children and teens that it does not trust them to be curious or interested in reading freely, and could discourage them from reading at all,” Freedom to Read program coordinator Madison Markham said. “At a time when reading rates by children and youth are plummeting, this is a terrible message for this board to be sending.”
 Obscenity discussion

Library directors, including Gosselink, said selection criteria for library materials include the Miller test, a three-pronged standard for obscenity created by a 1973 U.S. Supreme Court ruling.
An item must meet all three criteria to be considered legally obscene:

If the entire work “appeals to the prurient interest” based on “contemporary community standards,” as judged by the average person;
If it depicts or describes sexual behavior “in a patently offensive way”;
If the entire work “lacks serious literary, artistic, political, or scientific value.”

Encyclopedias, sex education books and depictions of nudity in art are not obscene by these standards, library directors told the State Library Board.
Board Chairman Clay Goff said he had never heard of the Miller test before Friday and was reluctant to incorporate it into the proposed rules because it would mean “no books are moved” to different library sections.
John McGraw, director of the Faulkner and Van Buren county libraries, said the Miller test ensures that “we do not have pornography in the library.” McGraw also said he appreciated that the proposed rules require libraries to ensure patrons under 16 are accompanied by adults.
“Everything that we do with minors in the library entails [and] presumes parental consent, but is that going to hold up in court if somebody wants to say Johnny checked out ‘The Diary of Anne Frank’?” McGraw said, noting that the book includes the teenage author’s curiosity about sex. “I don’t know, and that makes me nervous.”



Quotation







This policy sends a fundamental message to children and teens that it does not trust them to be curious or interested in reading freely, and could discourage them from reading at all.


– PEN America Freedom to Read program coordinator Madison Markham


Board member Emmaline Pilkington, wife of Republican state Rep. Aaron Pilkington, said she supported the proposed rules before Friday’s amendment because they are not aimed at “kids with great parental oversight.”
“We’re talking about maybe those kids that are kind of on the fringes, that are not going to have excellent parenting,” Pilkington said.
The rules include an exception for children 11 and older to access “age-appropriate information designed to prepare minors for the sociology of puberty” with parental consent.
This provision would block many girls’ access to books about menstruation until they are already experiencing it, said Abbigail Getty, a mother from Cabot who opposed the rules.
“That’s like saying you’re going to get a book about planning your wedding a year after you get married,” Getty said.
 Parallel policies

The State Library Board questioned if the proposed rules would interact or clash with Act 372 of 2023, which would allow anyone who “furnishes, presents, provides, [or] makes available” an item that is “harmful to minors” to be charged with a Class A misdemeanor, punishable by a maximum prison sentence of one year.
Act 372 would also give city and county governments the final say on the placement of a library book a community member seeks to relocate.

Arkansas Assistant Attorney General Aaron Lowrey (right) takes questions from Arkansas State Library Board Vice Chair Sydney McKenzie (center) at the board’s quarterly meeting on Nov. 13, 2026 while Chairman Clay Goff (left) and board member Emmaline Pilkington (second from right) listen. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)

Vice Chair Sydney McKenzie, wife of Republican state Rep. Brit McKenzie, asked if the board could “provide direction to local libraries just so there is some sense of uniformity in challenge cases.”
Assistant Attorney General Aaron Lowrey said a local dispute or court case regarding Act 372 would be outside the board’s purview.
Act 372 defines “harmful to minors” as “any description, exhibition, presentation, or representation, in whatever form, of nudity, sexual conduct, sexual excitement, or sadomasochistic abuse” if the content “appeals to the prurient interest,” is “patently offensive” or lacks literary or political value.
The proposed library funding rules instead use the federal definition of sexual content: a variety of physical contact “with an intent to abuse, humiliate, harass, degrade, or arouse or gratify the sexual desire of any person.”
Misty Hawkins, executive director of the four-county Arkansas River Valley Regional Library System, told the board it should spend its time and resources on other safety issues regarding libraries.
“Where’s the urgency to help libraries address practical needs, like safety training, for patrons and our staff who [might be] about to be arrested for something they didn’t do?” Hawkins said.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: NE auditor’s concerns turn to broader pandemic-era grant program: ‘We’ve got to dig deeper’
description: LINCOLN — Nebraska Auditor Mike Foley said that delving into a $1.2 million pandemic-era public grant — whose progress he described as “pathetic” — has him questioning the broader $234 million grant program of which it is a part. He said his office, the state watchdog of taxpayer dollars, at this point has no other […]
text:
Nebraska Auditor of Public Accounts Mike Foley speaks with reporters after a hearing before the Legislature's Government, Military and Veterans Affairs Committee on a bill brought at his request. Feb. 5, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — Nebraska Auditor Mike Foley said that delving into a $1.2 million pandemic-era public grant — whose progress he described as “pathetic” — has him questioning the broader $234 million grant program of which it is a part.
Gov. Jim Pillen, flanked by then-Omaha Mayor Jean Stothert and then-DED Director K.C. Belitz, leads a 2024 event announcing winners of the North and South Omaha Recovery Grant Program. (Photo by Cindy Gonzalez/Nebraska Examiner)
He said his office, the state watchdog of taxpayer dollars, at this point has no other investigations “in motion” regarding the North and South Omaha Recovery Grant Program managed by the Nebraska Department of Economic Development.
However, Foley said that given the complexity of the Legislature-approved initiative and the shrinking state agency charged with monitoring it — “there’s more work that we need to do.”
“Intuitively, you gotta say there’s more here,” Foley said. “We’ve got to dig deeper.”
‘Lavish’ salaries
He commented in the wake of a probe by his office into the Nebraska Startup Academy, one of roughly 130 entities that in January 2024 were awarded a piece of North-South grant funding.
Nebraska DED director defends grant management amid questions by state lawmakers

The program had a tumultuous start and more recently was a topic at an Oct. 21 legislative committee hearing during which DED defended its management but noted challenges with staff turnover. State Sen. Terrell McKinney of North Omaha, who helped shepherd the enabling legislation, said he had been contacted by grantees frustrated over what they said were shifting reporting demands. McKinney was concerned that some projects might not meet an end-of-2027 deadline to spend the money intended to lift economically disenfranchised communities hit hard by the 2020 pandemic.
Foley said his probe of the downtown-Omaha-based Startup Academy was sparked by concerns relayed to his office. Among Foley’s allegations against the nonprofit: unmet job creation milestones, commingling of funds, potential conflicts of interest and “lavish administrative salaries”—  including $387,126 over two years for the executive director.
For now, Foley said, he is satisfied with DED’s response to an 11-page analysis his team presented Tuesday to Maureen Larsen, DED executive director. That same day, the state agency formally suspended the Startup Academy’s contract and remaining $313,000 grant dollars.
The auditor team highlighted issues that “merit corrective action,” but said a more comprehensive financial audit was not necessary. 
Charlie Cuddy, executive director of the Startup Academy, told the Examiner his organization was taken aback, as it was unaware until Tuesday the auditor’s office was investigating.
Charlie Cuddy, executive director of Nebraska Startup Academy. (Photo courtesy of Charlie Cuddy)
“We found out with everybody else,” Cuddy said of the letter.
Cuddy said the Startup Academy’s grant funding effectively was suspended already. He said it hadn’t received any reimbursements since last December, and his team continues to work with DED to answer compliance questions.
The Startup Academy said it recognizes the responsibility to steward public funding, but believes Foley’s remarks created an incomplete picture. Cuddy noted that the findings did not establish “intentional misuse of public funds or fraudulent conduct.”
60 new startups?
Uncontested is an excerpt from the grant application, in which the academy said it would “directly help create and support 60 new startups” and that it anticipated 300-plus full-time jobs within three years.
According to the auditor team, the academy resubmitted forms that showed 42 fewer jobs created than originally reported to DED. Foley said amended reports showed that only two direct jobs and two indirect jobs were created over two years.
About 130 groups in North and South Omaha to share $235 million in development funds

According to Cuddy, the figures were modified as a result of guidance from DED. He said his team’s original reporting included jobs related to hires made by startups receiving academy support, but that DED changed reporting requirements to more narrowly ask for people paid by the grant. 
“We’ve had so many different people to work with at the DED and they’re all amazing in their own ways, but I just think there was no clear direction,” Cuddy said. 
He said the academy remained committed to working with DED to resolve outstanding matters.
Established in 2022, the academy says it has built a statewide entrepreneurship platform, offering education and mentoring that serve more than 750 entrepreneurs, including more than 80 from North and South Omaha ZIP codes. 
The bulk of its resources since 2024, according to the auditor report, has come from the North-South grant. It said that during 2024-2025, the academy’s director of entrepreneurship was paid $268,840 and two academy board members each were paid $79,000.
Maureen Larsen, director of the Nebraska DED and former general counsel to Gov. Jim Pillen. April 20, 2026. (Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Both Foley and the DED, in its notice of suspension, cited potential conflicts of interest that were not disclosed. They said the four academy administrators also hold leadership positions in Move Venture Capital.  
That is relevant, DED’s letter said, because of overlap between startups assisted by the academy and startups that Move has invested in. 
Foley said he was not comfortable with the “cozy relationship,” and that DED owes it to taxpayers to preclude even an appearance of impropriety in the use of public funds. 
“The academy spent most of the money on itself, leaving behind a trail of canceled paychecks but almost nothing in terms of meaningful results,” Foley said in a media release tied to the report.
In its response, the academy said, “We take these matters seriously and remain committed to providing appropriate documentation and clarification as needed.”
‘Too much money on its hands’
In an interview, Foley told the Examiner he suspects that some DED oversight challenges now coming to light are rooted in a “short-lived era where the state had too much money on its hands and couldn’t spend it fast enough.”
He cited a $5 million grant for a film about Chief Standing Bear, which originated from pandemic-era dollars flowing from the federal government. That money was separate from the North-South pot. After Foley’s office alleged a breach of contract, the DED stopped the contract with filmmaker, I Am A Man LLC.
Omaha moviemaker says state-funded venture paralyzed as DED stretches suspension of $5M grant

Another North-South recipient also has had its contract suspended for alleged mismanagement: Fallen Giant Films, Inc., which continues to battle for the remainder of its $5 million grant.
Fallen Giant founder Randy J. Goodwin has been wrangling with DED, and earlier this month reached out again to Gov. Jim  Pillen in a 16-page letter also sent to state lawmakers. 
Before its funds were frozen, the state had disbursed nearly $3.4 million to Goodwin’s venture, which was to build a Hollywood-esque industry in his hometown.
Goodwin told the officials that his group often doesn’t get a clear distinction between an activity that violates a grant requirement, one that requires more documentation or one that’s a film industry purpose the DED “simply does not understand.” 
A DED spokesman said there were no other North-South recipients under formal suspension. Brennan Hallock, the spokesman, said the agency has other remedies available under the grant program, including disallowing costs, contract termination and recouping dollars. He said the agency’s desire is to allow “curative” or least harmful repairs.
In DED responses included in the auditor report, the agency said it would strengthen procedures and training.
Foley believes a “perfect storm” arose with oversight demands and a more recent push by the governor to downsize state government. 
“When you write those checks, what really happens next?” he said.  “No question, there’s more work we need to do.”
