name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan’s Arab American News publisher sues Mike Rogers, campaign over alleged defamation
description: Comments made by Republican former U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers and members of his campaign during the 2026 cycle are the focus of a defamation lawsuit filed by Osama Siblani, the editor of the Michigan-based Arab American News. The lawsuit, filed Thursday in Wayne County Circuit Court, alleges that Rogers and his campaign published and […]
text:
Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers, takes a question from moderator and political reporter Rick Albin, during a televised debate with Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate Abdul El-Sayed, at WOOD-TV, on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026, in Grand Rapids, Mich. (AP Photo/Paul Sancya, Pool)Comments made by Republican former U.S. Senate candidate Mike Rogers and members of his campaign during the 2026 cycle are the focus of a defamation lawsuit filed by Osama Siblani, the editor of the Michigan-based Arab American News.
The lawsuit, filed Thursday in Wayne County Circuit Court, alleges that Rogers and his campaign published and disseminated false statements of fact about Siblani. The lawsuit claimed that Rogers’ campaign had falsely stated that Siblani had called on American Jews to “return to Poland,” that he justified the Hamas terrorist attacks against Israeli citizens on Oct. 7, 2023, and had defended acts of terrorism more broadly. 
Siblani’s attorneys also allege that the Rogers campaign suggested he had a “group” that provided hundreds of thousands of dollars to El-Sayed’s campaign.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rogers and his campaign were heavily criticized during the general election cycle for using Islamophobic rhetoric in its battle for the U.S. Senate seat against El-Sayed. Rogers also platformed several right-wing influencers and journalists who had produced stories claiming El-Sayed and his family had ties to terrorist networks or sympathizers, including the Muslim Brotherhood.
Three members of Rogers’ campaign team were asked to comment on this story and the lawsuit. None responded at the time of publication. A statement from Rogers’ campaign will be added to this story when it becomes available.
Aside from Rogers and his campaign, the lawsuit also names Together for Michigan, a group created to raise money and operate as “Democrats for Mike Rogers,” and outgoing state Rep. Karen Whitsett of Detroit. Whitsett was a member of the Democratic Party but left due to differences with her caucus. She became one of Rogers’ chief ex-Democrat surrogates on the campaign trail and helped run Together for Michigan and Democrats for Mike Rogers.
Whitsett hung up on a Michigan Advance reporter twice while seeking comment for this story by phone. A text message seeking comment from Whitsett went unanswered by publication. A comment or statement from Whitsett will be added to this story when one becomes available.
Michigan Rep. Karen Whitsett (D-Detroit) speaks alongside U.S. Senate nominee Mike Rogers at a “Democrats for Rogers” event in Detroit, Mich on Aug. 20, 2026 (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Christine Fort, counsel for Together for Michigan, told the Advance that the organization has not yet seen a copy of the complaint. Fort did, however, provide a response to a retraction demand sent by Siblani’s attorney, James Allen, on Nov. 2.
Fort said the response letter “addresses all of Siblani’s baseless claims.”
“TFM declines to issue the requested retractions because the statements made in the advertisement were not defamatory — they were true,” Fort wrote. “‘[S]ubstantial truth is an absolute defense to a defamation claim.’ Alternatively, even if that were not the case, Mr. Siblani cannot come close to establishing that the statements in question were made with actual malice, which — as a public figure — he must prove for any defamation claim to lie.”
Under a standard established by the U.S. Supreme Court, public figures must show that a defamatory statement was published either with knowledge that it was false or with reckless disregard for whether it was true.
According to the complaint, the controversy stemmed in part from a Washington Free Beacon article that Rogers shared on social media. The article described Siblani as, among other things, “an unapologetic supporter of Hamas and Hezbollah.”
The Free Beacon was not named as a defendant in the lawsuit but is referenced in the complaint.
Free Beacon Editor-in-Chief Eliana Johnson told the Advance in an email that the publication stands by its reporting.
“Siblani told Jewish Americans they should go back to Poland. Abdul said he was honored to have Siblani’s endorsement,” Rogers wrote in a post on X dated Oct. 27. “Abdul should disavow his endorsement and be held accountable for this hateful rhetoric that he champions. There’s no place for this in Michigan.”

Siblani told Jewish Americans they should go back to Poland. Abdul said he was  honored to have Siblani’s endorsement.
Abdul should disavow his endorsement and be held accountable for this hateful rhetoric that he champions.
There’s no place for this in Michigan. https://t.co/4yBv3cDsjl
— Mike Rogers (@MikeRogersForMI) October 27, 2026

Siblani’s comments about Poland came at a 2024 rally in which he said “And to Netanyahu who wants to bring their people to the north, we are going to take you back to Poland.” It was made following Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s statement concerning the safe return of displaced Israeli residents to northern Israel.  
The phrase ‘Go back to Poland’ has been characterized as antisemitic because it invokes the trope that Jews have no ancestral ties to Israel. CNN’s Jake Tapper made that argument when discussing Siblani’s remarks in October 2024.
Siblani’s lawsuit argues the comment was directed solely at Netanyahu, whose father was born in Poland. 
“Siblani did not demand that Jewish Americans return to Poland. His statement concerned only one individual, accused war criminal and Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu specifically,” the lawsuit states.
Some of Together for Michigan’s advertising for Rogers, which included TV spots and social media posts, was also a point of contention for Siblani. 
An Oct. 29 advertisement specifically named Siblani and called him a “notorious antisemite.” The ad also repeats the comments Siblani made at the 2024 rally.

The “big tent” that includes notorious antisemite Osama Siblani, who wants to send Jews back to Poland?
No thanks, Neera. There’s no room in the Democratic tent for virulent antisemites who sound indistinguishable from KKK members.  https://t.co/luy4ODPc8P
— Democrats For Mike Rogers (@DemsForMike) October 29, 2026

James Allen, Siblani’s attorney, wrote in the complaint that the allegations made against his client were “not merely unflattering descriptions, political opinions, or protected expressions of disagreement.”
“They include purported statements of historical fact, attributed quotations, descriptions of specific conduct, and representations concerning objectively verifiable financial transactions that, if true, would violate campaign finance laws,” Allen wrote. “Defendants’ publications transformed these alleged statements and transactions into a narrative portraying Siblani as a defender of terrorists, an individual hostile to Jewish Americans as a group, and a substantial financial patron of El-Sayed — all of these allegations being demonstrably false.”
The complaint states that Siblani acknowledges the First Amendment protects “robust political criticism” even if it is offensive or unfair. But his attorney argued that the U.S. Constitution “does not immunize the knowing publication of false statements of fact merely because they are deployed in a political campaign.”
In her response to Sibani’s request for a retraction, Fort said “his personal distaste for the content of the communication or the manner in which he was portrayed is irrelevant, and does nothing to undermine the truthfulness of its claims.”
“As stated above, the advertisement made no affirmative representations regarding Mr. Siblani’s sentiment toward Jewish Americans; rather, it simply allowed Mr. Siblani’s words to speak for themselves, accompanying them with an on-screen caption,” Fort wrote. “Having now demonstrated that the allegations and arguments you’ve presented herein fail to meet the minimum requirements of a defamation claim, let alone satisfy the actual malice standard that applies here, we will consider this matter closed.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: ‘What’s Next’ for Democrats? A 2028 supermajority, party leaders say in Denver.
description: Riding high from their success in the midterms, a constellation of rising stars in the Democratic Party gathered in Denver this week for a splashy summit seeking to set the terms of how the party can achieve an encore performance in 2028. The “What’s Next” conference brought together party leaders, consultants, influencers and media to […]
text:
Clockwise from top left: Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico; House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries; Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen; and Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin spoke at the What's Next conference hosted by Majority Democrats in Denver on Nov. 12 and 13, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)Riding high from their success in the midterms, a constellation of rising stars in the Democratic Party gathered in Denver this week for a splashy summit seeking to set the terms of how the party can achieve an encore performance in 2028.
The “What’s Next” conference brought together party leaders, consultants, influencers and media to rub elbows in a festival-like atmosphere at one of Denver’s top music venues, complete with concert-themed posters — “Cory Booker and The Revolution; Special Guests Democracy, Opportunity, Justice,” read one — and a busy merch booth.
The three-day event is a production of Majority Democrats, an influential new political action committee with deep-pocketed funders and a roster full of up-and-coming party favorites, most of whom took to the main stage inside Denver’s Mission Ballroom for speeches and panel discussions on the party’s next steps.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Sen. Elissa Slotkin of Michigan, one of the many What’s Next speakers considered a potential 2028 presidential candidate, said the recent Senate election in her home state, won by progressive Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, “gave a really clear demonstration” of the importance of party unity.
“Whatever side of the Democrats you feel like you’re on, that is not what is important right now,” Slotkin said. “Teamwork is what is important, and if you have elected officials who are spending all their time fighting progressive vs. moderate, then they have missed the plot of the election.”
But amid the sense of triumph, the conference put a spotlight on lingering disagreements within the party about how, exactly, to deliver on the promises it made to the swing voters who powered last week’s “blue tsunami.”
Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, fresh off announcing he would challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer of New York for leadership of the Democrats’ incoming Senate majority, told the crowd that following through on those promises meant “shaking things up.” At times, tensions boiled over, with a handful of protesters escorted from the venue during an appearance by House Minority Leader, and likely incoming House Speaker, Hakeem Jeffries, whom one demonstrator accused of being a “traitor” and “lapdog” for billionaires.
Majority Democrats bills itself as a group that champions “a different kind of Democrat,” with a focus on candidates who can compete in traditionally Republican-leaning states and districts. Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand, Texas Sen.-elect James Talarico and North Carolina Rep.-elect Jamie Ager were among the endorsees of the group who celebrated their midterm victories at the What’s Next conference.
Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand speaks on stage at the What’s Next conference hosted by Majority Democrats in Denver on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
Rep. Jake Auchincloss of Massachusetts, chair of Majority Democrats, sought to set the tone in a speech Friday morning that combined broadsides against the “bad ideas” some in his party have embraced — he named rent control, banning fossil fuels, “open borders” and a lack of attention to the national debt — with calls to “swing for the fences” on new proposals like a four-day work week.
“This is the moment to challenge and cast off these bad ideas and embrace the best and most radical one we ever had: equal opportunity for all and special privileges for none,” Auchincloss said. “Majority Democrats believe our responsibility is to make equal opportunity a real promise, and that means holding the line against special privileges for special interests, even the ones that have historically been on our team.”
Democrats’ big tent
Auchincloss is one of the House’s most conservative Democrats, and several other Majority Democrats members, including Ager and Montana Rep.-elect Sam Forstag, are set to join its centrist Blue Dog caucus. The What’s Next conference also had plenty of representation from the party’s liberal mainstream, along with a handful of progressive figures like Rep. Ro Khanna of California, another possible 2028 contender, who drew loud cheers for his calls to pass “Medicare for All” and abolish U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
Largely absent, however, were figures from the party’s left flank, like Denver’s representative-elect to Congress, 29-year-old democratic socialist Melat Kiros, and other insurgent candidates who scored a series of upset primary victories earlier this year.
Outside the venue Friday morning, Denver police faced off with protestors from groups like the Sunrise Movement and the Democratic Socialists of America, as buses ferrying conference attendees streamed in. Other demonstrators with the activist group Indivisible lined the sidewalk across the street throughout the day, holding up a banner opposing Schumer’s “coronation” as majority leader.
The What’s Next conference began Thursday and is scheduled to run through Saturday morning. Among the dozens of other party leaders featured during the event were former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg, former Attorney General Eric Holder, Georgia Sen. Raphael Warnock, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro.



Quotation







Get us out of the war. Get rid of the tariffs. Deal with the corruption.


– Sherri Stieg, Denver resident


Denver resident Sherri Stieg, holding a homemade sign supporting Van Hollen’s leadership bid, said she had “never missed a No Kings” demonstration over the last two years, and “for months and months” has urged Colorado Sens. Michael Bennet and John Hickenlooper to support new Senate leadership.
“Get us out of the war. Get rid of the tariffs. Deal with the corruption,” Stieg said when asked what she wants to see from the incoming majority, citing Van Hollen’s position in support of threatening a government shutdown in December to force an end to the Iran war.
Protesters with groups including the Denver Democratic Socialists of America and the Sunrise Movement demonstrated outside the What’s Next conference hosted by Majority Democrats in Denver on Nov. 13, 2026. (Photo by Chase Woodruff/Colorado Newsline)
“Americans have not given up on what their government can do,” Van Hollen said in his speech Friday. “They know our government and our democracy can make their lives better, but they have wholly lost faith that it will. … They want their government to work, and change to be worthy of their trust.”
Jeffries, who was interviewed onstage by Fox News’ Jessica Tarlov, sat impassively as a series of demonstrators interrupted to shout in favor of left-wing policies like Medicare for All, a Green New Deal and an end to arms sales to Israel. When asked by Tarlov about “some of the criticism — which we just saw with the young voters that were speaking out about their priorities — that perhaps your leadership is too timid for the moment,” he didn’t answer directly.
“In the last two years, we’ve worked hard to battle Republicans on every issue,” Jeffries said. “We’ve been working hard collectively across the House Democratic caucus, to do what was necessary to aggressively push back against MAGA extremism. And now we’ll have the collective responsibility to really get to work fighting for an affordable America.”
“So,” Tarlov said after another disturbance in which a demonstrator was escorted out of the venue. “How about permitting reform?”
Maneuvering for 2028
As Democrats begin to wade into the debates over policy and strategy that will shape the 2028 presidential race, the Majority Democrats PAC has staked out positions against some high-profile left-wing ideas like Medicare for All, which it says risks alienating Americans who don’t want to lose their employer-sponsored private insurance. That’s made the group a target of criticism from progressives hoping to see the party’s next presidential standard-bearer embrace those ideas.
Founded in July 2025, the PAC’s top donors are hedge-fund billionaire Stephen Mandel and his wife, Sue, who’ve contributed nearly $11 million. according to Federal Election Commission disclosures, The group has also received contributions from former New York City Mayor Michael Bloomberg and James and Kathryn Murdoch. The group shares some donors and advisers with the Searchlight Institute, a centrist think tank that says it’s pushing Democrats to “build a coalition big enough to enact our ideas and make them last.”
“Our party is on probation with voters who might not like us very much, or know exactly what we stand for, but who have given us a chance anyway,” said Stephanie Valencia, co-founder of Latino-focused polling and research firm Equis. “The clock is short. We maybe have the next year to 18 months to show voters who we are, or the pendulum might swing right back.”
What comes next for Democrats will depend in large part on how the party interprets what just happened — its best midterm performance in more than 50 years, powered by victories in traditionally deep-red states like Kansas, Texas and Mississippi. For many of those encouraging a more moderate approach, the results validated what the Searchlight Institute calls “supermajority thinking.”
“(Voters) are telling us loud and clear that they are real sick of Trump and his folks and the associated chaos,” Charlotte Swasey, the Searchlight Institute’s director of analytics, told What’s Next attendees from the stage Thursday. “But they’re not super hype for a wild swing in the other direction.”

Progressives, meanwhile, emphasize the economic populism embraced by many successful midterm candidates. That includes Talarico, who received a raucous reception at What’s Next on Thursday, delivering a speech in which he blasted an “economic system that only benefits the top 1%” and called on Congress to “unrig the political system so no billionaire, no trillionaire, can buy our elections.”
“Our candidates ran on platforms that are popular to the American people,” said Van Hollen. “But what they ran on was not so popular with many powerful special interests who profit from the status quo, and who deploy armies of lobbyists in Washington to defend that broken status quo.”
Colorado Gov.-elect Phil Weiser participated in a panel discussion Friday alongside several of his soon-to-be counterparts from other blue states. A two-term attorney general, Weiser prevailed over Sen. Michael Bennet — a Majority Democrats member — in the Democratic primary in large part by emphasizing his record of fighting the Trump administration. He said Friday that Democrats should stand firm on their principles as they set the agenda in Congress over the next two years.
“That’s why this election was so historic — the American people were fed up with the lawlessness, the corruption, the cruelty,” Weiser said. “We have to stay true to what our values are. Never bend the knee. Never try to give up on what we believe in, thinking we’re going to get something for it, because we won’t.”

title: Senator questions why feds paid so much for Appleton immigrant detention center
description: A member of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs asked the Trump administration to preserve all records related to the federal government’s recent purchase of the Prairie Correctional Facility in Appleton.  CoreCivic, a private prison company, was paid $496 million for the 1,600-bed facility after offering it to the state of Min[...]
text:
The watchtower of the CoreCivic’s former Prairie Correctional Facility, in Appleton, Minn., which will now be used as an ICE detention center, on Aug. 20, 2026. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)A member of the Senate Committee on Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs asked the Trump administration to preserve all records related to the federal government’s recent purchase of the Prairie Correctional Facility in Appleton. 
CoreCivic, a private prison company, was paid $496 million for the 1,600-bed facility after offering it to the state of Minnesota in May 2025 for just $75 million.
The Senate committee, where Democrats will soon be in the majority, is investigating whether Department of Homeland Security spending was “subject to improper influence, corruption, or other violations of federal law,” Sen. Maggie Hassan, D-N.H., wrote in a letter to Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Wednesday. 
Hassan sent the letter about a week after Democrats swept the midterms, winning majorities in both chambers of Congress. Party leaders have promised investigations into alleged corruption by the Trump administration, and the letter signals that the Appleton immigrant detention center — which accepted its first detainees this week — is already under scrutiny. 
KARE11 obtained emails from May 2025 between CoreCivic and officials with the Minnesota Department of Corrections, in which the company offered to sell the prison to the state for $75 million. The feds then paid more than six times that to buy the facility this year.  
Hassan described the deal in the letter. 
“The transaction raises additional concerns about DHS stewardship of taxpayer dollars, particularly in light of recent findings by the Government Accountability Office that DHS has wasted millions of dollars on failed detention initiatives,” Hassan wrote. 
DHS did not immediately respond to a request for comment. 
NBC News reported earlier this year that Homeland Security advisor Corey Lewandowski requested payments from another private prison company, GEO Group, in exchange for steering contracts to the company. Lewandowski is now under criminal investigation for his role in doling out Homeland Security contracts. 
CoreCivic, which also won a five-year, $536 million contract to run the facility, donated half a million dollars to President Donald Trump’s inauguration.

name: Washington State Standard
title: County violated WA law restricting coordination with ICE, judge rules
description: A judge ruled Friday that an eastern Washington county illegally aided federal immigration enforcement, in violation of a landmark state law restricting such coordination. The Adams County Sheriff’s Office is now barred from continuing to coordinate with civil immigration agents and must revise its policies to align with the Keep Washington Working Act, the [...]
text:
An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer's badge and weapon are seen as ICE conducts a vehicle checkpoint on Georgia Avenue on Aug. 30, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Photo by Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)A judge ruled Friday that an eastern Washington county illegally aided federal immigration enforcement, in violation of a landmark state law restricting such coordination.
The Adams County Sheriff’s Office is now barred from continuing to coordinate with civil immigration agents and must revise its policies to align with the Keep Washington Working Act, the state’s so-called “sanctuary” law, and train its deputies on the policy.
“This is a victory for the rights and dignity of all Washingtonians, regardless of where they were born, and an affirmation that local law enforcement cannot be co-opted by the federal government,” Attorney General Nick Brown said in a statement. 
In a lawsuit last year, Brown accused the sheriff’s office of flouting the law by sending nonpublic information about local jail inmates to U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement and Border Patrol agents. 
Sheriff’s office officials also allowed federal officials to interview people while in custody and detained people in jail based solely on civil immigration warrants or detainers, Spokane County Superior Court Judge Marla Polin found.
The information the sheriff’s office shared with the feds included inmates’ release dates, allowing federal immigration officials to take custody of them upon release.
The collaboration went on for at least four years, Polin wrote in her order Friday. Between May 2021 and March 2023, the sheriff’s office released at least half a dozen people directly to Border Patrol officials from jail. Three of them had no local charges pending against them.
In one example, a Border Patrol agent was allowed to speak to two people incarcerated at the jail who were not told they were talking to an immigration agent, according to court papers. When they were released, a Border Patrol agent was reportedly waiting for them. The county reportedly agreed to a $95,000 settlement this summer with one of the men after he filed a lawsuit over the transfer to federal custody. 
Adams County “violated KWW each and every time it sent a new in-custody list to federal immigration officials, as it did on a routine basis between 2019 and mid-2023,” Polin wrote.
Lawmakers passed the Keep Washington Working Act in 2019. It bars local law enforcement from helping federal immigration enforcement. Friday’s ruling marks the first time a judge has upheld the law in court, batting down a challenge from the county that the law is unconstitutional. Polin’s decision aligns with rulings on similar statutes across the country. It followed a court trial in July.
“Today’s ruling allows our state to continue building trust and confidence between law enforcement and immigrant communities as the federal administration undermines those efforts with its draconian policies,” Brown said.
After the law’s enactment, Sheriff Dale Wagner didn’t direct his deputies to change their practices, despite guidance from the state attorney general’s office that other sheriffs adopted.
State attorneys told Wagner in late 2022 that they were concerned his office might have been violating the Keep Washington Working Act. Two years of negotiations between the state and county followed to bring it in compliance with the law. During this time, Wagner told staff to stop sending jail custody lists to immigration officials.
After President Donald Trump retook office in January 2025, the county’s stance shifted, according to Brown’s office. The next month, county attorneys asserted in a letter to Brown that “Adams County has obligations under federal law that directly conflict” with the state law.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
The Trump administration has targeted local and state governments across the country that have laws similar to the Keep Washington Working Act, threatening to withhold federal funding from them. Trump has launched a campaign to deport as many immigrants as possible from the country and restrict them from coming in the first place.
In an email to many other Washington sheriffs in May 2025, Wagner asked them to “lawfully partner with the federal government,” and defy the state law.
Adams County is home to about 20,000 people in southeast Washington. Ritzville is the county seat. Its economy is driven by farming, and in turn workers without legal immigration status.
Wagner didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. The county’s attorney, Joel Ard, referred a request to Wagner.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: First working waterfront conference highlights lingering challenges from 2024 storms
description: Nearly three years since the devastating January storms that ravaged Maine’s coast, the state’s working waterfront says it is still feeling the effects.  Groups from across Maine’s coastal community gathered in Bar Harbor Thursday and Friday for the first ever Maine Working Waterfront Conference to discuss the lingering impacts of storm damage as well as […]
text:
The fishing vessel Tara Lynn II crashed into the rocky coast of Cape Elizabeth amid powerful winds and record-breaking tides on the coast of southern Maine. The crew was rescued. Jan. 13, 2024. (Photo by Jim Neuger/Maine Morning Star)Nearly three years since the devastating January storms that ravaged Maine’s coast, the state’s working waterfront says it is still feeling the effects. 
Groups from across Maine’s coastal community gathered in Bar Harbor Thursday and Friday for the first ever Maine Working Waterfront Conference to discuss the lingering impacts of storm damage as well as other pre-existing challenges facing the seafood industry. 
“We put a lot of work into that, and in a quick second, it was gone,” Milbridge business owner Amity Chipman said. Amity and Monica Chipman own Chipman’s Wharf seafood market, along with their husbands, brothers Chris and Jason Chipman. They bought their property in 2002, and over the years built the wharf themselves. 
“We lost the wharf about an hour before high tide, and basically, what happened was the surf took the building on the end first, and then it just lifted up the wooden structure, the whole thing like a raft, just came off from the pilings,” Amity Chipman said, recounting the devastation from the first of two Jan. 2024 storms.
The severe storms hit Maine’s coast just a few days apart, bringing rain and winds of nearly 60 miles per hour. Paired with a high tide, the storms brought severe flooding along the waterfront and caused extensive damage to piers and wharfs. 
Many coastal communities also had flooding into homes and businesses, damaging structures, electrical systems and more. 
While the brothers, fourth generation fishermen, were out on the boat Thursday, Amity and Monica Chipman attended the conference and spoke at the session on storm recovery. 
“We kind of felt like we are the poster children of devastation, and it’s really hard because we watched in a matter of seconds over 20 years wash away,” Monica Chipman said.
Maine communities receive $25.2 million in storm recovery grants

Although the loss of the wharf was “devastating,” Amity Chipman said the silver lining was how the community rallied around them. 
“The most amazing thing was the next morning I drove down there, and the parking lot was full,” she said. “I couldn’t find a place to park, and the community showed up.”
There were challenges to rebuilding, Amity Chipman said. They had insurance on the wharf, but it didn’t cover a wind event like the storm, so they weren’t compensated for the losses. They went through the federal Small Business Administration, and were told they could get a loan but would have to put their houses up as collateral. 
Luckily, Amity Chipman said, they were able to get a matching grant from the Working Waterfront Resiliency Grant Program. The program was launched in the spring of 2025, expressly aimed at rebuilding coastal infrastructure damaged in the storms, and making it more resilient to the impacts of climate change. 
“Honestly, I don’t think that we could have rebuilt without the help of that,” Amity Chipman said. 
But that hasn’t meant that the reconstruction has been fast or cheap, she said.
“We’re finally getting to the point of completing the permitting process, and I think right now we have spent over $50,000 on just permits in this project,” Amity Chipman said. 
And the rising prices of materials has caused further issues, Monica Chipman said. 
“Then there was a shortage,” she said, “we’re trying to order things as quickly as we can because we know everybody on the coast has been damaged.”
Amity Chipman said they were able to rebuild the wharf because they had set money aside over the years, but they haven’t been able to rebuild those savings. 
“Currently, we’re at the bottom of the barrel,” she said. “We have put everything that we can into rebuilding that wharf. Monica and I run the retail seafood market, and we serve lunch. And our motto is: We are building back the wharf one lobster roll at a time.”
Lewis Pinkham, town manager for Milbridge, which lies at the mouth of the Narraguagus River in Washington County, said the town was hit hard by the storms, including the town-owned pier. 
“The beginning of the pier almost disintegrated,” he said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Like the Chipmans, Pinkham said the local community showed up to help. 
“So we had almost two dozen fishermen that took the time and went down with my Board of Selectmen and other people, and they rebuilt ours, so our major pier, Jordan Pier, could be operational for every fisherman in town,” he said. 
It’s not just the piers and wharfs that the town has to think about, Pinkham said, there’s the other infrastructure that is affected. For example, he said the town recently got a grant to raise one of the roadways that frequently floods — leaving local residents trapped in town.
Jonesport Harbormaster John Church said their town, just north of Milbridge, was able to get funding support from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, but that hasn’t been a quick process either. 
“It is the slow process, the snail process that FEMA uses,” he said. “We spent the money. We’re still waiting for money to come back.”
He said Jonesport has started a project on its working waterfront, but is concerned the plans aren’t enough to prepare for future incidents of extreme weather.
“The height and the design that we built it for, we’re now questioning,” Church said. 
At another session focused on public and private collaboration, Curt Brown, owner of Bold Coast Seafood, said businesses rely on that public infrastructure. 
He said his company, based in Prospect Harbor, buys a substantial number of lobsters from Stonington. 
”If we don’t have the public infrastructure to get it over the causeway and then over the bridge — which, with some of the storms we’ve seen, is at risk, can be at risk, will be at risk in the future,” he said.
Other challenges facing coastal industries
Severe storms aren’t the only pressure on Maine’s working waterfront, said keynote speaker Colin Woodard. 
Woodard is a journalist and author of “The Lobster Coast: Rebels, Rusticators and the Struggle for a Forgotten Frontier.” He said there has long been pressure on waterfront real estate for development of high-end homes and for the hospitality industry. 
The pandemic was a “rapid accelerant” for that pressure, as people left cities to work remotely from more rural areas, Woodard said, putting home ownership out of reach for “most families with incomes tied to the local economy.”
And that can have ripple effects for the community, he said. 
“Local businesses, schools and nursing homes can’t find the workers they need to operate properly because there’s nowhere for the people to live on the incomes they receive,” Woodard said. “The coastal communities are generally the most impacted, which is a special problem for fishing families who have to drive all the way to the waterfront to start their day.” 
Linda Nelson, economic and community development director for Stonington, agreed with Woodard.
“It’s not just the people that work on the boats,” Nelson said. “The people that work on the boats need the schools for their kids to go to. They need the carpenters and the electricians and the plumbers because they can’t necessarily fix everything on their own.”
It’s particularly challenging in smaller towns, Nelson said.
“How do we balance the influx of people with a lot more money that they’re making in other places where the salaries are higher, that then inflate our property taxes and our property values?” she said, noting that towns can’t increase property taxes on those homeowners because of how the state constitution is structured. 
Brown said that he’s seen how the general uncertainty in the fishing industry and coastal communities is leading younger generations to question whether it’s a viable path for them.. 
“Without harvesters out on the water, none of what we do in the private sector works; it just doesn’t exist, and so that next generation is a concern,” he said. “So, how do we as an industry make that look appealing? Like, how do you draw the next generation into that? And I would say that would probably be my top concern right there.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Supreme Court denies Democrats challenge over de Soto seat in House of Delegates
description: West Virginia Democrats do not have standing in a legal challenge against House Speaker Roger Hanshaw and Gov. Patrick Morrisey over an appointment to the House of Delegates last year, the state Supreme Court ruled Friday.
text:
Joseph de Soto (West Virginia Division of Corrections and Rehabilitation)West Virginia Democrats do not have standing in a legal challenge against House Speaker Roger Hanshaw and Gov. Patrick Morrisey over an appointment to the House of Delegates last year, the state Supreme Court ruled Friday.
In a decision issued Friday afternoon, justices denied the writ of mandamus by state Democratic Party Chairman Mike Pushkin and Stephen Willingham over the appointment of Republican Ian Masters to fill a vacancy made after the arrest of Joseph de Soto.
De Soto was elected to the House of Delegates district 91 seat as a Republican in the November 2024 election. He switched his party to Democrat shortly before he was arrested the next month and charged with making threats to harm or kill Republican lawmakers. 
The House of Delegates passed a resolution Jan. 8, 2025 vacating de Soto’s seat. The resolution said that de Soto’s status on home confinement and at least two protective orders filed by lawmakers barring him from the state Capitol would make him unable to take the oath of office in the Capitol as required. It referred the appointment to the Berkeley County Republican Executive Committee to submit nominees to Morrisey, who named Masters to the role on Jan. 23, 2025.
In the lawsuit, attorneys for Pushkin argued that state law at the time required the appointment be made from the Democratic Party because de Soto was a registered Democrat before the vacancy. 
In the court’s opinion, Chief Justice Haley Bunn wrote that the court cannot order Hanshaw to seat de Soto, or alternatively, request a list of nominations to the seat from the Berkeley County Democratic Party and then compel Morrisey to appoint a Democrat. 
The Democrat’s claim lacks redressability, an element of standing. Redressability means the court has the authority to order the relief sought and that the relief is likely to correct the harm the party aims to fix. 
“We find that, under the circumstances of this case, this Court cannot order either Respondent to carry out these actions, and accordingly, the Petitioners’ purported injury is not redressable,” she wrote.
Bunn noted that the Democrats filed three separate petitions for writ of mandamus after a series of “flawed filings,” that included not providing notice of the lawsuit. Pushkins’ third petition — filed in September 2025, was the one that came before the Supreme Court.
She writes further that the Democrats’ did not make their case that Hanshaw has the authority to seat De Soto or the duty to request a list of nominations. In order to seat de Soto, Masters would have to be unseated, she wrote.
The party also does not have standing in case against Morrisey, Bunn wrote. Because Pushkin is not entitled to relief from Hanshaw, Morrisey has no vacancy for which he can appoint a nominee from a list of Democrats, she said. 
Justice Bill Flanigan, a former Republican lawmaker, disqualified himself from participating in the court decision. 
Senior Status Justice Beth Walker, sitting by special assignment, and Justice Charles Trump, concurred with Bunn in a separate opinion. Justice Bill Wooton also concurred in a separate opinion.
Since Masters was appointed, state law about appointments has changed. Lawmakers last year approved Senate Bill 586, Democrat-sponsored legislation that requires that when filling vacancies of state officials, justices, judges and magistrates, appointments be made from the same party that originally held the seat at the time of election, not the party to which the official may have switched to before he or she resigned.
Masters did not seek reelection this year. During the November general election, Republican Chris Claggett won the seat over Democrat David Michaels. Earlier this year Claggett’s racist social media posts drew the ire of House Speaker Roger Hanshaw and condemnation from Republican Party Chair Josh Holstein. 
In a statement Friday afternoon, Pushkin wrote that the party is disappointed by the court ruling, but not surprised. 
“The Court resolved this case on procedural grounds — standing and redressability — without addressing the merits of whether the Governor and Speaker violated the law,” Pushkin wrote. “From the beginning, Gov. Morrisey and Speaker Hanshaw used delay and procedural maneuvering to avoid accountability and run roughshod over the law simply because the law no longer benefited them. That should concern every West Virginian, regardless of party.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico bacterial outbreak spreads in unhoused population
description: A strain of a highly infectious intestinal infection in Bernalillo County has spread among unhoused people, who make up close to half the cases, according to the latest data from the New Mexico Department of Health.
text:
As of the end of October 2026, the New Mexico Department of Health reports 102 shigellosis cases centered in Bernalillo County, with nearly half among people experiencing homelessness. (Medical illustration of shigella bacteria by Stephanie Rossow and courtesy of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)A strain of a highly infectious intestinal infection in Bernalillo County has spread among unhoused people, who make up close to half the cases, according to the latest data from the New Mexico Department of Health. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
As of Oct. 28, the health department had identified 102 shigellosis cases since March 2025, 46 among people experiencing homelessness, Sarah Shrum Davis, NMDOH infectious disease epidemiology supervisor, told Source NM. Multiple outbreaks in recent years have contributed to rising shigellosis rates, she added.
Shigellosis, a highly infectious gastrointestinal infection, spreads through contact with the shigella bacteria, which is found in feces. It can spread through contact with surfaces; contaminated food or water; or person-to-person contact. Symptoms include diarrhea, abdominal pain, severe cramping and vomiting. Antibiotics are commonly prescribed to treat severe cases.
That current case number is likely an undercount, Shrum Davis said. 
“Not everybody that has diarrhea ends up going to the hospital and seeking care,” she noted, adding that of those who do go for treatment, “not all of them have the proper testing to diagnose the disease.”
Albuquerque Healthcare for the Homeless, which operates a medical clinic in the city to serve homeless populations, partners with NMDOH to tackle the issue, Kate Morton, the clinic’s chief clinical officer, told Source NM. 
“Our prevention efforts focus on promoting handwashing and hygiene, as well as early identification of symptoms,” she said. The clinic provides rapid access to antibiotic treatment and also assists local shelters with infection prevention efforts to “ensure that people experiencing homelessness have access to timely, compassionate health care without losing access to shelter or other essential services.”
It isn’t the first time the area has experienced a shigellosis outbreak. Between 2021 and 2025, the NMDOH reported more than 300 cases, also centered in Bernalillo County, including more than half in people experiencing homelessness. One person died from the infection. 
The particular strain of shigella in the previous outbreak was resistant to antibiotic treatment, but Shrum Davis said NMDOH has “not seen any indication of antibiotic resistance” in the current strain. The department has “some evidence” that the current strain may persist in the environment longer, but won’t know definitively until further investigation is completed, Shrum Davis said, adding that getting in front of shigellosis cases is difficult. 
“Shigella can be really tough to beat” from a public health standpoint “because there’s not a vaccine, so you can’t vaccinate your way out of it,” she said. 
Shrum Davis urged people to wash their hands thoroughly and seek care from a healthcare provider if they show symptoms of shigellosis: “We really want people to make sure they’re receiving appropriate care so they can recover,” she said.

title: Flights halted at Burlington airport and across US due to air traffic control communications problems
description:
The FAA notice on Friday afternoon said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Flights halted at Burlington airport and across US due to air traffic control communications problems.
text:
A commercial passenger jet lands at the Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport in South Burlington in Aug. 2021. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights in Vermont and nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
Federal officials have not indicated the stoppage is related to a hack or other nefarious activity. 
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a communications issue is affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers directing planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating. 
This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage.”
“Everybody’s safe. There’s no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying,” Mullin said.
There is no timeline for restarting flights. Mullin said investigators will look at whether there is any link to the FAA’s nationwide rollout of a new artificial intelligence system to help identify problems and reroute planes. But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers.
The outage had stranded about 400 passengers in the terminal at Patrick Leahy Burlington International Airport as of 5 p.m., according to Nic Longo, the airport’s director of aviation, who added that five aircrafts were on the ground with one confirmed cancellation. 
“We’re still holding onto a little bit of hope that things will get moving,” he told VTDigger, noting the last flight of the evening was scheduled to leave at 7:30 p.m. “We’ve got an awesome team, we’ve got a lot of contingencies in place.”
Longo said he did not know how long flights would be halted. He said that to his knowledge, the airport was not experiencing any communications issues. 
Passengers should contact their airlines to handle rebooking flights, Longo said. 
“People just need to be prepared, and we’re here to help,” he said.“ We just don’t have the answer either.”
Friday’s grounding appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.
Friday’s ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately, and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
___
AP writer Mead Gruver contributed to this report from Fort Collins, Colorado.

title: State health officials report second child’s death from measles in Wisconsin
description: A second Wisconsin child has died as a result of measles amid outbreaks that have sickened hundreds of people in 20 counties, the state health department reported Friday. The state Department of Health Services withheld demographic details about the child to protect the privacy of the child’s family. The death was reported in Grant County, […]
text:
Wisconsin health officials reported Friday that a second child in the state has died after getting measles, which health authorities say can no longer be considered "eliminated" in the U.S. Shown here, vials of measles, mumps and rubella vaccine are displayed on a counter at a Walgreens Pharmacy in Mill Valley, California. (Photo illustration by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)A second Wisconsin child has died as a result of measles amid outbreaks that have sickened hundreds of people in 20 counties, the state health department reported Friday.
The state Department of Health Services withheld demographic details about the child to protect the privacy of the child’s family. The death was reported in Grant County, located in the southwest corner of the state.
DHS reported Friday that measles has infected at least 649 people in Wisconsin, the highest number of cases in the state in more than 35 years.
Because not everyone infected with measles seeks medical care or gets tested for the viral illness, reported case counts may not reflect the full extent of the measles spread, according to DHS.
DHS officials reported a child’s death from measles Nov. 5.
The Wisconsin outbreaks coincide with the spread of measles nationwide. The New York Times reported this week that a consensus of medical experts concluded the illness can no longer be considered “eliminated” in the U.S.
Measles is highly contagious and spreads through the air and through close contact, according to the health department.
A measles infection typically begins with a fever, cough, runny nose and red eyes. Its most common symptom is a red rash over the body that shows up several days later. Measles can lead to permanent disability and death in some people.
“It can cause life-threatening complications including pneumonia and swelling of the brain,” DHS stated in its announcement of the second death Friday. “Although anyone can become seriously ill, children younger than 5 years old, pregnant people, and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications.”
The state health department is working with local and tribal health departments and other healthcare providers to respond to the measles outbreaks, identifying cases, tracking infections, testing people for the virus and supporting vaccination.
Measles vaccination is the most effective way to prevent the spread of the virus. Vaccination rates for measles in Wisconsin have fallen below the 95% of the population that ensures widespread protection from the illness, according to DHS.

title: Drake University, Blank Park Zoo receive estate gifts to support students
description: Drake University will use a million-dollar donation to support its students studying zoology and conservation science, with Blank Park Zoo planning to provide students with professional development opportunities. The Des Moines private university announced in a news release it has received a $1 million gift from the estate of Holmes and Marjorie Foster to es[...]
text:
Zoo and conservation science students at Drake University will have access to new scholarship funding from an estate gift. (Photo courtesy of Drake University)Drake University will use a million-dollar donation to support its students studying zoology and conservation science, with Blank Park Zoo planning to provide students with professional development opportunities.
The Des Moines private university announced in a news release it has received a $1 million gift from the estate of Holmes and Marjorie Foster to establish a new scholarship program for students accepted into Drake’s zoo and conservation science program.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Our students come to Drake because they want to spend their lives caring for animals and protecting wild places,” said Keith Summerville, Drake Department of Environmental Science and Sustainability chair, in the release. “The Fosters’ gift will help ensure financial barriers don’t get in the way of students pursuing that passion and making a difference in the world.”
The Holmes and Marjorie Foster Zoo and Conservation Science Scholarship will provide students in the degree program who are Iowa residents and have filled out a Free Application for Federal Student Aid with an annual scholarship of $5,000 for up to four years, as well as a $3,000 professional development stipend.
According to the release, the stipend will go toward activities like experiential learning and conferences, with potential opportunities for international travel. With two students already having received pilot scholarships, how many future students to receive the scholarship will depend on financial need and the number of applicants.
Blank Park Zoo also received $1.8 million from the estate, the release stated, to begin providing Drake student interns with stipends for their work at the zoo starting in summer 2027. Portions of the funding will also go to other projects and exhibits that have yet to be announced.
“Marjorie and Holmes’ generosity gives Blank Park Zoo an incredible opportunity to advance our mission, support the animals in our care and create meaningful experiences for future generations,” said Anne Shimerdla, president and CEO of Blank Park Zoo, in the release. “Our partnership with Drake University extends that mission beyond the Zoo’s grounds by giving students valuable, hands-on experience in conservation and helping prepare them to make a difference for wildlife.”

text:
Wartburg College surpassed its fundraising goal by more than $2 million. (Photo courtesy of Wartburg College)Wartburg College has completed its three-year fundraising campaign with more than $38 million, surpassing its original goal and supporting student scholarships, experiential learning opportunities and campus needs.
The private college, located in Waverly, announced in a news release it raised $38.2 million through its “Our Brightest Days: Realizing Purpose, Leading Change” campaign, which held the goal of $36 million when launched three years ago.
Wartburg President Rebecca Ehretsman said in the release the campaign and strategic plan that was developed with it “have been a labor of love” since she came to the college in 2022, and the campaign’s impact will last for generations of Wartburg students.

“Throughout our 174-year history, the pillars of our foundation — leadership, service, faith, and learning — have remained steadfast guideposts, shaping who we are and how we serve, even as the college changes to meet the needs of our students,” Wartburg President Rebecca Ehretsman said in the release. “We are deeply grateful to the alumni, parents and friends who have invested in Wartburg and our students through this campaign.”
Funding from the campaign has gone to establishing 50 new scholarship funds, the release stated, as well as a new initiative connecting students and alumni for mentoring, job shadowing and other activities. Donations also supported the Knight’s Experience Fund for experiential learning programs and technology and facilities upgrades across campus.
Wartburg senior Kameron Bergen, who is studying senior accounting and business administration, participated in the alumni connections program, according to the release, and worked with IPEX USA regional sales manager Jeff Herman. He said in the release the program was about more than just career advice, but “about building a real connection.”
The fundraising campaign received 10 gifts of more than $1 million, the release stated, and first-time donors made up more than half of all givers to the campaign.
“Their engagement tells us this campaign and our work has done more than raise money. We have expanded the circle of people who see themselves as part of Wartburg’s future, and that is invaluable,” Ehretsman said.

title: Flights halted at airports across US due to air traffic control communications problems
description: The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
text:
The Federal Aviation Administration grounded all flights nationwide Friday afternoon because of communications problems at regional air traffic control centers.
The FAA notice said the ground stop was being imposed “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.”
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said there is a communications issue affecting the 22 regional air traffic control centers that direct planes en route between airports nationwide. He said FAA technicians are investigating. This is the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when a key FAA computer system malfunctioned. Before that the last time had been after the Sept. 11, 2001, attacks.
Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication yet that “this was a nefarious attack against us. It’s just a telecommunications outage.”
“Everybody’s safe. There’s no reason to be concerned about your loved ones if they’re flying,” Mullin said.

But that system operates out of one location near Washington, D.C., and just sends recommendations to the air traffic control centers.
The government has been working to overhaul the outdated technology that air traffic controllers rely on since Congress approved $12.5 billion for the project last year. Miles of old copper wires have been replaced with fiber optic lines and old radio systems are gradually being replaced at airports across the country.
But much work remains. Duffy has said that another $30 billion will be needed to complete the work, and the White House has begun lobbying Congress to approve it.
The problem appeared similar to a regional air traffic control communication outage in September that snarled hundreds of flights across the Northeast, aviation safety expert Steve Arroyo said, except this time on a nationwide scale. It may be linked to the outdated technology used by air traffic controllers.
“If you don’t have that ability, whether it’s because the old wires that they have are just run down or for whatever reason, you’ve got to stop airplanes on the ground,” said Arroyo, who is a former United Airlines pilot. “And not put them in the air where you’re going to risk not being able to communicate with them.”
Friday’s ground stop was different than the one after Sept. 11 because planes were not being told to land immediately and pilots likely were able to communicate with ground controllers at airports, Arroyo said.
AP writer Mead Gruver contributed to this report from Fort Collins, Colorado.

name: VTDigger
title: Legal action against owner of Corinth’s historic village store building forthcoming
description:
The building’s owner owes more than $60,000 in fines related to the iconic structure that featured in the 1988 film “Beetlejuice.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Legal action against owner of Corinth’s historic village store building forthcoming.
text:
A photo of the Maitland Hardware Store from the movie “Beetlejuice” is affixed to a pole across from the filming location, the former East Corinth General Store, which is in disrepair in East Corinth, Vt., on Wednesday, Oct. 28, 2026. The Corinth Selectboard voted to find the building’s owner in violation of the Dilapidated Building Ordinance in August. Photo by Alex Driehaus/Valley News

This story by Sofia Langlois was first published in the Valley News on Nov. 12, 2026. 
CORINTH — Amid a years-long saga, the town plans to sue the owner of an out-of-use building in East Corinth that officials call a hazard to the public and the environment.
Town officials say the owner, Michele Walker, currently owes over $60,000 in fines — and counting — for failing to bring the property at 657 Village Road into compliance, particularly considering that it threatens the Tabor Branch of the Waits River, which runs directly behind the store.
“There is tremendous community concern about having a building in this condition,”selectboard member Stephen Devoto said Friday by phone.
Devoto also told the Valley News Friday that the town has received no responses from Walker regarding the violations. Her contact information was not publicly available.
East Corinth village was settled around 1783. Norm Collette, of the Corinth Historical Society, believes the Village Road building has been there since the late 1700s or early 1800s. It was originally a one-story structure that Nathan Blake and Susan Torrey purchased in 1817 and operated as a general store.
Through several owners, the building largely continued to serve as a general store — not to be confused with the East Corinth General Store on Route 25, which remains open.
The Village Road property was featured in the 1988 film “Beetlejuice” as the exterior of the story’s Maitland Hardware Store, alongside other Village Road buildings.
When the most recent owners before Walker, Jeff and Mary Martin, decided to sell the building, members of the historical society secured a commitment from Preservation Trust of Vermont for a low-interest loan to preserve the store and its architectural features.
“We got back to the Martins too late, as they had sold it to Walker at a reduced price,” Collette said Friday.
Walker purchased the now-2.5-story building in 2012, but it has remained inoperative and, according to town officials, begun falling apart. For at least four years, the Corinth Selectboard has tried to bring the property up to code to no avail.
A dilapidated building is one that is “hazardous to the health and safety of the public or presents a threat of damage to other buildings or property,” per the town’s ordinance.
Olivia Tillman, who sits on the board of the Congregational Church next door, told the Selectboard in a public comment that, despite having paid for dumpsters to help the owner clean up the property, the problem persists, according to April 4 meeting minutes.
In December 2022, the town issued a building safety order against Walker, with a second order raising her fines under the amended ordinance issued in June 2024.
The deadline for compliance was Aug. 4, 2024. On Aug. 3 of that year, the building safety officer confirmed that no substantial remediation had occurred and the hazardous conditions persisted, per meeting minutes from that August.
The next day, the Selectboard unanimously approved a motion by Devoto to find Walker in violation of the ordinance and responsible for civil penalties.
Hazards documented by the town’s building safety officer included “imminent collapse” of the barn structure into the river; threat of damage to the Village Road bridge and the neighboring East Corinth Congregational Church; and instability in the main store building.
Citing the public safety impact, the owner’s knowledge of the problems since 2022 and her record of non-compliance, the town assessed a one-time $150 penalty, $10 a day from March 11, 2023, through Aug. 6, 2024, and $75 a day since Aug. 7, 2024.
Fines continue to accrue at $75 a day, now reaching a total of over $67,000 as of Nov. 12.
The town’s counsel was continuing to collect information regarding the violations and taxes due over the years in order to serve Walker at the time of the Nov. 4 Selectboard meeting.
Devoto confirmed Friday that the lawsuit has not yet been filed in the Orange Unit of Vermont Superior Court, but he anticipates it will be filed in the next month.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Stock trading ban, veterans benefits and farm grants: CT politics news
description: Plus: How CT's House delegation voted on Pete Hegseth's impeachment and why workers at a West Hartford defense contractors are striking.
text:
These news briefs are part of The Connecticut Mirror’s 2026 political coverage. For more Connecticut political news, sign up here for The Issue, the CT Mirror’s weekly politics newsletter.
Bronin pushes for stock trading ban
Following his victory in the midterm elections, Luke Bronin said one of his priorities to combat corruption and self-enrichment in government was to ban members of Congress from trading stocks.
He joined dozens of other newly elected members this week in calling on House Democratic leadership to push for such a prohibition in the early days of the party’s majority next year.
Bronin and others want to see a rule barring members and their spouses from “owning or trading stocks, commodities, futures, derivatives, and other related securities.” Exceptions would include a diversified mutual fund or investments in a qualified blind trust. 
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
Major Richard Star Act passes U.S. House
All five Democrats in Connecticut’s congressional delegation joined an overwhelming majority in the House to pass legislation that would allow combat-injured veterans to collect full benefits.
Veterans who were medically retired and served less than 20 years cannot collect full retirement benefits when they also receive disability compensation. The Major Richard Star Act seeks to change that.
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal has tried several times to move the bill forward in the Senate through unanimous consent. But it was blocked each time since it only takes one member to object to such a request. He hopes Congress can get this fully passed by the end of the year. 
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
Round 2 open for farm disaster grants
A second round opened this week for eligible farmers to apply for funds from Connecticut’s $53 million federal disaster relief program. The application period runs from Nov. 9 through Dec. 9.
Farmers can access relief after experiencing damages caused by disasters and extreme weather events in 2023 and 2024. The money can be put toward crop production loss, damages to agricultural structures and farm infrastructure, or perennial crop losses that lead to multi-year production losses.
During the first round, 145 applications were submitted for a total of $67 million in requested relief. Those initial requests exceeded the total amount allocated to the state-run program. 
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
CT Dems vote to impeach Hegseth. The effort failed.
After a House Republican sought to impeach Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth, the GOP moved on a vote to effectively kill that effort. But all five Democrats in Connecticut’s delegation voted against referring the resolution to committee. Nearly a dozen other Democrats missed the vote, and Republicans ultimately had the numbers.
It’s unclear if House Democrats will take it up again when they’re in the majority. And broader questions remain among Democrats about impeachment of President Trump.
“I think impeachment could potentially be a blind alley, futile and frustrating,” U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal said Monday, “and also a diversion from the focus that we really need, which is on affordability and accountability.” 
— Lisa Hagen, Federal Policy Reporter
West Hartford aerospace workers hold strike
State officials and local legislators joined striking union workers in West Hartford on Veterans Day, more than a week after workers at Triumph Group first walked off of the job in protest.
The company, which builds components for military aircraft, employs more than 170 members of  UAW Local 405. The workers said despite recent profits, employees hasn’t seen corresponding growth in pay or benefits. This prompted workers to begin their strike at the company earlier this month.
On Veterans Day, workers continued to call for the company to meet them at the negotiation table, arguing that the company was failing to support its own workers, many of whom are veterans. 
— P.R. Lockhart, Economic Development Reporter

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho governor appoints agriculture official as House lawmaker to fill vacancy
description: Idaho Gov. Brad Little on Friday announced he appointed a longtime federal agriculture official to fill a vacancy for a state House seat in rural southwest Idaho. The governor named Kimberly Royer, who lives in Cambridge, to fill a Legislative District 9 House seat being left vacant by John Shirts, who recently stepped down after […]
text:
The exterior of the Idaho Statehouse as seen on Jan. 14, 2026, in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho Gov. Brad Little on Friday announced he appointed a longtime federal agriculture official to fill a vacancy for a state House seat in rural southwest Idaho.
The governor named Kimberly Royer, who lives in Cambridge, to fill a Legislative District 9 House seat being left vacant by John Shirts, who recently stepped down after he was named by the Trump administration as Idaho’s top federal prosecutor. 
Kimberly Royer (Photo courtesy of the Idaho governor’s office)
Royer will fill the seat until at least the end of the month, when Shirts’ current term as a state representative ends. 
It’s not immediately clear if Royer will fill Shirts’ upcoming term. He ran unopposed for his legislative seat in the Nov. 3 general election. Shirts resigned from the Legislature on Oct. 17, the governor’s spokesperson, Emily Callihan, told the Idaho Capital Sun in a text message. For a new appointment, Shirts would need to resign from his new term, Callihan said.
“I am honored by the opportunity to serve the people of Idaho in the Legislature,” Royer said in a written statement. “My years working alongside Idaho farmers and ranchers, serving on state boards, and being part of a rural community have given me a deep appreciation for the challenges and opportunities facing our state. I look forward to listening to the people I represent, working with my fellow legislators, and making decisions that keep Idaho strong for future generations.”
Royer recently retired from the U.S. Department of Agriculture’s Farm Service Agency, where she worked for 25 years, the governor’s office says. The office says she has also served in state government roles — as a governor-appointed member to the Idaho Sheep and Goat Health Board, and as chair of the Idaho Animal Damage Control Board, which prevents and controls damage caused by predatory animals and pests. 
Royer co-owns and operates a family farm and ranch, Dixie Creek Ranch LLC.
The governor’s office did not share the list of Republican candidates sent by local GOP officials to fill Shirts’ House seat. Under state law, the governor can pick from a list of three names submitted to him by local officials of the same party of the outgoing incumbent.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Family Dollar to pay $63 million to settle allegations that it routinely overcharged customers
description: The Family Dollar at 3336 Terry Road in Jackson during its closing sale on Wednesday, May 13, 2026.
text:
Family Dollar will pay $63 million to settle state and federal allegations that it routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on its shelves, website and mobile app.
The Federal Trade Commission and 17 states filed federal charges against the company Thursday and announced the proposed settlement the same day. The settlement must still be approved by a judge.
According to the FTC’s complaint, consumers from across the country have been reporting price discrepancies at Family Dollar for years. In January 2025, for example, consumers from at least seven states reported that Family Dollar refused to honor a “2 for $20” sale on a package of diapers, even though the price was advertised on its mobile app and on shelf tags.
One Michigan consumer took a picture of the “2 for $20” shelf tag and brought it to the register, but reported that the store manager said the price was wrong and quickly removed the shelf tag, the complaint said.
READ MORE: Mississippi joins lawsuit claiming Dollar General overcharged customers
Over the last five years, state and local regulators have cited Family Dollar for thousands of pricing violations, resulting in fines of more than $3 million, the complaint said. It has also entered into multiple settlements with state attorneys general and consumer protection agencies over inaccurate pricing.
Family Dollar said Friday it will work with the FTC and state agencies to meet the settlement’s requirements and provide clear information to customers about how the settlement could impact them.
“We take our responsibility to deliver a positive shopping experience seriously,” Family Dollar spokeswoman Janella Escobar said in a statement. “We remain focused on strengthening pricing accuracy across our stores and maintaining our customers’ trust.”
Family Dollar, which is privately owned and based in Chesapeake, Virginia, has more than 8,000 U.S. discount stores. It reported revenue of $13 billion in its most recent fiscal year, according to a company statement.
The case is similar to one the FTC and 20 states filed last month against Dollar General, a rival bargain chain. That case is ongoing.
Under the proposed settlement, Family Dollar will be required to establish a $40 million consumer redress fund payable to eligible consumers. The company must notify customers about the fund through notices in stores and on its digital platforms.
The settlement requires Family Dollar to establish a $20 million discount program for its customers and pay $3 million to the states involved in the case. Those states are: Alabama, Arkansas, Colorado, Florida, Illinois, Iowa, Kansas, Louisiana, Mississippi, Nebraska, Ohio, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, South Carolina, Tennessee, Utah and Wisconsin.
The settlement also requires Family Dollar to implement a pricing accuracy program that is independently assessed and annually certified.

name: California
title: CA Insurance Department accidentally reveals another judge complained about internal misconduct
description: Department responds to fired judge’s lawsuit, calling allegations ‘egregious.’ In doing so, it disclosed that a current judge also filed complaints with the State Bar.
text:
In summary
Department responds to fired judge’s lawsuit, calling allegations ‘egregious.’ In doing so, it disclosed that a current judge also filed complaints with the State Bar.


California’s Insurance Department reversed course Friday and chose to talk about a lawsuit brought by a former administrative judge against Commissioner Ricardo Lara and others, which accuses them of illegally approving rate increases.
In doing so, the department appears to have inadvertently disclosed that a current administrative judge, Karl-Frederic Seligman, also filed complaints about misconduct by attorneys in the department. 
As CalMatters reported this week, administrative law judge Kristin Rosi sued Lara and his former special counsel Lucy Wang in late September, alleging that they fired her in retaliation last year after she ruled in 2024 that they were improperly approving insurance companies’ requests to raise their customers’ premiums. 
Proposition 103, the 1988 voter-approved law that governs insurance in the state, requires the Insurance Department to hold hearings when an insurer requests a rate increase of 7% or more if a member of the public objects through the so-called intervenor process. 
Rosi’s “decisions found that Defendants had refused to conduct mandatory hearings, relied on unauthorized regulations, and circumvented rules requiring transparency in settlements,” according to her lawsuit filed in Alameda County Superior Court.
Rosi alleges Lara, Wang and other yet-to-be-named staff in the department tried to undermine the authority of administrative law judges after those decisions. That included asking the judge to change her rulings or to rule in certain ways, the lawsuit said. 
“While it is our policy to not comment on pending litigation, the egregious nature of these demonstrably false allegations and blatant inaccuracies requires a response,” Gabriel Sanchez, spokesperson for the department, said in an email to CalMatters. 
Sanchez said the department will “vigorously” defend itself: “At all times, Commissioner Lara and Department staff acted properly, legally, and within the decades-old framework of Proposition 103 to protect consumers and ensure accountability in its operations.”
Last year, Rosi filed complaints with the State Bar against Wang and three other department attorneys. The complaints, which are not public but were obtained by CalMatters, allege in detail repeated violations of law that include meetings that the judge said should have included all parties involved in rate hearings, including insurance companies and intervenors. 
Sanchez said the judge “misinterpreted… longstanding Proposition 103 procedures,” and that the State Bar has closed those complaints and did not find wrongdoing. He sent CalMatters a letter from a State Bar investigator dated July 14 that declared the matter closed. That letter said “The State Bar has completed the investigation of the allegations of professional misconduct reported by Hon. Kristin L. Rosi and Hon. Fredric J. Seligman.”
There appears to be no previous reporting that Seligman had also filed complaints with the State Bar. He is the only person listed as an administrative law judge on the department’s website. His staff did not immediately return CalMatters’ request for an interview.
Wendy Musell, Rosi’s lawyer, said her client appealed the State Bar’s decision to close the complaints.
“My understanding is the State Bar still has jurisdiction and the matter is still under appeal,” she said.
Rosi had been an administrative law judge with the department’s Administrative Hearing Bureau since 2007. She was appointed chief judge in 2016. In January 2025, the department placed her on administrative leave; her position was advertised as vacant in July 2025; and she received the department’s affirmation that she was fired in November 2025, according to her lawsuit.
Rosi sued Lara and Wang and other unnamed staff in their capacity as officials with the Insurance Department, so the state Justice Department is representing them in the lawsuit.
Lara’s second term as commissioner ends in January. Wang left the department in late 2025 and now works for a law firm that represents the insurance industry.

title: Flights grounded at T.F. Green as FAA halts departures nationwide
description: All departing flights at Rhode Island T.F.
