The rare FAA order, known as a ground stop, came shortly before 4 p.m., with the agency citing “extraordinary circumstan[...]
text:
A screenshot shows late departures at Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport on Friday afternoon.All departing flights at Rhode Island T.F. Green International Airport were halted Friday afternoon after the Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop amid communication issues with Air Route Traffic Control Centers.
The rare FAA order, known as a ground stop, came shortly before 4 p.m., with the agency citing “extraordinary circumstances” and safety concerns. Aircraft already in the air were still permitted to land, while international flights would be evaluated on a case-by-case basis.
An update to the FAA’s X account posted at 5:02 p.m. said, “There has been a temporary telecommunications outage – out of an abundance of caution all flights have been halted. Every flight has been accounted for and international flights will be handled on a case by case basis.” 
“The FAA has declared a nationwide ground stop related to frequency issues with air traffic control,” Bill Fischer, spokesperson for the Rhode Island Airport Corporation, said in an emailed statement shortly before 5 p.m. “Like every airport in the nation, PVD is impacted by this ground stop. All departures are halted at this time.”
Samantha Decker, a spokesperson for the Massachusetts Port Authority, offered a similar statement in an email Friday that the ground stop was affecting Boston’s Logan Airport as well. 
“We are monitoring the situation and working with the FAA and our airline partners,” Decker said.
U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said in an X post at 4:16 p.m. that FAA technicians were investigating the issue, and that updates would be issued as they became available. 
The length of the ground stop order or how many flights at T.F. Green would be delayed was not immediately clear.
Fischer said that travelers should contact their airlines for information on specifics impacts and delays regarding their flights.

Republican Byron Donalds celebrates his win in the Florida governor race on Nov. 3, 2026, flanked by his wife, Erika, and running mate Bryan Ávila. (Photo via Donalds Facebook page)Gov.-elect Byron Donalds, focusing on his transition from congressman to governor, said Friday that he’s been looking at the state’s agencies and considering “potential personnel.”
“There’s really good talent out there. People who can come in and help our state. And so we look forward to just vetting everybody, being very conscientious in that, so we can hit the ground running on Jan. 5.”
State departments or agencies are created in statute. Some are administered by secretaries appointed by and who exclusively work for the governor. Others fall under direct supervision of a board, such as the governor and Cabinet, and are run by  executive directors who serve at the pleasure of the board.
Those appointed to agencies that report to the governor require Senate confirmation.

Meanwhile, the Donalds campaign announced additional members of his transition team, charged with helping bridge the switch to his incoming administration from that of outgoing Gov. Ron DeSantis.
Donalds made transition team announcements earlier this week, also.
Meet Gov.-elect Byron Donalds’ transition team

name: VTDigger
title: Hunters prepare for major rule change in Vermont’s deer rifle hunting season
description:
Hunting antlerless deer has some seasoned hunters wary.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Hunters prepare for major rule change in Vermont’s deer rifle hunting season.
text:
Casey Morits of West Bolton examines the rack of a 165-lb. buck taken by Derek Villeneuve in Essex at the big game reporting station at the Jericho General Store in Jericho in November 2019. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

BARRE — Shoppers at R&L Archery knew what they were here for: a hunting license, a box of ammo, synthetic deer urine and, for some, a homemade pie. 
Vermont’s 16-day rifle deer hunting season begins Saturday. For Joe Sanborn, that means hundreds of customers through the door Friday at R&L Archery, the Barre outdoor sports store he manages. 
“It’s always busy, it’s always hectic,” Sanborn said. “Opening the door, we had six trucks in the yard ready to go.”
The state expects to see between 60,000 and 65,000 hunters out over the next two weeks, according to the Vermont Fish and Wildlife Department’s Deer Project Leader Nick Fortin. 
Some hunting regulations have changed this year, as they do every five years, he said. One rule change has left some seasoned hunters excited, and others wary. 
For the first time in 39 years, Vermont hunters can shoot antlerless and female deer during the regular season. Previously, antlerless deer harvest was limited to other seasons, such as archery and muzzleloader. 
State surveys indicated that a majority of hunters under 55 support the change, and a plurality of hunters 65 and older oppose the policy, according to previous reporting by VTDigger. 
“Some hunters are really nervous about it. They’re afraid we’re going to kill too many deer, or maybe they have safety concerns,” Fortin said in an interview Thursday. “We actually do need to kill more deer in some areas, but we also want to be sensitive to those concerns so that we don’t lose this tool again because we need this.”
The state’s deer population is relatively stable, but areas like the Champlain Valley, the Connecticut River Valley and the Barre-Montpelier area have more deer than can be supported by the ecosystem, according to Fortin. An overabundance of deer could mean increased deer-car collisions, tick-borne disease transmission and declining stability of forests from overgrazing, according to Penn State’s Department of Ecosystem Science and Management.
That’s what led to the Fish and Wildlife Board’s 2025 decision to issue 12,050 antlerless deer permits for the rifle season by lottery in August. Fortin said he estimates this will lead to about 3,000 female and antlerless deer killed during the regular season. Anyone with a hunting license can shoot a buck, but there are limits on how many total deer one hunter may harvest during the season. 
“This is one that we’re hoping will work long term, but we’re being really conservative because it is such a big social change,” Fortin said, speaking to the number of permits issued.
Sanborn said he’s been answering questions about the rule change all year and expects the discussion to continue through next year. 
“Every time they change anything, it gets people a little confused for a bit until we all settle into the new normal,” he said. “As avid as a lot of our customers are with their hunting seasons, the last thing they want to do is jeopardize that.” 
Melvin Pierson, who was shopping at R&L, said he hunts in Maine, New Hampshire and Vermont. He was at the store to buy gloves, a camouflage cushion seat and his Maine and Vermont licenses. He said he hasn’t killed a doe in 10 years. He won’t be breaking that streak this season. 
“I think if they’re going to shoot does, then they should shoot them earlier in the season,” Pierson said in the aisles of R&L Archery. “I’m a little against shooting them late season when they’re already bred.” Peak deer mating season occurs in November.
For Brandon Kennedy, another R&L shopper, the rule change is not a major concern. Leaving the shop Friday having purchased a new shotgun and other last-minute supplies such as ammunition, Kennedy said he assumes the state does its due diligence.
Vermont made seven other deer hunting rule changes this year, but most won’t impact the majority of hunters, Fortin said. Changes included moving youth and novice weekend — when new hunters and their mentors get to go out early — and allowing hunters who qualify to receive a second buck tag. 
Dylan Sickles sat outside R&L Archery all morning Friday. He’s not a deer hunter, but a fish culture operations manager for the state’s Fish & Wildlife Department. And he’s a scout master for Boy Scouts of America’s Troop 1. Rifle season for Sickles means selling pies. 
Sickles and Assistant Scout Master Joe Cannon had sold 37 pies by 12:30 p.m. The pies, baked by the Boy Scouts and their mothers and sold for $20 apiece, had brought in $740 to fund summer camps and other yearly activities. Sickles and Cannon knew many shoppers by name. 
Just like fishing does for him, Sickles said deer hunting creates community. “It’s all about your buddies,” he said.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Hunters prepare for major rule change in Vermont’s deer rifle hunting season.

text:
State Rep. Eric Emery, D-Rosebud, left, will serve as minority leader in the South Dakota House of Representatives in 2027. Rep. Mike Stevens, R-Yankton, is nominated as speaker of the House. (Photos by South Dakota Searchlight; illustration by Meghan O'Brien/South Dakota Searchlight) 


Searchlight Report is a podcast from South Dakota Searchlight. Reporter and host Meghan O’Brien works with other Searchlight journalists to take listeners inside politics and policy in The Mount Rushmore State.			




The ongoing struggle for power among factions of the Republican Party has resulted in new leadership for the South Dakota House, including historical firsts.
Rep. Mike Stevens, R-Yankton, is nominated to serve as speaker of the House, a role that’s nominated by the majority party and voted on by the full House. At 73 years old, he’s set to become the oldest speaker of the state House in South Dakota history.
Rep. Eric Emery, D-Rosebud, a member of the Rosebud Sioux Tribe, also made history with his election as House minority leader. He’ll be the first tribal member to lead a minority party in the state House.
When those and other leaders convene for the annual legislative session that begins Jan. 12, the membership will include 30 first-time legislators in the 70-member House and five first-time legislators in the 35-member Senate.
Searchlight Report Host Meghan O’Brien asked Stevens and Emery about their roles and legislative priorities. The next episode of Searchlight will feature new leaders in the state Senate.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Proposed federal change to SNAP puts more Oklahomans at risk of going hungry, advocates say
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans could be at higher risk of being food insecure if a proposed rule change to a federal food assistance program becomes reality, an advocate said.  The proposal, posted Tuesday by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, would end a current practice that allows automatic eligibility for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or […[...]
text:
A sign explaining restrictions on buying soda and sweetened drinks using Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program benefits is displayed in a grocery store in Bountiful, Utah on Feb. 11, 2026. (McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)OKLAHOMA CITY — Oklahomans could be at higher risk of being food insecure if a proposed rule change to a federal food assistance program becomes reality, an advocate said. 
The proposal, posted Tuesday by the U.S. Department of Agriculture, would end a current practice that allows automatic eligibility for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program, or SNAP, if they are meeting the requirements and receiving benefits from Temporary Assistance for Needy Families, another federal aid program. 
SNAP, commonly known as food stamps, provides aid to more than 36 million people across the country, including over half a million Oklahomans. The USDA estimates this rule change would impact over 17% of participants, which is about 3.2 million households or 6.3 million individuals by the 2029 budget year when the rule would be fully implemented. 
The change would reduce SNAP spending by $44.6 billion over five years and ensure the program benefits the truly needy, according to the proposal. 
But SNAP has already been subject to a series of Congressional changes that made millions ineligible and the rule change posted Tuesday could add to this number. 
Jessica Dietrich, director of government relations and public policy at Hunger Free Oklahoma, said its “terrible news” for Oklahoma and all states. Hunger Free Oklahoma  works to ensure all Oklahomans have access to affordable and nutritious food.
There are two aspects to the proposed change, she said. 
The change that would most impact Oklahoma families is reimplementation of strict asset limits to be eligible for SNAP, Dietrich said. This means assets that are available and could be used to purchase food, like a savings account, could count against a family’s eligibility, Dietrich said. 
Dietrich said that under current policy, if someone is slightly over income limits but qualifies for the Temporary Assistance for Needy Families Program, or TANF, it doesn’t matter but this rule change would create a hard cutoff at 130% of the poverty line – which equates to an income of $42,900 for a family of four. 
“If you don’t use SNAP or have a loved one that uses the program, it might be easy to think that it doesn’t affect you but that’s less money flowing into our local grocery stores,” she said. “And it could be the difference between a grocery store, especially in a rural area, staying open or having to close because they don’t have enough income.”
Oklahoma is already one of the most food insecure states, Dietrich said, with 1 in 5 people and a quarter of children in the state facing food insecurity. 
The change would also burden state agencies and make SNAP less efficient, she said.
“Our state, and every state, is already facing so many new rules that they have to implement into very antiquated technology that doesn’t pivot as easily as someone in the public might think,” Dietrich said. 
Adding another step where paperwork needs to be gathered will overload agencies and overwhelm families, she said. It will likely also impact the state’s error rate which could cost Oklahoma more money. 
SNAP has already been subject to a series of changes under the Big Beautiful Bill passed last year by Congress. This includes work requirements to maintain eligibility for SNAP as well as requiring states to lower their error rates or pay a larger share of the program’s cost. 
Error rates refer to payment inaccuracies, which are not necessarily fraud and can be underpayments or overpayments. 
The Oklahoma Department of Human Services, which administers SNAP, does not yet have a reliable estimate of how many Oklahomans would be impacted by the rule change, said Nazarene Harris, an agency spokesperson. They’re still reviewing the proposal to understand how it would impact eligibility for the program in the state. 
Since the passage of the Big Beautiful Bill, the Oklahoma Department of Human Services has worked to lower its error rate to 11.04% through additional training, oversight and quality control to improve payment accuracy, Harris said. An error rate of 6% is needed to prevent Oklahoma from shouldering a larger share of the program’s cost. 
Since November 2025, Oklahoma’s SNAP participation has declined by about 70,000 participants which is consistent with national trends, Harris said. While Congress made changes to eligibility, she said participation can change for many reasons and cannot entirely be attributed to the Big Beautiful Bill. 
The posted rule is open for public comment until Dec. 10.

name: National
title: US poised to lose its ‘measles elimination status’ after more than 25 years
description: The number of confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year has soared to 5,412 as of Nov. 12, more than double the 2,289 cases through all of 2025, according to the latest release of data from the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The trend is pushing the nation to the brink of […]
text:
Ethan Turner holds his 14-month-old son, Niko, while he gets the MMR vaccine from Raynard Covarrubio at a vaccine clinic put on by Lubbock Public Health Department on March 1, 2025 in Lubbock, Texas. (Photo by Jan Sonnenmair/Getty Images)The number of confirmed measles cases across the U.S. this year has soared to 5,412 as of Nov. 12, more than double the 2,289 cases through all of 2025, according to the latest release of data from the federal Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The trend is pushing the nation to the brink of losing its official “measles elimination status” in more than 25 years. 
“It’s pretty clear we’re hitting one grim milestone after the other,” Dr. Susan Kansagra, chief medical officer of the Association of State and Territorial Health Officials, a group representing local health officials, told Stateline. “It’s really, really just a hard time to see something that we know has been eliminated in the past, and to see this rapid growth that we have seen over these last two years.” 
The U.S. launched a national campaign to eliminate measles in the 1960s, around the time the first official measles vaccine was licensed to the public. In 1994, the Pan American Health Organization (PAHO), a regional office of the World Health Organization representing states across the Americas, set a goal of ending the measles epidemic through a concerted vaccination effort, and by 2000 a panel of experts had concluded that the United States had eliminated measles from its population. 
This elimination status means that the nation is able to squash instances of measles transmission for 12 months or more. To reverse that status, measles must be spreading for 12 months or more – and now that’s where the U.S. is headed. A panel of experts at PAHO was reviewing cases Friday. 
“And that means the disease has become what we call endemic again, meaning it’s just spreading in the community,” Katrine Wallace, an epidemiologist at the University of Illinois, Chicago School of Public Health, told Stateline. “I definitely blame it on the anti-vaccination kind of propaganda that’s been all over, and the lack of our (U.S. Department of Health and Human Services) really doing anything about these cases.
“There’s not been a real push for vaccination efforts to counteract the 5,000 cases or something that we have now,” Wallace said. 
Measles is a highly contagious respiratory virus that leads to symptoms of fever, rash, and other serious health complications, including death, but is entirely avoidable through the two-dose MMR, or measles, mumps, and rubella vaccine. Children, who generally don’t get vaccinated before a year of age, are highly susceptible. 
But in his time in charge, U.S. Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has been an outspoken vaccine skeptic who opposes many vaccine mandates. His agency has called into question the safety and efficacy of vaccinations and recommended fewer vaccines for children. Many Republican-led states have ended vaccine mandates for their populations. Thirty-nine states now have MMR vaccination rates below 95% – the percentage necessary for herd immunity. 
According to the latest CDC data, measles cases have been reported this year across 47 states, plus the District of Columbia, and New York City. Among those cases, 58% of them, or 3,134, are among people under the age of 19.
Among all cases, 96% are within people who are unvaccinated, and 11%, or 591 cases, have resulted in hospitalizations. The CDC has confirmed six measles-related deaths so far, though other investigations are continuing within individual states. 
Pennsylvania is experiencing a major outbreak, with 1,542 cases confirmed so far this year, including 37 cases since Nov. 9, according to the state’s health department. 
Just since Election Day, Pennsylvania has reported two “measles-associated” deaths, the most recent one announced Nov. 13. Two other deaths, in New York and Wisconsin, have been reported by state health agencies during the same period.
“Revoking our elimination status doesn’t really change the reality on the ground, right? We all know, you know, that we have measles in our community,” said Dr. Ali Khan, a medical epidemiologist and dean of the College of Public Health at the University of Nebraska Medical Center. 
“Measles has always been the sort of ultimate stress test for public health infrastructure,” Khan said in an interview. “And we’re failing that test … if you can’t get people vaccinated, that says something about the quality of your health system.” 
Khan said the real message behind the potential revocation of the elimination status is that the nation’s leaders desperately need to fund and promote public health infrastructure in communities, so that people can protect themselves. 
Kansagra, who works with local and state health departments, said it’s particularly worrisome that major federal public health grant programs and pandemic-era funds are expiring at the end of next year. 
“That type of core infrastructure support for public health is so important because these are exactly the types of threats that public health is dealing with and working to respond to,” Kansagra said.  
Wallace is hopeful on the heels of the 2016 midterm elections in November that Democrats, especially ones steeped in public health like Michigan Senator and Dr. Abdul El-Sayed, can change the direction of the country’s public health policy in time to prevent more death and spread of disease. 
“We’re voting these people in,” Wallace said. “So it seems like the country is moving towards wanting to rein this in.” 
Stateline reporter Shalina Chatlani can be reached at schatlani@stateline.org.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Data center policy a ‘ubiquitous’ and ‘pressing’ issue for state lawmakers
description: When Iowa lawmakers return to Des Moines in January for the 2027 legislative session, they’ll need to address the state’s role in regulating data centers, which while not new, have increased in the state alongside an explosion of technology such as artificial intelligence and cloud storage.  An Iowa legislator and utility stakeholders said recently in […]
text:
Data center policy is a pressing issue for state lawmakers as they head into upcoming legislative sessions. Pictured is construction at QTS data center in Eagle Mountain, Utah, on April 17, 2026. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)When Iowa lawmakers return to Des Moines in January for the 2027 legislative session, they’ll need to address the state’s role in regulating data centers, which while not new, have increased in the state alongside an explosion of technology such as artificial intelligence and cloud storage. 
An Iowa legislator and utility stakeholders said recently in a webinar that policy decisions to bring data centers online should consider stakeholders across the spectrum and take into account the long-term planning associated with connecting to the grid. 
The webinar was hosted by Legible, a platform that tracks legislation across states, with leadership of the platform stating that public policy around data centers has arisen as a “ubiquitous, as well as pressing, issue being talked about this year.” 
States, local governments and lawmakers in Washington, D.C., are grappling with data center policy. Some have initiated moratoriums on the projects, Congress has considered legislation aimed at protecting ratepayers from spillover costs associated with data centers, and policy stances around the tech-buildouts were an issue for voters in the recent midterm elections. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Rep. Hans Wilz, R-Ottumwa, said on the call there is a “punchlist” of factors a community must assess when determining whether a data center is fitting for the community: power, land, infrastructure, workforce, and state and local policy. But power, he said, is the “number one, overreaching” factor. 
Already, Iowa has seen a number of energy projects initiated to account for the energy demands created by large data centers. Google, for example, has an agreement with the Duane Arnold Energy Center in Palo to purchase more than 90% of the energy produced by the nuclear energy facility once it is restarted. 
Wilz said from a policy perspective, “you want to make sure that your state is also open and welcome to these opportunities.” He said high-energy users, be they a data center or a manufacturing facility, are beneficial — especially to rural communities.
Researchers expect ‘biggest year yet’ for energy siting bills in 2027

“We put in a hyperscaler (data center) in a rural area that makes sense with all those things we mentioned earlier, and that’s like building 1,000 homes as far as the taxation and the energy use,” Wilz said. “All those things are going to benefit the grid, the ratepayer and the community.” 
Proponents of data centers argue that increased energy demand on a system and a big user that can shoulder a larger percentage of the fixed cost of the system, can actually lower energy costs for ratepayers. 
Chaz Allen, executive director of the Iowa Utility Association, said that a number of large data centers, run by Microsoft, Google and Apple, have been operating in Iowa and the states’ major utilities have not had to shift costs to customers because of it. 
“Because of the way we’re regulated and the fact that we’ve signed large load tariffs and individual customer rates for these big load users to pay their way, we’ve not been hit as hard as other states have,” Allen said. 
A number of energy, environmental and community groups have opposed efforts from utilities to build additional natural gas plants that utilities say are not tied to data centers. One clean-energy group has raised concerns around the plants and argued the utilities should prove that the plants are in the public’s best interest before their permits are approved. 
Strategic locations to connect to the grid
Building a data center — or another high-energy user — and the power to support it, can be a long, complex process. Maison Bleam, the regional director of state regulatory affairs at the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, or MISO, said the regional grid operator is working with utilities, stakeholders and policymakers to address the energy build out, which he said doesn’t stop at state lines. 
“As data centers and AI drive unprecedented growth in electric demand, our role is to make sure, really, that the grid is prepared to support that growth, while maintaining reliability for the millions of people, that I mentioned, and businesses who depend on that delivery of energy,” Bleam said on the webinar. 
Bleam said historically, energy demand was “relatively predictable” but with data centers, reshored manufacturing and general increases in electrification, it means MISO has to “plan for both what we know today and what could happen tomorrow.”
Bleam said transmission projects, which are necessary if a site doesn’t already have a connection to the grid, can take seven to 10 years, which can create a “mismatch in timing.” Bleam said this is why the power pool is trying to send the “right signals” to utilities to “build generation that can be utilized, so that we don’t get caught in a situation where we have a mismatch.” 
DOE to loan up to $5.1 billion to Alliant Energy for Iowa and Wisconsin energy projects

Allen said big energy users, like a data center or the proposed $15 billion steel plant slated for southeast Iowa, are aware of these challenges and typically will talk to utilities early on in the process and try to pick sites that are along existing or planned transmission lines. 
Allen said much of the infrastructure in Iowa is being built out not for data centers, but for things like MISO’s Tranche 1.0 and Tranche 2.1 long-range transmission plans.
He said a lot of projects have been drawn to Iowa because it has this planned energy and transmission build out, not the other way around.
What will the legislature do?
Allen said mandates would “wrongly” impact economic development. 
“Iowa got to where it got with renewables not because it was mandated, but because it was the technology at the time that made the most sense,” Allen said, referring to Iowa’s status as a leader in wind energy adoption.
Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand has said legislation around data centers is something he hopes to see early on in the upcoming legislative session. Sand has called for an end to tax breaks for data centers, and for setback regulations, transparency in negotiations and assurances that data center operators pay for increases in utility costs. 
Environmental groups and community groups are urging local governments to initiate their own regulations on data centers, and a growing number of counties and municipalities have pass moratoriums and restrictions.
Wilz, who serves on the House Commerce Committee which typically tackles legislation related to utilities, said it will be important to have “everybody at the table” when drafting policy around the issue. He said industry, transmission, energy, the local community and water are all part of the discussion. 
“These are all things that have to be considered as we write policy, whether it be at the state level and/or working with our locals to make sure that we write something that’s not so restrictive that it doesn’t lead to a development agreement,” Wilz said. 
In a conversation with Iowa Capital Dispatch, Wilz said he has been in contact with Sand’s team about several issues already, but that he hasn’t had conversations with them yet about data center policy. 
“We need more conversation before we have legislation to ensure everybody has a seat at the table, to make sure we can create a path forward for Iowa that makes sense to keep Iowa moving forward,” Wilz said.

text:
South Dakota's Capitol in Pierre. (Makenzie Huber/South Dakota Searchlight)South Dakota’s Board of Economic Development this week approved a sales tax rebate of up to $65,804 for a Sioux Falls lab. 
The assistance for OmegaQuant comes from the state’s New Frontiers program, which supports qualifying research and clinical trials. 
The rebate will help fund additional research to develop blood fatty-acid-based algorithms to predict insulin resistance early, according to the Governor’s Office of Economic Development. The payment reimburses sales and use taxes paid on research and development costs associated with the project, including qualifying research equipment and supplies. 
Up to $6 million in tax rebates approved for South Dakota’s largest wind project

“The research has the potential to lead to new commercially viable testing tools developed and offered from South Dakota,” according to the office’s press release. 
The office said the project is also supported by a $1 million grant from the National Institute of Diabetes and Digestive and Kidney Diseases, which is part of the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services.
OmegaQuant employs 12 people in South Dakota. The company anticipates adding 14 new full-time positions over the next five years through this project, according to the release.
“Research and development projects like this demonstrate the potential of South Dakota companies to compete in specialized, high-growth industries,” said Commissioner of Economic Development Bill Even in the press release. “Supporting this work helps create opportunities to bring new technologies to market while growing skilled employment and strengthening South Dakota’s biotechnology sector.”
The board awarded OmegaQuant another rebate of up to $8,845.87 from the New Frontiers program in October. The Governor’s Office of Economic Development said OmegaQuant had been awarded a $320,864 National Eye Institute grant through the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services for that project to “develop blood fatty-acid-based algorithms for the early prediction of macular degeneration and glaucoma, with the potential to create new commercially viable testing tools developed and offered from South Dakota.”
OmegaQuant estimated adding eight jobs over the next five years through that project.

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Global Microsoft outage disrupts locally
description: The Narragansett Police Department could not access Outlook Thursday, but it could access Facebook. “Well, our work here is done. Outlook is down,” the department’s Facebook post read, punctuated at the end with a crying-laughing emoji. The department was but one entity with a frozen inbox Thursday due to a global outage of Microsoft 365, […]
text:
A Microsoft Outlook inbox without any new mail. (Photo by Alexander Castro/Rhode Island Current)The Narragansett Police Department could not access Outlook Thursday, but it could access Facebook.
“Well, our work here is done. Outlook is down,” the department’s Facebook post read, punctuated at the end with a crying-laughing emoji.
The department was but one entity with a frozen inbox Thursday due to a global outage of Microsoft 365, the cloud-based software suite with millions of enterprise users worldwide across businesses, governments and colleges and universities. The outage affected a still-to-be-determined number of users worldwide, although the number of people affected reliably appears to be in the millions. 
Grabbing many of the headlines was the inability for many users to access Outlook, 365’s email client and a longstanding flagship product for the Redmond, Washington-based Microsoft.
Lack of access to Outlook was one of the major headaches caused by the 365 outage for numerous Rhode Island state and municipal agencies Thursday, although most officials said they had recovered operations and it was business as usual Friday morning — including the Narragansett Police Department.
“Our department’s email service has been fully restored as of around 6 a.m. this morning,” Capt. Ryan Prest said over email Friday, noting that no other operations or communications beyond Outlook were affected Thursday.
At the state level, the Department of Labor and Training initially told Rhode Island Current Friday morning that the outage affected not only Outlook and 365 products but also phone queues for unemployment insurance and temporary disability insurance. 
The department’s employees had “continued processing claims behind the scenes to prevent any delays in service,” spokesperson Edwine Paul said.
Paul revised the claim about phone difficulties, however, in a follow-up email Friday afternoon, saying the claimant hotline had operated normally throughout the outage.
At Rhode Island College, the outage stretched from Thursday afternoon and into the evening, according to spokesperson John Taraborelli. He noted that while the overall impact was minimal, the college did make one concrete change, and gave students an extra day to withdraw from courses, since the deadline had been Thursday.
The command center of Rhode Island state government’s IT infrastructure — the Department of Administration’s Enterprise Technology Strategy and Services division — acknowledged statewide disruptions had occurred Thursday.
“Despite the inconvenience, State operations continued, and services were restored by Microsoft before the start of business this morning,” DOA spokesperson Karen Greco said Friday via email.
Contemplating the cloud
IT workers at state and municipal agencies weren’t the only ones with Microsoft-related migraines Thursday. The phones at the Roger Williams University help desk began buzzing promptly at 1 p.m. yesterday with complaints about email not going through.
RWU’s Chief Information Officer Daryl Ford said in a phone interview Friday that university IT staff quickly realized the problem was on Microsoft’s end, and not the school’s. 
“We’re basically completely dependent upon them for faculty and staff email,” Ford said. “So we couldn’t do much at all in terms of restoring Office 365 services.”
At RWU, Outlook was the only service down throughout the outage, Ford said, while other apps — like Teams, SharePoint and Copilot — were “radically up and down” over the course of the outage. 
Ford noted that while students primarily use Google’s Gmail instead, they still receive university-wide messages via the Microsoft 365 architecture. So the university pivoted and used its emergency notification system to inform students about the situation via text message.
“It’s basically supposed to be for emergencies — active shooters and weather alerts and so forth — but we consider this an emergency as well whenever communications are down,” Ford said.
The school uses Brightspace for its learning platform, and Ford said he was not aware of any significant academic disruptions or extensions to student deadlines because of the outage.
Ford also saw a lesson in the whole ordeal. He said some pressure has been applied for him to “consolidate on one platform, either Google or Microsoft.” 
“I’ve been reluctant,” Ford said, citing the Microsoft outage as one example that a “bifurcated” solution may be superior to putting all one’s eggs in a single basket. 
“If one’s down, we still have access to another, we still have some semblance of an operation going on,” Ford said.
The University of Rhode Island experienced a similar situation Thursday, according to spokesperson Dawn Bergantino. She noted that the school uses Google Workspace for email, thereby insulating university email from the Microsoft havoc, although other apps like Teams and SharePoint were intermittently slow, she said.
The decision to invest in multiple cloud services runs parallel to another trend in enterprise-scale IT which involves businesses moving certain services and data back to infrastructure they control, also known as “on prem,” instead of relying exclusively on a public cloud housed in a far-off data center.
A 2026 survey by S&P Global’s 451 Research found that 47% of respondents had moved data from public cloud providers back to their own data centers or privately owned ones in the previous year, up from 40% in 2024. The trend is driven partially by concerns about cost, data privacy and dependence on outside providers.
But for large, complex institutions like a school, Ford suggested there are limits, especially when it comes to email, on what can be brought in-house.
“We’re not trying to reinvent the wheel,” he said.
Still, the incident underscored for him how invisible the reliance on these platforms has become.
“The world revolves around electronic communication,” Ford said. “It’s kind of like electricity. We don’t miss it until it goes out.”
Microsoft works to restore service
An incident feed from Microsoft updated Friday traced the outage to an issue introduced during an earlier network capacity upgrade.
The update log on Friday afternoon noted that the underlying problem had been resolved but that the company was still working to restore service, an effort which included clearing backlogged emails.
“We’re seeing encouraging recovery progress, with service availability and email delivery performance improving across a growing portion of affected infrastructure,” Charles Lamanna, a Microsoft executive vice president, said in a statement provided to Rhode Island Current Friday morning. “We know our customers rely on our services to get important work done every day, and regret the impact these outages had on those who depend on us.” 
Microsoft plans to publish a full post-incident report. The current incident log is also available on Microsoft’s website. The University of Pennsylvania has a mirrored copy of the log across the incident’s duration. 
 



 What agencies reported disruptions? 

The following state offices reported varying degrees of disruption:

The Department of Children, Youth and Families was without email access Thursday afternoon and evening. The department posted a notice to its website advising providers to call instead and the agency’s hotline operated normally during the outage.
Email was disrupted Thursday afternoon for the Department of Transportation but the agency said operations continued as usual, and that the public could always reach the department directly via phone to report issues like potholes or roadway hazards.
The Executive Office of Health and Human Services had issues Thursday accessing its suite of Microsoft 365 applications, which are used by employees, but public-facing services like RIBridges were unaffected.
The Department of Health was swept up in the national outages as well, with access to Microsoft products interrupted. But the department uses redundancies — or identical systems which allow one copy to function and maintain operations should a primary copy fail — and was able to “maintain our critical lines of coordination with our hospital and healthcare partners,” spokesperson Joseph Wendelken said.
The Rhode Island Judiciary posted online Thursday that its email was down, and spokesperson Alexandra Kriss confirmed Friday that the courts had issues with Microsoft Office applications before functionality was restored on Friday.

title: Ten Iowa care facilities cited for abuse have federal ‘gold trophy’ status
description: Ten Iowa nursing homes eligible for abbreviated state inspections were cited for resident-abuse violations in 2025-2026, a new study has found. According to the nonprofit organization The National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care, a new analysis of federal data indicates that between April 2025 and July 2026, 173 of the 1,699 nursing homes currently[...]
text:
The Prairie Vista Village care facility in Altoona, Iowa. (Photo via Google Earth)Ten Iowa nursing homes eligible for abbreviated state inspections were cited for resident-abuse violations in 2025-2026, a new study has found.
According to the nonprofit organization The National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care, a new analysis of federal data indicates that between April 2025 and July 2026, 173 of the 1,699 nursing homes currently ranked as “high performing” by federal regulators were cited at least once for failing to protect residents from abuse and neglect.
The analysis was prompted by the federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ new initiative that calls for an abbreviated inspection process for facilities that CMS has designated as high performers.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
All 173 of the homes cited for failing to protect residents from abuse currently qualify for the abbreviated inspection process and have been awarded gold-trophy icons that are displayed on CMS’ Care Compare website — a search tool the public is encouraged to use to locate nursing homes and assess the quality of their care.
Beginning on Sept. 8, 2026, the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services began using a new risk-based inspection process for selected nursing homes across the country, replacing the traditional, more thorough process at those facilities that CMS considers higher performing, lower risk homes.
According to Consumer Voice, most of the relevant abuse-related citations, in Iowa and nationally, have involved allegations the homes failed to report to state inspectors incidents of resident abuse and neglect.
That specific violation was cited at 100 of the 173 care facilities, while failing to properly investigate abuse was cited at 53 facilities, and the underlying abuse and neglect was cited at 42 facilities. (Some homes were cited for more than one violation, with a total of 235 abuse-related citations being issued at the 173 nursing homes.)
Consumer Voice has opposed CMS’ new risk-based inspection system of performing less comprehensive inspections at homes considered to be high performers, arguing that the high-performing designation isn’t reflective of the quality of care provided in the past, present or future.
Last month, the Iowa Capital Dispatch reported that 75 of Iowa’s 393 nursing facilities were subject to the abbreviated form of government inspections under the new risk-based system. And while CMS’ criteria for selecting those facilities emphasizes favorable outcomes for infection control and staffing levels, a Capital Dispatch review of the 75 Iowa homes showed some of those facilities had been cited for violating both standards.
In June 2026, for example, inspectors visited the Good Samaritan Home in St. Ansgar, and cited the facility for insufficient staffing and for infection-control issues. The home, inspectors found, had failed on four separate days in one two-week period to meet the federal mandate of having at least one registered nurse on duty for eight consecutive hours each day.
In November 2025, inspectors conducted an annual inspection at Wapello Specialty Care and cited the home for infection control issues.



Iowa’s gold-trophy homes cited for abuse
The National Consumer Voice for Quality Long-Term Care’s analysis of federal data shows that these 10 Iowa nursing homes are designated high performers despite abuse-related violations being cited between April 2025 and July 2026:
Algona Manor Care Center, Algona: Cited for failure to develop or follow a policy on abuse.
Concord Care Center, Garner: Cited for failure to report alleged abuse.
Franklin General Hospital, Hampton: Cited for failure to develop or follow a policy on abuse.
Lamoni Specialty Care, Lamoni: Cited for failure to report alleged abuse.
Lone Tree Health Care Center, Lone Tree: Cited for failure to report alleged abuse.
Prairie Vista Village, Altoona: Cited for abuse through the misappropriation of resident property.
Sibley Specialty Care, Sibley: Cited for failure to report alleged abuse.
St. Francis Manor, Grinnell: Cited for a failure to develop or follow a policy on abuse.
Story Medical Senior Care, Nevada: Cited for failing to investigate allegations of abuse, and for failing to report alleged abuse.
Woodland Terrace, Waverly: Cited for resident abuse and neglect, and for failing to investigate alleged abuse and neglect.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: W. Hartford Mayor Shari Cantor to chair UConn Board of Trustees
description: UConn Board of Trustees Chair Dan Toscano has resigned, and Gov. Ned Lamont has appointed West Hartford Mayor Shari Cantor to take his place.
text:
University of Connecticut Board of Trustees Chair Dan Toscano has resigned, and Gov. Ned Lamont has appointed West Hartford Mayor Shari Cantor to take his place, the governor’s office announced in a press release Friday.
Toscano has served as chair since 2019. In a statement, Lamont said he picked Cantor to fill the role for her keen understanding of UConn’s needs and strong connections with Connecticut businesses, which he hopes to see translate into stronger ties between the university and state employers.
“[Shari Cantor’s] input is going to significantly benefit the university and its mission to develop the graduates who will flourish in today’s rapidly evolving, modern economy,” Lamont said.
The governor’s press release did not say why Toscano resigned from the board. Cantor and Toscano did not return requests for comment.

Chair of the UConn Board of Trustees Dan Toscano speaks during a news conference celebrating NSF Quantum Technologies Engine being awarded a National Science Foundation federal award at UConn Hartford’s campus on Wednesday, July 15, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Cantor was already a member of the board prior to her appointment as chair. She takes the leadership role following some uncertainty about the future of UConn’s President Radenka Maric. Speculation flared when news broke in October that House Speaker Matt Ritter was being considered as a possible interim UConn president; Ritter has since announced he will remain in his role as Speaker. 
“My understanding is there won’t be a vacancy, so there’s nothing to consider,” Ritter told The Connecticut Mirror on Wednesday.
The Hartford Courant reported on Nov. 6 that Maric was in the running for chancellor at the University of Wisconsin; a University of Wisconsin spokesperson told the Courant Thursday she was still a finalist there. Her contract with UConn is set to last until June 2027.
In a written statement, Cantor said she looks forward “to working collaboratively with President Radenka Maric, my fellow trustees, faculty, staff, students, and alumni to build on UConn’s remarkable momentum.”
Higher Education and Employment Committee co-Chair Sen. Derek Slap, D-West Hartford, said he’s “delighted” that Lamont has appointed Cantor — his mayor — as the new chair.
“I think her devotion to UConn is really unmatched,” Slap told The Connecticut Mirror. “I’ve seen how she leads. She does it by bringing people together. She’s just innately a consensus builder, so I think she’s going to be terrific.”
Slap also praised Maric for the work she’s done leading UConn through the turbulence of the second Trump administration. UConn is one of a host of universities around the country that have abruptly lost millions of dollars in research grants through sudden federal cuts. The questions about her future, he said, are “just kind of natural, especially because of the public nature of it.”
“So we see, OK, she’s interviewing at Wisconsin … That stuff is, I think, kind of unavoidable,” Slap said.
He did note that UConn has gone through several presidents in recent years.
“Ideally, whether it’s President Maric — and again, that’s the board’s decision — I think there is something important about having some stability at the top,” Slapp said.
Lamont’s director of communications, Cathryn Vaulman, said the governor remains confident in the university.
“UConn is headed in the right direction in terms of enrollment, fundraising, and its standing as a leading research institution,” Vaulman said.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ distributes $20M for legal aid for immigrants facing deportation, detention
description: State officials distributed more than $20 million to support legal help for immigrants facing deportation, money they said is needed as Trump's push increases.
text:
ICE agents by the Delaney Hall detention center in Newark on May 28, 2026. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)

New Jersey officials announced on Friday the allocation of more than $20 million to support legal services to help immigrants facing detention or deportation.
Gov. Mikie Sherrill, a Democrat, included $20.2 million for the so-called deportation defense initiative in the current state budget, more than double the amount provided last year. The money will now go to law schools, the state’s public defender office, and various immigrant advocates and support organizations, according to state officials.
Sherrill said that with the Trump administration’s push to detain and deport millions here illegally, New Jersey had to take action to protect people’s rights to a fair hearing. This includes representing low-income people held at Delany Hall, the 1,000-bed migrant jail in Newark that has faced growing scrutiny after three people died while being held or processed there.
“Our immigrant community should not have to face a complex and daunting legal system without anyone in their corner. I am proud that my Administration has quickly mobilized State resources and partnerships to help put legal counsel in reach for those who have been impacted by the federal government’s detrimental immigration policies,” Sherrill said in a statement.
Sherrill said the number of immigrants facing prolonged detention without a hearing or other protections is growing as ICE actions ramp up and more people are being held. The Trump administration is also pushing to convert a massive warehouse in Morris County into a migrant jail, a project opposed by residents, GOP local officials, and Democrats like Rebecca Bennett, who defeated GOP Rep. Tom Kean Jr. earlier this month and will represent the area in Congress come January.
“As ICE activity continues to impact immigrant communities, we remain committed to ensuring that those facing detention or deportation have meaningful access to counsel and the opportunity to be heard,” said Human Services Commissioner Stephen Cha, whose office oversees the program.
The state-funded deportation defense initiative provides free legal advice to low-income immigrants through a partnership with Legal Services of New Jersey, which provides pro bono legal aid; the social justice group American Friends Service Committee; and the law schools at Rutgers and Seton Hall. These groups will receive $13 million, state officials said.
The remaining funds will be distributed to the Office of the Public Defender and a handful of other advocacy or legal groups: Church World Service, NJ Consortium for Immigrant Children, Immigration and American Citizenship Organization, Catholic Charities Archdiocese of Newark, and the International Rescue Committee, according to the state.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Virginia runs $394 million ahead of revenue forecast through October
description: Virginia collected $141 million more in general fund revenue than expected in October, putting the state $394 million ahead of its revenue forecast just four months into the fiscal year. A new tax on data centers’ energy use brought in $66.5 million, accounting for about half of the month’s revenue growth from a year earlier.  […]
text:
Virginia’s general fund revenue was $394 million ahead of forecast through October. The state’s tax on data centers’ energy use brought in $66.5 million in October alone. (Photo by Getty Images)Virginia collected $141 million more in general fund revenue than expected in October, putting the state $394 million ahead of its revenue forecast just four months into the fiscal year. A new tax on data centers’ energy use brought in $66.5 million, accounting for about half of the month’s revenue growth from a year earlier. 
General fund revenue rose 6.3% from October 2025 to $2.19 billion, Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s office announced Friday. Collections through October totaled $10.47 billion, up 7.7% from the same period last year and 3.9% above projections in the current budget, according to the state’s October revenue report.
Corporate income taxes and individual income taxes paid outside payroll withholding accounted for most of the surplus. Together, the two sources generated $328 million more than expected, roughly 83% of the amount collected above forecast.
“October revenues came in $141 million above forecast, and every major tax source except recordation is running ahead of expectations for the year. That’s a great place to be heading into the budget cycle,” Finance Secretary Mark Sickles said in a statement. 
Sickles cautioned that corporate income taxes and nonwitholding payments, which include estimated income tax payments, are among Virginia’s most unpredictable revenue sources. 
He said the stronger collections could justify raising revenue projections, but the administration would remain cautious as it prepares the next biennial budget, citing persistent inflation and the possibility of another Federal Reserve interest rate hike in December. 
Virginia collected $91.4 million from the data center consumption tax in the first four months of the fiscal year. The state projects the tax will bring in $600 million by June 30.
Corporate income taxes also rose sharply, reaching $90 million in October compared with $8.3 million a year earlier. Through October, corporate receipts totaled $666.4 million, a 77.8% increase from the same period last year. 
Sales and use tax collections rose 3.9% for the month and were up 7.4% for the fiscal year to date.
But not every revenue source grew in October.
Payroll withholding, Virginia’s largest source of general fund revenue, fell 4.6% from a year earlier, a decline of about $72.8 million. Despite the monthly drop, withholding collections remained 3.6% higher through the first four months of the fiscal year.
Net individual income tax revenue, which includes withholding and other payments after refunds, declined 3% in October but was up 4.4% for the year to date.
The state entered October $253.7 million ahead of forecast, with September collections up 8% from the same period a year earlier. 
September included quarterly payment deadlines for corporate income and nonwithholding taxes, both of which exceeded expectations. Sales and use tax revenue had grown to 8.5% through September before easing to 7.4% through October. 
Despite this year’s strong start, Virginia was further ahead of its forecast at the same point in each of the two previous fiscal years. 
Through October 2025, general fund collections were up 5.5% from a year earlier and $497 million above forecast. 
A year before that, October 2024 figures showed collections running 8.6% above the previous year and $403.3 million ahead of forecast, even though corporate income taxes were $56.8 million below expectations. 
Virginia also finished the last fiscal year, which ended June 30, with a sizable surplus. 
According to preliminary figures released in July, general fund collections exceeded projections by $936.3 million after growing 6.7%, largely because of individual incomes and sales taxes. 
The two-year state budget incorporated $585.5 million of that surplus into the starting balance for the current fiscal year. 
Spanberger pointed to the latest revenue figures while renewing her criticism of federal economic policies. 
“With the war in Iran and reckless policies out of Washington burdening Virginians, my focus continues to be on saving money for families and protecting the long-term strength of our economy,” she said in a statement. 
Earlier this week, Spanberger and Democratic General Assembly leaders unveiled their Moving Virginia Forward agenda for the 2027 legislative session, including proposals to forgive medical debt and address housing costs.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Florence Griswold Museum kicks off $6.1 million renovation
description: The Florence Griswold Museum in Old Lyme has launched a  $6.1 million renovation of the Robert and Nancy Krieble Gallery.
text:
Expanded gallery and exhibition spaces meant to bring in new audiences. A collections study and research center for visiting scholars, museum curators, and students dipping into the archives. “Pocket galleries” for displaying additional artwork, and a 125-person space for lectures, gatherings and classes. Windows that overlook the Lieutenant River, and connect visitors to the surrounding environment. 
That vision is part of a $6.1 million renovation to the Robert and Nancy Krieble Gallery at the Florence Griswold or “FloGris” Museum, a former home of the Lyme Art Colony that first became a museum in 1947. Nestled on a 12-acre campus in Old Lyme, the museum features and teaches the history of American Impressionism in Connecticut, while also collecting work from modern and contemporary American artists. 
“What we’re adding to the museum is really important: new ways to find and experience art in our wonderful exhibitions,” Executive Director Peter Steere said at a groundbreaking ceremony at the museum Thursday afternoon. “This expansion brings new ways to inspire. Inspire us, inspire our guests, inspire you today.”
From now through the fall of 2027, the museum will work with Petra Construction Corporation and Oudens Ello Architecture, based in North Haven and Boston respectively, to transform the 10,000 square foot Krieble Gallery into a new home for visitors. The project will also add two accessible bathrooms and improved navigation to the museum’s eatery, Café Flo. 
It marks the first stage of a larger renovation project for which the museum is still fundraising, Steere confirmed in a phone call Friday.
In the initial phase, which received zoning approval from the town last December, the renovation includes a 2,740-square-foot expansion to the Krieble Gallery, a shed-and-gable structure from Centerbrook Architects that hasn’t been updated since it first opened in 2002. In addition, it will feature a long-awaited update to an existing 6,210 square feet of gallery space that has become too small for the organization’s growing collections and volume of visitors. 
Currently, the Krieble Gallery has a veranda that will become three midsize “pocket” galleries and one larger gallery that can accommodate groups of up to 125 people. In the larger gallery, Steere said he is especially excited about etched glass windows from the Easton-based artist James Prosek that double as code-compliant bird fritting, to reduce the risk of birds flying into the glass. 
In addition, Oudens Ello will build a collections study and research center and update lighting systems installed in 2002. That addition will create a dedicated space for archives, some dating back to the turn of the twentieth century, that have lived in the museum’s collection for eight decades. In addition, the study and research center brings the museum up to speed with many of its regional and national peers. 

Peter Steere, executive director of the Florence Griswold Museum, announces the first phase in a groundbreaking on Nov. 12, 2026.   Credit: Harold Shapiro / Florence Griswold Museum

That funding comes from donations to the museum’s $24.2 million “Inspiration Lives Here” capital campaign, which the board launched in spring 2022 and has steered through three leadership transitions since. Over the past four years, the museum said farewell to former Executive Director Rebekah Beaulieu, who led the museum from 2018 to 2022, and Joshua Campbell Torrance, who served as executive director from 2023 to 2025. 
Steere, who was named interim director last fall and has officially held the role since February of this year, said the campaign has brought in close to $12 million to date. “I’m over the moon” to finally see it through, he said in a phone call Friday morning. 
While the Krieble Gallery is temporarily closed, the museum’s multi-building campus will remain largely open, with exhibition space on the second floor of the eponymous Florence Griswold House. Those sites include the John and Dyanne Rafal Landscape Center, Kelly Bill and John W. Hartman Education Center, and William Chadwick Studio, as well as the museum’s grounds and gardens. 
The Robert F. Schumann Artists’ Trail, a half-mile loop that gives visitors the chance to experience the landscape as artists like Henry Ward Ranger and Childe Hassam once did, will also remain open. In that same spirit, the museum will open its annual “Holiday Magic” exhibition later this month. 
Conrad Ello, a founding principal of Oudens Ello, called the renovation part of “a more immersive museum experience,” where visitors can move more easily from one part of the campus to another and connect with the natural landscape. In that sense, he said, the Krieble Gallery is just a beginning: since 2024, Oudens Ello has worked with the museum to map out a multi-phase site plan for the campus. This moment marks the start of that work.
“This relationship between art and landscape has really always been here. It’s beautifully expressed in Ms. Griswold’s house and gardens, and our challenge was to extend that experience through the campus, including Krieble Gallery,” he said. “We’re truly thrilled to be part of this transformation and we look forward to the year ahead.” 
For many longtime fans of the museum, as well as board members, staff, and town officials, the renovation marks a continued commitment to teaching a history that is specific to Old Lyme, and national and international in significance and scope. 

The back of the Robert and Nancy Krieble Gallery, as i’s expected to look a year from now in the fall of 2027.  Credit: Courtesy of Oudens Ello Architecture

When New York artist Henry Ward Ranger founded the Old Lyme Art Colony at the turn of the twentieth century, he sought to create an American equivalent of the French Barbizon School, which preceded the artists of the Belle Époque. With colleagues who included Roger Wilson Dennis, Guy Wiggins, Bruce Crane, Hassam (perhaps the most famous among them), and hundreds of others, they built an enduring movement that connected Connecticut’s natural landscape with a new way of thinking about how painters document the world around them. 
Now, the museum’s expansion and renovation will carry on that legacy, several speakers said Thursday. Old Lyme First Selectwoman Martha Shoemaker noted the importance of Old Lyme’s history as a vibrant touchpoint for American Impressionism. 
“When Miss Florence opened the doors to the Lyme Art Colony over a century ago, she created a space where the unique light, the verdant landscape, and the bend of the Lieutenant River ignited a legendary creative energy,”  Shoemaker said. “Today, we’re keeping the fire burning bright. The expansion and renovation of the Krieble Gallery isn’t just about brick and mortar and new skylights. It’s about keeping our town’s cultural crown jewel forward-looking, open, and accessible to all.”
Steere said he hopes the museum can proceed with a second phase in the coming years, but it will require more fundraising.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Jackson City Council could censure Stokes for his incendiary remarks
description: Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes speaks during a council meeting at City Hall in Jackson on Tuesday, April 21, 2026.
text:
The Jackson City Council could consider whether to censure Councilman Kenneth Stokes for remarks he made to two women during a heated debate over a moratorium on data centers.
A resolution censuring Stokes for his conduct at council meetings was listed Friday on the planned agenda for next Tuesday’s meeting. 
If adopted by the council, the censure would be a rare rebuke of Stokes, the longest-serving member in Jackson who has a history of making chaotic statements and insulting people who question him. 
City Council President Vernon Hartley did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Hartley had shared the proposed resolution with Stokes in a letter earlier this week, asking Stokes to apologize for his recent remarks. 
Stokes responded at a press conference Thursday in which his attorney, Dennis Sweet III, said the proposed resolution infringes on the councilman’s right to free speech and that Stokes will sue his colleagues if they censure him.
Attorney Dennis Sweet III, left, sits next to his client, Jackson Ward 3 City Councilman Kenneth Stokes, as they prepare for a press conference on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026.  Credit: Aaron Lampley/Mississippi Today
The potential reprimand comes after some residents pushed for the council to condemn comments from Stokes, the longest-serving member who represents Ward 3 in west-central Jackson. 
Jacksonians have voiced opposition during public comment periods to Stokes’ behavior. One woman who lives in Stokes’ neighborhood gathered nearly 100 signatures on a petition calling on the council to censure him.
On Nov. 3, the council recessed a meeting after Stokes said he would “cuss that bitch out” in response to an indirect comment a woman in the audience made about his mother. He then told another woman, Candace Abdul-Tawwab, who was wearing a hijab, to “take the rags out y’all hair, y’all not Muslim.”
Abdul-Tawwab, executive director of an organization called Mississippi For a Just World, attended the meeting to oppose Stokes’ effort to repeal the city’s moratorium on data centers. 
Stokes’ remarks drew swift condemnation from some in the audience, who chanted “kick him out,” and from some of Stokes’ fellow council members. Kevin Parkinson, who represents Ward 7 near downtown, immediately exited the chambers. 
“Quite frankly, this was not the first time,” Parkinson wrote in a statement he issued later that night. “I felt I couldn’t, in good conscience, sit through such behavior as though it were acceptable.”
This would not be the first time the council reprimanded Stokes.
In 2003, Stokes’ colleagues censured him after he claimed during a council meeting that an unnamed member had requested a bribe from a permit applicant, according to archival news reports. 
Stokes, known for wearing oversized suits and a hat emblazoned with his last name, was first elected to the city council in 1989. Throughout his nearly four decades on the city council, his comments have repeatedly made national news. His behavior has often drawn comparisons to President Donald Trump.
In 2004, Stokes threatened to slap then-Councilman Ben Allen during a heated argument at a council meeting.
In 2010, Stokes staged a protest outside The Clarion-Ledger building near City Hall after the newspaper questioned his use of taxpayer funds for trips to Chicago, New York and Washington. 
In a 2015 interview with WLBT, Stokes told viewers to throw “rocks and bricks and bottles” at police officers who chase suspects from neighboring jurisdictions into Jackson. The following year, he called previous Rankin County Undersheriff Raymond Duke a “hog headed lying bastard” when Duke referenced the comment in a Facebook post.
Last year, Stokes repeatedly accused his nephew, Daniel Cooper, of being a “dope dealer” after Cooper opened a food truck in the Georgetown neighborhood, on a plot of land to which Stokes  has a potential claim through heir property law.
Cooper denied the allegation, and Mississippi Today found no Jackson drug sale charges in Cooper’s history.
Jackson City Councilman Kenneth Stokes, left, listens as City Council President Brian Grizzell speaks during a council meeting at City Hall in Jackson on Tuesday, April 21, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
In September, Stokes called another councilman, Brian Grizzell, a “sissy” after Grizzell opposed an effort from Stokes to rename a street. 
“If you see one, hit one,” Grizzell responded to Stokes. Grizzell, who represents Ward 4 in western Jackson, later apologized for the remark. Stokes has not apologized to Grizzell. 
This incident is why Norma Michael, who lives a few blocks from Stokes in Georgetown, organized the petition calling on the council to censure Stokes and fine him $500.
“He thinks he can do what he wants,” she said.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: State judge temporarily blocks prediction markets in Louisiana
description: A temporary injunction blocks companies such as Kalshi, Polymarket and Robinhood from doing business in the state.
text:
A Tangipahoa Parish court has issued an order that blocks prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket from accepting bets in Louisiana. Attorney General Liz Murrill argues that they aren't licensed to conduct gambling in the state. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Louisiana bettors with a varied taste for risk are out of luck for the time being after a Tangipahoa Parish judge issued a temporary injunction Thursday that blocks companies such as Kalshi, Polymarket and Robinhood from doing business in the state.
Attorney General Liz Murrill filed a complaint Thursday morning in Tangipahoa Parish against several prediction market companies, arguing they are not licensed to offer gambling in Louisiana.    
“It’s not complicated: If you aren’t a licensed gaming operator, you aren’t legal,” Murrill said in a statement Friday. “… Kalshi’s and the other operators’ attempts to make up new words to evade state gambling laws, regulators and taxes are not fooling anyone.”
Murrill added that illegal gambling is a crime in Louisiana, punishable by “jail time and significant penalties.” 
The state court order pauses what are known as event contracts, which allow bets on a variety of everyday occurrences, such as which actor will star in the next James Bond movie, future gas prices or whether the federal government will shut down next month. The platforms also accept sports bets, ranging from game outcomes to minutiae such as how many times Taylor Swift will appear on camera during a Kansas City Chiefs game.
Several states have pursued legal action to restrict or ban prediction markets within their respective boundaries. Some state courts, most notably in the gambling industry hub of Nevada, have ruled against the platforms, preventing them from taking event contract bets. 
Minnesota passed the nation’s first law in May to prohibit prediction markets, though a federal court has temporarily halted enforcement while the state appeals.
Polymarket sought relief from the U.S. District Court in New Orleans on Oct. 27 to prevent Louisiana from forcing it to shut down in the state. It maintains in its court complaint that its business is not subject to individual state laws.
“Prediction markets are regulated by the Commodity Futures Trading Commission under a federal framework, not a patchwork of state rules,” a Polymarket spokesperson said in an email Friday.
A spokesperson for Robinhood noted that the company is registered with the federal agency to allow “customers to access prediction markets in a safe, compliant, and regulated manner.”
Before Thursday’s ruling in Tangipahoa Parish, Jovy Dedaj, Kalshi’s head of litigation, posted on X that Louisiana was making an “unlawful attempt to stop Kalshi from operating in the state.”
“The operation of federally regulated exchanges is the exclusive province of the federal government. Full stop,” Dedaj wrote.
The next hearing in state court over the injunction Murrill obtained is scheduled for Nov. 30. 
U.S. District Judge Lance Africk, a federal court appointee of President George W. Bush, was assigned Polymarket’s preemptive action against the state. He has not yet set a date for what’s next in that matter.
