name: Rhode Island Current
title: FM to send workers to Massachusetts as part of HQ relocation
description: Downtown Providence isn’t the only target destination for FM’s planned departure from Johnston. The global insurance company, formerly known as FM Global, is also sending an unspecified number of local workers to Massachusetts as part of a regional approach that includes facilities in Norwood and Boston, the company confirmed in a statement to Rhode Island [[...]
text:
As part of FM's plans to relocate its headquarters to downtown Providence, some of its local workforce will also be sent to Massachusetts, with a small number of layoffs, the company confirmed Friday. (Photo by Christopher Shea/Rhode Island Current)Downtown Providence isn’t the only target destination for FM’s planned departure from Johnston.
The global insurance company, formerly known as FM Global, is also sending an unspecified number of local workers to Massachusetts as part of a regional approach that includes facilities in Norwood and Boston, the company confirmed in a statement to Rhode Island Current Friday afternoon.
“The specific timing of individual employee moves is still being determined, and we will continue to communicate directly with employees as those plans progress,” the company stated. 
There will also be a “limited number” of workers laid off in conjunction with the move, the company said.
Ahead of Johnston exodus, Polisena says FM to lay off local workers

The confirmation comes four days after the commercial property insurer revealed that it plans to move out of its wooded campus off Central Avenue in Johnston by the end of 2027, relocating its global headquarters to downtown Providence. In February, FM bought the 10-story office tower in Providence, colloquially referred to as the IGT building, for $69 million. 
The glass-and-metal building in downtown Providence will still house its global headquarters, serving as the primary location for corporate functions including finance, legal and human resources, FM confirmed. 
However, an unnamed number of other workers based in Johnston will move to other FM locations, including the recently redeveloped global training center, in Norwood, FM confirmed.
Hours before the company confirmation, Rhode Island Current spoke to two current and one former FM employee, who provided additional details and documents detailing the cross-state relocation and layoff plans. The workers spoke to Rhode Island Current under the condition of anonymity, fearing repercussions for their jobs and pension benefits. The information was confirmed through internal company portal updates shared with Rhode Island Current.
According to one administrative worker, roughly 100 people who previously worked in Johnston have already relocated to Norwood over the last year. Another 150 employees across multiple departments were given notice this week that they, too, will have to relocate to Norwood by the end of next year, or else lose their jobs, a separate, senior employee said. Severance packages and relocation benefits have not been offered.
The $593 million project to redevelop its Norwood campus, including a 320,000-square-foot building designated as the company’s global training center, has been years in the making. First solidified under a tax-financing agreement with the Massachusetts Economic Assistance Coordinating Council in 2023, the redeveloped 17-acre campus off Route 1 was completed earlier this year.
FM also leased office space in Boston’s South Station Tower last year.
A new, 40,000-square-foot science and technology center at FM’s Norwood, Massachusetts campus opened earlier this year. (Courtesy of FM)
But until this week, the Fortune 500 company never publicly indicated or told employees that it planned to abandon its Johnston headquarters or reduce its local workforce. Workers were informed at a global town hall held Wednesday, employees said.
Roughly three dozen corporate workers were laid off in October, unrelated to the relocation plans, FM said Friday. Employees who work in facilities services and the cafeteria within the 93-acre Johnston campus were also given notice this week that they would be out of work when the move is completed, expected by the end of 2027.
FM’s influence over the state as one of its largest employers, with a 1,500-person workforce in Johnston and its Glocester research campus, prompted lawmakers to rewrite a longstanding state law that capped investments by insurance companies in non-traditional assets. The 2025 law change benefits multiple local insurance companies, but was born out of a request by FM executives.
Senate President Valarie Lawson and House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Gov. Dan McKee’s office did not respond to requests for comment either. 
“Rhode Island has always been our home, and establishing our global headquarters in downtown Providence ensures the state remains central to FM’s future,” the company said Friday.
The cross-state move comes as Hasbro Inc. plans to abandon its Pawtucket headquarters in favor of the Boston Seaport by the end of the year. 
While FM is still maintaining a presence in Rhode Island, the unexpected loss of a local workforce stung Johnston Mayor Joseph Polisena Jr.
“It represents a very troublesome trend we’re seeing with Rhode Island companies that are leaving,” Polisena said in an interview Friday. “It seems like they tried to cover it up.”
Federal law requires employers with more than 100 full-time employees to give state and local officials at least 60 days notice before mass layoffs or facility closings. FM has not submitted any notices to the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training regarding layoffs or closings as of Friday morning, Edwine Paul, an agency spokesperson, said.
However, notice wouldn’t be required if fewer than 50 people were laid off under federal guidelines.
Polisena said he believes the workforce reductions were intentionally kept just below the minimum requiring state notice. 
“I will let the people who are reading this come to their own conclusion about that,” he said.
In addition to job losses for those who were laid off or who choose not to make the 40-mile drive to Norwood, Polisena is worried about the tax losses for Johnston. FM contributes around $3 million in property and tangible taxes to the town, equal to 2% of its $144 million annual budget. 
This story will be updated.

title: Kali Watson Is Stepping Down As Hawaiian Home Lands Director
description:
Kali Watson will not seek reappointment at the end of this year as director of the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands and chair of the Hawaiian Homes Commission, state officials announced Friday.  Appointed by Gov. Josh Green in 2023, Watson was responsible for overseeing the development of thousands of homes and the implementation of a […]
The post Kali Wats[...]
text:
Kali Watson will not seek reappointment at the end of this year as director of the Department of Hawaiian Home Lands and chair of the Hawaiian Homes Commission, state officials announced Friday. 
Appointed by Gov. Josh Green in 2023, Watson was responsible for overseeing the development of thousands of homes and the implementation of a $600 million state settlement with DHHL. He previously served as chair from 1995 to 1998 under Gov. Ben Cayetano. 
Under Watson’s leadership, the DHHL offered more than 5,300 leases. The department projects the offering of nearly 4,900 leases in 2027.
“That is some of the most important work we’ve done in our first term and Kali helped make it happen,” Governor Green said in the DHHL release Friday.
DHHL is tasked with administering a 100-year-old federal law guaranteeing land to Hawaiians who can prove a 50% blood quantum. Nearly 30,000 people are on its ever-growing waitlist. 
The department was recently sued over its blood quantum requirements. That lawsuit, threatens to undermine more than two dozen projects to develop thousands of homestead lots.
Watson had previously stated the department would fight that legal challenge. 
In July, Green announced he would be reappointing Watson as chair of the commission. The resignation letter gives no reason for Watson suddenly stepping down.
Kali Watson, chairman of the Hawaiian Homes Commission, is stepping down Dec. 31. (Blaze Lovell/Civil Beat/2024) Blaze Lovell/Civil Beat/2024
DeMont Kalai Manaole, a Native Hawaiian activist, said he wants a reason why. 
“I’m shocked,” he said. “And I’m entitled to answers as a trust beneficiary.”
Kalai Manaole suspects Watson was forced out due to a recent partnership between DHHL and the Office of Hawaiian Affairs to develop Kakaʻako Makai.  
OHA has long struck out on efforts to lift a ban on residential development that would allow it to construct housing units on lands it owns in Kakaʻako Makai. DHHL, however, has special development powers granted to it by Congress that make it exempt from the zoning restrictions that previously blocked the housing project. 
But there have been differing opinions over whether the housing should be built. The governor and some in the Legislature, Kalai Manaole said, don’t want to see Kakaʻako Makai developed. During the recent election, candidates for OHA trustee also expressed a wide range of opinions about the future of the Honolulu land.
“It’s an amazing thing that happened with DHHL and OHA joining forces, we’ve been wanting that for decades,” Kalai Manaole said.
Watson’s last day will be Dec. 31. In the DHHL release Friday, he said he planned to explore opportunities with OHA, the Aliʻi Trust and other community organizations.
“Governor Green, mahalo for your trust, your support, and the opportunity to serve,” Watson said in a DHHL release Friday. “You understood that behind every name on our waiting list is a person, an ʻohana, and a hope that has too often been deferred.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Supreme Court overturns 2025 law that gave Legislature more power over state Board of Education
description: In a 4-1 decision, the West Virginia Supreme Court overturned a 2025 law that attempted to give the Legislature more power over the state Board of Education.
text:
The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals. (West Virginia Legislative Photography)In a 4-1 decision, the West Virginia Supreme Court overturned a 2025 law that attempted to give the Legislature more power over the state Board of Education. 
The opinion, delivered by Justice H.L. Kirkpatrick, determined that a long established precedent that gave the state board the ability to act independently and not submit regulations for approval of state lawmakers would remain. 
“We conclude that this Court has previously decided the issue presented in this case and held that a statute enacted by the Legislature that required the Board to submit its rules to the Legislature for review constituted an interference with the Board’s rulemaking power and was therefore unconstitutional,” Kirkpatrick wrote. 
Only Justice Charles S. Trump dissented. In his opinion, he found the court’s prior rulings to be a “flawed constitutional premise.” He said while the school board can freely supervise schools, that doesn’t necessarily mean they can set their own regulations. 
“‘General supervision’ and ‘rulemaking’ are neither synonyms nor interchangeable powers,” Trump wrote. 
The Board of Education has enjoyed great independence from both the governor and the Legislature, following a Constitutional Amendment approved by voters in 1958. Since then, voters have had two opportunities to reverse this vote — in 1988 and 2022. Both times, voters rejected it. 
In 1988, the Legislature passed a law that would require the Board of Education to submit any regulations — which can range from which side of the hallway students should walk to the dimensions of school buses — to the Legislature for approval. 
Most agencies, like the Department of Environmental Protection and Department of Natural Resources, must submit their regulations to the Legislature for approval. 
The state Supreme Court at the time ruled the law unconstitutional. 
That case, referred to as Hechler, has become reigning precedent in West Virginia ever since. 
But in 2025, Del. Mike Hornby, R-Berkeley, successfully pushed a bill through the Legislature to once again give lawmakers more control over the Board of Education. At the time, he said the bill would spark a challenge against the Hechler ruling. 
Upon hearing the ruling Friday, Hornby said he didn’t agree with it. 
“I respect the decision of the court, however when I read the Constitution as a whole I still believe the Legislature has the ultimate rule making authority,” Hornby said. “We were also careful to draft this legislation in a way that created a significant difference to the Hechler case. That said, I thank the court for their time on this matter. I look forward to continuing to improve our education system moving forward.” 
Reacting to the ruling, the state Board of Education issued the following statement: 
“The West Virginia Board of Education  (WVBE) is grateful to the West Virginia Supreme Court for its decision to uphold the will of the voters and the State Constitution, which grants the State Board of Education authority over the rulemaking and oversight of education policy. The WVBE will continue its important work of providing leadership, oversight and support to the education system and children in West Virginia.”

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Polis warns budget writers Medicaid costs could eat up revenue from new graduated income tax
description: Gov. Jared Polis once again urged the Colorado lawmakers tasked with writing the state budget to slow state Medicaid spending, warning that new revenue from a recently-passed ballot measure would soon go entirely to the program if it’s left unchanged. “In three years, if you don’t rein in Medicaid, all that (Amendment) 87 money goes […]
text:
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis presents his budget request for the 2027-2028 fiscal year in his office at the Capitol in Denver on Nov. 2, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Gov. Jared Polis once again urged the Colorado lawmakers tasked with writing the state budget to slow state Medicaid spending, warning that new revenue from a recently-passed ballot measure would soon go entirely to the program if it’s left unchanged.
“In three years, if you don’t rein in Medicaid, all that (Amendment) 87 money goes to Medicaid. Zero for education. Zero for actually making people healthier. Zero for early childhood,” Polis told members of the bipartisan Joint Budget Committee on Thursday morning.
“None of it goes to the promises of why some people supported 87 — to support our schools and education and early childhood and better health outcomes for Coloradans. I hope that we can avoid that scenario,” he added.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Amendment 87, the voter-approved graduated income tax scheme where higher earners will pay a higher tax rate, will add about $2 billion in annual revenue to head towards health care, education and child care. There is no prescribed split between those allowable uses.
Thursday marked the last time Polis will present a budget proposal to the JBC, as he leaves office in January and Gov.-elect Phil Weiser, another Democrat, takes over. The governor is required to submit a budget request every November, even if there will be an administration change. Polis again suggested a hard growth cap on Medicaid spending tied to population growth and inflation. That would be 4.3% next year, the same amount state spending is allowed to increase overall under the Taxpayer’s Bill of Rights. It would still amount to about $250 million more for the program, but his budget proposal suggests measures like eliminating adult dental care to make the numbers work.
Lawmakers have already acknowledged that Amendment 87 will not fix the longtime budget woes caused by Medicaid spending. The entitlement health insurance program for low-income Coloradans takes up close to 40% of the state’s entire yearly budget.
“The projected Medicaid overage for the coming fiscal year was a billion dollars,” Rep. Kyle Brown, a Louisville Democrat on both the JBC and the Medicaid Commission, said during a Tuesday commission meeting. “(Amendment) 87 is expected to raise a billion dollars in its first year and $2 billion in the second year. If (Medicaid) continues to grow at 15% per year, we will eat up all that money unless we make changes.”
The commission this week started voting on recommendations to include in its final report on how to make Medicaid more sustainable. It rejected a hard growth limit on the state Medicaid contribution by an 8-1 vote. That suggestion had a legal note from the Department of Health Care Policy and Financing, which runs Medicaid, that the state is required to cover all eligible people and cannot enforce a growth cap by denying or reducing services.
“We have hard caps in our budget, and the piece of our budget that is growing the most should reflect those hard caps that we have to deal with,” Sen. Jeff Bridges, a Democrat who will be Colorado’s next treasurer and voted for the recommendation, said. “To just have Medicaid come back every year and say, ‘Oh, we’re $500 million over budget. Sorry,’ that is not a great way for any agency to run, and it’s not a great way for us to manage a budget.”
Polis will submit a revised budget proposal in early January before he leaves office. That should reflect the budget impacts from Amendment 87 and the other successful ballot measures that will either create more revenue or force the state to spend more money. The JBC submits a budget for the entire Legislature to vote on, typically in late March.

name: VTDigger
title: National hatchery closure in Bethel has Vermont officials concerned
description:
Other fish hatcheries across the state are already operating at capacity, officials say.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  National hatchery closure in Bethel has Vermont officials concerned.
text:
The White River National Fish Hatchery in Bethel held a re-opening ceremony on Friday afternoon after completing repairs from Irene damage. Speakers included Senator Patrick Leahy and Representative Peter Welch. (Herald / Ben DeFlorio)

This story by Wilder Grimes was first published in The White River Valley Herald on Nov. 12, 2026.
Plans to place the White River National Fish Hatchery in Bethel on inactive status have raised concerns among Vermont fishery officials, who say the state’s remaining hatcheries are already operating at capacity and could be affected by changes to federal programs.
A letter addressed to U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service Director Brian Nesvik from U.S. Sens. Peter Welch, Chuck Schumer, Bernie Sanders and Kirsten Gillibrand, and U.S. Rep. Becca Balint, shared early last month, detailed the federal agency’s plans to place the hatchery on inactive status.
The congressional delegation pleaded with the director to rescind that decision, advocating for the necessity of the hatchery in maintaining fish populations in Vermont and New York.
Federal officials have not publicly explained how the hatchery’s work would be handled following its deactivation. Paul Boynton, biological science technician and assistant project leader at the White River hatchery, was unable to comment on the announced closure and was instructed to forward all media inquiries to the U.S. Fish and Wildlife Service. Employees there were also unable to provide responses.
State perspective
Dylan Sickles, fish culture operations manager for the Vermont Fish & Wildlife Department, explained that the state’s five hatcheries operate separately from the federal facilities but have an agreement to work together to meet the needs of the state.
Though the Dwight D. Eisenhower National Fish Hatchery in North Chittenden was able to take on the work of the White River hatchery during its six-year hiatus following Tropical Storm Irene, Sickles isn’t confident that it has enough space to absorb additional responsibilities without affecting the programs it shares with the state.
While the Dwight D. Eisenhower facility primarily works with the state hatcheries to stock brook trout across Vermont, the White River hatchery provides brook trout eggs to them.
“We try not to move too many fish, but within the federal program they could do that within what they have from the White River (hatchery), potentially to the Dwight D. Eisenhower (hatchery).”
Despite that being a possibility, Sickles doesn’t believe there is adequate space to accommodate all of the White River hatchery’s work.
“They’d have to put those fish in the tanks that are already occupied by other fish they have. So their space is limited to do that as well,” he said. “There aren’t empty tanks laying around anywhere, or space available for additional fish we reared in our program. So that’s part of the big problem right now.”
Sickles explained that state hatcheries are at full capacity.
The White River hatchery contributes to restoration and conservation of lake trout in the lower Great Lakes, as well as landlocked Atlantic salmon in Lake Champlain. It is also used by researchers from Concordia, Purdue, Boston University and Dartmouth College for their studies, according to an interview with Boynton conducted by The Herald this past spring.
The federal hatcheries’ work is closely connected to state fishery programs, but the two agencies have separate responsibilities. Without details from the federal government about its plans, it remains unclear how much of the Bethel facility’s work might be transferred elsewhere or how those changes could affect the state’s cooperative programs.
Conservation concerns
Sickles explained that in recent years in Vermont, natural reproduction of lake trout in Lake Champlain has occurred, and because of that, the state has moved away from the broodstock program and is allowing fish to naturally stock the lake.
The White River hatchery currently holds a lake trout broodstock line, and the eggs are given to the Eisenhower hatchery and used to stock other lakes throughout the state.
Sickles added that even though things have improved in recent years for lake trout in Lake Champlain, conditions are always changing, and having the backup supply at the White River facility is important.
He mentioned a small fish known as a round goby that he said may be making its way toward the Lake Champlain area and would eat salmon and trout eggs if it arrived.
If that were the case, another location would have to be found for the fish. Sickles warned that if the Dwight D. Eisenhower facility were to take on that responsibility, “that would potentially reduce the capacity that we operate with them for the brook trout and the other fish that we stock that they help us out with.”
The possibility illustrates why Sickles considers the Bethel facility an important backup, even as some fish populations have begun reproducing naturally.
History of cooperation
The White River National Fish Hatchery in Bethel is one of two national hatcheries in Vermont and works closely with the Dwight D. Eisenhower Hatchery in North Chittenden.
In their letter, the members of Congress described how, after Atlantic salmon and lake trout populations disappeared from Lake Champlain around 1900 due to runoff and dam construction, Vermont and New York began reviving hatcheries to restore the populations.
In 1984, the White River National Fish Hatchery was established to provide federal support for this endeavor.
These efforts, the letter explained, “have only grown more critical since the introduction of aquatic invasive species like sea lamprey.”
The White River hatchery was severely damaged during Tropical Storm Irene and was forced to close in 2011 until a $2.4 million renovation allowed for reopening in 2017.
During that time, the Dwight D. Eisenhower facility filled the gap, “underscoring the importance of redundancy in the National Fish Hatchery System,” the letter read, as extreme weather grows more frequent.
That history is part of the congressional delegation’s argument for keeping both federal hatcheries operating. The earlier closure demonstrated how one facility could support the other’s work, but Sickles’ concerns about available space suggest that repeating such an arrangement could be difficult under current conditions.

text:
A sign at a University of Utah health clinic warns visitors about the spread of measles. (Photo by McKenzie Romero/Utah News Dispatch)The Pennsylvania Department of Health attributed another death to the state’s ongoing measles outbreak, this time in Montour County. It’s the seventh measles-associated death in the state. 
Though overall cases appear to have slowed, more than 1,542 people have been infected across 46 counties. Of those, just five people were vaccinated. 
Health officials emphasized that vaccination “remains the best protection against the measles virus,” in a Friday release, noting it is 97% effective at preventing measles for life after two doses. 
 
Learn more about measles, including its symptoms and information about vaccination, by reviewing this state-issued fact sheet.


DOH shared that the individual who died in Montour County was unvaccinated, but said state laws limited the department from sharing any more identifiable information. 
To qualify as a measles-associated death, the individual must die within 30 days after showing symptoms, have a positive laboratory test and not be attributable to an unrelated cause (such as a car accident). The agency also considers whether the person had been exposed prior to death or had supporting medical records. 
Another death in Franklin County reported last month, which the county coroner said could be associated, doesn’t meet the department’s criteria. 
The heart of the state’s ongoing outbreak, the worst in three decades, is in Lancaster County, where three have died and more than 500 people have been infected. 
On Thursday, state Secretary of Health Debra Bogen hosted a roundtable in Lancaster with local public officials, highlighting efforts to increase vaccination rates.
“State health data illustrate only part of the picture when it comes to Pennsylvania’s measles outbreak,” said Bogen in a release. “To fine-tune our approach, we are having deliberate discussions and listening to the people doing this work on the ground in Lancaster County … My team and I are committed to this all-hands-on-deck approach, working around the clock, so we can bring this outbreak to an end.”
A screenshot of the Pennsylvania Measles Dashboard taken on Nov. 13, 2026 shows case counts by county.
Roughly 300 DOH staff members and community members are responding to the outbreak, administering more than 7,000 measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccines at 244 pop-up clinics across the commonwealth since late April. 
The agency said private providers typically administer 25,000 MMR doses per month, but reported administering more than 56,000 and 61,000 doses in September and October, respectively. 
So far, providers reported administering 19,000 doses this month.
Measles is highly contagious and can be dangerous for the youngest Pennsylvanians, and DOH now recommends “an additional early zero dose,” for infants between six months and 12 months living in counties with sustained community transmission. 
People who believe they were exposed to measles, and are experiencing symptoms, should contact their health care provider or call DOH’s toll-free hotline at 877-PA-HEALTH (877-724-3258).

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana students see growth in reading, math proficiency
description: Nearly all counties in Montana saw year-over-year increases in the percentage of students grades 3 through 8 who are at or above grace-level proficiency standards in language arts and math.  That’s according to the second year of statewide results from the new standardized assessment protocol implemented during the 2024 school year.  The Office of Public […]
text:
A classroom at Woodrow Wilson Elementary School in South Salt Lake City, Utah, on March 12, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)Nearly all counties in Montana saw year-over-year increases in the percentage of students grades 3 through 8 who are at or above grace-level proficiency standards in language arts and math. 
That’s according to the second year of statewide results from the new standardized assessment protocol implemented during the 2024 school year. 
The Office of Public Instruction released the statewide scores of the Montana Aligned to Standards Through-Year Assessment, or MAST, this week and Montana’s average of students who tested at or above proficiency levels for their grade increased from the first-year scores. 
In language arts, 45.6% of students tested at or above grade-level proficiency, compared to 43% last year. And in math, proficiency levels increased from 36.8% to 40.8% this year, close to prepandemic scores conducted with a different assessment. 
“I think it’s very exciting to see the progress that we’re making,” state superintendent Susie Hedalen told the Daily Montanan. “And I do believe that the assessment and the information that’s being provided is very helpful to educators and parents in being able to understand where their students are, any misunderstandings they’re having, and address them.”
Hedalen, a Republican, oversaw the rollout of statewide MAST testing after a two-year pilot program was conducted under former state Superintendent Elsie Arntzen. 
As opposed to previous standardized testing formats, MAST involves “testlets,” smaller math and English Language Arts tests taking place during four testing periods in the school year, creating a “through-year assessment model.”
The goal is to offer more immediate feedback to educators, students, parents and administrators by providing multiple data points to track progress and alter curriculum or teaching strategies throughout the year to benefit students.
Hedalen said her office had worked to address challenges reported by educators during the first year of assessments, including the new testing protocol was time intensive and they hadn’t received adequate professional development on how to implement and utilize the new methods. 
“I came in with a solution-focused mindset on this,” Hedalen said. “We have professional development going on in many different forms across the state, and we had a lot of opportunities this summer for educators to get together and learn more about the assessment and the score reports and how to utilize them to improve student learning, so it is a huge advantage to educators.”
Hedalen touted one of the most useful parts of the MAST testing is by having more frequent assessments, educators get a look at how students understand the curriculum throughout the year, rather than receiving a single result usually after as school year ends. 
“Having gotten my students’ test scores in the summer after they were already gone and not being able to utilize that information was never very helpful as an educator,” she said. “It’s very exciting that within just a few days, educators have this information.”
Of Montana’s 56 counties, 41 saw increases in English scores from last year’s assessments, and 52 saw increases in Math scores. 
Counties that saw decreased average scores for the most part had exceptionally high first year tests, or saw only marginal declines.
The statewide gains in mathematics is the largest year-over-year increase in several years, Hedalen said. 
She also highlighted specific demographic breakouts of the assessment data which showed economically disadvantaged students showing a 3.2% increase in math proficiency and 1.8% increase in English proficiency; while Native American students saw a 2.6% jump in math and 1.6% increase in English. 
“It’s important just to see and make sure that we’re reaching all students and providing those additional supports,” she said. “I just always go back to it being really critical that all students have access to high-quality core curriculum, and then we take that additional time for any students that need an intervention in reading or math, and make sure that that’s put in place. So we’re supporting our schools across the state in making sure they have those systems in place.”
The Office of Public Instruction is currently piloting MAST testing protocols for science-based instruction, but Hedalen said it’s a more difficult subject to fit to a standard assessment model because various districts teach different science subjects at different grade levels. 
While the latest MAST scores are still below pre-COVID-19 levels (under a previous assessment), Montana students have had one of the highest bounce-back rates from COVID-19 era scores, according to the latest National Assessment of Educational Progress. In 2024, the national assessment showed Montana 9th graders ranking 10th in math proficiency and 4th in reading proficiently nationally. 
Full datasets from the 2025-2026 MAST testing can be accessed online and broken down by county, grade, district, school, and demographics.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Oklahoma law enforcement offers hard lessons as NC weighs cannabis legalization recommendations
description: Lt. Col. Mitch Smith with the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs says there have been many unintended consequences in the eight years since the Sooner state voted to legalize medical marijuana.  Smith, director of the bureau’s marijuana enforcement unit, said North Carolina should take those lessons to heart as it prepares final recommendations[...]
text:
On Tuesday, Nov. 17, the full N.C. Advisory Council on Cannabis will hold what is expected to be its last meeting before delivering final policy recommendations to Gov. Josh Stein in December. (Photo: Getty Images)Lt. Col. Mitch Smith with the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs says there have been many unintended consequences in the eight years since the Sooner state voted to legalize medical marijuana.  Smith, director of the bureau’s marijuana enforcement unit, said North Carolina should take those lessons to heart as it prepares final recommendations on a comprehensive cannabis policy.
Smith told members of the North Carolina Advisory Council on Cannabis’s public safety subcommittee Thursday that Oklahoma law required 75% of the ownership of any medical marijuana business to be held by an Oklahoma resident.
“What we found early on is that folks from out of state moving in would find local Oklahoma residents that would take any sum of money to be straw owners of a business,” Smith said. “It was the bad actors or foreign nationals that were actually operating the business itself.”
Lt. Col. Mitch Smith with the Oklahoma Bureau of Narcotics and Dangerous Drugs. (Photo: N.C. Advisory Council on Cannabis)
By 2021, Oklahoma had 8,400 commercial growers with no cap on how much could be grown.
“You could potentially grow an infinite amount of marijuana plants,” said Smith. “That led to an abundance and overproduction of marijuana, which was destined for the black market.”
Oklahoma also did not place a limit on the number of medical cannabis business licenses. The lack of restrictions in the early years did not go unnoticed.
“We’ve been inundated with individuals from foreign countries that come here to profit off that,” Smith said.
He told the committee his organization is aware of 27 different groups from at least 16 different countries that are operating illegally in Oklahoma.
Agents have been forced to deal with abandoned grow houses, large quantities of trash and banned pesticides that could taint well water and pose a public health hazard.
“There’s no recourse for that,” Smith said. “My fear is the state’s going to end up footing that bill, to get those things cleared up, cleaned up, to get back to its natural state.”
Smith said Oklahoma allocates about $10 million annually for 48 agents and analysts assigned to marijuana enforcement.
“What’s your evidence storage looking like?” asked Scottie Shoaf with North Carolina Alcohol Law Enforcement.
Smith said his agents last week seized more than 50,000 illegal plants, which the state is allowed to destroy, logging small samples into evidence. But additional storage is needed for vape products, cannabis consumables, black market items and seized cash.
The court system was also ill-prepared for an influx of foreign nationals who didn’t speak English and couldn’t understand the drug charges they were facing.
“Interpreters who speak Mandarin and Cantonese — there’s not very many of those in the state of Oklahoma,” Smith said. “There weren’t budgets set aside for those. And then we’d have jury trials and the jury instructions [in those languages] didn’t exist. They had to create them.”
North Carolina cannabis council considers public consumption policy for THC products

Rosanna Smart, co-director of the nonpartisan RAND Drug Policy Research Center, told the public safety subcommittee that North Carolina may find that it spends more money on cannabis enforcement in the first few years after the passage of legalization.
But research shows that legalization can make a major dent in the existing illegal market.
“Studies show people are willing to pay higher prices in the legal market, if they believe the legal products are of high quality and come with accurate lab testing,” Smart said.
Smart cautioned that much of the available research is based on early adopters of legalized cannabis, not states like North Carolina where cannabis is illegal, but intoxicating hemp products are widely available.
Smith told the subcommittee if he could make one recommendation, it would be for North Carolina to make its licensing as restrictive as possible.
“We have spent the majority of our time over the last six years trying to put the worms back in the can,” Smith said.
On Tuesday, Nov. 17, the full N.C. Advisory Council on Cannabis holds what is expected to be its last meeting before delivering final policy recommendations to Gov. Josh Stein in December. The General Assembly would need to agree on the legislation. House Speaker-elect Robert Reives, D-Chatham, said this week Democrats, who will have a majority in the state House in 2027, are interested in exploring marijuana decriminalization.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico housing leaders outline legislative agenda at Rural Housing Summit
description: At an event focused on rural housing challenges, New Mexico lawmakers and housing experts on Friday discussed measures the Legislature will consider at the upcoming session, including new tax credits and building incentives for developers.
text:
New Mexico Rep. Anita Gonzales speaks Nov. 13, 2026, in Las Vegas at the inaugural Rural Housing Summit, which she helped convene to spotlight rural housing issues ahead of the 2027 legislative session. 
At an event focused on rural housing challenges, New Mexico lawmakers and housing experts on Friday discussed measures the Legislature will consider at the upcoming session, including new tax credits and building incentives for developers.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
State Rep. Anita Gonzales (D-Las Vegas) helped organize the inaugural Rural Housing Summit in Las Vegas to highlight housing challenges particular to rural areas. She represents a district that lost hundreds of homes to the Hermits Peak-Calf Canyon Fire in 2022, followed by damaging floods and high rates of insurers refusing to renew area homeowners policies. 
“Our markets are just very different than you see in the urban cities,” she told attendees Friday. “As you all know, housing is the crux of so many things.” 
Rural areas have other housing challenges separate from natural disasters and insurance non-renewals, according to recent analyses. Rural counties collectively lack thousands of affordable ownership and rental units; are experiencing rising homelessness; and contain high concentrations of aging housing stock. 
The Legislature, in recent years, has dedicated historic sums of one-time funding for various housing-related projects across the state. Amanda Breiding, the budget director for the New Mexico House of Representatives, estimated in a presentation Friday that the Legislature has allocated $870 million to housing between 2024 and 2026, which is more than three times the amount the Legislature approved in the preceding decade.
About 40% of the recent housing funding has gone to rural communities, Breiding said. 
Despite the increased funding, lawmakers and experts said more needs to be done to ensure affordable housing gets built and gets built in the areas where it is most needed.
Some of the proposals lawmakers and experts laid out Friday included:

a property tax credit for developers who turn vacant or abandoned properties into homes;
long-term property tax relief for developers who reserve 20% of new units for low-income renters;
making municipal land transfers easier for new housing projects; and
incentives for towns and counties that adopt zoning changes that facilitate housing construction.

Gonzales said Friday she intends to introduce the bill establishing the vacant and abandoned property tax credit, as well as one that aims to give homeowners more transparency about the models insurance companies rely on to justify canceling policies. 
Sen. Cindy Nava (D-Albuquerque) told Source NM on Friday that she intends to introduce a bill at the upcoming session that would establish a statewide housing division within a state agency. 
The Department of Workforce Solutions currently oversees the state Office of Housing, but Nava said a better-staffer and -equipped division is necessary to ensure the state can effectively apply for and implement grant funding from the U.S. Housing and Urban Development and other funders.
“You’re able to accomplish 10 times more things if you have a built infrastructure where you bring all the game players to the table,” she said. “We haven’t had a hub like that where we bring everyone.”

name: Delaware
title: Your Delaware Weekend: Holiday Trains, Festival of Trees, Live Theater and Ways to Give Back
description: From holiday traditions and family entertainment to community fundraisers, concerts, writing day and charity walks, here’s what’s happening across Delaware and nearby communities Nov. 14–15 Editor’s Note:  Delaware LIVE covered each of these stories over the past several weeks.  Click through and read more about each of these events as Delaware LIVE continue[...]
text:
From holiday traditions and family entertainment to community fundraisers, concerts, writing day and charity walks, here’s what’s happening across Delaware and nearby communities Nov. 14–15
Editor’s Note:  Delaware LIVE covered each of these stories over the past several weeks.  Click through and read more about each of these events as Delaware LIVE continues to expand editorial coverage of the best things about living in our community. 
By George D. Rotsch, Delaware LIVE
DELAWARE — The holiday season is beginning to take shape across the First State, and this weekend offers plenty of ways to get out, have fun, and support local organizations.
The Festival of Trees returns to Wilmington, model trains begin rolling at the Brandywine Museum of Art, and Ebenezer Scrooge takes the stage in Middletown. Meanwhile, community fundraisers, live music, health screenings and historical programs offer something for nearly every interest.
Delaware LIVE News and Town Square LIVE have featured many of these events in recent weeks. We’ve gathered them into one weekend guide, complete with dates, times, and links to the original stories.
Holiday traditions begin
Delaware Hospice Festival of Trees — Wilmington
One of Delaware’s longtime holiday traditions returns this weekend as Delaware Hospice celebrates its 39th annual Festival of Trees at Brantwyn Estate, 600 Rockland Road.
The three-day event, running Friday through Sunday, features decorated Christmas trees, holiday shopping, musical entertainment and opportunities to support Delaware Hospice’s programs and services.
The festival has become a community tradition through the efforts of volunteers, businesses and families who return year after year. Visitors can also purchase remembrance ornaments honoring loved ones.
A second Festival of Trees celebration is scheduled for Dec. 4–6 in Selbyville.
Read the Town Square LIVE Festival of Trees story
Brandywine Railroad opens for the holidays — Chadds Ford
The trains begin rolling Saturday at the Brandywine Museum of Art as its popular Brandywine Railroad display opens for another holiday season.
A favorite for generations of families, the exhibition includes approximately 2,000 feet of track and more than 1,000 pieces, including locomotives, freight cars and trolleys traveling through miniature villages, farms, factories and a carnival.
Interactive buttons and foot pedals allow visitors to activate features throughout the display.
The railroad will remain on view through Jan. 10, 2027, with additional holiday activities planned throughout the season.
Read the Town Square LIVE Brandywine Railroad story
Live theater and music across the region
A Christmas Carol: The Musical — Middletown
Ebenezer Scrooge arrives in Middletown ahead of Thanksgiving as God’s Power & Light Company presents A Christmas Carol: The Musical at the historic Everett Theatre.
The production brings Charles Dickens’ familiar story of generosity, redemption and second chances to the stage.
Saturday’s 2 p.m. performance includes American Sign Language interpretation, providing an additional opportunity for theatergoers to enjoy the show.
Performances are scheduled for Saturday at 2 and 7:30 p.m. and Sunday at 2 p.m. Tickets are $20 for adults and $14 for children and students ages 3–17.
Read the Town Square LIVE A Christmas Carol story
Delaware lawyers take the stage for charity — Wilmington and Dover
Delaware’s legal community will trade courtroom appearances for stage performances with an original musical comedy called Flifferschmeep: Another Example of What Happens When You Get Lawyers Involved.
Presented by Profundo Bono, the production features judges, attorneys and other legal professionals performing to benefit the Combined Campaign for Justice, which supports civil legal services for Delawareans who cannot afford them.
Saturday’s performance begins at 7:30 p.m. at Tatnall School in Wilmington. Sunday’s show begins at 2 p.m. at Delaware State University in Dover.
Tickets are $25.
Read the Town Square LIVE Profundo Bono story
Brandywine Valley Symphony performs — Mendenhall
The Brandywine Valley Symphony continues its season Sunday with a 3 p.m. Masterworks concert at the Mendenhall Inn, just across the Delaware border in Pennsylvania.
Artistic Director Michael Hall will guide the audience through Georges Bizet’s Symphony No. 1, combining the performance with stories and musical examples intended to make classical music accessible and enjoyable.
Read the Town Square LIVE Brandywine Valley Symphony story
Community fundraisers offer ways to give back
Camping Out for Coats — Wilmington
Frawley Stadium will become a campground Saturday night as Sam’s KIDS celebrates the 10th anniversary of Camping Out for Coats.
The fundraiser supports Operation Warm, providing new winter coats to elementary school children throughout Delaware.
A kickoff celebration from 4 to 9 p.m. features live music, games, bonfires, refreshments and a silent auction. Registered participants can spend the night camping on the stadium field.
Since the event began in 2017, organizers say it has helped provide more than 17,000 coats to students at 37 elementary schools. This year’s goal is to raise enough money for another 2,000 coats.
Read the Town Square LIVE Camping Out for Coats story
Good KARMA 5K and One-Mile Walk — Wilmington
The Spread Good Karma Foundation will hold its inaugural Good KARMA 5K and one-mile walk Sunday morning at Conaty Park in Wilmington’s Trolley Square neighborhood.
Both events begin at 9 a.m., with race-day registration and bib pickup from 7:45 to 8:45 a.m.
The fundraiser supports free and donation-based wellness activities throughout Delaware, including yoga, Pilates, fitness classes, meditation and community walking groups.
Organizers hope to raise $25,000 to help keep those programs accessible to residents.
Read the Town Square LIVE Good KARMA 5K story
Southern Delaware Walk to End Alzheimer’s — Rehoboth Beach
Families, caregivers and supporters of the Alzheimer’s Association will gather Saturday at Grove Park in Rehoboth Beach for the Southern Delaware Walk to End Alzheimer’s.
Originally scheduled for September, the event was postponed because of severe weather.
Participants raise money for Alzheimer’s research, education and services while recognizing families affected by dementia.
The event is part of the Alzheimer’s Association’s national fundraising initiative. Participants should confirm the start time with organizers.
Read Delaware LIVE’s Southern Delaware Walk to End Alzheimer’s story
Health, history and activities for everyone
ChristianaCare offers lung cancer screenings — Newark and Wilmington
ChristianaCare will offer low-dose CT lung cancer screenings Saturday from 8:30 a.m. to 1 p.m. at the Helen F. Graham Cancer Center & Research Institute in Newark and Wilmington Hospital.
The screenings are intended for eligible adults with a history of smoking and are designed to detect lung cancer before symptoms appear.
Appointments are encouraged, but walk-ins will be accepted. Residents can call 302-623-0552 for information about eligibility and scheduling.
Read Delaware LIVE’s ChristianaCare lung screening story
Special Forces veteran speaks — Milford
Christopher VanSant, a retired Delta Force soldier and Caesar Rodney High School graduate, will speak Saturday at 1 p.m. at the Milford Public Library.
VanSant, who served in 11 combat deployments, will discuss his military experiences, injury and recovery, and the challenges of returning to civilian life.
The program is sponsored by the Milford Museum and Milford Public Library and offers an opportunity to continue recognizing veterans following Veterans Day.
Read Delaware LIVE’s Veterans Day events coverage
Hagley Museum offers daily cannon demonstrations — Wilmington
Visitors to Hagley Museum and Library can experience a new daily tradition as the museum fires its historic signal cannon at 1 p.m. each day it is open, weather permitting.
The demonstrations, which began Nov. 7, include an explanation of how signal cannons were used for communication during the 19th century.
The cannon firing takes place in Hagley’s historic powder yards, where the DuPont Co. manufactured black powder from 1802 to 1921.
Read Delaware LIVE’s Hagley cannon demonstration story
I Love To Write Day celebrates its Delaware roots — Statewide
A national celebration with Delaware roots returns Sunday.
I Love To Write Day was founded in 2002 by Delaware author John Riddle to encourage people of all ages to express themselves through writing.
The concept is simple: Write something.
It could be a letter, a poem, a journal entry, a family history or the beginning of a story.
Schools, libraries, families and individuals across the country can participate wherever they are.
Read Delaware LIVE’s story about the Delaware origins of I Love To Write Day
A weekend to enjoy Delaware and support your neighbors
From the holiday trains at the Brandywine Museum and the Festival of Trees to community races, live theater and nonprofit fundraisers, this weekend offers plenty of opportunities to explore Delaware.
Many of these events also demonstrate how much local organizations contribute to the communities they serve, whether through entertainment, education, health programs or direct assistance to families.
And while the holiday season is just beginning, these events provide an early reminder that some of Delaware’s strongest traditions are built around people coming together.
Readers can follow the links to Delaware LIVE News and Town Square LIVE’s original stories for additional information, registration details and ticket links.
Event schedules and availability are subject to change. Check with organizers before attending.

title: Utah’s on-time graduation rate gains are the highest in the country
description: Utah was the state with the most progress on a national index measuring on-time graduation rates this year. That’s one sign of promise seen nationally in higher education, according to an evaluation of higher education outcomes from the nonprofit Strada Education Foundation. According to the organization’s annual State Opportunity Index, about 70% of recent [...]
text:
The University of Utah campus, with Presidents’ Circle in the foreground, is pictured in Salt Lake City on Saturday, Aug. 23, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Utah was the state with the most progress on a national index measuring on-time graduation rates this year. That’s one sign of promise seen nationally in higher education, according to an evaluation of higher education outcomes from the nonprofit Strada Education Foundation.
According to the organization’s annual State Opportunity Index, about 70% of recent public college graduates throughout the country experience a positive return on their college investment within 10 years of completion.  
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
In Utah, the return on investment number is 67% for bachelor’s degrees, slightly below average, and 59% for associate degrees. However, the state shines above all others in its on-time graduation rate gains for bachelor’s degrees, which went from 28% to 37% this year. 
Hawaii followed Utah in those gains, going from 34% to 41%. Rhode Island was third, going from 47% to 52%, according to a news release from the Strada Education Foundation.
“Still, in most states, fewer than half of students complete a bachelor’s degree in four years,” the release says. 



Let us know what you think...


 


Despite its improvement in when students graduate, Utah didn’t fare well in the affordability measurements on the organization’s index. The average amount of hours a student needs to work to cover in-state attendance costs is 32 per week, for a $16,200 annual price. The national average price is $15,270, which amounts to 26 hours of work per week.
Among other positive results from Utah public universities is the percentage of bachelor’s degree holders who are employed in college-level jobs. 
“Its college-level employment rate is among the highest in the country at 63 percent (compared to a national average of 60 percent),” the report says of Utah, adding that the state has a good supply/demand ratio (of over 75%) in jobs for graduates in data analytics, information technology and cyber security, software engineering, nursing, engineering and manufacturing.
But, the supply/demand ratio for jobs in finance and accounting support is less than 50%, the state’s lowest ratio in the report.

title: Technical issues caused Oklahoma election result delays
description: OKLAHOMA CITY – A bogus security alert in one county and a failed hard drive in another county delayed the reporting of the Nov. 3 election results, said State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax. Ziriax said the two issues did not affect the counting of the votes or the validity of the vote count of […]
text:
(Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – A bogus security alert in one county and a failed hard drive in another county delayed the reporting of the Nov. 3 election results, said State Election Board Secretary Paul Ziriax.
Ziriax said the two issues did not affect the counting of the votes or the validity of the vote count of the midterm election results.
Paul Ziriax, election board secretary, speaks about candidate filing during a media briefing on Tuesday, April 2, 2024. (Photo by Janelle Stecklein/Oklahoma Voice)
A security alert in Cleveland County triggered security protocols that temporarily prevented the county from transmitting its results to the state, he said.
Officials were able to use an alternative method to process the file that triggered the alert and the results were posted to the state website shortly after 10 p.m., he said.
In Comanche County, a hard drive failure caused the delay and required manual entry, he said.
“Even with these technical issues and delays, Oklahoma still fully reported our unofficial election results statewide more quickly than most states around the country,” Ziriax said.
Officials do not like that the delays occurred, Ziriax said.
But he said he was proud of how the county and state staff did what was necessary to make the results available in a timely manner.

title: Beydoun faces 3 new charges in grant scandal, including alleged use of funds for her legal defense
description: Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced Friday afternoon three new charges against Fay Beydoun, the businesswoman who faces accusations of misusing $20 million in state legislative grant funding.  The new charges allege that she used hundreds of thousands of dollars in funds from her nonprofit organization, which was funded with state grant money, fo[...]
text:
The office of Attorney General Dana Nessel in the G. Mennen Williams Building in Lansing, Mich., on May 15, 2025. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Michigan Attorney General Dana Nessel announced Friday afternoon three new charges against Fay Beydoun, the businesswoman who faces accusations of misusing $20 million in state legislative grant funding. 
The new charges allege that she used hundreds of thousands of dollars in funds from her nonprofit organization, which was funded with state grant money, for her own legal defense fund, as well as for a membership to a professional organization and for personal furniture purchases. 
Beydoun was charged in May with 16 felonies — conducting a criminal enterprise, forgery, larceny by conversion of more than $20,000, six counts of larceny by conversion involving $1,000 to $20,000 and seven counts of uttering and publishing. At that time, Nessel’s office said that the investigation was ongoing and could result in additional charges.
Nessel’s press release detailed the background of the initial charges against Beydoun, which stem from a “Michigan enhancement grant” that she received through the fiscal year 2023 state budget to establish and operate a global business accelerator in Oakland County — her nonprofit, Global Link International (GLI).SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Now, Beydoun faces three additional charges related to the alleged theft of the funds, including two counts of larceny from a person, each a 10-year felony charge, “concerning an attempt to have GLI pay her legal expenses in defending herself against allegations that she stole from GLI, and for a donation to the Michigan Founders Fund alleged to be for personal reasons,” and one of larceny by conversion, a five-year felony.
“These newly charged allegations reflect the continued investigative efforts ongoing in my office, and a broader extent of Beydoun’s alleged expenses made with state grant funding,” Nessel said in a press release announcing the new charges. 
She noted that the case — which had initially been scheduled for a preliminary examination in January but will be postponed because of the new charges — will stretch beyond her term, which ends at the end of 2026, and stated that the case “remains a top priority within our Financial Crimes Division.”
Beydoun’s grant, which was administered by the Michigan Economic Development Corporation (MEDC), was secured while she served on the MEDC Executive Committee, and Nessel’s office has alleged that “no business relocated to Michigan through Global Link International efforts. Instead, Beydoun is accused of using the funds for personal gain and maintaining a $550,000 annual salary.”
“The new charges, like the old ones, are built on a house of cards,” attorney Todd Flood, whose law firm is representing Beydoun, told the Detroit News. Michigan Advance has requested a comment, but has yet to receive a response. This story will be updated once one is received.
“We allege Fay Beydoun sought and received a $20 million ‘Michigan enhancement grant’ from the state Legislature where she operated a criminal enterprise to use those funds for personal expenses and her own enrichment, and lied repeatedly when reporting how she used those funds, rather than using them towards the legally intended purpose of the grant,” Nessel said at the time of the initial charges.
The initial charges against Beydoun led to calls for change in the structure and administration of the MEDC, which have continued as controversies around the agency continue.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: Commentary: New federal rules proposed for food stamps are inhumane
description: The Trump administration, which is spending hundreds of millions on vanity projects for the president, wants to cut costs when it comes to food stamps.
text:
The Trump administration, which is spending hundreds of millions on vanity projects for the president, wants to cut costs when it comes to food stamps. (Photo by Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)As U.S. Senate Democrats bicker over who their next leader will be, the Trump administration is moving to ax food stamp benefits for millions of Americans.
A new federal proposal we just wrote about targets some of the nation’s poorest people while also pretending that it’s acting in the best interests of those same people.
Assembly Speaker Craig Coughlin, a Democrat whose top issue is food insecurity, balked at the Trump administration’s claims that its proposed rules are an attempt to shore up the food stamp system and prevent millionaires from taking advantage of it.
Coughlin, in a statement from his spokeswoman, said the White House is doubling down on policies that make working families’ lives harder by moving to make this change to food stamps, also known as the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program or SNAP.
“SNAP recipients aren’t gaming the system. They’re trying to survive. And punishing people for needing help is simply cruel,” he said.
The rules proposal takes aim at something called “broad-based categorical eligibility,” which allows people who are eligible for Temporary Assistance for Needy Families to be automatically eligible for food stamps. This idea was pitched by the federal government under President Barack Obama as a way to help families hurt by the Great Recession and also help governments with dwindling resources.
Because some states’ income limits for temporary assistance grants are higher than the federal income limits for food stamps, some people who make too much to be eligible for food stamps are able to get them. The Trump administration says its rule proposal is an attempt to fix this. State limits on temporary assistance can “sometimes far exceed” the same limits on food stamps, the administration says.
I think it’s helpful to dig into the numbers here. The federal income limit for food stamps is 130% of the federal poverty level, which amounts to $20,000 for a single person and $43,000 for a family of four. New Jersey’s limit for temporary assistance is 185% of the poverty level, which means $29,500 for a single person and $61,050 for a family of four.
The median household income in New Jersey is $107,797. I’m sure some folks would argue that someone making $61,050 is too rich to need government assistance to feed a family of four, but I am not one of them.
The number of people who receive food stamps but make more than the federal income limit is, relative to the program, small. The Trump administration estimates the total is 1.2 million households containing 2 million people. More than 40 million people are enrolled in SNAP nationwide.
Food stamps help about 848,000 people here in New Jersey, and the average benefit is about $200 a month. Nearly 80,000 of them are in danger of losing their benefits if the Trump rules go into effect.
The Trump administration also argues that rules surrounding income eligibility that don’t address an applicant’s material assets are harmful to the food stamp program. Its proposal says it is aware “of instances where millionaires have received SNAP benefits,” and for this it cites a single example of a Minnesota man who had little income on paper but owned $1 million in property and retirement accounts and secured food stamps in 2018.
“Because Minnesota doesn’t count those savings, I’m allowed to siphon unneeded welfare benefits,” the guy told CBS Minnesota.
There’s an argument to be made that food stamp eligibility should examine a person’s assets to prevent this kind of gaming of the system. But using this wisenheimer as a reason to kick 6 million Americans out of SNAP is ludicrous and cruel.
The Trump administration is spending $300 million in taxpayer dollars minimum on a White House ballroom, and those costs will no doubt balloon. It is considering millions in public funding for a great arch in D.C., potentially named after the president. Congress set aside $40 million for a statue garden Trump has wanted since his first term as president.
This is not an administration interested in saving taxpayer dollars — except when it comes to grabbing food stamps out of the hands of the poor.
Coughlin said he hopes the new Congress that takes over in January “recognizes the damage these policies are causing and takes action to reverse them.”
“Hunger is not a Republican or Democratic issue. It’s a human issue, and it’s long past time we started treating it that way,” he said.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho parents who got new private tax credit earned average of $178,000 per year, report shows
description: The average parent who received one of Idaho’s new private education tax credits made significantly more money than the average Idahoan and most of their children already attended private school before receiving the credit, according to a new report released Friday by the Idaho State Tax Commission.  Parents who received the Idaho Parental Choice Tax […]
text:
Members of the Idaho House of Representatives conduct legislative business from the floor on March 16, 2026, at the Idaho Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)The average parent who received one of Idaho’s new private education tax credits made significantly more money than the average Idahoan and most of their children already attended private school before receiving the credit, according to a new report released Friday by the Idaho State Tax Commission. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Parents who received the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit had an average adjusted gross income of $178,000 a year, which is more than double the income of an average Idaho family, the Idaho State Tax Commission’s Parental Choice Tax Credit Program Comprehensive Report found. (The U.S. Census Bureau reports Idaho’s median household income is $84,234)
The report was the first major state-analysis published on the $50 million new tax credit, which the Idaho Legislature created and Gov. Brad Little signed into law in 2025. 
The tax credit was one of the most discussed bills of 2025, and critics said it marked a major shift in education policy by making state funding available for private school tuition and expenses outside of the state’s K-12 public school system.
Idaho Republican Gov. Brad Little enters the House of Representative chambers to give his State of the State Address on Jan. 12, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
In Friday’s new report, the Idaho State Tax Commission reported that 55% of the 6,875 Idaho parents who received one of the tax credits earned more than 300% of the federal poverty level on their 2024 tax returns.
That compares to 45% of parents who were at or below 300% of the federal poverty level, which is the income level legislators said they would prioritize when they created the tax credit.
In conjunction with the release of the report, Little issued a statement saying that transparency and accountability around the tax credit are important. 
“Transparency and accountability are important to ensuring the Parental Choice Tax Credit works as intended and serves Idaho families well,” Little said Friday. “The Legislature called for transparency, and my administration went above and beyond to provide as much information and data as possible while protecting taxpayers’ personal information. This report gives policymakers and the public a clearer picture of the program and provides the best available data to evaluate its effectiveness, identify opportunities for improvement, and ensure it continues to serve Idahoans well.”
Other reaction to the report and the tax credit was mixed. 
Democrats renewed their calls to repeal the tax credit, or at least change the requirements so high income earners cannot benefit from the program. 
“Idahoans were sold a lie about this voucher scheme,” Idaho House Minority Leader Ilana Rubel, D-Boise, said in a written statement. “We were told this program would help low-income children leave public schools for supposedly better-performing private schools. Instead, more than half of the families awarded tax credits are above the income threshold Republicans promised to prioritize, and nearly three-quarters of students have never attended an Idaho public school.”
But the conservative Mountain States Policy Center, which backed the tax credit, said the report shows the tax credit is “a monumental success.”
“The Idaho Tax Commission has released its first in-depth report on year one of the state’s new parental choice tax credit, and the overwhelming evidence shows it has been a monumental success,” Mountain States Policy Center officials wrote Friday.
 Where did the money for the education tax credit go?

Two-thirds of the parents who applied for the tax credit lived in Idaho’s three biggest counties, the report shows. Of the 6,875 parents who applied for the tax credit, 4,527, or 66%, lived in Ada, Canyon or Kootenai counties. 
By comparison, there were just 48 applications from parents in eastern Idaho’s Bingham County and 31 applications from parents in southern Idaho’s Cassia County, the report shows. 
Almost one-fourth of the tax credit money spent for tuition at private schools went to just five Idaho private schools, the report shows.
Sen. Janie Ward-Engelking, D-Boise, takes her seat during the Joint Finance-Appropriations Committee meeting on Jan. 14, 2026, at the State Capitol Building in Boise. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
The five private schools where parents used the tax credits most are Cole Valley Christian School in Meridian, The Ambrose School in Meridian, Bishop Kelly High School in Boise, Nampa Christian School and Logos Classical Christian School in Moscow. Altogether, parents reported using almost $10.9 million in tax credits at those schools combined, or about 22% of the total money awarded.
“It’s hard enough for working parents to make ends meet without being asked to subsidize private school tuition for families who are better off than they are,” Sen. Janie Ward-Engelking, a Boise Democrat and retired teacher, said in a written statement Friday. “I want someone to explain to a rural parent why their child’s school can’t afford another teacher, but the state can afford to help a well-off family pay private school tuition. That’s a pretty lousy deal for rural Idaho.”
 How does the Idaho Parental Choice Tax Credit work?

The tax credit was created by the Idaho Legislature passing House Bill 93 in 2025.

CONTACT US



The tax credit provides up to $5,000 for qualifying expenses outside the public school system, including tuition and fees at a private school.
The tax credit provides up to $50 million annually in tax credits, minus administrative costs. 
After analyzing the tax credit program, the Idaho State Tax Commission reported that 6,875 parents received a tax credit, supporting a total of 12,216 Idaho students (some parents who received a tax credit had more than one student).
Among those 12,216 students, only 25.3% reported ever attending a public school previously. Just 4.3% of the students reported attending public school for the entire 2025 school year. 
Among those 12,216 students who benefited from a tax credit, less than 1%, or 600 students, had a disability. 
The overwhelming majority of the money for the tax credit has so far been spent on private school tuition, the report shows. More than 93.5% of funds went to tuition at private schools, while 2.8% of the funds have been spent on curricula materials, the report found. The remaining funds were split among tutoring, transportation, textbooks, prep courses and college placement, standardized tests and exams.

title: Democrat Eileen Laubacher unseats Rep. Lauren Boebert in Colorado’s 4th District
description: U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert will not return to Congress after voters of Colorado’s 4th Congressional District elected Democrat Eileen Laubacher to take her seat.  The Associated Press called the race at 12:53 p.m. Friday, when Laubacher had 48.8% of the vote over Boebert’s 47.9%. The AP estimated 99% of the votes in the race were […]
text:
Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert, left, and Democrat Eileen Laubacher appear at a debate hosted by 9News on Oct. 12, 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)U.S. Rep. Lauren Boebert will not return to Congress after voters of Colorado’s 4th Congressional District elected Democrat Eileen Laubacher to take her seat. 
The Associated Press called the race at 12:53 p.m. Friday, when Laubacher had 48.8% of the vote over Boebert’s 47.9%. The AP estimated 99% of the votes in the race were counted at the time.
Laubacher declared victory earlier this week, but Boebert declined to concede and emphasized that votes were still being counted to a group of reporters outside the Capitol Wednesday. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Boebert said she would not run in 2028 if she loses to Laubacher. She blamed the financial backing Laubacher received for her loss. 
“There’s a lot of money dumped on my head, and, I mean, I refuse to spend money like that again,” Boebert said. “I think it’s gross how much we dump into these races, and I was actually hoping to prove that seats just can’t be bought, but maybe I’ll be proven wrong. We’ll see.”
Laubacher attended orientation for new members of Congress this week. 
Since launching her campaign last year, Laubacher established a substantial fundraising advantage over her rivals, raising more money than every other candidate of either party in the race combined.
“This victory is historic. But making history means nothing if we don’t make a difference,” Laubacher said in a statement after she declared victory Monday. “My focus is simple: lower costs, protect healthcare, strengthen rural communities, take on corruption in both parties, and hold Washington accountable.”
The 4th District, which includes most of Douglas County and the Eastern Plains, was previously considered safely Republican. Some analyses of the Boebert-Laubacher race recently put the district in the “leans Republican” category. 
National Democrats looking to flip the district named it a top priority this election. The last Democrat to represent the district was former U.S. Rep. Betsy Markey, who was elected in 2008. She served one term.
Laubacher, a first-time candidate, is a retired Navy rear admiral and former National Security Council official. She was a longtime Republican and switched her party affiliation, first to unaffiliated, and then to Democratic in 2024. She defended that action at a debate against Boebert by claiming her belief in personal liberties is currently found in the Democratic Party and that the GOP she historically supported is “nearly unrecognizable.”
Boebert, of Windsor, was first elected to represent the 3rd District on the Western Slope, but she moved across the state after two terms when she nearly lost reelection in 2022. She is a longtime ally of President Donald Trump, but a rift arose earlier this year when Boebert campaigned alongside outgoing Kentucky U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, whom the president targeted for leading efforts to force a vote on releasing the Epstein files last year. 
Two other congressional seats in Colorado previously held by Republicans flipped to Democrats in last week’s election as part of a “blue tsunami” that swept the state and the country. Republican Rep. Gabe Evans lost his race to Democrat Manny Rutinel in the 8th District, and Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost his race to Democrat Jessica Killin in the 5th District. With Boebert’s loss, the state’s congressional delegation will favor Democrats 7-1.
Thursday was the deadline for overseas and military voters to submit their ballots and for voters with signature discrepancies to cure their ballots. County clerks have until the end of the day Friday to submit vote counts.
