name: National
title: Fueled by Democratic gains, women will hold a record of state legislative seats
description: The number of women serving in state legislatures will set a new record following strong Democratic performance in last week’s midterm elections.  Though many races remain too close to call, an analysis by the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University shows at least 2,559 women will serve in state legislatures. That represents […]
text:
Members of the Colorado House of Representatives work on the floor during session in May 2022. Colorado has among the nation’s highest rates of women serving in the state legislature. (Pema Baldwin for Colorado Newsline)The number of women serving in state legislatures will set a new record following strong Democratic performance in last week’s midterm elections. 
Though many races remain too close to call, an analysis by the Center for American Women and Politics at Rutgers University shows at least 2,559 women will serve in state legislatures. That represents nearly 35% of all state lawmakers and beats the 2026 record of 2,488 women in legislatures.
Election results also show a new record of six state legislatures will reach gender parity, or at least 50% women: Arizona, California, Colorado, Delaware, Nevada and New Mexico, the center found. 
Those gains follow a historic election in which Democrats swept control of Congress, flipped hundreds of state legislative seats and won a majority of governorships for the first time in 16 years. 
Women will hold a record number of seats in state senates and state houses, though the rise is driven solely by the increasing number of Democratic women elected. In fact, the number of Republican women will fall in state legislatures next year — from 867 today to at least 675 in upcoming sessions. 
“While these are impressive gains for the overall number of women and Democratic women in state legislatures around the country, this is a significant decline for Republican women,” Debbie Walsh, director of the Center for American Women and Politics, said in a Friday news release. “…It is past time the Republican Party put in the work to mitigate the ever-widening partisan gap in women’s representation.”
In historic night, voters elect 5 Black governors, including first woman, first Republican

Current election results show women will hold about 35% of all state legislative seats next year. That figure is currently 32.43%, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures. About 64% of the women currently in state legislatures are Democrats.
Across the political spectrum, research shows lower levels of political ambition among women. Women tend to underestimate their own qualifications, are more averse to competition and receive less recruitment and encouragement to run for office. Many women also work full-time and are primary caregivers. 
But the number of women serving in legislatures has increased nearly 40% over the past decade, according to government relations firm MultiState. Still, representation varies wildly: Women hold more than half of seats in Colorado, Nevada and New Mexico, but fewer than 15% of seats in West Virginia, South Carolina and Mississippi.
This election cycle also set a record for the number of women governors with at least 18 women slated to serve as their state’s executive. The midterms also notched other records: For the first time ever, five Black governors will serve simultaneously in the United States. Voters also elected the nation’s first Black woman governor, the first Black Republican governor and the first Native American woman governor. 
Congress will also see a record number of women serving. The center also tracked record numbers of Black, Latina and Native American women elected to Congress.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Prediction markets offered another way to forecast NC’s elections. But should voters trust them?
description: The growing popularity of platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket has brought prediction markets into mainstream political coverage, with their odds increasingly appearing on-screen alongside traditional polling and election forecasts. Those markets correctly anticipated Democrat Roy Cooper’s victory in North Carolina’s U.S. Senate race, but their performanc[...]
text:
Online prediction markets such as Kalshi and Polymarket are attracting scrutiny from state lawmakers, who argue the platforms are undermining state gambling regulations. (Photo by Alyssa Chen/Minnesota Reformer)The growing popularity of platforms such as Kalshi and Polymarket has brought prediction markets into mainstream political coverage, with their odds increasingly appearing on-screen alongside traditional polling and election forecasts.
Those markets correctly anticipated Democrat Roy Cooper’s victory in North Carolina’s U.S. Senate race, but their performance across the country was more mixed. 
Two North Carolina academics see both potential value and risks in their growing influence, particularly as the platforms become a more prominent part of how Americans follow elections.
Koleman Strumpf, an economics professor at Wake Forest University who studies prediction markets, said one of their biggest advantages is their ability to respond to new information in real time.
“The prediction markets are always open,” he said. “They’re always adjusting to information.”
Traditional polls offer a snapshot of voter preferences at a particular point in time. Prediction markets fluctuate as traders buy and sell based on what they believe will happen. 
Koleman Strumpf has taught in Wake Forest University’s Economics Department since 2017. (Photo: Wake Forest University)
A candidate’s odds can change as new polls are released, campaigns make announcements or election results begin coming in.
That continuous flow of information can make markets useful for tracking how a race is developing, Strumpf said. But he cautioned against assuming they are consistently more accurate than traditional polling. 
“Prediction markets and the poll modelers did about the same,” he said. “They each had their strengths and weaknesses.”
In North Carolina, prediction markets gave Cooper roughly a 97% chance of defeating Republican Michael Whatley ahead of Election Day. Cooper ultimately won by nearly 20 percentage points, defeating Whatley 58.8% to 39%.
But Strumpf said neither prediction markets nor traditional polling fully captured the extent of Democratic gains across the country. He pointed to several races where Democrats outperformed expectations, including contests in which markets had favored Republican candidates.
Still, Strumpf believes prediction markets will remain an important forecasting tool heading into the 2028 elections. 
Their ability to incorporate new information quickly, he said, gives them a role alongside polling and other election forecasts. 
Sean McKeever has worked in the Philosophy Department at Davidson College since 2005. (Photo: Davidson College)
Sean McKeever, a philosophy professor at Davidson College, is more skeptical of claims that prediction markets provide meaningful public benefit.
For markets to provide that broader value, they would need to offer better and more reliable information than traditional polls. McKeever said he has not seen convincing evidence that they do.
“I could be proven wrong in the future, but at this point I am not aware of any solid evidence that prediction markets perform better than polls,” he said. “The track records for both are mixed.”
McKeever said another measure of prediction markets’ value should be how far in advance they can provide useful information. Knowing who is likely to win just before Election Day offers limited benefit to voters, he argued.
“It is of little value to learn, say, 24 hours before election day who will win,” he said. “This is true of both polls and betting markets.”
A question of trust
Strumpf argued that concerns about manipulation should not be limited to just prediction markets. He said traditional polling can also be manipulated and influence political decisions.
“If we think we need to regulate and put the microscope on prediction markets, maybe we need to do the same thing with polls,” he said.
He pointed to a fabricated poll in Michigan’s 2026 Democratic U.S. Senate primary. Released by Wedgewood Polls in June, the poll showed state Sen. Mallory McMorrow trailing her opponents, U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens and Abdul El-Sayed.
McMorrow suspended her campaign less than a week later, saying the poll contributed to a loss of campaign support and momentum. 
Wedgewood later admitted that it faked the results as an experiment to demonstrate how easily false polling data could enter political coverage and election forecasts.
Strumpf said the stunt showed how misleading information can affect campaigns and public perceptions, even when it comes from a source presented as traditional polling.
Prediction markets diverge from traditional polls in NC races as Election Day nears

He also pointed to safeguards implemented by Kalshi, including identity verification and monitoring of accounts belonging to people who may have access to nonpublic political information. 
Kalshi is regulated by the U.S. Commodity Futures Trading Commission.
Strumpf said prediction market platforms have a financial incentive to prevent insider trading and manipulation because users are less likely to participate if they believe the markets are unfair.
McKeever said it’s true that people working closely with a campaign will often have access to insider information about a candidate that the public doesn’t, but the significance of that information is not always clear. 
He said campaign insiders might not be able to accurately predict which developments will matter most to voters.  
“Some scandals quickly sink a candidate while others quickly fade away,” he said. “Insiders might not be very reliable at telling one from another.

name: Florida Phoenix
title: Byron Donalds says he’ll address death penalty on ‘case-by-case’ basis
description: Among the more formidable responsibilities Byron Donalds will inherit upon being sworn in as governor of Florida in January is signing execution warrants once death-row inmates’ appeals and executive clemency processes have concluded. Florida and Pennsylvania are the only states giving their governors sole power to sign death warrants. And no governor has be[...]
text:
Corrections staff dismantle the death row lethal injection facility at San Quentin State Prison in San Quentin, Calif., in 2019. Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom this week announced a moratorium on the state’s death penalty. California is one of four states with moratoriums in place. (Photo by California Department of Corrections and Rehabilitation via Getty Images)Among the more formidable responsibilities Byron Donalds will inherit upon being sworn in as governor of Florida in January is signing execution warrants once death-row inmates’ appeals and executive clemency processes have concluded.
Florida and Pennsylvania are the only states giving their governors sole power to sign death warrants. And no governor has been more prolific in signing death warrants over the past two years than Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis. He signed 19 in 2025 and 22 so far this year.
Of the 37 executions that have taken place in the United States this year, more than half (19) have been in Florida, according to the Death Penalty Information Center. Three more are scheduled within the next month.
During a news conference in Hollywood Friday morning before he appeared at an education technology summit, Donalds was asked by a Phoenix reporter whether he would continue that pace of signing death warrants.
“For us, we’re just going to evaluate each case as it comes,” Donalds said. “I’m not trying to set a quota, or anything like that. We’re going to evaluate them on an individual basis, because you are talking about following through on a court decision for somebody who’s on death row. And so, we’ll just do that on a case-by-case basis. That’s the way that I’m going to proceed with that topic.”
Donalds’ comments came after he was asked to consider halting executions after he takes office.
Requests came from three exonerated death row inmates who during a press conference in Tallahassee Thursday called on the governor-elect to halt executions and review the state’s death penalty laws. Those three men are among 30 condemned prisoners exonerated in Florida since the death penalty was reintroduced in 1976.
Also, on Wednesday, the Rev. Dr. Jeff Hood, spiritual adviser to two of the death row inmates in Florida scheduled for execution in the next month, urged Donalds to commit to a six-month moratorium on executions.
“We’re asking for this to be a moment in which the state takes the opportunity to investigate what 40 executions in multiple years has cost,” Hood said during a remote press conference. “We are asking the governor to lead the way in taking the opportunity to see what pieces are not in place to support those who are being pushed and forced to carry these executions out. We should be knowledgeable about how much these executions are costing.”
Public approval for the death penalty for convicted murders in the United States has now dropped to 49%, the first time support has been below the majority level since 1971, according to a recent Gallup Poll. Gallup conducted the survey Oct. 1 -19, beginning the day after the failed execution attempt of Tennessee death row inmate Christa Pike.
Twenty-seven states still enforce the death penalty. However, four of them (Ohio, Oregon, Pennsylvania, and California), have executive holds on executions.
Jay Waagmeester contributed to this story.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: Fewer Kansas kindergarten students get measles vaccine as cases spiral nationwide
description: TOPEKA — Kansas has seen 14 cases of measles so far this year, avoiding the outbreaks being recorded in many states, even though measles vaccination rates for school kids dropped by four percentage points in the past five years. Measles cases have spiraled nationwide, topping 5,412 confirmed cases in a country where the disease was […]
text:
Cases of measles, shown here in a three-dimensional graphic represenatation of the virus particle, are growing nationwide even as fewer Kansas kindergarteners are receiving measles vaccinations this year than in the past five years. (Alissa Eckert/Centers for Disease Control and Prevention)TOPEKA — Kansas has seen 14 cases of measles so far this year, avoiding the outbreaks being recorded in many states, even though measles vaccination rates for school kids dropped by four percentage points in the past five years.
Measles cases have spiraled nationwide, topping 5,412 confirmed cases in a country where the disease was considered eliminated just 25 years ago.
Kansas reported eight cases in October and one in November, bringing the 2026 total to 14 cases, according to the state’s Infectious Disease Dashboard. 
Although the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention reported that 96% of cases nationally are outbreak-related, meaning they are being transmitted within the community, a Kansas Department of Health and Environment spokeswoman said Kansas cases were acquired primarily through travel.
“The Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE), in partnership with local health departments, have been investigating an increase in measles cases,” said agency spokeswoman Jill Bronaugh. “The cases are primarily linked to travel, with some secondary transmission within households.”
She said KDHE has been reaching out to healthcare providers across the state to increase awareness about measles. The agency also is providing rapid testing through the state public health laboratory, she said, and is offering the measles, mumps, and rubella, or MMR, vaccine.
Kansas tracks vaccination rates through its kindergarten enrollment data. MMR vaccinations dropped by just more than four percentage points since the 2019-20 school year when 94.47% of kindergarteners received the vaccine, compared to 90.26% in 2025-26.
Kansas parents claiming vaccine exemptions jumped from 2.12% in 2019-20 school year to 4.46% in 2025-26. 
Seven Kansas counties reported less than 75% required MMR vaccine coverage in 2025-26, compared to two in 2019-20.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Montana seeing increased hospitalizations, deaths from influenza
description: Influenza has killed three Montanans this year and resulted in 96 hospitalizations, a significant increase over last year, according to state health officials. Officials with the Department of Health and Human Services announced on Friday that last year, just four Montanans had been hospitalized from influenza and the state had recorded no deaths. All three [...]
text:
Montana Department of Public Health and Human Services (Photo by Eric Seidle for the Daily Montanan).Influenza has killed three Montanans this year and resulted in 96 hospitalizations, a significant increase over last year, according to state health officials.
Officials with the Department of Health and Human Services announced on Friday that last year, just four Montanans had been hospitalized from influenza and the state had recorded no deaths.
All three flu-related deaths occurred this month and health officials are urging Montanans to take precautions to protect themselves and their families.
“The same precautions that protect against flu also protect against COVID-19, pneumonia, and RSV,” said DPHHS Director Douglas Harrington in a statement. “Prioritize your immunizations, wash your hands, clean frequently touched surfaces, stay home when sick, and seek testing and treatment early.”
Between October 2025 and May 2026, Montana reported  more than 15,400 flu cases, 760 hospitalizations, and 32 deaths. Of those hospitalized, 75% had not received a flu vaccine or flu vaccine status was unknown. COVID-19 accounted for more than 5,300 cases, more than 350 hospitalizations, and 28 deaths.
Montanans can track respiratory illnesses cases in the state through the Respiratory Virus Illness Dashboard, maintained by DPHHS, which provides weekly data updates on flu, COVID-19, and RSV (Respiratory Syncytial Virus) activity statewide during respiratory illness season.
The department also recommends speaking with a doctor about getting vaccinated.
Effective vaccines are widely available through local health departments, pharmacies, and providers.

Influenza: Recommended every season for everyone 6 months and older. One dose protects through the entire season (October to May).
COVID-19 (2026-27): Recommended for all adults 18 and older and for children 6 months to 17 years with weakened immune systems. Other children may be vaccinated based on shared decision-making between parents and their provider.
Pneumococcal: Protects against a deadly form of bacterial pneumonia. Recommended for children under 5, adults 50 and older, and anyone at increased risk.
RSV: Adults 50 and older may be vaccinated after talking with their provider. Pregnant women at 32 to 36 weeks during RSV season may be vaccinated to protect their infants.
RSV antibodies: During RSV season, recommended for infants under 8 months whose mothers were not vaccinated during pregnancy, and for children 8 to 19 months with certain health conditions.

Symptoms of COVID-19, flu, RSV, and other respiratory illnesses are similar and include fever, cough, sore throat, headache, body aches, and fatigue. Anyone with symptoms or a positive test should stay home and limit contact with others while sick.
Health officials also recommend washing hands with soap and water often, covering coughs and sneezes, testing for disease before being around others, especially those at risk of severe illness, and wearing a mask in close settings if you cannot stay home.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Medicaid work rules don’t apply to Native Americans. They could still lose coverage.
authors: Andrew Jones, Katheryn Houghton, KFF Health News, Jazmin Orozco Rodriguez, KFF Health News
description: CHEROKEE, N.C. — Two months before the deadline to implement new Medicaid work requirements, states had yet to receive detailed guidance from federal health officials on how to exclude Native Americans from those rules, leading to a patchwork of eligibility checks that pose challenges for qualified enrollees trying to keep their health insurance. President D[...]
text:
Gwynneth Wildcatt and James Burns, citizens of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians, are leaders in the tribal-run healthcare system. They expressed concerns that work rules debuting in North Carolina next year could put tribal citizens’ Medicaid at risk. (Andrew Jones/KFF Health News)CHEROKEE, N.C. — Two months before the deadline to implement new Medicaid work requirements, states had yet to receive detailed guidance from federal health officials on how to exclude Native Americans from those rules, leading to a patchwork of eligibility checks that pose challenges for qualified enrollees trying to keep their health insurance.
President Donald Trump’s One Big Beautiful Bill Act excluded Native Americans from having to meet the work requirements to keep their Medicaid eligibility. But the rules issued by the Centers for Medicare & Medicaid Services didn’t provide a standardized system to help states identify Native Americans who should be excluded, leaving states to figure it out for themselves.
Native leaders fear the limited guidance will mean a repeat of the Medicaid “unwinding” in 2023, when states resumed checking qualifications for eligibility after a covid-era pause. An estimated 850,000 Native Americans lost coverage by May 2024, often for paperwork reasons.
The latest carve-out for American Indians and Alaska Natives also left out some Indigenous people, such as Native Hawaiians.
“I’m nervous. I’m extremely nervous,” said James Burns, who oversees the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ Medicaid managed-care program in the Qualla Boundary, the tribe’s sovereign land in western North Carolina. “When you look at any state that’s rolled out Medicaid work requirements, the unintended consequences have been vast, and that’s what we don’t want to happen.”
CMS published its guidance on work requirements in June, instructing states to use data they already have before potentially asking Native enrollees for additional records. But the rule didn’t set a standard process for states to prove Native American status, allowing states to raise the threshold for proof higher than federal requirements.
The rule also didn’t require states to share data with tribes, coordinate with Native health providers, or advise on managed-care plans like the one Burns oversees. Managed-care programs contract with the state to provide Medicaid benefits and connect patients to providers when they need care.
In July, a tribal advisory group for CMS recommended that the agency require states to allow Native Americans to self-attest to their eligibility as the standard proof. The group also wanted CMS to require states to share their Medicaid eligibility data with tribal health programs to catch when tribal citizens are mistakenly kicked off Medicaid. The National Council of Urban Indian Health pushed for similar guidance.
Native leaders expect additional guidance to come, said A.C. Locklear, CEO of the National Indian Health Board, which advocates for federally recognized tribes. But Locklear said that if CMS waits until December to issue more specific guidance on the exemption, states will have already determined their own processes. CMS did not respond to KFF Health News’ questions about whether it planned to provide more guidance.
“There’s 30-plus states who are independently repurposing their administrative processes for this, and they really all happen in a vacuum,” Locklear said. “That’s why it’s really important for CMS to provide guidance.”

The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians is based in the mountains of western North Carolina. Its citizens with Medicaid are exempt from the GOP’s work rules but could lose coverage if the program rolls out with flaws. (Andrew Jones/KFF Health News)
Falling through the cracks
KFF Health News asked 14 states how they would apply the exemption and found that they plan to ask tribal citizens to prove their status in different ways.
Arizona, Colorado, Montana, Nevada, New Mexico, and Washington plan to let enrollees identify their tribal status on their Medicaid application forms. The Arizona Health Care Cost Containment System, the state’s Medicaid agency, will continue to allow tribal members to self-identify, then will confirm their status through the state’s data on services received through the Indian Health Service or tribally run health centers.
South Dakota linked its claims system to identify people served by IHS, according to the state Department of Social Services. Oklahoma relies on a data-sharing agreement with tribes dating to 2022, according to Cherokee Nation Health Services. North Carolina requires a tribal enrollment card, a tribal census record, or confirmation from the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ Tribal Option managed-care program.
“There’s still going to be folks that fall through the cracks,” said Locklear, a citizen of the Lumbee Tribe of North Carolina.
In North Carolina, 3,400 Native Medicaid enrollees are verified as eligible for the exemption from the work requirement, health department spokesperson Summer Tonizzo said, and those enrollees will be automatically exempted. But the state doesn’t know how many more people might be eligible for an exemption through tribal citizenship.
And Native Americans who don’t live in states where their tribes are based may face challenges in affirming their status. About 87% of Native people live outside of what the U.S. Census Bureau calls tribal statistical areas, such as reservations, according to 2020 data.
A Navajo Nation citizen living in Connecticut, for example, may have a difficult time being identified by the state because it doesn’t have a close working relationship with the tribe based in the southwestern U.S., said Liz Malerba, director of policy and legislative affairs for the United South and Eastern Tribes. She’s a citizen of the Mohegan Tribe in Connecticut.
Most states didn’t say how many Native enrollees they had verified as exempt from the work requirement. Several said they don’t track tribal affiliation, noting that ethnicity questions that would show Native status on applications are optional. In a comment on CMS’ work requirements guidance, the National Council of Urban Indian Health warned CMS that “not all states collect data on their American Indian and Alaska Native residents.”
States, tribes prepare for workload
The Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ health system has spent five years building its managed-care program, which is the only tribal-run Medicaid managed-care program in the nation, said Gwynneth Wildcatt, a director with the Cherokee Indian Hospital Authority who sits on North Carolina’s Medicaid Beneficiary Advisory Council. All Medicaid enrollees in that tribe who need exemptions have them, thanks to that program, Wildcatt said.
A close connection with the state has made verifying its citizens for work requirement exemptions simple for the tribe, Wildcatt added, because its program is already integrated into the state Medicaid system. She’s a citizen of the tribe.

Work rules that begin in 2027 could risk health coverage for Native Medicaid enrollees in North Carolina, say Gwynneth Wildcatt and James Burns, leaders of the Eastern Band of Cherokee Indians’ health system. (Andrew Jones/KFF Health News)
In Montana, Native people who self-declare their tribal status for the work requirements won’t be required to provide additional proof, said Jon Ebelt, a spokesperson for the state Department of Public Health and Human Services.
The state has one of the highest percentages of American Indian and Alaska Native residents in the nation and began work requirement checks in July. It’s one of four states, alongside Nebraska, Arkansas, and Georgia, that are doing those scans ahead of the Jan. 1 federal deadline. Iowa begins its program on Dec. 1.
But Native leaders said Montana officials hadn’t clearly communicated how Medicaid enrollees could prove their Native status when those checks began. The state saw one of the nation’s sharpest declines in enrollment during the Medicaid unwinding as people struggled to navigate a backlogged system. Most enrollees who lost coverage did so due to paperwork problems, which rippled through Native communities.
Jason Smith, a citizen of the Confederated Salish and Kootenai Tribes who leads the Montana Consortium for Urban Indian Health, said clinics serving Indigenous patients are still working to reenroll members who lost Medicaid during that time.
Smith said the state has done a good job addressing tribal priorities while implementing work requirements. But he’s still concerned about whether its system is ready to handle the workload of the new mandates. As of September, Montana still hadn’t hired the number of workers officials estimated are needed to handle the workload. And federal data shows Montanans can face long waits on the state’s helpline.
“Have they improved their communication and outreach?” Smith said. “Will people be there answering phones? It will take time to see.”
Have you tried to prove your eligibility for Medicaid under new rules that require people to show they are working, going to school, or participating in another qualifying activity? Click here to contact KFF Health News.

title: ‘Extraordinary’ support saves Sternberg Museum as university develops new operational model
description: TOPEKA — After Sternberg Museum of Natural History received a lifeline through a $1 million matching grant, Fort Hays State University officials say more than $600,000 has been raised to help reimagine the museum’s future. “The future of the Sternberg Museum of Natural History is brighter today thanks to an extraordinary outpouring of support from […]
text:
Donations of $600,000 have flowed to the Sternberg Museum of Natural History in Hays, and with a matching grant of $1 million, will help to keep the facility open. (Submitted by Fort Hays State University)TOPEKA — After Sternberg Museum of Natural History received a lifeline through a $1 million matching grant, Fort Hays State University officials say more than $600,000 has been raised to help reimagine the museum’s future.
“The future of the Sternberg Museum of Natural History is brighter today thanks to an extraordinary outpouring of support from alumni, donors, community members, and friends of Fort Hays State University,” a university news release said.
The university announced in September it would close the museum this year because of funding cuts by the Legislature that made the annual shortfall in the museum budget difficult to maintain. Sternberg’s budget of $1.2 million is supported by just $400,000 in revenue.
Fans of the museum spoke out in support of keeping it open, and the Bob and Pat Schmidt Foundation offered a $1 million matching donation to save it. The new release said $600,000 has been raised from more than 1,400 donors, which when added to the matching donation, gives the university $1.2 million to support the museum.
“What began as a challenge became a powerful reminder of what is possible when people come together around a shared purpose,” said FHSU president Tisa Mason in a news release. “The response to Sternberg has been inspiring.”
The news release said university officials will create a new model that will support Sternberg’s future.
“This is an opportunity to strengthen the museum’s role as a center for learning, research, engagement, and inspiration,” Mason said in the news release.
Provost Jill Arensdorf and Werth College dean Mark Arant will work with museum faculty and staff to evaluate collections, operations, educational programming, and the museum’s broader academic mission. 
A volunteer advisory group including business, nonprofit and governmental organizations, will consider potential partnerships for the facility, the news release said.

name: VTDigger
title: The myth of the fleeing rich just won’t die
description:
If income taxes really drove the wealthy away, they’d have crossed into tax-free New Hampshire long ago.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  The myth of the fleeing rich just won’t die.
text:
Dear Editor,
Ali Jalili’s recent letter repeats a seemingly immortal contention: that raising taxes on high-income earners will drive them out of state. It’s simply wrong on all counts, but it just won’t die. In fact, the evidence against it is overwhelming. 
Americans move in large numbers every year. The Census Bureau tracks these moves and lists explanations. The top reasons given are housing, family, jobs and weather. Taxes do not even appear on the list.  
There have been numerous academic studies of Americans moving from one state to another. Most conclude that taxes are not a major factor. IRS data has long shown that people moving into Vermont earn more on average than those leaving. 
Common sense dictates the same conclusion. Surely, high-income people know Vermont has higher-than-average income taxes and New Hampshire next door has none. Even the anecdotal evidence confirms the same thing. Other than the old joke about the Vermonter who moves across the river because he “just couldn’t take another Vermont winter,” most stories are of Vermonters moving south, usually to Florida, not New Hampshire. If the old saw were true, then those with high incomes living here would have moved across the border long ago, and newcomers would gravitate to New Hampshire, not Vermont.
Jalili suggests that “unlike other very high-tax states, such as California, New York and New Jersey, Vermont simply doesn’t have many high-income individuals.” But since the top 1% (or whatever percentage is used) leaves out, by definition, 99% of the population everywhere — not just in Vermont — the number of people subject to the tax surcharge is always small everywhere. 
Jalili is particularly concerned about doctors, but there is a shortage of doctors everywhere in the country, not just in Vermont. This argument depends on two points, and I suspect neither is true. The first is simple demography: Does Vermont have fewer doctors per capita than other states? Are more of them leaving than coming? How does Vermont compare with other states? 

READ MORE

Second, even if the demographic answers show that Vermont has a larger doctor problem than other places, which I very much doubt, why? Are the reasons similar to those discussed for the population in general — i.e., family, weather and housing — or is there evidence that taxes are consequential? 
Finally, Jalili also cites “consecutive declines in population over the past two years following the pandemic bump” as evidence. But income tax rates in Vermont haven’t changed since 2018. Jalili’s statement contains a much more likely explanation: There was an incoming demographic bump during the pandemic years and then a slight decline as life normalized. 
As everywhere in America, high-income people have been the greatest beneficiaries of economic policies that have dramatically favored them while lower earners have seen little or negative change. Accordingly, high-income folks can afford to pay higher taxes. Depending on the specifics, they may not even have to give up all of their excess gains. 
It’s long past time to raise taxes on the highest-income earners in Vermont. 
John GreenbergMarlboro, Vt.

name: WyoFile
title: Dubois ranchers balk at oil and gas leases in treasured wildlife habitat in Shoshone, Bridger-Teton national forests
description:
Wildlife managers are navigating concerns over a new development two years after they opted not to designate a mule deer migration route in the Upper Wind River Basin.
The post Dubois ranchers balk at oil and gas leases in treasured wildlife habitat in Shoshone, Bridger-Teton national forests appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
After losing its last timber mill and seeing its economy sputter for decades, there’s a renewed vibrancy in the town of Dubois.
There’s been a stimulus effect from the National Museum of Military Vehicles, but the small community’s modern vitality is all wrapped up in the region’s outdoor splendors, a benefit of its location along the eastern slope of wildlife-rich Togwotee Pass. 
“This community is about tourism, hunting, fishing, outdoor recreation and second homes, certainly,” said Budd Betts, a former state lawmaker who represented Dubois in the Wyoming House of Representatives during the 1990s.
Betts, the longtime owner of Absaroka Ranch, is one of several large landowners who are vocalizing concerns about an oil and gas play in the Absaroka and Wind River Range foothills not far from the northwest Fremont County town of roughly 1,000 people.
“It’s just not consistent with where this community is heading,” Betts told WyoFile. “It’s not appropriate for this area, and I’m not speaking as some kind of ‘refuse to oil and gas’ — in my time in the Legislature, I established the bonafides for supporting this state’s energy industry.” 
The potential for oil and gas development in the Shoshone National Forest above Dubois could take a step toward reality as soon as next summer. 

Wyoming deer hunt area 128, which surrounds the town of Dubois, is known for producing trophy mule deer bucks. Expansive oil and gas leasing has been proposed within a migration corridor that cuts through the region. (Budd Betts)

Although there are no active oil and gas wells in the area, in August a company named Wyoming Energy Consultants nominated nearly 70,000 acres spread across 38 parcels for inclusion in a federal oil and gas lease auction that’s set for June 2027. 
The Casper-based business’ “expressions of interest” for leases on the national forest right around Dubois amounts to more than 55% of all the acreage proposed statewide for the quarterly auction, which is administered by the Bureau of Land Management. Across Wyoming, there are 104 parcels covering 123,166 acres being assessed for inclusion in the auction. 
WyoFile’s inquiry to Wyoming Energy Consultants yielded no response. 
The parcels near Dubois are located both to the north and south of U.S. Highway 26/287 and contain rich wildlife habitat used by the 7,000-animal Wiggins Fork Elk Herd and roughly 4,000-animal Dubois Mule Deer Herd. The mule deer herd in particular is renowned for producing trophy bucks. Acquiring a limited tag to hunt there, in area 128, is nearly impossible: There were 3,834 applicants for 60 licenses during this fall’s hunting season, a 1.5% draw rate. 
The landscapes those ungulates move through to reach their seasonal ranges are now at risk of being leased, a precursor to developing well pads. 
Trophy bucks on the go
Large reaches of the prospective drilling zone overlap with the Upper Wind River Mule Deer Migration Corridor. In 2024, under former director Brian Nesvik’s leadership, the Wyoming Game and Fish Department opted to “identify” that migration route but not designate and protect it under the state’s migration policy. At the time, agency staff reasoned that there were not substantial enough “threats” and “risks” to the “functionality” of the migration route to justify going through the time-consuming designation process. Some wildlife advocacy groups agreed that the corridor wasn’t in need of protection, but there were exceptions. 
Now, just two years later, a development threat that could disrupt the migration is emerging. 





Nearly 19,500 acres of the proposed oil and gas leases overlap with the Upper Wind River Mule Deer Migration Corridor, which has been identified but not protected. (Map from The Wilderness Society)

According to an analysis provided by Nick Dobric, a Wilderness Society employee who lives in Dubois, nearly 19,500 acres of the proposed oil and gas leases overlap with the Wind River deer migration corridor. Within that area, there are nooks and crannies that the smaller-than-desired deer herd particularly depends upon. More than 3,000 acres of the leases overlap “high-use” portions of the migration, more than 5,400 acres overlap “stopover” habitat and another 1,400 overlapping acres fall on joint high-use and stopover habitat. 
It’s not just mule deer that depend on the area, though. 
“It’s a major thoroughfare for everything that lives up [in the Shoshone National Forest] in the summer,” said Jon Robinett, who recently retired after more than three decades of managing the Diamond G Ranch. “Elk, deer, antelope, bears — everything that eats grass — comes through there.” 
Roadbuilding to access the exploratory “wildcat” wells would be particularly impactful on the area, Robinett worries. 
“Those roads would become more or less public,” he said. “You’d get an impact on recreation, hunting. To me, the downside is the detriment to wildlife.” 
Jeremy Prine, whose family has owned the Ram’s Horn Ranch for nearly eight decades, is on the same page. He supports the oil and gas industry and uses its products everyday, but said that the Dunoir Valley isn’t an “appropriate” spot for an exploration project.   
“I definitely don’t support oil and gas leases on the national forest in these proposed areas, just due to their wildness,” Prine said. “A lot of those places are starting to disappear.” 
Jon Robinett checks a trail camera in the wildlife-rich areas above the Diamond G Ranch at the head of the Dunoir Valley outside Dubois in 2014. (Ryan Dorgan)
Betts, Robinett and Prine all ranch on the north side of the highway, and they pointed out that companies have prospected for oil and gas in their corner of the Absaroka Range historically. Wildcat wells from the 1970s and 80s were a bust, Betts said, and were capped and reclaimed. 
“This was kind of puzzling,” he said, “because the Upper Wind River Valley has some of the lowest oil and gas potential in the state.” 
Longtime Dubois resident Robert Hoskins was also perplexed. 
“I have no earthly idea why Dubois is a target, other than that they’re going after everything,” he said. “This is the Trump administration.” 
Wyoming Energy Consultants’ bid to acquire drilling rights on tens of thousands of acres of the Wind River and Absaroka Range foothills isn’t the first time in the second Trump administration that there’s been an outcry over leasing environmentally sensitive parts of Wyoming. Last fall, another Casper-based company, Kirkwood Oil and Gas, sought to lease acreage in the Golden Triangle, among the most biologically rich reaches of the sagebrush-steppe biome remaining on Earth. Many of the most controversial parcels were deleted, however, because oil and gas leasing there wasn’t allowed under the BLM’s land-use plan. 
Next steps
That history could repeat. Roughly 39,000 acres that Wyoming Energy Consultants nominated for leasing in the national forest is located in areas that were closed to leasing in the Shoshone’s 2015 forest plan revision, according to calculations provided by Dobric.
Those nominations will likely be dropped by the BLM during the lease sale vetting process. The BLM’s taking public comment until Nov. 27. 
But another 30,200 acres of parcels are located in areas of the Shoshone deemed suitable for oil and gas leasing, including the migration corridor acreages listed above.





(U.S. Geological Survey/Ungulate Migrations of the Western United States, Volume 1)

Wyoming wildlife managers were also caught off guard by the oil and gas play. Will Schultz, Game and Fish’s habitat protection supervisor, told WyoFile that the proposed leases have put the department in a “unique situation.” 
“This is the first time in several years where we’ve seen leases proposed on national forests,” Schultz said. 
It’s also one of the first times, he said, that state wildlife managers have navigated oil and gas leasing in an “identified,” but not “designated,” migration corridor. 
If the corridor had been designated, the up-for-auction leases would be affixed with stipulations that recognized Wyoming’s migration policy. Although the policy is broadly permissive of development, those stipulations can also be restrictive, especially in the joint high-use and stopover habitat, where the policy states “surface disturbance should be avoided.” 
In the absence of a designation, Game and Fish will do what it can to protect the migration route, Schultz said. 
“It would take a lot of coordination to ensure the [migration] functionality is maintained,” he said.
For the time being, Schultz is in talks with the BLM and national forests. (A relatively small portion of the proposed leases, about 3,300 acres, is located west of the Continental Divide on the Bridger-Teton National Forest.) 
Another option for Game and Fish is to restart its process of formally protecting the migration corridor. 
“This particular leasing situation is an opportunity for us to reevaluate that,” Schultz said. 
Wyoming Game and Fish commissioners are tasked with making recommendations about migration designations. Ultimately, however, the decision would be made by Wyoming’s Gov.-elect, Eric Barlow, who takes office in January.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Secretary of State Watson faces criticism over Mississippi election management mishaps
description: Secretary of Sate Michael Watson speaks during the Mississippi Council on Economic Education’s 2026 Forum on American Enterprise at the Jackson Convention Complex on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026.
text:
Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson is facing criticism from voting rights advocates and lawmakers after his office applied error-filled consumer credit data to voter rolls, a move that led to a high number of Mississippians having to cast affidavit ballots on Election Day, or simply not voting. 
As the national press, election lawyers and voting rights groups flocked to Mississippi to watch a close U.S. Senate race between Democrat Scott Colom and Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Watson caught the brunt of criticism as deficiencies in Mississippi’s election laws were exposed.
Four Republican legislators told Mississippi Today they were disappointed in Watson and thought his handling of the credit data was a dereliction of conservative leadership.
One GOP lawmaker, who was granted anonymity to speak candidly about a powerful statewide official in the same political party, said he wasn’t angry with Watson, but believed the secretary’s idea to keep using the credit data was a poor decision “especially considering that clerks and commissioners have been saying for months that the data was not correct.” 
READ MORE:  Secretary of state ignored demands to reinstate voters inactivated by unverified Experian data days before midterms: ‘Harm is falling on eligible voters’
Watson defended the use of the credit data and said his agency the last two years had rolled out two pilot programs for local election workers to become acclimated to the data and that during that period they “didn’t hear a word” from the local leaders.
Laura Antonow, a Lafayette County election commissioner, previously told Mississippi Today that when Lafayette County became the first county to use the credit data, the commission informed Watson’s office that the data included incorrect information. 
The secretary of state speculated that the reason a firestorm has erupted over the credit data is because of the closeness of the U.S. Senate race. 
“We’ve got to have accurate data, and I don’t apologize for having clean voter rolls,” Watson told reporters Tuesday. 
When Watson was asked if he thought the credit company’s address data was still reliable, his communications director ended the interview, whisked the secretary away and said “we’re not getting into all of that.” 
A sample ballot is on display at Briarwood Presbyterian Church in Jackson during the midterm elections on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Watson, in a later written statement, called the anonymous Republican legislators “weak-kneed” and he continued to stand behind his actions. 
“The same ‘Republican’ legislators who voted for election integrity are now against clean voter rolls?” Watson said. “You cannot simply walk the conservative side of the fence when it’s convenient for you. You’re either for election integrity or you’re not.” 
The Secretary of State’s Office spent $50,000 to run nearly 2 million checks of Experian’s commercial data against registered voters’ addresses, and for the first time this election cycle that data was used to maintain rolls in every county. In the contract, Experian said it could not guarantee the “accuracy or reliability” of its data, and Watson’s office signed off on that disclaimer. 
Mississippi Today published an analysis in March that found incorrect information mistakenly led to the inactivation of legitimate voters ahead of the primaries. Experian has faced years of legal challenges at the state and federal levels, including a now-settled 2014 lawsuit by Mississippi, over errors in the company’s credit reports – including incorrect addresses.
READ MORE: Inside the secretary of state’s $50,000 deal to use Experian’s unverified information that he said would ‘strengthen’ election integrity
Watson said Tuesday that his agency dropped Experian at some point this year and switched to IDI Data, a company that sells identity records to businesses and the government, because he thought the new company offered “a better product.” 
The secretary of state has also pointed out that local officials are legally required to verify voter information before changing registrations, and any decisions to place voters on an inactive status is the decision of the local election officials. 
If local officials place a voter on inactive status, those voters are not purged from the voter rolls. Inactive status voters are still eligible to cast an affidavit ballot. 
But several Republican critics have pointed to the fact that Watson’s office chose to put credit data in front of counties in the first place and wonder if voters who were wrongly flagged as inactive grew frustrated by not being on the poll books and left without casting a vote at all.  
The problems with Experian weren’t the only mishap by Watson’s office that drew criticism as the final votes were tallied in the nail-biting U.S. Senate race. 
READ MORE: DeSoto County moved more voters to inactive in the leadup to Election Day than any other.
In the days following the Nov. 3 election, as only hundreds of votes separated the candidates, it became clear that the outstanding affidavit ballots could determine the outcome of the race. 
Affidavit ballots are filled out when a person doesn’t bring a valid form of ID to the polls, or there’s a discrepancy with their voter records. These ballots can then be “cured” to ensure they’re accepted, which had to be done by Nov. 10. 
Voting rights groups, student organizers and community groups sprang into action ahead of the deadline. They repeatedly called election officials and even organized carpools to the offices of local circuit clerks.  
Amid the chaos, the nonprofit law firm Mississippi Center for Justice noticed that the secretary of state’s election calendar did not include a deadline for “pending” voters to provide proof of citizenship so that their affidavit ballots are counted. 
That requirement imposed on voters arose due to the Legislature’s 2026 passage of the SHIELD Act, a law that requires local election officials to verify voters’ citizenship using a federal immigration database and to audit voter rolls for potential noncitizens.
Watson said he he was “especially proud” of the Legislature for passing the measure. In the days following the closely watched U.S. Senate race, it became clear his office did not know how to interpret parts of the law. 
An attorney with the Center for Justice noticed the deadline was absent from the secretary of state’s election calendar and emailed Watson’s office to request that it be added. The center said voters who had their ballots rejected due to the citizenship proof requirement were left in the dark about the deadline for ensuring their votes counted. 
In a Nov. 6 email to the center obtained by Mississippi Today, Laura Henderson-Courtney, an attorney with the secretary of state’s Elections Division, wrote that her office could not definitively state whether the deadline in the SHIELD Act was five calendar days or five business days. 
“Our office is not authorized to interpret statutes,” Henderson-Courtney wrote. “We intend to submit that issue for the Mississippi Attorney General’s office for review. Once we have some direction from the Mississippi Attorney General on this issue, we will be glad to move forward in the future with posting that to our calendar.”
That did not happen before the ballot curing deadline for voters, and state government officials still don’t have a clear answer. A person close to the situation in the AG’s office said on Thursday that they had no record of receiving anything from the secretary of state’s office. Watson told Mississippi Today on Friday that his office was still in the process of preparing the submission.
Ballot bags are piled on the floor, Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, at the Rankin County Election Commission in Brandon as the U.S. Senate race between Democratic candidate Scott Colom and the incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith remained uncalled.  Credit: AP Photo/Ellen Schmidt
In a statement, Harya Tarekegn, director of advocacy and policy for the Mississippi Center for Justice, said Watson has made elections less accessible to Mississippians who can vote. She said he used “unreliable Experian data for months to prevent thousands of eligible Mississippians from casting a regular ballot” and “championed the SHIELD Act, then never determined or published the deadline for voters who would be forced to vote by affidavit ballot then cure.” 
“His focus has not been on ensuring Mississippi has secure elections that all eligible Mississippians can vote in,” Tarekegn said. “It has been on implementing unnecessary barriers through unreliable means and it continues to show.” 
Sen.-elect Colom said on Tuesday that Watson needs to conduct a press conference to “answer some tough questions” and apologize to Mississippians.
“Nobody has gotten a straight answer from him as to why he used Experian to verify these voter rolls,” Colom said. “He created chaos. He created this problem.” 
Colom also said he believes the Legislature should pass a law banning Watson’s office from using commercial credit data if Watson won’t stop using it voluntarily.  
Democratic state Rep. Zakiya Summers of Jackson, a former elections commissioner, told Mississippi Today that she plans to introduce such a bill next legislative session. 
The secretary of state could face political headwinds over the recent election. Watson announced in April that he is running as a Republican for lieutenant governor, and was largely viewed as a shoo-in for the seat. 
Now, several Republican politicians are speculating whether the scrutiny of Watson’s handling of the recent election will attract a primary challenger or give a Democrat enough ammunition to mount a general election campaign.  
But the 48-year-old Republican has a lengthy political resume, would likely have his home region of the Coast supporting him, and is sitting on more than $2.4 million in cash, according to campaign finance reports. 
In his statement to Mississippi Today, Watson commended the work of election workers and said his office worked with them to ensure the election was secure. 
“We have followed the law as passed by the Legislature and the only reason it has come under such scrutiny is because of the razor thin margin in our U.S. Senate race,” Watson said. “Nothing has changed. The process is working and the law is being followed.”
Madeline Nguyen contributed to this report.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Black voters’ enthusiasm drives historic gains for SC Democrats
description: Black and straight-ticket voters propelled Democrats to their biggest election gains in South Carolina's modern history, according to an analysis of election data.
text:
State Rep. Jermaine Johnson, Democrats' nominee for governor, speaks at a rally in the McGirt Auditorium at Emmett Scott Recreation Center in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Thursday Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Katharine Wilson/SC Daily Gazette)COLUMBIA — Black and straight-ticket voters propelled Democrats to their biggest election gains in South Carolina’s modern history, according to an analysis of election data.
Annie Andrews’ victory over appointed U.S. Sen. Darline Graham marked Democrats’ first statewide win in 20 years, as well as the first time that South Carolina voters sent a Democrat to the U.S. Senate since Fritz Holling’s last re-election in 1998. Plus, Democrats flipped a U.S. House seat and 10 state House seats.
State Rep. Jermaine Johnson also came within 5 percentage points of becoming South Carolina’s first Black governor.
While he and other Black nominees for statewide office — a slate that included Democrats for superintendent of education, agriculture commissioner, treasurer, comptroller general, and secretary of state — fell short, the enthusiasm of Black voters made Democrats’ flips possible.
“Black voters are more than the base. They’re the heartbeat, the soul, and they showed up in a way that benefited all of our candidates,” Democratic Party Chair Christale Spain told reporters last week. “So, it was really the driving force behind our base turnout, and it was monumental.”
Black voters made up a quarter of all voters in the midterm, turning out in numbers close to the last presidential election, according to state election data certified this week. While it’s impossible to know precisely how many of them voted for Democrats, exit polls show Black voters overwhelmingly vote blue.
Election data shows a big jump in Black voters from the last midterm four years ago. Exactly how big is unclear, since it wasn’t until 2024 that the state separately reported the numbers of Black, Hispanic, Asian and Native American voters. Before then, the breakdown was simply white and non-white.
However, there were 29% more Black voters participating in this month’s election than all non-white voters in 2022. Given in numbers, the nearly 503,200 Black voters participating this year compares to about 390,500 non-white voters in 2022.
More Black voters cast a ballot for the Nov. 3 election than all non-white voters in any midterm election going back to at least 1986, the first midterm when the state reported demographic data.
Overall, fewer voters participated compared to 2024, which is unsurprising since more voters come out for presidential elections.
However, while total participation fell 20%, the number of Black voters decreased by just 7%, from about 542,200 in 2024.

Excitement for Johnson, only the second Black major-party nominee for governor in state history, benefited Andrews’ contest as well as down-ballot races, said Kwadwo Poku-Agyemang, director of the Public Opinion and Social Behavior Research Institute at Claflin University.
A poll he conducted in mid-October showed more than 40% of respondents most interested in the governor’s race, with Johnson winning.
“When a candidate really compels you to show up, often you take some of that love and spread it among all members of their party,” Poku-Agyemang said.
On Election Day, hundreds of students from Claflin and South Carolina State universities, two neighboring historically Black colleges in Orangeburg, marched together to the polling precinct on SC State’s campus chanting “My vote matters!” and carrying signs. Students lined up to cast their ballot.
Johnson was there to cheer them on. Ten days earlier, he and Andrews mingled with students at SC State’s homecoming football game.
“Every major change this state has ever seen started with young people deciding they were done waiting,” he wrote on social media after the march. “You are carrying that same torch right now, and I could not be prouder to have you at the front of this New SC.”
The “march to the polls” was indicative of a surge in the normally elusive young voters.
Almost 100,000 South Carolinians ages 18 to 24 voted this election, or nearly 30,000 more than in 2022. That represents a hike of more than 42%.
“They were energized and they were engaged,” said Roshanda Pratt, a communications strategist on Johnson’s campaign, noting her daughter was among Claflin students voting for the first time.
“It was no longer their ‘parents’ election,'” she said about young voters dealing directly with student loans and gas prices. “They knew their voice was just as important.”
The next age bracket, ages 25 to 44, saw the second-highest increase, with 28% more voters than four years ago.
But older voters still came out in higher total numbers, with people ages 45 and older making up 73% of all voters in the midterm, according to state election data.
The record participation topped more than 2 million total voters, or about 60% of all registered voters. Four years ago, about 51% of registered voters participated.
Straight tickets
Republicans have for years touted an increase in straight-ticket voting for GOP candidates.
South Carolina is among just six states nationwide that allow voters to simply pick a party for all partisan races on the ballot, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Straight-ticket voting accounted for 63% of all ballots cast in this election, the highest percentage since 2020.
More Republicans than Democrats still checked the party box. Of all straight ticket voters, Democrats’ share was 48%.
That represented a big jump in the number of Democratic straight tickets — 100,000 more than the presidential election two years ago.

That helps explain how the Democrats flipped 10 state House seats and came close to flipping others, even in districts normally deep red.
It’s also evidence of people who normally vote Republican crossing over to vote for Andrews, said Mark Owens, an associate professor of political science at The Citadel.
In the U.S. Senate race, straight tickets made up 59% of Andrews’ total and 70% of Graham’s total.
Democratic Party officials said they put an emphasis on selecting the straight party option this election.
“Republicans have long understood the value of straight-ticket voting, and this year, Democrats aggressively encouraged it as well,” Spain said in a statement to the SC Daily Gazette.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: New leaders elected for North Dakota Legislature’s Democrats
description: Two North Dakota lawmakers from the same Fargo-area district will lead the Legislature’s outnumbered Democrats in the upcoming session. House Democrats elected Rep. Austin Foss, D-Fargo, and Senate Democrats elected Sen. Jamie Selzler, D-Fargo, as their minority leaders Thursday evening, along with other leadership positions. They represent District 44, an a[...]
text:
Rep. Austin Foss, D-Fargo, listens to a Legislative Management meeting in the House chamber on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)Two North Dakota lawmakers from the same Fargo-area district will lead the Legislature’s outnumbered Democrats in the upcoming session.
House Democrats elected Rep. Austin Foss, D-Fargo, and Senate Democrats elected Sen. Jamie Selzler, D-Fargo, as their minority leaders Thursday evening, along with other leadership positions. They represent District 44, an area of north Fargo.
Democrats are a tiny minority in the Legislature, but they did gain a few seats in the general election. Republicans control the House 80-14 and the Senate 41-6.
Foss, 32, said he wanted the job to “keep going on the momentum” Democrats gained from the election. He is an architect first elected in 2024.
Foss succeeds Rep. Zac Ista, D-Grand Forks, who had been leader since 2023 and did not seek reelection to his House seat.
The new leader acknowledged Democrats have to work with Republicans on anything they want to pass, but said their job also is to be a voice for the voters who sent them to Bismarck. 
Democrats will prioritize lowering costs for North Dakotans, making government fair and accountable, strengthening public schools and retaining teachers, Foss said. Critics of Democrats “are going to see that we will have a voice,” he said. “It may not translate necessarily into legislative wins, but we’re taking it one step at a time.” 
Sen. Jamie Selzler, right, D-Fargo, speaks to Rep.-elect Corey Johnson, R-Williston, before a Legislative Management meeting on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Selzler, 48, is a certified personal trainer who coaches people for losing weight. He previously worked in senior leadership for Amazon and Walmart.
He said he became involved in politics at a young age as a Republican but left the GOP after 2000 when he perceived the party was out of touch with why North Dakota’s population was shrinking. He lost a close race as a Democrat for a Grand Forks-area legislative seat in 2006, and afterward became executive director of the state Democratic-NPL Party.
Selzler said he sought the leader post because of his skill set for communicating the Democrats’ wins and putting their priorities into action.
District Democratic leaders appointed him in August to serve the remaining two years of former Sen. Josh Boschee’s term after Boschee was elected mayor of Fargo in June. Selzler said he probably will run for a full term in 2028.
Selzler said it might be surprising to see a new lawmaker in leadership, but said he is comfortable in such roles based on his past work experience. He also cited his years in politics and campaigns. 
He succeeds Sen. Kathy Hogan, D-Fargo, who had been minority leader since 2022 and did not run for reelection this year. Selzler said he plans to work on common goals with Republicans.
State rep of 30 years will lead North Dakota House Republicans

“Our goal is not to fight with Republicans or get in the way. Our goal is to represent the issues that North Dakotans care about when it comes to lower costs or what we’re going to do to keep government accountable, focusing on schools,” Selzler said.
House Democrats elected Rep. Collette Brown, D-Warwick, as assistant minority leader and Rep.-elect Laura Dronen, D-Fargo, as caucus leader. 
Senate Democrats elected Sen. Ryan Braunberger, D-Fargo, as assistant minority leader and Sen.-elect Jayme Davis, D-Rolette, as caucus leader.
The Legislature’s Republicans are led by House Majority Leader Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, and Senate Majority Leader David Hogue, R-Minot.
Legislative leaders are paid an extra $20 per calendar day during the session.
The Legislature’s organizational session is Dec. 1-3, culminating in Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s budget address outlining his priorities.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.
