name: Michigan Advance
title: An interview with Abdul El-Sayed: ‘We cannot squander this governing opportunity’
description: For Abdul El-Sayed, winning the Nov. 3 election was never the ultimate goal — it was a good first step toward a seat at the table and a real chance to make change. Now that he’s U.S. Sen.-elect El-Sayed, he is not slowing down on his main policy goals. In an interview with Michigan Advance, […]
text:
WASHINGTON, DC - NOVEMBER 11: U.S. Senator-elect Dr. Abdul El-Sayed (D-MI) poses for a photo in his office on the U.S. Capitol on November 11, 2026 in Washington, DC. El-Sayed defeated Republican Senate candidate, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers (R-MI) in the midterm elections. (Photo by Salwan Georges/Getty Images)For Abdul El-Sayed, winning the Nov. 3 election was never the ultimate goal — it was a good first step toward a seat at the table and a real chance to make change. Now that he’s U.S. Sen.-elect El-Sayed, he is not slowing down on his main policy goals.
In an interview with Michigan Advance, El-Sayed said he’s urging his colleagues in the incoming Democratic majority to strike while the moment is hot to make lasting change for the American people before their window of opportunity closes.
Here’s what the senator-elect had to say about climbing “Mount Everest” to achieve his campaign promises and what’s next for the Democratic majority as it works to earn its mandate to govern.
This interview has been edited for length and clarity. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Michigan Advance: Given the lay of the land in the U.S. House and U.S. Senate for the next session of Congress, what is your read on the potential for getting some of your chief campaign promises at least on the board next year? Does it look like Medicare for All is more possible than rolling back Citizens United?
Abdul El-Sayed: I think there’s a lot of opportunity around a lot of these goals. Let’s focus on the affordability side. Ending the war, stopping dumb tariffs is a big goal for us, and that is going to put a lot more money back in people’s pockets. That’s a huge piece. The second, thinking about union protections, thinking about standing up to big corporate monopolies  — all things I’d lived to do, that I’m looking at colleagues to be able to do.
When it comes to Citizens United, I think there’s a lot of focus, given how expensive these midterms were, on addressing these challenges. I’ve already been talking to colleagues, frankly on both sides of the aisle, about how to do that.
When it comes to expanding healthcare, the first thing we’ve got to do is make sure that they don’t cut more through these Medicaid cuts. From there, I think there’s a real opportunity to start getting expansions, if not all the way Medicare for All. Now, I’m really looking toward how we build momentum through 2028, so we elect a president who’s ready to do this and be ready on day one with the legislation.
 
MA: You mentioned the potential for additional healthcare expansions first. How open are you to incremental changes as opposed to all-or-nothing changes? For example, if Medicare for All for kids is possible as a first step, would you support that, even though it doesn’t get everyone across the board?
AES: I’ve been clear that I want to climb Mount Everest, and to climb Mount Everest, you’ve got to get to base camp. So, I understand that you’ve got to take multiple steps. It’s a long journey, but I’m not going to lose sight of the fact that we want to climb Mount Everest. It’s that kind of commitment that I think is critical.
So yes, I’m going to take as much as I can get done within the space of where folks are willing to work, and then keep coming until we’ve gotten all the way there.
 
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, left, and U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, right, at a rally with U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders and U.S. House candidate William Lawrence in Lansing, Mich., on July 19, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
 
MA: Looking to 2028, there’s going to be a big push for many, and I mean many, Democrats to seek the office of president. We’ve already seen signs that people are energetic, it seems, for someone like your colleague, U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, to run. Which among the potential candidates that may be out there do you see as being in line with what you want to achieve in the U.S. Senate? Who would be best suited for this moment?
AES: I’ve yet to see who’s actually running, so it’s a bit premature. I want somebody who’s ready to get money out of politics, put money in our pockets, and pass Medicare for All. 
I’m looking for somebody who understands Michigan and wants to serve our state and wants to be a governing partner to try and address the role that Citizen United has had in corrupting our politics; who wants to stand with unions, wants to take on corporate monopolies and oligopolies, and wants to guarantee everybody healthcare through Medicare for All.
 
MA: As this new Democratic majority gears up to take over Congress next year, I think back to the early legislative trifecta of the Obama years. Looking back, Democrats wielded their power enough to get the Affordable Care Act, the American Recovery and Investment Act and Dodd-Frank signed into law, but then they lost the House in 2010. How important is it for you all to be as efficient, surgical and swift with your policy goals in this majority so you don’t lose the moment?
AES: That’s exactly what we need to do. We cannot squander this governing opportunity that the public has given us, and we have to understand that it wasn’t as much a vote for us as it was a vote against them. 
So we have to earn our mandate by actually demonstrating action, and every single one of those actions has to be about addressing the affordability crisis in people’s lives.
 
U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a rally in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. U.S. Sens. Elizabeth Warren and Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal also spoke at the event. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
 
MA: I know your primary opponent had framed her campaign as a “love letter to Michigan,” but on the campaign trail, you also showed Michigan a lot of love. An example: You had name-dropped a local shawarma shop that has seen a bunch of business since then. What does it mean to you, to know that there is a kind of excitement buzzing at a Michigan business simply because it was a place that you loved?
AES: We have so many amazing small businesses in Michigan, and they deserve a spotlight. I hope that I can continue to shine spotlights on so many of them, because small business is the heart and soul of our economy. Folks have an idea and they turn that idea — through blood, sweat and tears — into a business and into a commitment to their local community. 
I hope that our fellow Michiganders will go and engage in the incredible work that they do every single day. There’s nothing better than folks coming together around a meal they love, or a design that they’re excited about, some flowers to bring to mom. It’s one of the best parts of the job.
 
MA: Throughout the campaign, Republicans and others opposed to your candidacy made a lot of noise about your culture, your religion and your name. But your full real name — Abdulrahman — means “servant of the most Merciful” or “most Gracious” in Arabic. “The servant of God.” What does it mean for you, now as a member of Congress, to be in a position to serve a great many people, not just Michiganders, in the U.S. Senate?
AES: I’m deeply grateful, and it’s such an honor to earn the trust of nearly 3 million of my fellow Michiganders. My job is to go and earn that, every single day, in the work that I pursue here in the nation’s capital on behalf of our state. 
I keep saying, “we haven’t earned our mandate yet.” So let’s go earn it.

name: North Dakota Monitor
title: North Dakota Veterans Home audit questions meal prep in wake of choking death
description: A state audit of the North Dakota Veterans Home in Lisbon raises concerns on performance and finance issues, including the care required when serving meals after a resident choked to death. Other issues include thousands of dollars in overtime pay to a salaried administrator, insufficient performance evaluations and questionable approval of expenditures.  Th[...]
text:
North Dakota State Auditor Josh Gallion, right, speaks to Rep. Austen Schauer, R-West Fargo, during a Legislative Management meeting on Nov. 13, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)A state audit of the North Dakota Veterans Home in Lisbon raises concerns on performance and finance issues, including the care required when serving meals after a resident choked to death.
Other issues include thousands of dollars in overtime pay to a salaried administrator, insufficient performance evaluations and questionable approval of expenditures. 
The report released Thursday notes that the Veterans Home disputes several points in the audit. 
In a statement on Friday, the Veterans Home said it looks forward to addressing the findings during the Legislative Audit and Fiscal Review Committee meeting on Nov. 30.
A Medicare inspection report on the Veterans Home filed in September found no deficiencies at the home.
“This reflects the dedication, professionalism, and commitment of our employees who provide quality care and services to our Veterans and residents every day,” said Dane Grebel, administrator of the Veterans Home.
A report summary said the average number of deficiencies found at a North Dakota nursing home is 5.6; the national average is 9.2.
The home provides basic and skilled nursing care to military veterans. During the audit period, there were 110 residents at the Veterans Home. 
In preparing to conduct the audit covering the two-year period that ended June 30, 2025, Auditor Josh Gallion said his staff found a report from the North Dakota Department of Health and Human Services detailing the choking death at the Veterans Home in March 2025. 
He said that report is why the audit team, which includes a medical auditor, focused on meal service as part of its work. 
“We’re more than just numbers,” Gallion said Thursday. 
A resident died after a staff member did not chop the person’s food dietary restrictions required, the Health and Human Services report said. 
When the audit team visited the Veterans Home, it reviewed dietary restriction records and  inspected meals served to six residents with restrictions. 
The audit said that a printed dietary card for one resident intended to guide kitchen and staff did not match to the last updated dietary restriction from the resident’s doctor.
The Veterans Home response said the resident was not served an incorrect diet. It cited a recommendation from a doctor that was not consistent with the doctor’s notes. The recommendation was later corrected.
Gallion said the Veterans Home was not aware of the discrepancy until the audit team pointed  it out. 
Performance evaluations
Three employees were disciplined after the death, but those actions were not reflected in performance evaluations for two staff members who did not have any ratings below “meeting expectations,” the audit found. 
“The North Dakota Veterans home is not consistently considering previous performance during performance evaluations,” the audit report said. 
The Veterans Home response said disciplinary action was noted in their personnel files, that it believes it complied with state rules on performance evaluations and that a “meeting expectations” rating does not mean an employee had no performance concerns. 
Overtime
Other issues raised in the audit related to finances. 
The audit found that a salaried administrator at the home was routinely being paid overtime despite no written authorization. 
Gallion, in an interview, said the practice had been going on since the administrator was hired in 2003, resulting in nearly $360,000 in overtime pay. 
Overtime paid in the two-year audit period was $56,766, the audit says. 
The practice predates the hiring of Grebel, who has been the administrator since May 2024.
A response from the Veterans Home said that while there was no written authorization of the overtime, that it was approved by the administrator. 
The response also noted an administrative staff shortage.  
Other issues
The audit also found that some accounting practices were being performed by staff that were not qualified. 
An administrative assistant approved approximately $9.7 million of expenditures during the audit period. 
The Veterans Home response noted that the audit did not identify any errors in those approvals. It said that demonstrates that there are adequate controls in place. 
The audit also found that $37,412 in state money was used for purposes other than was intended by the Legislature. 
The Veterans Home disputed that finding and blamed part of the problem on expense coding errors. 
The Veterans Home received more than $6 million for the state general fund for the period covered by the audit.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV Supreme Court rules “deliberate indifference” in prison lawsuits can’t be used in court
description: The West Virginia Supreme Court has taken a step to strip away a key legal tool for families of inmates who have died in custody.
text:
The West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals. (Photo by West Virginia Legislative Photography)The West Virginia Supreme Court has taken a step to strip away a key legal tool for families of inmates who have died in custody. 
In a 3-2 ruling issued Thursday, the Supreme Court ruled that a circuit court committed a legal error when it let a claim of “deliberate indifference” in West Virginia’s jails and prisons move forward in a case. 
However, they didn’t outright kill the claim either. 
“We have not affirmatively disclaimed deliberate indifference to a clearly established law as a cause of action. However, were we to adopt such a claim, we would be the outlier, and perhaps the lone state to recognize deliberate indifference as a standalone claim under state common law,” Justice H.L. Kirkpatrick wrote for the majority. 
Deliberate indifference is when a jail or prison is aware that an inmate is in danger or ill and chooses to ignore it. 
Kirkpatrick and Justices Haley Bunn and Charles Trump ruled in the majority. Justices Bill Flanigan and Bill Wooton dissented. 
The ruling granted “writs of prohibition” – an order from a higher court to a lower court telling them they overstepped their legal bounds – against the Kanawha County Circuit for not dismissing deliberate indifference counts in two cases against the state Division of Corrections and Rehabilitation. 
While cases brought against DCR on grounds of deliberate indifference have been settled out of court or won in trial, the high court’s ruling means families or inmates in the system can no longer list it as a charge to seek damages for in court. 
The two cases brought before the state’s high court involved inmates who had died in the regional jails. 
In 2021 Jacquline Pyles, 24, who had a documented history of mental conditions on file with the Northern Central Regional Jail due to numerous arrests, was found dead in a cell with a bed sheet tied around her neck. Ronald Marvin Myers, 79, died shortly after attorneys say he did not receive medical care for numerous conditions while locked up at the Eastern Regional Jail. 
Writing for the majority, Kirkpatrick stated that deliberate indifference isn’t a reason to sue the state, but is actually a factor in proving a case in court. He noted that while other cases in West Virginia have used the factor, they did not go as far as to create it as something to sue. 
“If taken as true, the allegations in Mr. Pyles’s and Mrs. Myers’s pleadings ‘narrate a dismal series of events’ and we sympathize with the respondents’ tragic losses,” Kirkpatrick wrote. “However, the ‘objective tragedy of the allegations’ cannot determine this Court’s answer to the pure, legal question presented by DCR’s petitions: whether a common law cause of action for deliberate indifference to a clearly established law is a cognizable claim.” 
Kirkpatrick concluded it was not. 
Flanigan, writing for the dissenting opinion, said he didn’t believe the court really worked out if deliberate indifference is a grounds for a lawsuit or not before making the ruling to bar it from the two cases.  
He pointed out that an appeal to the Intermediate Court of Appeals approved a jury instruction including deliberate existence, which would imply it does exist in West Virginia law for purposes of filing a case. 
“It is difficult to understand how the circuit court’s order could be ‘clearly erroneous as a matter of law’ when this Court has never previously considered this issue,” Flanigan wrote.

name: Delaware
title: Festival of Trees opens with holiday displays and a volunteer’s enduring dedication
description: Brantwyn Estate welcomes visitors Nov. 13-15 as Delaware Hospice celebrates 39 years of community support and Laura Robelen’s three decades of service WILMINGTON — Delaware Hospice’s Festival of Trees opens Friday, Nov. 13, at Brantwyn Estate, inviting visitors to enjoy 63 decorated trees, shop for holiday gifts and treats, and support care for patients and [...]
text:
Photo by George Rotsch, Image created by AI on 11/13/2026
 
Brantwyn Estate welcomes visitors Nov. 13-15 as Delaware Hospice celebrates 39 years of community support and Laura Robelen’s three decades of service
WILMINGTON — Delaware Hospice’s Festival of Trees opens Friday, Nov. 13, at Brantwyn Estate, inviting visitors to enjoy 63 decorated trees, shop for holiday gifts and treats, and support care for patients and families across the community.
Running through Sunday, Nov. 15, the festival features a holiday marketplace, bake shop, musical entertainment and remembrance displays honoring loved ones. Behind the holiday sparkle is a year-round volunteer effort — and one woman who has helped sustain it for three decades.
Honoring a Volunteer with 30 Years of Service
Laura Robelen, a Delaware Hospice trustee, has volunteered for 30 of the festival’s 39 years and served as chair for 22. At Thursday evening’s preview, the organization recognized her dedication to an event that brings neighbors together while raising money for hospice care and family support services.
“We could not further our mission without this,” Charles McDonough, Delaware Hospice’s president and CEO, told Robelen during the Nov. 12 gathering.
McDonough said her commitment extends throughout the year, with the next festival already on people’s minds the day after the previous one ends. He also thanked committee members, sponsors, friends and families for supporting care for people at their most vulnerable.
For visitors, the result of that commitment is a building filled with holiday creativity. Robelen said volunteers assembled this year’s 63 trees in just a day and a half, following months of preparation.
“That doesn’t happen without a fantastic group of volunteers, especially my Festival of Trees committee, who worked all year long to make things beautiful for you,” she said.
Her response to the recognition was to share the credit — with committee members, sponsors, community partners and decorators whose work gives visitors a festive outing with a purpose.
Robelen’s involvement reflects the sustained volunteer effort behind the event. In a retrospective following its 35th annual festival, Delaware Hospice reported that the celebration had raised more than $2 million for its programs over the years.
That account described more than 100 volunteers contributing thousands of hours to making decorations, coordinating tree designers, staffing the festival and matching finished trees with nonprofit organizations that could enjoy them after the event.
Another longstanding partner received recognition Thursday: Hopkins & Sons Moving and Storage, which has helped transport festival trees since 1991.
Robelen thanked the company for moving the festival into and out of its venues and delivering decorated trees to recipient facilities. She estimated that its crews had delivered more than 1,500 trees over the years.
Hopkins & Sons Donates 
Photo by George Rotsch
Representing the company, Carly Sayers announced a $4,140 donation to Delaware Hospice from an anniversary fundraising campaign. Hopkins & Sons, founded in 1946, is celebrating its 80th anniversary this year.
“Every delivery carries a little joy while supporting such a meaningful mission,” Sayers said.
The Wilmington festival features trees sponsored and decorated by businesses and individuals, along with a marketplace, bake shop and musical entertainment. Specialty displays include Remembrance, Memorial Dove and New Hope trees.
The marketplace sells holiday decorations and gifts, with proceeds benefiting Delaware Hospice programs and services. For families missing someone during the holidays, remembrance ornaments offer a way to honor loved ones, with cards carrying personal messages.
The cause extends beyond end-of-life care. Delaware Hospice offers grief counseling, support groups and other resources to community members, including people whose loved ones did not receive care from the organization.
Its New Hope program serves grieving children and teens ages 6 to 17 through counseling, peer support and activities. Those services are available at no cost through donor support.
In Sussex County, Delaware Hospice is collaborating with the Selbyville Historical Society at a new festival location. A separate cocktail reception Dec. 5 will feature tree viewing, refreshments, entertainment, auction items and raffles. Tickets are $60.

Wilmington: Nov. 13-15, Brantwyn Estate, 600 Rockland Road. Noon to 4 p.m. Friday; 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday and Sunday.
Selbyville: Dec. 4-6, Selbyville Historical Society, 11 S. Main St. Noon to 6 p.m. Friday; 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Saturday; noon to 4 p.m. Sunday.
Selbyville reception: 5:30-7:30 p.m. Saturday, Dec. 5. Tickets: $60.
Participate: Attend, sponsor a tree, purchase a remembrance ornament or make a donation.
Details: Delaware Hospice Festival of Trees or 800-838-9800.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Missouri to end state-run developmental disability case management
description: More than 5,000 Missourians with developmental disabilities who rely on state employees to help them access services will be assigned to outside agencies by the end of 2027, a move that will eliminate 299 state positions.  The Department of Mental Health’s Division of Developmental Disabilities currently provides direct case management to 5,152 people statew[...]
text:
Support coordinators based in regional offices of the Missouri Department of Mental Health currently provide case management to more than 5,000 individuals with developmental disabilities, mostly in the Kansas City and St. Louis metro areas (Annelise Hanshaw/Missouri Independent).More than 5,000 Missourians with developmental disabilities who rely on state employees to help them access services will be assigned to outside agencies by the end of 2027, a move that will eliminate 299 state positions. 
The Department of Mental Health’s Division of Developmental Disabilities currently provides direct case management to 5,152 people statewide. About 87% of Missourians eligible for services through the division already work with contracted case managers employed by nonprofits or county disability boards.
Support coordinators work with individuals with disabilities and their families to develop and monitor individualized support plans, which identify the person’s needs and goals and, with approval from the division, help them access services, including those funded through Medicaid. 
Debra Walker, the department’s director of public affairs, told The Independent the change “will address caseload growth and focus (division) staff time on the division requirements of contract management, quality and compliance.”
The division has sought for years to shift support coordination to outside agencies as the number of Missourians eligible for services through the division has increased, citing the need to keep caseloads manageable. And the move is expected to save the state approximately $3 million annually, Walker said, as spending outpaces revenue and the pandemic-era surplus diminishes.
But some disability advocates worry the transition will disrupt services. Others are concerned that eliminating state-employed case managers could weaken oversight of organizations providing services to people with disabilities and make it more difficult for the state to follow federal rules barring individuals from receiving services from the same entity assessing their eligibility.
An Oct. 28 letter from the division obtained by The Independent tells clients to “continue to meet with your support coordinator as you usually would” and indicates they will be contacted by the division or their new case management provider once their case is transferred.
The transition, which will eliminate 299 state support coordination staff positions, including supervisors, is scheduled to be complete by Dec. 31, 2027.
Current employees will receive preference when applying for openings in the division’s regional offices, but none are guaranteed another position. 
Walker said the division has already confirmed contractors’ capacity to serve clients who will be transferred from state support coordinators  — 92% of whom are in the Kansas City and St. Louis metro areas. 
Larry Opinsky, a disability advocate based in St. Louis County whose daughter uses self-directed services, said he isn’t worried about his family’s transition because he knows how to navigate the state’s disability service system. But for families less familiar with the system, he worries the transition could interrupt or delay services.
“Most families are doing everything they can to get through the day, and this funding piece that case management and Medicaid is providing for them, this is bare minimum,” Opinsky said. “They’re going to take whatever they can get and only what’s offered because they’ve got 100 other things to worry about with helping their loved one.”
 A shift already underway

Contracted agencies have increasingly taken on case management for Missourians with developmental disabilities.
Lawmakers appropriated $7.6 million in fiscal year 2023 for the division to transfer 2,400 people from state support coordinators to contracted case managers “in an effort to right size caseloads,” according to the department’s fiscal year 2024 budget request. The average caseload of a state support coordinator dropped from 49 to 39 during the year the funding was approved and was 29 in fiscal year 2026. Contractors’ average caseloads have remained steady between 33 and 35 over the past five years.
For some families, the transition to contracted case management has been positive.
Victoria McMullen’s son was transferred from a state support coordinator to a private case manager during the earlier shift. McMullen told The Independent her son, who has cerebral palsy and autism, has received “exceptionally good case management” from the Center for Human Services, a nonprofit that serves individuals with developmental disabilities in over 60 counties across the state.
“We needed advocacy for a particular service,” McMullen said, “and it went up three levels of CHS administration weighing in on why this particular need had to be funded.”
Nancy Pennington, executive director of the Missouri Association of County Developmental Disability Boards, said that unlike the division, which can’t hire beyond its annual allotment of full-time equivalent positions, contractors can hire staff to keep up with caseload growth. 
“The role of support coordinators is the same no matter who does it,” Pennington said. “It’s just who has the flexibility, who might have the infrastructure established better and supported financially to do that, and then having people in the communities.”
For families who depend on support coordinators to access services that keep their loved ones safe and healthy, the change brings uncertainty.
Adam Sommer, of Warrensburg, told The Independent that without the state’s Sarah Lopez waiver, it would have been a lot harder for his 9-year-old daughter, who has Rett syndrome, to live safely at home and avoid institutionalization.
When his daughter recently stayed home from school with a cold, the family was able to manage her symptoms without a trip to the hospital, thanks to equipment and services they accessed through Medicaid.
“We’re able to essentially have a hospital room in our home with a suction machine and oxygen machine, so that we don’t have to constantly use hospital resources and emergency medical care for things that we know how to manage,” Sommer said.
A petition urging the department and Gov. Mike Kehoe to preserve state support coordination as an option gathered more than a thousand signatures in a week.
“Transferring responsibility to a private agency does not automatically guarantee equivalent service quality, continuity of care or effective oversight,” the petition says.
 Questions about oversight

For Opinsky, the concern extends beyond the immediate transition.
Even when contracted agencies are well-run, he worries that financial pressures could eventually lead them to increase caseloads at the expense of the people they serve.
The risk is heightened when the services are for vulnerable people, Opinsky said, who need the services to stay safe and healthy.
“Because it’s privatized, the concern that many families have is, what’s the motivation?” Opinsky said. “If the motivation is money, caseloads will increase. They’ll just keep dumping (cases) on the same people so that they’ll be able to bill more, but they won’t have to increase their functional cost. And if indeed they do get more staff, what’s the quality of that staff?”
A 2014 federal Medicaid rule required states to ensure individuals’ service plans are based on an “independent assessment of needs” and stipulated that individuals can’t receive assessments and services from the same source. 
The requirement is intended to ensure that the people assessing an individual’s needs and coordinating services are independent of the organizations paid to deliver those services.
Walker said Missouri is “conflict-free, meaning (outside case management) agencies cannot provide any other services under the waivers to individuals with developmental disabilities.”
Pennington said that while some county boards provide both services and case management, they don’t provide them to the same people.
For example, Lincoln County’s Community Opportunities for People with Developmental Disabilities provides residential services, day programs and employment services, but individuals participating in those services work with case managers from the Macon County disability board.
When Medicaid rules changed, Pennington said, “that’s where some of the county boards chose to retain case management. Some of them chose to retain service provision, and that’s where a lot of these nonprofits spun off from.”
Sommer said that even though the coming shift in support coordination isn’t “the biggest deal in the world,” he worries about future changes to the state’s safety net. 
Support coordination, he said, helps ensure people with developmental disabilities have fair access to state services regardless of their circumstances.
“Special needs kids are born every day, and they’re born to people of all walks of life and all abilities,” Sommer said, “and those people should have the same equitable opportunity as everybody else to access the system that’s going to keep their family afloat and keep kids safe in their home.”

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico officials report growth in medication treatment for inmates
description: A New Mexico program that provides medication-assisted treatment for inmates with substance abuse disorders has expanded its reach, a state legislative analyst told lawmakers Thursday.
text:
New Mexico Department of Corrections Health Services Administrator Wence Asonganyi and Legislative Finance Committee Senior Fiscal Analyst Allegra Hernandez update lawmakers on the state Legislature’s interim Health and Human Services Committee on Nov. 12, 2026, on a program providing state inmates with medication-assisted treatment for substance abuse disorders. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)A New Mexico program that provides medication-assisted treatment for inmates with substance abuse disorders has expanded its reach, a state legislative analyst told lawmakers Thursday. SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Nearly 24% of New Mexicans have substance use disorders, over half of which are opiate or alcohol disorders that can be treated with medication-assisted treatment, according to a Thursday presentation to lawmakers on the Legislature’s interim Health and Human Services Committee. 
Medication-assisted treatment uses medications, such as methadone or buprenorphine, in combination with counseling to treat substance use disorders. Patients receiving the treatment, research shows, are less likely to overdose, continue opioid use or have contact with the criminal justice system. 
A New Mexico Corrections Department survey found that 36% of inmates in the state — about 2,000 — require treatment. Wence Asonganyi, health services administrator for the Corrections Department, clarified to lawmakers that the figure represents inmates who meet the “medical criteria” for substance abuse disorder. The Corrections Department last year received a nearly three-year appropriation of close to $40 million from the state’s Government Results and Opportunity program to provide treatment for inmates in need.
This year, 1,407 of the 2,000 inmates identified received treatment, Allegra Hernandez, Legislative Finance Committee senior fiscal analyst, told interim HHS committee lawmakers Thursday. According to her presentation, seven of the eight state-operated prisons in New Mexico now provide MAT services, and 815 inmates continue to receive treatment in the program’s second year.
That represents an improvement from a year ago when the LFC reported only 176 inmates had received the treatment. 
“Corrections is doing an excellent job at rolling out the program,” Hernandez said.
Asonganyi told lawmakers he is confident in the program’s achievements, but said it has been “very challenging” to implement across the state.
One of those challenges, Asonganyi explained, is securing providers who can prescribe methadone, a controlled substance used as a treatment medication for opioid addiction.  Currently, the department can offer all other treatment medications in-house, Asonganyi said, but relies on an outside service provider to sign off on inmates’ methadone prescriptions, which leaves the Corrections Department “vulnerable.”
“If that service provider, for whatever reason, cannot supply the medication — we are left in a very difficult situation with our patients,” Asonganyi said.
In addition, Asonganyi said the department also has had trouble recruiting behavioral health staff for psychotherapy and counseling. As a result, the department has used telehealth providers to address gaps in treatment. Asonganyi said the department hopes to address these issues in the program’s third implementation phase next year. Its other goals include providing continuity of care after an inmate is released and collecting data on the program’s outcomes.
Sen. Elizabeth “Liz” Stefanics (D-Santa Fe) underscored the program’s importance: “I think this is extremely worthwhile if we are looking at a population that’s going to integrate back into our communities,” she said.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Will Bridgeport schools seek state financial oversight?
description: Bridgeport school board members are unconvinced state financial oversight is the right move going forward,
text:
The questions began in the spring: should Bridgeport seek more financial oversight? Could state intervention help bring the district more funding?
The answers, officials say, were not convincing enough to move forward at the time. And school board members remain unconvinced it’s the right move going forward, they told The Connecticut Mirror.
State law allows local and regional boards of education to request that the state Department of Education develop a fiscal intervention and oversight plan. The plan would be reviewed by the Municipal Accountability Review Board, known as MARB, and would require approval from the Office of Policy and Management and the State Board of Education. Although the process could make additional state funding available to participating districts, it does not guarantee additional money.
Board of Education member Rob Traber said the district explored the program in June while working to balance its budget and determine whether MARB could provide access to additional funding. At the time, he said, the program was not yet established and did not have money available. The district also determined it did not need the program to balance its budget.
Traber said there are still unanswered questions about how MARB would work and that the district has no immediate need to pursue it.
“There are serious questions that we need to have answered,” Traber said. “But two, we have no need to proceed with MARB right now. MARB isn’t ready for anybody to pursue at this point. So for those two reasons, it’s premature.”
Board of Education member Joseph Sokolovic raised concerns that participating in MARB could limit local control without guaranteeing additional funding. He said districts would have to submit financial plans for state review and could face pressure to make operational changes, including consolidating schools or reducing staff, to qualify for potential assistance.
“You basically gotta do what they want,” Sokolovic said, describing the process of submitting and revising financial plans to meet state requirements.
Sokolovic said Bridgeport’s financial challenges are largely the result of inadequate state funding, rising education costs and the expiration of federal pandemic relief. He argued that additional state oversight would not address those underlying funding problems.
Traber said the district’s focus is instead on advocating for additional education funding through the state legislature.
Bridgeport Public Schools has faced significant budget gaps in recent years. In November 2024, the district reported an approximately $38 million gap in its 2024-25 budget. The budget had initially been adopted with a $26 million shortfall, which the district planned to cover using reserves. 
A state-commissioned audit later projected an approximately $39 million deficit for the 2025-26 school year, partly tied to the expiration of more than $150 million in federal pandemic relief funding.
Interim Superintendent Royce Avery did not respond to a request for comment.
Bridgeport is already part of a separate state education intervention that began in 2025 after the district faced a multimillion-dollar budget deficit. That intervention is distinct from the fiscal oversight process. The district also completed an independent forensic audit that produced 34 recommendations to improve financial oversight and internal controls. A second team was brought in to help the district address those recommendations.
Bridgeport Education Association President Jeff Morrissey said the union recognizes the financial challenges facing the district but does not support voluntarily entering MARB oversight. Morrissey said the process could create more problems than solutions, noting that many questions remain unanswered. He also expressed concern that adding another layer of oversight could complicate decision-making as the district searches for a permanent superintendent.
For now, Traber said the district is focused on advocating for additional state education funding through the legislature.

name: Delaware
title: Cape Henlopen’s new Point Trail leads a wider push for Delaware walking and biking connections
description: Paved path and boardwalk will link Main Beach with The Point as DNREC pursues bridge improvements, trail extensions and local recreation grants LEWES, Del. — A new trail connecting Cape Henlopen State Park’s Main Beach area with The Point will add a dedicated walking and biking route to one of Delaware’s most popular outdoor destinations, part of a broader e[...]
text:
Paved path and boardwalk will link Main Beach with The Point as DNREC pursues bridge improvements, trail extensions and local recreation grants
LEWES, Del. — A new trail connecting Cape Henlopen State Park’s Main Beach area with The Point will add a dedicated walking and biking route to one of Delaware’s most popular outdoor destinations, part of a broader effort to expand and improve trails across the state.
DNREC’s Point Trail project will connect the Main Beach Bathhouse area with the northeast parking lot near The Point. State construction documents describe approximately 3,320 feet of trail, a little more than six-tenths of a mile, including a timber boardwalk section.
The plans specify a 10-foot-wide asphalt surface and approximately 480 feet of boardwalk measuring 11 feet, 5 inches wide. Work also includes new pavement where Prettyman Lane intersects Post Road. bidcondocs.delaware.gov
The Cape Gazette reported Nov. 6 that the project would cost $1.25 million, supported by statewide trails funding and the federal Recreational Trails Program. DNREC Parks and Recreation Director Matt Ritter told the newspaper the contract had been awarded and the contractor was waiting for materials, with completion targeted for the end of 2026 if work proceeds as planned.
The state’s procurement record lists an April 16 contract award. Bid documents allowed on-site work beginning Sept. 7 and called for completion before winter. The year-end target is not a confirmed opening date. mmp.delaware.gov
The new connection follows other Cape Henlopen trail work announced earlier this year. In March, DNREC outlined repairs to the Junction and Breakwater Trail, including fence replacement, edge grading and stone-dust resurfacing, followed by repairs to sections of the Gordons Pond Trail damaged by high tides. news.delaware.gov
Longer term, DNREC’s Cape Henlopen trail-planning page outlines 15.7 miles of additional trails beyond the park’s existing 19.3 miles. More than 12 miles of the proposed additions are west of the Lewes-Rehoboth Canal. Those figures describe a planning framework, rather than an immediate construction schedule. dnrec.delaware.gov
Other projects around the state
At White Clay Creek State Park near Newark, DNREC announced in August that it would replace Tweed’s Mill Bridge, an access point for hiking, nature programs and the park’s nature center area.
The approximately $1.5 million design and construction project will replace the bridge with a concrete structure intended to improve resilience. DNREC awarded the contract to A-Del Construction and projected an opening about six months after its August announcement.
The bridge work accompanies construction of a new discovery center. DNREC said trail access could close during working hours but should remain available evenings and weekends. State of Delaware News
The governor’s recommended fiscal 2027 capital budget also identified the Buck Jersey Trail extension at Lums Pond State Park, connecting Howell School Road to Area 1, and the Wheelwright Trail at Brandywine Creek State Park as priorities. The recommendation describes projects being built in segments over several years; it does not establish opening dates for those trails. www.budget.delaware.gov
In Dover, DNREC proposes a small trailhead and 2.75 miles of trails at Fork Branch Nature Preserve. The project would provide access to the 236-acre Anne McClements Woods Tract, which DNREC describes as the largest forested area within city limits. The project page does not identify a construction start or opening date. dnrec.delaware.gov
Local governments also are receiving DNREC assistance. Grants announced in January included $190,000 for Milford’s Deep Branch Park, covering trail construction, an entrance road, parking and other improvements, and $83,250 for Milton to redesign the Federal Street rail-trail crossing with wider ramps, warning signs and a more perpendicular alignment. State of Delaware News
Where the money comes from
The projects draw on several public funding streams, with different arrangements for state park construction and local grants.
State park construction receives funding through the state’s capital budget, commonly called the Bond Bill, alongside federal grants. Capital appropriations are separate from the annual operating budget, although the capital bill can include General Fund cash as well as borrowing and other funds. A reference to Bond Bill funding does not establish how much of an individual project is financed by debt. legis.delaware.gov
DNREC specifically identifies Bond Bill funding and federal Recreational Trails Program assistance for the Tweed’s Mill Bridge replacement. State of Delaware News
The federal trails program represents a portion of motor fuel excise taxes attributable to off-highway recreational fuel use. It supports both motorized and nonmotorized recreation, including hiking and biking trails. fpi.omb.gov
Milford’s and Milton’s grants come through DNREC’s Outdoor Recreation, Parks and Trails program. DNREC says the program is funded entirely by income generated by a trust established with real estate transfer tax deposits. Local governments supply matching funds. State of Delaware News
Available project summaries do not provide a complete breakdown of state cash, borrowing and federal dollars for every trail project.
To Go Box

What: New Point Trail connection at Cape Henlopen State Park

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi lion dancers bring cultural heritage to the National Folk Festival
description: Lion dancers from the White Tiger Lion Dance team practice their routine in the parking lot of the Vietnamese Martyrs Catholic Church in Biloxi, on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026.
text:
BILOXI – The lion blinks its fur-lined, hand-painted eyes as it approaches a set of red benches, stacked two on two. Nervous, it makes a few practice jumps, bounding from side to side as its fabric body ripples. Then, it rears up to stand on its hind legs before leaping forward, four sequined paws landing onto the narrow wood. 
Off to the side, musicians play furiously. The drummer beats out a steady da-dum as the lion grows more confident, and the gong follows the drum. The crash of cymbals rings in the air.  
After returning to the ground, the dancers lift off their costume to reveal two young men, who drop into a quick bow before transforming back into the large cat. One dancer manipulates the lion head, the other, bent over at the waist, acts as the tail.
This is lion dance, a cultural performance art that originated from China over a thousand years ago. Now performed as a way to symbolically ward away evil and spread good fortune, it is practiced throughout eastern and southeastern Asia, and the global Asian diaspora. In Mississippi, a state with a less than 2% Asian population, it was pursued by a troupe of self-taught Vietnamese American youth from Biloxi. 
This Saturday, five months after festival organizers reached out to them, the White Tiger Lion Dance team will perform on their first Jackson stage during the 2026 National Folk Festival. They are Mississippi’s only year-round lion dance performance troupe. 
The origin story
The White Tiger Lion Dance team originated out of a church teacher’s suggestion at the Vietnamese Martyrs Catholic Church in Biloxi, said captain Andrew Dang. At 22, he’s both the oldest member of the team and the longest running, having been a part of the group’s 2019 founding. He recalls that his church class wasn’t interested in forming a soccer or football team, but when the teacher mentioned lion dance, everyone was intrigued. But unlike most lion dance teams that form out of martial arts schools with experienced instructors, the students taught themselves the playful and acrobatic “Hok San” dance style. 
“We really didn’t have anyone to teach us the proper way of doing things, so we kind of just went on YouTube,” Dang said. “We kept redoing moves until we got it right.”
Three times a week, the dozen-strong group of youth, ages 13 to 22, drives out to their training space – the parking lot behind the church. While White Tiger outgrew the church in 2022, they still maintain a close relationship and perform at its annual Lunar New Year, or Tết, celebrations. 
Members of the White Tiger Lion Dance team pose after practice in Biloxi, on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026, a week before their performance at the National Folk Festival in Jackson. Credit: Bashirah Mack/Mississippi Today
In the summer, outdoor practices mean hot evenings and mosquitoes. In the fall when night comes early, they practice under the lot’s shoebox lights. Dang said he’s on the hunt for an indoor space. For now, they set up benches on concrete and store their lion heads at a nearby nail salon owned by a team member’s parents.
The group keeps busy with local performances, with the money they earn going back into equipment and meals for the team. One weekend before the folk festival, the team’s first national stage performance, they gather to practice a routine they’re performing at a wedding the next day. Warmup is filled with chatter, punctuated by exclamations of “Bro, what?” When they start a run-through, they become focused and serious. 
While routines on the ground can be challenging enough under heavy costumes and limited visibility under the lion head, the elevated benches add an additional level of difficulty. For today’s bench routine, William Van Lai performs as the animal’s tail while his lion dance partner, Minh Tran, is the head. To complete one common move called the head sit, Tran jumps while his tail dancer grabs a belt tied around his waist and lifts him into the air. Tran lands in a sitting position on Lai’s head, making it look as though the lion is standing. 
It takes time to build confidence in a partner, both to land the move and to keep each other safe, 18-year-old Lai said. 
“Especially when we do tricks like this, you have to trust your teammate,” he said. Lai started lion dancing during elementary school in the Gulf Coast, when members of a local Buddhist temple performed for Lunar New Year. Four years ago, he joined White Tiger. 
“I always loved lion dance,” he said. “It’s always in my heart.”
A family of lion dancers
For Tran, the team became a place to build community. He immigrated from Vietnam at age 12, and his parents were initially wary about letting him join the group as a sophomore in D’Iberville high school. Now, seeing the hardworking character of the team, they encourage him.
“My friends right here, I don’t really see them as teammates,” Tran said, watching the group practice a ground routine with two lions. “I definitely see them as a family.”
Other members described the team as a brotherhood, borne out of their shared love of lion dance and desire to spread the art form in Mississippi. 
When they offer public performances, even in Biloxi, people will come up to them saying that they loved the dance and have never seen it before, Dang said. That feedback helps motivate the team to improve their skills and create new routines each year. 
Andrew Dang, captain of the White Tiger Lion Dance team, prepares to play the drum during a practice run-through in Biloxi on Friday, Nov. 6, 2026. Credit: Bashirah Mack/Mississippi Today
Dang remembers watching lion dance performances as a kid and being amazed at the spectacle of lions jumping into the sky paired with percussive music. As he got older, he realized that practicing allowed him to stay connected with his culture. 
“My people, they do this back in Vietnam. They do it probably a lot better than us,” he said. “I was like, ‘OK, I’ve got to bring this tradition to Biloxi.’”
Crowded together after practice, the team expressed their eagerness to perform for a national audience at the folk festival. They plan to perform their ground routine and send lions out to interact with the crowd, blinking and flicking their ears and showing another corner of the world what it means to be a lion dancer.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: After migration delay, rare whooping cranes making yearly trek across Kansas
description: BARTON COUNTY — Each fall, around 500 endangered whooping cranes wing their way along the Central Flyway — a 2,500-mile avian superhighway over the Great Plains — from their breeding grounds in Canada’s Wood Buffalo National Park to their wintering grounds along the Texas Gulf Coast at the Aransas National Wildlife Refuge. But this fall, […]
text:
Whooping cranes soar over the Cheyenne Bottoms Wildlife Area in the fall of 2025. This year’s annual migration from Canada to Texas is underway, but it got a late start. (Photo by Dan Witt)BARTON COUNTY — Each fall, around 500 endangered whooping cranes wing their way along the Central Flyway — a 2,500-mile avian superhighway over the Great Plains — from their breeding grounds in Canada’s Wood Buffalo National Park to their wintering grounds along the Texas Gulf Coast at the Aransas National Wildlife Refuge.
But this fall, migration has been different, said Kansas Wetlands Education Center director Curtis Wolf. He should know, since his center sits across K-156 from the Cheyenne Bottoms Wildlife Area in Barton County, a wetland of international acclaim that hosts thousands of birds, including many of the cranes, that travel along the flyway every fall and spring.
“This has been an interesting year,” he said.
The cherished white whoopers prized by birdwatchers usually start showing up in early October at the state-managed Bottoms and its sister Quivira National Wildlife Refuge, 40 miles south along the Wetlands and Wildlife National Scenic Byway in Stafford County. However, the first local appearance wasn’t reported until last week.
“They spotted 15 at Quivira,” Wolf said, noting there had also been scattered reports in North Dakota, South Dakota and Nebraska. But none have been seen at the Bottoms.
With the flyway stretching up to 1,500 miles wide, not all of the migrating cranes choose to make a pit stop in central Kansas, “but it is odd to just now seeing them,” he said.
With the delay, Wolf said the cranes may arrive in one big mass or, feeling rushed, may bypass the refuges entirely.
The delayed migration is due to a warmer autumn in Canada, leaving the birds in no hurry to leave, said Mike Rader, wildlife education supervisor for the Kansas Department of Wildlife and Parks. “They are finding what they need there.”
With climate shifts, these delays are becoming more common, he said. The fall migration has been getting later over the past several years, with whoopers spotted at Quivira over Christmas 2025 when normally the last of the birds have passed by mid-November.
This same phenomenon is also affecting other crane species, such as the sandhill crane, Rader said.
Other than the whoopers being tardy, “this has been a good year for birding,” Wolf said. The water level at the Bottoms and the bird numbers are strong, with ducks, other waterfowl, and shorebirds flocking to the wetlands.
 
Cheyenne Bottoms Wildlife Area, shown Nov. 10, 2026, usually sees whooping cranes stop to rest on their fall migration. However, none have been spotted there yet this year. (Photo by Dale Hogg for Kansas Reflector)
Why so few?
The global population is estimated to be more than 800.
“The numbers have started to make a comeback in the past decade,” Wolf said, thanks to conservation efforts.
In the United States, about 550 make the Central Flyway journey, with a few more migrating along the eastern seaboard. There are also nonmigratory populations in Florida (around 80) and Louisiana (in the teens).
However, they remain threatened by illegal hunting (conviction for killing a whooper, a federal crime, can result in a $100,000 fine and a year in prison), natural predators, power lines, and habitat loss. Droughts and shortages in their food sources can also harm numbers.
In addition, it takes years for them to reach breeding age. Even then, not every pair succeeds in producing offspring, and females may raise only one surviving chick per season.
“They just don’t have the capacity to keep up,” Wolf said.
And, “It’s a slow process,” Rader said of rebuilding the population.
Whooping cranes can stand as tall as five feet with a seven-foot wing span. They are named for their loud, single-note, trumpeting calls — or “whoops” — made when they are alarmed or communicating.
 
The Kansas Wetlands Education Center at the Cheyenne Bottoms Wildlife Area in Barton County showcases the region’s importance in the migration of whooping cranes and other bird species along the Central Flyway. (Photo by Dale Hogg for Kansas Reflector)
A prized find
“People want to see the whoopers,” Wolf said, adding that it is a bucket-list find for birdwatchers.
In fact, participants in last weekend’s Audubon of Kansas annual Crane Festival, based out of Sterling, just east of Quivira, were the first to report the whoopers.
Like most migratory birds, whooping cranes fly south in the fall and back north in the spring. But there are more opportunities for sightings in the fall, Rader said.
Although they can make the entire trip in a matter of days with a good tailwind, they are more likely to linger while traveling to Texas, where they feed on blue crabs and wolfberries. When heading north, however, they are destined for their breeding grounds and have other priorities and make fewer stops, he said.
In the meantime, both Wolf and Rader said there is ample time for those wanting to spot the elusive birds. The 20,000-acre Bottoms and 22,000-acre Quivira form a wetland complex designated as Wetlands of International Importance under the Ramsar Convention and are considered among the most critical stopover areas in the Western Hemisphere for millions of migratory shorebirds and waterfowl along the Central Flyway.

title: Delaware’s new public health director brings broad policy background, questions about government’s reach
description: Dr. Harrison Hines takes charge of nearly 1,000 employees as Delaware links disease prevention with wider social conditions DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s new public health director is a neurologist whose federal policy work examined how housing, food and transportation affect health. His arrival puts an experienced physician and policy adviser in charge of an age[...]
text:
Dr. Harrison Hines takes charge of nearly 1,000 employees as Delaware links disease prevention with wider social conditions
DOVER, Del. — Delaware’s new public health director is a neurologist whose federal policy work examined how housing, food and transportation affect health. His arrival puts an experienced physician and policy adviser in charge of an agency whose decisions can affect patients, taxpayers and private businesses.
Dr. Harrison Hines became director of the Division of Public Health and state health officer Oct. 12, according to a formal appointment announcement issued Nov. 12. He oversees nearly 1,000 employees in the Department of Health and Social Services’ largest division.
The division’s responsibilities include communicable disease prevention, maternal and infant health, food and drinking-water safety, and public health emergency response.
“Our focus as public health professionals goes beyond disease prevention. My goal is to help individuals and communities flourish,” Hines said in the announcement. State of Delaware News
That broad outlook raises questions about how Delaware will coordinate health services and social policies, where authority will rest and how much room private providers, employers and community organizations will have to pursue their own approaches.
The appointment announcement does not describe a transfer of all health services or social policy to Hines. It also does not announce new regulatory powers or business mandates.
Hines previously served on the White House Domestic Policy Council, where he led an interagency team developing the U.S. Playbook to Address Social Determinants of Health. His professional biography places that work in 2022 and 2023 and describes subsequent senior leadership positions at the Department of Veterans Affairs.
He earned his medical degree at Stanford University and completed his neurology residency at the University of California, San Francisco. He also holds a master’s degree in theological studies from Duke Divinity School and undergraduate degrees in religion and chemistry from Duke University. astho.org
A broader structure already taking shape
Hines enters an existing public health office within a recently changed leadership structure.
Under the governor’s July order establishing the Office of the Surgeon General, the public health director reports to Surgeon General Dr. Neil Hockstein. Hockstein reports to the DHSS secretary and serves with the responsibilities of a deputy cabinet secretary.
The order directs the Surgeon General’s office to encourage collaboration across government and with health care organizations, employers and community groups. Its priorities include access to care, the health care workforce and social and environmental conditions affecting health.
The order preserves the DHSS secretary’s statutory authority. It also calls for the Surgeon General to identify opportunities to reduce unnecessary administrative burdens and eliminate barriers to care. State of Delaware
That creates a practical test: Will coordination simplify services and accountability, or add another layer of review for providers and businesses?
The public documents establish a chain of command. They do not establish that Hines controls every state program touching health, housing, food or transportation.
Authority with consequences for businesses
Public health leadership involves more than advice.
Delaware law gives DHSS authority over disease control, quarantine, drinking-water protection and public health nuisances. Lawfully issued departmental regulations and orders can have the force of law.
These are departmental powers whose exercise depends on the applicable law and delegation, rather than unrestricted personal authority attached to Hines’ title. delcode.delaware.gov
For food businesses, oversight can determine whether doors remain open. State guidance explains that an imminent health hazard can require immediate closure, while permit revocation based on inspections requires due process. dhss.delaware.gov
Such powers make consistency, clear standards, and timely review important to both consumer safety and business survival.
Where does the free market fit?
Hines’ background raises a policy question: How will the state weigh government programs against competition, consumer choice and voluntary partnerships when pursuing better health?
The federal initiative associated with his work promoted coordination between health and social services. An accompanying 2023 framework described housing and nutrition interventions for certain Medicaid beneficiaries. That history provides context for his experience; it does not establish a Delaware proposal. archives.hud.gov
Potential approaches deserve separate scrutiny. Contracting with a private transportation business to help patients reach appointments differs from requiring employers to provide transportation. Supporting a voluntary nutrition program differs from imposing new obligations on food retailers.
For Delaware, the questions include whether private practices, small businesses, faith-based organizations and independent nonprofits will have meaningful opportunities to participate — and whether administrative requirements will favor large institutions better equipped to handle them.
Another question is whether the state will examine barriers to competition and entry alongside proposals for additional spending or oversight.
Questions for the new leadership
The appointment announcement leaves several issues unresolved.
Which decisions will Hines make independently, and which require approval from the Surgeon General, DHSS secretary, governor or General Assembly?
What changes, if any, does he envision in the division’s work on housing, food access and transportation?
Would those changes involve voluntary partnerships, funding conditions, proposed regulations or requests for legislation?
How will the state assess effects on competition, patient choice, and small-business compliance costs?
What results will be published, and what would cause an ineffective program to be changed or discontinued?
How will Delaware distinguish temporary funding opportunities from commitments that require continuing state support?
Hines succeeds Steven Blessing after Dr. Tesha Quail served as interim director for more than three months. Quail returns to her position as deputy director and chief health equity officer.
His early priorities will provide the first indication of how Delaware’s broader health agenda translates into services, spending and expectations for the private sector.
To Go Box

Learn more: Read the state’s appointment announcement.
Review the structure: Read the governor’s order establishing the surgeon general’s office.
Participate: Follow proposed rules and public comment deadlines in the Delaware Register of Regulations.

title: Three in a Row: Tower Hill and St. Mark’s meet in DIAA Girls Volleyball State Championship for third straight season
description: The Tower Hill Hillers defeated the Archmere Auks and the St. Mark’s Spartans defeated the Middletown Cavaliers in the semifinals for a chance to compete for the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Championship title on November 16.   NEWARK, Del. — The 2026 DIAA Volleyball Championship matchup is set. The Tower Hill Hillers will take on the St. Mark’s Spartans[...]
text:
Tower Hill and Archmere warm-up before their semifinal game. Tower Hill won the match, 3-1, to advance to the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Championship game. Photo Credit: Ryan Colasanti
The Tower Hill Hillers defeated the Archmere Auks and the St. Mark’s Spartans defeated the Middletown Cavaliers in the semifinals for a chance to compete for the 2026 DIAA Girls Volleyball State Championship title on November 16.
 
NEWARK, Del. — The 2026 DIAA Volleyball Championship matchup is set. The Tower Hill Hillers will take on the St. Mark’s Spartans for the state title on Monday, November 16, at 7:00 p.m. The Spartans and Hillers will meet at the Bob Carpenter Center with a state title on the line for the third season in a row.
Tower Hill defeated Archmere, 3-1
Tower Hill senior Sydney Fischer stood to the left of the back line as Archmere junior Olivia Borsello started her serve. The serve tipped off the top of the net and was handled by Tower Hill senior Parker Lewicki. Lewicki passed the ball to Skylar Donohue and the junior set the ball to the front left of the net where Fischer was waiting.
Fischer rose up and hit the ball hard, right at Borsello in the middle of the court. Borsello only had time to react as Fischer’s kill moved at a ferocious pace. The ball hit off Borsello’s hands and landed way behind the field of play. 
Fischer recorded her third kill of the fourth set and increased the Hillers’ lead to 7-2, helping Tower Hill defeat Archmere and return to the state championship for the third season in a row.
“It’s so exciting,” Fischer said about moving onto the state championship game for the third straight season. “I really hope it goes well. Little nerve wracking again being in The Bob, but yeah I’m really excited.”
Fischer finished the game with 30 kills, with eight of them coming in the fourth set to go along with an ace that helped increase the Tower Hill total to 23. Hiller junior Cadence Davis scored the game winning kill on a strike from the left side after having to leave the game earlier due to an injury. The Hillers won the fourth set, 25-21.
“It was so cool,” Fischer said about Davis’ game winning play. “I think that’s exactly what we wanted. I mean in the huddle we told her like we all have her back, we’re all here for her even if she’s down or she’s hurting, like we have her, anything she needs she just needs to communicate with us and I think it really like spoke to how well our team culture is.”
With Davis’ short absence and the defense focused on limiting Fischer’s impact, the Hillers found an advantage in the middle with strong performances from senior Madison Squire and Jillian Truesdell. The pair combined for over 20 kills and three blocks in the semifinal.
“Seeing what they gave us and trying to just be aggressive especially when a key player like Cadence goes down,” Squire said. “I had to really step-up for my team and just be aggressive and just kind of take control of that front line.”
The Tower Hill versus Archmere matchup has been a staple in the past three DIAA tournaments. The Hillers won each of the last two matchups with sweeps of the Auks, but Archmere was able to win a set against Tower Hill in this year’s matchup, storming back from a seven point deficit to win, 26-24. It’s only the third set Tower Hill has lost this season.
St. Mark’s defeated Middletown, 3-0
Middletown junior Kaitlyn Haupt rose from the back line and hit the ball toward the St. Mark’s side of the court. The ball bounced off the hands of one Spartan then the hand of another before the kill fell to the ground past the back line. The score gave the Cavaliers a four point lead in the first set and forced a Spartan timeout to regroup. 
The timeout proved to be well timed.
St. Mark’s scored ten of the next 12 points of the set turning a four point deficit into a four point lead within minutes. The Spartans never trailed again and won the first set, 25-21. 
St. Mark’s carried the momentum from the first set win into the rest of the matchup, sweeping Middletown, to advance to the 2026 DIAA Volleyball Championship game.
“It feels so good, like me and my team have worked so hard to get here,” St. Mark’s junior Lina Clark said postgame. “There’s been a lot of pressure this whole season to just keep working hard and keep persevering and I feel like all of our hard work just really paid off and showed tonight.”
Clark played a big role in the Spartans closing out the victory with two kills and two blocks from her spot in the middle of the court. Freshman Anna Spofford led the Spartans with five kills in the third set including the game winner on a strike from the right side of the net that landed in the middle of the Cavalier defense. The Spartans’ sweep is their second in the tournament and 13th of the season.
A crucial part of the Spartans’ victory was their defensive play around the net. St. Marks finished the game with ten blocks, turning potential kills into points four times in both the first and final sets. Clark was a big part of that defensive effort accumulating four blocks in the game.
“We go over spots where people hit and how to get there. Me and Gia [Pezzullo] have really been working on pressing, being explosive and I feel like all of our training just came out tonight and it was great,” Clark said. 
Pezzullo finished the game as the Spartans leading scorer with 14 kills and paced an offensive attack that featured multiple players with five or more kills. 
The Spartans will need to take all their successes from this game along with the winning momentum into their battle against the reigning state champions. The Hillers and Spartans have met on this stage twice before in the same amount of years and the Spartans have come out as the runners-up each time without winning a set. 
The trilogy of this recent rivalry is scheduled for 7:00 p.m. at the Bob Carpenter Center on Monday, November 16.
