title: Commentary: ‘Get the hell out of here’: Rep. Tom Emmer’s post-election crashout
description: On Nov. 10, House Republicans voted 103-76 to keep Rep. Tom Emmer as whip. That makes him the No. 2 Republican in the new minority. At the press conference afterward, he told Democrats that “come January 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot.”  That night he told Fox News’ Laura […]
text:
WASHINGTON, DC - U.S. Rep. Tom Emmer, R-MN, was again elected party whip, though this time in the minority. Since the election, he's taken to right-wing national outlets to at-times castigate Minnesota. (Photo by Anna Rose Layden/Getty Images)On Nov. 10, House Republicans voted 103-76 to keep Rep. Tom Emmer as whip. That makes him the No. 2 Republican in the new minority. At the press conference afterward, he told Democrats that “come January 3, 2027, you will regret ever putting your name on a ballot.” 
That night he told Fox News’ Laura Ingraham that “prices are too high and wages are not high enough. And I think we need to listen to the American people.” The American people had just handed Democrats both chambers of Congress.
Over the next two days he gave four more: Fox & Friends, Newsmax, Matt Gaetz and Benny Johnson. 
MN-06 Watch transcribed all five. None were with Minnesota outlets. 
‘Get the hell out of here’
Emmer conducted a 23-minute interview with Benny Johnson — who was caught up in a Russian influence operation in 2024, though he said he was none the wiser. He also accused Emmer’s fellow Minnesotan Alex Pretti, who was disarmed and then shot dead by federal officers, of attempting to commit “mass murder.”
Emmer began the Nov. 12 interview by saying: “I’ve got basically the Somali civil war that’s come to the state of Minnesota.”
Johnson asked what Somali culture had brought to Minnesota and listed “rampant fraud,” “rampant crime” and “the humiliation of electing these Somalis,” and called it “such a scar on the face of Minnesota.” 
Emmer, who early in his congressional career defended Somali immigrants’ right to live in Minnesota, answered: “It really is.” He then said that more than 80% of Somalis “are still collecting on Minnesota welfare programs.” Census data roughly back the number: about 9 in 10 Somali Minnesotans receive some form of public assistance, most often Medicaid. But those programs are built to cover low-wage workers, and Somali Minnesotans are more likely to be in the labor force than Minnesotans overall. Many work in jobs that pay too little to keep them off those programs. Receiving benefits, PolitiFact noted, doesn’t mean someone isn’t working. Emmer also described Somali residents calling relatives elsewhere: “You’re never going to believe how gullible these people are… you can rip them off until the sun comes up the next day.”
On Rep. Ilhan Omar, he said: “She’s said in the past that she’s here to represent Somalia. Well, why don’t you go back to Somalia?… And if you don’t want to be an American, then you should just get the hell out of here.” That claim comes from a January 2024 speech Omar gave in Somali. A court-registered interpreter said the translation that critics circulated was wrong, and USA Today rated the “loyalty to Somalia” version false. Emmer used that same translation at the time to demand an ethics investigation. Nearly three years later, he’s still repeating it. He doesn’t seem to care that it’s been fact-checked and rated false. What would it take for him to stop?
It isn’t the first time he has told Somali Minnesotans to leave. On June 25, at a Faith & Freedom Coalition event in Washington, Emmer said: “Celebrate your culture, I don’t care — Italian, Polish, you know, Somali — but they don’t assimilate, and if they don’t assimilate, then they should go the hell back to where they came from.” Omar replied that she had “assimilated all the way to Congress.”
Johnson asked whether Emmer would support a ban on burqas “here in America or at least in Minnesota.” 
Emmer said America should have a dress code: “There should be no burqas. I’m sorry. If it covers up your identity, there should be nothing like that allowed.” 
He dismissed religious objections: “It is pure stupidity to say, oh, well, you know, this is what they believe.” 
Minnesota law already makes it a misdemeanor to conceal your identity in public. It exempts religious dress, so what Emmer is describing is removing a religious protection, an interesting contradiction from someone who has worried aloud about government interfering with his own faith. He told The Hill he voted for the Respect for Marriage Act because of its religious-liberty provisions, fearing Attorney General Keith Ellison could go after his kids’ Catholic school for “not teaching all forms of marriage.” When it’s his church, government should stay out. When it’s a Muslim woman’s clothing, the religious reason is “pure stupidity.”
His reasoning: “I want to know who the heck you are. It’s a matter of safety and security.” In February, when Democrats demanded that ICE agents identify themselves, Emmer called it “intellectually inconsistent” because Democrats oppose voter ID. Whether his standard of knowing who someone is applies to federal agents, he hasn’t said. I have asked. It’s among the dozens of questions I’ve put to his office this year, without a single response. 
‘Corrupt to the core’
On Nov. 10, Ingraham asked Emmer what was going on in Minnesota and answered her own question: “Fraud is like the biggest industry you have right now there.” Emmer didn’t push back, even though his home state features 18 Fortune 500 companies and the highest wages in the Midwest. 
He answered by referring to Minnesota Democrats, though he didn’t name them: “When you elect a Somali fraudster who ran a daycare and was guilty of fraud again in St. Cloud,” an attorney general “caught on tape essentially being bribed,” and “a gal who stood by Tim Walz’s side while the fraud was going on.” (More on this in a moment.) 
Two days later, on Johnson’s show, he went further: “Either fraud doesn’t matter or our election process in Minnesota is corrupt to the core. I’ll let you decide.” Later: “Something’s wrong with the election process in Minnesota, which I think we’re going to hear more about in the future.” That’s the election that just reelected him. He won by 11.5 points, down from 25 in 2024.
Minnesota ranked top in the country in MIT’s 2024 Election Performance Index, which measures election administration. After every election, the secretary of state and the counties conduct an exhaustive post-election review process, including hand-counting some precincts in each county, and the results year after year are nearly identical to machine tabulations that produce the official results. 
After Republicans lost the House in 2018, Emmer, about to take over the party’s House campaign arm, told Fox 9: “It is what it is. The voters have spoken.”
The evidence he offered for fraud this time was who won, not citing a single documented fraudulent vote or even a conspiracy theory: Attorney General Keith Ellison, Senator-elect Peggy Flanagan and Abdi Daisane, the first Somali American legislator elected from the St. Cloud area. On Fox, without naming him, Emmer said Daisane “was guilty of fraud.” Minnesota state court records show no criminal case against Daisane, and the reporting we found shows no federal charge.
The nonprofit that sponsored his day care’s federal meal funds settled a state fraud case, but his center was not named in that lawsuit. The attorney general’s office says investigations of people and sites connected to that sponsor are ongoing; nothing public ties them to Daisane.
Johnson asked about James O’Keefe — the right-wing activist charged in October over a primary-day video when he donned a burqa and unsuccessfully tried to participate in Minnesota’s primary election — and what Minnesota was “doing to him.” 
Emmer called O’Keefe’s stunt “brilliant.” His account: O’Keefe vouched for “five or six people,” and “they gave them all ballots. They didn’t vote.”
The Hennepin County attorney’s account is different. O’Keefe and Cam Higby gave election judges the names of registered voters, some of them dead. When the judges asked them to sign the oath, which carries a perjury penalty, “they made excuses to leave.” Vouching confirms an address, not an identity. Anyone registering that way still has to give a Minnesota driver’s license number, a state ID number or the last four digits of a Social Security number, and sign the oath. Every vouched voter is checked after the election. Fewer than 0.6% of votes in 2024 involved vouching.
Emmer also left this out: To vouch, you have to be registered in that precinct already. That is why O’Keefe and Higby had to impersonate other voters to get to the vouching portion.
That’s also what they’re charged with. They aren’t accused of casting fraudulent ballots. Each faces two felonies, unlawful voting and identity theft, under a state law that bars anyone from misrepresenting their identity when applying for a ballot. “You cannot go into a polling place and misidentify yourself, use other people’s identity, and say that to our election judges as you apply for the ballot, whether or not you intend to vote,” Moriarty said. 
O’Keefe calls the case “lawfare.” 
How “brilliant” is a stunt that ends in two felony charges?
Ellison
On Ingraham’s show, Emmer said Ellison was “caught on tape essentially being bribed.” He told Johnson the attorney general had promised “Somali fraudsters” protection from an investigation.
MN-06 Watch transcribed all 54 minutes of that December 2021 recording. In it, Ellison says he is hearing about the child-nutrition program complaints “for the first time.” When the audio became public in 2025, Reformer editor Patrick Coolican and Kayseh Magan criticized Ellison for being oblivious and inappropriately criticizing the Walz administration, which was his client. But no one in the recording discusses committing fraud. Some of the people in the room were convicted later.
Emmer also told Johnson that, “I’m told,” Ellison announced on his first day that there would be no more investigations without his approval, and “never approved any of them.” His office has also clocked more than 350 Medicaid fraud convictions since his tenure began in 2019. In September, Ellison’s office reached an $18.5 million settlement with Partners in Nutrition, another sponsor in the federal child-meal program, over fraud claims his office brought. You can’t settle a fraud case you never brought. And being told something doesn’t make it true.
‘They’re not going to be working with us’
Ingraham asked whether Democrats would work with Republicans on issues like gas prices. Emmer: “They’re not going to be working with us… I would not expect them to work with us. Where are we going to find middle ground…?” 
Emmer has often had trouble finding middle ground with members of his own party in the Senate. In five interviews, he didn’t name a single issue where he would seek Democratic votes. In 2020, as the party’s campaign chief, he told NPR that a narrow Democratic majority would have “no choice but to work with Republicans.” Republicans still control the executive branch, so any legislation that becomes law will need the White House’s signature.
The audience
All five interviews were on conservative outlets, and his language got sharper as the platforms got more partisan. 
On Fox & Friends, he stuck to the economy and the 2028 map; Minnesota never came up. 
On Ingraham’s prime-time show, Minnesota meant fraud, Ellison and Daisane. 
On Newsmax, Omar was “a dishonest, anti-American individual” and Democrats were “Marxist, socialist anarchists.” 
On Gaetz’s show, new Democrats were “terrorist sympathizers” who would “regret they ever put their name on a ballot.” 
The burqa answer, i.e., new American dress code, “gullible” and “get the hell out of here” came only on Johnson’s online show, the longest of the five. Hosts often set up the topic. Emmer didn’t push back on any of them. If anything, he leaned into the framing.
Promising aggressive oversight is standard for a House minority, and Democrats made similar promises when they were out of power. Minnesota’s fraud cases are real, too. Feeding Our Future produced federal convictions, and Emmer has pressed the issue for years. 
The record, however, doesn’t show that Minnesota’s elections were corrupted, that Ellison was bribed or that Daisane was charged. 
The fact checks and court records say otherwise, but Minnesota’s most powerful member of Congress, with the seat still at the table, repeats it anyway. 
Emmer’s office and campaign did not respond to questions sent Thursday.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Trump praises Democrat Scott Colom for courting MAGA supporters at Mississippi rally
description: President Donald Trump embraces Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith during his rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026.
text:
WASHINGTON — President Donald Trump on Thursday heaped praise on Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom for courting some of his hardcore MAGA supporters in the final days of the midterm election campaign, a rare example of the Republican president showing admiration for a Democrat.
When the president traveled to Corinth, Mississippi, last month to campaign for incumbent Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, Trump denigrated Colom as a “Marxist radical,” a “fake” and a “shameless phony who pretends to be a moderate.”
But on Thursday, during an appearance on Stephen A. Smith’s “Straight Shooter” podcast, Trump acknowledged that Colom demonstrated chutzpah by showing up to the Trump rally to mingle with some of the Republican president’s staunchest “Make America Great Again” supporters.
“I heard it the other day, where I had a rally there, and we had lines that went 10 miles long, and he campaigned on that line, telling everybody on the line what a good job he did,” Trump said of Colom, a 43-year-old local prosecutor who capitalized on the electorate’s discontent with the economy in his successful underdog campaign. “I give him a lot of credit for that.”
Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom greets people in line at a President Donald Trump rally for Colom’s opponent, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026 in Corinth. Credit: Special to Mississippi Today
Colom had walked along the lineup of Trump supporters waiting to get into the Corinth rally, introducing himself and asking about their concerns.
The move gained widespread media attention, stealing the spotlight from Trump’s barnstorming in Mississippi, a state Republicans had expected to easily win.
It also tracked with Colom’s strategy throughout the campaign of criticizing Trump’s policies — especially the Iran war that drove up gas prices and tariffs that caused headaches for Mississippi farmers — without taking personal jabs at the president or people who voted for him. Colom had sought to portray Hyde-Smith as a nonentity in Washington, while vowing that he would look out for the interests of people in his state.
The Associated Press called the tight race in Colom’s favor on Wednesday after local officials spent several days processing absentee and provisional ballots, which are called affidavit ballots in Mississippi.
With the win, Colom will become the state’s first Black U.S. senator since post-Civil War Reconstruction.

name: California
title: Newsom’s power move bruised Dems. Now, they look forward to the Becerra era
description: It’s Xavier Becerra’s honeymoon period, and he’s pledging to treat Democratic leaders in the Capitol better than the last guy. We’ll see how the promise holds come budget season. We have a new election result with Prop. 5 passing. That’s the Democratic-backed ballot measure that aims to shake up recall elections, presumably in a way […]
text:
Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra at a news conference at the state Capitol in Sacramento on Nov. 5, 2026. Photo by Miguel Gutierrez Jr., CalMatters




It’s Xavier Becerra’s honeymoon period, and he’s pledging to treat Democratic leaders in the Capitol better than the last guy. We’ll see how the promise holds come budget season.
We have a new election result with Prop. 5 passing. That’s the Democratic-backed ballot measure that aims to shake up recall elections, presumably in a way that helps political insiders.
And you don’t want to skip our story on a lawsuit that alleges real estate agents working both sides of the deal are giving the short end of the stick to buyers.
Gov. Gavin Newsom at times ticked off even his Democratic allies in the state Legislature by jamming big policy proposals down their throats right before deadlines, using the time crunch to generate urgency and discourage opposition.
But it appears that Newsom’s successor doesn’t want to work that way. At least that’s what he’s saying now, a couple months before he has to send a budget proposal over to the Capitol.
Standing alongside Democratic legislative leaders at the state Capitol rotunda last week, Gov.-elect Xavier Becerra signaled that he is embracing a more collaborative relationship with lawmakers, write CalMatters’ Maya C. Miller and Jeanne Kuang.
Lawmakers, in turn, are looking forward to the change up.

Assembly Speaker Robert Rivas: “It’s going to be a different type of relationship than what this Legislature has experienced over the past eight years. I fully expect and trust the governor-elect when he says that he’s going to do his best to … not drop stuff on us unexpectedly.”

Becerra’s push for cooperation between the two branches of government could stem from his experience as a California assemblymember and member of Congress. Since advancing from the primary as the Democratic candidate for governor, Becerra has met individually with several legislators, as well as the Senate and Assembly Democratic caucuses.
But where Becerra stands on major policy issues still is unclear, and both he and the Legislature have plenty on their plate to tackle, including how the state will deal with federal cuts to Medi-Cal; resolving the debate over who pays for wildfire damage caused by utilities; reining in artificial intelligence; and lowering the cost of living.
Even when asked if he would commit to one policy — reversing Newsom’s rollback of healthcare benefits for undocumented immigrants, which Becerra appeared to endorse in an interview with KQED earlier this month — Becerra lectured reporters for “playing politics.”

Becerra: “Guys, don’t play this game about asking me to commit, because I didn’t get elected doing that.”

Read more.



CalMatters Ideas Festival: 2027 Ideas Festival will expand to Los Angeles, Sacramento and San Francisco. One full day of candid conversations in each, with the leaders, innovators and changemakers shaping California’s future. Learn more.

Other Stories You Should Know


The next recall election will look different


A Newsom supporter holds up a sign against the recall at a campaign event in San Leandro on Sept. 8, 2021. Photo by Anne Wernikoff, CalMatters




California voters narrowly approved Proposition 5 Thursday, changing the recall process of state officials, reports CalMatters’ Kate Wolffe.
Currently, voters are simultaneously asked whether an official should be removed from office and who should replace the recalled official. But under Prop. 5, voters will now decide first whether to remove an official. If successful, they’ll vote again in a followup election on who the replacement should be.
Democratic lawmakers backed Prop. 5, arguing that the current system leads to unnecessary state expense and can lead to “undemocratic” outcomes, since the winner does not need a majority to win. The 2021 campaign to recall Newsom, for example, cost taxpayers about $200 million and the campaigns on both sides spent another $100 million total.
But Republican lawmakers said changing the recall process is unnecessary and would lead to additional costs because of the need to hold two elections.
Nevertheless, Prop. 5 passed with 52% of the vote.
Read more.



When real estate agents works both sides of the deal


A for sale sign in front of a residential home. Photo via iStock Photo




A Sonoma County lawsuit is bringing to light what appears to be a growing trend among real estate brokerage companies that are leaving some homebuyers worse off, writes CalMatters’ Ben Christopher.
“Dual agency” is a practice in which both buyer and seller are represented by the same agent or brokerage. Though it’s illegal in more than half a dozen states, it’s permitted in California — as long as both buyer and seller fully understand and consent to the arrangement.
But homebuyers in a lawsuit against W Real Estate, one of the largest brokerages in Northern California, are accusing the company of pushing new buyers of a Santa Rosa housing development into dual agency transactions without giving them any real choice in the matter. 
These deals could also hurt homebuyers’ pocketbooks: At a different W Real Estate brokered development where dual agency was not required of buyers, those with their own agents were four times more likely to receive concessions and credits, said the lawyer bringing the dual agency lawsuit. 
Some experts also say that dual agency deals operate in an ethical grey area.

Wayne Bell, a former commissioner at the California Department of Real Estate: “You can’t try to get the highest price for the seller and also try to get the lowest price for the buyer, it’s an inherent conflict of interest.”

Read more.

CalMatters columnist Dan Walters: Newsom insists that he respects voters, but his unilateral efforts to stop executions violate the promises he made, while running for governor, to honor voters’ support of the death penalty.
Gigantic acquisitions like Paramount-Warner and Fox-Roku have the potential to turn California’s entertainment industry into a handful of lumbering corporate behemoths that produce too much slop and not enough well-paying jobs, writes William Lockyer, a former California attorney general and state legislator

name: Mississippi Today
title: Will a north Mississippi man’s appeal sway the US Supreme Court?
description: Descriptions in the appeal Lane Mitchell's attorney filed in the attempted murder of Russell Rogers appear at odds with what was captured in the surveillance video.
text:
The parents of a Tennessee man nearly stabbed to death at a north Mississippi restaurant in 2019 are speaking out as the U.S. Supreme Court weighs this week whether to take on the defendant’s case, potentially halting a scheduled retrial. 
In 2023, a judge acquitted Lane Mitchell, who stabbed Russell Rogers at Tallahatchie Gourmet in New Albany, of attempted murder before the jury could deliberate. The state’s appeal led to a close decision by the Mississippi Court of Appeals. However, that decision was ultimately left standing by the state Supreme Court, paving the way for the retrial set for March 2027 in Union County. 
Mitchell’s attorneys asked the nation’s high court in October to hear his case, arguing that the state appeals court decision violated their client’s protection from double jeopardy. Typically, the U.S. Supreme Court accepts few petitions requesting review. 
Bob and Maridonna Rogers say the petition contains misstatements. These include the description of their son’s stabbing and the repeated assertion that Russell refused to show up or was intentionally kept from trial to testify, even though a Tennessee probate court ruled he was suffering from post-traumatic stress disorder as a result of the attack and was unable to testify. The judge used the victim’s absence as a basis for the acquittal. 
The couple had hoped the state would file its own brief to correct the record, as it did in the appeal. Instead, they said they were shocked to find that the attorney general’s office filed a two-page waiver saying it would not respond. 
“How can you (the court) make an informed decision when the information you’re being given is misinformation?” asked Maridonna Rogers, the victim’s mother. 
A spokesperson from the Mississippi Attorney General’s Office declined to comment, saying the office does not comment on active cases. 
In her victim’s impact statement, Maridonna Rogers said her son was given less than a 1% chance of survival. He had emergency surgery to repair a severed carotid artery and experienced a stroke. 
Months after the stabbing, Russell Rogers was placed under a conservatorship, which is a court-approved agreement for someone who is unable to care for their own personal affairs due to factors including illness. The court appointed his father, Bob, the conservator, in 2020 and that conservatorship overseeing medical matters remains in place today. 
Before the stabbing, Rogers had studied international politics in Washington, D.C., traveled to China and immersed himself in the language. Rogers left an international relations program in 2013 to take care of his father who had suffered a minor stroke and help his mother at home in Collierville, Tennessee. He stayed as his father experienced other health complications. 
An outdoorsman, Rogers liked to hike in north Mississippi, often bringing him to the New Albany area where he frequently ate at the restaurant. 
Today, he has ongoing symptoms of PTSD and sensory triggers that make him relive the stabbing, along with nightmares and hyper-vigilance, according to his parents. 
Their son also lives with the fear that the stabber will find him and try to kill him, his mother wrote in a victim impact statement. 
“He took my son’s life,” she said. 
Differing descriptions of the stabbing in court records and video
A 42-minute silent surveillance video from the restaurant from Feb. 9, 2019, shows interactions between restaurant staff and customers and the events that led up to the stabbing.  
In their petition, Mitchell’s attorneys state that Rogers had been drinking the afternoon and evening of the attack. 
About half an hour before the attack, video shows Rogers talking to three women at a table near the back of the restaurant. At trial, they testified that Rogers did not seem intoxicated and court transcripts show they did not feel threatened by him starting a conversation with them. 
Russell Rogers, seen top right in this surveillance video, talks with a female waitress at the Tallahatchie Gourmet restaurant in New Albany on Feb. 9, 2019, moments before Lane Mitchell, unseen sitting at the other end of the bar, stabbed Rogers in the neck. A judge acquitted Mitchell of attempted murder in 2023 and an appeal led to an order for a retrial. Mitchell’s attorneys have asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case. 
Later in their petition, the defense states that Rogers “corner(ed) a frightened teenaged server.” 
The server testified that she was 21 when Rogers was attacked, according to the trial transcript and local reporting. Prior to the attack, video showed Rogers attempting to talk with the woman.
The defense wrote that Rogers, who was told multiple times by restaurant staff to leave, became enraged and “charged aggressively at the bartender, (the) petitioner’s father.” 
The entire stabbing sequence happens in two minutes, video shows: 
The waitress, seen earlier offering Mitchell a hug, speaks with Rogers at a corner table as Mitchell watches.  
Mitchell, 18 at the time, takes a knife from the bar and holds it behind his back, keeping his eyes on Rogers and the waitress. A woman seated at the bar grabs the back of Mitchell’s t-shirt, but he stands and stops a few steps away from Rogers and the waitress. 
During the conversation, Rogers leans in, causing the woman to step back and lean away. She turns to go behind the bar, passing Mitchell’s dad, Torrey Mitchell, the bartender. Rogers takes a step to follow her, and Torrey Mitchell stops him, grabbing his arms. 
Lane Mitchell, seen top center, holds a knife behind his back while looking at Russell Rogers, top right, as he talks to a waitress at the Tallahatchie Gourmet restaurant in New Albany, as seen in video surveillance the night of Feb. 9, 2019.  A judge acquitted Mitchell of attempted murder on 2023 and an appeal led to an order for a retrial. Mitchell’s attorneys have asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case. 
At that moment, Lane Mitchell takes four steps toward Rogers from behind and sinks the knife into Rogers’ neck three times, dazing him. Torrey Mitchell pushes his son out of the way and wraps his arms around Rogers, holding him in place. 
Still holding Rogers around the abdomen, he walks them toward another end of the restaurant and eases Rogers to the ground. Video shows stains on the front of his pants and splatters of what is likely blood. Lane Mitchell and a customer peer at Rogers. Within two minutes, police officers arrive and tend to him: One gets a towel for the blood, another tries CPR. 
Russell Rogers is held around the abdomen after being stabbed in the neck on Feb. 9, 2019, at the Tallahatchie Gourmet restaurant in New Albany. The man holding Rogers is a bartender and the father of Lane Mitchell, the then-18-year-old who stabbed Rogers. A judge acquitted Mitchell of attempted murder in 2023, and an appeal led to an order for a retrial. Mitchell’s attorneys have asked the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case. 
The defense states that Mitchell acted in self defense “believing Rogers to be armed and seeing him charge at his father” and “to prevent any harm befalling his father, himself and any other patrons or employees at the Tallahatchie Gourmet restaurant.”  
Video shows that minutes earlier, Rogers had left the restaurant, prompting Mitchell, his father and the waitress to exchange looks. At trial, witnesses and Mitchell said they believed he retrieved a gun, according to court records. Court filings show a firearm was never found on Rogers. 
A representative from Mitchell’s legal team did not respond to a request for comment.
Victim’s absence at court argued as violation of defendant’s rights
Mitchell’s attorneys highlighted the trial judge’s order to support its argument to convince the U.S. Supreme Court to review his case. 
Union County Circuit Judge Kent Smith said Russell Rogers had never appeared at court hearings, spoke with law enforcement or communicated with the prosecution. The judge and both sides viewed him as a material witness and expected him to testify, with the defense issuing a subpoena to take Rogers into custody in Tennessee and bring him to Mississippi. 
Ultimately, his father acting as conservator, petitioned the Shelby County Probate Court, which oversees Rogers’ conservatorship. A judge quashed the subpoena, finding that Rogers was unable to testify due to his mental health. 
In lieu of Rogers, prosecutors called his mother as a witness, asking her about his injuries and recovery, according to the trial transcript. 
Rogers’ absence at trial meant the defense was not able to cross examine Rogers, which the defense argued was a violation of Mitchell’s Sixth Amendment right to confront a witness. Smith agreed. 
“(Rogers) is the complaining victim. Both the State of Mississippi and the defense announced their desire and intent to call Rogers as a witness at trial,” Smith wrote. “Nevertheless, he appears to be intentionally unavailable even though the Court is of the opinion that Mitchell has a fundamental right to call Rogers as a witness at trial and to examine him at trial in the presence of the jury.”
The state denied that characterization in its successful 2024 appeal. In the majority written by Judge John Emfinger, the court noted that the conservator acted accordingly when he stepped in to challenge the defense’s subpoena, even if it “may well have been at odds with the state’s interest in proceeding with the prosecution of the case.”
In its appeal, the attorney general’s office asked for a different judge or venue for the retrial, but the Court of Appeals did not order that, sending the case back to Smith.
New attorneys have not reached out about retrial 
The attorney general’s office has been part of the case since 2021, after District Attorney Ben Creekmore recused himself due to undisclosed conflicts. Multiple attorneys from the office worked on the case, including new attorneys now assigned to handle the retrial.
One of those attorneys is Special Assistant Attorney General Luke Williamson, who this year handled the cases of two former Capitol Police officers charged with manslaughter in the shooting death of Jaylen Lewis in a traffic stop in downtown Jackson. The jury deadlocked on whether to convict one, Michael Rhinehalt, while acquitting his co-defendant, Stephen Frederick, allowing both to walk free when the attorney general’s office announced it would not retry Rhinehalt. 
Bob and Maridonna Rogers said they had a positive experience communicating with Danielle Love Burks from the attorney general’s office who headed the appeal and took care in writing the appeal brief, but have not heard from Williamson or other attorneys assigned to the case. They said they learned about recent updates by reading Mississippi Today or by checking court dockets on their own to access new filings. 
A spokesperson for the attorney general’s office did not respond to Mississippi Today’s questions about its communication with the Rogers family.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: John Adams warned us against oligarchs
description: "He who had the deepest purse, or the fewest scruples about using it will generally prevail."
text:
OCTOBER 30 marked the 291st anniversary of the birth of John Adams in Braintree. This year we’ve been watching his fears come to life.  
With Elon Musk dumping nearly $500 million into the midterms and nearly 100 billionaires contributing to Susan Collins’s US Senate campaign in Maine, Adams’s warnings about wealth in politics were on vivid display.  
We may be tempted to call his warnings overblown after Musk’s millions, including $224 million spent backing Republicans in Texas alone, sank gurgling beneath the blue wave that saw huge Democratic gains, including the governor’s office and a US Senate seat in the Lone Star state. 
These outcomes would leave Adams unmoved. He would be quick to say that if Americans now think that by winning midterm battles against Musk and his fellow oligarchs we’ve won the war, we’re deluded. Adams saw the struggle against oligarchy as a permanent— and permanently acute—condition. 
Adams is often remembered as the most conservative of the Founders—as a borderline reactionary, morbidly anxious about the danger of too much democracy, and convinced that plebeian mobs could destroy the legal architecture of the new Republic. Adams is frequently contrasted with peers—Hamilton, Jefferson, Madison—who believed that by erasing hereditary titles and offices the United States had given birth to a stable new world of democratic rule by the people.  
Adams never amassed great wealth, and he always identified with the New England middling farmer and artisan class into which he was born. But it is certainly true that he did not trust the mass of people to run the government. He expressed this view with his characteristic impolitic pungency. At the arrival of pure democracy, Adams said: “The idle, the vicious, and the intemperate, will rush into the utmost extravagance of debauchery.” 
The unwashed crowds could be stupid and unwieldy. But what of an elite, composed of the well-born, the beautiful, and (especially) the rich, that could dominate, exploit, and mobilize those crowds?  That, Adams believed, constituted the permanent, aggressive, and existential threat to the Republic.  
As Luke Mayville showed in his 2016 book, John Adams and the Fear of American Oligarchy, what really distinguished Adams from his comrades at the founding was not a weakness for pro-aristocratic policies and institutions; it was his conviction that abolishing formal titles of nobility and explicit hereditary ranks did not remove the threat from ravenous elites.  
Adams saw that even in our new order the “goods of the mind” could not obliterate the “goods of fortune” —wealth, beauty, and family—that fuel metastasizing influence. John Adams saw Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos, and Peter Thiel coming.  
Adams thought that Madison, Jefferson, and the rest had naively substituted ideology for a cold-eyed examination of human nature, and in so doing had failed to account for the basic reality that “the power of privilege is so deeply rooted that it would persist even in modern democratic republics.”  
Adams’s criticisms of the Jeffersonian program arose not from admiration of Old World aristocratic structures, but from his fear of their sources. In Adams’s view, with or without titles, there always exists “a class of men who will not suffer themselves to be governed,” who would “Employ the commonality to knock to pieces any plan and model that the most honest architects in legislation can invent to keep them within bounds.”   
Adams saw all along that eventually these tycoons would say, as Peter Thiel put it, that they “no longer believe that freedom and democracy are compatible.”   
Yes, Adams agreed, now we will have elections, but, he warned, “He who had the deepest purse, or the fewest scruples about using it will generally prevail.” 
Adams would see the Democrats’ midterm wins as “the foam on the sea of history.” The fact that Musk was willing to squander $500 million and that others dumped $10 million into the Senate race in Maine shows us the eternal forces operating deep underneath.   
And Adams understood that wealth is politically powerful in modern societies not merely because money buys influence, but also because citizens admire and even sympathize with the rich. He thought that wealth is powerful in the same way that beauty is powerful—it distinguishes its possessor, and prompts approval, even veneration. MAGA might vote with the rich not because they hope to be rich one day themselves, but because they esteem the rich and submit to their wishes.  
John Adams would take sardonic pleasure from the fact that there is no John Adams Memorial or Monument in Washington, where we will soon see a Trump ballroom, and (perhaps) a Trump Arc of Triumph.  
But then, Adams would get to work. Adams would argue that 250 years after the Declaration of Independence, we’re still in a fight for our lives. He would be very sure whom the fight was against. And he would know which side he is on.  
Adams would welcome the midterms’ impressive frustration of oligarchy. Then, he would warn us to remain vigilant, for the oligarchs haven’t gone away, and that they never will.    
James Doyle is a Boston defense lawyer and author. He is former head of the public defender division of the Committee for Public Counsel Services and director of the Center for Modern Forensic Practice at the John Jay College of Criminal Justice.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Massachusetts braces for topsy-turvy winter energy
description: Looming over it all are soaring utility bills and the annual rinse-and-repeat cycle of turning to high-polluting oil-fired electric generation, as power demand is projected to keep rising across the region in the years ahead.
text:
A WAVE OF sky-high oil prices, the completion of significant additional renewable energy sources, and a Super El Niño weather event are threatening to collide and inject new uncertainty into Bay Staters’ electric bills this winter just as temperatures begin to dip.  
While the situation is clear for the 20 percent of Massachusetts households warmed by home heating oil, with costs up 60 percent compared to this time last year, it’s far more uncertain when it comes to electricity.  
Should New England burn oil for power generation at some point this winter, as it does every year, that would be a much more expensive endeavor this time.  
Those costs, to say nothing of the climate impacts, could soar if oil usage emerges anything close to last winter, the coldest in 20 years, when oil accounted for 28 percent of power generation. During a punishing cold snap in January and February, it even at times topped 40 percent.  
Looming over it all are soaring utility bills and the annual rinse-and-repeat cycle of turning to high-polluting oil-fired electric generation, as power demand is projected to keep rising across the region in the years ahead.  
Already, Massachusetts residents are grappling with energy bills up 38 percent on average since 2020 in a state ranked fourth-worst for energy insecurity among lower-income people. 
The good news is that this season, new offshore wind capacity from the recently-completed Vineyard Wind and Revolution Wind projects and forecasts of a milder winter could blunt the need to turn to oil in the first place. 
But if the coming winter is chillier than expected, or if anything fails, New England could again be forced to turn to oil. Recall the inconveniently-timed 12-day shutdown of the new hydropower transmission line just as frigid temperatures hit New England last winter, and the inexplicable two-week pause from May into June. 
Plus, ISO New England, the regional grid operator, is forecasting peak demands slightly higher than last winter, according to its newly-released outlook. 
“There are countervailing forces across the playing field,” said Dan Dolan, president of the New England Power Generators Association. “I have no clue what’s going to happen this winter on prices and costs.” 
Roughly half of the region’s power supply comes from natural gas. But in the winter, with half of Massachusetts homes using gas for heat, demand for the fuel — and prices — spike to the point that some generators turn to typically cheaper oil resources to meet New England’s electric needs. 
Last winter, more oil was burned than in any year since at least winter 2015, according to data from ISO New England. 
This year, though, oil may not be the cheaper option even when gas prices jump. Oil prices are significantly higher than this time last year, though they have dropped a bit of late, while natural gas prices in New England are currently lower than this time a year ago. 
Since ISO New England calls on the cheapest power sources to be deployed first, that could leave Bay Staters stuck paying higher gas prices should they jump, if oil is even costlier. Or it could leave them paying for expensive oil-fired electricity — which releases more than double the carbon emissions compared to gas — should it be necessary to keep the lights on, especially if another resource fails to deliver even for a short period of time. 
“This just reemphasizes the work that needs to be done to accelerate the clean energy movement so that we are able to insulate ourselves from these price spikes,” said Kyle Murray, Massachusetts program director at environmental nonprofit Acadia Center.  
Meanwhile on Beacon Hill, sweeping energy affordability legislation meant to deliver substantial savings to ratepayers and unclog supply shortfalls remains stuck in closed-door conference committee negotiations, where the House and Senate appear far apart. 
One of the largest points of disagreement is Mass Save, the state energy efficiency initiative funded through a fee on customers’ utility bills. The House approved a plan to cut $1 billion from the program, and the Senate advanced its bill with no cut at all. 
Eversource, the state’s largest utility company, warned in a 20-page letter last month to leaders of the energy committee that no legislation may be better than anything currently under consideration. Both the House and Senate versions “set the stage for dramatic cost increases,” executives wrote.  
If oil is burned this winter and costs stay high, some customers may be insulated from those price shocks through at least part of the winter.  
The state’s electric companies purchase power supply in six-month contracts that are approved by the Department of Public Utilities. So for the 1 in 4 customers in Massachusetts that receive electric supply directly from the utilities, known as basic service, the cost impact of burning any oil this winter would not likely show itself until the following six-month cycle, which starts in February. 
The 1.4 million customers that get electricity from municipal aggregation plans, accounting for about half of all customers in the state, state data show, could be even further insulated.  
These programs purchase power in longer-term 12, 24, or 36-month contracts, providing stability to the supply portion of their electric bills — about one-third of a customer’s overall bill. High oil prices would probably only affect them if their plan renegotiates its contracts in the near future. Municipal aggregation customers have saved $25 million over the last two years compared to basic service rates, according to the Department of Public Utilities.  
A limited reliance on expensive oil would likely go unnoticed on most customer bills, Dolan said. But sustained high prices and a grid strained to its maximum, like what the region endured last winter, translate into higher costs for consumers. 
Last winter wholesale electricity costs were up 45 percent from the one prior, higher than any other winter since 2014, ISO New England found, driven by a 31 percent surge in natural gas prices.  
“The issue right now is that the prices that consumers are going to be paying for this winter do carry some of the echoes of last winter,” Dolan said. “That has now introduced a level of operational risk that hadn’t been experienced on the electric grid in quite some time. The cost of having to absorb that is now a risk that generators have to embed.”

name: Nevada Current
title: Citing data center, tribal sovereignty fears, Nevadans push back against Trump-backed permit bill
description: A Trump-backed permitting revision bill is getting blowback from a growing coalition of Nevadans, who say its provisions will accelerate the buildout of new fossil fuel projects for data centers and cut tribes out of the regulatory process. The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BBAAJA) is a wide-ranging package aimed at easing the construction [...]
text:
Walker River Paiute Tribe flag blowing in breeze. (Photo: Jeniffer Solis/Nevada Current) A Trump-backed permitting revision bill is getting blowback from a growing coalition of Nevadans, who say its provisions will accelerate the buildout of new fossil fuel projects for data centers and cut tribes out of the regulatory process.
The Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act (BBAAJA) is a wide-ranging package aimed at easing the construction of new energy infrastructure and mines by rolling back environmental, judicial, Tribal, and historic preservation protections.
If passed, the bill would weaken certain provisions in the National Environmental Policy Act, the Clean Water Act, the Endangered Species Act, and the National Historic Preservation Act.
Nevada Democratic Sens. Catherine Cortez Masto and Jacky Rosen were among 19 Democrats voting with the Republican majority Monday to advance the bill, arguing it would help hasten the approval of renewable energy projects, bring down utility costs and require data centers to pay for the grid upgrades they trigger. 
But conservation groups warned the regulatory rollbacks would apply to all projects on public lands – everything from clean energy projects to fossil fuel pipelines built to fuel data centers.
Under the bill, federal land managers would be allowed to evaluate more projects on public lands using a less vigorous environmental analysis that requires a lower threshold for approval. 
“This means that data centers and gas power plants would almost certainly be analyzed using” lower-level of analysis, said Patrick Donnelly, the Great Basin Director of the Center for Biological Diversity.
Once approved, projects would also be more difficult to stop. The bill would drastically reduce judicial review for projects on public lands, including limiting judges’ ability to halt construction on public lands for environmental violations, even if it would cause imminent and irreparable harm.
Provisions in the bill would prevent future administrations from revoking permits for projects that have already been approved. In practice, conservation groups say that could embolden the Trump administration to accelerate AI data center construction on public lands. 
“If Trump tries to ram through a bunch of data centers on public lands in the next 2 years, and we get a new Democratic administration for whom that is not a priority, they would be hamstrung and unable to change course. It would lock in public lands data center approvals forever,” Donelly said.
Nevada became the first state to get a data center approved on public land in July, but the project was ultimately rescinded following a lawsuit from the Center for Biological Diversity and Boulder City. 
Donelly said, if passed, the environmental rollbacks in the permitting reform bill would “dramatically impact the permitting of Townsite Data Center” adjacent to Boulder City, “allowing the agencies to run roughshod over these laws while hobbling the enforcement mechanism that is meant to keep them honest.”
In a statement after her vote to advance the legislation, Cortez Masto criticized some of the bill’s provisions, saying she would not vote for final passage if changes to the National Historic Preservation Act — which protects historic properties and cultural resources — were not removed. 
Cortez Masto, Rosen among Democrats voting to advance overhaul of energy project permitting

Native rights advocates in Nevada are adamantly opposed to that portion of the bill.
Beverly Harry, who is Diné and a Native community organizer in northern Nevada, said the Trump-backed bill should not have advanced after voters made their position clear during the midterms.
“We thought the American voice on how we should proceed now was clear. It just seems like what we’re seeing is our Democrat senators being disingenuous with how they view Nevadans and people within Indian country,” Harry said. 
Under the bill, early consultation with Tribal Nations would be optional during the early stages of the permitting process, which would limit their ability to identify cultural resources and inform decision-makers of potential conflicts. 
“There are already not enough opportunities or notice for tribes to give input or to educate themselves about what projects are up and coming and the infrastructure being put in place. It’s already weak,” said Lisa Grayshield, a member of the Washoe Tribe of Nevada and California and an associate professor at New Mexico State University.
The bill would also limit what projects need to go through the Tribal consultation process and what sites would qualify as culturally important.
Native organizers say the legislation would not only weaken government-to-government consultation and alter long-standing historic preservation reviews, it would allow the Secretary of the Interior to suspend funding and override the functions of Tribal Historic Preservation Officers if they miss new stricter response deadlines.
“These roles are very important to our tribe because they protect our stories, our songs, our cultural lands and burial sites, and our history for the next generation,” said Josh Dini, a member of the Walker River Paiute Tribe and founder of Prayer Horse Inc., a nonprofit created to protect Indigenous culture, land, and sovereignty. “If this bill goes through, I don’t know what’s going to happen. We won’t be able to stand up to protect our land, protect the people, and protect our sovereignty.”
Harry and several other Native organizers will hold a protest at the Bruce R. Thompson Courthouse and Federal Building in Reno on Friday to pressure Nevada’s senators to vote against legislation they say will weaken government-to-government consultation and alter long-standing historic preservation reviews.
“We could be exposed to larger amounts of pollutants at a faster rate because now everything is open for the gas, oil, and mining industries to just come in and do whatever they want. They still want everything that we have. They are still trying to steal everything that we have, and that is what this protest is about,” Harry said, adding that it’s dedicated to the late Mary and Carrie Dann, both Western Shoshone activists in Nevada. 
Other Nevada officials have spoken out against the bill. Gov. elect and current state attorney general Arron Ford signed onto a letter warning that the permitting overhaul would weaken environmental protections and undermine state and Tribal Nation authority. 
Changes to the Clean Water Act under the bill would “unreasonably curtail traditional state authority and lead to dirtier, more polluted waters in our states,” wrote more than a dozen attorneys general in the letter.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Fuel vendors continue to leave CT’s winter heating program
description: This year, 192 fuel vendors are taking part in CT’s winter heating program, down from 325 in 2016-17, and demand for assistance is rising.
text:
State officials thought two years ago they’d stemmed the exodus of fuel oil vendors from Connecticut’s heating assistance program.
But those numbers continue to slip.
And with U.S.-Iran war driving oil prices sharply higher than last year, an industry leader said this week the state’s failure to fix compensation issues is putting the program’s future in jeopardy.
“Why shouldn’t we have a program that’s transparent? Why shouldn’t we have a program that’s fair?” Chris Herb, president of the Connecticut Energy Marketers Association, said Tuesday. “The price-volatility risk is no longer tolerable.”
But state Department of Social Services spokeswoman Christine Stuart said Wednesday programmatic reforms have been made — including increased compensation for vendors — and that enough fuel oil companies are participating.
“Though we may have fewer vendors overall, we expect to meet our statutory requirement to have an adequate supply of vendors who have historically indicated a willingness to take on new customers,” she said.
At issue is the Connecticut Energy Assistance Program, which is expected to help more than 94,000 households earning less than 60% of the statewide median income to keep warm this fall and winter.
Though run by the state, the program chiefly doles out federal funds, made available through the Low-Income Household Energy Assistance Program, commonly known as LIHEAP.
But while federal funding for energy assistance generally has grown modestly since the early years of the COVID pandemic in 2020 and 2021, demand has surged faster.
Gov. Ned Lamont’s administration estimated in August that Connecticut’s LIHEAP grant would be $86.3 million this heating season, up 5.6% from last year. Meanwhile, projected demand is up about 11%.
But even before COVID, fuel oil companies were beginning to leave a program they said often was costing them money.
CEAP relies on a complex system that limits how much participating businesses can charge program-eligible households. And that retail price isn’t set at the same time a fuel distributor purchases home heating oil at one of the terminals spread across Connecticut.
So, what happens when a vendor pays much more to a fuel wholesaler than it gets in reimbursement from the state?
CEAP lost more than one-third of its vendors, from 325 to 214, between the 2016-17 and 2023-24 heating seasons, according to the nonpartisan Office of Legislative Research.
Katie Childs, vice president of Tuxis-Ohrs Fuels in Meriden, said her company had participated in energy assistance for decades until it dropped out five years ago.
The unstable pricing mechanism was always problematic, and Tuxis-Ohrs did its best to manage. 
“We will do that because that is what we do,” she said. “We want people to be warm.”
But when the Russian invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022 and home heating oil prices jumped more than $2.50 per gallon in less than three months, the potential losses became too much for many small and mid-sized vendors to absorb, she added.
Connecticut lawmakers tried to fix the problem in 2023 and 2024, enacting laws setting county and regional pricing standards and mandating fair compensation for vendors.
Fuel distributors participating in heating assistance jumped up from 214 to 259 immediately after lawmakers finished those changes.
And while Stuart said Wednesday that vendors are paid “actual date of delivery prices,” the industry insists the price lag remains — and that the numbers back them up.
Vendor participation in heating assistance was down to 207 companies last winter, and Stuart said it now stands at 192.
Further complicating matters, the average retail cost of home heating oil stood at $5.71 per gallon earlier this week, as reported by the state Department of Energy and Environmental Protection. That’s 55% higher than where prices stood in early November last year and more than double the price when the war with Iran started on Feb. 28.
Nora Duncan, vice chairwoman of the state’s Low-Income Energy Water Advisory Board and director of the AARP’s Connecticut chapter, said it’s crucial this problem be addressed now.
“We can’t keep people warm with a program if they can’t get their fuel,” she said.
Lamont dedicated $12.7 million in state funds to the current CEAP program to allow more rounds of assistance grants to be issued earlier in the heating season.
And U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District, ranking member of the House Appropriations Committee, said in late October that many vulnerable households are at risk this winter because of “the president’s war of choice,” adding she’s hopeful both parties in Congress will support additional LIHEAP funding for states.
“This is not a partisan issue,” she said.
Stuart said the department has authorized a 15-cents-per-gallon increase in overall reimbursement for vendors this season.
The social services department “always wants to provide our residents with as much choice as possible in selecting vendors while staying within our budget,” Stuart said. “This is a constant challenge in administering a federally funded block grant program with fixed funding.”

name: California
title: What happens when real estate agents have split allegiances?
description: A Sonoma County lawsuit alleges that one of northern California’s largest real estate brokerages shunted buyers into “dual agency” contracts.
text:
In summary
A Sonoma County lawsuit alleges that one of northern California’s largest real estate brokerages shunted buyers into “dual agency” contracts.


Claudia Ochoa and Cesar Gonzalez thought it was odd when they were told to ditch their real estate agent.
Before the married couple could make an offer on the newly built single-family home on the west side of Santa Rosa, they were told that they would instead need to accept the services of a new agent who worked for W Real Estate. That’s the same brokerage, one of the largest in Northern California, that was representing the developer in the sale. 
But Ochoa and Gonzalez, first time buyers with full-time jobs and three young kids, were new to this. Having the same team of real estate agents represent both sides of the sale must just be another quirk of California’s mystifying home-buying process, they figured. Plus, this was the only way to make an offer, and they really liked the house, which was close to their kids’ school. 
Two years later, they no longer think the arrangement was simply odd. They say it was illegal.
Ochoa and Gonzalez are part of a lawsuit filed against W Real Estate that accuses the company and its owner, Randy Waller, of shunting new buyers into so-called dual agency transactions. 
Dual agency, in which both buyer and seller are represented by the same agent or brokerage, is illegal in more than half a dozen states. Though it’s allowed in California, state law requires that both buyer and seller fully understand and consent to the arrangement. The Sonoma County lawsuit argues that buyers like Ochoa and Gonzalez weren’t given a meaningful choice in this case.
Consumer rights advocates worry that dual agency sales are becoming more common across the country amid a wave of mega-mergers in the real estate brokerage industry. Even where legal, the practice occupies an ethical gray area, they say. 
“You can’t try to get the highest price for the seller and also try to get the lowest price for the buyer, it’s an inherent conflict of interest,” said Wayne Bell, a former commissioner at the California Department of Real Estate. An agent hoping to represent both sides is inevitably going to leave one side worse off, critics argue. 
According to the suit filed earlier this year, hundreds of buyers like Ochoa and Gonzalez spread across at least five new developments were, indeed, left worse off. 
Without someone exclusively representing their interests, buyers were less likely to receive credits and other concessions from the seller, the case alleges. Some of the buyers also argue that their W Real Estate agents, who were supposed to be representing their interests, failed to alert them to evidence of shoddy construction that is now the subject of separate construction defect litigation.
Four legal experts with no involvement in the case who were consulted by CalMatters all said the case, if accurately characterized in the lawsuit, raises serious ethical, if not legal, questions.
“Consent under duress or as an unnegotiable precondition to a  contract fails the legal requirement for the voluntary informed consent required for dual agency,” Bell said in a follow up email. The arrangement, as described, is “forced, involuntary, and not lawful (or ethical under the Realtor rules).”
Waller, W Real Estate’s owner and managing agent, directed questions to his attorneys, Doug Pettit and Sara Bloch. 
“W Real Estate can’t comment on any specifics since one attorney and his clients have sued the company and the matters are currently pending,” Pettit said in a written statement. Referring to both the dual agency lawsuit and a related construction defect lawsuit, he added: “W Real Estate disputes the allegations in those two lawsuits. The work the agents did for the buyers benefited their interests and all buyers had the right to consult with different agents if they wanted.”
Pettit further noted that the arrangement benefited developers who prefer to interact with agents “who have knowledge of the development.”
A jury trial is scheduled for next May.
‘Stop being involved’
The details of the dual agency arrangement were spelled out in a series of legal agreements and email exchanges unearthed as part of the legal proceedings and shared with CalMatters. 
“W Real Estate shall represent both buyer and seller in all transactions,” states the listing agreement between the brokerage and City 44’s developer, Dan Morgan. Another document specified that a buyer’s agent would receive a “referral fee” equal to 2.5% of the home sale price in exchange for bringing in their client and then ceasing to represent them.
“An outside agent would not act as a buyer’s agent,” one agent, Nalishma Carvelho, wrote in an email to a prospective buyer who asked whether he could retain his former Realtor. “Randy Waller and I are the agents for buyers and sellers in this community.”
In a separate email to another interested buyer, Carvelho explained that this was part of the “standard contract” and “pretty common” in Sonoma County.
Carvelho did not respond to multiple requests for comment by email, phone and text message.
Stephen Flynn, the lawyer bringing the dual agency lawsuit, said such arrangements are anything but common — and, in any case, illegal. While seller’s agents working a new development will often pay referral fees to Realtors for bringing in new buyers, a rule requiring those agents to then effectively go away and stop representing the interests of their clients is not something he’s seen in his 20 years as a real estate attorney. 
“That’s a level of brazenness that is quite astonishing to me,” he said.
Kerrin Shettle, a veteran Petaluma-based agent who entered into one of these contracts on behalf of an interested buyer, said she found the rule strange, too. She remembers calling W Real Estate shortly after signing with a question about the property. “‘You shouldn’t be calling us,’” Shettle recalls being told, though two years after the fact she said she doesn’t remember which agent told her this. “‘You’re not involved, so we need you to stop being involved.’”
Two-story homes with attached garages line a residential street near Tecado Drive in Santa Rosa on Oct. 19, 2026. Photo by Gustavo Hernandez Jr. for CalMatters
Getting independent agents like Shettle out of the picture ended up benefiting the seller at the expense of the buyers, said Flynn, the attorney. 
At a single W Real Estate brokered development where dual agency was not required of buyers, those with their own agents were four times more likely to receive concessions and credits, such as waived closing costs or appliance upgrades, Flynn said, summarizing sales date shared with him by W Real Estate as a part of the lawsuit’s pre-trial discovery process. Of those that did receive credits, the ones with their own agents got nearly six-times more on average: $3,252 compared to $554. 
Those sums aren’t much by California home price standards, Flynn admitted. But they prove that his clients were not receiving the representation they paid for. 
Other costs
There can be downsides to not having a dedicated representative that go beyond a home’s price tag.
Danny Matranga, a personal trainer and gym owner, had been saving to buy a home for nearly a decade. With interest rates hovering at historic lows in early 2022 he finally saw his chance. He and his fiancée fell in love with the model home at City 44 and put down a deposit. 
Then they waited. 
Months went by as construction dragged on past schedule. Carvelho, the W Real Estate agent officially representing him in the deal, was hard to reach and offered only occasional updates, he said. 
“This person is my Realtor, but it sure doesn’t feel like it,” Matranga thought to himself at the time. “If these people were Realtors that I had hired I would have fired them immediately.”
Things got so bad that Matranga’s loan officer stepped in on his behalf, asking Carvelho in an email why Matranga was being required to purchase solar panels at extra cost and why Carvelho had repeatedly failed to give him a firm close date.
Three months went by before Matranga finally closed. By then borrowing rates had nearly doubled. Matranga says he now pays more than a thousand dollars more each month than the amount he’d initially budgeted. 
What did they know?
Even so, he and his fiancée were happy to finally join the ranks of California property owning class — until they moved in.
First, the guy next door cracked a joke that the whole development was built out of “paper clips and bubble gum.” Another neighbor, who shares a wall with Matranga, texted a picture to the block of mushrooms growing out of cracks in her window frame. That winter he said he watched a bubble of water form in his ceiling. He later found more water pooled beneath his laminate flooring. 
Matranga also learned that shortly after his purchase, a City 44 construction superintendent had quit in a rage, explaining in a text message to one of Matranga’s neighbors that buyers were “being sold homes that are substandard.” Court records show that those texts were also shared with the builder, Morgan, and with W Real Estate’s head, Waller.
“Where homeowners have raised concerns, we are working through the legal process to evaluate those claims and address any valid issues,” Morgan wrote in a statement.
“My own experience working with W Real Estate has been entirely positive and straightforward, but W Real Estate is best positioned to speak to its agency relationships and practices in individual transactions,” he added.
Matranga said he now spends a lot of time wondering exactly how much the team at W Real Estate knew about the construction issues at the same time they were purporting to represent him in the sale. 
“I don’t want to say ‘impossible,’ but it seems super improbable that they would have not been aware,” he said.
In an additional statement, Pettit, W Real Estate’s attorney, flatly denied that: “W Real Estate was not aware of any construction defects at any developments that its agents hid from buyers.” 
Is dual agency always a bad deal?
Having a buyer and seller represented by the same person does tend to speed things up. 
There’s reduced wait time as the two parties exchange information and negotiate, since all the haggling is passing through one intermediary, not two. With only one agent collecting a fee from both sides, there’s also room for an “educated consumer” to negotiate down the total commission, said Bennie Waller, a professor of real estate at the University of Alabama. 
Dual agency is also a favored practice when a home is being sold between two friendly parties — say, between members of the same family. (In many states that ban dual agency, such sales can be facilitated by a specialized “transaction broker,” who mediates between buyer and seller without representing either).
But dual agency comes with the obvious downside that a single agent, even one operating in good faith, may struggle to represent the interests of both buyer and seller simultaneously.
In California it’s considered dual agency whether buyer and seller are represented by the same individual agent or by different agents working for the same brokerage, an arrangement sometimes referred to as a “double-ended” transaction. In the Sonoma case, most transactions were double-ended, though at least two prospective buyers at City 44 signed agreements in which the same individual agent represented both buyer and seller.
Double-ended arrangements also raise ethical red flags, said Wendy Gilch, a fellow at the Consumer Policy Center. Because the same brokerage is set up to receive commission fees from both ends of the transaction, the firm has a strong incentive to close the deal as quickly as possible, not necessarily to get the best outcome for either client.
A “for sale” sign is posted in front of a home in Sacramento on March 3, 2022. Photo by Rich Pedroncelli, AP Photo
Consumer advocates like Gilch worry that such arrangements are becoming increasingly common across the United States. The last decade has seen a wave of consolidation sweep across the industry. Compass, most notably, now stands as the largest brokerage in the country, owning smaller brand names such as Coldwell Banker, Century 21 and Christie’s International Real Estate. 
When one firm dominates a market, the odds that two of its agents represent both sides of the same deal become much more likely. Critics say Compass has been boosting those odds further by encouraging sellers to first list their properties on Compass’ private listing networks where only other Compass agents can see them. The issue has become the subject of congressional inquiries, state probes and lawsuits.
“Private listing is a way to basically create a mechanism for dual agency,” said Mischa Fisher, chief economist at Zillow, which has been feuding with Compass in both the courts of law and of public opinion for more than a year.
The ultimate goal of this strategy is to capture commissions from both sides of each sale and “make each transaction more lucrative to help the stock price,” said Jonathan Miller, a real estate consultant and frequent critic of Compass.
A spokesperson for Compass responded in an email that the company’s goal is not to produce double-ended deals, but to give sellers flexibility in the way they list their homes. Even if “private” listings aren’t found on Zillow or Redfin “all Compass listings are publicly available on our website or by contacting Compass,” wrote Devin Daly Huerta. “Our goals are to sell more homes and fulfill our fiduciary duty to our clients.”
Experts weigh in on Sonoma case
By out-and-out requiring buyers to agree to dual agency and paying the buyer’s independent agent to withdraw, the alleged W Real Estate arrangement represents a more extreme version of an industry wide problem, said Gilch at the Consumer Policy Center.
“Oh gosh, this case is bad,” she said when shown a copy of the complaint.
Bess Freedman, the CEO of the New York brokerage Brown Harris Stevens and a public critic of Compass’ private listing strategy, agreed. “That sounds to me very un-kosher,” she said.
Anthony Ventura, a veteran real estate attorney in the Bay Area who is not involved in the case, said the alleged arrangement may not clear the legal bar that requires that both buyers and sellers understand and agree to dual agency contracts.
“The buyer has the right to pick their own agent or to not have an agent at all, so I don’t think you can condition someone’s right to make an offer on having you as their agent,” he said. “I’m pretty certain that that would not be legal.”
Though one could argue that the buyers did consent, as they could have walked away, the arrangement, at the very least, runs counter to the spirit of how real estate transactions are typically regulated in the United States.
“There should be a free market where everything is negotiated,” he said. “The idea that an agent can come in and say ‘you can only make offers through me’ is just counter to that entire public policy.”
‘We just trusted a lot of people’
Christopher Ortiz, Ochoa and Gonzalez’s original agent, said that in his decade of work as a Santa Rosa-area Realtor he’s come across dual agency arrangements at new developments at least twice before. “It was as easy as just bringing them in there and I got paid for it,” he said of those deals. “It was almost too good to be true. I almost didn’t feel right about it.”
In Ochoa and Gonzalez’s case he said he nevertheless continued to advise them informally, explaining certain terms or hopping on the occasional phone call, even after he no longer officially worked for them. “I was basically just being a communicator,” he said, a characterization that Ochoa and Gonzalez confirmed.
Since buying the house, the couple have spent a lot of time wondering what, if anything, they lost by not having Ortiz at their side at all times. 
Would they have gotten a lower price? A better deal on the home’s appliances? Would Ortiz have spotted the alleged defects they say have left them with a leaky roof, a persistent mold problem or a downstairs bathroom that has twice flooded with raw sewage? And what, exactly, did they get in return for the $17,500 in commissions they paid to their new agent?
“I’m certain that anyone who has a little bit of experience buying a house probably would have caught some funky things,” said Ochoa. “We just trusted a lot of the people involved in this process when in reality they were not in our corner.”

name: California
title: California needs to better resist job-killing megamergers in entertainment
description: Mergers like the recent ones between Paramount and Warner Bros and between Fox Corp. and Roku are endanger jobs and hurt consumers.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

William Lockyer
William Lockyer is a former California attorney general and member of the state Assembly and Senate, where he served as president pro tempore.


The architect of the recent Paramount-Warner Bros. megamerger, Gerry Cardinale, initially downplayed the possibility of layoffs once the two companies finished joining together. 
Not long afterward, the CEOs of the merged company, Skydance, sent emails announcing “difficult decisions that affect our workforce” — and later offered voluntary buyouts in anticipation of layoffs. 
Many of the job cuts will naturally affect California, where Skydance has its headquarters. Concerns over job losses was one reason California Attorney General Rob Bonta sued earlier this year to try to stop the merger. 
That lawsuit ultimately was settled out of court, and the merger is a done deal. But if we’re to protect jobs in California — to say nothing of one of our legacy industries — we need to resist these gigantic acquisitions from becoming the norm. 
Hollywood’s corporate consolidation trend threatens to yield fewer opportunities for workers and higher entertainment costs for consumers. 
The just-completed $22 billion purchase of Roku by Fox Corp. is in line with other mergers, where large media companies join forces with streaming services to build entertainment empires. 
Whereas Paramount-Warner received enormous attention in the press and among lawmakers, the Fox-Roku deal has relatively flown under the radar. That’s concerning given its implications for our state and for entertainment law. 
Fox Corp. employs more than 10,000 employees globally and has a major studio presence in Hollywood. Roku, meanwhile, is headquartered in San Jose and has other offices scattered across our state. 
That means the writing is likely on the wall for hundreds, if not thousands, of California jobs. Roku has already been laying off workers, slashing its workforce by 10% in 2023 alone. 
It couldn’t come at a worse time. California’s unemployment rate is 5.1%, a percentage point over the national average and among the nation’s highest. The state is stuck in a trap: its economic growth remains high but its job market doesn’t reflect that expansion.
This has some economists warning about a so-called K-shaped economy, where California’s rich get richer and its poor and middle class go the other way. 
If we want to arrest this trend, we need to do more than worry about AI taking jobs. We need to challenge the giant corporate mergers that portend more layoffs.
Even without the job losses, Fox-Roku could be a bad deal thanks to its naked conflict of interest. Most media deals where a content provider seeks to join with a content streamer carry this risk.

Logo at the main entrance to the FOX News Headquarters at NewsCorp Building in Manhattan on Oct. 18, 2022. Photo by Erik McGregor, LightRocket via Getty Images

Streaming services such as Roku are supposed to be content-neutral, recommending channels and shows based on user preference and overall popularity, rather than on corporate or political bias. But Fox recently said it will continue carrying non-Fox content on Roku for at least three years and won’t discriminate against that content in its search results.
Afterward the incentive will likely be to prioritize Fox channels, such as Fox News and FS1 —  and to deprioritize their competitors. Fox News’s ratings have been sinking in recent months, but with Roku that might become less of a problem. 
Worse, the merger could destroy the precedent of TV provider neutrality, leading other media companies to place their thumbs on the scales. 
Ultimately the question behind these megamergers is what kind of entertainment industry do we want for California: A dynamic job-creator where competition ensures viewers have plenty of thrilling and smart shows to choose from, or a handful of lumbering corporate behemoths that produce too much slop and not enough well-paying job opportunities?

name: California
title: By emptying death row, Newsom broke a promise and disregarded the will of voters
description: Despite promising to respect voters' support for capital punishment, Gavin Newsom moved to empty death row in the waning days of his governorship.
text:
