name: Alabama Reflector
title: Alabama infant mortality rate increases slightly, remains above national average
description: Alabama’s infant mortality rate worsened slightly in 2025 and remains above the national average, according to data released Thursday by the Alabama Department of Public Health. State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris said that the state’s infant mortality rate, the number of infants who died in the first year of being born, was 7.4 deaths […]
text:
Dr. Scott Harris, Alabama State Health Officer, at the Oversight Commission on Opioid Settlement Funds meeting on Feb. 18, 2026, in the Alabama Statehouse in Montgomery, Alabama. Harris on Thursday said that the state’s infant mortality rate was 7.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2025, an increase from 7.1 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024. (Anna Barrett/Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s infant mortality rate worsened slightly in 2025 and remains above the national average, according to data released Thursday by the Alabama Department of Public Health.
State Health Officer Dr. Scott Harris said that the state’s infant mortality rate, the number of infants who died in the first year of being born, was 7.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2025, an increase from 7.1 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024.
“When we’re dealing with all these statistics, we talk a lot about statistical significance, and did things really change, or does the number look a little different,” Harris said during a meeting of the State Committee on Public Health. “But it’s not really statistically significant. Please understand what we mean when we say insignificant. Every death of a child is significant.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
He said that while the rate increased, it was not statistically significant. The three-year average gives a “smoother curve” with 0.2 to 0.4 jumps over the last 10 years, and showed improvement from 2003 to 2015, when the state’s rate was between 8.3 deaths per 1,000 live births and 9.5 deaths per 1,000 live births.
Alabama’s infant mortality, a three-year average, from 2003 to 2025. (Alabama Department of Public Health)
Harris said the infant mortality rate is an indicator of overall health in Alabama and is a fair way to compare states. 
“There’s so many different factors that go into this number that you’re going to see that you can look at that number and sort of get an idea of how public health is looking in Alabama,” Harris said.
The nation’s infant mortality average is 5.5 deaths per 1,000 live births, up from 5.4 deaths per 1,000 live births in 2024. Harris said the gap between Alabama and the national average has always been there, but the state roughly matches the nation’s trend.
In 1970, about 20 babies died per 1,000 births nationwide and about 24.5 died in Alabama. The rate started to descend after the implementation of Neonatal Intensive Care Units in the 1960s. In the late 1980s, Medicaid coverage was extended to pregnant women.
Infant mortality rates for the United States and Alabama from 1970 to 2025. (Alabama Department of Public Health)
Harris said in an interview that the gap could close, and the state got close at its lowest rate in 2022 of 6.7 deaths per 1,000 live births.
“We absolutely have the ability to improve that, and we have a lot of people working on it,” he said. “We have a lot of people in Alabama outside of our agency who are really invested in these projects, but it’s going to take all of us.”
There were 57,192 total births in 2024, and 422 of those babies died before reaching their first birthday in 2025. The 2026 rate is still being calculated because all babies born in 2025 have not yet reached their first birthday. 
A ‘stubborn statistic’
Racial disparities continue to be a challenge. Of the 422 infant deaths, 229 of them were white babies while 183 were Black babies. The mortality rate for Black babies in Alabama is 13.1 deaths per 1,000 live births, nearly 2.5 times as high as that of white babies at 5.5 deaths per 1,000 live births, Harris said.
“This is a really stubborn statistic. We spend a lot of time and effort thinking about how to address this. We’ve not really made a big difference in that,” he said. “The white infant mortality rate is right at the U.S. average, but because we’ve not done the job we should do with the Black infant mortality rate, we’re typically in that bottom tier of states overall, unfortunately.”
About 72.1% of babies were born to white mothers in Alabama, and about 24.5% of babies were born to Black mothers in 2025, according to the data. Harris said the birth rate, regardless of race, has been on a steady decline since 2021.
Alabama’s infant mortality, by race, from 2016 to 2025. (Alabama Department of Public Health)
Dr. Marquisha Jarmon, a Hoover-based pediatrician and member of the committee, said the department should work directly with Black groups to raise awareness to reduce the mortality rate.
“I love hearing this information about infant mortality because it just sheds a light on the problem, especially in the African American community,” she said. “The question that we’re all asking is: What really is the problem in our community when everyone else is getting better and we’re staying the same?”
Harris called closing the racial gap the “million dollar question.” He said in an interview that some of the social determinants – poverty, race, education, ZIP code – is not something that the health department can address, but it can educate mothers-to-be on a healthy pregnancy.
“It’s challenging to know how to address that. The way we address it is by trying to find specific reasons that we’re losing our babies that we can intervene with,” he said. “That might be prenatal vitamins and safe sleep education, trying to get people connected to healthcare for chronic disease management. That’s our approach.”
Risks and causes of death
Harris said that ensuring adequate prenatal care is crucial for a successful pregnancy. According to the data, 75.7% of live births in 2025 received adequate prenatal care, and only 2.8% of pregnancies with no prenatal care resulted in a live birth. 
The top three causes of infant deaths are congenital abnormalities, preterm births and low birth weights, and sudden infant death syndrome, according to the data. About 23.2% of infants died by SIDS, a 7-point increase over 2024 when the cause of death was the lowest ranked. The deaths often occur while the infant is asleep, often caused by accidental suffocation, strangulation or an unknown cause.
“We really believe that sleep-related deaths ought to always be preventable. We think education is the way to get there,” he said.
Harris said safe sleeping, babies sleeping alone, on their back and in a crib, is important to prevent SIDS.
Many things can contribute to infant mortality, like maternal age, smoking and chronic disease; preterm birth, low birth weight and congenital abnormalities. A mother’s income, race, level of education and ZIP code impact her baby’s chance of survival, according to the data. These factors also impact a mother’s access to health care. 
Alabama’s infant mortality, by county of residence for 2025 (right), and a map of counties with delivering hospitals for 2025. (Alabama Department of Public Health)
According to the data, the infant mortality rate is much higher in rural counties like Pickens, Sumter, Hale and Washington in the Black Belt, and Geneva County in the southern part of the state. Those counties directly correlate with counties without hospitals that can deliver babies, according to the data.
According to the University of North Carolina’s Sheps Center, nine rural hospitals have closed in Alabama since 2009. Only 30% of the state’s rural hospitals have labor and delivery units, leaving many expectant parents to drive long distances for care. One labor and delivery unit in Mobile closed this summer. 
“We aren’t necessarily able to prove a statistical association because the numbers are really small, but it doesn’t seem like a coincidence that when you live really far away from a delivery hospital your infant mortality rate is higher, and that’s what we see,” Harris said.
The department has nine programs related to infant mortality: Safe Sleep initiatives; Well Woman; family planning services; newborn screening; sexually transmitted infection/disease diagnosis and treatment; Women, Infant and Children program; Children’s Health Insurance Program; Fetal and Infant Mortality Review; and Pregnancy Risk Assessment Monitoring System.

name: Idaho Capital Sun
title: Idaho independent Achilles fell short against Republican US Sen. Risch. Can independents win here?
description: Idaho’s Todd Achilles was one of a handful of major independent U.S. Senate candidates in red states to generate national attention ahead of the 2026 general election.  Although he and the other high-profile independents lost their races, Achilles argues there’s still a future for independents to be a competitive alternative in a two-party system, and […]
text:
Campaign signs greet attendees at the election night watch party for independent U.S. Senate Candidate Todd Achilles on Nov. 3, 2026, in Garden City, Idaho. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)Idaho’s Todd Achilles was one of a handful of major independent U.S. Senate candidates in red states to generate national attention ahead of the 2026 general election. 
Although he and the other high-profile independents lost their races, Achilles argues there’s still a future for independents to be a competitive alternative in a two-party system, and a viable way to win in such a Republican state. 
U.S. Sen. Jim Risch, R-Idaho, talks to an Idaho News 6 reporter at the Idaho GOP election night watch party at the Grove in Boise, Idaho, on Nov. 8, 2022. (Photo by Otto Kitsinger for Idaho Capital Sun)
Achilles, a former Democratic state legislator, ended with 33.57% of the vote, compared to incumbent Republican U.S. Sen. Jim Risch’s 56.6% in the four-way race with no Democrat on the ballot. The other independent candidate, Natalie Fleming, received around 7% of the vote. 
In an election year where many Republicans struggled in nationwide federal races, Idaho voters stood by their GOP incumbents. 
“Idaho is different because, it’s just the advantage for Republicans among voter behavior is so outsized compared to even states in the South,” said Robert Jones, a partner and political strategist at Boise-based GS Strategy Group.
Nearly 62% of Idaho voters are registered with the Republican Party, and 12% are registered Democrats, according to the Idaho secretary of state’s office. More than 24% aren’t affiliated with either party. 
Voters who deeply align with a major political party tend to stick with that party, even when they aren’t necessarily satisfied with their performance, said Idaho State University political scientist Edward Greer. Greer researches American politics, political psychology, and political behavior. 
“If a political party is not meeting those needs, then there’s not typically going to be a lot of crossover to the other side,” Greer said. “Usually, people will just kind of sit out.” 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
 Was this race different from past Idaho U.S. Senate elections? 

The win, although still comfortable, was Risch’s closest general election race since he first won his U.S. Senate seat in 2008. 
In 2008, Risch won with 57.7% of the vote against Democratic challenger and former congressman Larry LaRocco, who had 34.1% of the vote, with three other candidates on the ballot. 
Achilles, speaking to the Idaho Capital Sun the day after the election, said his campaign “built a great foundation” for the independent movement in Idaho. 
Independent candidate for U.S. Senate Todd Achilles speaks with attendees at an election night watch party on Nov. 3, 2026, at Iconic Bistro and Bar in Garden City. (Photo by Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
“We went from zero to 33% in 18 months,” he said. “… We got a lot of people excited. We had hundreds of meetings and town halls and events across the state. Everything I’m seeing in my inbox this morning is, ‘Let’s keep going.’ ‘We like what this independent movement is about.’” 
Achilles said he hasn’t decided if he would run again, but that he plans to continue to be involved in politics. 
His campaign garnered a similar share of votes as Democrats in other statewide races. Risch’s last challenger, Democrat Paullet Jordan, finished with a similar vote share, with 33.2% in the 2020 election.
Achilles this year narrowly outperformed Democratic gubernatorial candidate Terri Pickens, who won 32.25% of the vote in her five-way contest against incumbent Republican Gov. Brad Little. 
In two-way statewide races, Democrats consistently won about 34% of the vote, with the highest coming from attorney general candidate Lori Hickman, who received 40.21% against incumbent Republican Attorney General Raúl Labrador.  
 Some Idaho Dems pressured their candidate to drop out of the Senate race and rally around Achilles, then Achilles lost. Now what? 

After he won his May primary, Democrat David Roth withdrew from the U.S. Senate race in August, days ahead of the deadline to have his name removed from the general election ballot. He told the Sun he dropped out because he lacked support from his own party.
Leaders of the Ada County Democrats wrote Roth a letter asking him to drop out, arguing Achilles had the better chance to oust Risch, the Spokesman-Review reported. 
Jared DeLoof, executive director of the Idaho Democratic Party, speaks to attendees during the general election watch party Nov. 5, 2024, in Boise. (Pat Sutphin for the Idaho Capital Sun)
Ada County Democrats Chair Jared Deloof told the Sun he’d still probably send the letter today, because Roth wasn’t raising the money to be competitive. But he also thinks the future lies with more work within the Democratic party, and not with independents. 
“This was, I really think, an experiment year, given the stakes of what’s going on in the country,” DeLoof said. “Folks seeing is this a path forward to confronting the threats that we’re seeing to freedom across the country?  So I totally understand the want to try to do something new.”
“I will say now the results are in after last Tuesday, and we saw across the country independent candidates not doing well against Republican opponents, and actually saw Democrats in some of the deepest, reddest parts of the country fare very well, even in places like South Carolina, Mississippi, and Texas,” he said. “And so, my takeaway from this is that in deep red places like Idaho, we have to continue to do the work within the Democratic Party to build a party that can win here.” 
Idaho Democratic Party Chair Lauren Necochea told the New York Times ahead of Nov. 3 that she thought “independent candidates will generally fade away after the election.” 
“The Democratic Party will still be here doing the work to hold Republicans accountable,” Necochea said. 
 Is there a meaningful way forward for major independent candidates? 

The Achilles campaign raised nearly $2 million, more than any other Senate challenger in recent years. However, Risch’s campaign surpassed $5 million, as of Oct. 14 Federal Election Commission data. 
Greer, the political scientist, said it’s not impossible for independents to win in Idaho, but it is more difficult without the party infrastructure Republicans and Democrats have. 
“I wouldn’t completely rule out the possibility of independents potentially doing better down the line,” Greer said. “There are some notable independent senators that have gotten elected before, closer to the East Coast. But it could be a question of, if the Democratic brand is unpopular in states like Idaho, it would be a matter of if independents could win over would-be Democrats while still keeping the Democratic brand at arm’s length to make it credibly seem that they’re not Democrats.” 
The nation saw a blue wave this election. Idaho saw a ripple.

“And then at that point,” Greer said, “they might be able to win people over that are truly independents that aren’t wanting to align cleanly with either party.” 
Jones, with GS Strategy Group which has worked with Republican-aligned campaigns and PACs, said Republicans are likely to keep winning in statewide elections in Idaho for the foreseeable future. 
“Those things take a long time to change,” Jones said. “It doesn’t mean there won’t be a candidate or a single race where something happens that’s anomalous and somebody can get elected. But structural change, where Democrats are competitive up and down the statewide ballot, is a fair ways off.”
DeLoof noted that even among some victories for Idaho Democrats this year, it’s a “really tough uphill battle” to win in statewide elections. 
“This is a similar trajectory to what Georgia did, what Texas did, states that you never could imagine showing up blue on the map,” he said. “I believe if we stick to it, we’ll eventually get there someday.” 
Jones noted that Risch’s victory against Achilles was the slimmest among statewide general election contests in Idaho. One could argue he had a better chance than a Democrat, he said.  
“So Achilles did the best, I guess if you want to put in that framework,” Jones said of the vote margins, “but an independent campaign is still a long way off from beating a Republican.”

name: Arkansas Advocate
title: Even solidly red Saline County saw a shift toward Democrats in Arkansas’ midterm election
description: Located a short drive from Democrat-leaning Little Rock, Saline County has been a Republican stronghold of central Arkansas for years. The county hasn’t voted for a Democrat for president since Bill Clinton’s 1996 reelection, and has been the epicenter of fights over book restrictions. But an unexpected thing happened in the county that Donald Trump […]
text:
Campaign signs for the 2026 midterm elections line the grass outside the Saline County Courthouse in Benton, Arkansas on Oct. 19, 2026, the first day of early voting. (Photo by Tess Vrbin/Arkansas Advocate)Located a short drive from Democrat-leaning Little Rock, Saline County has been a Republican stronghold of central Arkansas for years. The county hasn’t voted for a Democrat for president since Bill Clinton’s 1996 reelection, and has been the epicenter of fights over book restrictions.
But an unexpected thing happened in the county that Donald Trump won with 69% of the vote just two years ago. The county’s voters swung 17 percentage points in favor of Democrats. The GOP nominees for U.S. House and Senate saw their numbers drop from two years ago, and a Republican state lawmaker in the county barely survived a bid to oust him. 
And a Republican-led effort to cut the county’s library funding failed.
The results don’t amount to a blue wave in a county where Republicans still control county offices. But last week’s midterms in Saline County highlight how even the reddest of counties were touched by an election where Republicans suffered major losses around the country.
How Trump and Republicans lost the 2026 midterm elections, according to The AP Voter Poll

Former state Republican party chairman Richard Bearden said it’s too early to draw conclusions about Arkansas’ political trajectory.
“I don’t know that we can look at one election cycle and say, ‘Golly, the state’s trending back to being sort of a yellow-dog Democrat state that it was 20 years ago,’” Bearden said.
National polling has indicated that Democrats’ takeover of congressional seats and governor’s races across was a repudiation of the president and his policies. Arkansas voters chose Trump in the past three presidential elections, winning about 69% of Saline County’s vote each time.
Despite Democrats’ attempts to tie U.S. Sen. Tom Cotton and U.S. Rep. French Hill to the increasingly unpopular Trump, Saline County’s double-digit voter shift isn’t necessarily a rebuke of the president, at least not in elections for state-level offices, said Shane Broadway, chairman of the Saline County Economic Development Corporation.
“One thing I noticed watching all of the ads [was], especially on the Democratic side, they were focusing on costs of gas, groceries, those kinds of things, and nobody ever mentioned Donald Trump on either side,” Broadway said.
Sen. Kim Hammer (R), candidate for Arkansas Secretary of State, answers questions at the press conference following the debate at Arkansas TV studios on Thursday, Oct. 15, 2026 in Conway, Arkansas. (Photo by Katie Adkins/Arkansas Advocate)
But Republican Sen. Kim Hammer of Benton, who won his race for secretary of state last week, said Saline County voters’ leftward shift might have been simply “a protest vote” against Trump. 
Nearly 44,000 Saline County residents voted in the midterms, with nearly 34,000 setting a county record for early voter turnout, County Clerk Doug Curtis posted on Facebook. Turnout is typically lower in midterms than general elections, and nearly 58,000 Saline County residents voted in 2024.
Broadway, a former longtime Democratic state legislator and former House speaker, said his decades of experience in Arkansas politics have taught him that the state’s voters “tend to have an independent streak.”
“I’ve seen red waves, I’ve seen blue waves, and I’ve seen a lot of times where Arkansas was not a part of either,” he said.
 Changes in northeast Saline County

Republicans kept all 13 seats on the Saline County Quorum Court, with seven members and the county judge running unopposed. All six state House seats and both Senate seats in the county will continue to be held by Republicans.
Gina Thomas-Littlejohn (Courtesy of the Arkansas Secretary of State)
But GOP Rep. RJ Hawk of Bryant won reelection over Democrat Gina Thomas-Littlejohn by only 96 votes, two years after he defeated her by more than 2,300 votes.
Hawk’s razor-thin victory in the Saline County district closest to Little Rock came on a night when most of the state capital’s northern suburbs voted blue. Democrats flipped two House seats and one Senate seat in north Pulaski County, breaking Republicans’ House supermajority with 10 House seat flips statewide.
Democrats nationwide ran on lowering the cost of necessities such as gasoline and healthcare. Saline County residents of all political persuasions shared frustrations about the cost of living, said Thomas-Littlejohn, a former Alexander city council member, and Joshua Irby, a Democratic first-time candidate who ran for Hammer’s Senate seat.
NORC polling takeaways: Arkansans worried about economy, healthcare, data center impact

“Some Republicans [said] they have voted Democrat this year,” Thomas-Littlejohn said. “I’ve never heard that before. The two years prior, I never heard that.”
Bearden said independents who voted Republican in the past likely chose to vote Democrat this year because they believed the GOP wasn’t sufficiently “addressing kitchen table issues.”
Demographic changes in Saline County might have played a role in the election results. The northeast part of the county that includes Bryant, Alexander and Shannon Hills has seen an influx of new residents moving from Little Rock seeking a lower cost of living, said Thomas-Littlejohn and Lela Chism, who won a Shannon Hills city council seat last week.
This means the area doesn’t have the “reactionary Republican voting base” present in other parts of Saline County, so voters are less receptive to right-wing talking points about immigrants and the LGBTQ+ community, said Chism, one of the most vocal opponents of the failed ballot measure to reduce library funding.
“The culture stuff might hype you up and get reactionary people out to the polls because it scares them, but the policy itself isn’t popular,” she said.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Shane Broadway, vice president for university relations has been appointed, interim chancellor of ASU Three Rivers. (Photo courtesy of Arkansas State University)
 Increased Democratic presence

Democrats held a majority of Arkansas’ state and federal offices from 2006 to 2012, but Republicans had taken over by 2014. The Democratic Party of Saline County “pretty much died out” around that time, said Broadway, who unsuccessfully ran for lieutenant governor in 2010.
However, the party has been rebuilding a presence in the county over the past few years. Broadway said he’s seen Saline County Democrats man booths at local festivals, and Thomas-Littlejohn said the party knocked down a wall in its Benton headquarters to make room for new members.
Chism said the issues that motivated Arkansas’ Democratic voters this year are not going away anytime soon.
“If the Republicans in Arkansas continue to neglect the needs of working people and average people, they’re going to lose again,” said Chism, who ran for a quorum court seat as a Democrat in 2024.
The four Saline County quorum court members who ran in both 2024 and 2026 defeated their Democratic opponents by lower margins this year, according to the secretary of state’s website.
Hammer said he believes Democrats’ progress in Saline County will be short-lived over the next two years.
Joshua Irby (Photo courtesy of Arkansas Secretary of State)
“I think we’re going to see the pendulum swing back the other direction because people will realize we were going in the right direction” under Republican leadership, Hammer said.
Saline County Sheriff Rodney Wright defeated Irby in the race for Hammer’s Senate seat, but Wright received 3,321 fewer votes than Hammer did in 2022.
Irby said he learned while campaigning that Arkansans want “solutions and not sound bites” from their elected officials.
“People are just feeling like, ‘Where’s the help?’” Irby said. “Where are the people who are representing us, and what are they doing to improve this situation? I think that was the key takeaway, the biggest concern anyone and everyone had.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Tennessee’s gerrymandered election maps hold up, but not as well as in past cycles
description: Tennessee Republicans won the popular vote in down-ballot races last week, but gerrymandering  allowed them to win even more seats than vote totals would have indicated. The GOP received around 54% of the vote in Tennessee’s nine congressional races while likely winning eight of them, or 89% of the seats, an analysis of election data […]
text:
Tennessee Republican won more seats then the party's popular vote totals in Tennessee's U.S. House and state House elections. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee Republicans won the popular vote in down-ballot races last week, but gerrymandering  allowed them to win even more seats than vote totals would have indicated.
The GOP received around 54% of the vote in Tennessee’s nine congressional races while likely winning eight of them, or 89% of the seats, an analysis of election data by Lookout shows. In the state House, state Republicans received 58% of the votes cast while winning 69 of the 99 districts, or 70%.
Republicans achieved this outcome by drawing a state House map in 2022 and a U.S. House map in 2026 that gerrymandered districts to dilute Democratic Party votes. Democrats won 44% of congressional votes cast and 41% of state House votes. But Republican margins of victory were narrowed, particularly in the state’s congressional races.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
During the 2022 and 2024 election cycles, Republicans handily won eight of the state’s nine congressional seats. This year’s mid-cycle redistricting narrowed Republican margins of victory in U.S. House districts 5 to 9 because of gerrymandering.
Democrats lost those five districts by less than 5% this year, compared to 2024, when President Donald Trump won those same districts by 20-25% over Democratic Vice President Kamala Harris. 
The narrow margins were also boosted by a political environment in which Democrats won the popular vote by 13%, versus 2024, when the party lost it by 1.5%. 
Kent Syler, a political science professor at Middle Tennessee State University, said Republicans were fortunate to lose only one congressional seat Tuesday night. 
“Tennessee was an afterthought, but this is what can happen in wave elections,” he said. 
The new map, enacted during a May legislative session, allowed Republicans to flip Tennessee’s 9th Congressional District, previously held by Memphis Democratic U.S. Rep. Steve Cohen. But the party likely lost Tennessee’s 4th Congressional District, resulting in no numerical change in House seats held by each party statewide.
Democrat Victoria Broderick currently leads U.S. Rep. Scott DeJarlais in the 4th district by about 285 votes, but the race has not been officially called. About 700 provisional ballots remain to be counted in the 4th as of Nov. 12, and about 600 are in the Democratic stronghold of Nashville, where Broderick won about 75% of the vote on election night. 
Those ballots will be counted on Monday, Nov. 16, after which the race can likely be officially called.
Broderick’s win would be the only Democratic win in Tennessee’s U.S. House map. It would effectively neutralize the redistricting enacted to help Republicans win all nine of the state’s congressional districts. 
Democrats did manage to flip six state House seats, and should control up to 30 of the lower chamber’s seats. The party officially won 29 seats, but in a Memphis state House district, Democrat G.A. Hardaway’s death meant neither party nominated a candidate, and write-in candidate John Bradley won.

name: Mississippi Today
title: What did Colom get right in his win over Hyde-Smith? Pretty much everything
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom greets people in line at a President Donald Trump rally for Colom's opponent, Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026 in Corinth.
text:
Democratic challenger Scott Colom’s upset win over Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith, in red, red Mississippi of all places, will be studied by Deep South politicos from both major parties for years to come. 
I predict it will be a blueprint, a road map for Democrats and a bogeyman of what not to do for Republicans.
So what did Colom’s campaign get right? Well, pretty much everything, it would appear as the dust settles.
First, and foremost, he worked. He campaigned hard, while Hyde-Smith hardly campaigned, at least until the homestretch.
Colom crisscrossed the state nonstop, shook every hand and kissed every baby, so to speak (and he didn’t get the two mixed up, lol). He met the voters where they were, and he listened to them. That’s becoming more and more rare, in the age of big-money campaigns.
Colom adopted a clear message, and he stuck to it: It’s affordability, stupid. When you get a gift from Republicans, don’t overthink it. He expanded his messaging here and there, but he kept the main thing the main thing.
READ MORE: Turns out, Mississippi voters were paying attention in the Colom, Hyde-Smith Senate race
Speaking of money, Colom had little to start with, and national Democratic interests had, as usual, written Mississippi off as too Republican to bother with.
But what resources he did secure early on, he deployed wisely. If he and his crew ever want a new career, they could start an ad agency. The don’t pick another protein/pick another senator, and other ads drew national attention and campaign donations. 
His wise use of resources and sticktoitiveness helped convince national Democrats to sink resources into his campaign. It was kind of late in the game, but he was ready and seized on it.
In Mississippi, even before national resources flowed in, Colom didn’t try to reinvent the wheel. He relied on decades of others’ organizing work before him, and he united many different groups that helped organize and get-out-the-vote. If there was infighting, it didn’t spill out into the public or slow the campaign’s momentum. That is a feat.
Colom also appeared to keep his own counsel. He most certainly was advised to follow some conventional Mississippi Democratic campaign wisdom, and appeared to often ignore it. For many years, some statewide Democratic candidates have tried to keep the national party and its leaders at arm’s length. I recall one time many years ago when a Democratic candidate tried to keep it under wraps that the chair of the Democratic National Committee was coming to Mississippi, and their campaign folks got a little perturbed when news of it leaked to the media.
Colom read the tea leaves correctly: Americans wanted change from the current GOP led by President Donald Trump, including those in Mississippi. He embraced support from his party. He reportedly shrugged off advice to not have former Vice President Kamala Harris campaign for him. He embraced a who’s who of national party leaders past and present.
But Colom also appeared to get a sizeable amount of crossover votes. It’s hard to say exactly how many, but he overperformed other Democratic candidates by more than 25,000 votes. That wasn’t all just turning out Democrats.
He campaigned in Republican strongholds, didn’t write them off. For God’s sake, the man gladhanded with folks in line for a Trump rally in Corinth. Hyde-Smith, by the way, didn’t.
He flipped seven counties from R to D, including some big ‘uns. DeSoto County, which Hyde-Smith had previously won by 16 points, saw a well over 20-point swing, with Colom winning the normally GOP stronghold. He thwarted Hyde-Smith from running up big numbers on the Coast. 
Colom won in many of the suburbs, including Madison County and the aforementioned DeSoto, and he did well in college communities in Lafayette, Forrest and Oktibbeha counties. He held his own in many rural Republican areas, and he amped up turnout in the Delta and other rural Democratic areas.
Over many years in Mississippi, we’ve seen many Democrats play the woulda-shoulda-couda game and do some fingerpointing after (or even during) elections, even ones where they lost by fairly narrow margins. I think we’ll be seeing a good bit of that from Republicans now, although most of their fingers could point to President Trump.
It would appear Colom, of course building on the work of others over many years, helped solidify some infrastructure for the state Democratic Party and get the national party’s attention and resources, the lack of which Mississippi Democrats have long lamented. 
Will it last? Time will tell, but having a Democratic U.S. senator from Mississippi, and a blueprint that worked in the Deep South, will help.

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Stockard on the Stump: Senate finance chief takes Tennessee ‘DOGE’ talk with grain of salt
description: Tennessee’s chief numbers cruncher is downplaying Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn’s plan to take a DOGE-style cleaver to “skinny up” the state budget. Blackburn boasted about her plan after barely beating Democrat Jerri Green in the gubernatorial race and again in her first press conference with Gov. Bill Lee. But Sen. Bo Watson, chairman of the Senate […]
text:
Sen. Bo Watson. a Hixson Republican and chair of the Senate Finance Committee, suggests Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn might not find much to cut in the state's budget. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)Tennessee’s chief numbers cruncher is downplaying Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn’s plan to take a DOGE-style cleaver to “skinny up” the state budget.
Blackburn boasted about her plan after barely beating Democrat Jerri Green in the gubernatorial race and again in her first press conference with Gov. Bill Lee.
But Sen. Bo Watson, chairman of the Senate finance committee, said this week every new governor takes a hard look at the state’s finances and spending, regardless of whether it’s a “top-to-bottom review” done by former Gov. Bill Haslam or a “DOGE” deal, the Department of Government Efficiency used by President Donald Trump in his second term with the help of Elon Musk, some of which ran into constitutional problems.

SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX. 
“I think once she learns about how we do our budget that she’s gonna find that we run pretty lean anyway,” Watson said this week. 
Watson acknowledged there are always ways to improve but said he didn’t know anything about the possibility that Blackburn could hire an outside firm to go through the state’s spending plan.
Blackburn, though, is likely to bring in a consulting company to pore over the $58.3 billion budget, because there’s nothing like spending money to save money. 
As Watson said, it wouldn’t be anything new.
Lee’s administration hired McKinsey & Co. with a $9 million no-bid contract during his first term in office to find ways to streamline the budget, as he fought press efforts to find out exactly what was in the report. The governor followed that up with a contract totaling $3.7 million with McKinsey to handle the state’s COVID-19 response, even though the Attorney General’s Office was investigating the company’s role in consulting with opioid manufacturers on drug sales.



Quotation







I think once she learns about how we do our budget that she’s gonna find that we run pretty lean anyway.


– Sen. Bo Watson on Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn's plans streamline the state budget


Lawmakers questioned multiple no-bid contracts that slipped by McKinsey as well as the deal it received to pore over the budget in search of waste.
Blackburn, who is nothing if not repetitive, plans to put Tennessee on a “government lessening plan.” The governor-elect said she believes the state has been “well-led,” but that “periodically it’s good to get inside the numbers” and study items such as unfilled positions, ineffective programs and state contracting through a “deeper dive.” 
During her time in the state Senate in the early 2000s, as lawmakers were going through the income tax battle, she said she recommended a 5% across-the-board cut annually to make sure the state wasn’t getting lax with programs.
“The legislators are excited about doing this, and I’m excited about working with them on it,” she said.
The question is: How long will the honeymoon last if she and her advisors try to ram things down their throats?
I pledge allegiance …
Republican Senate Speaker nominee Jack Johnson says his heart lies with the Senate, not with Blackburn, even though they’re close friends and have the same political consultant, Ward Baker.
Johnson, who narrowly warded off Sen. Paul Bailey in the speaker’s race this week, might have been handicapped by his close relationship with Blackburn and Baker. Senators don’t want the political consultant telling them what to do all the time.
In addition to that albatross, Johnson was handcuffed by top-down management within the caucus, a bad case of rank-and-file senators sitting on the sidelines waiting for marching orders until the last second. 
Ward Baker is the chief strategist for both Gov.-elect Marsha Blackburn and Sen. Majority Leader Jack Johnson. (Photo by John Partipilo/Tennessee Lookout)
In addition to promising better communications with the full Senate, Johnson is trying to allay concerns that Blackburn and Baker will dictate Senate moves.
“Our loyalty is to the state Senate, regardless of who the governor is, regardless of who any other officeholder is,” Johnson said. “So we’re accountable to our members, and we’re gonna advocate for the positions and policies that our members support.”
He predicted they would be aligned on most issues but would work out disagreements between the Governor’s Office and the House. Of course, things always start out happy and peppy and bursting with love, but then they crumble when one side starts dictating to others who love power as much as they do.
To the victor …
The Blackburn camp wasted no time this week in showing how things will be done. The governor-elect appointed a cadre of her campaign and Baker Group Strategies people to the new transition team and inaugural committee, the latter of which will be raising enough money to float a battleship because we all know that some folks like to drink and dance all night, which is tough in tuxedo rental shoes.
None other than Baker, who likes to keep things within the family, will chair Blackburn’s inauguration executive leadership team, accompanied by Amy Pass, Blackburn’s campaign fundraiser, Melina Settles, a Blackburn finance director, Anna Katherine White, communications for Baker Group Strategies, and Mary Morgan Ketchel, Blackburn’s daughter.
Co-chairs are Daphene and Scott Andrew from the Tri-Cities, Anita and Tom Decosimo (member of the state’s Transportation Modernization Board, which approved a toll lane project and bid), Stephanie and lobbyist John Ingram of Nashville and Anne and Mike Keeney of Memphis.
Former Nashville auto dealer magnate Lee Beaman and his wife, Julie, will serve on Blackburn’s transition team, which is also loaded with her campaign group and Baker people. Blackburn’s campaign manager, Abbi Sigler, will be a senior adviser.
A mild prediction is that these folks will follow the natural evolution by becoming gubernatorial staffers once Blackburn takes office, then moving into the lobbying world where they can make real money. 
Everybody does it, and it’s not illegal.
Outgoing Lt. Gov. Randy McNally’s daughter, Maggie McNally Kimball, received a Blackburn appointment to an advisory committee for the Department of Children’s Service to be chaired by former Sen. Jim Henry, an ally of Lee and Haslam.
McNally denied making phone calls Tuesday morning to lobby for Johnson as Senate speaker in a vote that was exceedingly close by all accounts (the caucus refused to give the tally). 
But there’s absolutely no doubt that Blackburn was pulling for Johnson to win. (He still has to claim the full Senate vote but has a 27-6 supermajority). Otherwise, she and Baker would be dealing with Bailey, and they didn’t want that.
Reaching to the middle?
Creating an advisory group to delve into the Department of Children’s Services’ persistent problems with housing kids in state custody doesn’t seem a very Blackburnian thing to do. She didn’t campaign on it and didn’t bring it up after her win.
Considering she bested Green by only 2.5 percentage points and failed to capture a majority, maybe Blackburn is ready to govern as a moderate.
Besides talking about workforce housing and child safety, Blackburn is encouraging people to participate in a University of Tennessee Extension Service, forestry service and state Department of Agriculture to collect white oak acorns and plant them as part of an effort to replenish forests.
It’s a noble effort. But one must ask: Don’t oaks drop acorns to perpetuate themselves? And will anyone be around to see if they grow?
But if you’re looking for nuts, we have a pretty good idea where to find some without venturing into the woods.
“For the maples want more sunlight / And the oaks ignore their pleas” * 
* “The Trees,” Rush

title: Alabama public schools show improvement on state report card
description: Alabama’s public, K-12 schools saw slight improvement on the state’s report card released Thursday afternoon. The Alabama Department of Education, which determines policies for public schools in the state, received an 88 on the 2025-26 state report card. That is up one point from the 2024-25 school year report card. “We’re real proud,” said Alabama […]
text:
Members of the Alabama State Board of Education as seen on Nov. 12, 2026. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Alabama’s public, K-12 schools saw slight improvement on the state’s report card released Thursday afternoon.
The Alabama Department of Education, which determines policies for public schools in the state, received an 88 on the 2025-26 state report card. That is up one point from the 2024-25 school year report card.
“We’re real proud,” said Alabama State School Superintendent Eric Mackey after the meeting. “This would be the highest score on the state report card we’ve ever had. And one of the things I’m most proud of is where the points went up, is in academic achievement.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The report card measures academic achievement, academic growth, graduation rate, progress in English learner proficiency, chronic absenteeism and college and career readiness. 
According to the state report card, the state saw an increase in academic achievement going from 67 in the 2024-25 school year to 69.20 in the 2025-26 school year.
“It’s much harder to move achievement because to move achievement, students have to actually move from level one, level two, two to three, three to four,” Mackey told board members. “So this is a significant change as students are moving from band to band to make that number change.”
English language proficiency also increased – receiving 49.92 in the 2025-26 academic year – up from 45.65 in the 2024-25 school year.
Other improvement areas include chronic absenteeism, graduation rate and college career readiness.
The graduation rate went from 91.56 in the 2024-25 school year to 92.77 in the 2025-26 school year. College career readiness also increased, receiving a score of 90.70 in the 2025-26 school year, up from 87.88 in the 2024-25 academic year.
Chronic absenteeism decreased over the past two school years going from 12.05 in the 2024-25 year to 10.54 in the 2025-26 year.
Schools under statewide intervention also improved on the state report card.
Bessemer City Schools, which was placed under state intervention due to the board’s dysfunction, went from an overall score of 75 in the 2024-25 year to 77 in the 2025-26 year.
A message seeking comment was left with Bessemer City Schools Thursday afternoon.
Dallas County also saw an increase going from 77 in the 2024-25 school year to 79 in the 2025-26 year. Dallas County was placed under state intervention due to financial and board governance concerns.
Dallas County Schools Superintendent Corey Jones said in a statement Thursday that the increase “a step in the right direction for (the) Dallas County School System.”
“Although we recognize that there is still work to be done, we are encouraged by the progress reflected in this year’s accountability results,” Jones said in the statement. “This improvement represents the dedication of our educators, the hard work of our students, and the continued support of our families and community. We are not satisfied with simply maintaining a letter grade. Our goal is to continue moving forward, strengthening instruction, increasing student achievement, and ensuring that every child has access to opportunities that prepare them for success.”
Sumter County Schools, which was placed under intervention due to a population decline in the area among other reasons including board governance and academics, received a 70 for both the 2024-25 and 2025-26 academic years.
Sumter County Schools recognized the report card score in a statement Thursday.
“While we recognize this achievement, we also understand that there is more work to be done. We remain committed to strengthening classroom instruction, improving student achievement, and providing opportunities for every student to succeed,” the statement said.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: West Virginia politicians cutting taxes while not providing needed infrastructure improvements
description: Well, the midterm elections are over and have proved to be exactly as predicted — a disaster for President Donald Trump and Republicans.
text:
West Virginia is the worst state for bridge infrastructure, with 13% of bridges in poor condition. A road crew works on the Eugene A. Carter Memorial Bridge on Interstate 64  in Charleston, West Virginia in June 2025. Work to replace the deck of the bridge began last month and is scheduled to be completed by spring of 2028. (Photo courtesy of the West Virginia Division of Highways)“West Virginians sent us to tackle real problems and deliver real results.” — Gov. Patrick Morrisey (March 2026)
Well, the midterm elections are over and have proved to be exactly as predicted — a disaster for President Donald Trump and Republicans. The Democrats prevailed in a number of conservative, formerly red states. Like Georgia, where the Senate, the governorship and all statewide races were won by Democrats. But that did not happen in West Virginia, which over the last decade has become a Republican stronghold. The key question is will it remain that way if clearly needed services are not provided by the Republicans in charge? 
Gov. Patrick Morrisey and the GOP controlled Legislature cut taxes earlier this year, declaring above that tax reduction was what the state’s voters wanted. Sure, everybody wants their taxes cut and services expanded. That is why Trump is projected to run up a $2 billion deficit this year. 
However, Morrisey and the state GOP have downplayed areas in which West Virginia must improve to help the state’s citizens. In past columns, I have addressed the issue of highly inadequate healthcare services in West Virginia, especially mental health. But in this column, I will zero in on infrastructure problems.
A recent study has found West Virginia to be the worst state in the nation for infrastructure. Specifically, it is by far the poorest regarding bridge maintenance and power outages. Nearly 13% of the state’s bridges were found to be in poor condition. For comparison purposes, let’s examine Nevada and Arizona, where less than 1% were found to be in disrepair. And West Virginia had 17 hours of power outages annually, the highest in America. Nevada was at 2 hours and Arizona at 1 hour.
Undoubtedly, some of the discrepancy is due to the nature of West Virginia, a mountainous state. Still, Colorado was much better than West Virginia on both measures, with only 11% in disrepair and power outages at 5 hours versus 17 in West Virginia. So, it is not just topography that is causing the bridge and power problems.
The state also ranked poorly regarding community water system health violations and the availability of broad band systems. Only 89% of state residents get broadband, one of the lowest percentages nationally, ranking 47th. Only Montana and Alaska were worse, with 85% coverage. However, they are much larger states and more rural.
West Virginia has other issues which may be directly related to infrastructure. For example, the state has the highest number of crash rate per capita for seniors (over 65) in the nation, 42 accidents per 100K, which is double the national average. At the same time, it has one of the worst road pavement quality ratings, ranking 37th, according to the study by Davidoff Law Personal Injury Lawyers.
Obviously, West Virginia’s politicians must address these issues which include but extend beyond just inadequate state expenditures. However, they are not widely enough discussed or solutions proposed by the governor or Legislature. 
Instead, primarily for political purposes, the state’s GOP has pushed tax cuts. Objectively, West Virginia’s taxes are not high compared to other states. For example, of the states surrounding it, only one has lower taxes — Kentucky. The other four are higher regarding taxes (including Pennsylvania, Virginia, Ohio and Maryland). 
The only way that this situation will change is for voters to put facts and results above party. West Virginia’s GOP leadership needs to hear from its citizens.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Van Hollen says he will challenge Schumer to be next Senate majority leader
description: After a week of “actively listening” to progressive Democrats who were calling on him to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for Senate majority leader, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) confirmed late Thursday that the race is on.
text:
Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) speaks to reporters in El Salvador in April 2025, where he met with Kilmar Abrego Garcia, a Maryland resident erroneously detained and deported there. (Screenshot from Van Hollen's social media)After a week of “actively listening” to progressive Democrats who were calling on him to challenge Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) for Senate majority leader, Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) confirmed late Thursday that the race is on.
“In this election, the American people called for change. They called for a change from [Republican President] Donald Trump’s disastrous policies – but even bigger than that, a change from the status quo that isn’t working for working people,” Van Hollen said in a statement posted to social media late Thursday evening.
“It’s now on us to meet this moment, and to do that we need new leadership. This is not about any one person – it’s about answering the call of the American people,” Van Hollen’s statement said. “That is why I’m running for Senate Majority Leader.”
Within minutes, Schumer had a social media post of his own that did not name Van Hollen or specifically mention a challenge, but that said he looked forward to “leading our new Democratic majority.”
“I welcome any discussion about the future of our caucus and the important work ahead,” Schumer’s post said. “I’m proud of what we’ve accomplished together — 55 seats and counting is an amazing result — and I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.”
Schumer ‘confident’ he’ll lead US Senate Democrats again, despite criticism

Schumer’s supporters point to those Democratic seats as one reason to keep him: Democrats will go from the minority in the current Congress, when they have 45 seats and two independents who caucus with them, to the majority next year with at least 55 seats. They could pick up one more when the Senate race in Alaska is decided.
Despite that, some progressives have been looking to replace Schumer, who they see as too moderate, too friendly with Israel and not aggressive enough when it comes to challenging President Donald Trump and his policies.
Michigan Democratic Sen. Elissa Slotkin and Vermont independent Sen. Bernie Sanders announced this week that they would not support Schumer’s reelection. Even though he will not have a vote in the selection of the new leader, which will happen behind closed doors this year, Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed (D-Mich.), has called on Van Hollen to run. Van Hollen was an early supporter of El-Sayed’s candidacy, Schumer was not.
Schumer, 75, was elected to the Senate in 1998, after 18 years in the House, and has been majority or minority leader of the Senate Democrats since 2017. Van Hollen, 67, was first elected to the Senate in 2016, after 14 years in the House. He represented Montgomery County in the House of Delegates from 1991 to 1995, and was in the state Senate from then to 2003.
Until Thursday, Van Hollen had been saying only that there should be a discussion of what Democrats want in a leader, not a coronation, and that he was not ready to make an announcement. He did not say Thursday what caused him to change his position.
One day before Van Hollen’s announcement, a number of progressive organizations – Baltimore Rapid Response Network, Charm City Indivisible, Allies for Democracy and IfNotNow Baltimore – scheduled a Saturday rally in Baltimore to urge Van Hollen to run for majority leader.
“Some people are saying, ‘Well, Chuck Schumer played an instrumental role in in winning the midterms,’” said Ryan Harvey, with Baltimore Rapid Response. “Well, thank you. You should have done that because you’re one of the leaders of the Democratic Party, and that’s what’s expected of you.
SUPPORT: YOU MAKE OUR WORK POSSIBLE
“Leadership should be … a democracy. It should be a conversation. That’s what Van Hollen’s been calling for,” Harvey said.
He said Van Hollen is more vocal about not only challenging Trump and his administration, but also speaking publicly in support of issues such as Medicare for all.
Van Hollen has been a vocal critic of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, and made headlines last year when he traveled to El Salvador to demand the release of Maryland resident Kilmar Abrego Garcia, after he was erroneously swept up by ICE agents and deported there.
“Sen. Van Hollen has really stepped up since Trump took office a second time, and has really kind of distinguished himself as somebody who’s willing to fight and trying to push the Democratic Party to be to be tougher and more assertive,” Harvey said.
“Van Hollen is not some radical, progressive guy. He’s a Democrat who seems to have been listening quite closely to what people in the party, voters, his constituents have been saying and wanting,” Harvey said. “This is about the future of the Democratic Party, and it’s about defining what this blue wave mandate means.”
Another group, Progressive Maryland, started a change.org petition Thursday afternoon calling on Van Hollen to run for majority leader position. Without naming Schumer, the petition says that “if the caucus defaults to the leadership that has run it since 2017, this [blue] wave will fade into business as usual.”
Van Hollen has also said recently that he was “kicking the tires” on a potential 2028 presidential bid. It’s not clear how a leadership bid might affect that.
Despite their losses in the midterm elections, Senate Republicans this week retained Sen. John Thune (R-S.D.) as their leader for the next Congress, when they will be in the minority. Thune reportedly did not face a challenger.

name: Michigan Advance
title: El-Sayed backs Maryland’s Chris Van Hollen as US Senate majority leader battle begins
description: Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland on Thursday evening announced that he would challenge the party’s U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York for the majority leadership position — and Michigan’s incoming junior senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed, has offered Van Hollen his support. El-Sayed (D-Ann Arbor) previously said he would suppo[...]
text:
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen and U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed speak to reporters after a rally in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)Democratic U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland on Thursday evening announced that he would challenge the party’s U.S. Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer of New York for the majority leadership position — and Michigan’s incoming junior senator-elect, Abdul El-Sayed, has offered Van Hollen his support.
El-Sayed (D-Ann Arbor) previously said he would support Van Hollen if he sought the leadership position of the caucus. As the Democrats regained control of the U.S. Senate in the Nov. 3 election, it was unclear if someone would challenge Schumer, who has led the caucus since 2017.
In an interview with Michigan Advance, El-Sayed reaffirmed his support on Thursday afternoon, hours before Van Hollen jumped into the race.
“I was the first to be calling on him as the next leader, so I would love to see him run, and I’d love to see him as our next leader,” El-Sayed said.
Following Van Hollen’s announcement, El-Sayed said in a news release that Michiganders rejected “the failed status quo and the politics that too often leaves families behind” when they voted last week to give Democrats a majority in Congress.
“But we need to earn our mandate. That demands new leadership,” he said in a statement. “Senator Chris Van Hollen offers both the courage to go toe-to-toe with the Trump administration to deliver for working people and the experience to maneuver the Senate caucus.”
U.S. Sen. Chris Van Hollen speaks at a rally for U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed in Ferndale, Mich., on July 25, 2026. U.S. Sen. Elizabeth Warren and U.S. Rep. Pramila Jayapal also spoke at the event. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)
U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) also has called for new leadership for the Democratic caucus, but she has not publicly backed Van Hollen. 
Slotkin said she is not actively seeking the position. Schumer said Tuesday he’s “confident” he will be reelected as Democratic leader for the next Congress.
The International Association of Machinists and Aerospace Workers said in a news release that it also supports Van Hollen.
“He’s a proven champion of working people who will fight to unrig an economy stacked against working families,” IAM President Brian Bryant said in a statement. “Senator Van Hollen understands this is a fight of Workers vs. Billionaires, and has the courage to deliver the change voters demanded. Workers did their part on election night. Now it’s Senate Democrats’ turn. Senator Van Hollen is the right choice.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Civic group finds KY lawmakers made some transparency improvements but more work is needed
description: In its latest report on legislative transparency, the Kentucky League of Women Voters found some improvements in 2026, but still says there is more work to be done.  During the 2026 legislative session, the General Assembly lessened the use of surprise meetings, declining from 47 surprise meetings in 2024 to 28 in 2026, the League […]
text:
The Kentucky Senate meets on Feb. 28, 2024 in the Capitol, now closed for renovation. The legislature is meeting this year in temporary quarters. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Arden Barnes)In its latest report on legislative transparency, the Kentucky League of Women Voters found some improvements in 2026, but still says there is more work to be done. 
During the 2026 legislative session, the General Assembly lessened the use of surprise meetings, declining from 47 surprise meetings in 2024 to 28 in 2026, the League said. Committees held 90% of their meetings at scheduled times this year, compared to 79% in 2024. 
The League also said more legislative journals were published. In 2023, the most recently published journal was from the 2019 legislative session. As of 2026, the most recent journal is from the 2025 session. 
However, the group’s latest full report continues to highlight ways the public is excluded from the legislative process, such as fast-tracking of bills through the General Assembly. 
Some methods to do that include giving bills a reading shortly before it appears in a committee meeting, adding last-minute changes to committee versions of bills, having same-day floor votes after a bill moves out of a committee and the House and Senate making substantial changes to a bill in a free conference committee near the end of the session. Both the House and Senate used fast-tracking maneuvers on about 20% of all bills that became law this year, the report said.   
“Kentucky lawmakers work for the people of Kentucky,” said Jennifer A. Jackson, the LWVKY president, in a statement. “Although our latest transparency review shows areas of improvement, decades of expedited lawmaking tactics continue to limit participation. We must remain committed to ensuring that Kentuckians play a meaningful role in shaping the laws that affect them.”
The League has been tracking legislative transparency in the General Assembly since 2023. 
In response to the report, a Senate Republican spokesperson said the caucus appreciated “the League’s latest report acknowledging positives of committee scheduling and access to legislative journals.
“The timing of a bill’s final steps does not always capture the public discussion and committee work that preceded them, including work during the interim,” the spokesperson added. “Kentucky’s part-time legislature operates under firm constitutional deadlines, and it has used these procedures for many years. That context should be considered when evaluating the process. Committee meetings remain open to the public, with committee and floor proceedings livestreamed. Bill texts, votes and extensive legislative history are available online. We encourage Kentuckians to contact their senators throughout the year.
“We remain committed to being accessible and responsive to the people we serve.”

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Too many bears? Some want to expand black bear hunting in Eastern Kentucky
description: Over the course of his decades in Harlan, Mayor Joe Meadors has seen a resurgence of wildlife, including deer, elk, and turkeys that he never really saw as a kid growing up in Eastern Kentucky. He’s glad to “have them all” around his community.   But there’s another animal making a comeback that Meadors is less […]
text:
A black bear seen on Ivy Street next to a trash bag and a knocked over trash bin in Harlan, Kentucky. (Courtesy Joe Meadors)Over the course of his decades in Harlan, Mayor Joe Meadors has seen a resurgence of wildlife, including deer, elk, and turkeys that he never really saw as a kid growing up in Eastern Kentucky. He’s glad to “have them all” around his community.  
But there’s another animal making a comeback that Meadors is less happy about: black bears.
“Right now, the bear population is plum out of sorts. There’s so many of them in the city of Harlan,” said Meadors. “They’ve just gotten out of hand because the population’s kind of been unchecked for a while.”
Meadors said what used to be an occasional black bear sighting in his city of 1,100, has become near constant. The bears, attracted to scraps of food in garbage, roam around almost everywhere imaginable in the city. They’re by the schools. They’re by the library. They’re being chased away by the city police department at night. 
Meadors said he’s not portraying bears as the “bad guys”, but he is among some local elected officials in Eastern Kentucky who believe something needs to be done to manage or reduce the population. He said a friend’s kid had an encounter about a month ago with a protective mother bear with three cubs who growled at the kid, scaring the kid “to death.” 
A black bear seen along a local street in Harlan County, Kentucky. (Courtesy Joe Meadors)
Black bears usually are very shy, have a solitary nature, and avoid people. Black bear attacks on humans are also exceedingly rare, though not unprecedented. 
In 2010, a hiker in the Red River Gorge area of the Daniel Boone National Forest described what officials believed was the first bear attack in Kentucky in modern history. In September, Kentucky State Police said a trooper shot and killed a bear in Harlan County after the trooper said it lunged at him after finding its way into an elementary school’s field house. 
Bell County Judge-Executive Albey Brock told the Lantern that he believes the black bear situation is “flirting” with the potential for a “horrific encounter” because of how often some bears are interacting with people. 
Brock and Meadors have been in favor a further expansion of bear hunting in Eastern Kentucky, something that the chair of the state commission that crafts state hunting rules says he’s interested in.
Though both say addressing the problem is more complex than just increased hunting, including better management and containment of trash. 
“We have to put enough pressure on the bear that they stay in the remote woods. I’m all for that,” Brock said, mentioning he doesn’t want to “eradicate” the bears. “They’ve got a natural instinct to be fearful, but it’s not strong enough. It will not override a stale box of Little Debbie’s that got thrown in the garbage.”
The problem of ‘problem bears’
The Kentucky Department of Fish and Wildlife Resources, the state’s wildlife management agency, considers the resurgence of black bears in Eastern Kentucky over the past 20 years to a “true wildlife success story” after they were essentially wiped out in the 1800s due to widespread logging of forests and colonization by settlers moving into the state. 
Larry Cornett, the president of the Kentucky Bear Hunting Association, which represents hunters, including those who use dogs to chase and hunt bears, told the Lantern that black bears generally are afraid of people. 
But the issue is what he calls “problem bears” that have formed a habit of getting into garbage as a food source. 
“When a bear gets to where it’s not scared of humans, it’s a potential hazard,” Cornett said. 
Cornett said he would be in favor of expanding black bear hunting opportunities in Kentucky to help control the population, something that the Kentucky Fish and Wildlife Commission could potentially look at in upcoming meetings. 

Commission chair Chuck Meade told the Lantern the expansion of bear hunting was a “priority” of his and would be the “next topic of discussion” for a subcommittee of the commission. The issue has been on his radar since last year when he met with local elected officials in Eastern Kentucky. 
He said some of the potential ideas to be considered could include adding a spring bear season, extending hunting season days and adding more youth hunting opportunities in “overpopulated areas.” About eight states have spring bear hunting seasons in the Western U.S., but none east of the Mississippi.
Earlier this year, the commission had already approved a smaller expansion of bear hunting by extending the days of the season when hunters can train dogs to chase bears, along with adding a short youth hunting season. But Meade doesn’t believe it has alleviated “any of the problems that some of the complainers are having about nuisance bears.” 
Around that time, a Kentucky lobbyist with an animal welfare group had raised concerns about the stability of the state’s bear population because of the state’s “increasingly permissive” hunting regulations. The number of black bears killed in the state has sharply risen in recent years, with more than 200 bears killed in both 2024 and 2025. In 2015, hunters in Kentucky killed just 46 bears. 
But for Meade, who represents Eastern Kentucky counties on the commission, he said there’s a “fine line of cohabitation” between bears and people. He said the commission would have to work with biologists within the department on potential solutions.  
 “If we’re overpopulated now and we don’t do anything, how much more overpopulated are we going to be next year?” Meade said.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Va. crime panel recommends tougher penalties for license plate reader misuse, stops short of ban
description: New recommendations from the Virginia Crime Commission on governing automatic license plate readers will likely spark debate when lawmakers convene in January, as public calls for an immediate ban mount. On Tuesday, the Virginia Crime Commission, which includes state lawmakers, recommended several changes to the ALPR state law focused on data sharing and pen[...]
text:
A view of an automated license plate reader. (Photo by Nathaniel Cline/Virginia Mercury)New recommendations from the Virginia Crime Commission on governing automatic license plate readers will likely spark debate when lawmakers convene in January, as public calls for an immediate ban mount.
On Tuesday, the Virginia Crime Commission, which includes state lawmakers, recommended several changes to the ALPR state law focused on data sharing and penalties, but did not recommend a ban.
Cases of alleged misuse and local government disagreements over these crime-investigation tools have fueled proposals to ban the devices in the commonwealth. Earlier this year, Virginia Crime Commission staff found fewer law enforcement agencies were non-compliant with state law, but concerns remained, including prohibited data sharing in some cases. 
Law enforcement agencies’ use of license plate reader data faces fresh scrutiny

“It’s important that there’s sufficient consequences, not just for individual police officers that are looking up their neighbors or boyfriends or girlfriends, or whatever, but also for the law enforcement agencies that don’t seem compelled to follow the laws that we pass,”  Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell, D-Fairfax, said at the meeting.
Hampton Commonwealth’s Attorney Anton Bell noted, however, that most ALPR violations do not involve personal misuse, such as accessing information about former partners. Instead, he said, they involve officers sharing information with other officers or agencies to address ongoing criminal activity.
“With this statute … we’re thinking of ex-boyfriends, ex-girlfriends, and they are accessing this information to use it in a nefarious manner, but that is not the majority of the violations,” Bell said. “The majority of the violations is a law enforcement officer giving that information to another law enforcement officer or agency to address a criminal act that is currently going on.”
As part of its ALPR package, the commission recommended that the General Assembly consider allowing data-sharing requests to be made electronically. State law allows data sharing under certain circumstances, but it does not allow electronic requests. 
The commission also recommended treating each unlawfully shared record as a separate violation and establishing a $5,000 minimum civil penalty per violation, increasing the financial stakes. 
The law establishes a Class 1 misdemeanor for intentional unauthorized access, use, or sharing of ALPR data, but does not include a financial penalty.
“There’s a lot of public concern,” said Bruce Cruser, commission member and an appointee of Gov. Abigail Spanberger, on Tuesday. “If we really want to try to address those concerns, we need to make the fine or the fee … it needs to reflect the importance of this violation.”
The commission voted to establish standards for officer decertification for unlawfully accessing or sharing ALPR data, with final procedures to be addressed during the legislative session. 
In addition, the commission recommended expanding enforcement authority to local prosecutors and, in emergencies, allowing emergency data-sharing without a court order when there is an imminent threat of harm.
Ahead of the next General Assembly session, some lawmakers, including Sens. Glen Sturtevant, R-Chesterfield, and Lashrecse Aird, D-Henrico, have publicly expressed interest in banning the readers, signaling bipartisan interest in further action. Others have called for more transparency.
“The crime commission is proposing more guardrails for a surveillance system that never should have been installed in the first place,” Sturtevant said in a statement to the Mercury following the meeting. 
“We tried guardrails last year, and we’ve already seen the abuses. But even if everyone followed the rules, these cameras would still be collecting information on where law-abiding Virginians drive. The government shouldn’t be building that kind of surveillance network.”
 What’s next

Lawmakers will return to Richmond on Jan. 13 to discuss related legislation and proposals the commission endorsed, including a measure to allow attorneys to share unredacted records with defendants and procedures to scientifically test evidence discovered during the review.
They will also consider giving the panel authority to consult independent experts.
Lawmakers could also pursue reforms to clarify and streamline criminal record-sealing procedures, including a 30-day waiting period before automatic sealing takes effect. 
They could also require individuals to petition the court to seal past misdemeanor dismissals, because electronic records cannot distinguish between complete dismissals and deferred dismissals involving admissions of guilt in serious cases.
