name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: Scout Motors’ SC factory is 85% complete and first test vehicles are rolling off the line
description: EV-maker Scout Motors has started its transition from building a factory to building vehicles in South Carolina.
text:
Covered by a sheet, one of Scout Motors' first test SUVs undergoes testing for wheel and headlight alignments Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at the nearly complete electric vehicle assembly plant in Blythewood. It marks one of 30 test vehicles to be assembled this year at the plant, with more planned for early 2027. This vehicle is not a finished product that will be sold to customers in 2028. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)BLYTHEWOOD — South Carolina-based electric vehicle maker Scout Motors has started its transition from building a factory to building vehicles, with plans to hire a few hundred more assembly line workers over the course of the next year.
The Volkswagen subsidiary is nearly finished putting together its first round of 30 to 40 test vehicles and will begin a second round of testing in early 2027, CEO Scott Keogh said Thursday, following a tour of the nearly complete $2 billion assembly plant in Blythewood.
One of the assembly lines Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at the nearly complete Scout Motors electric vehicle assembly plant in Blythewood. The assembly shop is the final building in need of completion at the plant. At full capacity, 2,000 assembly workers will build about 40 Scouts per hour. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)The view from inside one of the glass paint booths Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at Scout Motor's nearly complete electric vehicle assembly plant in Blythewood. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)
“This is the very first prototype, the prototype that’s working its way out to America to get the software installed, start going on roads, and testing and validating things like durability, things like safety, and all of the electronic hardware,” Keogh said.
Testing will continue in phases throughout 2027. The first vehicles are now expected to hit the market in 2028.

At full capacity, Scout plans to produce 200,000 vehicles annually. That will include a mix of fully electric and hybrid-like models.
Some 212,000 people have already signed up and paid the deposit to buy the first Scouts that roll off the line, Keogh said. Most of those are asking for the Scout Traveler SUV and 95% want the combination gas and electric option.
Today, Scout employs upwards of 18,000 workers across its three locations — the Blythewood assembly plant, corporate headquarters in Charlotte and an engineering and design center in Michigan.
Of those employees, 900 work in South Carolina: 600 in engineering and management and 300 factory workers.
That South Carolina number will grow to 4,000 workers when the assembly plant reaches full capacity.
Meanwhile, German-headquartered Volkswagen, the financiers of the Scout project, and Swedish automaker Volvo, which has an assembly plant in the Lowcountry, are both struggling financially.
Volvo posted larger-than-expected operating losses last month and Volkswagen’s profit margin fell to its lowest in at least a decade, as both face joint headwinds from increased competition in China — the world’s largest electric vehicle market — and global tariffs increasing the cost of vehicles in the U.S.
“We are not in a naive position. We quite know the automotive dynamics are tough and you have to compete,” Keogh said.
But unlike Volvo’s Ridgeville plant, which is operating at less than 20% of its capacity as it shifts from building electric vehicles for export to building them for the U.S. market, Keogh said Scout won’t need to be at full capacity — or even 80% capacity — before it expects to start turning a profit.

And unlike other startup electric vehicle brands, such as Rivian, Scout benefits from the cost savings that come with tapping into Volkswagen’s bulk buying power.
While Keogh declined to name the capacity percentage the factory needs to reach before its profitable, he said “we can make money at dramatically less volume.”
Scout did face a recent setback in its plans to sell its vehicles directly to consumers, similar to Tesla, rather than through the traditional dealership network.
Tennessee, this month, denied the company a license, and legislation allowing direct sales in South Carolina stalled in a House committee in February 2025. The bill officially died earlier this year with the end of the legislative session. To renew the effort, the bill would need to be reintroduced next year.
Laws governing direct sales vary by state — 18 expressly allow it and 17 expressly ban it, with the rest falling somewhere in between, according to the National Conference of State Legislatures.
Still, Scout is confident it can still reach all buyers, even if customers have to cross state lines to test drive them and have them shipped at a later date.
One of about 900 robots, pictured Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, inside the body shop of the Scout Motors electric vehicle assembly plant in Blythewood. The robots work in teams to put together the parts making up the vehicles frame, with a new frame moving between each station every 90 seconds. Between 150 to 180 workers also will work alongside the robots in this shop, largely loading parts into the machines. (Photo by Jessica Holdman/SC Daily Gazette)

name: Michigan Advance
title: Detroit residents urge delay as city council advances RenCen redevelopment agreement
description: DETROIT – City council members advanced an agreement between developers and residents tied to a $2.2 billion plan to transform Detroit’s Renaissance Center and surrounding East Riverfront into a residential and entertainment district.  In a 3-2 vote, the City Council’s Planning and Economic Development Committee voted to send the community benefits agreement[...]
text:
Teron Haynes Jr. was amongst the protestors demanding that the city council delay its Nov. 12, 2026, vote on the $43.5 million community benefits agreement. He is the only member of the NAC who didn't approve the agreement. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)DETROIT – City council members advanced an agreement between developers and residents tied to a $2.2 billion plan to transform Detroit’s Renaissance Center and surrounding East Riverfront into a residential and entertainment district. 
In a 3-2 vote, the City Council’s Planning and Economic Development Committee voted to send the community benefits agreement to the full council without a recommendation.
Committee Chair Latisha Johnson said sending the agreement to the full council would allow members to raise additional questions and concerns during a public discussion.
“If we determine that we’re not ready to move forward, then we know how to address that in the committee of the whole,” Johnson said. 
Councilmember Gabriela Santiago-Romero opposed advancing the agreement, saying she wanted more time to review the proposal and ensure questions raised by council members and residents are answered.
“People don’t move to cities for their downtowns. They move to cities because of their transportation, their neighborhoods, their culture, their people, all of that,” Santiago-Romero said. “That’s what I’m trying to make sure that we have at the forefront here and this does feel very, very rushed.” 
Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield joined members of the project’s nine-member Neighborhood Advisory Council at a press conference on Nov. 5, where they signed the CBA, which dedicates $15 million to housing, $10 million to small businesses, $8 million to a community hub, $6 million to workforce development and education, and $4.5 million to parking, totaling $43.5 million. 
Developers also pledged an additional $90 million in voluntary payments in lieu of taxes or “PILOT” payments over 30 years, bringing the total announced commitments to $133.5 million.
Dozens of residents, community organizers and business owners urged the city council to delay its vote on the community benefits agreement and give the community more time to provide input. 
“There are things that we have asked for over the last 10 weeks and all of a sudden they have disappeared out of the CBA,” said Nicole Small, of Save the RenCen, during a rally outside of the Coleman A. Young Municipal Center Thursday morning.  “This is not a community benefits agreement, this is a developer benefits agreement. The mayor should be outraged. City Council should be outraged and the people of Detroit should definitely be outraged,” Small said. 
Protestors chanted “Whose riverfront? Our riverfront!” during a rally outside of the Coleman A. Young Municipal center on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)
The agreement is part of the city’s Community Benefits Ordinance, which requires developers of large-scale projects to engage residents who could be affected by the development. The Neighborhood Advisory Council is responsible for representing residents throughout that process. Its nine members include three City Council appointees, four appointees from the city’s Planning and Development Department and two elected neighborhood representatives.
Still, some residents felt that they were left out of the process, especially after released text messages between council members showed they agreed not to make public the recordings or transcripts from closed negotiations with developers, at least until after the council voted to approve the CBA. 
“We got two months of public input on this process for a project that’s about to exist for the next 50 years,” said Jeremiah Wheeler of Detroit Action during the rally. “The money is coming from all around the city but the benefits are not going all around the city. The benefits are limited to … downtown and that’s not acceptable,” Wheeler said.
Not every member of the NAC is in support of the agreement. Teron Haynes Jr. was the only council member who didn’t sign the CBA. 
“Those buildings don’t look obsolete to me. They’re standing and I’m not waiting for them to collapse,” Haynes said during the rally, pointing to the Renaissance Center. “We shouldn’t be waiting for Detroit to collapse either but that’s what’s going to happen if we keep giving billionaires this money and not investing into the community.” SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The agreement follows weeks of negotiations between the council and developers Bedrock Detroit and General Motors. During Thursday’s committee meeting, officials described it as the largest community benefits agreement in Detroit’s history.
“We have community benefits in the agreement but the reason why I voted no was because I did not think that the benefits were substantial enough for, what we are giving to these developers but also what people in Detroit … have missed out on in the past decade as far as community development and investment,” Haynes told the Michigan Advance. 
The project calls for the demolition of two of the complex’s five towers, with plans to convert the remaining three into 934 mixed-income housing units and office space. Additional plans include a marina, an observation deck and 18 acres of proposed civic space across the broader 46-acre development site.
Bedrock and GM are expected to invest more than $1.6 billion in the project, while the Downtown Development Authority will contribute $75 million. The remaining $505 million is expected to come through debt.
Developers are also seeking more than $473 million in tax breaks over 30 years. Additional commercial tax incentives would bring the total requested subsidies to approximately $548 million.
If approved by Detroit City Council, demolition work is expected to begin next summer. The project is expected to take at least 10 years to complete. City Council members are aiming to approve the plan before Thanksgiving, when the council will go on recess until next year. 
Billionaire Dan Gilbert, who founded Bedrock, pledged an additional $1 billion to establish a new nonprofit organization dedicated to redeveloping and operating the Renaissance Center and East Riverfront.
Despite the donation, protesters said they would rather the new development be publicly owned and that there be more investment into developing housing throughout the city instead of downtown. 
“If the word philanthropy meant anything, then he (Dan Gilbert) would pay property taxes,” said Russ Bellant, of Detroiters for Tax Justice during Thursday morning’s protest. “Why isn’t he using those tax benefits that he’s looting from us … for an investment instead of coming back to us and saying, ‘Let me screw you for another half a billion dollars.’”
Bedrock is the largest private property owner in Detroit, operating roughly 100 properties, most of them in the downtown area. 
Dozens of community leaders, advocates and residents spoke during public comment at Thursday’s Planning and Economic Development Committee meeting, with many urging council members to delay the proposed Renaissance Center redevelopment and give the community more time to weigh in on the project. Despite commenters being limited to 45 seconds, the meeting lasted more than five hours. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)
The redevelopment has drawn both support and concern from residents. Some question whether the project represents another major investment in downtown Detroit while neighborhoods elsewhere in the city continue to grapple with vacant lots and deteriorating homes.
Another major concern, especially early in the community benefits process, was that the estimated area of impact was too small and did not include residents in surrounding areas. The Renaissance Center, located along Woodward Avenue in the city’s downtown area, is in District 5. Developers estimate that nearly 4,700 residents live in the impacted area.
“The NAC should have considered bus riders who use Jefferson as a route. If this project goes through without any consideration, it would jeopardize access to jobs, access to city and county services and transit connections across Detroit and our county,” said Renard Munchinski, an organizer with Detroit People’s Platform, during virtual public comment at Thursday’s committee meeting. 
Supporters view the development as an investment in Detroit’s future. 
“In TechTown we see every day that local entrepreneurs don’t lack talent. They lack affordable storefronts, capital and coaching and this CBA delivers all three,” said Ned Staebler, President and CEO of TechTown.
Ryan Sullivan, CEO of the Detroit Riverfront Conservancy also spoke in support of the project and urged the committee to pass the agreement. 
The project marks a significant turning point for one of Detroit’s most recognizable landmarks.
The Renaissance Center opened in 1977, featuring a 73-story central hotel tower surrounded by four office towers. Two additional office towers opened in 1981. General Motors purchased the entire complex in 1996 for $73 million and established its global corporate headquarters there.
But as hybrid work schedules became more common following the COVID-19 pandemic and office occupancy declined, GM announced in 2024 that it would relocate its global headquarters to Hudson’s Detroit, another Bedrock development. The 49-story skyscraper was also developed by the Detroit-based real estate firm, owned by billionaire Dan Gilbert.
GM’s planned departure raised questions about the future of the Renaissance Center. Now, those questions have evolved into a multibillion-dollar redevelopment proposal that could reshape Detroit’s riverfront for decades.

name: National
title: This time, rural voters ‘just weren’t there’ for the GOP
description: LAMPASAS, Texas — Standing at the edge of his family’s 300-acre cattle ranch in Central Texas, Clayton Tucker is characteristically attired in a white Stetson western hat, a beige shirt with pearl snaps, and lightly faded Wrangler jeans. At 35, Tucker is poised to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to serve […]
text:
Clayton Tucker, elected last week as Texas agriculture commissioner, poses at his ranch in Lampasas, Texas. Tucker is the first Democrat in more than three decades to hold the position. Across the country, rural voters — staunchly Republican in recent decades — either defected to Democrats or stayed home. (Photo by David Montgomery/Stateline)LAMPASAS, Texas — Standing at the edge of his family’s 300-acre cattle ranch in Central Texas, Clayton Tucker is characteristically attired in a white Stetson western hat, a beige shirt with pearl snaps, and lightly faded Wrangler jeans.
At 35, Tucker is poised to become the first Democrat in more than three decades to serve as Texas agriculture commissioner, a post from which he will oversee policies affecting much of rural Texas. The last Democrat to serve as agriculture commissioner left office in January of 1991— a month before Tucker was born.
Tucker, who takes office in January, benefitted from the Democratic wave that swept across Texas and other states in the midterm elections, propelled by widespread disenchantment with Republican policies, both in the cities and on the farm.
Across the country, rural voters — staunchly Republican in recent decades — either defected to Democrats or stayed home to protest the spread of data centers, rising fuel prices, the war in Iran and other grievances.
In Texas, about 90% of the counties where turnout decreased were rural, according to The Texas Tribune. While many rural voters stayed faithful to GOP candidates, their diminished numbers at the polls helped clear the way for Democratic victories: In the state’s U.S. Senate race, the Democrats improved their performance in all 254 Texas counties, compared with the 2024 U.S. Senate contest.
“People felt like they were being treated as sacrificial lambs for Wall Street, for Silicon Valley, for all these tech bros and oligarchs and everyone else,” Tucker said in an interview behind the steering wheel of his parked 1982 GMC pickup truck, “and they just weren’t being supported by our government anymore.”
Rural disenchantment also helped drive epic Democratic victories in other states.
In Kansas, Methodist minister Adam Hamilton was elected to the U.S. Senate, the first Kansas Democrat to win a Senate seat since 1932. Analysts attributed Hamilton’s victory to a rural backlash over high fuel and fertilizer prices and cheap imported beef. In Montana, former smoke-jumper Sam Forstag flipped one of the state’s two congressional seats, becoming the first Montana Democrat to win a U.S. House seat since 1994.
Partisan control also shifted in Iowa, where agriculture-related jobs employ roughly 1 in 5 residents. Iowa Democrats won the governor’s race, a U.S. Senate seat and three of the state’s four congressional seats. Republicans maintained their grip on both chambers of the state legislature, but Democrats narrowed the gap.
Iowa Republican U.S. Rep. Ashley Hinson won just over half of rural and small-town voters in her unsuccessful bid for one of Iowa’s U.S. Senate seats, according to The Associated Press. But that was a smaller percentage of rural and small-town voters than the GOP got in 2022, and the diminished margin helped secure a victory for Democratic candidate Josh Turek.
“It was a setback for Republicans and now they have to figure out how they’re going to get back some of the voters they probably lost,” said Abhishek Chatterjee, an associate professor of political science at the University of Montana.
Texas the epicenter
Texas, the nation’s second-largest state, was an epicenter of the midterm upheaval. Voters there turned against three-term Republican Gov. Greg Abbott to choose state Rep. Gina Hinojosa as the state’s first Latina governor and the first Democrat to hold the office since Ann Richards left in 1995.
Texas voters also elected Democratic state Rep. James Talarico to the U.S. Senate and placed Democrats, including Tucker, in all of the top statewide offices. Democrats also took over the Texas House, which has been controlled by Republicans since 2003.
Republicans still hold the majority in the Texas Senate and are considering rule changes to undercut the power of incoming presiding officer Vikki Goodwin, a Democratic legislator who defeated incumbent Republican Lt. Gov. Dan Patrick for the state’s number two post, which includes leadership of the legislature’s upper chamber.
Young, diverse voters showed up for midterms as older, Trump voters stayed home

In the aftermath of what she called a “nationwide Republican defeat,” Texas Republican Party Chair D’rinda Randall announced the formation of an invitation-only Texas Mandate Committee composed of statewide leaders charged with “examining what occurred and developing a strategy to win Texas back.”
“This is not about placing blame,” she said in a statement. “It is about planning to win.”
Kendall Scudder, chair of the Texas Democratic Party as well as the Democratic National Committee’s Rural Council, told Stateline that his party’s Texas triumph resulted in part from a concentrated campaign that included a heavy focus on rural Texas.
“What I think happened was folks in rural Texas gave Democrats an opportunity to state our case, and we hadn’t had that in while,” said Scudder, who grew up in Sulphur Springs in largely rural East Texas.
“I think we started making inroads, and part of that could be because Republicans weren’t worth showing up and voting for. But I think another piece is that Democrats were talking about things that were important to rural Texas.”
Top issues that resonated strongly in rural Texas, he said, included the spread of data centers, “mass surveillance” by mounted Flock cameras that read license plates, and inadequate funding for state schools. As result, he said, 21 largely rural counties that voted red in previous elections “went blue this time.”
“I think we moved the needle in a good way, and I think if Democrats deliver for those communities, we can start to unlock more and more gains,” he said.
Outgoing Agriculture Commissioner Sid Miller, a Republican who lost his primary race for re-election, echoed Tucker and Scudder’s assertions that rural voters are up in arms over data centers, artificial intelligence, Flock cameras, and soaring fuel prices. Tucker says he will push for a moratorium on data centers after he takes office in January.
“We’ve never had any real property tax relief,” Miller said in a phone interview “Diesel’s the highest it’s ever been. Fertilizer’s the highest it’s ever been. I don’t think the Democrats took anything away from the Republicans,” Miller said, “we basically gave it to them.”
Miller put much of the blame for rural dissension on Abbott’s policies.  Abbott endorsed Miller’s Republican primary opponent, Nate Sheets, who in turn was beaten by Tucker in the general election.
A $1 billion publicly funded private school voucher program that Abbott pushed through the Texas Legislature in 2025 also stirred dissent in parts of rural Texas, amid fears that it will siphon money from public schools.
Voters across the country reject data centers

“There was a lot of hard feelings about the voucher program out there,” said Snapper Carr of Austin, a managing partner and general counsel of Focused Advocacy, a lobbying firm that represents cities and communities throughout the state. The Republican downturn, he said, was particularly evident in what he said are typically “bright red areas of West Texas,” where residents “talk about the price of diesel like we all talk about the weather.”
“The Republicans still carried them,” he said, “but their margins were much less than what they’ve been in the past…There was a large number of past Republicans that didn’t show up this time.”
‘Totally surprised’
In Briggs, an unincorporated Central Texas community with around 100 residents, Ray Bizzell, 83, offered his thoughts on the election outcome as he left Sunday’s services at the Briggs Baptist Church. Bizzell, who runs a floor covering business about 20 miles away in Georgetown, Texas, said he voted “Republican, straight ticket” and “was totally surprised” by Democrats’ strong showing in the state.
“I really thought we might hold it,” he said. “I just think my beliefs align better with the Republican Party.”
In Williamson County, which stretches from the high-growth Austin suburbs to patches of rural Texas further east, the unexpected Democratic surge propelled first-time candidate Chris Jimenez, 42, into a state legislative victory over a Republican incumbent backed the governor.
In this year’s U.S. Senate race, Williamson County swung nearly 19 points toward the Democrats compared with the Senate race in 2024, according to The Associated Press.
Jimenez, who lives on a pecan farm with his wife and 16-year-old daughter near the town of Elgin, is headed to the statehouse after defeating Republican state Rep. Caroline Harris Davila for the House seat once held by Talarico. Jimenez’s opponent was endorsed by Abbott.
Jimenez grew up on a ranch near Sanderson and served in the Marine Corps. He said his thoughts of running for office intensified after he was “pulled over and profiled by a police officer,” he told Stateline. “I was very concerned on multiple levels. I  figured, ‘Hey, if this is happening to me, a Marine Corps veteran just trying to make my life here on the farm, it’s got to be happening to multiple people.’”
“Did I expect to win? I felt our message resonated with people, regardless of their political affiliation,” he said. “It was never about being red or blue.  It was about survival in Texas and it’s gotten hard for a lot of folks.”
Democrats romped in state elections. What will they do with their newfound power?

Jimenez has joined other incoming lawmakers in pre-filing bills before the January start of the legislature. His measure call for repealing “the private school voucher scheme,” eliminating a sales tax exemption for data centers and expanding Medicaid benefits in Texas.
Republican data analyst Derek Ryan said Republicans needed to win by “a very large margin” in rural counties to counter strong turnout in predominately Democratic urban areas.  The GOP only had 32-point advantage in those counties in this year’s mid-term elections,  he said, compared to 55 points in 2022 and 46 points in 2018.
Ryan estimated that about 625,000 Republicans sat out the election, according to the Texas Rural Report.
“We knew there was going to be a slight shift towards the Democrats in rural Texas,” Ryan told Stateline. “I didn’t think it was going to be this significant, but it comes down to the economy and gas prices.
“When you live in rural Texas, it’s a long drive anywhere you go. So when it’s costing you more to fill up your tank, you know you’re going to vote with that in mind.”
Suzanne Bellsnyder, who owns and runs a newspaper in the small town of Spearman near the Oklahoma state line, said she has analyzed all 184 Texas counties with a population under 50,000 and found signs of Republican slippage in areas that have typically served as Republican bulwarks.
“Republicans have always depended on the rural counties to kind of be their firewall, their insurance policy,” she said. But this time, she added, “they just weren’t there.”

name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Engineers give Indiana infrastructure a D+ amid warnings of aging systems, funding gaps
description: Indiana’s roads and bridges are holding up better than those in much of the country, but aging water systems, deteriorating dams and mounting pressure on the state’s electric grid have earned its overall infrastructure a D+ in a new assessment released Thursday. The 2026 Report Card for Indiana’s Infrastructure, prepared by the American Society of […]
text:
Indiana Secretary of Transportation and Infrastructure Matthew Ubelhor speaks Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, at the Indiana Statehouse during the release of a new infrastructure report card. (Photo by Casey Smith/Indiana Capital Chronicle)Indiana’s roads and bridges are holding up better than those in much of the country, but aging water systems, deteriorating dams and mounting pressure on the state’s electric grid have earned its overall infrastructure a D+ in a new assessment released Thursday.
The 2026 Report Card for Indiana’s Infrastructure, prepared by the American Society of Civil Engineers, found that years of transportation investments have helped preserve highways and bridges. But engineers warned that billions of dollars in needed repairs, increasingly severe weather and growing demand for electricity are threatening other critical systems.
The findings also raise concerns about how Indiana will pay for future improvements as federal infrastructure funding winds down and the state’s suspension of gasoline taxes creates additional uncertainty for road construction and maintenance.
The D+ grade falls below the C assigned to the nation’s infrastructure in 2025. The national assessment, however, covers 18 infrastructure categories, compared with seven evaluated in Indiana.
Engineers presented the findings Thursday at the Indiana Statehouse, joined by state transportation officials, as well as representatives from U.S. Sen. Todd Young’s office and Indiana American Water.
Story continues below.
2026-indiana-report-card-full
 
The report examined seven areas: bridges, dams, drinking water, energy, roads, stormwater and wastewater.
Bridges earned the highest grade, a B-, followed by roads and drinking water at C-. Dams, energy and stormwater received D grades, while wastewater received a D+.
The analysis says D means poor and at risk.
“A ‘D+’ grade is a reminder of the importance of Indiana’s infrastructure and the successes in some areas and challenges other sectors face in the future,” said James Tradup, a report card co-chair. “This report card shows the positive impact investment has sparked in some sectors, while a reminder of where additional funds are needed to improve these systems every Hoosier depends on.”
The assessment is the first state-specific infrastructure report card published by the engineering group for Indiana. Engineers said they evaluated infrastructure conditions, capacity, funding, future needs, maintenance, public safety, resilience and innovation.
The report notes that while Indiana has benefited from more than $9 billion in federal infrastructure investments under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act, those resources are temporary — and the engineers said sustained funding will be critical for preventing infrastructure from deteriorating.
Roads and bridges outperform, but funding questions remain
Transportation was among Indiana’s strongest areas in the report card, following years of state investment and efforts meant to maintain existing infrastructure before major repairs or replacements become necessary.
About 95% of Indiana’s more than 19,500 bridges are in fair or good condition, according to the report. State-owned bridges generally fare better than those maintained by counties, cities and towns.
Just 1% of state-owned bridges are rated poor, compared with 7% of bridges owned by other agencies.
Still, the report identified a substantial funding gap for locally maintained bridges.
Engineers estimated that local bridges need approximately $580 million annually to reach a state of good repair, but receive only about $67 million, leaving a $513 million annual shortfall.

Local roads face similar challenges. While the state’s major highways are generally in relatively good condition, nearly one-third of city, town and county roads are rated poor.
The report estimates that deferred roadway maintenance costs Indiana motorists $1.6 billion annually through additional vehicle repairs, fuel consumption and depreciation.
Funding is another concern.
The engineers warned that the ongoing suspension of Indiana’s gasoline taxes threatens a major revenue source for transportation improvements at a time when aging infrastructure already requires significant investment.
Indiana Secretary of Transportation and Infrastructure Matthew Ubelhor, who spoke at Thursday’s announcement on behalf of Gov. Mike Braun, said the extended suspension is expected to create a roughly $1.1 billion funding shortfall.
He said the administration intends to use available reserves to keep planned transportation work moving, including projects and maintenance scheduled for fiscal year 2027. Lawmakers will have to make that happen, though.
Ubelhor said no projects have been removed from the state’s construction schedule because of the funding uncertainty.
“We are not taking one project off,” Ubelhor said, emphasizing that Braun has insisted the state’s planned construction and maintenance work continue despite the revenue losses.
He also acknowledged that Indiana will need to identify a sustainable source of transportation revenue in the longer term, particularly as fuel efficiency improves and more electric vehicles enter the market.
“We need to look at that yesterday,” Ubelhor said of finding alternatives to the gasoline tax, which he indicated will become a less dependable source of revenue as vehicle technology changes.
The administration is examining possible alternatives, including tolling, although Ubelhor said questions remain about the potential approach and federal approvals.
He said the state is still awaiting a federal waiver decision related to a proposed I-70 reconstruction and rehabilitation program.
The report’s recommendations include expanding programs such as Community Crossings, providing local governments with additional revenue options and establishing more predictable long-term transportation funding.
Billions needed for drinking water, sewer systems
Some of Indiana’s largest infrastructure challenges are underground.
The report estimates that Indiana needs more than $8 billion in drinking water improvements and more than $10 billion for wastewater infrastructure.
Those needs include replacing aging water mains, removing lead service lines, addressing emerging contaminants such as PFAS, upgrading treatment plants and repairing deteriorating sewer systems.
Much of the funding for drinking water systems comes from customers’ utility bills, which must also cover daily operations. That leaves utilities facing difficult decisions about how to finance major improvements without making water service unaffordable.
Indiana’s wastewater systems face similar pressure.
Americans’ water bills are growing faster than groceries, overall inflation

More than 4 million Hoosiers rely on municipal wastewater systems, many of which are approaching the end of their intended service lives.
In 2024, communities sought more than $2 billion in wastewater funding, but only about $300 million was available statewide, according to the engineers’ assessment.
Stormwater infrastructure also faces growing challenges as heavy rainfall overwhelms drainage systems built decades ago.
The report estimates $531 million in stormwater infrastructure needs, with available funding covering only a small share.
Engineers recommended expanding state revolving loan programs, pursuing additional federal grants, encouraging partnerships among utilities and investing in flood-management improvements.
Matthew Hobbs, senior director of engineering for Indiana American Water, said Thursday that the utility plans to invest more than $1 billion in water and wastewater infrastructure across Indiana over the next five years.
The company serves approximately 1.5 million Hoosiers in more than 75 communities.
“Water infrastructure is fundamental to public health, fire protection, economic development and quality of life,” Hobbs said. “Maintaining that infrastructure requires consistent, long-term investment — not simply responding when something breaks.”
Hobbs pointed to a new $60 million water treatment plant in Seymour, expected to enter service this month, as an example of the investments underway.
He emphasized that replacing aging infrastructure before it fails can help prevent emergencies and reduce long-term costs.
“Proactive investment is also more efficient than waiting for infrastructure [to] fail,” Hobbs said, adding that replacing aging equipment and pipelines before emergencies occur can reduce service disruptions and costly repairs.
But he also said affordability must remain central to decisions about future upgrades.
“Infrastructure investments and affordability cannot be viewed as competing priorities,” Hobbs said. “We have to do both.”
Data centers add pressure to Indiana’s electric grid
Indiana’s energy infrastructure earned a D. Engineers noted increased electricity demand rises, aging coal-fired power plants near retirement and higher utility bills for Hoosiers. They warned that the state’s power grid will need significant upgrades to keep pace with growing demand while maintaining reliable service.
One of the biggest concerns is the growth of data centers.
The report projects that data centers could account for approximately 41% of Indiana’s electricity consumption by 2030, dramatically increasing demand on a grid already facing major changes.
At the same time, coal-fired power plants are approaching retirement, requiring utilities to replace generation capacity while maintaining reliable service.
The engineers also pointed to growing electricity costs for households.
Tradup said the projected growth of data centers is a major driver of future electricity demand, alongside the retirement of existing power plants and rising costs for customers.
Residential energy costs increased by more than $28 per month between 2024 and 2025, according to the report, prompting an investigation by the Indiana Utility Regulatory Commission.
Severe storms present additional risks to transmission and distribution systems, potentially leaving homes and businesses without power.
Engineers recommended investing in transmission infrastructure, modernizing the electric grid, expanding energy storage and diversifying power generation sources.
Jessica Eichhorst, with ASCE Indiana, said growing demand from data centers, industrial development and electrification will require investments in transmission infrastructure and grid modernization.
She also emphasized the need to diversify electricity generation and improve the system’s ability to withstand disruptions.
The report further outlined workforce shortages as a concern across infrastructure sectors, with retirements, competition for skilled workers and limited training pipelines making it harder to maintain and operate increasingly complex systems.
Aging dams raise safety concerns
Indiana’s dams were another area of concern, earning a D.
The state has 1,641 regulated dams, nearly two-thirds of which are privately owned.

Of those, 278 are classified as high-hazard dams, meaning their failure could result in loss of life or significant property damage. The designation reflects the potential consequences of a failure, not necessarily a dam’s current condition.
Only 55% of Indiana’s high-hazard dams have emergency action plans, compared with a national rate of 83%, according to the report.
State-owned dams also have a maintenance backlog exceeding $80 million.
The engineers warned that many dams are approaching or have exceeded their original design lives, while private owners often lack access to financial assistance for expensive repairs.
Indiana does not have a dedicated loan or grant program to help rehabilitate privately owned dams, according to the assessment.
The report recommends expanding rehabilitation funding, increasing inspections and prioritizing structures that present the greatest potential risks to public safety.
Engineers call for long-term planning
Beyond individual infrastructure categories, the report emphasizes that Indiana’s challenges can’t be addressed just with short-term spending.
Its six broad recommendations include:

more dedicated local transportation funding;
faster modernization of water and wastewater systems;
stronger flood protection;
electric grid improvements;
dam rehabilitation; and
more coordinated infrastructure planning.

The engineers also urged policymakers to account for changing weather patterns and future demand when designing projects, rather than relying on conditions that existed when much of the state’s infrastructure was originally built.
Even so, the funding question extends beyond Indiana.
The federal Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act provided billions of dollars for projects across the state, but its authorization expired Sept. 30. Congress has not yet approved a comparable long-term replacement.
ASCE representatives said Thursday that they plan to take the report’s findings to Washington in March 2027 as federal lawmakers consider future infrastructure legislation.
Jennifer Sharkey, an Indiana ASCE leader and report card co-chair, said the assessment is intended to give policymakers a clearer picture of where investments have worked and where additional attention is needed. She urged state leaders to consider the findings when making decisions about future infrastructure spending, particularly as communities confront growth and increasingly severe weather.
“The future of our state relies on our ability to maintain and improve upon the current conditions of our infrastructure, while also maintaining focus on that growth for our state and for our communities,” Sharkey said. “These systems, they drive economic growth, they create jobs, they improve our public health, and they also protect us from environmental threats.”

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Offshore wind offered a ‘limitless’ future for CT. Trump scuttled the plan
description: New London was poised to become a regional hub for offshore wind development. The Trump administration's war on offshore wind changed things.
text:
This article was produced in collaboration with ProPublica’s Sustainability Desk, a project of the Local Reporting Network. The Connecticut Mirror, The New Bedford Light and Ocean State Media worked together to understand how the Trump administration’s war on offshore wind has hurt workers and communities across New England.From The New Bedford Light: Fishermen’s offshore wind work drying upFrom Ocean State Media: Offshore wind saved a struggling New Bedford union. Now its future is uncertainAnd in ProPublica: Trump’s war on offshore wind has hurt thousands of workers
On a tour a few years ago through the North Sea coast of the United Kingdom, New London Mayor Michael Passero caught a glimpse of what a resurgence of manufacturing might look like back home in Connecticut.
At a factory in Hartlepool, he watched workers assemble underwater cables that deliver power from the country’s numerous offshore wind farms to shore. To the south, he visited a workforce development center run by the shipping giant Maersk, where workers received specialized training to work at sea on gigantic turbines.
There was even a lab developing submersible robots capable of completing jobs in rough seas that are too dangerous for humans, Passero recalled. 
In the port of Blythe — which, like New London, had seen its maritime trades wither due to decades of deindustrialization — the harbor had been repurposed as a staging area for the UK’s surging offshore wind industry, one of the world’s largest.
“I think the future just looked limitless,” Passero said. “You could almost look to Europe and really see the future here, see everything that can be done. And we have some of the best wind in the world right off the Northeast here, so the industry really looked good there for a while.
“Until Donald Trump got reelected,” he said.

New London Mayor Michael Passero poses for a portrait along New London Waterfront Park with New London State Pier in the background on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026.  New York’s Sunrise Wind, an Ørsted project, is currently being staged at the pier but beyond that there are no projects planned. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

Before last year’s efforts by the Trump administration to grind America’s offshore wind industry to a halt, New London was poised to become a regional hub for developers looking to take advantage of the Atlantic’s abundant winds.
The state of Connecticut, through the use of public borrowing, invested more than $211 million to expand a state-owned pier in the city to handle the loading and offloading of parts onto specialized installation vessels. The Danish energy developer Ørsted, partnering with local utility company Eversource, signed on to launch its first three U.S. offshore wind projects from New London, kicking in another $100 million toward the redevelopment of the State Pier.
In addition to employing thousands of workers during construction, the wind projects were billed as a way to wean the region off its historic dependence on oil and natural gas to meet its growing energy needs.
Revolution Wind, the second of the three Ørsted projects launched from New London, is contracted to sell 704 megawatts of electricity — enough to power 350,000 homes — to customers in Connecticut and Rhode Island. The other two projects, South Fork and Sunrise Wind, are connected to New York through underwater cables.
As those connections get up and running, much of the work will dry up. If the Trump administration succeeds in its ongoing efforts to end future offshore wind development in the United States — which by recent accounts is likely — it will eliminate thousands of current and future jobs on America’s waterfronts from Massachusetts to Virginia. Many of these jobs are located in struggling seaports like New Bedford, Mass., and New London, Conn., where states invested hundreds of millions of dollars in port infrastructure and workforce training to court giant offshore wind companies.
The resulting uncertainty has led international wind developers to redirect investment towards other countries or even sell back their leases. Workers who have undergone specialized training or pinned their futures on the promise of steady offshore wind construction could find themselves unable to continue working in the industry. Meanwhile, the states that invested heavily in offshore wind infrastructure are at risk of seeing their purpose-built piers sitting empty, as is the case in New Bedford. 
Today, the State Pier in New London remains a bustling hive of activity. Turbine blades that stretch the length of a football field are stacked on the heavy-lift platform, ready to be transported out to sea on the specialized installation vessel Wind Scylla — named for one of the mythic sea monsters from Homer’s “Odyssey.”
That initial run of offshore wind projects is only scheduled to last through 2027. Officials are searching for a future tenant that can take over Ørsted’s position at the pier, but no contracts have been announced.
Just a few years ago, however, the investment in wind was touted by local leaders as a long-term vision for New London’s waterfront. 
“This is going to be a major facility for decades and decades to come,” Connecticut Gov. Ned Lamont triumphantly declared during a visit to the then-active construction site in 2022.

Elements of wind turbine towers for offshore wind projects are staged at New London State Pier is seen on Friday, Sept. 18, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

A new purpose for the port
New London is an old port city of irregular streets and 19th-Century buildings squeezed into a 10-square-mile strip of land where the Thames River meets Long Island Sound. Like New Bedford, the city was once home to a large whaling fleet but struggled to compete with larger trading ports like New York and Boston after that industry declined.
Across the river, in Groton, the waterfront is dominated by the Navy’s primary East Coast submarine base and General Dynamics Electric Boat’s sprawling shipyard.
But prior to the launch of the offshore wind industry, New London’s maritime trade had mostly dwindled to a few ferries shuttling passengers to and from Long Island alongside the underutilized State Pier, which had been used to import wood pulp, road salt and other products.
All that seemed destined to change by the time Passero joined a delegation of state and local officials on a tour of the U.K.’s offshore wind industry in 2024.
Between community host agreements, docking fees and crews coming ashore to spend money in the bars and restaurants along Bank Street, Passero said he estimated the economic benefit would amount to around $1 million a year for the city — a modest sum that would nonetheless provide a boost to Passero’s efforts to reinvigorate the city’s struggling downtown. 
“You’re not going to fit much in New London, but we got the pier,” Passero said.
Passero was thinking beyond the city’s borders, too. North of New London, the Thames River once powered textile mills that served as one of the birthplaces of the Industrial Revolution.
“We’d get our share of what was appropriate to put in New London, but then the whole area — think of this whole river, all the empty factories along the river — I had visions of these factories being repurposed, you know to be able to, provide some of the materials and equipment that’s needed for this industry,” he said.
Before entering politics, Passero worked as a union laborer on several area projects, including the redevelopment of an old railroad bridge and erecting a new laboratory building at Pfizer’s research campus across the harbor in Groton. 
“It was good money,” he said. “My BA wasn’t going to get me anything.”
Passero’s son, Thomas Passero, followed his father into the building trades and wound up working on both the redevelopment of the State Pier and the subsequent staging of offshore wind projects through Laborers Local 547. 
With the exception of a short diversion to work on an unrelated highway project, the younger Passero said the activity at the State Pier has provided him with a steady stream of income for more than five years, a rarity in the industry. Even when the Trump administration ordered its halt to the work taking place miles offshore, he said workers at the pier never experienced even a single-day layoff. 
“As a New London man, I’ve never seen it so busy,” the younger Passero said. “And it’s not just the pier, you go down to Ocean Beach and see the cargo ships — cargo ships! It’s pretty cool.” 

Staging for Sunrise Wind, an Ørsted project, is seen at New London State Pier on Friday, Sept. 25, 2026. Credit: Sarah Gordon / CT Mirror

30 gigawatts by 2030
By all accounts, the revitalization Mayor Passero imagined on that trip to the U.K. had hit a few bumps before Trump took office the following January.
Ørsted, the developer behind the three New London-based projects, pulled out of two similar projects off the coast of New Jersey in 2023, citing rising interest rates and supply chain issues that plagued much of the industry during the COVID-19 pandemic. Elsewhere cost overruns, project delays and technical challenges threatened to slow the progress toward reaching President Joe Biden’s goal of deploying 30 gigawatts of offshore wind power by 2030.
Still, work was moving forward on projects off the coast of Massachusetts, Rhode Island, New York and Virginia.
The first of those projects, Ørsted’s South Fork Wind, began sending power to the electric grid in 2023. It was followed over the last year by Revolution Wind, Dominion’s Coastal Virginia Offshore Wind and Avangrid’s Vineyard Wind. The final two projects under construction, Ørsted’s Sunrise Wind and Equinor’s Empire Wind, are scheduled to reach commercial operation sometime next year.
Trump’s unsuccessful efforts to halt each of those projects have scuttled the long-term outlook for U.S. offshore wind. The completed projects are slated to supply a total of 6 gigawatts to the grid by the end of next year, far from the 30-gigawatt goal established by Trump’s predecessor.

Instead of planning new projects in American waters once its current work in New London is complete, Ørsted announced last year that it would instead shift its focus to “core markets” in Europe and Asia. During an earnings call with the investors in February, Ørsted chief executive Rasmus Errboe delivered a blunt assessment of his company’s future in the U.S.
“We have no expectations whatsoever to increase our exposure to offshore wind in the U.S.,” he said.

Worker Thomas Passero speaks to reporters at the Connecticut State Pier in New London on Aug. 25, 2025. Credit: Dana Edwards / CT Mirror

Standing on the sidelines
Thomas Passero, the mayor’s son who works at the pier, said he wasn’t too anxious about the future of offshore wind construction. “Being in the trade unions… it’s kind of beaten into us that we’re gonna just build ourselves out of a job and go to another one anyway,” Passero said. “So how permanent is anything, you know?”
Still, he said it was hard to find a job site like the one he had — with consistent hours, years of work, and all only a 10 minute drive from his home and two young children. 
“I hope it stays busy forever. I hope they keep building windmills or something that we can participate in here.” 
Speaking at Yale University in May, Eversource’s president of transmission Bill Quinlan said the industry had been severely weakened by macroeconomic forces and “nonconstructive federal policy.” (Eversource exited the offshore wind industry in 2024, selling its stake in two projects for $745 million.)
While the current slate of projects is likely to be completed, he said, it would could some time before any new projects are announced. 
“I would set that aside for the time being, I don’t see [wind] making a significant comeback in the near term in this country,” Quinlan said. 
“I think developers — the international developers who have the expertise — are probably going to stand on the sidelines for a period of time here in the U.S.”

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: SEIU Wisconsin calls for bill to restore UW Health union rights
description: After a seven-year campaign to reinstate union rights at UW Health hospitals in Madison, organizers are looking to the incoming Democratic governor and majority in the Legislature to help finish the job. Service Employees International Union’s Wisconsin branch mobilized support across the state for winning candidates — from Gov.-elect David Crowley on down t[...]
text:
Madison residents posted yard signs in 2022 in support of a campaign by nurses at UW Health seeking union representation. SEIU Wisconsin and the union's UW Health members are urging Democrats who will control the Legislature starting in January to enact a law restoring their union rights. (Photo by Erik Gunn/Wisconsin Examiner)After a seven-year campaign to reinstate union rights at UW Health hospitals in Madison, organizers are looking to the incoming Democratic governor and majority in the Legislature to help finish the job.
Service Employees International Union’s Wisconsin branch mobilized support across the state for winning candidates — from Gov.-elect David Crowley on down to incoming Assembly members who flipped seats on Nov. 3 and put the Democrats in charge of both houses in the Legislature.
In an announcement issued Thursday, SEIU Wisconsin members and leaders spelled out their next goal: passing legislation to restore collective bargaining rights at the UW Hospital and Clinics Authority — the corporate parent of UW Health hospitals and clinics.
“This moment represents the beginning of a new era,” Colin Gillis, SEIU Wisconsin vice president for nursing and a nurse at UW Health for nine years, told the Wisconsin Examiner.
“I’m really excited to have the opportunity, at long last after years of organizing and campaigning — knocking doors, doing phone banking, organizing with my co-workers — to have the opportunity to have a Democratic trifecta that can restore our collective bargaining rights,” Gillis said, “so that we can advocate for our patients and our community and ensure that Wisconsin has the healthcare system it deserves.”
The UW Health hospital system’s employees are not classified as state employees. Nevertheless, former Gov. Scott Walker’s 2011 Act 10 — which stripped collective bargaining rights from most public employees in Wisconsin — also eliminated state laws that had guaranteed union rights for UW Hospital & Clinics Authority employees since 1996.
SEIU Wisconsin is calling for the new Democratic majority in the Legislature to reintroduce and pass a bill that would “restore full collective bargaining rights for thousands of nurses and over 25,000 total UW Health employees,” the SEIU Wisconsin announcement Thursday said.
An email inquiry to UW Health about the SEIU announcement and the prospect of such a law did not get a response Thursday.
Nurse cites assurances from Dem leaders
Legislation to restore UW Health employees’ union rights was last introduced in February, toward the end of the current legislative session. The bills, AB 999 and SB 965, were never taken up. The SEIU announcement Thursday identified them as the union’s objective.
Gillis said that at campaign events before the Nov. 3 election, he and other SEIU members spoke with the Legislature’s Democratic leaders, Sen. Dianne Hesselbein and state Rep. Greta Neubauer, along with David Crowley, now the governor-elect.
“And they gave me and my coworkers, assurance, directly to our faces, verbally, that this would be a top priority,” Gillis said. He said he hasn’t yet heard about a timeline, however.
Rep. Lisa Subeck (D-Madison), who has been the lead Assembly author on the previous bills, said Thursday the timeline for action and the exact form it might take still has to be determined.
“I’m definitely still committed to restoring collective bargaining rights for our UW Health nursing staff and others,” said Subeck. “I think there is broad support among Democrats for restoring collective bargaining rights broadly.”
Subeck, who has been elected Speaker Pro Tempore in the next legislative session, added that it is “a little too soon to say exactly how these bills may be introduced and exactly what that timing would be.”
She also said that it “remains to be determined” whether simply repealing Act 10 — as Democratic leaders have said they intend to do — would be sufficient for restoring the UW Health workers’ union rights.
“It’s unfortunate that this hasn’t happened already,” Subeck said. “We all know that when the people who care for us, and in this case that’s our nurses at UW, have a voice in their workplace and can have a role in working conditions, it is good for patient care.”
Gillis said that he and other union members believe the legislation introduced in February would offer stronger protections for the rights of UW Health employees to union representation than simply repealing Act 10.
AB 999/SB 965 include provisions that would allow a majority of employees to win union recognition by signing a petition rather than through an election — the only mechanism for unionizing under current state law, according to the Legislative Reference Bureau analysis of the bill.
The measure, if enacted, also would require UW Health to allow unions that represent current employees to provide information at new employees’ orientation sessions, and to allow them to use the work email system to discuss workplace issues, administer union contracts and organize employees.
After 2019 launch, union drive escalates
After Act 10 ended the UW hospital system’s collective bargaining guarantees, the last contracts expired in 2014. Five years later, in 2019, UW Health nurses announced they were joining SEIU Wisconsin.
Initially they sought voluntary talks on working conditions with the hospital system’s management. UW Health rejected their demand.
A series of legal memos followed arguing that, despite Act 10, there was a stronger case in existing Wisconsin laws to support union rights for UW Health employees.
Encouraged by those arguments, nurses sought union recognition from the hospital system’s management and were rebuffed. On the verge of a threatened three-day strike in September 2022, Gov. Tony Evers brokered a deal between UW Health and nurses affiliated with SEIU Wisconsin.
That agreement set in motion a court case that concluded with a unanimous 2025 decision in which the Wisconsin Supreme Court affirmed that because of Act 10, state law does not require the hospital system to recognize or bargain with unions representing its employees.
The 2022 agreement also included a provision for voluntary meetings between union representatives and UW Health management. Gillis, who has participated in those meetings, said they have continued since then.
“Every other month we sit down for a process, a two-hour meeting called ‘meet and discuss,’” Gillis said. “We have enjoyed a productive and collaborative relationship with our counterparts across the table in that process, but that process is no substitute for negotiation at the bargaining table.”
That’s because it doesn’t lead to a formal contract, he said.
“Nurses know that a contract is, collective bargaining is, the most powerful tool they have to advocate for their patients and their co-workers and their communities,” Gillis said.

name: Maine Morning Star
title: How Maine’s two-decade old school consolidation effort continues to unravel
description: Next year, the town of Kingfield will leave MSAD 58 to form its own school district. The move will allow the western Maine community of roughly 1,000 people to keep its elementary school building and operate its own district, which will serve about 80 students. Kingfield was the only one of more than a dozen […]
text:
A classroom at Woodrow Wilson Elementary School in South Salt Lake City, Utah, on March 12, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps/Utah News Dispatch)Next year, the town of Kingfield will leave MSAD 58 to form its own school district. The move will allow the western Maine community of roughly 1,000 people to keep its elementary school building and operate its own district, which will serve about 80 students.
Kingfield was the only one of more than a dozen Maine towns to successfully withdraw from or reorganize its school district in the Nov. 3 election. At least 12 other communities considered similar changes, driven by concerns that their schools could close, that their local tax dollars were being spent on improvements at other schools in their district, or that they lacked control over school governance.
Kingfield voters overwhelmingly supported the ballot measure to withdraw from the district, with  over 70% voting in favor.
The trend highlights a broader trade-off facing small towns: leaving larger districts can give communities more control over their schools, but smaller districts may struggle to provide the specialized services and academic support available in larger ones. 
It is the latest chapter in a decades-long debate about how to govern rural school districts, since former Gov. John Baldacci signed sweeping school consolidation legislation in 2007, penalizing those that chose to go their own way. 
In a state facing enrollment declines and aging school buildings with insufficient state funding available for improvements, that challenge is only expected to get worse.
“A lot of communities place a really big value on their schools, which is wonderful because schools, in my opinion, are the backbone of public education,” said Laura Columbia, superintendent of MSAD 58.
“But I think what’s really important for people to think about is: At what cost? At what point are we keeping buildings at the expense of not providing services to students?”
The challenges for smaller districts extend beyond student services to the cost of maintaining a certain level of funding, said Janet Fairman, a University of Maine professor and co-director of the Maine Education Policy Research Institute.
“The state’s funding formula gives (small districts) enough money based on a certain staff-to-student ratio, and when these communities choose to be smaller than that, they have to pay the difference,” she said. “That means they have to tax themselves more or they have to somehow come up with more revenue to cover the difference in cost.”
When a town decides to separate, Columbia explained that it can also strain the existing school district.
Most rural districts in Maine are already facing a yearslong staffing shortage, and starting next year, MSAD 58 will have to compete with the newly formed Kingfield district for the few special education teachers, bus drivers and occupational therapists in the area. Under the agreement, Kingfield will still send its students to the MSAD 58 high school, so Columbia expects staffing challenges to be most acute at the elementary level.

“People really like to have local schools, I think that’s kind of aligned with a lot of Mainers’ philosophy on local control,” she said. “But we have limited resources to start with in many of our rural schools, and so it can often stretch those resources even further when we have smaller districts in the same area.”
Financial repercussions
School districts are financially incentivized to leave their larger consolidated school units, according to Amy Johnson, a professor at the University of Southern Maine and co-director of MEPRI along with Fairman. 
Most Maine districts, 109, are typical school administrative units, with more than one school. But there are also 81 districts that have only one school. This typically means these districts operate their own schools for younger grades and use a tuition model, under which the Maine Department of Education mandates towns pay tuition for their residents to go to another town’s public school, or an approved private school. 
One-school districts enroll anywhere between 2 and 600 students, with the median student population being 129, according to MEPRI data.
That’s similar to the plan for Kingfield, where the new school will enroll about 80 students.
But there are also 59 school units with no schools. That means a town withdraws from a school unit and does not form its own, instead choosing to send all of its students to other districts under the tuition model.
“What they gain from that is they only have to pay for the costs for their students, and they only have a handful of students,” Johnson said.
These school districts have the lowest per pupil spending, according to MEPRI data. 
A typical school unit spends about $18,000 per student, not including transportation or career and technical education. Costs jump up for a one-school district to about $21,000, because, as Johnson explained, “you’re not sharing any costs, you’re trying to be an entire school district with one school plus some tuition students.”
But zero-school districts spend the least, about $15,000 per student, which is the higher end of the state average for tuition. But even at that level, that tuition often does not cover the cost of special education or other services that their students may need, leaving the district accepting them to cover those costs.
“There is this real financial benefit to pulling out of a school unit and becoming your own district, because then you can pay less towards the cost of education because you have fewer kids,” Johnson said. “Because all they’re doing is taking their tax dollars and sending their kids elsewhere.” 



Quotation







“There is this real financial benefit to pulling out of a school unit and becoming your own district, because then you can pay less towards the cost of education because you have fewer kids. Because all they're doing is taking their tax dollars and sending their kids elsewhere.


– Amy Johnson, professor at the University of Southern Maine and co-director of Maine Education Policy Research Institute


Similarly, Kingfield’s withdrawal from MSAD 58 will create a financial burden for the district, Columbia said. 
Not only will it reduce per-pupil state funding, but also because Kingfield’s local contribution to the district was relatively large because of the town’s high property values. 
And because the roughly 60 students being pulled from the district are spread across multiple grades, Columbia said it won’t result in any reduction in staffing or classroom space, and their associated costs.
Towns attempting joint withdrawal 
Three towns about an hour south of Kingfield also attempted to leave their consolidated district, RSU 10, to form their own smaller school unit. 
Buckfield, Hartford and Sumner proposed forming their own district because RSU 10’s central office is about a 40-minute drive away. Buckfield voters approved the change, but since the other two towns did not, all three will stay with the district. 
This is not the first withdrawal from that regional district. In 2017, four towns — Canton, Carthage, Dixfield and Peru — withdrew from the district to form their own. 
In the case of the Buckfield-area towns, they did not want to spend tax dollars on improvements within the district that their students would not benefit from, said RSU 10 Superintendent Matt Gilbert. 
“They’re the smaller communities within our district, and they also have the smallest tax base,” Gilbert added. “They were focusing on the desire for control of their tax dollars to be closer to home.”
If the three additional towns had withdrawn and formed their own school district, Gilbert said they would have had about 500 students, which may have been a challenge, “and they would have lost all the benefits that they get from being part of a larger district and the economy of scale that comes with that, like central office services and supports.”
In the aftermath of last week’s election, the withdrawal committee discussed an alternative budgeting model with Gilbert, under which they would have more autonomy over improvements to schools in their communities, but share administrative costs with the larger district. 
That means if they want to build a track or add a foreign language program to a school in their community, they would not rely on approval from the entire district school board. 
“We were all forced into this consolidation because of the threat of being penalized financially,” Gilbert said.

According to Johnson from MEPRI, school consolidation is a reality many towns have to face due to declining enrollments, due to aging populations and people moving away from rural areas. 
Baldacci attempted to address this challenge by mandating that roughly 300 districts be consolidated to 80. Even though that effort was not completely successful, as there are now more than 200 districts, Johnson said it’s not realistic to expect all towns to be able to independently meet their students’ needs.
“In small communities, you don’t start with an economy of scale. If there’s only one school to begin with, it’s much harder to close because there would be nothing left,” Johnson said. “But it’s more expensive to operate that way, and it’s less efficient.”
Consolidation vs. local control
Mount Desert Island-area schools still operate under an alternative organizational structure or AOS. That model allows each of the 10 schools to pass their own budgets but share a superintendent. 
The AOS model was offered as an alternative to Baldacci’s consolidation mandate, but there are currently only eight AOSs left in Maine, according to the Maine School Management Association. 
Several towns and islands around Mount Desert Island considered consolidating into a regional school unit, but many communities last week rejected the plan.
Superintendent Michael Zboray said many communities were reluctant to give up control over their community schools. 
“I tried to argue that all the same people that are caring for your school now will continue to be the people caring for your school, you’ll just have a larger pool of money to help in that care if something catastrophic happened to your building,” Zboray said, “rather than having to rely on the tax base just within your town.” 
Zboray said at least some communities on the island as well as neighboring Tremont agree they will eventually need a consolidated school unit because of declining class sizes and lower enrollment in all schools except Bar Harbor.
“It’s a very challenging situation, and we can apply that to police departments, fire departments and school departments,” said Maine School Management Association Executive Director Eric Waddell.
Waddell said he heard from people all over the state struggling to maintain local services amid affordability challenges and declining populations.
“I don’t know what the answer is other than to find alternate revenue sources for funding schools other than leaning so heavily on local property taxes.”
