name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Amid clash with U.S. attorney, Sen. Blumenthal says he won’t be ‘bullied’
description: A U.S. attorney warned the CT senator over his inquiry into the White House ballroom. Blumenthal pushed back that he won't be 'intimidated.'
text:
U.S. Sen. Richard Blumenthal engaged in a written back-and-forth this week with a U.S. attorney over the role of congressional oversight, setting up an early preview of when Democrats regain the majorities next year and prioritize investigations into the Trump administration.Blumenthal, in his capacity as the leading Democrat on the Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee’s Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has already launched a number of congressional inquiries from the minority, including one looking into private donors helping to finance the construction of a ballroom at the White House and whether they got preferential treatment from the administration.
He expects to return as chairman of that panel next year in the Senate.
But this week, the White House and the U.S. Department of Justice are giving a prelude into how they plan to respond — and fight back — against investigations and inquiries conducted by congressional Democrats over the final two years of Trump’s term.
“They’re clearly trying to intimidate us and deter and discourage our uncovering the truth about corruption,” Blumenthal said in an interview on Thursday. “It would be ludicrous if it were not so serious, and they’re misusing and weaponizing the prosecutorial power of the Department of Justice.”
Aaron Reitz, the U.S. attorney for the Southern District of Texas, posted a letter on social media Wednesday afternoon that was directed at the Connecticut Democrat and how he’s conducted an inquiry into the ballroom project. Reitz accused Blumenthal of threatening citizens who are donating and associating themselves with the president.
Reitz requested that Blumenthal preserve all documents, communications and “all potentially relevant evidence related to your efforts to suppress associational activities for philanthropic projects throughout the nation’s capital.”
“Failure to do so may result in sanctions, adverse-inference instructions, or other penalties, and may carry significant legal consequences,” Reitz wrote. “This demand applies to you, your staff, employees, agents, consultants, campaign personnel, and any other person acting on your behalf or in concert with you.”
Blumenthal said he sees that request as a threat of initiating an investigation, arguing it’s an attempt “to intimidate members of Congress for engaging in constitutionally protected activity.” He wrote back that Americans deserve to know who’s donating money to Trump’s projects “and whether lawsuits were dismissed, contracts were awarded, or regulations went unenforced in exchange for that money.”
In an interview with The Connecticut Mirror Thursday, Blumenthal said one of those donors, Nvidia, will be “front and center.” The tech company donated $25 million to the project, according to The Washington Post. 
Blumenthal said his subcommittee will investigate whether Nvidia “received more favorable treatment on its requests for chips” and whether Trump ignored intelligence about the company’s CEO Jensen Huang and his ties to a suspected Chinese spy, with whom he had an affair. Huang resigned on Thursday following those revelations.
The Connecticut senator sent his own letter responding to Reitz on Wednesday night with a request similar to the prosecutor’s: preserve all correspondence, documentation and “all communications with the White House or senior officials at the Department of Justice, related to the decision to draft and post your letter.”
“Not only are these appropriate subjects for congressional oversight, but such inquiries are among the constitutional duties that members of Congress must undertake to become informed about matters on which legislation may be necessary,” Blumenthal wrote.
When reached for comment about Blumenthal’s letter, Reitz referred to his response to the senator over the platform X.
“Received. Valid investigations must be conducted for a legitimate legislative purpose,” Reitz posted. “I believe that your threatenings may constitute the initiation of unconstitutional investigations conducted for reasons other than a legitimate legislative purpose. Semper Fidelis.”
The pushback to Blumenthal and his inquiries comes as the White House more broadly seeks to set the tone on how it plans to respond to investigations stemming from Congress.
White House counsel William Scharf sent a letter earlier this week to U.S. Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the incoming chairman of the House Oversight Committee, warning about what they see as the  limitations of congressional oversight and implications of criminality, according to The New York Times.
“Beyond being inconsistent with the clear, well-recognized constitutional limitations on your investigative functions, threats to executive branch officials designed to deter them from public service, or process designed merely to abuse or instill fear in the recipient may cross the line into blatant criminality,” Scharf wrote in the letter. “And issuing unlawful subpoenas with the intention of depriving citizens of their constitutional rights and privileges may warrant further investigation.”
Garcia had a similar response to Blumenthal and noted in a statement that the Constitution provides the legislative branch with the authority to conduct oversight.
Blumenthal has co-led a series of public forums with Garcia, seeking to cast a light on the practices and conduct of federal immigration agencies, such as U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, under the Trump administration. Blumenthal said he expects a “very cooperative working relationship” with Garcia from the majority next year.
As Democrats gear up for majorities in both the Senate and House in early January, Blumenthal won’t likely be the only member of Connecticut’s delegation who will conduct oversight from their committee perches.
Several Connecticut lawmakers are expected to claim the gavel of committees that have varying levels of jurisdiction and issue areas. But there’s a common theme: They plan to wield their influence around oversight of the administration.
U.S. Rep. Rosa DeLauro, D-3rd District, appears poised to return next year as the head of the House Appropriations Committee. U.S. Rep. Jim Himes, D-4th District, will likely be appointed as the chair of the House Intelligence Committee. And U.S. Rep. Joe Courtney, D-2nd District, is expected once again chair of the Armed Services’ Seapower and Projection Forces Subcommittee.
U.S. Rep. Jahana Hayes, D-5th District, is also running in a contested race to become chair of the House Committee on Education and the Workforce.
The House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence has oversight over U.S. intelligence agencies as well as some issues concerning the Pentagon and other government agencies. As a potential chairman, Himes has previewed oversight as a main objective.
Himes has already issued warnings to defense companies about cooperating with congressional oversight, specifically on a potential investigation into corporate donations for the construction of the White House ballroom.
DeLauro has said she envisions handling some oversight “in my lane” by taking a look at where federal dollars are flowing and whether some money “has been transferred illegally.”
Courtney also see opportunities for oversight, whether that’s on the Air Force One plane gifted by Qatar or the White House’s battleship proposal. He believes oversight over the war in Iran and U.S. Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth’s tenure will be “front and center” for the full House Armed Services Committee. (House Republicans blocked an effort on Tuesday to impeach Hegseth over his handling of the war.)
Blumenthal said Thursday he and his colleagues will move forward with their investigations for the remaining weeks of the session and as they move into the majority in the 120th Congress.
“The whole purpose of this letter is simply to intimidate,” Blumenthal said. “I absolutely refuse to be bullied or threatened in this way. We’re going to continue our investigation undeterred.”

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Conservative group sues UNC-Chapel Hill over access to course materials
description: A conservative group is suing UNC-Chapel Hill, accusing the university of violating state public records law by failing to provide reading lists and other instructional materials for 29 courses. Defending Education filed the lawsuit this week in Orange County Superior Court. The group says the university failed to properly respond to two public records reque[...]
text:
UNC Chapel Hill. (Photo: Clayton Henkel/NCNewsline) A conservative group is suing UNC-Chapel Hill, accusing the university of violating state public records law by failing to provide reading lists and other instructional materials for 29 courses.
Defending Education filed the lawsuit this week in Orange County Superior Court. The group says the university failed to properly respond to two public records requests, submitted in October, seeking materials used in courses during the fall 2026 semester.
The courses span several departments, including African American studies, history, political science, sociology and women’s and gender studies. They include “Defining Blackness,” “Black Feminism,” “Feminism and Political Theory,” “Critical Food Studies,” and “Slavery and the University.”
Defending Education’s complaint does not explain why the group selected these 29 courses. NC Newsline has reached out to the group for an explanation.
The first request, submitted Oct. 16, sought materials for 19 courses. The second, submitted Oct. 23, sought materials for 10 additional courses.
UNC-Chapel Hill closed both requests without providing additional documents, according to the lawsuit. Instead, the university directed the organization to Simple Syllabus, an online platform where faculty members post course syllabi.
Defending Education argues that the platform does not include all the materials used in courses. The requests also sought reading assignments,  course plans, materials shared with students through email and documents posted on Canvas, the university’s learning management system.
The complaint says UNC’s policy requires faculty members to use Simple Syllabus, but limits the information they must include. For example, faculty members are directed to list course materials students are required to purchase, while other instructional materials can be shared through other means, including Canvas and email.
The organization says that the university failed to conduct a reasonable search for the requested records, including materials maintained by instructors and documents stored on university systems.
UNC system faculty condemn proposed policy disclosing course materials to public

UNC-Chapel Hill did not immediately respond to NC Newsline’s request for comment. 
Sarah Parshall Perry, vice president and senior legal fellow at Defending Education, said the university’s alleged refusal to provide the materials prevents taxpayers from understanding what public universities are teaching. 
“The University of North Carolina’s sleight-of-hand over production of its course materials is no excuse for shirking its obligations under the North Carolina Public Records Act.” Perry said in a statement. “Taxpayers in the state have every right to know what their money is funding at North Carolina’s institutions of higher education, and we look forward to the university finally complying with its statutory obligations.”
Defending Education is a national conservative education advocacy group founded in 2021. It says it works to promote transparency, free speech and parental rights in K-12 and higher education. 
This is the latest chapter in a broader effort by conservative groups to scrutinize teaching at universities in the state and across the country. Last year, The Oversight Project, a conservative group affiliated with the Heritage Foundation, requested course materials from 74 UNC-CH classes, seeking content related to diversity, race, gender. 
The university denied the request, citing faculty intellectual property rights.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Advocates renew push for Minnesota Equal Rights Amendment
description: Democratic lawmakers gathered with advocates for an Equal Rights Amendment at the Minnesota Capitol Thursday to launch their latest campaign to add to the state Constitution sweeping protections that prohibit discrimination based on race, national origin, disability, gender identity, sex and pregnancy — including one’s decision to become pregnant or terminat[...]
text:
Rep. Leigh Finke, DFL-St. Paul, spoke at a press conference surrounded by Equal Rights Amendment advocates at the Minnesota Capitol on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Michelle Griffith/Minnesota Reformer)Democratic lawmakers gathered with advocates for an Equal Rights Amendment at the Minnesota Capitol Thursday to launch their latest campaign to add to the state Constitution sweeping protections that prohibit discrimination based on race, national origin, disability, gender identity, sex and pregnancy — including one’s decision to become pregnant or terminate a pregnancy.
During the last Democratic-Farmer-Labor trifecta in 2024, the Minnesota Equal Rights Amendment nearly passed but stalled at the last minute because of disagreements among Democrats about the amendment’s language. Democrats will enter the 2027 legislative session with another trifecta — this time with greater margins — and ERA advocates are confident that they will be able to pass legislation next year to put the question before voters. 
“Equality shouldn’t depend on who holds office, who’s making those laws,” said Sen. Mary Kunesh, DFL-New Brighton, who is a chief author of the legislation. “It’s clear that those words must be enshrined in our Constitution, not just for today, but again for the future generation.”
If the Minnesota ERA passes the House and Senate, Minnesotans would be asked on the 2028 ballot to support or oppose the ERA. The measure would require a majority of total votes cast — not voting on it would be akin to a “no” vote.
Democratic lawmakers on Thursday said passing the ERA legislation is among Democrats’ top priorities in 2027 and anticipate early passage; the session begins Jan. 12.
Dozens of states have passed legislation to add gender, race and class protections to their constitutions, but Minnesota’s proposed amendment will be inclusive of more classes, such as gender identity and abortion rights. Minnesota’s ERA advocates say their ballot measure will be similar to New York’s, which went into effect last year.
Ballot measures do not require the governor’s signature, but Gov.-elect Amy Klobuchar has expressed openness to supporting the latest ERA effort.
Critics of Minnesota’s ERA proposal say that including gender identity and abortion rights protections in the state Constitution infringes on their religious freedom. The current ERA language does not include religion as a protected category — though religion is already protected in the Minnesota Constitution’s Bill of Rights.
The Minnesota Human Rights Act, which is in statute and not the Constitution, currently protects Minnesotans from discrimination — in employment, housing, public services, public accommodation and education — based on race, color, creed, religion, national origin, sex, gender identity, marital status, disability, sexual orientation and status with regard to public assistance.
Some critics also say the measure gives too much authority to the judicial branch, which will be responsible for remedying alleged violations of the ERA’s protections.
Minnesota’s ERA advocates say they are finalizing the language, but note it will largely match the language lawmakers considered and nearly passed in 2024.
“It is long past time for us to recognize the values represented in the Equal Rights Amendment and to put them into the Constitution,” said Rep. Leigh Finke, DFL-St. Paul, who is also a chief author of the legislation. “No matter who you are, where you come from, or why you are here, you deserve to be treated equally under the law. That is what we are fighting for.”

name: Delaware
title: Delaware home-care providers seek $26.6 million in rate increases
description: Providers and families say higher payments would help retain nurses and aides who support people receiving care at home DOVER, Del. — Delaware home-care providers are asking the state to increase reimbursement rates in the next budget, saying higher payments would help keep nurses and aides with the families who depend on them. The Delaware Association for H[...]
text:
Delaware Association for Home and Community Care’s proposal calls for a 25.5% increase in private-duty nursing rates and a 10% increase in personal care service rates. Association Executive Director Sue Getman estimated the respective costs at $7.3 million and $19.3 million.
Providers and families say higher payments would help retain nurses and aides who support people receiving care at home
DOVER, Del. — Delaware home-care providers are asking the state to increase reimbursement rates in the next budget, saying higher payments would help keep nurses and aides with the families who depend on them.
The Delaware Association for Home and Community Care estimates the requested increases would cost the state $26.6 million, according to WMDT’s report on testimony at the Nov. 10 public budget hearing at the Delaware Public Archives in Dover.
The proposal calls for a 25.5% increase in private-duty nursing rates and a 10% increase in personal care service rates. Association Executive Director Sue Getman estimated the respective costs at $7.3 million and $19.3 million, WMDT reported.
Those amounts are the association’s estimates, rather than figures confirmed by the state. www.wmdt.com
The appeal comes as the Department of Health and Social Services develops its fiscal 2028 spending request. For providers, the issue is retaining workers. For families, it is maintaining dependable care that allows loved ones to remain at home.
Families describe the stakes
Providers, nurses, parents and disability advocates testified about the importance of consistent care and the disruption families face when a nurse leaves, according to WMDT.
Heather Holveck, the grandmother and legal guardian of a child with disabilities, described the uncertainty that comes with possible staff turnover.
“Knowing that there is a potential that even our current nurses could leave is terrifying for him because then we’re starting over,” Holveck told WMDT. www.wmdt.com
The testimony highlighted how reimbursement decisions can affect daily life for people who rely on in-home support. Retaining familiar caregivers can help families preserve established routines and relationships.
Different services, different rate histories
The providers’ appeal also raises questions about how Delaware has adjusted payments for different types of home care.
State records, however, describe more recent increases for some services.
In February 2024 testimony to the Joint Finance Committee, the Division of Medicaid and Medical Assistance said it would implement personal care service increases retroactive to July 1, 2023. dhss.delaware.gov
That testimony does not establish whether the increases applied to every service or provider covered by the current request. The scope of the 18-year statement remains unconfirmed, and it cannot be applied broadly to all home-care payments based on the available records.
The association is seeking separate increases for private-duty nursing and personal care services, making the distinction between those payment categories important to evaluating the request.
State proposes additional funding
DHSS’ Nov. 10 budget presentation includes approximately $2.6 million for a first-phase home and community-based services rate increase among its discretionary requests for fiscal 2028.
The presentation does not explain how that proposal relates to the association’s request or which portions of the providers’ proposal it might address.
DHSS also identified improving services for people with complex needs and lowering health care costs among its priorities. budget.delaware.gov
The providers’ request will compete with other spending proposals as the governor and lawmakers develop the budget.
What happens next
The November public hearings help shape the governor’s recommended budget, which is released in January.
Joint Finance Committee hearings follow, with legislative budget work continuing through the spring and final budget bills considered in June. www.budget.delaware.gov
For families who testified, the request puts a personal question before budget writers: whether the payments supporting care at home are sufficient to keep the workers they rely on.

Request: A 25.5% increase for private-duty nursing and 10% for personal care, with an estimated $26.6 million state cost, according to the association’s figures reported by WMDT.
Budget documents: Delaware fiscal 2028 public hearing documents.
Follow legislative budget hearings: Joint Finance Committee hearing information.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: Tentative contract averts Brigham nurses’ strike at the last minute
authors: Sam Drysdale | State House News Service
description: The tentative agreement remains subject to ratification by nurses in the bargaining unit, and the MNA said the union's committee has recommended that Brigham nurses vote to ratify the contract.
text:
MORE THAN 4,000 NURSES at Brigham and Women’s Hospital reached a tentative contract agreement late Wednesday night, avoiding what could have been the largest open-ended nurses strike in Massachusetts history.
Nurses represented by the Massachusetts Nurses Association and hospital officials left negotiations Monday without a resolution, and ended up back at the table Wednesday to avert the strike at the last minute. The walkout was scheduled to start Thursday.
The tentative agreement remains subject to ratification by nurses in the bargaining unit, and the MNA said the union’s committee has recommended that Brigham nurses vote to ratify the contract.
“I’m incredibly proud of the Brigham nurses who stood strong to protect the world-class patient care we provide,” Kelly Morgan, BWH MNA Bargaining Committee chair and a labor and delivery nurse, said. “We secured this agreement with the help of countless community members, patients, unions and elected officials who supported us for many months. By standing together, we protected patients and the future of union nursing care at the Brigham.”
The hospital says the agreement “was reached within the financial limits of the hospital’s last, best and final offer presented on October 10.”
“We deeply value our Brigham nurses and believe this agreement recognizes their important contributions while supporting the long-term sustainability of our hospital and our ability to care for our patients and communities,” the hospital said in a statement.
The tentative agreement follows months of negotiations, including a July 8 one-day strike, after which the thousands of nurses who went on strike were locked out of the hospital for four additional days. The union voted September 24 to authorize an open-ended strike. They voted late last month to reject MGB’s “last, best, and final” contract offer.
Nurses will receive wage increases and lower health insurance costs under the tentative contract.
All nurses below the top step would receive a $1,000 bonus prorated based on their full-time-equivalent hours upon ratification, while new top steps with greater pay are added to the pay structure. Nurses also defeated a proposed health insurance premium split increase, the MNA said.
Nurses agreed to a compromise on 40-hour nurses on individual plans. Current nurses working 40 hours will retain premium-free coverage while newly hired 40-hour nurses will contribute 2.5 percent of the premium.
The new agreement includes contract language that the hospital does not intend to replace permanent Brigham nurses with temporary nurses, per the MNA.
The hospital’s dependence on temporary and floating nurses has been a central flashpoint in the labor dispute. Union nurses frequently raised concerns that temporary nurses — who are also paid higher wages — undermine permanent union jobs and are unfamiliar with patients and hospital systems.
Hospitals use temporary nurses primarily to quickly fill critical staffing gaps and maintain safe patient-to-nurse ratios when local hiring falls short.
MGB agreed in the tentative contract to post 20 new 36-hour float pool nurse positions to help limit the reliance on temporary nurses. The hospital will track floating into and out of each unit and the use of temporary nurses, the MNA said. It will also provide the union with data that will be reviewed by a new joint Staffing and Resources Committee that will look for ways to reduce floating and the use of temporary staff.
There are other provisions in the contract to restrict reliance on temporary staffing, such as requiring the hospital to provide the MNA with a rationale whenever more than 15 percent of the full-time-equivalent positions in any hospital unit are covered by non-permanent nurses.
It also builds in more protection for nurses responsible for coordinating care at greater capacity, and reduces the acute patient assignment workload for nurses in charge or overseeing others. Other benefits include adding grandchildren to bereavement leave, adding paid time for workplace-related court appearances, and adding language that all nurses can attend conferences.
Gov. Maura Healey released a statement Thursday morning saying she was pleased the two sides reached a tentative agreement and avoided a strike. Healey and Boston Mayor Michelle Wu made appearances at Monday’s negotiating session.
“I appreciated the opportunity to meet with both sides and urge them to stay at the table and continue working in good faith toward a resolution,” Healey said Thursday. “I want to thank and congratulate everyone involved for their hard work, commitment and willingness to reach an agreement. Our nurses are essential to our health care system, and this is an important step toward ensuring stability at the hospital and the continuity of care that patients depend on.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Barboursville School to reopen as a residential treatment facility for children, Morrisey announces
description: The former Barboursville School will reopen next year as a residential treatment facility, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday. The state has entered a five-year lease with Youth Health Associates to operate the school. The facility plans to start accepting kids in early 2027.
text:
Gov. Patrick Morrisey on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, announces that the Barboursville School, a residential treatment facility for children, will reopen next year. The school closed earlier this year. (West Virginia Office of Gov. Patrick Morrisey video screenshot)The former Barboursville School will reopen next year as a residential treatment facility, Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday. The state has entered a five-year lease with Youth Health Associates to operate the school. The facility plans to start accepting children in early 2027. 
“Bringing our children home has been one of my highest priorities since taking office,” Morrisey said in a news release. “For too long, our kids were sent hundreds or even thousands of miles away to receive the care they need. Reopening Barboursville is an important step toward changing that, and our goal is to replicate this approach across West Virginia so we can bring all our children home.”
The Cabell County facility closed earlier this year, decreasing the number of beds the state has available for children experiencing severe mental health crises. 
Youth Health Associates has hired a facility director and is recruiting additional staff, the governor’s office said. When it’s fully operational, the school will accommodate up to 36 children and employ 50 to 60 people. Many of the beds are projected to be filled by the end of March.
Morrisey said the Barboursville facility will be a model for similar facilities throughout the state, part of his A Home for Every Child initiative. Additional announcements are expected in the coming weeks and months, Morrisey’s office said. 
Foster care officials have said that West Virginia doesn’t have enough in-state treatment options for children in need of specialized mental health or behavioral care, leading the state to send hundreds of children out-of-state for help. It has also led to some children living in hotel rooms while in the state’s care.
As of early November, the number of West Virginia children receiving residential treatment outside the state was down from 400 earlier this year to 372 in early November, the governor’s office said.  
Morrisey also announced Thursday the state will end its longstanding practice of applying Social Security survivor benefits belonging to children in foster care toward the state’s foster care costs beginning Jan. 1, 2027. Instead, those funds will be preserved for the children who receive them to provide them a financial foundation as they transition into adulthood, the governor’s office said.
About 42 West Virginia children in foster care receive survivor benefits totaling about $402,700 annually.
“When a child loses a parent, the benefits they receive should help provide a foundation for their future,” Morrisey said in the news release. “We’re ending a longstanding practice and making sure those funds remain available to the children who need them. It’s another important step toward giving West Virginia’s children the support and opportunities they deserve.”

name: Rhode Island Current
title: Ahead of Johnston exodus, Polisena says FM to lay off local workers
description: FM is laying off an unknown number of employees in conjunction with plans to relocate its global headquarters from Johnston to Providence, Johnston Mayor Joe Polisena Jr. said on Thursday. Polisena told Rhode Island Current in a phone interview that he met with an FM employee earlier in the day, who said she and at […]
text:
FM is leaving its 93-acre corporate campus on Central Avenue in Johnston, for downtown Providence amid a report the company has already given some workers layoff notices. (Photo by Michael Salerno/Rhode Island Current)FM is laying off an unknown number of employees in conjunction with plans to relocate its global headquarters from Johnston to Providence, Johnston Mayor Joe Polisena Jr. said on Thursday.
Polisena told Rhode Island Current in a phone interview that he met with an FM employee earlier in the day, who said she and at least a handful of other workers for the insurance giant had received layoff notices. The employee was not immediately available for comment.
A spokesperson for FM, formerly known as FM Global, acknowledged but did not immediately respond to requests for confirmation and details on layoffs.
FM revealed on Tuesday that it will be moving from Johnston to the IGT office tower in downtown Providence. At the time it bought the 10-story glass and metal building for $69 million in February, FM executives said it was part of a planned expansion, with no implications for its existing, 93-acre corporate offices in Johnston.
On Tuesday, the company confirmed it will abandon its Johnson campus, moving its 1,500-person local workforce in a portion of the Providence office building on Memorial Boulevard. The announcement did not say when the relocation would happen, or how it would affect employment.
Federal law requires employers with more than 100 full-time employees to give state and local officials at least 60 days notice before mass layoffs or facility closings. A spokesperson for the Rhode Island Department of Labor and Training did not immediately respond to requests regarding any notices submitted by FM.
Polisena said Thursday he has not received any layoff notices.
“This explains why they have been so quiet about it,” Polisena said of the layoffs.
Having learned of the company move when he was contacted by Rhode Island Current on Tuesday, Polisena blasted the company for what he called a “corporate sneak attack.” 
He also alleged that when his office called FM Thursday morning, following his conversation with the employee who received a layoff notice, the person who answered the phone hung up on his assistant.
Polisena was most concerned about the financial implications for the town, which relies on property and tangible tax revenue from the company’s Central Avenue headquarters. The tangible tax, which reflects office equipment, technology, furniture and other physical assets within the office space, amounts to $1.4 million per year, Polisena said.
Combined with a $1.5 million property tax bill in 2025, FM contributes nearly $3 million in annual tax revenue to Johnston, representing roughly 2% of its $144 million budget.
However, FM has challenged the tax bill based on the 2025 property revaluation, alleging the $53.4 million assessed value exceeds the “full and fair cash value” of its property and that the assessment method was “arbitrary and capricious,” according to the Providence County Superior Court complaint filed in April. The town tax board already rejected FM’s appeal, according to the complaint. The town denied the claims in a response to the Superior Court suit filed in May.
The case remains open, according to the public docket.
In 2025, the Rhode Island General Assembly agreed to rewrite a longstanding state law at FM’s request. Former House Speaker K. Joseph Shekarchi later revealed the global insurance giant had contemplated leaving Johnston without the law change, which lifted the cap on insurance company investments in nontraditional, long-term assets. 
House Speaker Christopher Blazejewski and Senate President Valarie Lawson did not immediately respond to requests for comment on the layoffs Thursday.
Gov.-elect Helena Buonanno Foulkes, who has centered her campaign on economic growth and jobs, also did not immediately respond to requests for comment. Polisena is part of her 23-person transition team.
FM opened its current headquarters in September 2009, spending $154 million to build the corporate offices on land it already owned, according to news reports. 
The new headquarters in downtown Providence also houses the state’s lottery contractor — formerly known as IGT — along with Fidelity Investments Inc., and the Capital Grille.
FM previously said the move will not affect its research campus in Glocester. 
This story will be updated.

title: Advance Notice for Thursday, Nov. 12
description: Michigan Democrats rally around Curtis Hertel as he seeks reelection as party chair — Hertel is seeking to lead the Michigan Democratic Party into the next election cycle after monumental wins in the Nov. 3 election, which saw the party expand its state Senate majority, take back the majority in the state House, retain the […]
text:
News in brief

Michigan Democrats rally around Curtis Hertel as he seeks reelection as party chair — Hertel is seeking to lead the Michigan Democratic Party into the next election cycle after monumental wins in the Nov. 3 election, which saw the party expand its state Senate majority, take back the majority in the state House, retain the top executive offices, and flip three key Congressional seats. The party also elected U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El Sayed. Hertel’s reelection has been endorsed by, among others, El-Sayed, Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson, U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) and UAW President Shawn Fain. 

 

Greater Lansing DSA is encouraging AOC to run for president — As U.S. Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (D-New York) signals her possible interest in jumping into the 2028 presidential race; the Greater Lansing Democratic Socialists of America on Thursday encouraged her to do so. Ocasio-Cortez is a member of DSA. The Greater Lansing chapter said it adopted a resolution calling on her to seek the Democratic nomination, saying DSA was ready to assist a candidate that shared its values.

 

 Citizens Research Council of Michigan calls for new Democratic leaders to prioritize affordable healthcare — Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson and the new leaders of the state Legislature must find ways to address the immediate need for affordable healthcare in the upcoming 104th legislative session, the Citizens Research Council of Michigan said in a call to action email. The CRC said that a mix of federal policies and industry-wide cost pressures will drive up the cost of health insurance, which could also drive up the rate of uninsured residents next year.

 
ICYMI

Michigan’s Black voters sent a message to candidates in midterms: ‘You’ve got to earn it’ — Michigan Advance’s Katherine Dailey explored what Black voter turnout looked like in the 2026 election, and the hard work that went into Democrats earning the community’s vote.

 

Michigan’s U.S. Senate results challenge claim that criticism of Israel alienates Jewish voters — Senior Reporter Ben Solis dug into how the vast majority of Jewish voters stuck with the Democratic Party in the 2026 election despite an active campaign to dissuade the community from voting for U.S. Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed.

 
Stories in the works

MEA releases findings on disruptive, dangerous behaviors among Michigan students — The Michigan Education Association presented new data from a recent survey of teachers on student behavior issues in classrooms across Michigan, and called on Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson and the incoming Democratic-led Legislature to address the issue head on with potential new pilot programs and appropriations in the next budget cycle.

name: Mississippi Today
title: New York startup’s move to Mississippi pays off. Two of the state’s largest banks to merge: Mississippi Marketplace
description: According to state records, Elon Musk's company began construction in Southaven before it received proper permits. It now faces fines up to $6 million.
text:
Earlier this week, Mississippi entrepreneurs and investors gathered in Jackson for the annual startup conference put on by Innovate Mississippi. There are two pitch competitions as part of the event, one for early stage startups and another for later stage companies. 
The later stage competition featured 10 Mississippi companies pitching their goods and services to a panel of investors. The winner, receiving $15,000 plus attention from investors, was LOA Carbon, which recently relocated from New York to Mississippi. 
Katherine Lin
“We thought we were likely to land in either Texas or Alabama, and we didn’t really even pay attention to Mississippi,” said Ryan Shearman, the company’s CEO. But the research and development at the state’s universities, the manufacturing capacity, labor market and programs such as Innovate ultimately pushed them to choose Mississippi.
SpaceXSI Updates
Elon Musk’s artificial intelligence company with an ever-changing name, SpaceXSI, formerly SpaceXAI, formerly xAI, said that it expects to invest $45 billion in Mississippi, double its original announcement.
According to Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality records, SpaceXSI began construction in Southaven before it received proper permits. It now faces fines of up to $6 million.
But in a separate matter, a federal judge in an NAACP lawsuit against the company found that MDEQ misinterpreted federal clean air statutes around the company’s temporary natural gas turbines it is currently using to power its data centers.
This week, the MDEQ permit board rejected an appeal of its decision to approve an air permit for SpaceXSI’s permanent power plant. Among the permanent turbines are eight converted jet engines. It appears to be the first power plant using converted engines that has come before the permit board. 
Other news:

The Mississippi Council on Economic Education held its annual forum to celebrate personal finance and economic education in the state.
A mechanical and electrical fabrication contractor is investing $4.25 million to expand its operations in Greene County.
The city of Madison approved a tax increment financing plan for a $60-million mixed use development, called the Gallery. It approved up to $11.74 million in borrowing to help pay for public infrastructure for the development. Property taxes are higher in a TIF district with the excess money going to repay the bonds, as well as sales tax revenue from within the development. Madison County may also join.
Trustmark announced Thursday that it will merge with Hancock Whitney in a deal estimated to be valued at $3.2 billion. Together the two Mississippi headquartered banks will create a $58-billion in assets bank across six Southeastern states and an $8.9-billion market cap that the companies said would be the “premier Gulf South bank.” The deal is estimated to close in the first quarter of 2027.

name: Oklahoma Voice
title: Rural Oklahoma hospitals at risk of closure from Medicaid cuts, lack of revenue
description: OKLAHOMA CITY — Over a dozen rural Oklahoma hospitals are at immediate risk of closing, according to a national report.  Nationwide, 260 rural hospitals are at immediate risk of closure and 17 of those are in Oklahoma, according to a report from the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform, a national policy center. Oklahoma […]
text:
More than a dozen rural Oklahoma hospitals are at risk of closure, a threat exacerbated by congressional cuts to Medicaid. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)OKLAHOMA CITY — Over a dozen rural Oklahoma hospitals are at immediate risk of closing, according to a national report. 
Nationwide, 260 rural hospitals are at immediate risk of closure and 17 of those are in Oklahoma, according to a report from the Center for Healthcare Quality and Payment Reform, a national policy center. Oklahoma also has 44 rural hospitals the report classifies as “at risk” of closing, but not as immediately as the other 17. 
Rich Rasmussen, president and CEO of the Oklahoma Hospital Association, said the report doesn’t necessarily reflect the full financial picture for these hospitals, but the risk of their closure becomes more real if congressional cuts to Medicaid from the Big Beautiful Bill take effect. 
The report focuses on whether a hospital is making money on delivering care but doesn’t take into account supplemental Medicaid and tax payments that help push them into the black, he said. Rasmussen said federal cuts to programs, such as the Supplemental Hospital Offset Payment Program which allows the state to draw down additional federal Medicaid matching funds to offset revenue losses, puts rural hospitals at risk. 
Without supplemental Medicaid payments, Oklahoma’s critical access hospitals are operating with a negative margin, Rasmussen said. Critical access hospitals, which are specially designated rural providers, are the “smallest and most frail” hospitals, he said. 
“I think what the report tells us is that we have hospitals that are at risk today, based on the fact they lose money delivering care because the reimbursements are inadequate,” Rasmussen said. “Now, those hospitals survive because of the special Medicaid payments that unfortunately Congress has cut. So the challenge that we have going forward over this next decade is how many hospitals will we lose because of these Medicaid cuts that Congress passed.”
Closures are often caused by hospitals losing money delivering patient services, insufficient revenue to cover costs and low financial reserves, according to the report. Rasmussen said other factors that contribute to rural closures are slow or untimely payments from health plans and below cost reimbursements from Medicare Advantage plans. 
He said the newly elected Congress could respond to the cuts made last year and potentially rescind part of them if there’s a desire to do so. 
“Oklahoma is not alone,” Rasmussen said. “This is being felt across the nation, and perhaps most acute in states that have rural hospitals.” 
Hospitals are being forced to evaluate what services they might need to cut to stay afloat, he said. 
There’s one critical access hospital in Oklahoma that delivers babies, a service that loses money, Rasmussen said. 
“Now that one hospital, will they be able to continue to deliver babies with these cuts? That is going to be a gut wrenching discussion that that board will have to have over whether or not they continue to do that,” he said. 
The impact of Medicaid cuts and service reductions impacts everyone, even if they don’t live in rural areas, Rasmussen said. When services or specialty programs are cut and hospitals close, people in rural areas have to travel further to seek healthcare and create more pressure on providers in urban areas, he said. 
“It means people will drive further,” he said. “It means we’ll have higher mortality, meaning more people will die. We will have more incidents of illness that could have been addressed earlier in their disease state, which is not good for patients.”

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan reproductive justice advocates lay out priorities for incoming Democratic trifecta
description: Danielle Atkinson, the founder and executive director of Mothering Justice Action Fund, said that she is “cautiously optimistic” about the incoming Democratic trifecta to work with organizations like hers on prioritizing legislation to support caregivers and to improve maternal and child health outcomes.  She also described some of these policy priorities as[...]
text:
Danielle Atkinson, the founder and executive director of Mothering Justice Action Fund, speaks at a roundtable of advocates discussing priorities for the incoming Benson administration and legislative term on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)Danielle Atkinson, the founder and executive director of Mothering Justice Action Fund, said that she is “cautiously optimistic” about the incoming Democratic trifecta to work with organizations like hers on prioritizing legislation to support caregivers and to improve maternal and child health outcomes. 
She also described some of these policy priorities as having the potential to be impactful early wins for Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson’s administration — such as passing paid leave laws, which Atkinson noted her organization has done the research and feasibility studies to put them on the table. 
“You have the support. You have the majority. Something that can be done really quickly that can be meaningful, and then stop the bleeding,” she said. “Unfortunately, it’s not the sexiest thing. But these cuts that are coming down from the federal government are going to be really harmful, and people are going to feel it, and they’re going to feel it silently, and they’re going to blame this incoming administration, deserve it or not. So they have to stop the bleeding and make sure that Michigan has an answer to what has happened at a federal level.”
Atkinson joined other reproductive justice advocates in Lansing Thursday to discuss policies and priorities that they hope to see taken up in January when Democratic majorities take power in the Legislature alongside Benson assuming the governor’s office. 
Shanay Watson-Whittaker, the director of Michigan campaigns with Reproductive Freedom for All, for example, laid out two specific pieces of legislation that she hopes to see passed. She advocated for establishing a state-level Freedom of Access to Clinic Entrances (FACE) Act, which would make it a criminal offense to interfere with access to a health facility that provides reproductive health services, as well as a state-level shield law, which provides legal protection for both reproductive healthcare providers and patients who receive reproductive care coming from states where it is illegal. 
Paula Thornton Greear, the president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Action Fund, speaks at a roundtable of advocates discussing priorities for the incoming Benson administration and legislative term on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
Paula Thornton Greear, the president and CEO of Planned Parenthood Action Fund, similarly mentioned shield laws as a priority — including for providers of gender-affirming services — as well as access to medication abortion and telehealth services. She also pushed for legislators to end the 24-hour waiting period for abortions and parental notification requirements.
With Democrats set to control both chambers of the Legislature as well as the governorship, the advocates described a ‘mandate’ from Michigan voters to enact legislation that expands access to health care, including reproductive healthcare.
“Incremental progress is not enough anymore, and Michigan has a real opportunity to take a lead across this country,” Thornton Greear said. “We need things written into law. Executive orders are not strong enough; they can be torn down and broken, and they end. So we need to collectively push to have things written into law. An executive order is a promise written in pencil.”
Cassy Jones-McBryde, founder of the Michigan Chamber for Reproductive Justice and executive director of the Michigan Equity Action Fund, warned against the same problems that the last Democratic trifecta, from 2023 to 2024, faced. 
“I was heartbroken when we also had a trifecta not so long ago, and we still didn’t get the promise of what the trifecta was,” she said. “We need to be audacious with our asks now. We have learned a few things from this administration. We know that we can be just as aggressive as the ways they took things from us, we can advocate and get things passed now that we have the promise of what this new administration here in Michigan will be.”
Cassy Jones-McBryde, founder of the Michigan Chamber for Reproductive Justice and executive director of the Michigan Equity Action Fund, speaks at a roundtable of advocates discussing priorities for the incoming Benson administration and legislative term on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance)
But Atkinson, speaking to Michigan Advance after the roundtable conversation, expressed hope about the bigger majority that the Democrats now hold and how it will prevent any one legislator from stalling key priorities.
“We are hopeful that this cohort of elected officials will not be as worried and timid because there’s only a few people holding the majority together, and we have weak legislators,” she said, “We don’t need legislators like that, and we have fewer of them in this — well, we’ll see. True colors will show, but because there is a nice cushion. I’m really hopeful that the leadership will be able to hold a core together to get these ambitious but meaningful and funded policies across the finish line.”
Thursday’s conversation also considered how policies outside of healthcare access do directly impact those conversations — including the harsh immigration policies of the Trump administration. 
Dr. Seydi Sarr, an advocate and the founder and CEO of the African Bureau for Immigration and Social Affairs, described how immigrants in Michigan — including many who worked to mobilize voters for the Benson campaign and state-level Democratic candidates — are living in a culture of fear of being detained by ICE.
“Driving without a license in Michigan is a deportable offense. Taking your children to the hospital, taking your children to school, going to do grocery shopping can get you arrested,” she said, referencing stalled efforts to allow undocumented residents of Michigan to obtain drivers licenses. “You can end up in detention, and you could be deported. So when we have a trifecta, we have to make sure that we hold our community, our elected officials, accountable to their promises.”
Jones-McBryde also discussed social determinants of health impacting access to reproductive health outcomes that she hopes to see addressed under the Benson administration — including legislation to address water affordability and eviction protections.
Atkinson, who was announced as a part of Benson’s inauguration team on Thursday, said following the roundtable that, while she hopes to take her position on that team to celebrate the victory for Benson’s supporters, she also intends as an advocate to “stay visible in the administration, so that they see me and I’m a squeaky wheel.”
Whitmer directs state agencies to strengthen privacy protections for reproductive health data

Benson’s transition team — which is distinct from the team on which Atkinson holds a position — has faced criticism over her choice of members with strong ties to DTE Energy and the controversy-ridden Michigan Economic Development Corporation. 
“I understand the criticisms and I also have concerns, but it’s about the undue influence that they might have, and the best way to combat that is with more representation,” Atkinson said. “So you know, just asking who’s there for childcare, who’s there for wages.”
Accountability was a strong theme throughout the conversation, with Thornton Greear noting that she has seen a trend of greater “self-accountability” among incoming leadership, who understand the message from voters about what is expected of them in the next term.
“You can have hope, but it is really quite useless without strategy,” she said. “The governor-elect’s office knows full well that the federal administration is not done coming after Planned Parenthood or other providers. Just look around the corner, and you’ll see that they are poised to do something once again detrimental to Title X, which will impact so many Michiganders. I think it’s incumbent upon us to continue having that dialogue, to work with the governor-elect’s office to plot a course forward, to be around the table collectively with her, and actually plot out what we can get done.”
Atkinson, who often advocates specifically for the “sandwich generation” — people responsible for both childcare and for elder care of parents — also added that she hopes to see Benson establish task forces to examine the actual administration of policy and the nuances of how different departments can work together. 
“They have to deliver. They have to be specific,” she added. “They have to be able to say with their full chest, Black women need this, and when we do this for Black women, it will affect and help everyone.”

name: Washington State Standard
title: WA House member unseats fellow Democrat to join Senate
description: While Washington’s state Senate Democrats didn’t lose any seats this year, one incumbent did fall to a member of his own party.  State Rep. Cindy Ryu, D-Shoreline, defeated two-term Sen. Jesse Salomon, also a Democrat from Shoreline, in the 32nd Legislative District. Votes are still being tallied, but Ryu has a comfortable lead of more […]
text:
State Sen. Jesse Salomon, left, and state Rep. Cindy Ryu. (Photos courtesy of Washington State Legislature)While Washington’s state Senate Democrats didn’t lose any seats this year, one incumbent did fall to a member of his own party. 
State Rep. Cindy Ryu, D-Shoreline, defeated two-term Sen. Jesse Salomon, also a Democrat from Shoreline, in the 32nd Legislative District. Votes are still being tallied, but Ryu has a comfortable lead of more than 3 percentage points, or nearly 2,100 votes.
Ryu is considered more progressive than Salomon, though the incumbent often voted with his party on the most contentious policies, such as the income tax on high earners, limits on residential rent increases and unemployment benefits for striking workers. However, Ryu attacked Salomon for voting against a lower rent cap.
Ryu has said she supports lowering the million-dollar threshold for the income tax to $250,000, while Salomon argued the Legislature “blew a long-term opportunity” by not dedicating enough of the tax’s proceeds to tax relief.
The campaign was an expensive one, with Ryu raising $364,000 to Salomon’s $314,000. Salomon was also the beneficiary of $395,000 in independent spending supporting his campaign, mostly from business-aligned groups. Over $49,000 was spent backing Ryu, most of it coming from the American Civil Liberties Union of Washington.
“I want to thank the voters for their support and for placing our communities’ needs at the core of this campaign, despite hundreds of thousands of dollars in outside spending. I am honored to serve as their next Senator,” Ryu said in a statement.
“The results so far in this race show that our elections cannot be bought and the voters of the 32nd Legislative District remain committed to progressive policies, including capping rent, helping small businesses and workers thrive, and ensuring our schools are fully funded.”

An endorsement from right-wing commentator Brandi Kruse backfired and hurt Salomon’s chances, said Sen. Manka Dhingra, who chairs the Washington Senate Democratic Campaign committee. 
“I think that probably played a big role,” Dhingra said. “When she ended up endorsing in that race, I remember thinking ‘Uh oh, that’s done now.’”
Salomon didn’t respond to requests for comment.
When Ryu announced her campaign last year, Senate Democratic leaders bristled. 
Senate Majority Leader Jamie Pedersen, of Seattle, was frustrated that Ryu was wasting resources that could be spent elsewhere by challenging a fellow Democrat. 
“My personal belief is that as the leader of the caucus, I am going to be loyal to and stand up for any member of my team,” Pedersen said this week. 
But Pedersen called Ryu a “valued colleague,” and that she’ll now get the same loyalty when she joins the caucus. 
“I met with her early on and told her if the voters of her district elected her that she would be our colleague and we’d be happy to work with her, as well,” he said.
The campaign committee doesn’t spend money protecting incumbents like Salomon in intra-party battles. Salomon also got into the Senate by defeating a Democratic incumbent, Maralyn Chase, in 2018.
Ryu has been in the state House for 15 years, and is the chair of the Technology, Economic Development, and Veterans Committee. Before that, she was the mayor of Shoreline.
Her bid to unseat Salomon meant her House seat was left open. Attorney Danica Noble defeated Shoreline City Councilmember Keith Scully in the Democrat-on-Democrat battle to replace Ryu.
The 32nd District is safe territory for Democrats, and includes northwest Seattle, Shoreline, Lynnwood, Edmonds and Mountlake Terrace.
While Democrats in the state House achieved a two-thirds supermajority in this election, the balance of power in the upper chamber will likely remain the same, with 30 Democrats and 19 Republicans. 
Carolina Mejia, a Democrat and Thurston County commissioner, appears to have fallen just short of unseating Republican Sen. Drew MacEwen in the 35th Legislative District.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Commentary: Will we finally expand Medicaid in Georgia?
description: “Medicaid still remains a top priority in this state… It continues to be a priority and will be a day-one priority for me to prepare our state agencies for that expansion.”- Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms I’m the increasingly rare Georgia bird: a proven fiscal conservative and social liberal. Take a picture before we go extinct. […]
text:
Guest columnist Jack Bernard makes the case for fully expanding Medicaid in Georgia. Jill Nolin/Georgia Recorder“Medicaid still remains a top priority in this state… It continues to be a priority and will be a day-one priority for me to prepare our state agencies for that expansion.”- Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms
I’m the increasingly rare Georgia bird: a proven fiscal conservative and social liberal. Take a picture before we go extinct. I’m OK with expending tax money. But it must be for a good cause and we must budget for it.
Georgia has the third highest rate of uninsured in the nation. It is simply unacceptable that 14% of Georgians under 65 are uninsured compared to a national rate of 8% in states with full expansion. That’s why I have supported full Medicaid expansion in our state as  envisioned in the Affordable Care Act.
We are one of the nation’s best states for business, which may or may not have much to do with our governor doing things like preventing state taxation of Georgia’s data centers. However, we are one of the worst for healthcare coverage directly due to Gov. Brian Kemp’s policies. To the benefit of Georgians, that Kemp era – notable for him willfully ignoring our healthcare deficiencies – will come to a halt very soon. Gov.-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms has said she will make expansion a priority.
Many Georgians are not aware that Georgia originally refused to accept federal money to expand health insurance via Medicaid with no matching requirement for the first three years. It was a major mistake on the part of both the Legislature and Kemp, one that he purposefully continues to ignore to this day. And one that will haunt him if he makes a run for the GOP nomination for president in 2028.
Why are we among the worst states for healthcare coverage? The short answer is partisan politics. Several years ago, Kemp submitted a waiver to the Affordable Care Act. That waiver became the disastrous “Pathways” program.
The purpose of Medicaid expansion is to provide insurance coverage, but the overly complicated waiver implemented by the governor doesn’t do that to the extent it should. Normal expansion would have provided coverage to nearly a half million uninsured Georgians…most in working families with low incomes. Instead, the Kemp administration chose to cover only 13% of them, or 18,527 people, as of June.
Medicaid expansion caused the rate of uninsured to go down dramatically in 40 states while ours has not. Every state that refused to expand is red, including most of our neighboring states. Thus, the short-sighted, ideological views of Kemp and our MAGA politicians caused federal tax money (billions of our dollars) to be spent in New York, California and other states rather than here.
It’s not possible in this short commentary to go into detail as to costs and funding sources. But funding full Medicaid expansion in Georgia is financially feasible, if we have the will. Much of the expense is picked up by the federal government and we have a large budget surplus.
Our choice is either to expand Medicaid or to let lower income people, most in working families, continue to go without needed healthcare. Is that what we really want in our thriving state? With the recent blue tsunami in Georgia and the election of Governor-elect Bottoms, I remain hopeful that Medicaid will be fully expanded in Georgia.
