name: California
title: California voters overhaul recall elections, pass Democratic-backed Prop. 5
description: After a tight race, Californians sided with Democratic leaders, approving their proposed change to the recall process. The recall will take place in two parts: first, whether an official should be recalled, then, who should replace them.
text:
In summary
After a tight race, Californians sided with Democratic leaders, approving their proposed change to the recall process. The recall will take place in two parts: first, whether an official should be recalled, then, who should replace them. 


California will change its election recall process after voters approved Proposition 5, a ballot measure backed by Democrats who argued the process was too open to partisan exploitation. 
The recall process will now take place in two parts: Voters will first decide in an election whether an official should be removed from office. If successful, they’ll vote again in a follow-up election on who should replace the recalled official. Under the previous system, voters were asked both questions at the same time. 
About 52% of voters approved the measure and 48% were against it with about 91% of the vote counted Thursday, 9 days after Election Day.
Democratic lawmakers placed the constitutional amendment on the ballot in 2024, arguing the current system leads to unnecessary state expense, confuses voters, and can lead to ‘undemocratic’ outcomes, since the winner does not need a majority to win. 
Republicans used the recall process in recent years to challenge Democratic politicians. Gov. Gavin Newsom, who survived his own attempted recall in 2021, endorsed the ballot measure to change the rules. 
Voters in Democratic enclaves such as San Francisco, Alameda and Los Angeles counties passed the measure by a wide margin. More rural, Northern California counties like El Dorado and Shasta favored keeping the current system. 
The origins of Prop. 5
Democratic lawmakers and Secretary of State Shirley Weber began advocating for changes in the aftermath of the failed recall of Newsom in 2021. The recall effort cost taxpayers about $200 million and the campaigns on both sides spent another $100 million. Newsom walked away unscathed, with 62% of voters electing to keep him in office. 
The measure got on the ballot after lawmakers passed Senate Constitutional Amendment 1 in 2024. Democratic Sen. Josh Newman, who was recalled himself in 2018, carried the proposal in the Legislature.
Republican lawmakers voted against it, arguing the reform was not needed, would dilute the power of voters and lead to additional special election costs because of the need to hold two elections. 
Unlike some of the tax measures on the ballot that spurred multimillion-dollar spending sprees, no group spent any money on the effort. 
Although recalls are often initiated, they rarely make it to voters. Only 11 recalls have made it to the ballot in California since 1913, and only six have been approved by voters. The current recall process is how Republican Gov. Arnold Schwarzenegger came into power, replacing Gray Davis in 2003.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Mississippi wants to build a statewide health data network. It’s been here before
description: Singing River Health System is seen here on Wednesday, May 17, 2023, in Pascagoula, Miss. The healthcare system was a part of the pilot health information exchange on the Gulf Coast after Hurricane Katrina that laid the groundwork for a statewide network.
text:
Mississippi is again working to build a statewide system that will help hospitals, health providers, pharmacies, laboratories and emergency medical services securely share patient health data.
“We’re creating the infrastructure to improve care coordination, to support emergency preparedness, to strengthen public health decision making and to give healthcare professionals the information that they need to deliver even better care,” Gov. Tate Reeves told reporters at an Oct. 21 press conference.
The exchange will initially be funded by the federal Rural Health Transformation Program, a $50 billion, five-year program to spur innovation in rural healthcare and offset cuts to Medicaid that was signed into law in 2025 by President Donald Trump. Reeves has called the health information exchange the “backbone” of the state’s plan for the funds. 
Health information networks help to create a “person-centric” health record system, where health records are linked to a patient rather than a hospital or clinic, according to Dr. David Kendrick, chair of the medical informatics department at the University of Oklahoma School of Community Medicine. 
“It should be expected that patients have their full medical story with them throughout life,” said Kendrick, who is also the the founder and former CEO of MyHealth Access Network, Oklahoma’s statewide health information exchange. 
This is not the first time Mississippi has worked to develop such a system. The Mississippi Health Information Network was funded with a federal grant and established by state lawmakers in 2010. It was growing until the state Legislature declined to renew it in 2019 — an abrupt decision stakeholders said came as a surprise.
Other health statewide exchanges emerged to fill the gap around the time the state network shut down, including the Mississippi Hospital Association’s IntelliTrue and the Mississippi Health Access eXchange, a physician-led network established in partnership with the Mississippi State Medical Association.
The federal government has pushed states to improve healthcare data sharing among providers for decades. The efforts can help bridge parts of a fragmented healthcare system and improve patients’ health, allowing clinicians across systems to spot dangerous prescription drug interactions and reducing duplicate services.
But despite the benefits for patients, health information exchanges, or HIEs, often face challenges with funding and incentivizing providers to participate, said Julia Adler-Milstein, a professor of medicine at the University of California-San Francisco.
“Building a successful HIE requires not just technical infrastructure, but governance, incentives, and a lot of pieces that have to come together and align for an exchange to be successful,” Adler-Milstein said.
In some states, expanded health data sharing has raised questions about patient privacy, in particular because of cases in which patient data has been used by immigration and law enforcement agencies. 
Mississippi’s application for a vendor to create and operate a new health information exchange, with services expected to begin in January, closed on Nov. 3. 
The contractor is expected to build and operate an exchange that “aggregates, enhances, and distributes health data as a public good,” according to a request for proposals. Core goals are to improve care coordination in trauma response, access to clinical information and centralized imaging services. Beyond serving individual patients and providers, it will also support the state’s study of public health. 
“It’s a game changer for those of us studying population health outcomes,” State Health Officer Dr. Dan Edney said at an Oct. 14 Board of Health meeting. 
How Katrina spurred Mississippi’s first exchange
Plans for a statewide health information exchange in Mississippi were spurred in 2005 by Hurricane Katrina, which damaged paper-based medical records and left thousands of patients unable to access them.
In 2007, then-Gov. Haley Barbour established a task force to plan for a statewide health data exchange. The group recommended a pilot network in the six-county area along the Gulf Coast most heavily affected by Katrina to lay the groundwork for a potential statewide network. 
Mississippi House Speaker Pro Tem J.P. Compretta, D-Bay St. Louis, left, and Speaker Billy McCoy, D-Rienzi, applaud Republican Gov. Haley Barbour, who waves to spectators before delivering his State of the State speech to the Legislature at the Capitol in 2010.  Credit: AP Photo/Rogelio V. Solis
State lawmakers authorized the Mississippi Health Information Network in 2010. That year, Mississippi received about $10.4 million in funding through a federal program to help states build health information exchanges.
Mississippi’s network generated a repository of patient data and sent real-time alerts to providers when patients were admitted, discharged or transferred to or from emergency departments or hospitals. It also supported public health reporting and disease surveillance efforts, said Mike Garcia, the network’s former interim executive director who was involved in the project from its early days and has since retired. 
By 2014, the system included 13 hospitals, 39 clinics and more than 600,000 patients, according to a report from the Joint Legislative Committee on Performance Evaluation and Expenditure Review.
But as it grew, the system struggled to achieve buy-in from some key stakeholders. Like many health information exchanges, providers paid a user fee to participate, with the expectation that the network would one day become self-sustaining. Hospitals were charged $100 per bed to participate, according to budget documents for the 2017 fiscal year. That year, the agency collected roughly $660,000 in user fees. Federal funding ran dry and legislative appropriations declined over time. 
Sen. David Blount, a Democrat from Jackson, authored the bill necessary to reauthorize the network in 2019 — what he believed would be a “routine matter on something important and needed.” 
The Senate passed the bill, but it died without a vote by the full House.
“To me, it was a needless failure, and I was puzzled by it at the time,” Blount said. 
When the Mississippi Health Information Network lapsed, it had roughly 30 million patient records, Garcia said. He said the records were stored in a vault and immediately began to lose their value.
“It was all very anticlimactic,” Garcia said. 
Building demand before infrastructure
The challenges Mississippi faced in keeping a health information exchange alive — including funding and participation — mirror those faced by similar networks across the nation. 
Although data networks can help improve the quality of patient care, hospitals aren’t always incentivized to share information, because patient data is a key asset that ties patients to hospitals, said Adler-Milstein.
For an exchange to succeed, it must also create value for providers, such as helping them meet quality metrics tied to payments and motivate them to participate. 
“There aren’t really strong incentives to share patient data across competing health systems,” Adler-Milstein said. “So you really have to build the demand, and then build infrastructure that supports it.”
Exchanges also need sustainable funding models, Garcia said. He said he believes government support should incentivize providers to participate without making them pay to participate, particularly because they are already contributing value by supplying data. 
“The burden can’t be put on the users,” Garcia said. 
Under some Mississippi Rural Health Transformation Program grants, providers receiving funding are required to participate in the exchange. State officials have not explained how the system will be funded after the federal funds, which must be spent by 2032, are expended.
Shelby Wilcher, a spokesperson for Reeves, whose office is overseeing the plan, did not respond to a request for comment about the state’s long-term plans to fund the exchange.
During the application period for vendors, one potential contractor asked whether the Mississippi State Department of Health or the Division of Medicaid would require or incentivize providers to participate, and whether funds would cover the providers’ onboarding costs. 
In response, the state Health Department, which oversaw the procurement process, said it “can not speak for RHTP requirements.” 
Beyond funding and incentives, experts said, a successful exchange requires buy-in from stakeholders across the health system — including those who receive, deliver and pay for care. Those stakeholders must first come together to establish a shared vision for the exchange and ensure it provides value to everyone involved to ensure sustainability. 
“Governance is what comes first, and that means convening actual people that live in the community to do the work,” Kendrick said.

name: WyoFile
title: Trump administration plan to sell public lands draws congressional pushback
authors: By Matthew Brown, The Associated Press
description:
Officials have not offered details about the potential sale of public lands managed by the Interior Department. The agency oversees a third of Wyoming’s land.
The post Trump administration plan to sell public lands draws congressional pushback appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
President Donald Trump’s administration wants to sell public lands to states, tribes and local governments as part of an effort to “decrease the size of the federal estate,” according to a new plan presented by the Interior Department.
Agency officials said the sale of federal property would allow the government to focus resources on “nationally significant” lands, which were not defined. They offered no details on what parcels could be sold, nor the scope or location of potential sales.
The proposal drew quick pushback from some lawmakers, including Trump’s former Interior secretary, Republican Rep. Ryan Zinke of Montana, showing it faces strong headwinds in Congress even before Democrats assume the majority in January.
The McCullough Peaks, public lands in Park county managed by the BLM as a Wilderness Study Area, emerge from the fog at sunrise. (Lisa Marks/BLM) 
The plan could face strong headwinds in Wyoming, where past proposals to sell off public lands drew a strong public backlash.
The Interior Department’s five-year strategic plan also calls for land transfers and exchanges to support greater energy production, a centerpiece of the administration’s pro-fossil fuel policies. It reflects the Trump administration’s view of most public lands as assets to be used, rather than to be set aside for preservation.
The Interior Department oversees more than 750,000 square miles of land — an area greater than Texas and California combined — along with vast underground mineral reserves. That puts the agency at the center of a contentious, decades-long debate over whether the government controls too much land.
The Associated Press sent emails to Interior officials Wednesday requesting comment and further details.
Most public lands are in Western states. In some, the government controls the vast majority of land, protecting it from potential exploitation but also hindering growth. Nevada, for example, is almost 80% under federal control.
Nearly half of Wyoming is federally owned. About a third of land in the state is managed by Interior Department agencies. 

U.S. Interior Secretary Doug Burgum speaks in June 2025 at the Western Governors’ Association conference in Santa Fe, New Mexico. (Ellen Jaskol)

Interior officials said a portion of any land sale proceeds would be returned to the buyer for conservation purposes elsewhere.
Yet it’s uncertain if Interior Secretary Doug Burgum can achieve the administration’s goals without cooperation from Congress.
Federal law puts significant constraints on public land sales, said Mark Squillace, a professor of natural resources law at University of Colorado Law School.
Land cannot be sold if it’s under protected status. And before a sale can occur, it must be deemed appropriate under certain criteria. Those include cases of land that is uneconomic to manage or where a sale would “serve important public objectives, including but not limited to, expansion of communities and economic development.”
Zinke’s office said in a statement that he “remains firmly opposed to the sale or transfer of public lands.” It said Zinke would vote against any legislation on the issue if it happens before the lawmaker leaves Congress after this term.
The ranking Democrats on the House and Senate natural resources committee — buoyed by their party’s success in last week’s midterm elections — pledged to fight any land sales.
Democratic New Mexico Sen. Martin Heinrich said federal lands “belong to the American people, not private interests looking to cash in.”
California Democratic Rep. Jared Huffman said Democrats would resist the move.
“Americans love their public lands and sent a clear message last week: the Trump administration’s schemes to auction off our treasured resources and silence opposition must stop now. Democrats in Congress are going to deliver,” Huffman said.
Some Western lawmakers last year sought to sell vast tracts of land in Utah and Nevada, saying that could generate revenue and ease growth pressures in booming cities. Among the proposals, Utah Republican Sen. Mike Lee suggested selling more than 2 million acres to states or other entities.
Those efforts failed amid bipartisan opposition.
The plan sets out a road map for the Interior Department’s priorities and actions between 2026 and 2030. Future administrations would not be bound by it.
The department regulates mining, drilling, grazing, recreation and other activities that many state and local officials want greater control over. Interior includes the Bureau of Land Management, National Park Service, Fish and Wildlife Service and Bureau of Indian Affairs.
The agency’s strategic plan was last updated four years ago under former Democratic President Joe Biden.
Burgum and Housing and Urban Development Secretary Scott Turner last year proposed using “underutilized” federal land for affordable housing. Turner said some 7 million homes were needed. Officials under Biden also sought to use public lands for affordable housing, although on a smaller scale.
WyoFile editor Joshua Wolfson contributed to this report.

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: NJ regulators approve virtual power plant, battery storage programs
description: The Board of Public Utilities approved programs Thursday aimed at putting less strain on the grid and lowering energy costs statewide.
text:
The Board of Public Utilities approved programs Thursday aimed at putting less strain on the grid and lowering energy costs statewide. (Photo by Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)The Board of Public Utilities on Thursday unanimously approved the launch of an interim virtual power plant program and the next phase of the state’s energy storage program.
The approved programs make up PowerUp New Jersey, the state’s bid to tap into smart devices and smaller-scale battery projects to soften the impact peak demand has on power prices by paying for reductions in power use or stored energy transmitted to the grid.
“Residents and businesses can lend power from their homes — through smart devices, in-house batteries, solar panels, and other energy sources — to help support the grid when they are not using them, and we will pay you for that energy. That means more money in your pockets, less strain on the grid, and lower energy costs across our state,” Gov. Mikie Sherrill said in a statement.
Virtual power plants seek to remotely reduce the power draw of certain devices, like smart thermostats or electric vehicle chargers, during the parts of the day that grid demand is highest and compensate ratepayers for their reduced electricity use.
Price effects are magnified when demand for electricity approaches the grid’s capacity to generate power. Relatively small amounts of additional generation can have an outsized impact on per-kilowatt-hour rates under those conditions.
The project aims to reduce peak energy use at each of the state’s four regulated utilities —companies like PSE&G or Atlantic City Electric that transmit electricity to ratepayers — by 3%.
Existing devices paid for by state energy efficiency or electric vehicle charger programs could already meet up to 82% of the sought-after reductions at each of the utilities if three-quarters of the eligible devices were enrolled in the virtual power plant program. The state is seeking an overall reduction of 547.1 megawatts across the four electric distribution companies.
“I don’t know if everyone in New Jersey understands, but it is the most expensive hours of the year that are driving the really unsustainable price hikes in the utility and electricity bills that we saw in the last few years,” Board of Public Utilities Commissioner Emma Rebhorn said Thursday.
The order approved by the BPU Thursday requires the state’s four regulated utilities to stand up their interim virtual power plant programs by Oct. 1, 2027. Those programs would run until Sept. 30, 2029, after which they would be replaced by more permanent versions.
By approving PowerUP New Jersey, the board also approved the first block of the second phase of the state’s energy storage program, which seeks to stand up new capacity by expanding residential battery storage in New Jersey.
That program would pay $200 per kilowatt of residential or small-scale commercial new storage capacity, or $100 for each kilowatt of existing storage capacity that joins the program, with adjustments for how much power those batteries actually put into the grid.
Overall, block one seeks to collect 150 megawatts of new storage and 100 megawatts of existing storage. New Jersey’s energy storage program aims to build 2,000 megawatts of capacity by 2030.
Individuals or businesses enrolled in the distributed battery program would receive payments through a distributed energy resource manager, while those enrolled in the virtual power plant program could be paid directly by their utility or through such a manager.
Thursday’s votes are the latest in a series of actions across administrations that have sought to curb spikes in electricity costs driven by the mammoth power demands of artificial intelligence data centers.

name: Daily Montanan
title: Commentary: Who owns the Montana Democrats?
description: Last week’s midterms were historic, one of the biggest sea-changes in U.S. history. Much-needed checks and balances soon will be returned to our federal government. At the state level, Montana will send its first Democrat, Sam Forstag, to Washington in two years. But the state Democratic Party is in a bad way. Notwithstanding Forstag’s U.S. […]
text:
Nearly every Montana county voted more Democratic that in 2024. Last week’s midterms were historic, one of the biggest sea-changes in U.S. history. Much-needed checks and balances soon will be returned to our federal government. At the state level, Montana will send its first Democrat, Sam Forstag, to Washington in two years. But the state Democratic Party is in a bad way.

Notwithstanding Forstag’s U.S. House win, Montana did not share in the blue wave to the extent a number of other “red” states did. Kansas, Texas, Ohio, and Iowa each elected a Democratic senator and governor. South Carolina and Mississippi each elected a Democratic senator.

Montana made only small gains in the state legislature (four seats) and did not pick up any Public Service Commission seats.
Why did the big blue wave largely pass us by? A principal reason is the flawed strategy adopted by several leading Montana Democrats — for example former U.S. Sens. Jon Tester and Max Baucus, former Gov. Steve Bullock, and former Superintendent of Public Instruction Nancy Keenan — of running independent candidates instead of Democrats in major races.

The argument is, to quote a leaked January 2026 text from Tester, that the Democratic brand is “poison” in Montana and only an independent can win.

Montana Democrats have been split by independent bids three times in the last four years. Gary Buchanan’s run for the eastern district Congressional seat in 2022, Michael Eisenhauer’s bid for the same seat this year, and Seth Bodnar’s challenge for the Senate seat this year. The results have not been good. Buchanan netted 21.9% of the vote; Eisenhauer received 9% and Bodnar 37.7%. All lost to the Republican, and in so doing divided the state’s Democrats while hurting down-ballot Democratic candidates.

Not only has the “independent strategy” proven ineffective, it has involved a good deal of shady, behind-the-scenes maneuvering and skullduggery, the sort that only increases divisions, mistrust, and cynicism within and about the Montana Democratic Party.
The state party, now in disarray, has been deeply divided by the just-concluded U.S. Senate race. The now-former party chairwoman, Shannon O’Brien, resigned last month on the eve of the election, slamming the party nominee for Senate, Alani Bankhead, and endorsing independent Seth Bodnar, on her way out the door. Bankhead struggled to raise money throughout the campaign, while Bodnar and the Republican, Kurt Alme, each raked in millions. Bodnar raised around $7 million and Alme roughly $4 million, not counting the millions in PAC money supporting each.
The official Democratic nominee couldn’t raise money. Why? Well, as it turns out the only reason Bankhead, a retired Air Force officer who moved to Montana in 2023, was the Democratic nominee was because the behind-the-curtains, Democratic string-pullers decided she would be.
There had been another candidate, Reilly Neill, a former state legislator who,, as of the June primary, had been running for 19 months. Neill had conducted more than a hundred town halls across the state, garnered around 5,600 campaign donations amounting to nearly $300,000, and out-raised Bankhead by more than 10-to-1. It was widely presumed that Neill would be the Democratic nominee, but the Bodnar-backing heavyweights had other ideas.
Knowing Neill was a substantial, extremely hard-working, grassroots candidate, unlikely to drop out following the primary to create the toe-to-toe with Alme the Bodnar forces desired, they hatched a plan. They would raise and deploy dark money to boost Bankhead and trash Neill. After using Bankhead to knock off the frontrunner, Neill, they would cynically discard Bankhead and get her to drop out of the race.
It all worked according to plan, except for the part about Bankhead dropping out. The Bodnar bigwigs recruited, among others, billionaire tech tycoon Jason Carroll to give more than $1 million, per Montana Free Press reporting, to fund a new dark money front, Progressive Vet PAC, with strong Tester ties. Its treasurer, former Helena Democratic legislator Moffie Funk, is close to Tester and her son is a former Tester staffer.
In early May, the Progressive Vet PAC began flooding the state with tv and social media ads, mailers and personal phone calls that elevated Bankhead and slammed Neill. Paid calls informed Montana voters, “Reilly Neill is a Republican.”
Until recently nothing was known about who, exactly, had recruited Carroll and other big money donors central to the pro-Bodnar folks’ effort to kneecap Neill and make Bankhead the Democratic nominee. The Oct.26 episode of NPR’s “This American Life,” however, shed some light. On the program, former Sen. Max Baucus admitted that he was privy to some of the behind-the-scenes dealings, as the following dialogue reveals:

        BAUCUS: I do know some people who were involved.
INTERVIEWER: Who was involved?
BAUCUS: Some people I know, been involved in Montana campaigns. Really wonderful people. Um, they, they were part of some organizations that directed the money.
INTERVIEWER: But they told you that they were gonna pick somebody who would be more likely to withdraw? Somebody told you that?
BAUCUS: That’s— yes, that’s correct.    
In the end, of course, all of the machinations of Baucus and Tester, and the other string-pullers, came to naught. Bodnar may claim, as he did last week on the heels of his defeat, that, “We showed Montana, and the country, that there’s a different path forward for our politics.” The unfortunate fact, however, is that he lost by more than 51.000 votes (10.6%). About all he really demonstrated is that a campaign can raise many millions and still lose big.

Montana is sending yet another “Trumplican,” Kurt Alme, to the Senate. The state Democratic Party is in disarray and more disunited than ever. And we have the continuing legacy of shady, backroom, dark money string- pullers like Baucus, Tester, and Keenan, with their deep cynicism about democracy and their continued, hubristic belief that they know best and will decide whom our candidates will be. Keenan even had the effrontery to crow, on the night of Bodnar’s historic defeat, about how Democrats will need to get used to supporting Independent candidates going forward.The “smoke filled rooms” with party bosses who hand-picked candidates in the late 19th and early 20th Centuries were more transparent and open than what we have today in Montana with this reign of behind-the curtains, Democratic string pullers. The Montana politicians who wore the Anaconda Company’s ‘copper collar’ were well-understood as compared with the shady forces that run today’s Montana Democratic Party.
Montanans deserve fair choice. We want real democracy in our great state. We want the people to have their say. Right now, at least when it comes to Montana Democrats, we have a cynical, obscurantist politics of, “Daddy (Baucus, Tester, et. al.) knows best.” With the Democratic string-pullers in charge, the party rank-and-file really don’t have a meaningful say over our candidates for high office, at least not whenever the ‘heavyweights’ choose to put their fingers on the scales.
Is this how we want to do democracy in Montana? “The Company” — Anaconda and Montana Power — ran the state’s politics and government for decades, but Montana escaped that capture and emerged into the light of self-government. We face the prospect, at least on the Democratic side of the aisle, of being captured once again. But, if our history is any guide, we can break free from these bonds as well.


Brad Snow is an Assistant Teaching Professor of History at Montana State University.

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Weeks before Alaska gets a new governor, its economic development arm goes on a spending spree
description: A $25 million investment in a nuclear energy startup. Another $36 million for a controversial mining road. And up to $75 million for a new state-owned company promoting broadband. Those are among the multi-million-dollar decisions that GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s appointees and state officials have made as part of a spending blitz by Alaska’s economic developme[...]
text:
The Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority has led the state's participation in an array of controversial projects during GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy's administration. (Nathaniel Herz)A $25 million investment in a nuclear energy startup. Another $36 million for a controversial mining road. And up to $75 million for a new state-owned company promoting broadband.
Those are among the multi-million-dollar decisions that GOP Gov. Mike Dunleavy’s appointees and state officials have made as part of a spending blitz by Alaska’s economic development arm just weeks before Dunleavy leaves office.
The spending announcements have totaled more than $200 million since August — and reflect an aggressive push by state officials to advance projects that could come under fresh scrutiny after Dec. 7, when Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins is set to become Alaska’s next governor.
“We’re trying to push everything forward, Mr. Chair, as our mission statement tells us to do — and frankly, as our Alaska Constitution tells us to do,” the executive director of the Alaska Industrial Development and Export Authority, Randy Ruaro, told board members at a Nov. 6 meeting.
The export authority, known as AIDEA, is a state-owned corporation that’s promoting some of Alaska’s biggest and most contentious resource development projects. Under Dunleavy, the agency has faced sharp criticism over investments in oil and gas exploration in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, as well as in controversial mining road proposals.
The recent spending decisions have drawn scrutiny from skeptics. But AIDEA officials say they reflect months of work and staff time rather than a slapdash effort to get funds out the door. The corporation is self-funded and its finances are separate from the state’s operating fund.
Supporters say AIDEA’s investments will create jobs and generate new revenue for Alaska’s budget; they point also to a dividend that the agency pays to the state government annually — some $15 million this year.
Critics, though, say the export authority’s leaders have gone rogue, spending on speculative projects with limited oversight at a time when the rest of the state government has been strapped for cash.
Kreiss-Tomkins has said he would “completely reassess” AIDEA if elected and that he’s likely to change its leadership.
“We will have more to share once additional additional votes have been counted and the transition progresses,” a Kreiss-Tomkins campaign spokesperson said in a texted statement. The campaign declined an interview request.
In addition to authorizing tens of millions of dollars in entirely new investments, AIDEA is also ramping up a contentious plan to search for oil in the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge, starting as soon as January if it can secure necessary permits.
The agency has already signed a contract for advanced geologic studies, and it “will incur significant financial impact if it is forced to terminate the program” after Nov. 29, lawyers representing the corporation said in a recent court filing.
Rep. Ashley Carrick, a Fairbanks Democrat who has pushed for stronger legislative oversight of AIDEA, said she’s broadly concerned about the corporation’s direction.
“I just feel like this administration is taking some actions on their way out the door that could have some pretty large implications for upcoming AIDEA projects and AIDEA spending,” Carrick said. “I’m not sure that’s the direction that most Alaskans want to see AIDEA go.”
In late October, AIDEA announced a $25 million investment in NuCube Energy, an Idaho-based startup that’s designing small nuclear reactors. That money has already been committed, AIDEA spokesperson Andrew Jensen confirmed in an email, and it gives AIDEA an ownership stake in the company. Neither AIDEA nor NuCube has publicly disclosed the size of that stake. NuCube is in the middle of a deal to become a publicly-traded company and “can’t comment beyond what has been publicly filed” with U.S.securities regulators, a company spokesperson said in an emailed statement.
AIDEA’s board, also in October, authorized staff to create a subsidiary focused on improving broadband in Alaska, and to transfer up to $75 million to it. Those funds have not yet been committed, Jensen said in an email.
A couple of weeks later, the authority’s board approved up to $10 million for a second equity deal — this one to acquire a stake in GeoAlaska, a small company studying geothermal energy potential beneath Augustine Island, a remote volcano in Cook Inlet.
Then, late last week, the board approved an estimated $86 million in spending on preliminary work on the proposed Ambler Road, a 211-mile haul road across northern Alaska that’s drawn fierce opposition from environmental groups. That figure includes $50 million that the agency had previously authorized.
Board members also in recent weeks have greenlit more than $50 million in cash and loans for shipyard projects in the Southeast Alaska towns of Wrangell and Ketchikan.
And on Nov. 9, AIDEA launched an investment platform run by a new subsidiary, Alaska Data Corp., in partnership with a San Francisco-based finance firm called Plural. The platform is designed to let Alaskans invest directly in specific projects, with the aim of financing data centers and other infrastructure. (It lists no offerings yet.)
AIDEA allocated $20 million for Alaska Data Corp. earlier this year. A web page for the subsidiary lists Brandon Brefczynski, AIDEA’s deputy director, as its president and another AIDEA official, former conservative talk radio host Dave Stieren, as its vice president.
AIDEA declined to make Ruaro available for an interview.
In an emailed statement, Jensen said AIDEA’s staff and board “take seriously their roles as fiduciaries” and have a “statutory mandate to advance economic growth and general well-being for Alaskans.”
The recent announcements “are proof we’re meeting that obligation,” the statement said, noting that the agency generated more than $60 million in annual net income and $52 million in total dividends over the past three years.
The spending decisions come after “months of staff work and due diligence,” the statement added.
The board has at least one more meeting, on Dec. 4, before a new governor takes office.
Jensen would not say whether the corporation would sign more deals between now and then. But the statement he emailed said that AIDEA “will continue to follow its fiduciary responsibilities and conduct all due diligence required, building on the countless hours of staff time that have brought” proposals forward.

name: California
title: Este condado de California alberga a la mitad de los delincuentes sexuales violentos del estado. ¿Existe una mejor manera de alojarlos?
description: Mientras un juez de San Diego sopesa la posibilidad de reubicar a dos depredadores sexuales violentos en un barrio rural, un supervisor del condado propone un nuevo plan para alojar mejor a estos delincuentes.
text:
This article is also available in English. Read it here.
Boulevard, California, es una comunidad rural de aproximadamente 750 habitantes, ubicada en montañas desérticas cubiertas de maleza, a una hora al este del centro de San Diego.
 Pronto podría albergar a dos depredadores sexuales violentos: una categoría estatal utilizada para describir a los delincuentes sexuales con alto riesgo de reincidencia.
 Reynaldo Delrosario, de 71 años, fue sentenciado a 12 años de prisión estatal por “actos lascivos e indecentes” con un menor de 10 años. Michael Poulsom, de 67 años, cometió actos lascivos con víctimas menores de 14 años en Georgia y San Diego, y fue sentenciado a 15 años de prisión estatal en California.
 Ambos fueron diagnosticados con trastorno de pedofilia y, tras cumplir sus condenas, fueron internados en un hospital estatal para recibir tratamiento. El jueves, un juez de San Diego decidirá si concede la libertad condicional y los ubica en residencias estatales en la pequeña comunidad.
 Si se aprueban sus solicitudes, se unirían a otros siete delincuentes sexuales violentos en barrios residenciales de la zona rural de San Diego, lo que dejaría al condado con más de la mitad de todos los centros de detención de este tipo en California.
 El supervisor del condado de San Diego, Joel Anderson, un republicano que representa la región sureste del condado, tiene otra idea.
Él quiere que el condado adopte un modelo utilizado en el estado de Washington, en el que los agresores sexuales violentos se alojan en residencias grupales con vigilancia las 24 horas del día. Según él, ubicarlos juntos en áreas más aisladas proporcionaría una mejor supervisión y servicios, y reduciría el riesgo para los vecindarios circundantes.
 El jueves, el juez del Tribunal Superior de San Diego, Theodore Weathers, decidirá si concede la libertad condicional a Poulsom y Delrosario. Anderson espera convencer al tribunal de que implemente el modelo de vivienda colectiva como programa piloto.
“La seguridad es mucho mayor”, dijo Anderson. “Pero hay más libertad para los depredadores sexuales violentos porque viven en una zona donde a nadie le molesta que estén allí”.
 Depredadores sexuales violentos se concentran en San Diego.
 El término depredador sexual violento describe a una persona condenada por delitos sexuales violentos, como violación o agresión sexual a un menor, que tiene un diagnóstico de enfermedad mental que la hace propensa a cometer nuevos delitos.
 En California, los delincuentes sexuales violentos, conocidos por las siglas SVP, cumplen condenas en prisión y, posteriormente, suelen ser internados en un hospital estatal para recibir tratamiento de salud mental tras cumplir su condena.
 Si todo sale bien, pueden solicitar la libertad condicional. La empresa contratista del estado, Liberty Healthcare, busca vivienda en el condado de origen del delincuente o en el lugar donde cometió sus delitos, y luego le alquila una casa.
 El sheriff y la fiscalía dan su opinión sobre el lugar de liberación, y la fiscalía solicita comentarios de los miembros de la comunidad. Un juez considera la ubicación propuesta y revisa las medidas de seguridad, como el monitoreo GPS, los registros sin previo aviso, las pruebas de polígrafo y de drogas, y luego decide si concede la libertad condicional.
 Este proceso se ha convertido en algo habitual en el condado de San Diego, donde se concentra la mitad de los depredadores sexuales violentos del estado.
 Seis de ellos ya viven en zonas rurales de San Diego, en las comunidades desérticas de Borrego Springs, una comunidad de aproximadamente 2700 habitantes rodeada por el Parque Estatal del Desierto de Anza-Borrego, y Jacumba, con 740 residentes, según una lista mantenida por la Fiscalía del Distrito de San Diego . Un séptimo delincuente también ha sido autorizado para ser reubicado en Borrego Springs. 
 Palmeras y casas en la comunidad de Borrego Springs, cerca del Parque Estatal del Desierto de Anza-Borrego, el 24 de marzo de 2022. Foto de Mario Tama, Getty Images.
 Otro individuo, Merle Wakefield , se quitó el monitor electrónico del tobillo mientras trabajaba en un almacén de Amazon en Rancho Bernardo y escapó el 25 de septiembre. Fue hallado muerto semanas después en el lecho de un río de San Diego, según anunció el sheriff de San Diego el 20 de octubre.
 Actualmente, hay un total de 14 depredadores sexuales violentos en libertad condicional en distintos condados de California, según informó el Departamento de Hospitales Estatales en un correo electrónico enviado a CalMatters. Si el tribunal aprueba la libertad condicional de Poulsom y Delrosario, nueve de ellos se encontrarían en San Diego.
 La Defensoría Pública de San Diego representará a los hombres en sus audiencias judiciales este mes, según informó Alexandra Knudson, supervisora de internamiento civil de la oficina de la defensoría pública. La defensoría pública no hizo comentarios sobre las ubicaciones, pero Knudson indicó que revisarán la propuesta de Anderson. 
 Peleas por los puestos
 Vecinos y líderes locales han expresado su preocupación por la liberación de depredadores sexuales violentos. Los residentes de estas pequeñas comunidades de bajos ingresos suelen oponerse a compartir su vecindario con un delincuente sexual de alto riesgo, pero sienten que tienen poca voz en el asunto.
 “Se trata de comunidades rurales”, dijo Anderson. “No tienen los medios para resistir ni para defenderse”.
 En 2021, la Junta de Supervisores del Condado de San Diego votó por unanimidad en contra de cualquier plan para liberar a delincuentes sexuales violentos en las comunidades de San Diego, a menos que el condado tuviera voz y voto en cómo y dónde serían liberados. Pero esa votación no modificó la política estatal sobre la reubicación de delincuentes sexuales.
 El senador estatal Brian Jones, cuyo mandato termina este año, dedicó años a intentar perfeccionar el proceso. El año pasado, el gobernador Gavin Newsom firmó uno de los proyectos de ley de Jones que exige al Departamento de Hospitales Estatales que analice opciones de alojamiento transitorio para depredadores sexuales violentos liberados bajo libertad condicional.
 Sin embargo, su otro proyecto de ley para exigir responsabilidades por la liberación de delincuentes sexuales quedó estancado en la Asamblea de California, después de haber sido aprobado por el Senado estatal.
 La ley habría exigido que el director de los hospitales estatales aprobara los contratos de alquiler de los reclusos para evitar su reubicación en lugares inapropiados o peligrosos. Asimismo, habría priorizado la seguridad pública en la reubicación de delincuentes sexuales violentos. La Unión Estadounidense por las Libertades Civiles y la Asociación de Defensores Públicos de California se opusieron al proyecto de ley, argumentando que, en la práctica, impediría a los reclusos obtener la libertad condicional tras cumplir sus condenas.
 Ahí es donde Anderson cree que el modelo del estado de Washington para albergar a depredadores sexuales violentos podría ser útil. 
 Las instalaciones del Centro de Internamiento Especial del estado de Washington en McNeil Island, Washington, el 20 de octubre de 2015. El centro alberga a depredadores sexuales violentos. Foto de Ted S. Warren, AP Photo.
 En Washington, los delincuentes sexuales violentos que cumplen sus condenas penales son enviados a internamiento civil en un centro de máxima seguridad en la isla McNeil. Allí reciben un tratamiento intensivo destinado a prevenir nuevos delitos sexuales y se les realiza una evaluación anual para determinar si reúnen los requisitos para ser ubicados en una “alternativa menos restrictiva”.
 Existen dos centros de transición comunitarios seguros, propiedad del estado, con personal las 24 horas y capacidad para albergar entre 12 y 24 reclusos. El estado de Washington también gestiona hogares comunitarios privados, que suelen alojar a varios reclusos y pueden incluir supervisión permanente y personal que acompaña a los residentes fuera de las instalaciones.
 Anderson cree que eso ofrecería una opción de vivienda más estructurada y segura para los depredadores sexuales violentos, y los disuadiría de reincidir.
 “Hay que brindarles esa constante seguridad y aliento positivo para que se mantengan por el buen camino, protegiendo a la comunidad”, dijo.
 En Washington, al igual que en San Diego, los programas de reubicación comunitaria han generado controversia. Un plan para alojar hasta cinco delincuentes sexuales en una gran granja en la ciudad de Tenino, Washington, fue cancelado debido al aumento de los costos y al rechazo de la comunidad.
 Cynthia Shipley, responsable de prensa del Departamento de Servicios Sociales y de Salud del Estado de Washington, afirmó que el departamento colabora con miembros de la comunidad, funcionarios municipales, las fuerzas del orden y proveedores privados para atender sus inquietudes. Anderson está al tanto de las controversias en torno al modelo de Washington y las abordará en su plan, según declaró su jefe de comunicaciones, Matthew Phy.
 Pero se muestra optimista y cree que existe una manera de alojar a los depredadores sexuales violentos que podría resultar en mejores resultados para los infractores y mayor seguridad para las comunidades aledañas. En su distrito hay varios complejos turísticos y ranchos privados de gran tamaño que podrían alojar a los reclusos liberados en zonas remotas, lejos de los barrios residenciales. También piensa que esto podría suponer un ahorro económico.
Un informe de 2024 de la Auditoría Estatal de California reveló que California gastó 93 millones de dólares en dos décadas para liberar a 56 delincuentes sexuales de alto riesgo. Los costos se dispararon de 5.3 millones de dólares en 2018-19 a 9.4 millones de dólares en 2022-23, debido al aumento de los precios de la vivienda y a los pagos a Liberty Healthcare.
 Según Anderson, alojarlos juntos podría reducir esos gastos, a la vez que ofrecería mejores servicios y supervisión. Tiene previsto presentar su plan ante el Tribunal Superior el jueves y someterlo a la consideración de la junta de supervisores el próximo mes.
 “La comunidad se beneficia”, afirmó. “El costo disminuye. Y la calidad de la atención para los pacientes con enfermedades terminales aumenta. Estadísticamente, el modelo de Washington ha sido mucho más exitoso. No presenta inconvenientes en ningún aspecto”.

name: Nebraska Examiner
title: ‘Best cat ever’: Commission approves project honoring Cameron, Nebraska’s ‘Capitol Cat’
description: LINCOLN — The Nebraska State Capitol’s longtime unofficial feline mascot will soon have a statue outside the building after a governing commission approved the idea Thursday. The Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission, which oversees development, sculptures and public art in the cardinal directions of the Capitol, voted 6-0 to allow the proposal to move forwar[...]
text:
Supporters of a statue and landscape area honoring the unofficial Nebraska State Capitol mascot, Cameron the "Capitol Cat," joined at a public hearing Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, in the Capitol to urge a commission to approve the project. Octavia Hampson, 9, holds a black-and-white photo of Cameron taken by Lincoln photographer John Shaw, who is standing at back. Shannon Hampson, center, is joined with three kids from her daycare, Wild Child Daycare, and her son, Kingstin Ferguson, at center. Flanking the group and holding renderings of the project are state Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, left, and former state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln, right. Back right is Scott Shafer of the Nebraska Commission on Indian Affairs and at left is Courtney Wittstruck of Lincoln wearing a shirt with Cameron's likeness. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)LINCOLN — The Nebraska State Capitol’s longtime unofficial feline mascot will soon have a statue outside the building after a governing commission approved the idea Thursday.
The Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission, which oversees development, sculptures and public art in the cardinal directions of the Capitol, voted 6-0 to allow the proposal to move forward. One commissioner was absent. 
Dianna McGinnis of Lincoln with her cat, Cameron, who became a celebrity around the Nebraska State Capitol and Lincoln and gained the status of “Capitol Cat” and unofficial greeter. (Photo courtesy of John Shaw)
The statue would honor 11-year-old Cameron the “Capitol Cat,” a tabby who for nearly a decade regularly trotted to the Capitol and greeted his own sort of constituents.
In May, Cameron and his owner, Dianna McGinnis, moved into assisted living, and Cameron retired from his public duties.
“This is so much better than what we started with,” state Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, a leader in designing the project, told the commission. “I feel like we’ve landed where it needs to be.”
An evolving project
Commissioner Dave Landis, a Lincoln state senator from 1979-2007, and other commissioners praised the proposal’s evolution, which now came with formal renderings from Olsson, an engineering and design firm, rather than AI mockups.
“This seems to be very much like what a cat owner would do,” said Landis, noting how the public could sit and enjoy the green space next to Cameron.
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward testifies before the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Thursday, Nov. 12, 2026, in Lincoln, Nebraska. At left is Commissioner Dave Landis, a former state senator from Lincoln who served from 1979-2007. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
The final proposal calls for a life-size bronze statue of Cameron on the south side of the Capitol atop granite slabs. Those rectangular pieces were originally curbs on streets near the Capitol building and have been safely stored ever since the City of Lincoln put in concrete curbs.
“It really pulls it together, and I’m really, really excited about that piece of it,” Hughes said.
A plaque honoring Cameron and the values he brought to the Capitol, such as bringing together Nebraskans and officials who might have just disagreed vehemently during debate, will be installed on the ground in front of his statue.
‘An awesome viewscape’
Benjamin Victor, an Idaho-based sculptor, is poised to sculpt Cameron’s bronze statue, assuming enough private funds are raised. As of Thursday morning, more than $6,500 had been collected. No public dollars will be used to create or maintain the project. 
State Sen. Jana Hughes of Seward, at the podium, to the left, and former state Sen. Anna Wishart, at the podium, to the right, testify before the Nebraska Capitol Environs Commission on Aug. 28, 2026, in Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
Other sculptures by Victor are displayed in the Capitol Environs District, including bronze statues for Ponca Chief Standing Bear and Dr. Susan La Flesche Picotte on Lincoln Mall north of the Capitol. Victor has also sculpted four statues in Statuary Hall in the U.S. Capitol, including the Chief Standing Bear statue for Nebraska.
Supporters had originally proposed a more monument-style tribute to Cameron, a statue on a limestone pedestal in homage to the Capitol building. Then the idea moved toward a more formal bench with Cameron. The project landed instead on a green space, which Olsson will spruce up in the immediate vicinity of the sculpture while also refurbishing an accessibility ramp. 
Hughes said the corner will serve as a focal point for fourth graders visiting the Capitol from across the state.
“It’s an awesome viewscape for photos because you’re far enough away from the Capitol that you can kind of capture the whole structure behind you,” Hughes said.
Designers will take into consideration final commissioner comments, including how to put together the granite slabs to be more uniform and how to prevent wayward skateboarders.
“I’d hate to see him clobbered by a skateboarder,” said Commission Chair Kile Johnson.
‘Best cat ever’
Speaking in support of the project was Octavia, a 9-year-old from Lincoln who attended the commission meeting with her mom, Shannon Hampson, brother Kingstin and three other children from Wild Child Daycare, which Hampson runs in Lincoln.
A handwritten comment letter in support of a statue for Nebraska’s Cameron the Capitol Cat written by Kingstin Ferguson, a 12 year old from Lincoln. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)
When someone feels down or upset, Octavia said, they can go to the statue, pet Cameron and be OK.
“Every person I know really wants a statue of him,” Octavia told the commission. “Did you know that he has been at the Capitol for 10 years? He’s the best cat ever.”
An unexpected fire alarm went off after Octavia spoke. Rather than delay the vote, commissioners abruptly ended public comment and gave unanimous final approval.
In a prewritten letter of support, Kingstin, 12, said he felt the statue was important so future generations will know about Cameron and how important he was to Lincoln. Kingstin said many historical figures have statues, “so why don’t we have a statue of Cameron?”
“I thought he was so special I made a trading card for him with some help,” Kingstin wrote. The daycare created trading cards to learn more about the Legislature and state senators, too.
Cameron’s ongoing lesson
After the meeting, Hampson said the daycare visits the Capitol quite often and that Cameron gave the kids a chance to learn more, not just through senators. In one exchange, when kids asked a lawmaker their favorite part about the Capitol, one senator said Cameron, and Hampson said it became a “fun little scavenger hunt” to find Cameron in each future visit.
“Even when two parties weren’t in agreement on something, that was a moment that they could be in agreement and find something that they both liked, and it could be that meeting point,” Hampson said. 
“I think that’s a very important lesson in life that even when you don’t agree with someone, you can still find something that you agree on. And so it’s just kind of that continuation of what we want when we come to the capital.”
With the final vote Thursday, designers need no further approval, but former state Sen. Anna Wishart of Lincoln, who helped Hughes, said the group would probably continue to update the commission as the project moves ahead.
Cameron the Capitol cat sits inside the vestibule of the south entrance to the Nebraska State Capitol on Nov. 24, 2025. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron the Capitol cat sits on a reporter's lap at the west entrance to the Nebraska State Capitol on Aug. 7, 2024. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron, the Nebraska State Capitol's "Capitol Cat," poses on a ledge on the south side of the building. (Photo courtesy of Katie Quintero)Cameron the Capitol Cat, shown in December 2024. (Photo by Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron, the Nebraska State Capitol's "Capitol Cat," trots down a ledge on the south side of the building. (Photo courtesy of Katie Quintero)Cameron the Capitol Cat was a common sight around legislative sessions. (Photo by Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron the Capitol cat looks up at a reporter's phone on the south steps of the Nebraska State Capitol on the evening of March 18, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Nebraska Gov. Jim Pillen holds Cameron, the Nebraska State Capitol's unofficial mascot, on the south steps of the building in spring 2023. (Photo courtesy of the Office of Governor Jim Pillen)Cameron the Capitol cat outside the south entrance to the Nebraska State Capitol on Feb. 20, 2026. (Photo by Zach Wendling/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron the Cat, a fixture at the Nebraska State Capitol.
(Photo by Aaron Sanderford/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron the Capitol Cat. (Photo by Erin Bamer/Nebraska Examiner)Cameron the Capitol Cat with Diana McGinnis. (Photo courtesy of Diana McGinnis)

title: Commentary: How the election results may have saved the planet
description: Among all the reasons to celebrate the wonderful midterm election results, I would particularly like to emphasize how they have literally created an opportunity to save mankind’s future on this planet — that is, by stopping Trump’s race toward climate destruction and allowing the United States to once again become a leader in positive climate […]
text:
The Michigan State Capitol, visible through wildfire smoke. July 16, 2026. | Photo by Katherine Dailey/Michigan Advance.Among all the reasons to celebrate the wonderful midterm election results, I would particularly like to emphasize how they have literally created an opportunity to save mankind’s future on this planet — that is, by stopping Trump’s race toward climate destruction and allowing the United States to once again become a leader in positive climate policies. This could not be more timely. Let me explain.
First, some data on the extent of the climate crisis.
While the issue of climate change unfortunately received almost no attention during the election campaign (in part due to some dubious recommendations by campaign advisors for “climate hushing”), one might have still noticed the almost weekly occurrence of climate-related weather disasters throughout the year … both in the U.S. and around the world.
The evidence that massive global climate change is happening is absolutely incontrovertible. Every year now brings new temperature records, and just this past October was globally the warmest October ever recorded. Atmospheric CO2 rating on Election Day (Nov. 3, 2026) was 428.84 ppm, continuing a pattern of record-high ratings (vs. about 280 ppm in “pre-industrial” times). CO2 ratings have now been climbing every year for decades, with trends increasing from less than 1.0 ppm/year in the 1960s to over 2.5 ppm/year in the 2020s.
Indeed, climate scientists are warning that Earth’s “life support systems” are breaking down, and that “The climate emergency is already here.” A new United Nations report concludes that we have already missed the original goal of limiting global temperature increase to 1.5 degrees Celsius. However, with urgent and stringent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions (e.g., 18% by 2030 and 45% by 2035), we could limit the increase to a level of 1.7-1.8°C and return to 1.5°C by the end of the century.
This is where the crucial importance of the recent U.S. election comes into play. As the world’s largest economy, the United States is positioned to have a massive influence on world policy and actions regarding climate. Hence the positive actions that President Biden took toward reducing greenhouse gas emissions were vitally important … and, in contrast, the immensely negative steps during Trump’s second administration are tremendously damaging.
Trump EPA to strip greenhouse gas limits for power plants, a key Biden climate policy

It is no exaggeration to say that if the U.S. continued Trump’s recent path regarding climate-related actions, those urgent savings targets would be completely unfeasible. Indeed, Trump’s actions to undermine climate policy and increase greenhouse gas emissions are so numerous and so extensive that it is not possible to summarize them all in one editorial. But here are a few examples.
In terms of international agreements, Trump not only has withdrawn (again) from the Paris Agreement, but also from the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC), the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) and the Green Climate Fund (GCF).
Domestically, Trump has pursued an incredible list of actions to support, finance and deregulate coal and oil interests, while also removing funding and blocking development of wind and solar energy projects. (Trump actually said in January 2026, “My goal is to not let any windmill be built.”)
This past September, Senators Schumer and Whitehouse released an extensive report detailing the dozens of ways that the Trump administration has rewarded the fossil fuel industry for its huge support of Trump’s presidential campaign. Some examples include:

26 senior officials across EPA, the Department of Energy (DOE) and the Department of the Interior (DOI) previously worked for fossil fuel or other polluting industries.
Trump weaponized his EPA, DOE, DOI, DOJ, etc., on the fossil fuel industry’s behalf — from canceling grants for renewable energy projects on false pretexts to leasing swaths of public land to fossil fuels.
Trump attacks clean energy to take out fossil fuel’s competitors: The Trump administration attacks fossil fuel’s competitors, especially wind and solar. More than $1.8 billion in taxpayer funds have been paid to companies to cancel wind projects, and over 160 projects are frozen.

Among the most consequential of Trump’s many actions is his rescinding of the “endangerment” finding by the EPA, that was the core basis for the government to be able to regulate greenhouse gas emissions.
States can also be important leaders in advancing climate action. In that regard, the 2026 election is also very significant in that it produced five new states that now have Democratic “trifectas” (i.e., Democrats control the governorship as well as both chambers of the legislature). Michigan is one of those five states (the others being Minnesota, Nevada, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin).
The existence of Democratic trifectas has become very important, due to the unfortunate shift in the Republican Party under Trump to be against any pro-climate policies.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The Michigan story in that context is very illustrative. Back in 2023, when Michigan had a Democratic trifecta, we passed a very significant legislative “climate” package. It established for the first time a clear state policy relating to climate change, as well as making some important additions to Michigan’s landmark renewable energy and energy efficiency law (PA 295 of 2008).
When Michigan passed that climate policy package in 2023 (PA 235 to strengthen the renewable energy requirement and PA 229 to strengthen the utility energy efficiency standard), not a single Republican voted in support of either of those pieces of legislation. Since the Republicans captured control of the Michigan House of Representatives in 2024, not a single piece of climate-friendly legislation has been passed. Re-establishing a Democratic trifecta in Michigan and those other key states should provide excellent opportunities for advancing pro-climate policies.
Bottom line: We are at a crucial crossroads for the future of this planet. With these outstanding election results, we’ve been given an opportunity to reverse our current path toward a climate crisis. Among the many issues that our newly elected representatives need to deal with, let’s hope that they make sure that one of the priorities is the climate.
Postscript: It is important to note that the primary policy solutions to the climate challenge … renewable energy and energy efficiency … are both cheaper than fossil fuels, and also create more local jobs. So saving the climate is also good economic policy.
Let’s get to it!

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Secretary of State Warner calls for ‘uniformity’ in elections, hints at opening Republican primary
description: The West Virginia Secretary of State all but asked the state GOP to return to open primaries.
text:
An early voting sign sits outside of the Girl Scouts of Black Diamond Council building at 321 Virginia St. W in Charleston, West Virginia, on Oct. 29, 2026. (Photo by Leann Ray/West Virginia Watch)The West Virginia Secretary of State all but asked the state GOP to return to open primaries. 
Secretary of State Kris Warner, a Republican, issued a press release Thursday calling for uniformity in primary elections between the two major parties. He specifically called on his own party to change its primary. 
“The Republican Party has an opportunity to swiftly take-up this issue for the betterment of our State,” Warner said.  
Warner added, “Speaking as Secretary of State, this is not a political issue. If both major political parties in the State don’t have the same rules for primary elections, the voters suffer. Poll workers suffer. Election administration suffers. And ultimately, the public’s trust in our processes and outcomes will be diminished.” 
He said having an open Democratic primary — where unaffiliated or no party voters can cast a ballot — and a closed primary for only registered Republicans may have contributed to low turnout and legal challenges in the May elections. 
“There is a basic principle in elections that the same rules must be fairly applied to everybody,” Warner said in the release. “So when we see not one, but two legal challenges filed as a result of inconsistent standards, it’s a major red flag.” 
The West Virginia Republican Party voted to close its primaries in 2024, with the 2026 cycle being the first time it would take effect. 
The Secretary of State’s Office noted candidates in the GOP primary filed challenges in Fayette and Harrison counties on the basis that non-affiliated voters had been allowed to vote in their primary. A new election had to be ordered in Fayette County, while the Harrison County challenge was resolved on its own. 
“Objectively, it is clear that a lack of uniformity between political party primaries hurts election integrity,” Warner said. “Not only did we see legal challenges based on inconsistent applications of the closed primary rules, but turnout in the 2026 elections was the lowest in over a decade. I suspect that the lack of uniformity is partly to blame for that.”
Warner chalked up issues in the Republican primary to voter and poll worker confusion. 
Turnout in the 2026 primary was the lowest since in more than a decade, according to Warner’s office. 
Warner also mentioned that 42 states have uniform primaries — either all primaries are open to non-affiliated voters or all primaries are closed to only registered party members.
Josh Holstein, a state delegate and chairman of the Republican Party, did not return a request for comment.

title: Ameren plans three more Missouri battery plants
description: Utility company Ameren has received the green light to add a new-to-Missouri type of infrastructure to the electric grid: batteries. The utility is expanding energy storage in the state. It is currently building its first battery facility in Missouri and recently received approval from state regulators for three more. Last month, the Missouri Public Service [...]
text:
(Dana DiFilippo/New Jersey Monitor)Utility company Ameren has received the green light to add a new-to-Missouri type of infrastructure to the electric grid: batteries.
The utility is expanding energy storage in the state. It is currently building its first battery facility in Missouri and recently received approval from state regulators for three more.
Last month, the Missouri Public Service Commission, the state agency that regulates corporate energy companies, approved Ameren’s plans to build two large-scale solar power plants and three battery systems throughout the state.
Ameren’s battery facilities are the first of their kind approved in the state of Missouri, said Sarah Fontaine, the commission’s communications director.
Ameren’s Director of Renewable Development Scott Wibbenmeyer said the new solar and battery energy storage facilities are needed to replace electricity lost from the company’s recently retired coal plants — and to meet the significant power demand from artificial intelligence data centers.
“They’re really critical for us to meet the reliability and energy needs of the state … as we look long-term into the growth in the state, the region and replacing our aging infrastructure … these two facilities work together to really meet that energy need,” he said.
State energy regulators approved the company’s plans to build battery facilities in St. Louis County and Lincoln County and a solar power facility in Stoddard County. Additionally, Ameren is preparing to start construction on a large-scale solar power plant and a battery system to store excess electricity in Audrain County.
The utility’s battery system in Audrain County, named “Huck Finn,” will be built on 22 acres of land. According to the company’s application for the project, the facility will “improve system reliability, support renewable energy integration, reduce reliance on fossil fuels, and enhance overall grid stability and flexibility.”
In total, Ameren received approval to build 545 megawatts of battery capacity and 400 megawatts of solar power generation. By some estimates, one megawatt can power for 600 to 1,000 homes.
In a news release, environmental group the Sierra Club praised Ameren for these investments and said “renewable energy remains the cheapest way to generate electricity.”
“The exciting reality of matching solar and wind with storage is that we can generate electricity during the day and use it at night when the sun goes down,” said Jenn DeRose, Missouri campaign representative for Sierra Club’s Beyond Coal Campaign. “We can power our lives safely and affordably with renewable energy and storage, and we need more of these smart investments in our state.”
The Audrain County solar project, named “Tom Sawyer,” will be built on 1,200 acres of agricultural land that Ameren leased or purchased. This will be the company’s second solar farm in Audrain County. It also operates a gas plant in the area.
Wibbenmeyer said Audrain County has been an “absolute great asset” for the company.
Audrain County Commissioner Alan Winders said while the large-scale solar and gas power plants are taxed locally, the battery storage infrastructure is not.
“It will be state assessed and our taxing jurisdictions will realize very little — very, very, very little — revenue from it,” he said. “So that’s kind of a point of contention.”
The project didn’t require any local government approval, Winders said, but Ameren representatives met with community leaders to answer questions about the projects, including safety measures for the batteries.
“As we’ve looked at really any development project, including energy projects, there are three things that we always insist upon,” he said. “One is that the people of the community are protected. Two is that the infrastructure of the county is protected, and three is that they pay their fair share.”

Revenue from the forthcoming large-scale solar power plant will be split among the local taxing jurisdictions, Winders said, with the local Van-Far R-1 School District receiving the largest share.
 Battery safety



At public hearings throughout the state, Missouri residents raised concerns about the safety of the relatively new technology of large-scale batteries. Similar facilities have experienced lithium battery fires that are difficult to put out.


“It’s just a technology that we’re not familiar with here, so we’re trusting that you will do your part in terms of vetting the safety of these sorts of things,” Winders told Ameren officials at a public hearing in Vandalia in July.


Wibbenmeyer said Ameren is working to communicate with the communities where they’re building to “reduce some of that anxiety or fear” around large-scale batteries. He said the company will install large water tanks on the battery facility site for use by local fire departments in an emergency.


“Part of what we do with any project is one: we meet with fire departments. We do full assessments on what is the fire risk for our particular design and then what do the fire workers have? What do they need to meet that response?” Wibbenmeyer said. “How do we blend in our emergency response plan with a county response emergency plan?”
 Power for AI



Some state officials, including Geoff Marke, a chief economist for the Office of Public Counsel, the state’s utility consumer advocate, have raised concerns the new power facilities are solely for the benefit of power-hungry AI data centers.


“To be clear, the only reason we need to purchase excess solar generation and complementary battery storage systems at this moment in time and under these inflated prices is to meet the need for projected data center load,” Marke said in testimony before the Missouri Public Service Commission.


When regulated monopolies such as Ameren build power plants and upgrade infrastructure, the company can later come before the Missouri Public Service Commission and ask to recoup the costs of those investments through their customer’s utility bills.


Marke said the cost of power plants built to meet new demand from hyperscale data centers should not be borne by residential electricity customers in Missouri.


“Absent a firm commitment for participating data centers to put up the funds to cover the entire costs of the project, I do not believe it is prudent for Ameren Missouri to move forward with these projects,” he said.


State energy leaders have set goals to produce more than double the amount of power Missouri currently makes — in part to meet the needs of existing and future AI data centers. Repeatedly in his testimony, Marke cautioned against what he called “overbuilding for a wildly unpopular industry that is seemingly bleeding money.”


Ameren predicts electricity demand from data centers “will result in a roughly 60% increase” in the company’s energy needs.


Wibbenmeyer called Marke’s concerns about overbuilding for the AI industry “a fair thing to watch and monitor.” But he said Missouri is in “a really good spot” thanks to lawmakers passing data center regulations last year.


“Our legislators got ahead of this with Senate Bill 4 and really put one of the leading laws into place that requires by law for those data centers to pay for their fair share,” Wibbenmeyer said.


How the costs of Ameren’s new solar power plants and battery storage facilities are spread out among customers will be decided when the company aims to recoup the cost of these investments in a future rate case before the Missouri Public Service Commission.
This story was originally published by KBIA.

name: South Carolina Daily Gazette
title: SC man sentenced to prison time for flying drone over prison yard
description: The 47-year-old from Sumter pleaded guilty to operating an unregistered drone and will spent the next year in federal prison.
text:
A man from Sumter was sentenced to a year in prison after pleading guilty to operating an unregistered drone over a prison yard. (Photo courtesy of South Carolina Department of Corrections)COLUMBIA — A Sumter man will spend just over a year in federal prison after pleading guilty to flying a drone over a state prison yard, a federal judge decided Thursday.
U.S. District Judge Richard Gergel sentenced Quinzell Robinson, 47, to one year and one day after he pleaded guilty to operating an unregistered aircraft, which violates Federal Aviation Administration laws, according to the U.S. attorney’s office.
Early in the morning of March 14, 2025, police received reports of a drone flying over Lieber Correctional Facility in Ridgeville. Officers spotted Robinson leaving the woods with a drone and a bag, and security footage later showed inmates retrieving a package dropped in the prison yard.
Bill banning drones from flying too close to prisons, military installations advances in SC Senate

Flight data on Robinson’s drone showed it flying over the same spot where the package landed at the same time, according to prosecutors.
Robinson’s cellphone had photos and videos of the high-security prison, as well as text messages with an inmate about delivering contraband using drones.
“Correctional facilities cannot safely operate when individuals on the outside coordinate with inmates to deliver contraband over prison fences using drones,” said U.S. Attorney Bryan Stirling, who has personal experience as the previous head of the state’s prison system. “This case sends a clear message that those who attempt to use technology to undermine prison security will be investigated, prosecuted, and held accountable for their actions.”
A law passed unanimously by legislators earlier this year strengthens state penalties for flying a drone over a prison. It takes effect Jan. 1, 2027.
Since 2018, anyone convicted of flying a drone too close to a prison could face up to 30 days in jail. But law enforcement officers told legislators the law lacked teeth, allowing many people to escape prosecution.
The new law expanded the punishments to as many as six months in prison for a first offense, one year for a second offense, and two years for any further offenses.
Using the drone to deliver contraband or to map out a prison in an effort to find security gaps could face up to five years in prison.
