name: West Virginia Watch
title: Gov. Morrisey announces multibillion-dollar investment in West Virginia power plants
description: Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday a $24 billion investment by Appalachian Power into natural gas and coal fire power plants throughout the state.
text:
John E. Amos Power Plant, seen in June 2013, is a coal-fired plant owned and operated by Appalachian Power, a subsidiary of American Electric Power in Winfield, West Virginia. (Getty Images)Gov. Patrick Morrisey announced Thursday a $24 billion investment by Appalachian Power into natural gas and coal-fired power plants throughout the state. 
Appalachian Power, which serves most of the state south of Sutton and parts of the Northern Panhandle, will invest $17 billion into new natural gas generation, generating 3.3 gigawatts — enough to power 2.4 million homes for a year. 
The project is expected to create a little more than 2,000 construction jobs and 100 permanent jobs. It will be completed in 2031. Morrisey said in a video announcement that there are three plans for projects that will be “geographically dispersed” across the state. 
Location and further details will be forthcoming, he said. 
Additionally, Appalachia Power will be investing $7.5 billion into its coal plants to keep them operational until 2050. The company currently owns three coal-fired plants in the state: John Amos in Winfield, Mountaineer in New Haven and Mitchell in Moundsville. 
The projects will “increase energy supply to lower costs,” Morrisey said. 
The governor said the projects will not be paid for by customers. 
“Power bills will not go up; they must not go up because of these new additions,” Morrisey said. “And we’ve been assured that they will not. And I will look to enforce that any way I can.” 
Emmett Pepper, policy director of Energy Efficient West Virginia, a consumer advocacy group focused on electricity billing, said he wants to see more details. 
“First Energy has a proposal for a gas plant. It’s not good for the rate payers,” he said. 
That proposal, in Monongalia County, is for a $2.5 billion gas plant that residents say will result in higher power bills.

name: Iowa Capital Dispatch
title: Commentary: The Sand trap: Will Rob Sand become the next Chet Culver?
description: Gov.-elect Rob Sand may have just been handed the keys to Terrace Hill in a situation reminiscent of the last Democrat to hold the office, the one-termer Chet Culver. During the Great Recession, Culver faced massive budget shortfalls, rising unemployment and declining revenues. He made deep spending cuts that proved unpopular and became a political […]
text:
Gov.-Elect Rob Sand. (Photo by Robin Opsahl/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Gov.-elect Rob Sand may have just been handed the keys to Terrace Hill in a situation reminiscent of the last Democrat to hold the office, the one-termer Chet Culver.
During the Great Recession, Culver faced massive budget shortfalls, rising unemployment and declining revenues. He made deep spending cuts that proved unpopular and became a political liability in his unsuccessful 2010 re-election campaign.
Sand faces his own financial peril. He inherits the consequences of years of deliberate tax reductions that have substantially reduced state revenue and limited the money available for government services. With Republicans controlling both chambers of the Legislature, Sand will have to be a world-class negotiator if he’s going to keep his promises to help struggling Iowans.
In October 2009, after state revenue estimates plunged, Culver ordered a 10% across-the-board reduction in covered state appropriations to keep the budget balanced. The cuts totaled about $564 million. They hit virtually everything, including typically sacred education and public safety budgets.
K–12 education lost about $238.5 million in state foundation aid, along with a $49.4 million reduction in state support for special education. School districts, already struggling with the recession, faced another round of painful financial decisions.
Culver took a huge political hit and ultimately lost his job to former Gov. Terry Branstad in 2010.
Voters tend to hold governors responsible for the condition of their state, even when the governor doesn’t control all the decisions that created the problems. Sand takes his turn in the crucible in January. And he won’t have much wiggle room.
A decade of Republican control of the executive and legislative branches effectively tied off and padlocked the purse strings, sealed them in an iron vault and dropped them in the deepest spot of the Des Moines River.
Iowa’s 3.8% flat individual income tax, which took effect in 2025, is part of a series of tax reductions that have substantially reduced state revenue.
The state collected about $635 million less in general fund revenue in the 2026 fiscal year than it did the year before. Meanwhile, projected revenue for the 2027 fiscal year is approximately $1.11 billion below the state’s budgeted spending. Assuming modest revenue growth and no spending increases, that gap would narrow to approximately $820 million in the 2028 fiscal year.
Those gaps cannot be attributed entirely to the flat tax. But the tax reductions have contributed to the state’s revenue pressures.
To be fair, the outgoing governor, Kim Reynolds, and Republican budget officials have argued that the reductions were deliberate and that Iowa accumulated billions of dollars in reserves to help finance the transition to lower income taxes.
At the close of the 2026 fiscal year, the state’s Taxpayer Relief Fund held approximately $3.2 billion, with another $1.6 billion in its ending balance. Those reserves give Sand and lawmakers some breathing room.
But reserves are not an endless source of money. Eventually, recurring revenue and recurring spending have to come closer together. That will make any new initiatives Sand proposes all the more difficult.
Urban and rural areas face challenges
Iowans, urban and rural, have different problems, and all of them are looking to the state for help. Growing urban and suburban counties face rising housing costs, development pressures, changing demographics and increasing demand for schools, roads and public services. Meanwhile, many rural counties struggle with population loss, aging residents, declining school enrollment, long bus routes and difficulty recruiting teachers.
Urban hospitals face demands for behavioral health care, emergency services and the costs of treating patients who cannot pay. Rural hospitals face questions about their survival, shortages of doctors and nurses, ambulance coverage and longer travel distances for patients.
Growth demands new infrastructure in urban and suburban counties. Across rural Iowa, the challenge is maintaining thousands of miles of secondary roads, aging bridges and water systems with limited resources. Broadband access remains a challenge in some rural communities, even as statewide coverage improves. And water quality is everybody’s problem.
Urban areas struggle with flooding, stormwater runoff and drinking water contamination. Rural counties face agricultural runoff, soil conservation needs and increasingly expensive damage from extreme weather.
Don’t look to local governments to solve these problems on their own. The Reynolds administration and the Republican-controlled Legislature have already tightened restrictions on local governments’ ability to raise revenue.
A property tax law passed this year generally limits annual growth in revenue from certain city and county property tax levies to 2%, with exceptions, including new construction. The nonpartisan Legislative Services Agency estimates the cap could cost Iowa cities approximately $103.7 million in property tax revenue over its first four budget years.
Other provisions of the law, including an expanded homestead exemption and changes to state reimbursements, could further reduce local government revenue.
Earlier Republican legislation also restricted when local governments can hold bond referendums, generally requiring those elections to take place in November.
Cities must figure out how to provide services to growing populations while facing new limits on property tax revenue. Rural communities must try to maintain essential services with stagnant or shrinking tax bases. And communities with little new construction may have an even harder time making up lost revenue than fast-growing suburbs.
Thes problems all share one need: money. Where Sand is going to get that money may well be the question that defines his governorship.
Iowans sent state government a clear message about income taxes in November. By a margin of roughly 56% to 44%, voters approved a state constitutional amendment requiring a two-thirds majority in both chambers of the Legislature to increase individual or corporate income tax rates or establish new state income taxes.
Everybody needs something from state government. Nobody wants to pay for it — a classic American dilemma.
The burden now lands squarely on Sand’s shoulders. If the governor-elect doesn’t figure something out, he could become the next one-termer in a state that adores long-serving governors.
Good luck and godspeed, Gov.-elect Sand.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: Beshear tells Trump to nix RFK Jr., pick health secretary without ‘a worm in their brain’
description: Kentucky Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear told Republican President Donald Trump that Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has got to go.  Beshear announced in a Thursday press conference he sent the president a letter dated Nov. 12 asking him to immediately remove Kennedy from his post, adding the secretary is “woefully […]
text:
U.S.  Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. came to Lexington on Aug. 5, 2026 to announce the decertification of a Kentucky organ donation group, Network For Hope. (Kentucky Lantern photo by Linda Blackford)Kentucky Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear told Republican President Donald Trump that Secretary of Health and Human Services Robert F. Kennedy Jr. has got to go. 
Beshear announced in a Thursday press conference he sent the president a letter dated Nov. 12 asking him to immediately remove Kennedy from his post, adding the secretary is “woefully unqualified” and “is putting American lives at risk.” The request comes as Kentucky and the nation are experiencing an outbreak of measles. As of Thursday, Kentucky had more than 200 cases of measles. 
Beshear said Kentucky has had more cases of measles this year than the last 35 years combined. He also pointed to the U.S. experiencing spikes in foodborne illnesses and whooping cough this year. In September, Kennedy told members of an anti-vaccine group they would have “a strong and steadfast friend at the White House.”
“Elections are good barometers of public opinion and the results of last Tuesday’s elections are clear: The American people want change from your Administration,” Beshear wrote to Trump. Democrats are set to regain control of the U.S. House and Senate in January after midterm elections. 
Later in response to questions, Beshear said “somebody who has resurrected measles in the United States certainly shouldn’t continue in this role.” The U.S. had eliminated measles 26 years ago, but that official designation could be removed by a panel of scientific experts meeting this week. 
The governor said he had not discussed the possibility of impeaching Kennedy with Kentucky’s federal delegation, but he’d support it. Beshear added that he is asking Trump to “just do the right thing to not have to go there.” 
“Just choose someone qualified. Choose someone who will give actual medical advice about vaccines. Choose somebody that won’t spread conspiracies,” Beshear said, before continuing to list issues with Kennedy. 
“How about this? Choose somebody that doesn’t have a worm in their brain. Choose somebody that didn’t put a dead bear in the back of their car and drive into New York City, choose somebody that didn’t put a whale head on top of his car and drive somewhere else. Choose somebody that didn’t swim in a polluted creek with one of their grandchildren. Choose somebody that didn’t snort cocaine off a dirty toilet at one part in their life,” Beshear said. “Just choose somebody better than this clown.”
Asked about Beshear’s letter, a White House official pointed to Trump encouraging vaccinations in 2025 and discussing vaccinations at a Medicaid MFN (most-favored-nation) event. There Trump said he would like to further space out shots during the childhood vaccination schedule, media reports say.   
“President Trump and Secretary Kennedy have both stated that vaccination is the best way to prevent measles infections,” said White House spokesperson Allison Schuster. “In response to outbreaks, the President and Secretary have repeatedly encouraged measles vaccination, coordinated with states, and facilitated the deployment of vaccine doses across the country.”
Beshear, who is considering a run for president in 2028, said he also believes the president should fire Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth, who faced an impeachment effort this week led by outgoing U.S. Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Kentucky. Massie’s articles of impeachment alleged Hegseth waged unlawful war against Iran. The congressman lost his primary earlier this year to Trump-endorsed Ed Gallrein, who later won the general election. A failed procedural vote effectively blocked the effort until the new Congress convenes in January. 
“I was saddened by the recent vote on Pete Hegseth. It was brought by a Republican, yet every other congressional Republican ended up defending the war in Iran, the current Secretary of Defense and the President, and they had just lost by a historical margin because of it,” Beshear said. “I’d hope that maybe losing a job would help them grow a spine, but apparently we’re not seeing that.”

name: New Jersey Monitor
title: New NJ law aims to better protect domestic violence and stalking victims
description: The law requires social media and communications companies to more quickly comply with search warrants in domestic violence and stalking cases.
text:
Supporters of a law signed by Gov. Mikie Sherrill on Thursday say it will help the justice system keep up with the digital age. (Photo by Anne-Marie Caruso/New Jersey Monitor)Gov. Mikie Sherrill signed a new law Thursday meant to help domestic violence and stalking victims by requiring social media and communications companies to more quickly comply with investigators’ search warrants seeking digital information.
The new law amends the New Jersey Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Control Act to require social media platforms to respond within 72 hours of receiving search warrants related to investigations of domestic abuse, stalking, and violations of protective orders. Providers of phone, internet, and other communications get five business days to comply.
Assemblywomen Marisa Sweeney (D-Morris), Heather Simmons (D-Gloucester), and Luanne Peterpaul (D-Monmouth) sponsored the measure.
“For victims of domestic violence and stalking, every day spent waiting for information can feel like an eternity,” Sweeney said in a statement. “We know that sometimes the most critical evidence is stored online, and when investigators can’t get to that information quickly, it can slow down the efforts in place to protect victims and stop abuse before it escalates even more.”
Peterpaul said the new law helps the justice system keep up with the digital age.
“While digitization has changed the way crimes are committed, it must also change the way they are investigated,” Peterpaul said in a statement.
The law is modeled after “Kristil’s Law” in Oregon, which lawmakers passed earlier this year. That law was inspired by Kristil Krug, whose husband Daniel digitally stalked, harassed, and impersonated her ex-boyfriend before murdering her in their Colorado home in 2023.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: NH House Democrats nominate Simpson to be next speaker ahead of Dec. 2 vote
description: Rep. Alexis Simpson, who has led the New Hampshire House Democrats as minority leader for two years, is the caucus’ pick for speaker of the House. House Democrats met in Concord Thursday to vote on who to rally behind to lead the chamber. On Dec. 2, the entire New Hampshire House of Representatives will meet […]
text:
Democratic House Leader Alexis Simpson speaks to reporters Nov. 12, 2026, immediately after her caucus voted to nominate her as speaker of the House. The full chamber will meet on Dec. 2 to officially elect the position. (Photo by William Skipworth/New Hampshire Bulletin)Rep. Alexis Simpson, who has led the New Hampshire House Democrats as minority leader for two years, is the caucus’ pick for speaker of the House.
House Democrats met in Concord Thursday to vote on who to rally behind to lead the chamber. On Dec. 2, the entire New Hampshire House of Representatives will meet to officially elect the speaker. After Democrats won a supermajority in last week’s elections, the party controls who holds the speaker’s gavel. Thursday’s meeting was an attempt by Democrats to get on the same page before the final vote. Still, fractures have emerged within the party in recent weeks after Rep. Jim Maggiore, a former Republican candidate who now represents North Hampton as a Democrat, unsuccessfully challenged her for the role and rallied a group of supporters unhappy with Simpson’s leadership.
The final vote was 200-75.
Simpson is a Christian minister who represents Exeter. This will be her fifth term in the House. Simpson’s priorities as a lawmaker have typically aligned with that of her party at large: protecting abortion rights, opposing Republicans’ education freedom account program and funding the state’s Housing Champions program, for instance.
“When the people in this room knocked on thousands and thousands and thousands of doors, and they know their constituents, they bring those conversations and those stories with them,” Simpson said. “And we know that people are struggling, needing lower property taxes, needing more affordable housing, needing to lower the cost of childcare, and to find accessible, affordable childcare throughout the state. So those are just a few things that we will be working on.”
She said that starts with the upcoming budget and will be working with her team in the coming weeks on the spending plan.
Her pitch to fellow representatives relied on her previous leadership. She argued that she and her team had spent the last two years preparing for this moment and were ready to put the party’s agenda in motion. Maggiore cast Simpson as an uncollaborative leader and argued he would do a better job of gathering input from the entire caucus. Maggiore’s voting record became a point of contention. The former Republican was one of few Democrats to vote in favor of Medicaid work requirements, cutting the Office of the Child Advocate budget and tabling a minimum wage increase, among other things.
Asked about the criticisms of her leadership style, Simpson said she was “sorry that that debate took place” but is “going to spend some more time thinking about that” and contended that she has “always had a collaborative approach.” She said she’ll “make an extra special effort to reach out to those who have felt that way.”
The speaker’s wide-ranging duties include presiding over votes, making committee assignments and controlling how bills work their way through the Legislative process. The speaker also serves as the leader of the chamber and caucus. That includes administrative tasks such as hiring and managing House staff, but it also means leading negotiations with the Senate or governor’s office at times and setting the tone for how the chamber will operate. With a whopping majority totaling 291 Democrats (pending recounts), she’ll likely face challenges finding consensus at times and could see intraparty factions she’ll have to mediate.
Simpson characterized that as a positive, saying the caucus was “a big tent even when we were a smaller caucus, and so we have experience with ideological diversity that we’ll lean on.”
While the goal Thursday was to coalesce around one candidate, it’s possible that last-minute jockeying over the position will continue heading into December’s full chamber vote.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan’s US Senate results challenge the claim that criticism of Israel alienates Jewish voters
description: As Jewish voters overwhelmingly supported Democratic candidates in last week’s midterm elections, new polling data shows that the Democratic Party’s Jewish support was not an outlier and likely won’t change anytime soon. At the same time, growing opposition to unconditional U.S. support for Israel could create opportunities for Democratic candidates in 2028 [...]
text:
Former Wayne County Health Director Abdul El-Sayed speaks at a primary election night watch party in Detroit, Mich., on Aug. 4, 2026. (Photo by Andrew Roth/Michigan Advance)As Jewish voters overwhelmingly supported Democratic candidates in last week’s midterm elections, new polling data shows that the Democratic Party’s Jewish support was not an outlier and likely won’t change anytime soon. At the same time, growing opposition to unconditional U.S. support for Israel could create opportunities for Democratic candidates in 2028 who take a more critical approach to the Israeli government’s policies. 
Polling data released after the election by J Street, a progressive Jewish organization that advocates for a two-state peace solution between Israel and Palestinians, indicated that 72% of Jewish voters cast ballots for Democrats in the 2026 midterm election. That number has remained consistent compared with past cycles. The organization’s polling also found that 70% opposed unconditional U.S. aid to Israel. That’s comparable to the 68% who in 2022 said they supported restricting aid if it expanded Israeli settlements in the West Bank.
The survey of 800 self-identified Jewish voters was conducted by GBAO Strategies from Oct. 28 to Nov. 3 among those who cast their ballots on Election Day or prior to Election Day. It has a margin of error of +/- 3.5 percentage points.
J Street polling data on Jewish voters opinions in the 2026 midterm election about aid to Israel. (J Street PowerPoint)
Jewish voters remain reliably Democratic, even as views on U.S. aid to Israel shift
Some 2026 candidates were critical of the Israeli government over conflicts with its Arab neighbors, as well as the outsized spending against them from the American Israel Public Affairs Committee, or AIPAC, including U.S. Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan. 
That stance exacerbated tensions among Michigan Jewish Democrats, some of whom called for voters in the U.S. Senate race to leave their ballots blank or vote instead for the Republican nominee, former U.S. Rep. Mike Rogers. Although J Street did not specifically poll Michigan’s U.S. Senate race, Tali deGroot, the group’s vice president for digital and political strategy, said those factors did not sway Jewish voters in Michigan from supporting El-Sayed.
“The vast majority of Jews voted for Democrats across the country,” deGroot said. “It was just another chapter, ‘Will the American Jewish community abandon the Democratic Party?’ And the answer is no. The American Jewish vote is a reliably Democratic vote.”
Tali deGroot, vice president of digital and political strategy at J Street. (Photo courtesy of J Street)
In terms of the moral conflict that faced American Jews at the ballot box this year, deGroot said “American Jews support a relationship with Israel that is grounded in values and shared interest.”
Few races better illustrated those tensions than El-Sayed’s contest against Rogers, following a contentious Democratic primary against U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens (D-Birmingham) that appeared, at least on the surface, to damage his standing with some Michigan Jewish voters. But once all the votes were counted, El-Sayed defeated Rogers by 7 percentage points, a much wider margin compared to the Senate race between U.S. Sen. Elissa Slotkin (D-Holly) and Rogers in 2024, which was within a single percentage point in a Republican wave election. 
An analysis by Millions of Michiganians, the super PAC for Progress Michigan, a nonprofit that supports progressive policies, found that El-Sayed’s share of the vote in 72 precincts with large Jewish populations was just 1.3 percentage points lower than Slotkin’s share in those same precincts in 2024.
That said, Jim Gerstein, the principal at GBAO, in a call last week presenting J Street’s polling data, cautioned against looking at precinct-level data in areas with a large Jewish voting population as a way to distill how the community voted in the 2026 election.
“These precinct level data, they also have non-Jews in those precincts, so we don’t know which way those votes went and what percentage of those were moved by Jewish voters versus the larger number of people in those precincts that are not Jewish,” Gerstein said. “The other thing is, in the precincts where they are overwhelmingly Jewish, those Jews are going to have different perspectives than Jews who live in less Jewish-dominated precincts.”
Millions of Michiganians also argued that El-Sayed performed well among Jewish voters despite an active campaign by Nonnegotiable Michigan. The coalition of rabbis and Michigan Jews said they could not vote for El-Sayed unless he publicly recognized the right of Israel to exist as a Jewish state, and ensured the safety of American Jews if elected. Nonnegotiable also championed a write-in campaign for “Emma Lazarus,” a 19th-century author and Jewish political activist.
Jewish groups disagreed over what the election results showed
Millions of Michiganians noted that there were only 470 anti-El-Sayed write-in votes across the 72 precincts that it polled, and just 253 undervotes, meaning that less than 0.25% of total voters in the governor’s race, decisively won by Democrat Jocelyn Benson, chose to leave the ballot blank for El-Sayed. 
Nonnegotiable Michigan represented Michigan Jews who opposed El-Sayed, but deGroot said that opposition represented only a small portion of Jewish voters who considered Israel a top issue. She believed El-Sayed did well to shift his general election campaign away from Israel and AIPAC toward “the issues that affect the vast majority of Michiganders: affordability, healthcare, cost of gas, issues that the American Jewish community is actually voting on.”
That notion tracks with the J Street polling, which indicated that the future of democracy and the cost of living were by far the top concerns for Jewish voters, at 44% and 34% respectively, while policy toward Israel stood at just 14%.
J Street polling data on top priorities for Jewish voters in the 2026 midterm election. (J Street PowerPoint)
Debbie Rosenman, a member of the progressive Michigan Indivisible Fighting 9 activist group, supported El-Sayed because of his progressive values and the issues he championed. Rosenman said Jewish voters like her shared those values and voted accordingly.
David Kramer, a Democratic fundraiser and member of Nonnegotiable Michigan who ended up publicly supporting Rogers, said he had “zero regrets” about the stance he and other Jewish Democrats had taken during the election.
“I think that we spoke from a point of moral clarity and a position of caring about Jewish safety and security, and our place in the community,” Kramer said. “Even though Abdul failed to meet us on those points, we still put an important marker down, and it’s a template for other candidates and for other elected officials. It was never about just one race and one person.”
Israel policy could reshape the Democratic coalition heading into 2028
While there was no way to avoid the U.S.-Israel relationship being a political football in the years to come, deGroot warned candidates and outside groups against the “instrumentalization and weaponization” of the Jewish vote, because the data shows that younger American Jewish voters are becoming more progressive, and are shifting toward ending military aid to Israel.
“Something we found in this cycle is that a candidate’s willingness to buck AIPAC was an indication of their general willingness to buck the status quo, and I expect that to continue,” deGroot said. “Voters want to see candidates say the status quo is not right, and we’re going to change it.”
Rosenman said that Jews who supported El-Sayed could easily transfer their support to another progressive candidate in the presidential election if they had preconditions on the U.S.-Israel relationship. That was especially true if that presidential candidate possessed qualities they saw in El-Sayed, like his ability to communicate complex issues.
State of the Race: Democratic U.S. Senate race pits old guard, vanguard in battle for party’s soul

Rosenman also said that many American Jews were waiting to give the Israeli government a chance to reform itself before they fully agreed to completely reexamine its ties. That could depend in part on the outcome of Israel’s recent parliamentary elections, which left Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s governing bloc short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset. Opposition parties and Arab-led parties collectively won enough seats to prevent Netanyahu’s bloc from securing a majority, leaving the formation of a new governing coalition uncertain. 
If Netanyahu were to lose power, Rosenman said progressive Jews like her could be more “patient” with Israel if it becomes more “open-minded and responsive to the needs of the Israeli people and their neighbors.”
Another factor is El-Sayed’s performance as a senator, and if he can deliver on his baseline promises for healthcare and ending the corrupting influence of money in politics.
“I think there were a lot of people who were elected who he can find partners with, and so we’re going to be watching him,” Rosenman said. “And based on how he does, or what the impression is of how he’s doing, that will have an effect on how people feel, because I don’t think Jewish voters are changing their values.”

name: Mississippi Today
title: National Folk Festival brings wide sweep of traditions to Jackson
description: Local bluesman Eddie Cotton Jr. poses at a Mississippi Blues Trail marker honoring his legacy, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Clinton. Cotton will be performing at the 83rd National Folk Festival in downtown Jackson this weekend.
text:
For centuries, the customs and traditions of the Choctaw nation have been passed from one generation to the next. About two decades ago, William Dan Isaac, a member of the tribe’s Mississippi band, helped form the Mystic Winds Social Dance Group to hand down traditions of dance, music and storytelling to Choctaw youth. 
The endeavor not only exposed Choctaw youth to the wider world but also shared their culture and traditions across other communities.
Another opportunity comes this weekend when Mystic Winds joins dozens of other groups for the 83rd National Folk Festival, which returns Friday and runs through the weekend in downtown Jackson.
This year’s festival commemorates the country’s founding 250 years ago, but Mystic Winds provides a reminder of the Indigenous cultures that existed across the Mississippi River valley before Europeans settled the area.
Members of the Mystic Winds Social Dance Group, which will perform at the 83rd National Folk Festival in Jackson.  Credit: Courtesy of William Dan Isaac
“A lot of our people were removed from here,” Isaac said. “But the state itself, its rivers and creeks and the names of the counties, hold our roots here.”
Taking part in this year’s folk festival, he said, will “honor and share this connection to our homeland.”
The festival showcases early Indigenous and African American traditions alongside folk traditions from Hawaii and the U.S. Virgin Islands, offering “a snapshot of the nation’s cultural fabric” woven over two and half centuries, said Blaine Wade, the executive director of the National Council for the Traditional Arts, which puts on the national festival. 
“I cannot think of a better place to celebrate America at 250 than Mississippi,” he said.
“You cannot tell the story of American popular music, and really cultural achievement, from food to music, literature – all forms of artistic expression – without Mississippi,” Wade said. 
Last year’s inaugural Jackson gathering, organizers said, was the first time the festival has taken place in the Deep South.
The festival features genres that span the blues and hip-hop to country, as well as other traditions such as Brazilian capoeira, Cajun, Filipino rondalla, Mardi Gras Indian and Texan conjunto.
“A few years back we were invited to the B.B. King Museum,” Isaac recalled, noting a connection between the “call and response” pattern of blues and the rhythm of native stomp dancing the Choctaw call “chahta hihla.” 
Geno Lee poses for a portrait outside the Big Apple Inn on Farish Street in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. Geno will be taking part in a food panel during the National Folk Festival. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Geno Lee, the fourth-generation owner of the Big Apple Inn on Farish Street, usually arrives at events as a vendor selling food, but this time he’ll be more directly part of the festivities when he offers a food demonstration on the Mississippi Folklife Narrative Stage on Saturday. 
“Folk history is passed down through stories,” Lee said, and this festival is important because “it centers on stories passed down through music and culinary traditions.” 
There are ancillary events outside of the festival, such as the art museum’s exhibition featuring Tom Pich’s portraits of folk masters, which runs until January, and a community block party Thursday that runs until 3 p.m. at the Medgar and Myrlie Evers Home National Monument. 
“We also see how business owners within the festival’s footprint” benefit from the increased foot traffic, said Thabi Moyo, a Jackson native serving as a local festival manager. 
The Rookery, an event space a couple blocks from the new Shivers Creek Catfish House on East Capitol Street, will host an open house during festival hours. Tony Davenport, a visual artist and educator from Vicksburg, will be a part of the festival’s marketplace. He has one of his largest murals in the Rookery.
Eddie Cotton Jr., who lives in Clinton, is a nationally recognized blues musician who has performed at several national folk festivals.
Local bluesman Eddie Cotton Jr. poses with his guitar, Wednesday, Nov. 11, 2026, in Clinton. Cotton will be performing at the 83rd National Folk Festival in downtown Jackson this weekend. Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
“I’ve played in Richmond, Virginia, and Maryland, even drove to Montana,” said Cotton. “I’ve seen a lot in my career traveling for 30 years, but there’s nothing like playing at home.”
Cotton said the festival is good at bringing in talented artists who represent different cultures. “I’ve seen amazing Japanese musicians, and I didn’t know what they were saying, but you see the authenticity and can tell they are the best at what they do.” 
Raiatea Helm is one such master of her craft, having gained international fame performing traditional Hawaiian falsetto. “From the early 1900s Hawaiian bands were traveling with string, brass, and woodwind instruments,” Helm said. 
Noting the influence of the lap steel guitar, a traditional Hawaiian instrument, on early blues music, Helm said that Hawaii has long had a presence in Mississippi. 
“It’s my first time visiting Mississippi,” Helm said, but the musical traditions she participates in and “the stories of our ancestors passed down in them” spread across the country long ago.

title: Iowa Board of Regents approves first steps in UNI president search
description: The Iowa Board of Regents has approved a national search to replace the University of Northern Iowa’s leader as President Mark Nook prepares for retirement. Board Counsel Aimee Claeys said during the Nov. 12 board meeting that with board approval, which was given unanimously, board staff will seek applicants Friday for potential search-firm partners and […]
text:
University of Northern Iowa President Mark Nook speaks to the Iowa Board of Regents on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)The Iowa Board of Regents has approved a national search to replace the University of Northern Iowa’s leader as President Mark Nook prepares for retirement.
Board Counsel Aimee Claeys said during the Nov. 12 board meeting that with board approval, which was given unanimously, board staff will seek applicants Friday for potential search-firm partners and also begin developing a search committee.
“We fully anticipate that this search will follow the cadence and process that we have used quite successfully in recent searches,” Claeys said, referring to the search that ended with David Cook being selected as Iowa State University’s new president in 2025.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
On Oct. 23, Nook announced his plans to retire at the end of the 2026-2027 academic year, with the promise of staying on until a new president is chosen and comes to campus.
Claeys, joined by board Chief Academic Officer Rachel Boon and Senior Communications Director Josh Lehman, will “spearhead” the search with board staff, she said, and will work with search committee chairs to establish a timeline for the search process.
The goal is to have a new president on campus by the end of Nook’s contract period on July 1, 2027, Claeys said, by bringing finalist selections to the board during its April meeting on the UNI campus.
Nook will have spent a decade at the Cedar Falls university as its president by the time he retires, with the president saying in his announcement that serving UNI and Iowa has been “one of the greatest privileges” he’s had.
“We’ll have … another opportunity in our next meeting or two to say all the nice things about President Nook, but we do appreciate all your work,” Board President Robert Cramer said.

title: Swastika found on Hartford veterans monument on Veterans Day
description:
The monument honors Hartford residents who served in the Korean War, the Vietnam War and the post-1975 era.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Swastika found on Hartford veterans monument on Veterans Day.
text:
A swastika seen on Veterans Day on the side of a monument honoring Hartford residents who served in conflicts after World War II. Alex Ebrahimi/Valley News

This story by Alex Ebrahimi was first published in the Valley News on November 11, 2026
WHITE RIVER JUNCTION — A swastika drawn in what appeared to be black marker was visible on a monument in Veterans Park on Veterans Day.
The graffiti was on the park’s newer monument, which honors Hartford residents who served in the Korean War, the Vietnam War and the post-1975 era. It was dedicated on Memorial Day this year and completed the work of the Hartford Monument Committee. The park’s other monument, which honors the town’s World War I and World War II veterans and was installed in 2024, was not vandalized.
Last week, a flagpole was installed in the park, completing the Eagle Scout project of a 16-year-old Hartford High School sophomore.
The Hartford Police Department did not respond to phone calls and an email as of Wednesday afternoon.
Vermont recorded 137 antisemitic incidents between 2021 and 2025, according to ADL New England’s annual Audit of Antisemitic Incidents. Vandalism made up 33% of those incidents, and swastikas appeared in 53% of the state’s vandalism cases.
Similar vandalism happened recently across the Connecticut River from Hartford.

READ MORE

In September, swastikas and a “Heil Hitler” message were spray-painted at several sites in Lebanon, including near Ledyard Charter School on the Lebanon Mall, a Water Street parking lot, Logan Field and a cemetery on Dulac Street. The first report came in on Sept. 13, the last day of Rosh Hashanah. Lebanon police said they had surveillance footage of two juvenile suspects and that the vandalism appeared to be an isolated act, not the work of an organized group.

title: Trump administration pursues a second round in the courts on birthright citizenship
description: WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia on Thursday seemed weary of the Trump administration’s arguments that it should be allowed to proceed with its second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship. During the hearing, Judge Christopher Reid Cooper pressed Department of Justice attorneys to clarify when the sec[...]
text: WASHINGTON — A federal judge in the District of Columbia on Thursday seemed weary of the Trump administration’s arguments that it should be allowed to proceed with its second attempt to redefine the constitutional right to birthright citizenship. During the hearing, Judge Christopher Reid Cooper pressed Department of Justice attorneys to clarify when the second executive order went into effect, because no date was included when President Donald Trump signed his executive order in August. Cooper also questioned the advocacy groups that brought the suit, led by the American Civil Liberties Union, if he should make a decision on whether to grant a preliminary injunction or wait, as he was concerned about issuing a ruling that would be redundant because there is a similar case out of Maryland. He noted that the judge who handled the first challenge to the president's executive order in 2025 was also presiding over the second attempt and had more knowledge about the issue.This is the Trump administration’s second try at curbing birthright citizenship. In June, the U.S. Supreme Court struck down the president's executive order that would deny citizenship to babies born to parents who were either in the United States on a temporary visa or were immigrants without legal status. The case was brought by the ACLU, ACLU of New Hampshire, ACLU of Maine, ACLU of Massachusetts, ACLU of the District of Columbia, Legal Defense Fund, Asian Law Caucus and Democracy Defenders Fund. They are representing immigrants and their children who could be subject to the new executive order, and the groups previously challenged the first executive order relating to birthright citizenship. Trump’s recent executive orders would deny citizenship to babies born in the United States to parents deemed part of a designated terrorist organization and to parents who purposefully came to the United States to gain citizenship in what critics call “birth tourism.” The executive order also aimed to deny citizenship to children born to foreign diplomatic staff and children born in U.S. territories where Congress has not passed a law granting citizenship.Passports potentially revoked?Cooper, who was appointed by former President Barack Obama, wanted to know when children would be subject to the second executive order, which Trump signed on August 6. Lucia Goin, an ACLU staff attorney, said there is concern that the second executive order is retroactive and that children who were issued passports would have them revoked by the State Department if the order went into effect. She added that the order does not have a set date, compared to the first executive order that made clear that any child born 30 days after the order was signed would be subject to it. Ty Turley Trejo, a DOJ attorney, said the Trump administration views the order as going into effect when it’s published. Cooper questioned if that meant a child who was born before the Aug. 6 order was published, such as on Aug. 4, would be subject to the order. Trejo said the executive order would not apply to the newborn, or any child born before the executive order was signed. Cooper said if he decided to proceed with the case, he would issue an order soon.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Bridgeport officials say Mayor Ganim failed to tell them about trip to Turkey
description: Bridgeport Mayor Joe Ganim is in Turkey this week for COP31, the UN climate change summit. His plans weren't shared with city officials.
text:
Bridgeport Mayor Joe Ganim is in Turkey this week for COP31, the U.N. climate change summit.
His plans for the trip weren’t shared with city officials, including City Council President Jeanette Herron, who is supposed to fill in for Ganim while he’s gone, until he was already there.
“Typically, the City Council President would be formally notified of the Mayor’s planned absence,” city Communications Director Constance Vickers said in a statement to WSHU. “This was an oversight in direct communication, and we will ensure better communication ahead of any future planned events.”
The U.S. did not send a delegation to COP31 for the second year in a row. However, some American leaders attended on their own; they include Ganim, California Governor Gavin Newsom (D) and Minnesota Governor Tim Walz (D).
Ganim participated in a panel on Thursday with other American mayors titled “US Climate Mayors Building Resilient Communities and Thriving Economies.”
“There may not be every national leader of every country at this event; ours from the United States government is missing,” Ganim said. “But we said this when we were in Rio as well: the mayors have shown up on a local level where subnationals are making a difference and having an impact. And why? Because we want to get things done.”
On the panel, Ganim spoke at length about the city’s journey to closing the PSEG power plant, one of the last of its kind in New England.
It was shut down in 2021 and mostly demolished last year.
“Not only did we see reductions in things like asthma for children who lived around the plant, but we were able to garner millions of dollars from the company in order to put money back into the community and try and do what we call environmental justice,” Ganim said.
“But also today on those 33 acres of waterfront, formerly industrial with that power plant, we’re now servicing our residents, creating jobs, attracting investment, and bringing what I like to call exciting opportunities to that part of the city, our South End,” he continued.
The city has received $22 million from the state of Connecticut to demolish and redevelop the site. In its place will eventually be housing, commercial space, and public access to the waterfront.
Whether to tear down the red-and-white smokestack, known as the “candy cane,” has been an ongoing conversation amid redevelopment talks. Demolition has been delayed while the city works on a fortification project to stop coastal flooding.
Some residents favor keeping it.
This story was first published Nov. 12, 2026 by WSHU.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Black University of Mississippi students wrestle with forgiveness in wake of racist gestures
description: The University of Mississippi in Oxford, Monday, Dec. 1, 2025.
text:
Three Black University of Mississippi students who shared a now-viral Ring camera video of two white students making monkeylike sounds and gestures outside their front door say they received an apology from one woman.
But the other only amplified her behavior, they said, divulging details of the rest of the encounter that weren’t captured on camera.
“She continued to make the gestures after the girl was apologizing. It was like a slap in the face,” Victoria Johnson told “CBS Mornings” in an interview that aired Wednesday.
Johnson was joined by her roommates, Jakiyra Metcalf and Kaiyden Caldwell, to talk about the incident that has ignited a firestorm on the Ole Miss campus and across social media. The animalistic gestures and sounds are seen as racist because they were reminiscent of ugly, old stereotypes comparing Black people to simians.
For it to happen at a college community in the Deep South with a long history of racism has added to the raw emotions.
The University of Mississippi in Oxford, Monday, Dec. 1, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
Metcalf saw the video Friday and she and Johnson went outside to talk to the two women, who had another friend with them. She was only seen glancing at the door in the video.
They said one woman, Alaina Kunes, apologized but said they had been making animal-like noises and gestures in front of other doors in the apartment complex. But the second woman, who lives in the complex, purportedly kept the antics going off camera.
Metcalf’s TikTok post has been viewed over 13 million times in four days. On Monday, the university posted a statement condemning the actions in the video as “offensive, hurtful, and unacceptable behaviors that conflict with our university values.” School officials also said the incident is being investigated and they are dedicated to “maintaining a safe and welcoming environment.”
Kunes, 18, issued a public apology Tuesday through a law firm.
“Before the incident on Nov. 6, I never met the women involved and was unaware of their race, however I recognize my actions were insensitive, inappropriate and deeply harmful,” Kunes said. “I would have never intentionally made those noises or gestures toward a person of color. I have apologized to the women and I pray they will forgive me.”
She has since withdrawn from school. She also said she would fully cooperate with any investigation.
The statement was originally posted on the firm’s website, but it had to be taken down because of ongoing harassment, said Kate Gardiner, a spokesperson for the firm.
Kunes will not be speaking beyond the statement, Gardiner added.
Outrage at taunting prompts opposition to social media shaming
The outrage against Kunes and the second woman, who has not publicly identified herself, has also stirred up opposition against using social media to malign them.
Tom Hennessey, an influencer tied to online fundraisers for people criticized for making xenophobic remarks, is credited with starting a fundraiser for the other woman on Christian fundraising platform GiveSendGo. It has raised over $30,000 as of Wednesday afternoon. The fundraising page states the “online mob (is) treating a juvenile stunt as a hate crime because the residents were Black.”
The University of Mississippi in Oxford, Monday, Dec. 1, 2025. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
The fundraiser also says it could possibly be canceled if the woman “disavows our support and bends the knee” and apologizes.
When contacted via X, or Twitter, DM, Hennessey said there is a double-standard and less attention is given to Black-on-white crime. He declined to say whether he had been in touch with the student about the fundraiser.
This is not the first time the university has been the backdrop for a Black student dealing with taunting animallike mimicking. In a May 2024 campus demonstration over the Israel-Hamas war, a counterprotester made monkey sounds and gestures at a Black, female student. The interaction was filmed by a student journalist. The video got the attention of outgoing Georgia Republican U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, who appeared to praise the behavior in a tweet.
University has ties to nation’s desegregation movement
Ole Miss also has a long history with racism, civil rights and segregation. In 1962, activist James Meredith was the first Black person to be admitted to the school after the U.S. Supreme Court ruled in his favor.
Then-Gov. Ross Barnett tried to block his admission but could not disobey federal law, according to the National Museum of African American History & Culture. Still, white objectors instigated a riot on campus. Two bystanders died and over 200 arrests were made.
Metcalf, Caldwell and Johnson hedged when asked if they forgive Kunes.
“I still have very mixed feelings about it,” Metcalf said.
Caldwell said she appreciated the apology but said it doesn’t change what happened.
“It’s still hurtful, and it’s still devastating that someone would go to our camera and do that,” Caldwell said.

name: Kansas Reflector
title: U.S. Senate chiefs of staff peel back layers of election in terms of causes and consequences
description: Chiefs of staff to GOP and Democratic U.S. senators consider leadership change in Congress and what to expect in final two years of President Trump's term.
text:
Colleen Shogan, a fellow at the Dole Institute of Politics at the University of Kansas, leads a Nov. 11, 2026, discussion at the institute with Reema Dodin, chief of staff to Democratic U.S. Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii, and J.T. Jezierski, chief of staff to Republican U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, on the outcome of the 2026 midterm election. (Kansas Reflector screen capture from Dole Institute of Politics video)TOPEKA — A pair of U.S. Senate chiefs of staff say failure of Republicans to retain control of Congress hinged on President Donald Trump’s inability to outrun an affordability crisis prompting the stampede of independents and Democrats voting in the November election.
Reema Dodin, chief of staff to Democratic U.S. Sen. Brian Schatz of Hawaii, and J.T. Jezierski, chief of staff to newly reelected Republican U.S. Sen. Shelley Moore Capito of West Virginia, peeled back layers of the midterm election resulting in Democrats crafting majorities in the Senate and House. They were part of a program Wednesday at the Robert J. Dole Institute of Politics at the University of Kansas.
“We, on the Republican side … may have thought it might be a long night, but it actually wasn’t. The margins were pretty decisive,” said Jezierski, who worked in the administration of President George W. Bush.
“You can do all the analysis you want, but high gas prices are high gas prices,” he said. “The president won two years ago, this is my personal opinion, on two measurable statistics: border crossings and affordability. Those statistics are still measurable. The border is one thing, but on affordability, I just think that’s tough to get around.”
Dodin, who was deputy director of legislative affairs for President Joe Biden, said the foremost determinant of the 2026 election was affordability. Other factors were candidate quality, immigration enforcement overreach and the Trump administration’s “outlandish and in-your-face” corruption, she said.
Dodin and Jezierski said the war initiated by Trump against Iran was a factor in undermining GOP turnout and motivating Democratic and unaffiliated voters.
“What we were seeking in a lot of polling was even the president’s own supporters from two years ago felt the war was a betrayal of the philosophy he had espoused on the campaign trail,” Dodin said.
The final composition of the Senate and House in Washington, D.C., has yet to be determined as votes continued to be counted. At this juncture, Democrats secured 55 seats to Republican’s 44 in the Senate with a Democrat leading in Alaska’s undecided race. The House would have at least 255 Democrats and 168 Republicans with a dozen House races not finalized.
Jezierski and Dodin agreed the Nov. 3 outcome was consequential because the final two years of Trump’s presidency would occur with both chambers led by Democrats and lawmakers under intense pressure from voters to deal with inflation in terms of fuel, health care and grocery costs. Progress on basic appropriations bills and complex policy shifts could be made if Congress and the president engaged in meaningful negotiations, they said.
“In all this, the president is the first mover in that he will set the mood and he will sort of set the tone of the political marketplace,” Dodin said. “There are deals and bills to be had. There are going to be some places where there is a lot of disagreement. The fact that the president accepted last Tuesday’s results was huge.”
Dodin said interplay between Trump and Congress during the lame-duck period between the election and when Republicans surrendered power in January would influence the approach of Democrats in 2027.
Jezierski said he wasn’t certain what to expect from the Senate’s evolving relationship with the White House.
“We have to work together,” he said. “We absolutely have to do that.”
The chiefs of staff indicated the ballot-box results offered both political parties an opportunity to recalibrate heading into the presidential election cycle.
“As a country, we are all different post-President Trump,” Dodin said. “From 2016 to now … the voters are different, the electorate is different, the way politics is done is different. The next two years, it will be a chance for both parties to decide, ‘What are we post-Trump?’ ”
The two-year window could lead to a free-for-all among Republican and Democratic candidates seeking to replace Trump, they said. Dodin suspected both parties could field as many as 20 candidates for president.
In response to questions from moderator Colleen Shogan, the archivist of the United States under President Biden, Dodin said she longed for more robust Senate floor debate on legislative issues.
“I wish we were on the floor more doing live debate,” she said. “They’re from 50 different states. They should have different perspectives.”
Jezierski said it was time for the nation to reclaim civility in politics. The climate had grown too hostile as elected officials and their families were placed at risk, he said. He pointed to abusive communications fielded by members of Capito’s staff.
“The comments and calls and the things that people say to our team, it’s despicable,” Jezierski said. “It’s absolutely unbelievable what has happened and what people do. Our discourse has gotten so bad. I have no respect for someone who can curse and yell at a 22-year-old kid who just graduated from college because you’re angry about something.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: In Bradford, a community reels after hospital closes
description: For Port Allegany native Alyssa Osani, the string of healthcare closures in McKean County feels “like everything around us is dying a slow death.” Osani and her husband returned to the area after finishing college and both work as educators. But several months into her first pregnancy, she’s wondering if it’s time to leave her […]
text:
The Bradford Regional Medical Center emergency department closed on May 17, 2026, the latest loss for local healthcare services in McKean County. (Photo by Noah Trapp for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)For Port Allegany native Alyssa Osani, the string of healthcare closures in McKean County feels “like everything around us is dying a slow death.”
Osani and her husband returned to the area after finishing college and both work as educators. But several months into her first pregnancy, she’s wondering if it’s time to leave her hometown. 
“Our five-year plan is to try to get out of here because we’re worried about healthcare. When it comes to welcoming our son, what if he needs something? We have family who, when they have an emergency … they have to try Buffalo,” said Osani. “Or, God forbid, Pittsburgh.” 
Port Allegany native Alyssa Osani, pictured in late September, is wondering if she has to leave her hometown to raise a family. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
The first option is a two-hour drive while the latter is more than three hours.
In the last 18 months, the labor and delivery unit in Coudersport closed, and Kaleida Health shuttered inpatient services at its Bradford hospital — leaving Olean General Hospital in Olean, New York as the nearest birthing option. 
“I’ve been not really thinking about it too much and hoping that everything will go according to plan,” said Osani, adding that she worries about having to give birth in the backseat of a car during the 30-minute drive. “It’s kind of scary to think … we do have that long drive and who knows what the weather will be like at that time of year.”
Osani spoke in late September ahead of a prenatal appointment at Universal Primary Care (UPC), which has a clinic that sits across the street from the former site of the Bradford Regional Medical Center. 
The Bradford hospital ended its emergency services on May 17, with a release noting that primary and specialty care services would remain available alongside the 95-bed long-term living facility, The Pavilion. 
A sign at the former Bradford Regional Medical Center directs people to go elsewhere after the emergency department closed in May 2026. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
“While this transition marks the end of emergency and inpatient services, BRMC will continue to play an important role in supporting the healthcare needs of the region,” unnamed hospital leaders said in a statement. “Healthcare — especially rural healthcare — continues to face many challenges. Over the 139-year history of the hospital, healthcare delivery has changed with the most recent shifting significantly toward outpatient services. We remain committed to building a sustainable model that continues meeting as many of the community’s healthcare needs as possible.”
The same week Osani spoke to the Capital-Star, Kaleida announced it would be closing The Pavilion, another loss for local services. 
“These facilities keep closing, and where do we go for help?” Osani asked. 
 Pressure on those left

Mike Austin, UPC’s chief operating officer, shared that demand has increased as Kaleida continues to end services. A handful of times, people have wandered into the clinic with high-level crises looking for help. 
In those situations, UPC staff will try to triage and call an ambulance, but often emergency services are tied up transporting patients to far-flung hospitals, especially if their insurance doesn’t permit them to seek treatment in Olean.
“It’s really a domino effect of a lot of bad things that are putting more strain on an overstrained healthcare system,” Austin said. 
Universal Primary Care has five clinic locations in the area, one of which is in Bradford across from the former hospital site. (Photo by Noah Trapp for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
It makes it more difficult to recruit providers to the area, added Bretty Lawton, UPC’s CEO, especially in a specialty like obstetrics, where there should be hospital-level backup. 
The Center for Rural PA projects that rural counties will lose 5.8% of their population over the next 30 years, even as the demand for services — especially healthcare for older adults — increases.
“Healthcare support is leaving faster than the population is declining, and I feel like one thing probably contributes to the other,” Lawton said. “It’s harder for people to stick around when they see a decline.” 
But Austin, who grew up in the area, said there’s still a lot of community left that needs the support, noting that there’s a University of Pittsburgh branch, as well as Zippo Manufacturing Company’s flagship location and other industry. 
“The skeleton is there to have a thriving community … I think we could stop the population decline if the investment in healthcare was at the forefront. Because that’s kind of the heart that’s going to pump life throughout,” Austin said. “The (healthcare services) that are remaining, we’re picking up the bill.” 
UPC is attempting to turn the tide, fundraising for a new space that’ll triple the size of its primary care services and house a dental residency program with the University of Pittsburgh. 
Dr. Anil Pradhan has practiced in Bradford for 45 years, but is now one of just two pediatricians left. (Photo by Noah Trapp for the Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
That’s on top of a separate UPC dental clinic that opened in January and still has a waitlist of more than 1,000 people — including some people from New York. 
As a federally qualified health center, UPC regularly conducts community needs assessments, identifying dental care as a gap. But unlike most of Pennsylvania’s other federally qualified health centers, a large share of their patients have private insurance, reflecting the lack of alternatives. 
In 2025, roughly a quarter of all Pennsylvanians visiting federally qualified health centers had private coverage, compared to 42.5% at UPC, which includes four New York clinics. 
“We’re the only game in town,” said Lawton. 
Anil Pradhan has been an area pediatrician since 1981, retiring briefly in 2020. After three years, he came back to work part time at UPC’s Bradford clinic. 
“I really missed the interactions with the kids,” Pradhan said. “Just about every child I see, the parents used to be my patients.” 
He’s one of just two pediatricians practicing locally now, he said.
“Lately, of course, we have no hospital. No (emergency room). You may not get an ambulance if you need it because they’re busy,” he added.
 A slim ray of hope

To many locals, Kaleida Health’s decision to close the Bradford hospital’s inpatient services is seen as a tactic to divert services to the Olean location, which it also owns. Kaleida didn’t respond to a request for comment.
It’s a suspicion that the area’s local officials have asked the attorney general’s office to investigate after Lake Erie College of Osteopathic Medicine (LECOM) pulled out of a purchase deal for the former hospital and adjoining long-term facility. According to reporting from The Buffalo News, Kaleida tried to insert a noncompete agreement that would limit LECOM’s ability to offer services at the facility.
The letters spelling out Bradford Regional Medical Center are still visible under the banner bearing the healthcare facility’s new name: Bradford Medical Park. (Photo by Whitney Downard/Pennsylvania Capital-Star)
Rep. Martin Causer (R-McKean) said the health system “failed to negotiate in good faith,” adding noncompetitive language that would “effectively ensure that BRMC would never again operate as a hospital.” 
Causer, Sen. Cris Dush (R-Jefferson), who has also called for an investigation, and the attorney general’s office didn’t respond to requests for comment.
But according to the lawmakers, the state agency has “pledged to explore all aspects … (of) the closure and failed sale,” including potential antitrust violations. 
“The situation facing patients throughout the entire Bradford region is unacceptable, particularly when you consider Kaledia’s significant reductions in lifesaving healthcare services – most notably the closing of Bradford Regional’s emergency room,” said Dush.
Both lawmakers are part of a Healthcare Access Team attempting to restore care. 
For Austin, with UPC, the federally qualified health center must continue to think outside of the box to be sustainable, because the alternative is unacceptable. 
“Just about everyone, we live in these communities that we’re serving. The patients are our family members; they’re our friends; they’re our neighbors,” Austin said. “It’s pretty easy to get up every day and have that mindset and know what you’re doing, why you’re doing it and who it’s for.” 
This story was reported as part of the National Press Club Journalism Institute Public Health Reporting Fellowship, funded by the Common Health Coalition.

name: WyoFile
title: Wyoming water district sues landowners to condemn private property for Alkali Dam and reservoir project
description:
To obtain easements to enable the proposed $103M dam, the Nowood water district sued landowners in Big Horn County.
The post Wyoming water district sues landowners to condemn private property for Alkali Dam and reservoir project appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
A Bighorn Basin water district filed condemnation lawsuits Tuesday seeking easements on private property to enable construction of a canal system and a reservoir for the proposed $103 million Alkali Creek Dam near Hyattville.
Nowood Watershed Improvement District filed eminent domain documents in Big Horn County District Court in Basin, board member Todd Jones told WyoFile on Wednesday. The suits seek temporary and permanent easements across property owned by at least five separate people or entities.
“Despite efforts by the district to acquire the permanent and temporary easements … Defendant has declined to allow [the] district to purchase the described permanent and temporary easements,” one complaint viewed by WyoFile states. “The taking and use of the premises as set forth … is necessary and appropriate for the project,” the document reads.
A summons accompanying the document states that the landowner targeted for condemnation has until five days before a Dec. 7 court date to contest the water district’s right or necessity to take the private property “for public use.”
The document describes that public use as “late season irrigation, water, reliability, recreation, opportunity, enhancement of wildlife and riparian, habitat, downstream, flood, attenuation, and economic benefit to [the] local community.”
“We feel we did our part.” John Joyce
The easements would enable enlargement and or construction of a canal or pipeline system to carry water from Paint Rock and Medicine Lodge creeks to the proposed reservoir. One permanent easement is necessary to enable the reservoir to inundate 4.5 acres of private land on one ranch.
While the legal action is ongoing, the district is expected to meet with the landowners to discuss obtaining the easements or rights of way without condemnation, according to Tom Shirran, one of the targeted landowners. He expressed relief that the two sides were going to “sit down and negotiate.”
The district has offered the landowners a total of $97,000 for right-of-way easements on 35 acres, to be adjusted according to appraisals.
The legal action comes after the impasse worked its way to a joint meeting of the Wyoming Water Development Commission and Wyoming Legislature’s Select Water Committee, where panel members refused to endorse another $44 million to complete the project. Lawmakers and commission members appeared wary of condemnation of private property and gave the feuding parties until Dec. 17 to settle differences at which time the $44 million will again be considered.
Whether the parties can overcome a history of acrimony and resolve the issue without condemnation is uncertain.
“We feel we did our part,” John Joyce, a member of the Nowood Watershed Improvement District board, said after the lawmakers and commissioners tabled the $44 million request last week. “We’re starting to come around to the conclusion they aren’t negotiating in good faith.”
Landowners have raised the same question about the water district board, accusing it of threatening condemnation instead of working to resolve differences.
Condemnation “is not the Wyoming way,” landowner Michelle Hamilton, whose property is targeted in the eminent domain action, told lawmakers last week.
Mitch Vigil, a Nowood Watershed Improvement District board member said time is of the essence. “We have a short window to negotiate,” he said. A Nov. 3 water district election for three board seats saw voters choose a majority who backed eminent domain.
“The results of the election speak for themselves,” said Vigil, an incumbent who won reelection. “I believe the vote is a clear indication of the direction the community wants the board to take.”
“This reservoir has the potential to benefit thousands of people,” he said, “but is hung up by a few.”
The reservoir would hold about 9,000 acre feet of water impounded by an earth embankment 100 feet high and half a mile long. The resulting reservoir would be 312 acres when full, providing late-season irrigation for some 33 families in eight out of 10 years. It would always have at least a 132-acre pool for recreation.

name: Colorado Newsline
title: Commentary: Colorado, hate state 2.0
description: As voters last week demanded an end to Republican darkness, a deep shadow marred the otherwise bright light of Colorado ballot returns. Coloradans flipped at least two congressional seats to Democrats. They gave Democrats another term of trifecta government in the state capital, the longest period of one-party dominance in state history. Like voters in […]
text:
A person holds a "Support LGBTQ+" sign during a rally at the Colorado Capitol to protest Trump administration policies last year in Denver. (Quentin Young/Colorado Newsline)As voters last week demanded an end to Republican darkness, a deep shadow marred the otherwise bright light of Colorado ballot returns.
Coloradans flipped at least two congressional seats to Democrats. They gave Democrats another term of trifecta government in the state capital, the longest period of one-party dominance in state history. Like voters in virtually every county in the country, they rejected Trumpist values, including cruelty and bigotry — except when it came to Propositions 134 and 135, which will ban transgender students from playing school sports and gender-affirming surgeries for minors, respectively.
The measures both passed by modest margins. Enactment of these bigoted policies recalled the state’s adoption in 1992 of a constitutional amendment that prohibited state and local governments from enacting protections for LGBTQ+ people. The U.S. Supreme Court struck down the amendment, but not before Colorado earned a reputation as the “hate state.”
The anti-trans measures reanimate the state’s mean streak, and with Tuesday’s election, Colorado has launched hate state 2.0.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The measures purport to protect children and families, but it takes little reflection and understanding to conclude they are products of pure bigotry. Anti-trans hate, especially on the right, particularly as defended as a religious imperative, is unconcealed and aggressive in the Trump era. 
From the president to Cabinet members to state lawmakers, Republicans are eager to advertise their hostility to the very existence of trans people, and in leveraging their hate for political advantage they create an environment where their targets are physically threatened.
That’s what the Colorado propositions are about.
Maybe the best evidence that the measures had little to do with “protections” is that they solve a problem that doesn’t exist. Reliable figures are hard to come by, but it’s clear that the number trans student athletes is negligible, and in cases when trans student athletes are controversial it’s typically parents or government officials who make it so, not coaches or teammates. The same goes for gender-affirming surgeries for youth. They virtually never happen.
The measure on school sports updates state law to define boys and girls based on physical anatomy and exclude transgender people. School sports teams will have to be designated for men, women or co-ed participation, and the schools will be required to adopt policies to implement the law. But how, exactly? This is an area where voters might not have thought through the implications of voting “yes.”
State Rep. Brianna Titone, an Arvada Democrat who is the first trans lawmaker in state history, notes that implementation could involve expensive DNA testing. 
“Does everybody need to be tested?” she asks. “Are we going to single out certain people who have features that don’t fit the actual aesthetic of what a woman’s supposed to be? And when we do that, right, what happens? We’re now policing women of all different types, and we’re setting a standard of what is a woman, what she’s supposed to look like, what she’s supposed to be like.”
Some women have more “masculine” features than others, and those features are different across races, Titone said, adding, “Are we going to be singling out women of different races more than others?”
Physical inspections of prospective student athletes are understood as another implementation method. Titone said genital inspections could expose all girls to abuse, citing the case of Larry Nassar, the former U.S. women’s national gymnastics team doctor who was convicted of sexually abusing athletes in his care.
Democratic Gov.-elect Phil Weiser last week, the day after he was elected, said he was uncomfortable with the prospect of inspections. “I don’t believe it would be acceptable for Colorado to have every student athlete have to go through full-body examinations or other invasions of privacy,” he said.
That’s partly why, in an unusual move, he endorsed potential legislative changes to the new anti-trans laws. State leaders typically refrain from interfering with the direct-democracy will of the people. But in this case, Weiser said, “We’re going to have to take a look at these anti-trans measures, and what adjustments are necessary and appropriate.”
Titone, though she’s term-limited and will be out of office when the new legislative session starts in January, said she agrees that lawmakers should explore ways to delay, blunt or eliminate the noxious effects of the laws. Her position is partly based on her belief that many voters made a mistake. 
“I think there’s a lot of people who just didn’t know what they were actually voting for in this case,” she said. “If we had the time to give them the proper information about it, maybe they would actually say, ‘Yeah, maybe I was wrong.'”
It should not take another Supreme Court smackdown for Colorado to avoid a return to hate-state status. The decent, humane path forward would be for it, whether through elected bodies or the electorate itself, to admit that the codification of anti-trans bigotry was wrong.
