name: North Dakota Monitor
title: State rep of 30 years will lead North Dakota House Republicans
description: One of the toughest jobs in North Dakota’s Legislature has a longtime figure taking charge. Rep. Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, is the new House majority leader after House Republicans elected their leadership team Wednesday night. Senate Republicans reelected Sen. David Hogue, R-Minot, as their majority leader. Both men ran unopposed.  “It will be an outstandin[...]
text:
Speaker of the House Rep. Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, listens to a Legislative Management meeting in the House chamber on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)One of the toughest jobs in North Dakota’s Legislature has a longtime figure taking charge.
Rep. Robin Weisz, R-Hurdsfield, is the new House majority leader after House Republicans elected their leadership team Wednesday night. Senate Republicans reelected Sen. David Hogue, R-Minot, as their majority leader. Both men ran unopposed. 
“It will be an outstanding relationship because it already is,” Hogue said of their roles together.
They will lead the two Republican supermajorities as perhaps the most visible members of the Legislature. The majority leaders steer the biennial legislative session, meet frequently with the governor, talk to the media and keep tabs on the Legislature’s work between sessions.
Weisz has been speaker of the House for nearly two years, presiding over the 94-member chamber during floor sessions. He will hold both jobs simultaneously until a new speaker is elected in early December.
The 70-year-old lifelong farmer was first elected in 1996, representing a large rural district in the middle of the state. He owned a grain elevator business for 15 years. He has a patent for a product he and a partner invented for agriculture. 
For more than a decade, Weisz chaired the House Human Services Committee, which has handled bills on everything from abortion regulations to medical marijuana to vaccines.
Voters reject higher bar to amend North Dakota’s constitution

Last year, Weisz was the main sponsor of the legislation that became Measure 1, a proposed constitutional amendment that sought to require 60% voter support to change the state constitution. Voters rejected the measure by about 56%. 
Weisz said his 30 years of experience and calm approach will help the House. 
“I think that’s an advantage I’ve had, you know, chairing over the years and stuff is that, yeah, I’m not always going to be happy with things, but keep that even temperament, keep the even keel and work out the issues and go forward,” he said.
Weisz will be wrangling an 80-member Republican caucus, an enormous group of lawmakers who don’t always agree.
“To me, that means I have to be able to listen to the broad range of my caucus. We have ultraconservative to maybe relatively liberal but they’re all part of our caucus. They have a voice,” he said.
Weisz succeeds Rep. Mike Lefor, R-Dickinson, who did not seek reelection to his House seat. Lefor, 70, said he is retiring to spend more time in Arizona and with his grandchildren.
Lefor was elected majority leader in 2022 and spent much of the time traveling the state on his own dime to meet with different groups and learn about everything from aging university buildings to agricultural research to educate himself for when the session comes around.
“The job is what you make it,” Lefor said.
During Lefor’s tenure, he helped lead the Legislature’s response to adverse court rulings on redistricting and a catchall budget bill. He also helped plan three special sessions to redo the budget bill, approve federal rural health funds and restrict kratom products. His predecessor, former GOP Rep. Chet Pollert, dealt with impacts of the coronavirus pandemic and helped lead the first expulsion of a North Dakota lawmaker in state history. 
Weisz said he was heavily involved in many of those issues even though he wasn’t the majority leader. He said he would deal with bad situations fairly to reach the best outcome.
“Who knows what this session may bring,” he said.
Senate Majority Leader Sen. David Hogue, left, R-Minot, speaks to House Majority Leader Rep. Mike Lefor, R-Dickinson, before a Legislative Management meeting on Nov. 12, 2026. (Photo by Michael Achterling/North Dakota Monitor)
Hogue, who has led Senate Republicans since 2022, said his approach is to mentor and delegate as leader of his caucus.
He and Weisz, who will reach their chambers’ term limit in 2028, will guide one of the last legislative sessions with longtime incumbents who will mostly be gone by 2031. Term limits restrict lawmakers to eight years apiece in the House and Senate.
The 2027 Legislature is “going to be an interesting dynamic where we’re starting to see lots of new faces and not just a few,” said Hogue, who added he is concerned about the loss of institutional knowledge of agencies, budgets and recurring, rejected legislation.
Weisz said he won’t run for Senate. Hogue said he hasn’t decided his future.
Lawmakers take office Dec. 1. Republicans control the House 80-14 and the Senate 41-6.
The Legislature’s majority and minority leaders are paid an extra $20 per calendar day during sessions.
New faces, new leaders and a few more Democrats will shape North Dakota’s next Legislature

House Republicans elected Rep. Greg Stemen, R-Fargo, as assistant majority leader and Rep. Jim Grueneich, R-Ellendale, as caucus leader. They also nominated Rep. Brandy Pyle, R-Casselton, for speaker.
Senate Republicans reelected Sen. Jerry Klein, R-Fessenden, as assistant majority leader and Sen. Kristin Roers, R-Fargo, as caucus leader. 
House and Senate Democrats will elect their leadership teams Thursday night.
The Legislature’s organizational session is Dec. 1-3. Some of the most important events are the election of a House speaker and Gov. Kelly Armstrong’s budget address laying out his priorities for the next two years.
Reach North Dakota Monitor reporter Jack Dura at jdura@northdakotamonitor.com.

title: Wyoming’s Barrasso secures No. 2 GOP post as Senate Minority Whip
description:
Not all GOP Senators participated in the vote, calling instead for a delay to reflect on Republicans’ stunning defeat in the midterm elections. 
The post Wyoming’s Barrasso secures No. 2 GOP post as Senate Minority Whip appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
Republican senators have elected Wyoming Sen. John Barrasso to serve as minority whip in the incoming 120th Congress. 
As the No. 2 party leader next year, Barrasso’s job will look different than his past two years as majority whip after Democrats swept the midterm elections and won control of the Senate as well as the House. 
“As the opposition party in the Senate, we must be equally clear about what we stand for and what we will fight against,” Barrasso said in a Monday letter to colleagues obtained by Politico. “We need to draw sharp, principled contrast with the left-wing Majority. We need to do it in our message, the legislation we advance, the votes we demand, and our conversations at home.” 
The effectiveness of Senate Republicans, Barrasso wrote, will depend on their ability to unite. 
“We will not agree on everything, but we remain united in our purpose,” he wrote. “When we stand together, we are stronger, our positions carry greater weight, and our ability to shape legislation and stop bad ideas is greater. A united Conference has a meaningful voice in the Senate with the strength to use it.”
Senate Republicans also voted to reelect South Dakota Sen. John Thune to lead their party. Some members, however, asked that leadership elections be delayed until Republicans could meet to reflect on their stunning defeat. 
“Holding leadership elections without engaging in a robust discussion and evaluation of how those running for leadership intend to lead would be political malpractice,” Wisconsin Sen. Ron Johnson wrote in a Monday letter.
Johnson did not ultimately participate in Tuesday’s leadership election, he said in a post on X, “because a defeat of this magnitude demands serious reflection and change.”  
“Holding a rush election ignores the message our voters sent,” Johnson said. “We must acknowledge where and why we failed and develop strategies to succeed.”
Barrasso, who campaigned with Trump ahead of the midterms and supported a slew of Republican Senate candidates, did not directly address the call for a delay in his letter or his Tuesday remarks to the press, but said the GOP “will waste no time.”
“We’re going to make every second count. And that means all these judicial appointments. We’re going to do everything we can to get every single one of them confirmed,” he said. “Remember, these are lifetime appointments. We will leave no vacancy behind.”

description: OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma County killer James Pavatt was put to death by lethal injection Thursday at Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester. text:
Barbed wire and fencing surrounding the Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester is pictured on Sept. 5, 2025. (Photo by Emma Murphy/Oklahoma Voice)OKLAHOMA CITY – Oklahoma County killer James Pavatt was put to death by lethal injection Thursday at Oklahoma State Penitentiary in McAlester.
The time of death was 10:12 a.m., according to the Oklahoma Department of Corrections.
“We carried out the court’s orders according to our high standards of professionalism and respect for those in our custody, ensuring dignity for everyone involved in the process,” Oklahoma Department of Corrections Executive Director Justin Farris said in a statement.
The execution process had no complications, said Kay Gallamore, a DOC spokesperson. No members of Pavatt’s family or the victim’s family attended, she said.
Pavatt, 73, and his love interest Brenda Andrew, 62, were both sentenced to death for the 2001 shooting death of advertising executive Rob Andrew as he attempted to pick up his two children for a holiday visit.
Oklahoma County killer James Pavatt speaks during his October clemency hearing. (Photo by Barbara Hoberock/Oklahoma Voice)
Brenda and Rob Andrew were going through a divorce. Prosecutors alleged Brenda Andrew and Pavatt were having an affair. They allege a $800,000 life insurance policy Rob Andrew had was part of the motive.
Brenda Andrew, the only female on Oklahoma’s death row, is appealing her conviction and death sentence.
Brenda Andrew and Pavatt fled to Mexico with the Andrews’ two children after the killing, prosecutors said.
“Justice has been served for Rob Andrew who was taken from his children and his family far too soon,” said Oklahoma Attorney General Gentner Drummond.
The Oklahoma Pardon and Parole Board in October denied clemency on a 2-3 vote.
Pavatt, who served in the U.S. Air Force, told the panel he was not guilty of murder, but guilty of falling in love.
“Jim long professed his innocence and the absence of credible evidence against him is stark,” said Hunter S. Labovitz, his attorney.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: Former top NC lawmaker faces indictment related to Kentucky bourbon tour
description: The indictment charges former state Rep. Jason Saine, a Republican from Lincoln County, with felony embezzlement of more than $100,000 and obtaining property by false pretense.
text:
The North Carolina Legislative Building (Photo by Clayton Henkel/NC Newsline) A lobbyist and former top North Carolina lawmaker is facing criminal charges from a Wake County grand jury stemming from an April 2024 bourbon tour for North Carolina lawmakers in Kentucky.
The indictment, handed down earlier this week, charges former state Rep. Jason Saine, a Republican from Lincoln County, with felony embezzlement of more than $100,000 and obtaining property by false pretense. He was also charged with aiding and abetting the same acts by the group’s executive director, David Coble, who was indicted as well this week.
Former Rep. Jason Saine (Photo: NCGA)
“I do not understand why I have been charged in this case,” Saine said in a statement. “The indictment claims that I ‘aided and abetted’ a crime committed by someone else — I did not do that.”
Saine declined to provide further comment, but said in the statement, “I did not commit any crime and I look forward to clearing my name.”
The junket was arranged and funded by Greater Carolina, a 501(c)4 advocacy group connected to Saine and founded by a former Saine staffer. It’s sometimes referred to as a dark money group because it doesn’t publicly disclose its donors.
Greater Carolina described itself as a nonprofit conservative social welfare organization aiming to promote pro-business and free-market policies in North Carolina. The group no longer has an online presence. 
Federal tax law allows for 501(c)4 social welfare groups to lobby for legislation, but they cannot intervene in political campaigns or have political activities as their primary purpose.
The Kentucky trip gained attention across the Tar Heel State after a Louisville-area hospitality worker made an anonymous social media post saying the group had booked a private bourbon tasting, but was already inebriated when they arrived.
Four prominent NC lobbyists indicted over bourbon-tasting junket

Wake County District Attorney Lorrin Freeman said the charges come from an ongoing multi-year investigation into Greater Carolina. 
“From the beginning, the focus of this investigation has been to determine what, if any, laws were violated in the operation of this organization,” Freeman said in a statement. “This case serves as a reminder that the law places restrictions on the way they operate and sets forth that they should not be used as an end run around the statutory framework embodied in our state’s Ethics Act and lobbying regulations.”
Freeman said when her term ends, the case will transition to District Attorney-elect Wiley Nickel. 
Earlier this year, four prominent North Carolina lobbyists were also indicted on criminal charges related to the 2024 trip. They each faced a misdemeanor charge of solicitation to commit violations of the offense of giving gifts by lobbyists and lobbying principals.
Three of those four lobbyists had their cases cleared in September, while pending charges remain against the fourth, Kevin Wilkinson of The Southern Group.
The indictment against Wilkinson claimed Greater Carolina paid for the trip “with the intent that an ultimate beneficiary of those contributions would be legislators.” 
At the time of the Kentucky trip, Saine was a top state budget writer in the North Carolina House. He resigned from the legislature in August 2024, joining The Southern Group lobbying firm. 
Saine now leads his own firm, Saine Strategies.

name: Mississippi Today
title: State permit board rejects appeal of SpaceXAI air permits in Southaven
description: Shannon Samsa gives her comments during a Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality public hearing on an xAI permit application at Northwest Mississippi Community College in Southaven on Tuesday, Feb. 17, 2026.
text:
After hearing hours of testimony over two days, Mississippi’s permit board rejected an appeal of an air permit awarded earlier in the year to SpaceXAI’s data center hub in Southaven.
The board, which makes decisions over permits issued by the Mississippi Department of Environmental Quality, issued its decision Tuesday, the last day of the hearing. 
In March, the board approved air permits for 41 permanent gas turbines that will power SpaceXAI’s data center operations in the area, which cross over the state line into Memphis.
The Safe and Sound Coalition — comprised of Southaven residents — the NAACP and Young, Gifted & Green appealed the decision shortly after. 
On behalf of the appellants, the Southern Environmental Law Center argued that MDEQ erred in writing the permit in three ways: The agency relied on limited modeling, it didn’t require SpaceXAI to use less-polluting turbines, and it didn’t require emission offsets. In areas with poor air quality — referred to as “nonattainment areas” — the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency requires any new sources of air emissions to also include offsets mitigating those emissions.
The site of a planned xAI facility at 2400 Stateline Road in Southaven, Tuesday, Feb. 17. 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
While DeSoto County isn’t listed as a nonattainment area, SELC attorney Patrick Anderson argued federal law still requires offsets because the area fails to meet national air quality standards.
“All of this makes sense,” Anderson said Monday in his opening argument. “If the air is too dirty, MDEQ should not wait for action from the federal government. And, in fact, they can’t wait, they’re required to treat the source accordingly.”
MZX Tech LLC, a subsidiary of SpaceXAI that received the air permit, disagreed. Trudy Fisher, a former executive director of MDEQ who argued on behalf of MZX Tech, said the agency underwent extensive modeling of the turbines’ emissions and consulted with EPA throughout the permitting process.   
“This was not a permit that was approved without careful consideration,” Fisher said. 
The board’s lone dissenting vote came from state Agriculture Commissioner Andy Gipson, also a Republican candidate in the 2027 gubernatorial race. Gipson voted against approving the permit because he didn’t get “answers to all the questions I have posed.”
Commissioner of Agriculture and Commerce Andy Gipson speaks to media members at the Neshoba County Fair on Thursday, June 25, 2026, near Philadelphia. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
One of the few state officials to publicly question Mississippi’s data center growth, the commissioner published a memo over the summer “requiring” data centers give certain information, such as around water use, before receiving a permit from MDEQ. 
In response, MDEQ spokesperson Jan Schaefer told Mississippi Today that Gipson’s memo “does not alter” what information permit applicants need to submit to the agency. 
During the hearing’s first day, Gipson tried to ask about MZX Tech’s water usage, yielding objections from MZX Tech’s attorneys who argued the questions were outside the scope of an air permit hearing. Kim Turner, the state’s hearing officer, agreed with the objection. 
“I want to get an answer on the water usage, which I deem, as a member of this board, relevant information for me to ask,” Gipson fired back. “And if I’m not allowed to do that, there’s no point in there being a permit board.”
Shannon Samsa, a Safe and Sound Coalition member and Southaven resident, said after the hearing that the board’s decision was “reprehensible.”
“Whoever’s interests they are serving, it certainly doesn’t appear to be those of the people who actually live here,” Samsa said in a written statement. 
Reporter Katherine Lin contributed to this story.

text:
The Maine state flag flies outside the State House in Augusta. (Photo by Jim Neuger/ Maine Morning Star)As Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree and her transition committee work to fill her future cabinet, she announced Thursday that Jesse Connolly will serve as her chief of staff.
Jesse Connolly will serve as Gov.-elect Hannah Pingree’s chief of staff. (Courtesy photo)
The longtime political strategist has most recently served as chief of staff for Hannah Pingree’s mother, U.S. Rep. Chellie Pingree, overseeing her Washington, D.C. and Maine operations, managing legislative and constituent service teams, and serving as a senior adviser on policy and political strategy. 
Prior to that, he worked for Hannah Pingree for four years as chief of staff during her time as speaker and majority leader of the Maine House of Representatives.
“Jesse is one of the most capable, strategic, and trusted leaders I have ever worked with, and I am grateful he is joining my administration,” Hannah Pingree said in a press statement. “When I was speaker and majority leader, he helped me manage a complex legislative agenda and build a team that delivered for Maine people. He has since held some of the most demanding roles in Maine and national politics, and he understands how to turn big goals into real results. I can’t think of anyone better to lead my team.”
Connolly, who lives in South Portland, also previously managed several statewide and national campaigns, including two Maine gubernatorial races and the successful 2005 campaign to defeat a referendum repealing Maine’s LGBTQ+ nondiscrimination law. 
Earlier this week, the governor-elect announced the members of her transition committee, who will work with committee co-chairs former Republican state Sen. Roger Katz and former Penobscot Ambassador Maulian Bryant to identify candidates to serve in her administration. 
Hannah Pingree will be sworn in as Maine’s 76th governor on Jan. 6.

title: Commentary: Laura Lee Brown transformed natural spaces, urban cores with art and imagination
description: Laura Lee Brown, who died Nov. 10, 2026, at the age of 85, was a true daughter of the Commonwealth. In her long and purposeful life, she successfully combined the grace of an old Kentucky lineage with an unapologetically modern vision for the arts, civic preservation, and the environment. She was born in Louisville on […]
text:
Laura Lee Brown of Louisville died on Nov. 10, 2026 at the age of 85. (Photo provided)Laura Lee Brown, who died Nov. 10, 2026, at the age of 85, was a true daughter of the Commonwealth. In her long and purposeful life, she successfully combined the grace of an old Kentucky lineage with an unapologetically modern vision for the arts, civic preservation, and the environment.
She was born in Louisville on June 12, 1941, into a family whose name had long been synonymous with the growth and character of the city. Her father, George Garvin Brown II, from 1951 to 1969 led Brown-Forman, the spirits empire founded by her great-grandfather, George Garvin Brown, in 1870. Her mother, Gertrude Polk Brown, was an active cultural force in her own right. Laura Lee Brown was a great-great-great-granddaughter of the 16th governer of Kentucky, William Owsley.
Young Laura Lee was reared at Sutherland, the family’s riverfront farm, in an environment where civic responsibility and corporate stewardship were viewed as fundamental obligations. Growing up alongside the rolling waters of the Ohio, she developed an early, profound reverence for the landscapes of the region. It was a connection that would define much of her later life. 
In 1993, when the beloved grounds of Sutherland faced the threat of subdivision, she joined with her siblings, Dace Polk Brown Stubbs and George Garvin Brown III, to purchase and protect a critical 46-acre riverfront tract. Deeded to the River Fields land trust, it became the Garvin Brown Nature Preserve, ensuring that the meadows and wetlands of her childhood would remain open to the public forever. She was celebrated by River Fields, where she was an honorary trustee, at a dinner last month.
Though her family legacy was estimable, Brown was never content to simply inhabit a comfortable inheritance. Instead, she chose to use her resources to dramatically reshape the cultural landscape of her hometown and her state.
She was educated at Sweet Briar College, where she graduated in 1963 with a degree in French. In her early adulthood, she spent time in San Francisco before returning home to Kentucky to focus on her own work as a photographer and painter. It was a deeply personal practice—her camera capturing everything from the stark, quiet beauty of the South Pole to intimate portraits — and it was this shared love for the creative process that ultimately brought her together with her husband of 29 years, Steve Wilson.
Her initiation into the institutional art world began at the side of her mother, who helped found the New Collectors group at the Speed Art Museum. Joining those trips to New York to scout what was current and vibrant, Laura Lee learned early on how to cultivate emerging talent. Her loyalty to the local creative ecosystem deepened through decades of unwavering support for the Actors Theatre of Louisville, where she championed regional playwrights and performers.
Yet, she understood that art should not be a cloistered luxury, but a public experience. 
The result was her greatest entrepreneurial and cultural triumph. In 2006, she and Wilson revolutionized downtown Louisville by opening the inaugural 21c Museum Hotel. They created an entirely new global paradigm: a boutique hotel operating as a contemporary art museum, free and open to the public 24 hours a day. 
By stepping forward in 2012 to rescue a row of historic 19th-century tobacco and bourbon warehouses on West Main Street from the imminent threat of the wrecking ball, the couple along with other local philanthropists preserved the architectural majesty of Whiskey Row.  That complex includes the Old Forester distillery and museum. The project injected vital energy into the urban core, serving as a beacon of renewal that eventually expanded across multiple American cities.
Her civic engagement did not end at the city limits. Ms. Brown possessed an enduring attachment to the rolling pastures of her native landscape. At Woodland Farm and Hermitage Farm in Oldham County, she and her husband championed sustainable agriculture and thoroughbred culture. Their reintroduction of bison herds became a popular source of organic meat in the region.
Whether funding the nascent Kentucky College of Art + Design or sitting in the audience of a local gallery opening, she was a gentle, inspirational force. Her mother’s love of history was memorialized with the Filson Historical Society’s Gertrude Polk Brown lecture series, a staple of Louisville’s intellectual framework.
Ms. Brown died following an illness at her beloved Woodland Farm in Goshen, Ky., surrounded by the fields she labored to preserve. She is survived by her husband, Steve Wilson; her three children, Laura Lee Gastis (George), Polk Deters (Sarah), and Garvin Deters (Pritchett); seven grandchildren; her sister, Dace Polk Brown Stubbs of Bedford, Ky., nieces and nephews. In addition to her parents, she was preceded in death by her brother, George Garvin Brown III.
A private family burial is planned, and a formal public memorial service will be conducted in the spring, when the Kentucky bluegrass returns to full bloom.

name: New Hampshire Bulletin
title: Commentary: What are key challenges facing New Hampshire as we head into 2027?
description: From rising housing, childcare and healthcare costs to a labor force with many workers reaching retirement age, New Hampshire faces some big challenges heading into 2027. For many Granite Staters, the growing cost of living makes it increasingly difficult to afford the basics, pay monthly bills and save for the future. As lawmakers prepare for […]
text:
"Addressing these challenges could require difficult decisions, particularly as lawmakers develop the next state budget." (Photo by Dana Wormald/New Hampshire Bulletin)From rising housing, childcare and healthcare costs to a labor force with many workers reaching retirement age, New Hampshire faces some big challenges heading into 2027. For many Granite Staters, the growing cost of living makes it increasingly difficult to afford the basics, pay monthly bills and save for the future.
As lawmakers prepare for the upcoming legislative session, they have an opportunity to address these challenges and improve residents’ lives and livelihoods. With limited state resources and competing priorities, the decisions ahead may not be easy. 
Overall inflation faster in the Northeast
Prices increased nearly 26% between 2019 and 2025 in the Northeastern United States. In September 2026, overall consumer prices were 4.2% higher than a year earlier, compared with 3.7% nationally. Energy costs have been a significant factor, with gasoline prices in the Northeast rising 37% over the year and home heating fuel oil prices increasing 74% nationally. 
Cost of paying for the median-priced house surges 160% in 10 years 
Housing costs have risen even faster. The median sale price for a single-family house statewide increased 114% between 2015 and 2025. Accounting for mortgage rates, property taxes and a 5% down payment, the monthly cost of a median-priced house surged 160%, from approximately $1,500 to about $3,900. A full-time worker would have needed to earn approximately $75 an hour to afford that house without spending more than 30% of income on housing. Renters have also faced rising costs, with median rent and utilities for a two-bedroom apartment increasing by 58% from 2015 to 2024, faster than inflation and income growth. 
Price of childcare rises to nearly a quarter of median income for a family with young children
For families with young children, childcare can be the second-largest expense after housing. The average cost of care for an infant and 4-year-old was about $30,000 annually during the 2022–2025 period, equivalent to 24% of median income for a married couple with two or more children under age 5. That is substantially above the federal affordability benchmark of 7%. While the expanded New Hampshire Child Care Scholarship Program is helping more families, thousands of eligible households remain unreached, and providers continue to face financial pressures and limited capacity. 
Out-of-pocket healthcare costs for families increasing 
Healthcare is another growing expense. Out-of-pocket healthcare costs reported by consumers in the Northeast increased by 44% from the 2014–2015 average to the 2023–2024 average. In New Hampshire, the average family deductible in an employer-sponsored health insurance plan increased by 323% between 2005 and 2024, while the average employee contribution to family premiums rose by 116%, reaching approximately $6,220 in 2024. 
Average private-sector wage lost 2.2% of purchasing power in 2025, still behind in 2026
Granite Staters would be more able to absorb these rising costs if incomes were keeping pace. However, New Hampshire’s inflation-adjusted median household income in 2025 was statistically unchanged from 2021. The average private-sector wage fell behind inflation in 2022, 2024, 2025 and the first nine months of 2026, with purchasing power dropping 2.2% in 2025 alone. 
More than 200,000 Granite Staters near retirement ages
The age composition of the state’s population could also spur economic changes. Approximately 206,000 Granite Staters could reach traditional retirement ages within the next 10 years. With New Hampshire relying on in-migration for all population growth since 2017, helping ensure that workers and families can afford to live here will be increasingly important to the state’s economic future. 
Fiscal constraints and state budget opportunities 
Addressing these challenges could require difficult decisions, particularly as lawmakers develop the next state budget. 
The current budget required approximately $113 million in unspecified reductions and other savings, lowered funding for several key services, and raised 125 fees and fines. New Hampshire also continues to face significant potential costs. Compliance with a July 2025 Supreme Court ruling could increase state spending on local public education by about $448 million in the first year if the court’s suggested minimum were implemented without other changes. Separately, settlements for alleged abuse at the Youth Development Center had reached $239.3 million by August 2026, with 1,684 claims still pending and the potential for more court-ordered payments. 
Recent state revenues are ahead of expectations, potentially giving policymakers more fiscal space than during negotiations over the current budget. However, reductions to the state’s two primary business tax rates and repeal of the Interest and Dividends Tax reduced revenue by an estimated $500 million to $800 million during the current budget cycle.
The challenges facing New Hampshire are significant, but so are the opportunities to address them. The decisions lawmakers make in 2027 about how to raise and invest public dollars will have consequences well beyond the next two-year budget. These decisions could help shape whether Granite Staters can afford to live, work, raise families and retire in the communities they call home. With thoughtful, data-informed choices and a clear understanding of the challenges facing residents, policymakers could make meaningful progress toward a more affordable and prosperous New Hampshire for Granite Staters.

name: North Carolina Newsline
title: North Carolina vows to hold Chemours accountable for contamination ‘no matter how long it takes’
description: This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here. FAYETTEVILLE, N.C.— North Carolina environmental regulators this week sent a scathing critique to Chemours, which is responsible for contaminating at least 10 counties with to[...]
text:
An aerial view of the Chemours Fayetteville Works plant in northern Bladen County. For more than 30 years Chemours and its predecessor, DuPont, discharged “forever chemicals” into the Cape Fear River. (Photo: Chemours)This article originally appeared on Inside Climate News, a nonprofit, non-partisan news organization that covers climate, energy and the environment. Sign up for their newsletter here.
FAYETTEVILLE, N.C.— North Carolina environmental regulators this week sent a scathing critique to Chemours, which is responsible for contaminating at least 10 counties with toxic “forever chemicals,” arguing that the company’s cleanup proposal violates the terms of a consent order.
The state Department of Environmental Quality detailed multiple inadequacies in the company’s plan to remediate widespread, decades-old groundwater and soil contamination from PFAS chemicals in southeastern North Carolina.
“Today’s direction to the company makes clear that DEQ expects Chemours to clean up all the areas they have polluted,” said DEQ Secretary Reid Wilson in a prepared statement. “DEQ will hold Chemours accountable no matter how long it takes.”
The company’s predecessor, DuPont, is responsible for some of the contamination emanating from the Fayetteville Works plant, but it shielded itself from liability when it spun off Chemours in 2015. An international company, Chemours manufactures chemicals used to make Teflon cookware, data center coolants and grease-, water- and stain-resistant consumer products.
DEQ’s letter said the agency also determined the company could not justify how it assessed the public health and environmental risk of PFAS exposure. The letter cited numerous instances of what DEQ described as missing data, substandard sampling methods and flawed analyses in Chemours’ reports. In some cases, these errors led the company to reach conclusions that lacked a factual, scientific or legal basis, according to the letter.
The groundwater and soil remediation must be detailed in a corrective action plan, a key component of a 2019 consent order between the company, DEQ and the nonprofit Cape Fear River Watch. The agency rejected the company’s draft corrective action plan in 2020, calling it “inadequate” and lacking a “thorough technical basis.”
Progress on the plan stalled for six years until September, when the state announced it had reached a half-billion dollar settlement with Chemours that included a provision accelerating progress on its completion. The settlement required DEQ to provide written feedback to Chemours.
A Chemours spokesperson told Inside Climate News that with DEQ’s formal feedback to its 2019 corrective action plan, risk assessment and other studies “now in hand, we can move forward. We are reviewing the comments in detail and will respond through the established process.”
Because of shortcomings in Chemours’ data and analysis, DEQ wrote, neither the company nor the agency knows the full extent of the PFAS contamination in the Lower Cape Fear River Basin, nearly 10 years after the public first learned of it through media reports.
Over 36 pages, DEQ rebutted the company’s conclusions about the extent of the contamination and the public health and ecological risks.
Chemours told DEQ that current concentrations of the PFAS chemical GenX near the Fayetteville Works plant were unlikely to harm human health even without treating the groundwater. However, the state said, Chemours failed to evaluate all PFAS originating from the plant, as legally required. DEQ said the company also used outdated toxicological data for GenX, one of 15,000 types of PFAS compounds.

What are forever chemicals?

There are more than 15,000 types of PFAS—per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, the so-called “forever chemicals.” They are found in many consumer products, such as microwave popcorn bags, pizza boxes, stain- and water-resistant clothing and furniture, and lithium-ion batteries, including those used in electric vehicles.
They’ve been linked to many serious health conditions, including several types of cancer.
PFAS also disrupt the ocean’s ability to sequester carbon, a driver of climate change. PFAS manufacturers emit thousands of tons of greenhouse gases into the atmosphere each year.
In 2022, the Chemours Fayetteville plant emitted 52,000 tons of greenhouse gases, according to EPA data.




Chemours’ health risk assessment excluded people who regularly fish in the Cape Fear River for food, and the company didn’t account for other ways people could become exposed, such as eating contaminated vegetables, touching water or soil that contains PFAS or inhaling the compounds, the state added.
Image: Adobe Stock
DEQ also requested that Chemours complete its investigation about biosolids—sewage sludge—that could have originated from the plant and have been applied to farm fields. The agency requested comprehensive information about where and when the biosolids were shipped offsite and their quantities.
Sewage sludge is often used to fertilize farm fields. When the sludge is contaminated, the PFAS can seep into the soil, groundwater and drinking water wells.
“The agency is asking the company to look into how their contamination is truly going to harm communities,” said Jean Zhuang, senior attorney for the Southern Environmental Law Center, which represents Cape Fear River Watch. “It demands much more of Chemours than the company has ever done so far.”
Over the past six years, Chemours has spent about $1.2 billion on complying with some provisions of the consent order. The company installed a thermal oxidizer to remove 99.9 percent of all PFAS emissions from the air, offered free water filtration systems to more than 10,000 homes with contaminated wells and built a mile-long underground barrier wall to prevent contaminated groundwater seeping from the site and into the Cape Fear River.
These projects have reduced, although not eliminated, the amount of PFAS entering the environment. Contaminated groundwater continues to seep from the Fayetteville Works plant into the river and other surface waters; PFAS are still entering the air.
The magnitude of the contamination is so vast that Chemours has previously told DEQ it is “technologically and economically infeasible” to comply as closely as possible with the state’s groundwater rules.
However, DEQ told Chemours in the letter that the company has not provided sufficient evidence to support that conclusion. “While DEQ recognizes that the geographic scope of the contamination caused by Chemours is enormous and unprecedented in this state,” DEQ Deputy Secretary Sushma Masemore wrote, “the vast scope does not release Chemours of its obligation to thoroughly evaluate all remedial alternatives.”
Chemours’ sampling methods to determine health and ecological effects were also flawed, according to the letter. For example, contractors sampled soil along roadways, which is often trucked in from other areas. And instead of collecting earthworms to assess exposure risks in the soil, contractors evaluated grasshoppers, crickets and dragonflies—which don’t live in the dirt.
Contractors also wiped loose dirt off leaves before collecting them, which likely removed PFAS bound to the dust that was deposited through the air, the state said.
Chemours failed to sample aquatic plants and organisms and excluded animals from its studies due to time constraints, which DEQ called “an inadequate justification.”
Questions about air emissions 
Chemours has also failed to identify all of the PFAS compounds it is emitting into the air from the Fayetteville Works plant, which is continuing to contaminate the groundwater, Michael Abraczinskas, director of the state’s Division of Air Quality, wrote in a separate letter.
Nor do the company’s sampling and reporting methods meet quality control standards, Abraczinskas wrote, adding that “the issues identified in this letter require immediate attention and corrective actions.”
There is a direct link between air emissions that contain PFAS and contaminated groundwater. After the compounds enter the air, they can travel on the wind and fall to the earth, where they seep into soil and groundwater. PFAS traced to the Fayetteville plant, such as PFMOAA and GenX, have been detected in private drinking water wells as far as 25 miles away.
“Chemours has acted like it’s done everything it needs to do on air emissions, and even asked to expand its facility,” Zhuang said, “and DEQ is saying, ‘No, they are continuing to be an issue, and we’re going to take this really seriously.’”
NC AG Jackson calls on residents to weigh in on Chemours’ ‘backroom deal’ over PFAS

Chemours has underestimated its air emissions at least twice before, DEQ records show. In 2018, state regulators found Chemours was emitting 2,700 pounds of GenX into the air—amounts 40 times higher than the company had originally reported in early 2017, and four times higher than the company’s revised estimates.
In 2021, the company again underreported its GenX emissions by 40 percent. The next year, DEQ fined Chemours $305,000 for failing to maintain air pollution control equipment, which allowed excessive amounts of GenX to enter the air.
Chemours plans to expand its Fayetteville Works plant, which DuPont opened in the early 1980s. The company filed an air permit application with the state in 2022 and revised it last year. However, environmental advocates, including the Southern Environmental Law Center, objected to the application because it redacted key information that Chemours claimed was confidential, including emission rates from stack testing, hours of operation and production figures.
DEQ notified Chemours nearly a year ago that the application was on hold until the company could submit revised emission calculations necessary for the Division of Air Quality to conduct review. Chemours has yet to submit this information, an agency spokesman said.
Based on the new deficiencies identified in its letter, the division could request additional data.
Chemours has until February to file a plan to address the state’s air concerns listed in the letter. As for the groundwater and soil cleanup plan under the consent order, DEQ has asked Chemours to respond to the state’s critique within 60 days.
There still is no timeline for the work to be completed. Given the scope of the contamination, it could take decades.

name: Source New Mexico
title: ICE increases arrests at New Mexico home construction sites, putting workers on edge
description: New Mexico homebuilders are reporting a sharp increase of federal immigration raids at home construction sites across Albuquerque and Santa Fe in recent weeks, resulting in arrests and project delays across the industry during a statewide housing shortage.
text:
U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcements agents targeted workers building these single-family Habitat for Humanity homes in Albuquerque on Nov. 10, 2026, according to the organization’s CEO, amid an apparent increase in ICE activity at home construction sites across the state. (Photo by Patrick Lohmann/Source NM)New Mexico homebuilders are reporting a sharp increase of federal immigration raids at home construction sites across Albuquerque and Santa Fe in recent weeks, resulting in arrests and project delays across the industry during a statewide housing shortage.
Miles Dylan Conway, CEO of the New Mexico Home Builders Association, told Source NM that he’s received approximately 20 calls or texts from developers in the last week reporting that U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement agents have descended on home construction sites, often in unmarked SUVs, and have arrested multiple workers at a time.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“The level of activity I’ve had on my phone, the calls from members who are sometimes calling on behalf of their subcontractors, are telling me that the pace and intensity of the immigration enforcement is significantly escalated,” he said.
ICE officials did not respond to Source NM’s emailed request for comment Tuesday about whether the agency is stepping up its activity at home construction sites and how many people it has detained.
But Source NM’s interviews with home developers, immigration advocacy groups and homebuilder organizations suggest at least five such operations netting more than a dozen arrests have occurred at construction sites over the last month. Social media video has also shown ICE agents leading handcuffed workers away from partially built homes in Santa Fe and Albuquerque in recent weeks. 
The raids have occurred at large, multi-family developments as well as at least one small project site in a low-income Albuquerque neighborhood.
On Tuesday morning, ICE agents arrived in Albuquerque’s San Jose neighborhood as workers were pouring concrete for driveways on two nearly complete, single-family Habitat for Humanity homes, Bill Bidal, CEO of the Greater Albuquerque Habitat for Humanity, told Source NM on Wednesday. 
“Out of the blue, the federal authorities showed up,” Bidal, who said he arrived at the site shortly after workers fled, relayed. “We’ve heard rumors all over town for the last couple weeks about activity, but to have it hit home like this was very, very sudden.”
ICE didn’t detain any Habitat for Humanity contractors, Bidal said, and the two low-income families the homes are built for will likely be able to move in after Thanksgiving. But he said he remains “in total shock.”
Sales employees from Twilight Homes, which is developing several large subdivisions in Albuquerque and Santa Fe, told Source NM on Wednesday that ICE targeted their subcontractors in recent weeks and those of other developers at adjacent sites. 
Pauline Hansen, a sales counselor for Twilight Homes in Mesa Del Sol, said ICE agents have been out “several times” in the last few weeks to hers and other companies’ sites in the subdivision south of Albuquerque. ICE detained four subcontractors doing concrete work for Twilight Homes several weeks ago, she said, and she witnessed an additional raid last week for another company during which ICE arrested an additional four workers on a different development. 
“They’re going everywhere, apparently,” she said. “It’s quite disturbing.”
Federal immigration agents have increased their arrests at New Mexico home construction sites in recent weeks, including at Los Brios in Santa, a Twilight Homes development pictured above Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Matt Mondschein/Source NM)
Fear of ICE arrests has prompted workers not to show up to job sites, even in locations that ICE hasn’t targeted, Conway said. 
“A lot of projects this week are not operating,” he said. “It’s oftentimes even folks with documentation — visas and work permits — are not coming to work because the potential for them to get swept up in one of these actions is very real.”
Johanna Gilligan, the CEO of nonprofit developer Homewise, told Source NM on Wednesday that workers on Homewise projects, particularly those contracted for stucco work, have shown up at low rates over the last month or so. She said her organization is anticipating at least weeks of delays in projects being completed.
“It has the potential to have a knock-on effect, just out of people taking an abundance of precaution,” she said about workers afraid to show up to job sites. “So we are definitely concerned about how this could be exacerbating what’s already a hard process of building homes.”
The National Association of Home Builders estimates that the industry relies on a workforce that is approximately 30% foreign-born. In a state that lacks approximately 58,000 affordable housing units, Conway said he is hoping homebuilders will prevail upon President Donald Trump’s administration to stop the crackdown. 
The administration has revoked millions of immigrants’ work permits in the last two years, including in the construction industries. But Trump also said he was open to making a deal on work permits in certain industries in an interview shortly after the midterm elections last week in which Democrats reclaimed control over both chambers of Congress. 
Conway said he hopes New Mexico homebuilders will speak up more in the coming days to pressure Trump to make a deal. 
“When I get that many calls and texts, there just seems to be an overwhelming energy to try and find a strategy forward,” he said. “We just really need a strategy forward that’s different than what’s happening now.”

name: Tennessee Lookout
title: Commentary: The fine art of constitution writing, and the continued lengthening of Tennessee’s Constitution
description: Tennessee voters this month grew our state’s constitution by 442 words.  Amendment One, expanding the number of crimes for which the accused can be held without bail, passed by better than a two-to-one margin. It added 152 words and deleted 53.  Amendment Two, banning a statewide property tax, also passed more than two-to-one. It added […]
text:
The U.S. Constitution is a model of brevity, but Tennessee lawmakers can't stop adding to that of the Volunteer State. (Illustration: Getty Images)Tennessee voters this month grew our state’s constitution by 442 words. 
Amendment One, expanding the number of crimes for which the accused can be held without bail, passed by better than a two-to-one margin. It added 152 words and deleted 53.  Amendment Two, banning a statewide property tax, also passed more than two-to-one. It added 36 words and deleted 20.  Amendment Three, a victim’s rights measure, passed by better than a three-to-one margin. It added 517 words and deleted 190.
Let’s put aside, for a moment, the merits of each of these public policy questions and instead ask ourselves what kind of things belong in state constitutions and which are better placed in statutes (laws) or left to judicial discretion (interpretation of laws)?
The U. S. Constitution is a model of brevity. The original draft contained just 4,543 words, including the signatures of the 39 signing delegates. It has 27 amendments, the first ten of which —the Bill of Rights — have been with our republic since the start. Add in those amendments and 17 subsequent ones and our Constitution grows to 7,591 words — still one of the shortest national constitutions in the world. The original handwritten text fit on just four large parchment sheets.
Tennessee voters will decide whether those accused of some felonies lose right to pretrial bail

By contrast, the average state constitution is about 26,000 words, more than three times as long. Alabama’s state constitution is a behemoth at an estimated 388,882 words. The recent additions send Tennessee’s state constitution over 14,000 words, still rather modest compared to many other states — Texas at nearly 87,000, Oklahoma’s topping 81,000, Louisiana and Missouri both clocking in at more than 69,000.
The impulse when crafting a constitution is to put a lot of things in there to be certain you get the kind of society you want. Some of these provisions don’t age well and look silly or worse in retrospect. We still have a provision, one hopes unnecessary, preventing those who fight in or challenge others to duels from holding public office in our state (Article IX, Section 3). In 2022 Tennessee voters quietly removed a provision that allowed slavery or involuntary servitude as a criminal punishment. That same year we also removed an obsolete (and long held unenforceable by federal courts) ban on the clergy serving in the General Assembly.
Several states have “zombie” provisions that remain on the books but are unenforceable, including literacy tests for voting, restricting certain offices only to men and disqualifying atheists from public office.
Amended: All four amendments to Tennessee’s Constitution pass overwhelmingly

Florida’s Constitution (Article X, Section 21) prohibits the cruel and inhumane confinement of pregnant pigs on farms. Now, before anyone squeals that I am for inhumane treatment of pigs, let me reiterate this column is not about the merits of the policy; it’s about what needs to be in a constitution and what works just fine as a statute.
Constitutions set out the basic functions of government (done at what level and by what body) and also protect against government overreach by delineating what rights exist, are held by the people, and cannot be abridged by the government. 
The U.S. Constitution is far from a perfect model, especially when one considers the democracy twisting potential of the Electoral College and some of the interpretation abuses by the current Supreme Court. Nevertheless, it remains a good work in progress and usually a coherent structure.
Elected officials, new members of the military, and naturalized citizens all take an oath to uphold the Constitution. Many groups give out pocket copies of it, and many Members of Congress repeatedly point out how they carry those pocket copies with them. This “less is more” approach works so long as some neutral court is given the task of interpreting constitutional application. The founders, for example, did not and could not envision video recorders, much less streaming services, but they did set out a provision, Article I, Section 8, Clause 8, for Congress “To Promote the Progress of Science and the Useful Arts, by securing for limited Times to Authors and Inventors the exclusive Right to their respective Writings and Discoveries.” Past precedent regarding copyrights and patents thus can guide courts in these matters.
In Tennessee, we could and should let judges weigh the merits of when to hold without bail those not yet convicted of anything. We could and should also pass laws about victim rights and the procedures to assure them. We probably do not need to doubly and triply assure our fidelity to no state income tax ever. We have made all of these constitutional matters, however, and just for a moment or two let us ask ourselves, what really requires constitutional amendment and what is pompous pandering.

name: West Virginia Watch
title: WV school officials ask Supreme Court to halt Logan court proceedings regarding school closure
description: West Virginia school officials are asking the state’s highest court to step in and stop a lower court’s decision temporarily preventing the closure of a Logan County elementary school.
text:
(Getty Images)West Virginia school officials are asking the state’s highest court to step in and stop a lower court’s decision temporarily preventing the closure of a Logan County elementary school.
The state Department of Education and the Logan County school board this week filed an emergency writ of prohibition with the state Supreme Court of Appeals. The legal action seeks to halt proceedings in Logan County Circuit Court, where Judge Sabrina Deskins last week granted a temporary restraining order preventing school officials from taking further action to close South Man Elementary School.
The Logan school board is considering consolidating the school into Man Elementary School, a decision that would require the approval of the state school board.
School officials are also considering closing Hugh Dingess Elementary and Justice Elementary, all of which have fewer than 100 students and need repairs to bring them up to code, school officials have said.
Deskins granted a temporary restraining order requested by parent Lauren Browning and community member Donna Thibault, who asked the judge to stop school officials from moving forward with closing South Man until the resolution of legal challenges over the state school aid formula and the 2027 legislative session, which is expected to focus on the school aid formula.
The American Civil Liberties Union of West Virginia filed a lawsuit in September over the funding formula, asking the the West Virginia Supreme Court of Appeals to require lawmakers to correct it.
Deskin’s order last week directed the Logan school board to cancel a public hearing on the school closure scheduled for Nov. 4, and not to move forward with a vote on the proposed closure that had been planned for Thursday.
In the emergency petition filed Thursday, attorneys for the school boards argued that they are empowered by law to close and consolidate schools in the state, and that Deskin’s order prevented them from complying with the laws.
“That result cannot stand — this Court should issue a writ of prohibition undoing the Circuit Court’s temporary restraining order and prohibiting it from blocking Petitioners from complying with West Virginia law governing school closure,” the petition said.
“This case implicates core separation of powers principles. The Legislature creates laws that govern the school system. The West Virginia Board of Education creates the policies and rules to manage the day-to-day operation of the school system, including ‘clos(ing) and consolidat(ing) schools when it deems necessary.’”
In their lawsuit, attorneys for Browning and Thibault argue that the judge should grant the restraining order until after the Legislature has time to address the school funding aid formula.
“It would be tragic to deny the (temporary restraining order) and South Man Elementary School closes, and then in six months the legislature fixes the funding formula solving the very funding issues the defendant publicly states are inadequate to keep SMES open and thriving,” attorneys wrote in the petition.
“Granting the relief of a temporary restraining order would permit the Supreme Court time to address the numerous legal challenges to the current school funding formula, as well as the Legislature time to allocate resources to counties that meet the mandate required by the West Virginia Constitution of providing a thorough and efficient system of free schools. If neither happens, the defendant is no worse off.”
School officials told lawmakers this week they would need an increase of $410 million in state aid for public schools to stabilize public school finances, which are in dire straits and have prompted a wave of school closures across the state.
The Logan County court has indicated it could not hold a hearing in the case until Dec. 8, a date the state school board said is too late
“If this Court does not issue a writ of prohibition now, Petitioners cannot follow the law and resolve whether to consolidate South Man Elementary School into Man Elementary School effective for the 2027-2028 school year,” the school boards wrote.
“Time is of the essence. School closure decisions must be made shortly, or it will be too late to issue a closure decision affecting the 2027-2028 school year,” the petition said. It added that if the decision to close the school is postponed, state taxpayers will pay an $1.3 million for each additional year the school remains open.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: Outgoing DFL Rep. Dan Wolgamott arrested again on suspicion of driving while impaired
description: Rep. Dan Wolgamott, DFL-St. Cloud, was arrested by the St. Cloud Police Department on Wednesday on suspicion of driving while impaired. The fourth-term legislator was arrested just after 9 p.m. on Wednesday and booked into the Stearns County Jail. He was arrested on three DWI-related charges, including criminal vehicular operation, bodily harm under the infl[...]
text:
Then-House Speaker Pro-Tempore Dan Wolgamott, DFL-St. Cloud, hands the omnibus supplemental education finance and policy bill to Chief Clerk Pat Murphy on April 27. (Photo by Paul Battaglia/Minnesota House Information.)Rep. Dan Wolgamott, DFL-St. Cloud, was arrested by the St. Cloud Police Department on Wednesday on suspicion of driving while impaired.
The fourth-term legislator was arrested just after 9 p.m. on Wednesday and booked into the Stearns County Jail. He was arrested on three DWI-related charges, including criminal vehicular operation, bodily harm under the influence of alcohol; third-degree driving while impaired; and operating a vehicle under the influence of alcohol.
The circumstances surrounding Wolgamott’s arrest are unclear, but a charge for bodily harm criminal vehicular operation indicates police judged that someone was injured, according to state statute.
Wolgamott did not answer a Reformer call seeking comment, and his voice mail box was full. He did not immediately respond to a text message seeking comment. The Stearns County Jail roster indicates Wolgamott was still in jail as of Thursday morning.
Wolgamott is leaving the Legislature after an unsuccessful run for state auditor.
In 2023, Wolgamott was arrested by the state patrol on suspicion of DWI in Kanabec County. Wolgamott pleaded guilty to a 4th degree DWI charge after a Minnesota State Patrol trooper pulled him over and arrested him near Mora, Minnesota. In that incident, Wolgamott acknowledged that his blood alcohol concentration was above the .08 legal limit.
The 2023 arrest came after someone called in a complaint about a person drinking in a liquor store parking lot in Mora. The trooper later saw the car weaving within its own lane, according to the state patrol’s incident report, and the trooper pulled the car over. Wolgamott was identified as the driver.
In security camera footage of the liquor store parking lot, Wolgamott appeared to take a drink out of a bottle, put it in his trunk, get back in his car and drive away.
In a statement at the time, Wolgamott said he had undergone professional testing and received “an assessment that I do not have an alcohol-use disorder.” In addition, Wolgamott said he attended an eight-hour alcohol education class and a Mothers Against Drunk Driving victim panel.
A number of Minnesota lawmakers have been arrested on suspicion of drunk driving in recent years. Most recently, then-Rep. Elliott Engen, R-White Bear Lake Township, was arrested in March on suspicion of DWI. Rep. Walter Hudson, R-Albertville, was a passenger in his vehicle and he was not charged with a crime. Hudson was carrying a firearm while impaired, which is against the law, though he was never charged.
Other current lawmakers arrested include DFL Rep. Brion Curran, DFL-White Bear Lake, DFL Sen. Tou Xiong, DFL-Maplewood, and Sen. John Jasinski, R-Fairbault.

name: Maryland Matters
title: Maryland environment secretary to step down, in latest shakeup to Moore’s Cabinet
description: Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain and Emergency Management Secretary Russell Strickland both announced their departures Thursday, as the Moore administration continues remaking its leadership ahead of a second term.
text:
Maryland Environment Secretary Serena McIlwain speaks at an Oct. 2, 2025, event at the Conowingo Dam. McIlwain announced Thursday she is stepping down, the latest Cabinet departure as Gov. Wes Moore prepares for his second term. (File photo by Christine Condon/Maryland Matters)Serena McIlwain, who has led Gov. Wes Moore’s (D) environmental department since shortly after his inauguration in 2023, will step down at the end of this year, she announced Thursday.
McIlwain, who came to the department from the California Environmental Protection Agency, said in an email to staff on Thursday morning that she would be resigning “after 38 rewarding years in public service and four incredible years serving as your Secretary.”
“When I returned home to Maryland to lead this agency, my priority was to support and empower the dedicated professionals who protect our state’s air, land, and water every single day. Thanks to your tireless efforts, we have accomplished extraordinary things,” McIlwain wrote.
Lee, Scruggs, Rothstein depart Moore’s Cabinet

Deputy Secretary Adam Ortiz will step in as acting secretary on Jan. 1, McIlwain said in her email. Ortiz previously served as a regional administrator for President Joe Biden’s (D) Environmental Protection Agency, overseeing the regional office for Maryland and four other states, plus the District of Columbia.
Also departing is Secretary of Emergency Management Russell Strickland, who will retire on Dec. 8. Moore announced he will appoint Montgomery County Assistant Chief Administrative Officer Earl Stoddard to serve as acting secretary, beginning Dec. 9.
Since winning a second term on Nov. 3, Moore has announced a new chief of staff as well as other changes to his Cabinet: Last week, the secretaries of State, Veterans and Military Affairs, and Public Safety and Correctional Services all cleaned out their desks and were replaced immediately by interim directors.
Additional changes are expected before the General Assembly reconvenes and Moore is sworn in for a second term in January. Such changes are not uncommon.
