name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Remembering Professor Mike Shea, a quiet champion of the arts
description: SCSU Professor Mike Shea, who taught at the university for 41 years and became a cheerleader of arts and culture, died last month.
text:
Mike Shea never missed the chance to make a connection. 
Teaching Shakespeare to his students at Southern Connecticut State University, he brought actors along with him, to make sure a scene came vividly to life. In the popcorn-scented lobbies of movie theaters, he stayed to talk with staff long after the final credits had rolled. If he was late — to a class, to a meeting, to an opening night — it was because he had met a friend along the way, or made one somewhere between the front door and his destination.
Shea, a steadfast champion of the arts who taught English at SCSU for 41 years and chaired the department for nine of them, died on Oct. 24, following a hit-and-run incident earlier that month in New Haven’s Westville neighborhood. In the wake of his death, a community of friends, family, students, professors, and lifelong theater kids have come forward to grieve a man who they describe as quietly generous, sharply brilliant and utterly himself. 
He was 74 when he died, and his colleagues, family and friends said he possessed a knowledge of theater, film, and literature that often seemed vast enough to last a person three or four lifetimes. He is survived by his wife of 29 years, Central Connecticut State University Professor Candace Barrington, their two adult children, his three siblings, and thousands of people who adored him, from nonprofit arts leaders to SCSU staff and alumni still reeling from the sudden news of his death.   
In his honor, friends and family have set up “Let’s See a Play: Mike Shea Student Performance Fund,” which will cover the cost of theater tickets for students who can’t afford to see a live performance. A memorial is also planned at the John Lyman Center for the Performing Arts on November 15, from 1 to 3 p.m. 
“Mike believed that you bought art from artists, and it didn’t have to be an investment. The investment was in the artist, not the art,” Barrington said in an interview at their New Haven home last Wednesday. ”And you went to plays, and you bought the tickets, and you went to the movie theater to keep the movie theaters going. It was like, ‘If you want these things [to survive], you have to go. You have to pay for it, and you have to support it.’”
“He knew how to look and listen, and observe,” she added. “He wasn’t interested in what things meant, but how they meant. How they created meaning.” 
Shea’s commitment to others, and his interest in asking questions, began in his very first years of life. The inquisitive youngest of four children (“and they thought he hung the moon,” Barrington said of his adoring siblings), Shea was born and raised in Baltimore, where he later attended Loyola College. As a kid, he grew up in the Jesuit tradition, a branch of Catholicism that is committed to social justice, education, and public service. 
While Shea stopped formally attending church in high school, he never lost that tie to public service and community building. He was constantly checking in on people, from childhood friends to elders who had survived his parents, to students who were in the midst of a tumultuous life transition. Somehow, there was always room for more: Shea could not get through a semester, or sometimes even a dinner out with his family, without inviting someone new into his orbit. 
“He’d say [to a waiter], you know, ‘How long have you been working here? Do you go to school?’ Because most servers do, right?” Barrington remembered. “If they look like they’re under 30, that’s a pretty safe question. [He’d say,] ‘Oh, what are you studying? Where do you go? Do you like it? What made you just choose that? And we would know the server’s entire life history” by the end of the evening. 
In the last three and a half decades of his life, he often ended the conversation by pulling a card emblazoned with the sun out of his wallet, and inviting them to the solstice parties he and Barrington hosted at their home. By last year, the invite list included hundreds of people: actors Shea had met backstage, movie theater staffers, SCSU faculty and alumni, theater makers and film nerds, chefs and servers from local restaurants.
“It was his commitment to making a richer life for everyone, without any sense of self-aggrandizement at all,” his oldest sister Maureen Fry said of his wide-open, magnanimous spirit. “I think of it as a gift he was always giving to someone, either individually or to students, or to the community as a whole.” 
“He Was Truly The Best Of Us”

Professor Mike Shea leading an English class at SCSU. Credit: Isabel Chenoweth / Southern Connecticut State University

Shea moved to Connecticut in the 1980s, after earning both graduate and doctoral degrees in English literature at Miami University of Ohio. Shea became a professor at Southern in 1985, where his students and colleagues quickly learned that he was as kind as he was rigorous, with a curiosity that was contagious. 
“He was just so charming, and his enthusiasm was just so incredible,” said Rob Harmon, who first met Shea in 1999, when Harmon was working as the manager at the York Square Cinema and toying with the idea of going back to school. \ His advice that Harmon pursue the school’s “Media Studies” major helped steer him to Best Video Film & Cultural Center, where he’s now the video archive director.
Shea was constantly thinking about how to make the texts he was teaching feel alive, from in-classroom performances of Shakespeare to field trips around the state, and sometimes on and off Broadway, complete with dinner that he covered out of pocket (colleagues Joel Dodson and Phil Smith, who have known him since 2011 and 1985 respectively, estimated that Shea spent thousands of dollars of his own money so that students could experience live theater; more on that below).
Laura Kirk, now the director of audience services at the David Geffen School of Drama at Yale University, remembered meeting Shea three decades ago, when she was a young thespian at SCSU and Shea was a new professor. With a group of other young, bright-eyed  theater nerds, Kirk became an early member of the Naked Theater, a grassroots company that existed for just a few years. Shea was one of its first boosters and board members, eager to cheer actors on even after the company disbanded.
When Kirk left acting to start a family, ultimately working in arts and educational nonprofits, Shea eagerly pulled her back in, asking her to act out scenes with friends during his Shakespeare classes. Once, she remembered with a laugh, he proposed Helena and Hermia’s fight from “ A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” but asked actors to play it as if they were on the Jerry Springer show. That was just who he was, Kirk said: he wanted to show students the same level of joy and delight he felt every time he returned to the Bard. 
Shea’s love for literature, and care for his students, never waned. For some students, now alumni, it looked like frequent visits to his office hours, during which he helped steer them toward majors they hadn’t ever considered. For others, it was the way he made clear how bitingly funny and trenchant Shakespeare and his contemporaries could be, once students got the hang of the 16th-century language. 
“You could just tell he was absolutely enamored with it,” said Justin Ayora, a high school English teacher in Danbury who took Shea’s introduction to Shakespeare in the fall of 2025, when he was finishing his studies in SCSU’s college of education. “I learned from him that the best way for students to be invested in the learning is simply being in love with the thing that you’re teaching yourself. Because he loved it so much, you wanted to show him, ‘Hey, I love this too.’”
Now, Ayora brings the same verve to his classroom, including a unit on magical realism and the author Gabriel García Márquez that the class just finished. It may seem far from Shakespeare, he acknowledged, but the core of how to teach the material remains the same. 
“He truly got the best out of us, as learners and human beings,” he said. “He’s truly the best of us. You talk about an educator who helps you light a fire within yourself … that’s Mike. I want to show these kids, ‘I love this and I care for you,’ because that was Mike. What a privilege it is to have known him.”
“When In Doubt, Go To The Show”

The door outside Mike Shea’s office now bears notes and remembrances from students and fellow faculty, including a note that says simply, “Good night, sweet prince,” a reference to Horatio’s parting words to Prince Hamlet. Credit: Contributed Photo

While Shakespeare was Shea’s specialty, his interest in the arts spanned media and centuries, from early modern drama to modern and contemporary German and Japanese film to obscure and popular folk music. He had an insatiable hunger for the cinematic and performing arts, as eager to see a student show in Southern’s tight black box theater as he was to attend two off-Broadway plays in a single afternoon. 
At least once a week, he caught a double or triple feature at the movies, a habit that made him a beloved fixture at the now-shuttered Criterion and York Square Cinemas in downtown New Haven, as well as Hartford’s Cinestudio, the Madison Art Cinemas, Regal Branford, and Regina A. Quick Center for the Arts in Fairfield, among others.  
Rai Bruton, a former Criterion employee who is now the executive director of Hamden’s Best Video Film & Cultural Center, remembered seeing Shea each week, one of a handful of movie theater faithfuls she could count on before the theater ultimately closed in October 2023.  
What stood out to her, and still does years later, was how genuinely friendly Shea was, and how curious he always seemed to hear what she and fellow staff members thought of the same film. It was only after he learned that she had left college under financial duress and was juggling multiple jobs with dreams of finishing a novel that she learned that he was a tenured professor.
“He tried to give me a little bit of a roadmap,” she remembered. “I had been in school to be a teacher, and it was very much what a good teacher would do. He was just so kind, and he talked to everyone.”
He was, in that same way, a quiet and unassuming supporter of Connecticut’s arts ecosystem, with a fondness for theater that never stopped at the state’s borders. At the time of his death, Shea was a season regular at the Yale Repertory Theatre, Yale Cabaret, Collective Consciousness Theatre, Long Wharf Theatre, Hartford Stage, the Brooklyn Academy of Music (BAM), Theatre for a New Audience, and the Red Bull Theater, among others. 
In addition, he was a longstanding board member at Elm Shakespeare Company, with a particular dedication to its educational programming. Elm’s Artistic Director, Rebecca Goodheart, who referred to him as “the quiet glue for our community,” fondly remembered how Shea was often the only board member who seemed to fully read and weigh in on the minutes   
Joel Dodson, an early modernist and professor of English and Arts Administration at SCSU who Shea hired in 2011, estimated that the two saw “ conservatively 10,” and likely closer to 20 or 30, movies together every year, in addition to several live performances across Connecticut, New York, and the Northeast. 
In 2021, the two made the trip to New York to see a marathon performance of Shakespeare’s Roman tragedies, including “Julius Caesar,” “Antony & Cleopatra,” and “Coriolanus,” at BAM. This month, the two had tickets to see Ann Carson’s translation of Sopocles’ “Elektra” at the Theatre for a New Audience in New York 
“Mike’s main ethos was, ‘When in doubt, go to the show,’” Dodson said. Whatever the outcome, Shea often left with the same five parting words: “I’m glad they did that.” 
It wasn’t just that the two both studied and loved Shakespeare, Dodson added: Shea was something of a “social father figure in the arts,” who encouraged him to donate to organizations he liked, and “taught me what it meant to tie the academic work of loving Shakespeare to the public work of loving Shakespeare.” 
He was often in awe of Shea’s three-week summer intensive “Shakespeare Alive,” in which he and students would read a Shakespeare play, watch a film adaptation, and then see a live performance before the end of the course period. Following Shea’s injury and death in October, Dodson took over his “Intro to Shakespeare” courses, in which students are reading “Twelfth Night” after starting the semester with “Much Ado About Nothing.” 
“He believed in the liberal arts,” Dodson said. He pointed to Shea’s syllabi, in which the words “serendipity” and “community” often appeared together. “People can be so protective of their areas of specialization,” but Shea never was. He wanted to share his love for the subject matter, and so he did. 
His belief in both the liberal and the performing arts, from cinema to experimental theater, often spilled over into the generosity he showed his students. In the summers, Shea was known and adored for “Shakespeare Alive,” which often ended with bug spray, picnic blankets and live Shakespeare in the August twilight of New Haven’s Edgerton Park. In the fall, he brought students into “Ambiguity in the Arts & Sciences,” an Honors College course that fused live theater and literature with Socratic-style dialogue.    
From the 1980s until his sudden death last month, Shea paid largely out of pocket so that his students — often first-generation college kids, working one or two jobs in addition to a full class load — could take an afternoon or evening off, eat lunch or dinner with the class, and see a play. If the show was in New York, that included an all-expenses trip to the Oyster Bar in the basement of Grand Central Station, where feeding students could quickly amount to hundreds of dollars. 
“There are some people whose presence strikes you as very noticeable, and Mike was not that way,” said Smith, who had hired Shea during his tenure as the dean of the College of Arts & Sciences, and remained close with him for four decades. “But he made a huge difference.”
Barrington, who Shea first met when she came in for an interview in 1997, saw him extend the same kindness to his colleagues, in and far beyond the English department. 
That first job went to an internal candidate, but then a second opened up months later. After the two began working together, Shea would answer her administrative questions, connect her with the right people in the travel or HR offices, and steer her to fellow faculty members who had the answers she was looking for. 
“And so after one semester, I knew everybody at Southern, because Mike had marched me around and introduced me to people,” she said. 
At the time, she was a single mom of two young children, with a degree in Medieval literature, and Shea quickly became both an academic cheerleader and a devoted partner. Barrington can still remember him visiting their Cape Cod style house in North Haven for the first time, and going right down to the basement to play Nerf guns with her son. 
That was it: the two spent the next 29 years learning from each other, from near-empty movie theaters to her academic conferences, where he was the life of the party in a crowd of Medievalists.
“He did that everywhere we went,” she said. “He just was so interested in people. And I think that that’s what the arts did for him, right? They allowed him to work with people and find out why they were interested in.”
In his 41 years at SCSU, Shea served as English department chair, president of the university’s chapter of the American Association of University Professors (AAUP), a member of the SCSU faculty senate, and a member of the Connecticut State University’s AAUP Faculty Union among other appointments.  
“He never missed an opportunity to speak out publicly about his concerns — to the press, to the BOR [Board of Regents], and to state legislators,” wrote Louise Williams, a professor of history at CCSU who is also the president of the school’s AAUP chapter.  
Now that he’s gone, friends and family members are thinking about how to keep his legacy alive. In addition to his memorial, which will feature a scene from “A Midsummer Night’s Dream,” a guided writing exercise, and tributes from many of the people who loved him, “Let’s See A Play” is committed to opening up opportunities for as many students as possible at a time when seeing a show can be prohibitively expensive.   
“He was always this joyful, bright spirit,” Kirk said. “It was so clear that he adored meeting people and he loved taking it all in … There must be thousands of people who can just take that bright light and turn it around. It’s just an immense ripple effect.”
A public memorial for Shea is planned at the John Lyman Center for the Performing Arts on November 15, from 1 to 3 p.m. More information is available here.

name: Louisiana Illuminator
title: ‘Very passionate, very principled’: St. Bernard state Rep. Mike Bayham dies
description: Mike Bayham, who represented St. Bernard Parish in the Louisiana House of Representatives, died Wednesday, according to a statement from his family.   He was 52 years old.
text:
State Rep. Mike Bayham represented St. Bernard Parish since 2024. (Louisiana Legislature photo)Mike Bayham, who represented St. Bernard Parish in the Louisiana House of Representatives, died Thursday, according to a statement from his family. He was 52 years old.
A lifelong Chalmette resident, Bayham had served House District 103 since January 2024. He held a seat on the St. Bernard Parish Council from 2001-04 and at the time was the youngest person elected to the office.    
Bayham got his start in state GOP politics in 1996 when he was elected to the Republican State Central Committee and remained a member for 30 years. He was secretary of the Louisiana Republican Executive Committee from 2008-12 and served as a presidential elector, which meant he cast a vote in the Electoral College on behalf of Louisiana, during 2008 and 2012 presidential elections. .
Bayham briefly acknowledged his health challenges in a social media post Saturday. Bayham’s legislative aide, Catherine Brinkman, sent out a followup email Wednesday stating he was “gravely ill and facing a serious health challenge.” 
Friends said Bayham considered his biggest professional triumph to be the recent approval of Constitutional Amendment 4, which establishes term limits for the Louisiana governor. It passed with 56% of the vote on the Nov. 3 ballot.
The measure, which Bayham authored during the 2026 legislative session, prevents a governor who has served one and one-half terms from running for the office again. Bayham had worked tirelessly over the past few months to gain voter approval, friends and colleagues said.  

“He considered it his political legacy,” said Susan East Nelson, a child welfare advocate who became close to Bayham when they were both LSU students in the 1990s. 

A lifelong Republican, Bayham was known as an independent thinker with a passion for politics that began at an early age. 

“His love for St. Bernard is unmatched,” Lt. Gov. Billy Nungesser said in an interview Wednesday. 
State Rep. Brian Glorioso, R-Slidell, attended secondary school and college with the Chalmette representative. He recalls Bayham tracking down conservative talk radio personality Rush Limbaugh on a Bacchus Mardi Gras parade float in New Orleans in the 1980s when they were in middle school.

“I had no idea who Rush Limbaugh was when we were in seventh grade, but Mike knew who he was,” said Glorioso, who shared a fraternity house room with Bayham at LSU. “I don’t even know if I could find the talk radio station in my car.” 
Bayham was interested in meeting political figures of all types, several of his friends said. It’s apparent from Bayham’s extensive collection of photos he shared on social media of himself with some of the world’s most famous people. The shots include Bayham with former President Ronald Reagan, former British Prime Minister Margaret Thatcher and Pope Leo XIV. 

During their freshman year at LSU, Bayham dragged Glorioso out of bed early one morning in 1992 to drive to downtown Baton Rouge and meet Al Gore, who was then a candidate for vice president. 

Bayham ran straight past the security barriers set up for Gore’s appearance and yelled out, “Hey, Al!” to get Gore’s attention. The future vice president stopped what he was doing and came over to talk to them, Glorioso said. 
A staunch Republican activist, Bayham enjoyed talking with people who held opposing views and had several decades-long friendships with Democrats. 

“He was the king of Free Speech Alley,” said longtime friend Jason Redmond, referencing the area near LSU’s Student Union where students, faculty and staff have held political debates and demonstrations since the 1960s. 

Redmond and Bayham met when they were working side-by-side booths for the Democratic and Republican parties at LSU in 1992. Redmond was supporting Bill Clinton for president, and Bayham was backing Republican Pat Buchanan, a conservative Catholic who lost in the GOP primary to President George H.W. Bush that year. 

“He was kind of a bull in a China shop,” said Redmond, who was roommates with Bayham toward the end of college. “He was very feisty, very passionate and very principled.” 
Nelson, who was also active in the Democratic Party while at LSU, said she was pleased to see Bayham win his election to the Louisiana Legislature in 2024, even if her politics differed from his. 

“I knew that he was the kind of person that we needed in the legislature. He was the kind of person that wasn’t going to be motivated by ideology but really what was best for the people,” she said.

In 2025, Bayham authored a new law that will require private insurance companies to pay for home visits after births for newborns and parents starting next year. Nelson, who worked for the Louisiana Policy Institute for Children at the time, asked Bayham to sponsor the legislation. 

“Louisiana will be the first state in the South to have universal home visits after the birth of a child,” Nelson said. 
Following the death of Dolly Parton in September, Bayham announced his intention to introduce legislation in 2027 to pay for a children’s literacy program funded with fees from a new specialty license plate in the country music icon’s honor.   
One of the first laws Bayham passed as a freshman legislator in 2024 outlawed the use of nondisclosure agreements in employment contracts to cover up sexual misconduct and other hostile acts in the workplace. 
Prior to joining the legislature, Bayham worked in St. Bernard Parish government for several years, where he most recently oversaw the parish’s public transportation services. 
Friends said Bayham’s had an ardent interest in transit systems, which he developed after traveling the world extensively. He had been to every country in Europe multiple times, Glorioso said, and attended the recent New Orleans Saints game in Paris.  
A devout Catholic, Bayham never missed Sunday Mass while traveling, friends said. He was a parishioner of Our Lady of Prompt Succor Catholic Church in Chalmette.
Born in New Orleans, Bayham graduated from Holy Cross High School and earned a bachelor of arts degree from LSU with minors in journalism, political science and history.

name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Dems, industry groups press for immigration changes post-midterms
description: Democrats and business leaders called on the Trump administration  to prioritize work permits and other protections for long-term immigrants.
text:
WASHINGTON — Democrats and business leaders publicly lobbied the Trump administration Wednesday to prioritize work permits and other protections for long-term immigrants during the lame-duck session of Congress and beyond.
Citing the midterm elections, when Democrats flipped the U.S House and Senate, and President Donald Trump’s recent admission that his immigration crackdown hurt Republicans at the ballot box, Democratic lawmakers argued that voters were clear about wanting immigration reform before the start of the next Congress. 
Congress has a lengthy to-do-list for the lame-duck session, possibly including government funding, the annual defense policy bill, the farm bill, a measure to regulate the college sports landscape and permitting reform to ease regulation on large construction projects. 
“We owe it to these families to try anything, and I’m willing to try anything,” Arizona Democratic Sen. Ruben Gallego said. 
He was joined by American Business Immigration Coalition Action, which lobbies for work permits and legal pathways for long-term immigrants, and the South Texas Builders Association, a local trade group that represents the construction industry that has a workforce that is 30% immigrant nationwide, and Democratic U.S. House members from Texas.
Asked how receptive the White House would be to work permits for immigrants, which the administration has vigorously worked to limit, Gallego didn’t directly answer.
Trump’s mixed signals 
The administration has revoked millions of immigrants’ work permits in the last two years. Many were workers in hospitality, healthcare and the construction industries. 
But shortly after the midterm elections, the president said he was open to making a deal on work permits in certain industries. 
At the same time, though, he elevated Stephen Miller, an official who has crafted some of the president’s harshest immigration policies, to White House chief of staff. 
“I think right now the best thing the White House could do is to actually try to send some type of signal, besides talk, that they’re serious about this, and the way to do that is to have some reforms already at (Immigration and Customs Enforcement),” Gallego said. 
“Whether it’s shutting down the detention centers, giving (a) certain level of protections, whether to veterans so they don’t get deported, to maybe parents of U.S. students so they don’t get deported, something to show that it’s not just talk, and this isn’t going to be a policy that’s led by Stephen Miller,” he added.
The vice chair of South Texas Builders Association, Benny Melendez, had a pointed message for Miller.
“If you want to continue harassing our communities, prepare yourself not only to lose your job, but … these same communities you are now harassing will make sure you lose the White House” in 2028, he said. 
Next Congress
If lawmakers are unable to get any major reforms through the crowded end-of-year session, Democrats are looking ahead to when they control both chambers next year.
House Republicans on Tuesday elected Ohio Rep. Jim Jordan, a staunch Trump supporter who has not supported immigration reform, to lead them in the minority. 
Texas Democratic Rep. Henry Cuellar, the incoming chair on the subcommittee that handles government funding for the Department of Homeland Security, said he’s not worried about Jordan because  Democrats will have a majority in January.
Cuellar, whom Trump pardoned after he and his wife were indicted on charges of bribery, money laundering and conspiracy, said he’s going to use his subcommittee gavel to add guardrails on ICE and clear the backlog at U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services, which processes legal immigrants.
Gallego said he thinks the Senate will be able to get to 60 votes on some type of immigration reform legislation in the 120th Congress, when Democrats will have at least 54 and up to 56 seats depending on races that are still too close to call.
Whether that overhaul is in one bill or a series of increments is up for debate, Gallego said. 
“If we can pass a big, beautiful conference immigration reform bill, the Trump immigration reform bill, and if that gets them on our side or not, then let’s do that,” Gallego said. “But if that doesn’t work, then I do think incremental passes to start protecting different communities I think is also an option. We should not avoid that either.”
This story was first published Nov. 11, 2026 by States Newsroom.

name: Nevada Current
title: Inmates’ families, advocates plead with state not to block delivery of physical mail
description: As correction officials wait for final legislative approval to restrict physical mail from being delivered to people who are incarcerated, prison advocacy groups are asking lawmakers to block the restriction. In response to a rise of drugs entering prisons and an increase in overdose among those incarcerated, the Nevada Department of Corrections proposed lim[...]
text:
(Photo: Nevada Department of Corrections)As correction officials wait for final legislative approval to restrict physical mail from being delivered to people who are incarcerated, prison advocacy groups are asking lawmakers to block the restriction.
In response to a rise of drugs entering prisons and an increase in overdose among those incarcerated, the Nevada Department of Corrections proposed limiting mail. Officials proposed to digitize the mail and give it to incarcerated people electronically. 
“NDOC is also aware that processing offender mail by digital scanning will likely not eliminate the introduction of contraband,” said prison director James Dzurenda in October, adding that it “will lessen the risk and allow for a greater focus on other avenues of contraband introduction.”
Return Strong and the Nevada Fines and Fees Justice Center have also questioned the evidence officials presented to the Board of Prison Commissioners in October justifying the regulation.  
“The director has been clear that taking away physical mail will not address demand for drugs, and it will only increase violence and the price of drugs, making compromising staff an even bigger reality than it already is,” Jodi Hocking, the founder of Return Strong, told commissioners. 
The Board of Prisons Commissioners, which includes Republican Gov. Joe Lombardo, Attorney General and now Governor-elect Aaron Ford, and Secretary of State Cisco Aguilar, both Democrats, unanimously approved the regulation to proceed. 
The regulation needs final approval from the Legislative Commission, which is slated to meet in December. 
Dzurenda  told the board the department used opioid settlement funds to conduct a study. 
The funds were used to place a drug detection device “at the High Desert State Prison to detect abnormalities in the mail,” he said, adding “233 were positively identified as containing contraband substances.”
Return Strong and the Nevada Fines and Fees Justice Center authored an analysis of study on prison mail, which it shared with Nevada Current.
The analysis argues that NDOC’s study should have inspected “mail selected at random and tested across facilities and security levels” rather than what NDOC prepared, which inspected 20% of mail at only High Desert State Prison “with no explanation of how pieces were selected.” 
“Statewide numbers were reached by simple multiplication,” according to the analysis findings, adding that the one-year study period ended after nine months and “before the holiday mail season.”
Hocking told the board in October it shouldn’t consider a regulation at all  “but especially not until all questions have been answered and problems resolved.”
“We know from history that we can’t go backwards and fix things that have already been passed,” she said. “We’re not even close to the point that this is ready to be moved forward.”
The analysis shared with the Current from prison advocacy groups also notes that “the study does not control for other possible causes: drugs coming in through other routes, changes in drug potency, changes in how overdoses are reported, population shifts, or access to medication-assisted treatment (MAT).” 
The full analysis is expected to be released publicly ahead of next month’s Legislative Commission meeting. 
NDOC originally tried to restrict mail in 2022, but the move was blocked by then Gov. Steve Sisolak.
Lawmakers in 2023 passed Assembly Bill 121 that not only requires all incarcerated people receive physical and original copies of their mail but mandates corrections officials submit a study “and any evidence or data” prior to adopting a regulation that restricts mail access. 
Hocking said the Legislature set a bar for NDOC to pursue a regulation, and it has not met that.  
“We’re not here to deny that the overdose crisis exists,” she said. “People are dying. Other incarcerated individuals, families, and staff are carrying that with them. We want it to stop as much as anyone in this room, but the law sets a bar.”
NDOC held its first public workshop on the proposed regulation in April despite not releasing any public study mandated by the law. The findings were released in May. 
Scoffing at state law requiring a study first, NDOC plans more limits on prison mail

The board was originally slated to hear the proposed regulation during the summer, but the item was withdrawn before re-emerging at the October meeting. 
If the regulation receives final legislative approval, Drzurenda said NDOC would pilot its new approach to mail, which would be scanned and given to inmates electronically, at High Desert State Prison first. 
“There’s going to be a 60-day notice to the offenders and their families with the address of where they send it to,” Dzurenda said at the October board meeting. “The process will begin after 60 days.” 
In addition to restricting physical mail, the new regulation also blocks people who are incarcerated from receiving picture drawings, which would instead be digitally scanned and uploaded on a person’s tablet. 
“This is unfortunately a necessary safety and security measure given that synthetic drugs are being added into the color ink and soaked into the paper,” Dzurenda said. 
People will still be able to send photographs, but Dzurenda said they would first have to use a yet-to-be determined company that specialized in printing photos.
“While this contract has not yet been finalized, the price for this service will be similar to the cost of reproduction photographs that are already in commercial photo centers such as Walgreens and CVS and similar convenience stores,” he said.
During an emotional public comment, family members of those incarcerated and formerly incarcerated individuals pleaded with the board not to approve the restriction.
Among those opposed to the regulation was Nathaniel Williams, who said he was incarcerated in Nevada four times. 
Williams said he struggled with addiction throughout his life, including while incarcerated in Nevada.
“I didn’t do heroin until I was in the Nevada Department of Corrections and never used a syringe until I was in the Nevada Department of Corrections,” he said. “That heroine and that syringe did not come through the mail.”
The only thing he received in the mail were letters from his grandmother and son, which he brought with him as he testified in October. He was released from prison three years ago, and said he will always keep those letters because of what they meant to him while incarcerated. 
Prior to his vote in October, Ford said he understood his support of restriction mail would “disappoint a lot of people out there, I think this is a very important step to take,” 
“I do think that the study that has been utilized is sufficient for purposes of satisfying the statutory requirement as well,” he said.

name: CommonWealth Beacon
title: The House bid to expand gambling is not just a bad idea. It’s a stealthy move that underscores what the public hates about the Legislature.
description: The plan is a giveaway to special interests that has received none of the scrutiny of earlier casino legislation.
text:
TO PUT IT in fitting terms, the Legislature’s handling of a potential expansion of gambling in Massachusetts has a less-than-subtle “tell” that signals how they prefer to govern in general: quietly, behind closed doors, and with as little public engagement as possible.  
Arguably, no one is more tired of talking about expansion of gaming in Massachusetts than I am. As the co-chair of the group that blocked a Suffolk Downs casino bid in 2013, a proponent of the failed 2014 statewide repeal initiative aimed at ousting gaming altogether, and the chair of the ballot question opposition that blocked an international dark-money-financed bid to expand gaming licensure in Massachusetts in 2016, I was pretty sure that nothing had been left unsaid.   
Unfortunately, the Massachusetts House has us back at it as they attempt to override their own carefully crafted casino legislation through a barely public, backroom maneuver.   
As a House-Senate conference committee negotiates differences in their respective versions of a sweeping economic development bill, one of the biggest, most tangible stumbling blocks appears to be a provision in the House version that would allow so-called historical horse racing machines at former race tracks – the Suffolk Downs horse track, which straddles the Boston-Revere border, and the former dog racing track in Raynham.  
It’s a bad idea on the merits. But beyond that, this proposal to significantly alter state gambling law has gone through none of the public review and debate that all meaningful pieces of legislation should be subjected to, and it should be killed on that important principle alone.  
Historical horse racing is roughly defined as machines that allow gamblers to bet on previously run horse races. With that narrow definition, and the image it conjures of some kind of nostalgic niche apparatus, they are not classified as casinos but as track-betting operations. Google a photo of these machines, however, and it’s clear that they look, operate, and function just like slots, with no indication that there is any relationship to racing – save for the statistics on past races embedded somewhere in the coding.   
Greenlighting these would be equivalent to giving the holders of track licenses permission to open a slots parlor without a license, without host community agreements, and without the mandated taxes or dividends required by rightful casino and slots licensees.   
It not only would cut into licensed gaming action from casinos and slots parlors, 15 to 40 percent of which goes to the state, but would further cannibalize state lottery dividends that return up to 93 percent of revenues to the state economy. 
If accepted by the Legislature as written, a prime beneficiary of the amendment would be the Sterling Suffolk Group, which hasn’t held a live horse race at Suffolk Downs since 2019, although they still operate simulcasting there. (They’re already cashing in on millions from the state-mandated Race Horse Development Fund, which is funded by casinos.)   
The historical horse race amendment, sponsored by state Rep. Adrian Madaro of East Boston, would be a giveaway to the biggest losers in Massachusetts’s short gaming history – Sterling Suffolk Group lost out to Wynn Resorts in the competition for the Boston region casino license.     The stealthy initiative — which is being championed by House Speaker Mariano, is poised to upset the existing gambling industry, face an outcry from gambling opponents, and possibly legal action from existing licensees and tribal interests – could actually have a much bigger impact on the larger Massachusetts political stage. If this quiet, backdoor change is allowed to casino legislation that underwent rigorous public review at the time of its original passage, it would set a dangerous precedent for untold numbers and types of legislative tweaks going forward.   
The Massachusetts casino law gave voters a clear view of how legislation gets done. From its inception and the empaneling of the state gaming commission in 2011, it has been one of the least ambiguous laws in the state. The legislation authorizing casinos provided a road map for developers and opponents alike to engage in the process.  
Underscoring that point is the fact that East Boston activists were able to organize and defeat a 2013 referendum on a proposed casino at Suffolk Downs that had the backing of gambling giants Caesar’s Palace and Mohegan Sun. That showed that David could defeat Goliath, and that perhaps the deck wasn’t entirely stacked in favor of deep-pocketed interests.  
In sharp contrast to that more open process, which ultimately resulted in the awarding of three casino licenses statewide, the Legislature is taking the current conversation behind closed doors, excluding the public, and hoping to minimize attention.  For lawmakers, the biggest takeaway from that earlier history apparently was not that a fair and balanced process makes for good governance.  It was that excluding the public from the conversation ensures the outcomes insiders want.   
The biggest takeaway from the current House effort isn’t simply that the Legislature will stop at nothing to advance gaming.  It’s that the Legislature will stop at nothing to advance the goals of special interests.   
The new gambling effort is just the latest example. There are 4,844 lines in the economic development bill.  Amendment #386, which would authorize gambling on “historical horse racing,” only takes up a handful of them.  If you don’t get worked up over gambling in Massachusetts, or if you’re not concerned about the House attempt to quietly expand its reach in the state, you might take exception to their blatant efforts to divert existing gaming revenues to benefit special interests.   
Or you might, like me, wonder what’s in the remaining 3,754 lines of the economic development bill, who will benefit, and how you might be impacted.    
Celeste Ribeiro Hewitt was co-chair of No Eastie Casino, the citizen-led ballot question committee that led the opposition to the referendum on a casino at Suffolk Downs, and chair of the Committee for Sustainable and Responsible Economic Development, the ballot question committee opposing the 2016 ballot question to expand gaming licensing in Massachusetts, aimed at siting a slots parlor near Suffolk Downs.

name: Minnesota Reformer
title: What’s going on with Minnesota Medicaid funding? (reprise)
description: The Trump administration recently said it’s permanently denying over $112 million of Medicaid money to Minnesota, part of the $259 million it had threatened to claw back in February. The denied payments are for services provided from July 2025 to September 2025 and have largely been paid out. Minnesota will now be on the hook […]
text:
Dr. Mehmet Oz, Administrator of the US Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, speaks alongside other Trump administration officials during a press conference on Friday, Oct. 30, 2026 in St. Cloud, Minn. CMS recently said it’s permanently denying over $112 million of Medicaid funding to Minnesota. (Photo by Nicole Neri/Minnesota Reformer)The Trump administration recently said it’s permanently denying over $112 million of Medicaid money to Minnesota, part of the $259 million it had threatened to claw back in February.
The denied payments are for services provided from July 2025 to September 2025 and have largely been paid out. Minnesota will now be on the hook for paying that money back, unless the denials are somehow reversed.
The federal government has repeatedly threatened to freeze or claw back payments, but this sum is the first time the administration has permanently denied payments. It’s the latest episode in a yearlong fight between the Trump administration and Minnesota over Medicaid funding.
Here are a few things to know, plus a timeline to get caught up.
The funding fight centers around 14 Medicaid services deemed high-risk to fraud, waste and abuse
Medicaid is a sprawling public insurance program. It’s known for providing medical insurance for low-income people, but it also pays for nursing homes and long-term care services for seniors and disabled people. It’s jointly funded by federal and state money, but administered by the state.
The ongoing funding fight centers around 14 Medicaid services that were deemed in October 2025 by the Walz administration to be high risk for fraud, waste and abuse. Those services largely provide critical long-term care to disabled and elderly people.
Federal investigations have found that in the high-risk Medicaid services, some providers billed for services they didn’t provide. For example, an autism service provider is alleged to have paid kickbacks to families for enrolling their children while delivering a fraction of the services billed. One of the services, Housing Stabilization Services, was considered so riddled with fraud that the Walz administration shut it down in 2025.
Since then, the state has created a slew of program integrity measures, such as a prepayment claims review process and a re-screening of all providers in those 14 services.
Though federal funding actions have focused on those specific services, state officials have said that the freezes could deliver a serious blow to the state’s budget, health facilities and Medicaid enrollees in general. Medical Assistance, which is what Minnesota calls its Medicaid program, cost $20 billion in 2025, and is projected to outpace the state’s growth in tax revenue.
The funding actions are separate from Medicaid provisions in the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, which will result in less federal funding for the state. The OBBBA may also result in some possible savings, since some Minnesotans will lose their Medicaid coverage due to new, administratively burdensome work requirements.
The federal government extrapolated from a small group of claims when deciding how much to deny
The federal Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, known as CMS, looked at just 330 invoices from over 6 million Medicaid claims submitted by providers. CMS found that 78 of the 330 claims were deficient, according to an official notice from the federal agency.
CMS then extrapolated from the 78 deficient claims — which totaled about $112,000, according to Minnesota Department of Human Services Temporary Commissioner John Connolly — to conclude that over $112 million in claims was deficient.
The deficiencies include missing provider signatures in agreements and missing notes in treatment plans.
It’s unclear how the agency chose the 330-claim sample, which it described as “statistically valid” despite scant explanation. It’s also unclear how the agency extrapolated to $112 million in deficient claims.
What’s going on with Minnesota Medicaid funding?

Connolly, in a Tuesday email to his agency, said that the state human services department has “more questions than answers right now,” and called the denials “deeply concerning.”
“We remain concerned about the transparency and fairness of the process CMS is using to deny reimbursements for claims the state has already paid,” Connolly wrote.
In the notice, CMS also said it was releasing the remaining $131 million it deferred in February.
A timeline
The publicly available view of the fight is largely through official letters sent between CMS and the state’s Department of Human Services, and videos posted to CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz’s X account. Starting in January, the two agencies have also had regular virtual meetings.
December 2025: CMS ordered Minnesota to propose and implement a “corrective action plan,” i.e., an anti-fraud plan. Minnesota sent its first plan later that month.
January 2026: On Jan. 6, the Trump administration rejected Minnesota’s first corrective action plan.
In the Jan. 6 rejection, the administration said that it intended to withhold $2 billion of annual funding toward the high-risk Medicaid programs. Connolly said that was an overestimation of what the programs cost, which is $1.2 billion per year.
In the rejection, Oz wrote: “The withholding will end when the Minnesota Medicaid agency fully and satisfactorily implements a comprehensive (corrective action plan)” for the high-risk Medicaid services.
The state submitted a revised plan on Jan. 30.
February 2026: CMS announced that, in addition to the $2 billion withholding, it would defer $259 million from Minnesota. In the deferral process, the federal government can withhold funding when questioning the justification of specific claims already billed to Medicaid. The questioned claims were from July 2025 to September 2025.
The process has previously been used for individual claims and not entire service areas, the state noted in a press release.
Of the $259 million, $242 million comes from the 14 Medicaid services deemed a high risk for fraud and found questionable by the feds. Most of the rest come from services given to people who, according to CMS, lack “satisfactory immigration status.”
March 2026: Minnesota state officials sued the Trump administration over the $242 million, arguing that deferring the money before a hearing for the $2 billion freeze effectively denies Minnesota due process. That lawsuit is ongoing.
The federal government approved Minnesota’s corrective action plan later that month.
The federal approval of Minnesota’s plan appeared to be good news for Minnesota’s Medicaid funding. Oz had said that the government would let go of its funding threats after Minnesota proposes and implements a corrective action plan.
April 2026: CMS deferred $91 million more, stemming from services from October to December.
July 2026: CMS deferred $199 million more, for services from January to March of 2026.


October 2026: Connolly sent a letter to CMS on Oct. 2, asking for more clarification of how CMS identified high-risk providers, among a slew of other questions that were unanswered as of Oct. 30.
November 2026: The Trump administration permanently denied $112 million of the February deferral.
Eric C. Tostrud, chief judge for the District of Minnesota, has given CMS and the state human services department until Jan. 4 to try to resolve the lawsuit.
