name: Connecticut Mirror
title: ICE arrests 18-year-old in downtown New Haven
description: Immigration agents detained an 18-year-old Tuesday after he left a hearing in his criminal case at the state courthouse on Elm Street.
text:
Federal immigration agents detained an 18-year-old New Haven man Tuesday shortly after he left a hearing in his criminal case at the state courthouse on Elm Street — boxing in the car he was riding in, breaking a window, and pulling him out, according to the driver.
The driver said an agent also slammed the young man’s relative’s head when he got out to ask what was happening.
The young man, identified by advocates as Jaime, is in U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement custody, according to ICE’s online detainee locator.
Jaime was at the courthouse at 121 Elm St. Tuesday morning for a hearing in a pending criminal case — not an immigration matter. According to court records, New Haven police arrested him on Aug. 30 and charged him with first-degree assault, interfering with an officer, and evading responsibility in a crash that caused serious injury. He was released after posting a $200,000 bond and has not yet entered a plea.
John Lugo of Unidad Latina en Acción (ULA) said Jaime, who is from Guatemala, entered the country without authorization and is separately fighting an immigration case in federal immigration court. Lugo also said that ICE took Jaime to Hartford on Tuesday.
“It’s the same old story,” Lugo said. “It was a very terrifying situation for our volunteer” and the relative.
That volunteer, a veteran organizer with Black and Brown United in Action named Catherine John, was driving Jaime and his relative home after the hearing, which was scheduled for 10 a.m. She said volunteers had watched the area while Jaime met with his attorney, and that the three left through a side entrance without incident.
Around 11:30 a.m., on State Street near Court Street, Catherine John said, several vehicles boxed in her car — she estimated about seven — and roughly 10 agents surrounded it. Some were masked.
She said agents cursed at her and demanded she open the door, and that one appeared to be holding a gun. She locked the doors and told her passengers to stay inside.
Agents then broke a rear window, she said, tried to pull Jaime through it, and finally opened the door and dragged him out.
When Jaime’s relative got out of the front passenger seat to ask what was happening, Catherine John said, an agent asked him if he wanted to fight, then grabbed him and threw him, hurting his head in the process.
Agents told them in Spanish that Jaime would be taken to Hartford, she said. The whole thing, she said, lasted about a minute and a half.
“You didn’t need seven agents for one little kid like that,” Catherine John said. “Watching them get dragged like that, as a mother, that hurts my soul. Nobody should be treated that way.”
Catherine John said she believed the agents deliberately waited until the car was away from the courthouse. “They knew not to be very close to the courthouse,” she said.
She also said a New Haven police officer working at a nearby road-work site watched the arrest but did not intervene.
Afterward, Catherine John said, Jaime’s relative complained of a headache and was walking unsteadily. She urged him to go to the hospital.
While she was driving him there, she said, a New Haven police officer stopped her for using her phone. She said she told the officer what had happened, and that he called a supervisor and documented the incident. 
She was not charged.
City spokesperson Lenny Speiller said the city had no information about the arrest. Police spokesperson Officer Christian Bruckhart said he had heard rumors of an ICE arrest but had no report on it, and no information about the traffic stop Catherine John described. 
Bruckhart said ICE is not required to notify the city or local police before conducting operations in New Haven.
[RELATED: Video shows downtown ICE arrest]
ICE did not respond by publication time to questions about the arrest, how it was carried out, or the allegation that an agent struck Jaime’s relative. A video of the encounter appears to show a man, boxed in by law-enforcement vehicles, get out of a car on State Street before being thrown to the ground by two masked agents.
Jaime’s attorney in the criminal case, Nicole Shepter, did not respond to a request for comment.
This story was first published Nov. 10, 2026 by New Haven Independent.

name: California
title: HOA boards often make decisions behind closed doors. California should require they meet in public
description: HOAs have become another form of local government, assessing fees and fines while providing its members services cities and counties can’t.
text:
Guest Commentary written by

William Fulton
William Fulton is a professor of practice at UC San Diego and a condo owner. He is a former mayor of Ventura.


Like millions of other Californians, I live in a community governed by a homeowners association. In my case the HOA operates a tall condo building in downtown San Diego. 
My wife and I pay a lot every month in assessments, and we get a lot in return: 24-hour concierge service, beautiful common areas, two full-time engineers who keep the building running, janitorial service and more.
But we don’t really know what our HOA board does. We don’t know how they build our budget, why they enter into contracts or how they make many other decisions that affect our financial investment in our building.
Our board meets almost exclusively in closed session, communicates with us mostly via email, delivers a budget to us with an increased assessment each year without much explanation and provides information mostly through carefully curated “town halls,” rather than real board meetings.
That’s because the Davis-Stirling Act, the state law that governs homeowner associations, doesn’t require more. The law is so loose when it comes to transparency that if our HOA is sued — or sues somebody else — the board is under no obligation even to reveal this information to us.
When you talk to HOA board members around the state, they emphasize that they are volunteers serving on a nonprofit board, which is factually true.
But what’s also true is HOAs have become another form of local government. They provide services that cities and counties can’t. 
It’s about time the Legislature forces HOA boards to shine a light on what they are doing.
This year, a significant bill on HOA transparency almost got through. Assembly Bill 1184, by Assemblymember Joe Patterson, a Rocklin Republican, would have required HOA boards to reveal far more information to homeowners — for example, revealing the lawsuits the board discusses in closed session.
Patterson’s bill died on the last day of the session. 
The Legislature should pass the bill next year and go even further by requiring that HOA boards make far more information available to members.
In theory, Davis-Stirling is patterned after the Brown Act, the state’s open meetings law for cities and counties. Davis-Stirling limits the topics that can be discussed in closed session to things like litigation, personnel and what the law calls the “formation” of contracts.
But there’s little enforcement because no HOA member wants to sue an organization they belong to. 
That’s why in practice, HOA boards are far more opaque than cities and counties. They often discuss practically everything in closed session, frequently using the “formation of contracts” loophole to talk about things covered by HOA contracts. And most HOAs contract with third parties to do practically everything.
HOAs are under no obligation to even inform the people paying dues about pending litigation. 
Although homeowners may legally obtain contracts and other documents related to an HOA’s activities, the organization only needs to provide it in response to an individual’s request. 
For example, I recently learned our HOA manager had been providing contract information to a few people who asked for it, instead of putting the contracts on the building’s internal web site. Only after pressure from a number of residents were the contracts made available to everybody.
In short, the Davis-Stirling Act is set up to protect HOA boards when dealing with the property owners they serve. That perverts the whole purpose of the law and makes it nearly impossible for rank-and-file HOA members to know what’s going on with the organization they are investing their money in.
The Legislature needs to finally acknowledge that HOAs are, in effect, a form of local government and to hold HOA boards to the same transparency requirements as cities and counties. If Patterson brings back AB 1184 next year, legislators must wave it through.

name: California
title: How we found the instructors making more than $400K at community colleges
description: Our analysis found 72 community college instructors who worked at five or more campuses in 2024, with 10 of them taking home more than $340,000 in pay.
text:
In summary
Our analysis found 72 community college instructors who worked at five or more campuses in 2024, with 10 of them taking home more than $340,000 in pay.



CalMatters’ in-depth analysis of 2024 payroll data from the California Community Colleges system found records showing at least 72 instructors were on payroll at five or more community college districts or California State University/University of California campuses. Ten of the 72 instructors we identified earned more than $343,000, the median salary of a community college president or chancellor in the same year.
Each California community college district is independently governed, and no one tracks who teaches across districts or how many classes they teach. Community colleges have no way of knowing what an instructor’s full course load is. The top earner in our analysis was listed as the instructor for at least 69 course sections across nine community college districts, according to course catalog records from 2024 reviewed by CalMatters.
We also reviewed payroll data from the California State University and University of California systems and found many of the same instructors identified in our community college analysis.
Data collection
CalMatters used 2024 employee compensation data from Transparent California, part of a nonpartisan think tank advocating for limited government. Transparent California obtained the data directly from the colleges and universities using public records requests.
Data cleaning
CalMatters normalized job titles and names, removing non-alphabetic characters and standardizing letter case to lower in the compensation data.
Methodology
Our analysis relied on a computer algorithm grouping payroll records that shared highly similar names followed by CalMatters’ reporters verifying an employee’s identity and employment using publicly available records or confirmation from college press contacts. We contacted any instructors we identified as working at five or more college districts or university campuses.

Pay record clustering
The community college payroll records included name, campus, job title, total pay and benefits. We compared all payroll records that shared either a middle or surname. A pair of records were considered as a possible match if (1) they shared the same first name and (2) the remainder of the names were a perfect or near-perfect match, barring a single name and excluding initials. We grouped the matched pairs based on transitive relationships. 
For example, a group of names, which we refer to as a cluster, could contain pay records for Bob Smith, Bob J. Smith, Bob M. Smith, and Bob Williams Smith. The four records were grouped together because they all shared the same first name and last name with the record for “Bob Smith”. We built a single group because we couldn’t determine whether the plain “Bob Smith” was the same individual recorded in the remaining records based solely on payroll data.
We excluded 61 clusters that matched records solely based on sharing a very common name. (See: High frequency surnames excluded.) That left 272 clusters that were associated with payroll records for five or more college districts or university campuses.
Manual evaluation and validation
CalMatters manually reviewed the remaining 272 clusters and further grouped records that could reasonably represent a single instructor. We made these judgments by relying on name, title, employer, department and course subject.
We determined which payroll database entries represented a single instructor by independently verifying the named instructor’s relationship with the associated campus or district. We established this by locating at least one current or previous course listing at each school, a faculty directory profile, LinkedIn profile or college hiring documents. (See: Contract renewals.)  
We sent at least two emails to share our findings and request comments for each instructor who met our criteria, identifying instructors who taught at five or community college districts or university campuses. Most of the professors did not respond to CalMatters’ requests for comment. Others asked CalMatters not to publish the data, which is publicly available, for fear of how it might affect their employment.
California State University and University of California payroll records
After completing the manual evaluation and validation of the community college records, CalMatters ran a similar process with payroll records from California State University and University of California. We cross-referenced names in the validated community college data against records in the CSU and UC data that share a middle or surname. If there was a perfect or near-perfect match, then we ran the same manual evaluation and validation process to determine whether the CSU or UC record represented the same instructor we identified in the community college payroll data.
Findings
CalMatters found 72 instructors who were paid by five or more districts or university campuses in 2024. Median pay for those instructors was $191,000. The top earner, Thien-Huong Ninh Villarreal, was found on payroll records for 11 college districts or university campuses, and earned more than $793,000 in 2024. She was the listed instructor for at least 69 course sections, according to course catalog archives we reviewed for the community colleges and universities where she was on payroll that year.
In total, we found 10 instructors, including Ninh Villarreal, who earned more than $343,000, the median salary of a community college president or chancellor in 2024.
Limitations
High frequency surnames excluded
We excluded candidate pairs where the match was based solely on a middle initial, middle name or surname that appeared 500 times or more  in the community college payroll data because we could not validate the individual records in a reasonable timespan. (See: Manual evaluation and validation.) This approach excluded 61 clusters from manual evaluation. Among the surnames were many of Spanish language origin, including Garcia, Rodriguez and Gomez, as well as the surnames Nguyen, Brown, Johnson and Smith. There could be other instructors from those clusters who taught at five or more college districts or university campuses but evaluating those records fell outside the scope of our analysis.
Validation limited to clusters with five or more records
We limited our analysis to instructors we suspected may have been employed at five or more districts or university campuses in 2024. This is not a comprehensive analysis of community college instructors teaching at multiple schools. 
Contract renewals
We used colleges’ searchable Fall 2026 class schedules as our primary source to confirm where an instructor taught. We used this as a proxy for teaching location in 2024 because the colleges we reviewed typically didn’t maintain archives of past class schedules. If the instructor was not listed in the Fall 2026 schedule, we reviewed other corroborating documentation. (See: Manual evaluation and validation.)
Teaching assignments may change from one academic term to the next, so the 2024 payroll data does not represent the definitive list of campuses where an instructor has taught. An instructor could have been paid in 2024 for a course taught in 2023. An instructor could be teaching at fewer or more schools in 2026 than they did in 2024.
Name changes or variations
We expected the payroll database to use employees’ legal names consistently across multiple schools, but we found instances where instructors we verified as the same person were listed under different name variations. For example: Thien-Huong Villarreal, the top earner on our list, had five different name variations across 11 different schools. This means there may be instances where our approach didn’t catch a name variation of an instructor.
The payroll data obtained by Transparent California is gathered on a year-to-year basis as reported to the Internal Revenue Service. If an instructor teaches at multiple districts or university campuses and changes their name between terms then their pay record will be updated at only the schools they are a returning instructor.
Note on AI-assisted work
We used AI coding tools to assist with the analysis. All code and results were manually reviewed by a member of our data team. You can access and download our analysis here.
Appendix

name: California
title: These part-time professors make big money teaching dozens of classes online. Are their students learning?
description: There are no rules governing how many classes community college professors can teach. Some are cashing in.
text:
In summary
There are no rules governing how many classes community college professors can teach. Some are cashing in.


As online classes proliferate, community college professors have found a hack — repackaging similar courses for hundreds of students at a time and teaching more than a dozen classes in a single semester.
Professor Thien-Huong Ninh Villarreal has at least two tenured, full-time community college jobs, plus recurring part-time gigs over the past 12 months at UC Berkeley, Cal State Sacramento, and seven other community colleges. This fall, she’s teaching 30 sociology, ethnic studies and business classes to about 1,100 students.

In 2024, with roughly the same courseload, she made nearly $800,000, according to public payroll records. CalMatters reached out to her three times for comment, but she never responded.
Community college professors are expected to evaluate student progress and provide direct support without the help of teaching assistants, though that’s nearly impossible at such a scale, said Sarah Thompson, president of the Faculty Association of California Community Colleges. “Obviously no one has enough time in a week to teach 30 classes and do a good job, so that’s very problematic.” 
However Chris Ferguson, an executive vice chancellor at the office overseeing California’s community colleges, said having multiple teaching jobs is not, by itself, evidence of poor instruction. In an emailed statement to CalMatters, Ferguson, who leads finance and strategic initiatives for the office, said multiple jobs would be a problem if the “faculty member’s workload is preventing the required level of engagement, feedback, assessment, or student support.” In that case, he said the college district — not the statewide college system — should be accountable. 
CalMatters analyzed public payroll records from the non-profit Transparent California and corroborated those records with college course data. The analysis found at least 70 adjuncts, or part-time professors, who were paid by five or more community college districts, California State University or University of California campuses in the same year, including many who taught more than 10 classes in a semester. 
Some of these professors were among the highest paid employees across California’s 116 community colleges. Ninh Villarreal made more than every community college administrator in 2024, even more than Sonya Christian, the chancellor of the state’s community college system, according to CalMatters’ analysis.
Most of the 70-plus professors did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Others asked CalMatters not to publish the data, which is publicly available, for fear of how it might affect their employment.
These professors aren’t breaking any rules. In fact, there are no rules that prevent community college adjuncts from teaching at more than one district.
Andrew Vanden Heuvel, an adjunct astronomy professor, told CalMatters he teaches roughly 50 online classes and labs from the office above his garage in a small town on the shore of Lake Michigan. 
Almost all of his lectures are pre-recorded, and students can listen at any time. It’s called asynchronous instruction. At the UC, Cal State and especially at the state’s community colleges, these kinds of online classes are popular and widespread, a major shift since the COVID-19 pandemic. 
Vanden Heuvel said he has taught as many as 1,000 students a semester across the country, including in Santa Monica, Salinas, San Jose and Visalia, plus schools in New Mexico, Michigan, Washington and Florida. He said the classes use different iterations of the same, largely introductory content about stars, galaxies and the solar system. Students read information online, interact with online astronomical simulations, watch videos or submit labs. 
“In its current form, I am not grading anything (by hand),” said Vanden Heuvel. All quizzes are multiple choice and computer-graded — a common feature among many online classes, not just Vanden Heuvel’s. Some students also submit written assignments, which he said he usually grades using an algorithm that only checks whether the work was submitted or not. 
About 20% of his course load is in California, he said. “In California, I can get paid as much as eight times as much as I can in Florida.” In 2024, California schools paid him a total of about $320,000, according to the CalMatters analysis. Nationally, he made much more, he said. “Looking over my records, I can tell you that 2024 was the high water mark.” He said he made  $758,485.12 that year. 
Full-time professors cash in 
By law, adjunct faculty are generally limited to teaching three classes per semester at a single community college district, with each district setting its own rules. Most part-time jobs are precarious, with no healthcare, no guarantee of employment and all work assigned on a contract basis. Colleges can strip adjuncts of their classes — and their wages — with little notice.
For union and faculty leaders, who have long said adjuncts are underpaid and overworked, the workload of professors like Ninh Villarreal and Vanden Heuvel comes as a shock. “I don’t know how you can earn that much money, how you can have that many assignments. I mean that’s pretty wild,” said Jim Mahler, the president of the community college council for the California Federation of Teachers. He said he suspects some professors are simply recording their lectures and “just hitting play.”
Students on their laptops in the quad area at Fresno City College on Aug. 13, 2025. Photo by Larry Valenzuela, CalMatters/CatchLight Local
To make more than $400,000, many of California’s highest earning adjuncts had full-time tenure or tenure-track positions too, the records show. For example: 

Bobby Seals, an ethnic studies professor, has a full-time position at Evergreen Valley College in San Jose. He also teaches 14 more courses across four other community college districts, plus San Jose State — a total of about 930 students this semester. 
Faramarz Mortezaie is the chair of the computer science department at Mission College in Santa Clara. Part time, he also teaches 11 classes at other campuses, including San Jose State. 
Nicholas Nardi, a full-time psychology professor at Santa Ana College, is teaching 11 more classes at six other schools, including Cal State Los Angeles.
Timothy Durfield, a full-time business professor at Citrus College, teaches an additional 10 classes at four other community college districts. 
Walter Meyer, a full-time art history professor at Santa Monica College, teaches 10 additional online classes to students in Los Angeles and Kern counties.

None of these professors responded to requests for comment.
Ninh Villarreal, the top earner, has often had at least two full-time jobs, according to college officials and public records. She’s been a tenured professor at Cosumnes River College in Sacramento since 2016. In 2023, she got a second full-time job at Reedley College near Fresno, though she returned to part-time status less than a year later. In 2025, she got tenure at San Joaquin Delta College in Stockton, and the same year, official college documents show she was the inaugural tenure-track faculty in the ethnic studies department at West Valley College in Saratoga near San Jose. Cade Story-Yetto, a spokesperson for the district encompassing West Valley College, said Ninh Villarreal is no longer employed there and refused to answer other questions.

CalMatters reached out to nearly every one of the state’s 73 community college districts, seeking feedback on our methodology before publication. Transparent California, part of a nonpartisan think tank advocating for limited government, obtained payroll information directly from the college districts. CalMatters then used that data to compile a list of professors who taught at five or more community college districts, Cal State or UC campuses in 2024, which is the most recent data. The data was corroborated using course catalogs, faculty directories and college hiring documents.
While some of the professors taught a few in-person classes, usually at Cal State or UC campuses, CalMatters’ analysis found that many of those who taught at five or more college districts relied heavily on online, asynchronous instruction. 
No one is tracking it 
Universities treat online courses the same as in-person classes: students get the same amount of credit, and teachers are generally paid the same amount. As online courses have become more common, the UC, Cal State and community college systems have spent millions in state funding to ensure they have the same rigor as in-person courses. 
Community colleges evaluate the quality of all courses, but they have no way of knowing what a professor’s workload really is. California’s community college districts are independently governed, and no one tracks who teaches across districts or how many classes they teach. 
The Cal State and UC systems, which are smaller and more centralized than the community colleges, track employment and limit the number of courses each professor can teach. If the instructor is also teaching at a community college, however, they may have no way of knowing. 
Vanden Heuvel, the astronomy professor, said he believes his students are getting an excellent education. “I teach at a certain number of schools because that portfolio gives me the stability I need as an adjunct to survive and thrive,” he said, pointing to his three kids, his wife, who is an elementary school teacher, and the need to be present with his family instead of driving from campus to campus each day. “Now, did I push it further than some people think is morally conscionable? I don’t think so.”
Researchers say it’s not clear whether online courses are worse, or better, than traditional in-person education. Students, especially working adults who predominate the community college system, praise online courses for their convenience, but there are known drawbacks. Asynchronous classes in particular have historically offered students less interaction with their professors, which research has found is detrimental to student success.
Students work in the library at San Bernardino Valley College on May 30, 2023. Photo by Lauren Justice for CalMatters
How to teach 50 classes in a semester
Vanden Heuvel posts much of his course material on YouTube, where his channels collectively have nearly 5 million views, spread out over more than 300 videos. In his videos, he’s charismatic and personable, taking students into his car, even posting videos while on vacation at Disney World. His location isn’t a secret, he said — he has always been open about where he lives, both with California’s colleges and his students. 
In fact, the first lesson in one of his classes is a video in which he introduces himself and takes students to his favorite place, Lake Michigan, where he first developed a love of astronomy. 
State and federal laws require professors to interact with their students, especially in asynchronous online courses. Interaction could include fostering engagement in the classroom or monitoring students’ academic performance, wrote Ferguson, the finance vice chancellor, in his emailed statement. “These requirements apply to every course, regardless of how many colleges or districts employ the instructor.” The federal government has strengthened its own rules for online classes over the past few years.
Vanden Heuvel said he gives out his personal cell phone to all students and gets as many as 30 emails a day from them, mostly asking to extend assignment deadlines. He said he answers every email. 
It would be very easy for students to cheat using AI, he said, especially because quizzes are multiple choice and most written assignments are graded only on completion. “The logic is the equivalent of the Scantron (a multiple-choice grading machine) at the large lecture hall. It’s a defensible instructional practice to assess that way. It’s how lots of assessments are run, be that the GRE or LSAT. I don’t love it.”
The promise of online education is to reach students at scale and lower the cost-per-student of education, he said — and that’s exactly what he’s doing by teaching 50 online classes and labs to as many as 1,000 students across the country. In some schools, especially in rural areas, Vanden Heuvel is the only astronomy professor. 
He said his large-scale teaching practices represent his “most successful” experiment, though he acknowledged that many faculty won’t look so favorably upon it. 
‘I’m not a factory of education like that’ 
Part-time faculty, who are cheaper to employ, outnumber tenure-track professors at every one of California’s 73 community college districts, in some cases by more than 5-1. The same imbalance is evident at many Cal State campuses, though their adjuncts, known as lecturers, can work full time and receive benefits. The UC, with a focus on research, has faculty categories that don’t exist at the Cal State or community college system, making comparisons tricky. 
It’s well-known that adjuncts teach at multiple districts, but unions often say that they do it out of necessity. Tina Leonard, who teaches American Sign Language, is a perfect example. In 2024, she made just over $84,000 teaching at five community college districts.

“I am Deaf,” she wrote in an email, “and it is very difficult and competitive for a Deaf educator to get a full-time tenure-track position in ASL.” She said she took additional teaching jobs in 2024 to cover the cost of her taxes. “Each college withholds as if it is your only job, so when you add them all together, you can end up owing.”
K. Frindell, the president of a federation of faculty unions, the California Community College Independents, said she wasn’t surprised to see many faculty teaching in multiple districts, even some who are earning hundreds of thousands of dollars. “A loophole has been created,” she said — one that allows districts to cut costs by hiring adjuncts and allows adjuncts to teach at multiple districts.
In fact, the total number of community college adjuncts in California is unknown because statewide tallies do not account for professors who teach at multiple districts, said Ferguson. The Cal State system has the same data problem.
Adjuncts are often hired for the academic year and then rehired each fall. Numerous legislative proposals have tried but failed to give adjuncts opportunities for additional pay, benefits or full-time employment. In 2022, legislators tried to increase benefits for community college adjuncts, sending $200 million to districts that would then reimburse part-time faculty for health insurance. In the 2024-25 academic year, nearly 7,000 adjuncts used the program, very few of whom were teaching at multiple districts. Many districts chose not to participate, and most of the money remains unspent. 
Noah Thomas, a professor in the art department at Long Beach City College, on campus in Long Beach on Aug. 3, 2026. Photo by Ariana Drehsler for CalMatters
Noah Thomas, a community college art professor, said he looked into the new healthcare benefits but found them lacking. “It’s such a convoluted system and the subsidies are kind of pretty low,” he said. “The coverage only applies to me and not to any of my dependents and it’s only for 10 months out of the year because my contract is only 10 months.”  
Thomas made just over $100,000 in 2024 by commuting among five community college districts in Orange and Los Angeles counties, where he taught in-person studio arts classes. Sometimes, the drives are so long, and the days so jam-packed that he eats lunch in his car, he said. “Financially I’d love to teach as many classes as I could. $800,000 sounds amazing. But I’m not a factory of education like that. I really love teaching students one-on-one and showing them how to actually cut out a piece of cardboard and use a band saw.”
The moral dilemma 
Frindell, who represents the independent community college unions, said the solution is not to focus on the professors who teach multiple online classes and earn high six-figure salaries. She wants to see an end to the low pay, precarious employment, and restrictive laws that force adjuncts to teach at multiple districts in the first place. 
CalMatters asked the leaders of the state Assembly and Senate higher education committees about adjuncts who are teaching at multiple schools. Alhambra Democratic Assemblymember Mike Fong, San Diego Republican Assemblymember Carl DeMaio and Riverside Democratic Sen. Sabrina Cervantes did not respond.  
Because of state and federal rules that require professors to engage with their students, Vanden Heuvel redesigned some of his courses, adding new types of assignments. At times, he said the rules seem like they were “invented to prevent people from doing what I’m doing,” though he added that they are often ineffective if so. “What it feels like in practice is an administrative checked box that is not really connected to meaningful student experience.”
Still, he said he has sought reassurance from other educators about the moral implications of teaching so many students in so many classes, even if legally he is within bounds. “What they say to me, whether they’re just being nice or not, is this sense that adjunct faculty are systematically taken advantage of by higher education, and if you have built a system that allows you to thrive while still providing excellent education, then more power to you.”
At the end of each semester, Vanden Heuvel said he asks his students to evaluate the course and that they consistently say it’s far above average in quality and knowledge gained and about average in difficulty. “There’s always the sense of like, ‘Is what I’m doing OK or not OK? Am I pushing it a little too far or not?’”
He self-published a 600-page book that collects student reflections, mostly about how their relationship with planets, stars and galaxies changed because of his class. He said the book sits in his office, right near his desk.

name: California
title: This California county holds half the state’s violent sex offenders. Is there a better way to house them?
description: As a San Diego judge weighs placing two sexually violent predators in a rural neighborhood, a county supervisor offers a new plan to better house these offenders
text:
In summary
As a San Diego judge weighs placing two sexually violent predators in a rural neighborhood, a county supervisor offers a new plan to better house these offenders


Boulevard, California is a rural community of about 750 people set in brushy desert mountains an hour east of downtown San Diego.
It may soon be home to two sexually violent predators: a state category used to describe sex offenders with a high risk of reoffending.
Reynaldo Delrosario, 71, was sentenced to 12 years in state prison for “lewd and lascivious acts” with a child under age 10. Michael Poulsom, 67, committed lewd acts with victims under age 14 in Georgia and San Diego, and was sentenced to 15 years in California state prison. 
Both were diagnosed with pedophilia disorder and committed to the state hospital for treatment after serving their sentences. On Thursday a San Diego judge will weigh whether to grant conditional release, and place them in state-funded homes in the tiny community.
If their requests are granted, they would join seven other violent sex offenders in residential neighborhoods of backcountry San Diego, leaving the county with more than half of all such placements in California.
San Diego County Supervisor Joel Anderson, a Republican who represents the southeast region of the county, has another idea.
He wants the county to adopt a model used in Washington State, which houses sexually violent predators in group homes with round-the-clock supervision. Placing them together in more secluded areas would provide better monitoring and services, and reduce the risk to surrounding neighborhoods, he said.
On Thursday, San Diego Superior Court Judge Theodore Weathers will decide whether to grant conditional release to Poulsom and Delrosario. Anderson hopes to persuade the court to pilot the group housing model.
“The security is much greater,” Anderson said. “But there’s more freedom for the SVPs because they’re living in an area that no one’s upset that they’re there.”
Sexually violent predators clustered in San Diego 
The term sexually violent predator describes a person convicted of sexually violent offenses such as rape or sexual assault of a child, who has a diagnosed mental illness that makes them likely to commit new crimes.
In California sexually violent criminals, referred to by the acronym SVP, serve terms in prison, and then are often consigned to the state hospital for further mental health treatment after completing their sentence.
If that goes smoothly, they can petition for conditional release. The state’s contractor, Liberty Healthcare, scouts housing in either the county the offender came from, or the place they committed their crimes, and then rents a home for them.
The sheriff and district attorney’s office weigh in on the release site, and the D.A. seeks comment from community members.  A judge considers the proposed placement and reviews security measures such as GPS monitoring, unannounced searches, polygraph and drug tests, and then decides whether to grant conditional release.
This process has become routine in San Diego County, which houses half of the state’s sexually violent predators.
Six already live in the San Diego backcountry, in the desert communities of Borrego Springs, a community of about 2,700 surrounded by Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, and Jacumba, with 740 residents, according to a list maintained by the San Diego District Attorney. A seventh offender is also cleared for placement in Borrego Springs.
Palm trees and homes in the community of Borrego Springs, near Anza-Borrego Desert State Park, on March 24, 2022. Photo by Mario Tama, Getty Images
Another, Merle Wakefield, removed his ankle monitor while working at an Amazon warehouse in Rancho Bernardo and escaped on Sept. 25. He was found dead in a San Diego riverbed weeks later, the San Diego Sheriff announced on Oct. 20.
There are currently a total of 14 sexually violent predators on conditional release in counties throughout California, the Department of State Hospitals stated in an email to CalMatters. If the court approves conditional release for Poulsom and Delrosario, San Diego would house nine of them. 
The San Diego Public Defender will represent the men at their court hearings this month, said Alexandra Knudson, the civil commitment supervisor for the public defender’s office. The public defender did not comment on the placements, but Knudson said they will review Anderson’s proposal.
Fights over placements
Neighbors and local leaders have raised red flags over the release of sexually violent predators. Residents in the small, low-income communities often object to sharing their neighborhood with a high-risk sex offender, but feel they have little say in the matter.
“These are rural communities,” Anderson said. “They don’t have the means to push back or fight back.”
In 2021, the San Diego County Board of Supervisors voted unanimously to oppose any plans to release sexually violent predators into San Diego communities unless the county had a say in how and where they were released. But that vote didn’t change state policy on sex offender placements.
State Sen. Brian Jones, who terms out of office this year, spent years trying to tighten the process. Last year Gov. Gavin Newsom signed one of Jones’ bills requiring the State Department of State Hospitals to analyze options for transitional housing facilities for sexually violent predators freed on conditional release.
However, his other bill to force accountability for sex offender releases stalled in the California Assembly, after passing the state Senate.
It would have required the director of state hospitals to sign off on rental leases for the offenders, in order to avoid placements in inappropriate or dangerous locations. It would also have made public safety a top priority in placement of sexually violent predators. The American Civil Liberties Union and California Public Defenders Association opposed the bill, arguing that it would effectively ban the offenders from gaining release after serving sentences.
That’s where Anderson believes the Washington state model for housing sexually violent predators could be useful.    
The grounds of Washington state’s Special Commitment Center on McNeil Island, Washington, on Oct. 20, 2015. The facility holds sexually violent predators. Photo by Ted S. Warren, AP Photo
In Washington, violent sex offenders who serve out their criminal sentences are sent to civil commitment at a secure facility on McNeil Island. They undergo intensive treatment aimed at preventing new sex offenses, and get a yearly evaluation to see if they qualify for placement in a “less restrictive alternative.”
There are two state-owned secure community transition facilities with 24-hour staffing that can house 12 to 24 offenders. Washington also operates community homes run by private businesses, which often accommodate several offenders and may include round-the-clock supervision and staff who escort residents off premises. 
Anderson believes that would offer a more structured and secure housing option for sexually violent predators, and deter them from re-offending.
“You have that constant reassurance in positive encouragement for them to stay on the straight and narrow, protecting the community,” he said. 
In Washington, as in San Diego, community placements have sparked controversy. One plan to house up to five sex offenders in a large farmhouse in the Washington city of Tenino was cancelled because of cost increases and community backlash.
Cynthia Shipley, a media manager for the Washington State Department of Social and Health Services, said the department works with community members, city officials, law enforcement and private providers to address their concerns. Anderson is aware of the controversies with the Washington model and will address them in his plan, his communications chief Matthew Phy said.
But he’s optimistic there’s a way to house sexually violent predators that could yield better outcomes for the offenders with greater safety for surrounding communities. There are various large private resorts and ranches in his district that could potentially house the released offenders in remote areas away from residential neighborhoods. He also thinks it could save money.
A 2024 report by the California State Auditor found that California spent $93 million over two decades to release 56 high-risk sex offenders. Costs ballooned from $5.3 million in 2018-19 to $9.4 million in 2022-23, as housing prices rose, along with payments to Liberty Healthcare.
Housing them together could trim those expenses, while offering better services and supervision, Anderson said. He plans to propose his plan in Superior Court Thursday, and bring it to the board of supervisors next month.
“The community benefits,” he said. “The cost of it decreases. And the quality of care for the SVPs increases. Statistically, the Washington model has been far more successful. There’s no downside across the board.”

name: VTDigger
title: Chronic wasting disease found in wild New York deer for first time in decades
description:
With northern New York deer season in full swing, Vermont officials want to keep the illness — which is similar to mad cow disease — at bay.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Chronic wasting disease found in wild New York deer for first time in decades.
text:
Stuffed deer heads mounted on the walls inside Choiniere’s Hunting Camp in Brownington in November 2025. File photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger

Theo Wells-Spackman is a Report for America corps member who reports for VTDigger.
Chronic wasting disease, a fatal illness in deer, moose and elk, has been discovered in a wild New York doe for the first time in decades.
The disorder, which stems from defective proteins called prions, has never been spotted in Vermont, and with northern New York’s deer season in full swing, officials want to keep it that way.
Following the discovery of the infected animal, the Vermont Department of Fish and Wildlife issued a statement Tuesday reminding hunters to follow policies against bringing deer meat without proper processing into Vermont from areas where the disease has been observed. Those include New York, Pennsylvania and Québec, among other states and provinces.
“It’s a really funky kind of disease,” Nick Fortin, the department’s lead deer biologist, said in an interview. It’s in the same class of disorder as the infamous “mad cow” disease, he said, and Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease in humans.
In deer, chronic wasting disease causes symptoms like emaciation, listlessness and disorientation. It has never shown the potential for animal-human crossover, Fortin said, though people should not eat infected deer. His worry about the disease is centered on Vermont’s deer and their habitats, he said.
“Those prions that cause CWD can remain in the soil for decades, essentially,” Fortin said. “The persistence is the biggest concern.”
The malformed proteins in question can outlast the deer they kill and be stored in the earth, scavengers’ waste and even in surrounding plant life, he said. 
Other states have struggled to control the fatal disease’s spread in deer and elk. Nearly 15% of all deer and elk tested in Wyoming returned a positive CWD result in 2024, with one herd in particular registering about 66% average infection rate over the course of five years.
New York state officials discovered the CWD-riddled deer last week in Livingston County, nearly 300 miles from the Vermont border, during an annual testing program. The disease had not been detected in New York since 2005, save for one captive deer in 2024.
Fortin said Vermont hunters commonly disregard state policy about transporting deer across state lines — including from New York.
“We hear about it anecdotally all the time,” he said.
Successful hunters can bring back parts of deer under certain conditions, including if the meat is packaged and labeled correctly or is boneless, or if a person is transporting cleaned teeth or antlers.
Essentially, Fortin said, “We let hunters bring back the parts that they’re not going to dispose of on the landscape.”
Vermont’s regular deer hunting season runs Nov. 14 to 29, and the season in northern New York runs Oct. 24 to Dec. 6.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Chronic wasting disease found in wild New York deer for first time in decades.

name: Utah News Dispatch
title: ‘I didn’t expect it at all’: The blue wave hit a portion of red Utah County
description: The November election's blue wave reached parts of conservative Utah County that voted to send an LGBTQ+ candidate to the state Legislature.
text:
David Chappell, the Democrat who unseated a Republican incumbent in a reliably red state legislative district, speaks at a forum at Rugged Grounds in Provo on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)That a blue wave rolled into the Utah Legislature and washed out its Republican supermajority was a surprise. That it seeped into conservative Utah County and handed over a reliably red seat to a 27-year-old Democrat was a shock even to him. 
“I didn’t expect this at all,” David Chappell said Tuesday night at a coffee shop in Provo, where he’d invited constituents to help hash out his priorities for the coming legislative session. 
“A lot of people who voted for me voted for Donald Trump,” Chappell added. “I think that makes sense. We’re voting for change candidates. We want people to shake things up and make it so that it’s easier to live here.” 
Chappell wants Utah to provide school meals at no cost and free up funding to help make home ownership affordable. He plans to make housing his focus at the Capitol. 
“Now that there’s no supermajority, I have so much hope that we actually can deliver, and that Republicans will listen to us,” Chappell said. “And I think that they will.” 
David Chappell, the Democrat who unseated a Republican incumbent in a what is typically a reliably red state legislative district in Utah County, takes ideas at Rugged Grounds in Provo on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)
Top Republican legislative leaders last week said the losses were humbling, with Senate President-elect Evan Vickers acknowledging “the public has lost some trust.” 
Still, they noted their party retains more than a two-thirds majority in the Senate and a lesser, albeit significant margin in the House. 
Pundits cited the intense rebuke of Trump and his administration as one force propelling Utah’s blue wave, in addition to frustration in the state with the overwhelmingly Republican Legislature’s moves asserting power over redistricting, ballot initiatives and unions. 
‘Blue tsunami’ hits Utah: House Republicans on pace to lose 17 seats, breaking supermajority

Chappell, who identifies as queer and said he sees himself more as a progressive independent than a Democrat, had never run for office before. He will represent parts of Provo — home to Brigham Young University, his alma mater — and Springville. 
It’s a part of the state that has long voted red and where the state’s predominant faith, The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints, is particularly concentrated. The church views same-sex relationships as a serious transgression. 
“One of the districts by BYU is now represented by, you know, a flaming homosexual. I think that’s great,” Chappell said. He grew up in a conservative family in the Arizona ranching community of Lehi, he said, before attending the university himself. 
He’s set to join a small but growing number of openly LGBTQ+ representatives in the Utah House, alongside fellow incoming Democrat Drew Howells of Sandy and Rep. Sahara Hays, D-Millcreek. 
He said his victory shows that Provo is accepting — and that voters in the district were more focused on issues like the cost of food and housing than matters of identity. 
Attendees listen at a forum hosted by David Chappell, the Democrat who unseated a Republican incumbent in a reliably red Utah legislative district, on Tuesday, Nov. 10, 2026. (Annie Knox/Utah News Dispatch)
At the coffee shop in Provo Tuesday, Chappell wrote down topics on a white board that included data centers, abortion rights and the drying Great Salt Lake as a few dozen attendees reviewed what they want him to focus on. 
Among those in attendance was Rep. Norm Thurston, the Republican incumbent who conceded and congratulated Chappell last week after serving almost 12 years in the House. He’s one of 16 Republicans set to lose their seats in that chamber, in addition to two in the Senate, though results are not official until a canvass next week. 
In an interview, Thurston recalled advising Chappell that “you have no idea how long it’s going to last. So enjoy every minute of it for whatever time you’re given.”
In a moment that resembled mentorship at the coffee shop, Thurston chimed in from his seat in the crowd to shed light on the time it takes for state lawmakers to draft a bill with help from legislative attorneys. 
Thurston carried 65% of the vote in the district in 2024 but lost to Chappell’s 53% in last week’s election. Now he’s working with fellow Republicans to figure out how to reclaim their lost seats for the GOP in 2028. 
Rep. Norman Thurston, R-Provo, rises to present S.B. 1011, for which he was the House sponsor, during a special legislative session at the Capitol in Salt Lake City on Monday, Oct. 6, 2025. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)
“We’re all in the same boat, and it’s like, wow, what happened?” Thurston said. 
He noted the toll of national issues such as the war in Iran and gas prices and President Donald Trump’s White House ballroom construction. That’s in addition to a Utah development authority helmed by top Republican lawmakers ushering in a 20,000-acre data center proposal in Box Elder County.
Provo Mayor Marsha Judkins said Wednesday the victory for Chappell, who volunteered on her campaign last year, is surprising considering past elections. 
“However, David started early in the cycle working very hard, knocking doors, energizing volunteers, and taking every opportunity to reach voters,” she said. 
Judkins, a former Republican state lawmaker, said those efforts combined with frustration with the GOP to push him ahead. 
“My district is extremely young and it’s extremely Hispanic, and those are two groups that really shifted towards Democrats,” Chappell said in an interview. 
He recalled voters telling him about their concerns for education funding and their opposition to Utah’s school voucher program and book bans. Some of the same issues motivated him to run, he said, along with his broader sense that state lawmakers weren’t listening to Utahns. 
“That’s what I’m most excited for, is to pass things that people want,” he said.

name: Washington State Standard
title: Newly elected, WA’s first openly transgender legislator ready to ‘stand on business’
description: When Jaelynn Scott arrives in Olympia in January, she doesn’t want to be labeled a one-note legislator.  Elected by voters last week, Scott will be Washington’s first openly transgender state lawmaker, and the first Black transgender legislator in the nation. But she doesn’t want to be seen as only focused on LGBTQ+ rights. Scott, who […]
text:
Jaelynn Scott will represent the 37th District in the Washington state Legislature. (Photo courtesy of the Jaelynn Scott campaign)When Jaelynn Scott arrives in Olympia in January, she doesn’t want to be labeled a one-note legislator. 
Elected by voters last week, Scott will be Washington’s first openly transgender state lawmaker, and the first Black transgender legislator in the nation. But she doesn’t want to be seen as only focused on LGBTQ+ rights.
Scott, who will also be one of two members of the Democratic Socialists of America in the Legislature, wants to be a leader on tax reform, housing policy and criminal justice reform.
“I’m going to stand firmly and stand on business for (the) LGBTQ community and trans rights, but we’re going to be talking about the agenda for working people and the poor,” she said in an interview this week. “I think it will be challenging to resist from whatever, whichever, directions the tokenizing of me as a trans woman and trans elected, but I’m doggedly committed to this agenda for working people.”
Scott, who leads the Black trans advocacy organization the Lavender Rights Project, is sailing into office with more than 87% of the vote in the 37th Legislative District, which covers diverse south Seattle communities like Beacon Hill, Rainier Valley, Columbia City and the Central District.
She’s one of six transgender and nonbinary legislators elected this month who will make history as their state’s firsts. 
“It is very important and powerful that we have a representative in Jaelynn Scott,” said Vanessa Clifford, of the Working Families Party. “And not only is that great for Washington, but I think that’s important to show to the rest of the country.”
Election night was emotional for Scott, 49, not just because of her trailblazing victory but because of the success of a conservative-backed ballot measure to stop transgender girls from competing in girls’ school sports. She figures people who voted for her must’ve also voted for Initiative 638, which she sees as bringing about “legalized segregation,” though it faces a legal challenge filed this week to stop it from taking effect.
She hopes the lawsuit will be successful. She’s reminded of the role the legal system played during the civil rights movement; Scott is originally from the South. 
“I’m very hopeful that at least the law will find balance and give us time and room to actually have a cultural conversation about what type of Washington we want to live in,” she said. 
“Do we want a commonwealth where all of our children feel welcome and loved, and can just have fun with their friends, or do we want to build a society where we use the law to bully a handful of kids out of playing sports?” she continued.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Scott said she had it “slightly” easier than other transgender candidates in terms of death threats and harassment — especially since she doesn’t read social media comments. 
After the August primary, Scott said she felt being the first was a “heavy burden.” Now she feels differently. It’s “a privilege that is not afforded to a lot of people like me,” Scott said.
“It’s not feeling heavy,” Scott added. “I’m feeling very well supported, and I’m excited about the opportunity of bringing the entire community’s needs forward, and the power of having Black women in office, and trans women in office, and representation in office that understands the urgency of this moment and the critical crises that our communities are in.”
She’ll join a Democratic caucus that will have a supermajority for the first time in decades, potentially allowing transformational changes to state law. Scott hopes the growing majority will help the Legislature deliver on her goals, such as reducing recent cuts to childcare funding.
“We’ll have no excuses if in the end we are passing down an austerity budget with serious cuts that threaten the social safety net for communities,” she said. “I think the supermajority is a mandate not to do business as usual.”
Scott is part of a triumvirate of new representation in the 37th. Rep. Chipalo Street is moving to the Senate to replace Sen. Rebecca Saldaña, who won election to a seat on the Metropolitan King County Council. Educator Kelabe Tewolde, a progressive Democrat, defeated Rep. Sharon Tomiko Santos, the House’s longest-serving active member. He’ll serve in the House alongside Scott.
Tewolde said he “couldn’t be luckier to have a seatmate like Jaelynn.”

name: WyoFile
title: Detective: Man suspected of stabbing Sikh trucker asked ‘so he didn’t die?’
authors: by Hannah Romero, Green River Star, with WyoFile
description:
The attempted murder case against Andrew Bzdak advances as authorities describe case against defendant. A court hearing doesn’t touch on motive for attack, which caused concern within the broader Sikh community. 
The post Detective: Man suspected of stabbing Sikh trucker asked ‘so he didn’t die?’ appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
ROCK SPRINGS—When officers arrested the man suspected of stabbing a Sikh truck driver inside a southwest Wyoming rest stop in September, he wanted to know why, according to Sweetwater County Sheriff’s Det. Stephanie Cassidy. They told Andrew Bzdak he faced an aggravated assault charge. 
That provoked another question, Cassidy testified Nov. 4 at Bzdak’s preliminary hearing on what’s now an attempted murder charge. Bzdak, she told the court, “answered something along the lines of ‘So he didn’t die?’”
Cassidy described the circumstances of Bzdak’s arrest, as well as the stabbing that spurred it, at a Sweetwater County Circuit Court hearing. At the conclusion, Magistrate Ed Newell ruled enough evidence exists for Bzdak, himself a trucker from California, to face trial for attempted first-degree murder.
The stabbing drew national headlines, in part because the driver who was attacked is a Sikh. While authorities have not offered a motive, the stabbing took place amid a national rise in vitriol directed at immigrant truck drivers and four days after the U.S. Department of Homeland Security posted an image on social media that showed the Transformers’ leader Optimus Prime facing off against a Sikh man with the tagline that said, in part, “get off our roads.”
Jasjit Singh, left, attorney and director of legal services for Jakara Movement, an organizaiton that supports the Punjabi Sikh community, visits with Mr. Singh, a truck driver from Sacramento, Calif., who survived a knife attack at a rest stop along Interstate 80. (Jakara Movement)
During the hearing, Cassidy explained she was the on-call detective and received a call around 4 a.m. on Sept. 13, advising that someone had been stabbed at the Bitter Creek Rest Area at 144 eastbound on Interstate 80 in Sweetwater County. 
The victim himself, a truck driver from Sacramento, California, named Gurvinder Singh, reported the stabbing, as did a family who had been at the rest stop during the incident. Singh had been lifeflighted to the hospital before Cassidy arrived on the scene, but she spoke to him the next day. He reported that he had stopped at the rest stop and gone into the bathroom and was at the sink when a man punched him in the head. Cassidy reported that Singh said he turned and the man punched him in the face, there was pushing between the two men, the attacker patted down the front of Singh’s pants, and when Singh tried to leave the man began “punching him with the knife.” 
When defense attorney Steven Anselmi-Stith later questioned Cassidy about this statement, she explained that was the way Singh structured his words. She added that there wasn’t exactly a language barrier, since she could understand Singh, but that was the phrasing Singh used. 
Cassidy confirmed that records showed Singh had been stabbed 15 times, which included cuts above his left eye and on his cheek, a puncture to his neck area, and several punctures on his arms, chest and flank. Cassidy also said his left wrist was degloved and his right hand and face were “super swollen” when she spoke to him. Cassidy explained that most of Singh’s wounds had been treated and were covered when she spoke to him in the hospital, but that EMS had taken photos of the wounds after the incident, which she had seen and which looked like punctures rather than cuts to her. The hospital had also indicated that the wounds were punctures, according to Cassidy. 
Singh told Cassidy that he left and the suspect ran. A family, which Cassidy identified as the Anchado family, was at the rest stop during the incident. The adult son, who was in the car at the time, gave a witness statement and translated for his parents, who don’t speak English. The family reported that the mother had been in the women’s restroom and heard grunting, so she left and saw Singh, who was bleeding. Seeing the suspect’s truck leaving, the family got in their car and followed the truck for long enough to get a description and the license plate number, after which they returned to the rest stop, where they provided the information to dispatch, Cassidy explained.  
Information on the truck was shared with Wyoming Highway Patrol, and Highway Patrol officers were able to pull the truck over at the Flying J in Rawlins, where they detained the driver, who was identified as Bzdak. Cassidy identified Bzdak in the courtroom as the defendant in the case and the suspect from the incident. 
A search warrant was obtained for Bzdak’s truck, and Cassidy said that detectives searched the vehicle and found a plastic Walmart bag with jeans and wet wipes that both appeared to have blood on them, as well as a pair of shoes with apparent blood on them. 
Authorities obtained video footage of the incident from both the dash cam of Bzdak’s truck and another semi parked at the rest stop. Cassidy said the videos show when Bzdak’s truck parks at the rest stop before midnight and when Singh shows up close to 3 a.m. As Singh begins walking toward the rest stop, Bzdak gets out of his truck and follows him from a different sidewalk, Cassidy explained. The video then shows Bzdak running back to his vehicle and leaving on the interstate. 
While Bzdak’s dash cam footage from his truck faces outwards, it shows reflections of the inside of the cab from the windshield, Cassidy explained. This footage shows Bzdak using his phone, and after Singh gets out shows the reflection of Bzdak appearing to grab something, holding his hands in his lap in a fist, and appearing to manipulate his sweater before he gets out, Cassidy said. After Bzdak returned to his truck and began driving, the footage shows two instances where he quickly turns the dome light in his vehicle on and holds out his hands, as if to examine them to see if they are hurt or have something on them, according to Cassidy. 
The sheriff’s office also obtained GPS records from Bzdak’s trucking company, JKC Trucking, for Bzdak’s truck, and a search warrant for Bzdak’s phone and its GPS data. Cassidy said the GPS records from both the truck and phone line up with the timeline of events described by witnesses and observed in the dash cam footage. 
When questioned by Anselmi-Stith, Cassidy said that Singh had told her he had no idea who Bzdak was, and he had asked her why he was attacked. When Anselmi-Stith asked about what Singh was wearing at the time, Cassidy said he had a dark Nike T-shirt, pants and tennis shoes, and that he walked with his hands in his pockets. 
In closing statements, County Attorney Daniel Erramouspe said he believed the state had met the burden for probable cause on the case and that Bzdak had purposefully attacked Singh. Erramouspe added that questions of intent and malice are for a jury to decide, but he believes intent to kill can be inferred from repeated stab wounds in vital areas, and that malice can be inferred from the use of a deadly weapon.
Anselmi-Stith countered that he didn’t believe the state had met the burden, pointing to the facts that there was no witness to the actual event, the victim hadn’t identified the suspect, and there was no testimony of a knife being found or used. Erramouspe responded that there are very few cases of murder or attempted murder with direct witnesses. He pointed to the dashcam footage and GPS data lining up with the timeline of events as described. Erramouspe also added that whether a murder is premeditated is also a question for a jury, but pointed out that premeditation doesn’t have to be for more than a second, and that Bzdak was sitting in his truck before seeing Singh and following him inside, then fleeing. 
“He went in there and started stabbing,” Erramouspe said. 
Magistrate Newell said that the court had determined enough evidence exists to advance the case to district court. 
Bzdak remains detained at the Sweetwater County Detention Center under a $1 million bond.

name: Missouri Independent
title: Commentary: What the midterm elections could mean for Missouri’s economy
description: Wall Street’s initial optimism following Tuesday’s midterm elections quickly turned into a sharp selloff, driven largely by concerns about the future of AI and data-center investments. But beyond the market’s volatility, the election results sent a message that leaders in Washington and Jefferson City should take seriously: Americans want relief from rising [...]
text:
President Donald Trump's unpopularity, due in part to an inability to execute his campaign promise to lower costs, is likely to hurt Republican congressional candidates in the midterms, according to political scientists and analysts (Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images).Wall Street’s initial optimism following Tuesday’s midterm elections quickly turned into a sharp selloff, driven largely by concerns about the future of AI and data-center investments. But beyond the market’s volatility, the election results sent a message that leaders in Washington and Jefferson City should take seriously: Americans want relief from rising costs and a more stable future.
Democrats made major gains in Congress as many people voiced frustration about the cost of living, economic uncertainty, and national and foreign policies. Missouri’s results also showed a changing political landscape. Democrats gained seats in the state legislature, while Republicans lost their supermajorities in Jefferson City.
These results should not be seen only as a win for one party or a sign of political gridlock. They offer a chance to rethink policies that affect Missouri’s workers, farmers, families, and businesses. And the economic concerns behind that opportunity are real, not speculative.
Months before the election, an August 2026 Saint Louis University/YouGov survey of 900 likely Missouri voters documented widespread financial anxiety. 69% worried about affording health care, 66% about groceries and gasoline, 62% about utility bills, and 59% about property taxes. Only 25% rated Missouri’s economy as good or excellent, while just 21% gave the national economy similarly positive marks. The same survey found that 68% opposed construction of a new data center in their community.
The war with Iran added to economic pressures. As I discussed in my March analysis and June follow-up, the conflict’s effects on energy markets, transportation costs, and economic uncertainty extend well beyond the Middle East, reaching Missouri families, farmers, and businesses. Those economic consequences have since become part of the broader political debate, with even administration officials acknowledging the war’s role in the midterm backlash.
These findings do not establish why every Missourian voted as they did. But they show that economic dissatisfaction and concerns about the costs of technological development were already widespread before Election Day. The challenge now is to translate the demand for change into policies that deliver meaningful economic improvements.
 Tariffs: An opportunity to reconsider the costs

Few policies show the gap between promises and reality as clearly as tariffs. The Trump administration says tariffs protect American industries, support domestic production, and improve the country’s position in trade talks. These goals may appeal to manufacturing states like Missouri, but tariffs can also raise costs for businesses that rely on imported parts, materials, and equipment.
As I explained in my earlier analysis of Missouri’s trade relationship with Canada, these costs are particularly significant because Missouri’s manufacturers depend on deeply integrated North American supply chains.
The new Congress can review the effects of current tariffs, strengthen oversight, and help shape a clearer trade strategy. The president has broad authority over trade, but Congress can influence policy through laws, hearings, and budget decisions.
 Missouri farmers need markets, not just assistance

Trade is vital to Missouri farmers, who rely on global markets to sell soybeans, corn, and livestock. Trade disputes can prompt retaliation, costing farmers access to markets and putting them at a disadvantage compared with producers whose trade relationships are more stable.
Government assistance can provide temporary relief when markets are disrupted, but it cannot replace steady buyers and reliable export markets. Trade uncertainty also makes it harder for farmers to plan or make commitments extending well beyond a single growing season.
The new political balance in Washington offers a chance to rethink how trade policies affect agricultural competitiveness. Instead of relying mainly on assistance after disputes hurt farmers, policymakers should prioritize restoring predictable access to international markets.
For rural Missouri, that would represent a meaningful economic response to the frustrations surrounding the election.
 Data centers and AI: Missouri voters are asking who benefits and who pays

The August SLU/YouGov poll found that 68% of likely Missouri voters opposed construction of a new data center in their local community, compared with just 17% who supported it. Opposition had increased by 17 percentage points since February.
The concern also crossed partisan lines, with majorities of both Republican and Democratic respondents opposing a data center in their community.
Large data centers can attract substantial capital investment, create construction employment, and expand local tax revenues, but they require enormous amounts of electricity, significant water resources, and costly infrastructure improvements. Their permanent employment benefits may be modest relative to the size of the initial investment.
As I have argued previously, attracting technology investment should not require communities to accept financial obligations without adequate transparency and accountability.
The new Congress can examine the national implications of AI-related electricity demand, energy infrastructure, and investment incentives. Missouri lawmakers, meanwhile, have an opportunity to strengthen transparency surrounding utility costs, local incentives, and infrastructure commitments.
Beyond data centers, AI brings both opportunities and risks to Missouri’s economy. It can boost productivity and create new opportunities, but it also threatens to displace workers, eliminate certain jobs, and widen economic inequality. Policymakers, businesses, and educational institutions must work together to prepare students and workers for these changes, help displaced workers transition into new careers, and ensure that small businesses can benefit from emerging technologies. They should make sure that innovation creates better jobs, raises living standards, and benefits communities, not just a few companies.
 The voters have spoken. Economic policy must respond.

The midterm blue wave emerged against a backdrop of widespread economic dissatisfaction. Missouri’s own polling confirms that concerns about affordability, economic conditions, and the costs of technological development were firmly established before voters went to the polls.
These problems will not go away just because control of Congress has changed. But the election has created an opening for a different economic conversation, one focused less on political victories and more on measurable improvements in people’s lives. What matters most now is how policymakers respond to voters’ concerns and turn that response into economic progress.
