name: Alabama Reflector
title: Scott Colom wins Mississippi U.S. Senate race
authors: Taylor Vance, Michael Goldberg, Mississippi Today
description: This story was originally published on Mississippi Today.  Democrat Scott Colom has won a hard-fought U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, breaking Republicans’ dominance of statewide offices, ousting one of the state’s sitting senators for the first time since the 1940s and becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction. Colom, a district attorne[...]
text:
District Attorney and U.S. Senate candidate for Mississippi Scott Colom speaks as he gives an update on state of Senate race against Cindy Hyde-Smith November 4, 2026 in Jackson, Mississippi.  Colom, a district attorney, was declared the winner of a hard-fought battle for the Senate seat, and will be the first Black U.S. senator from Mississippi since Reconstruction. (Rogelio V. Solis/Getty Images)This story was originally published on Mississippi Today. 
Democrat Scott Colom has won a hard-fought U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, breaking Republicans’ dominance of statewide offices, ousting one of the state’s sitting senators for the first time since the 1940s and becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.
Colom, a district attorney in north Mississippi, defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and independent Ty Pinkins. Colom on Wednesday secured a come-from-behind triumph that has stunned pollsters, pundits and forecasters across the nation. Hyde-Smith has held the Senate seat since 2018. Mississippi has elected only Republican senators for the last 40 years.
The Democratic victory is an extraordinary upset in a state that President Donald Trump won by 23 points two years ago, and where Republicans have long maintained a stranglehold on state government and every statewide elected office.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
A source close to the Colom campaign said the Hyde-Smith had called him to concede on Wednesday evening. She did not immediately release a statement of her own.
RESULTS: Mississippi 2026 midterm election results
Democratic leaders see Colom’s victory as a stinging rebuke of the Republican Party’s agenda under Trump, who visited the state in the election’s closing days and pleaded with voters to send Hyde-Smith back to the Senate to help advance his agenda.
The Associated Press called the race with 99% of precincts reporting. Colom led 49.2% to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7%. He led Wednesday night by 4,645 votes.
Colom will now be the 55th Democratic senator to join the chamber, with Alaska’s Senate election still too close to call.
The AP called the race for Colom based on uncertified results, and the campaigns have said legal challenges are possible.
Colom’s long-awaited win caps more than a week of the nation waiting on Mississippi’s county election officials processing by hand thousands of affidavit ballots to determine the winner.
Colom, 43, will be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John Stennis in 1982. He is also the first Black person elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since Reconstruction, when the state Legislature elected Hiram Revels in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875. He is also the first Black person elected to any type of statewide office since Reconstruction.
When asked about possibly becoming the first Black man in more than a century to win a U.S. Senate race in the state, Colom said he only wants to make sure he won’t “be the last.”
“I don’t want anybody to say that I did anything to hurt the next person that has the talent, the work ethic, the ability to be able to reach for their dreams,” Colom said. “That’s my focus.”
Most forecasters rated the Mississippi Senate race as safe Republican. But on the issues defining the midterms, voters left little doubt the elections would be a referendum on soaring consumer prices exacerbated by tariffs and the president’s unpopular war in Iran.
Colom believed his strategy of tying Hyde-Smith to the high cost of gasoline and consumer prices would be enough to pierce the Republicans’ dominance in the Magnolia State. He began to pick up steam rapidly in the campaign’s closing weeks, receiving endorsements and resources from national Democrats.
Colom traversed the state from end to end and, in the election’s homestretch, engaged in a near-nonstop media blitz aimed at galvanizing any voters tuned into traditional cable news shows or following the race on social media.
In one viral ad, he mocked Hyde-Smith for suggesting voters upset over the rising price of beef should “pick another protein,” with Colom supporters saying they’d rather pick another senator. Another ad riffed off the Oscar-winning movie “Sinners,” which is set in Mississippi and his final ad before the election featured the home of slain civil rights hero Medgar Evers.
Colom mobilized the Democratic base through energetic rallies and appearances with high-profile national Democrats. He also tried to persuade skeptical Republicans. In one 24-hour span just over a week before Election Day, Colom roamed the line outside a Trump rally for Hyde-Smith in northeast Mississippi, spoke to some of the president’s supporters, then headed to the other end of the state for a rally with former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.
Dan Pffeifer, a political commentator and former senior adviser to President Barack Obama, said Colom “has run a campaign that is a model for Dems trying to flip very red states.”
And his strategy worked. Colom managed to crack the GOP’s iron grip on the state by turning out large numbers of Black voters, flipping several crucial swing counties blue and convincing Republicans to cross over and vote for him.
The most surprising feat was Colom winning DeSoto County, a reliably Republican stronghold in a Memphis suburb, by seven percentage points, something Democrats would have viewed as unthinkable last year.
Colom also tempered his losses in Harrison County, a populous coastal county that has swamped statewide Democratic candidates over the last decade and become a red firewall for the state GOP.  He also flipped Lafayette and Madison counties, two majority-white, affluent areas of the state that have become swing areas in recent elections.
In a joint statement, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said Colom’s victory was historic and vowed to work with him “to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs, and future in the 120th Congress.”
“Scott is a seventh-generation Mississippian, proud husband and father of two, and District Attorney who has dedicated his life to keeping communities safe,” Schumer and Gillibrand said. “He has never stopped fighting for his neighbors, because Mississippi Matters – and he’ll continue to be a champion for Mississippi in Washington.”
For many pioneering Black officials in Mississippi, Colom’s victory is the culmination of decades of organizing, campaigning and civil rights activism. It’s a moment that many never thought they would see in their lifetimes.
Mike Espy, the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the U.S. House since Reconstruction and the first Black person to become U.S. agriculture secretary, unsuccessfully ran against Hyde-Smith twice.
The former cabinet secretary served as an advisor to Colom, handed over his donor and voter lists to the campaign and hoped his losses “paved the road” for the soon-to-be senator, he told Mississippi Today in an interview.
“There is a time and place for everything,” Espy said. “This is Scott Colom’s time, and his place is in the U.S. Senate. I’m so pleased with the way he ran his campaign, and I was happy to support him.”
For Colom’s supporters, his victory brought a sense of poetic justice. Then-President Joe Biden in 2022 nominated Colom to a federal judgeship in northern Mississippi. A bipartisan coalition of Mississippi officials supported the nomination, but Hyde-Smith used her home-state “blue slip” privilege to oppose it.
Had Hyde-Smith not blocked Colom’s nomination, he likely would have served on the federal judiciary for the rest of his life and never run for the Senate.
But Colom decided to run and cast her as an out-of-touch politician who doesn’t represent Mississippi’s values. Hyde-Smith’s campaign called him a puppet of far-left national Democrats, with a spokesman calling Colom a stooge of Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and to billionaire donor George Soros.
Hyde-Smith, a Brookhaven cattle farmer, was first appointed to the Senate in early 2018 by then-Gov. Phil Bryant to succeed longtime Republican Sen. Thad Cochran, who retired about halfway into the six-year term. She won two races against Espy, a special election in late 2018 to fill the end of the term Cochran started and a regular election in 2020, and hoped she would gain a third victory.
Hyde-Smith left little doubt that she hoped to stymie Colom’s future as a judge. But in the end, her decision to block him from the federal judiciary cost her a seat in the Senate.

title: Republicans win two open Alabama State Board of Education district seats
description: Two Republicans won open Alabama State Board of Education seats last week, maintaining GOP holds on the districts.  The board, which determines policies for public schools in the state, is composed of nine members. The governor also serves as a member of the board. In State Board of Education District 8, Republican candidate Emily Jones […]
text:
Members of the Alabama State Board of Education pose for a picture after its meeting on Oct. 8, 2026. Two Republican candidates won open seats on the board during last week's election. (Andrea Tinker/Alabama Reflector)Two Republicans won open Alabama State Board of Education seats last week, maintaining GOP holds on the districts. 
The board, which determines policies for public schools in the state, is composed of nine members. The governor also serves as a member of the board.
In State Board of Education District 8, Republican candidate Emily Jones defeated Democratic candidate Shatika Armstrong. According to unofficial election results, Jones received 123,654 (53.7%) votes to Armstrong’s 106,282 (46.2%) votes. District 8 covers Madison, Limestone, Jackson and DeKalb counties.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Jones thanked voters in a statement posted to social media last week.
“This campaign has always been about putting students first, strengthening academic excellence, and ensuring parents have a voice in their children’s education,” the statement said. “I’m excited to get to work, and I promise to serve the families of District 8 with dedication, integrity, and a commitment to making a meaningful difference over the next four years.”
Jones campaigned on school counseling reform and transparency in communication with parents.
Armstrong said in a social media statement last week that despite the loss, her work “continues without a title.”
“Give me a minute to readjust my crown, tighten my laces, and catch my breath because I’m not done,” the statement said.
Armstrong campaigned on looking into the needs of rural schools, increasing teacher salaries and improving mental health access for students.
Jones will succeed Wayne Reynolds, who decided not to run for re-election to the board.
In District 6, Republican nominee Cathi Bradford bested Democratic candidate Angela Morgan with 137,123 (71.3%) votes to Morgan’s 54,834 (28.5%) votes. District 6 covers Cullman, St. Clair and Etowah counties and a majority of Talladega County.
Bradford said in a statement last week her campaign was “about something much bigger than winning an election.”
“It has been about standing up for our children, respecting the rights of parents and making sure our teachers have the support they need to do what they do best — educate. The people of District 6 have spoken, and I intend to work every day to honor the trust they have placed in me,” the statement said.
Bradford ran on school counseling reform and instilling patriotism in students.
Morgan said in a social media post last week while she didn’t win, the support she got “is a strong foundation to build upon. So, let’s build upon it anyway.”
“I will use this experience and all that I have learned to continue to help improve public education for ALL children in Alabama and to better love ALL my neighbors. I will do it with a glad heart anyway,” the statement said.
Morgan campaigned on student well-being, ensuring clear communication from schools to parents and safe and welcoming schools
Board member Tracie West won reelection to State Board of Education District 2 with 115,373 (61.5%) votes. Her opponent, Democratic nominee Jamie McCurry, received 72,056 (38.4%) votes.
West said in a statement last week she was “very grateful to everyone that supported our campaign!”
West’s priorities included seeking safeguards on artificial intelligence and continuing to make gains in literacy.
McCurry, a student at Auburn University, thanked voters in a social media statement last week.
“Over 72,000 votes is something I never would have expected and it means a lot. I enjoyed running this campaign and being able to meet so many wonderful people,” the statement said.
McCurry ran on advocating for complete and accurate textbooks and funding for neglected schools.
In the only non-contested race, Board Member Yvette Richardson won re-election with 98% of the vote.
Richardson said in a social media post Tuesday “it is an honor to continue serving District 4 on the Alabama State Board of Education and advocating for our children.”

name: West Virginia Watch
title: Commentary: A court introduces Attorney General McCuskey to the First Amendment
description: Pursuing political opponents through government-sponsored “investigations” is quite the thing in Washington, D.C., and Charleston these days.
text:
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey
speaks to the Legislative Oversight Committee on Health & Human Resources Administration during legislative interims on Aug. 11, 2026 in Charleston, West Virginia.
(Photo by Perry Bennett/West Virginia Legislative Photography)Pursuing political opponents through government-sponsored “investigations” is quite the thing in Washington, D.C., and Charleston these days. In September, West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey issued sweeping subpoenas to two environmental advocacy groups opposed to fossil fuels, claiming their advocacy was deceptive and violated the West Virginia Credit and Consumer Protection Act. The legal rationale for this claim is so flimsy that its true political purpose is clear. McCusky, a staunch supporter of the energy industry, simply disagrees with their point of view and seeks to disable the groups. 
Federal Judge Joseph R. Goodwin was having none of it. On Oct. 29, 2026, he entered a temporary restraining order barring McCuskey from enforcing the subpoenas or issuing new ones until Nov. 12, when a hearing will be held on whether the injunction should be extended. I’d bet that it will be.
McCuskey learned his approach to the job of attorney general at the knee of his predecessor, Patrick Morrissey. Both have used the legal machinery of the Attorney General’s Office to promote right-wing political goals and, in the process, to advance their own political careers. We have seen the same weaponization of state legal machinery on the national stage, and it should frighten us. 
Both Morrissey and McCuskey have joined or led coalitions of other attorneys general (all from red states) in lawsuits on newsworthy national political issues that have nothing to do with West Virginia. They have accompanied this with skillful publicity to project faux outrage and position the attorney general as an action hero. But McCuskey has gone further, using deprecating names to undermine his ideological opponents, like “insane leftist greeno’s” and a “green cabal” full of people “willing to destroy our economy.”  This is Trump-style schoolyard stuff.
McCuskey claims authority to issue the subpoenas under the West Virginia Credit and Consumer Protection Act. This makes unlawful “unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive acts or practices in the conduct of any trade or commerce.” The trade or commerce referred to must be related to the sale of goods or services. 
But according to Judge Goodwin, the Act doesn’t apply to the operations of the two advocacy groups — West Virginia Rivers Coalition and 350.org. Their missions are public education and dissemination of information. Their speech consists of public advocacy on important topics, not commercial speech. They are not financial institutions, lenders or creditors. They are not seeking to make a profit by engaging with consumers. They do not sell services of any kind. Their only sales are trivial items like T-shirts and coffee mugs displaying their logos. 
But here is where this dispute takes a serious turn beyond the usual West Virginia right-left political controversy. The subpoenas are “shockingly broad.” They demand more than10 years of records, including originals and drafts of 25 different document types in any way relating to a fossil fuel climate claim, or identifying a West Virginia energy business. This kind of burden would cripple a small advocacy organization and chill its ongoing work. McCuskey surely knows this.
The most alarming aspect of the subpoenas is that they probe into the relationships of the advocacy groups with others. They seek documents related to work with third parties to develop communications and strategies, documents relating to contacts with or funding by renewable energy companies or associations, and documents pertaining to dealings with other advocacy groups active in West Virginia on the fossil fuel-climate connection. This must have triggered the red First Amendment fire alarm on Judge Goodwin’s desk.
The First Amendment protects the right of peaceable assembly. This necessarily includes the right to associate with others. When the government intrudes into the ability of an individual or group to work with others toward a common political goal, the protected right of association is abridged. 
The First Amendment is not absolute, and McCuskey is right that some speech does not deserve protection. But when the government seeks to probe into speech and association like these subpoenas do, it had better have a very good reason. McCuskey’s reason is limp. He asserted only that there might have been a violation of the West Virginia Credit and Consumer Protection Act, and admitted that it is possible there was none.
Judge Goodwin has now held that the consumer protection act — a statute that prohibits deceptive and unfair commercial acts — can only apply to the type of commercial speech in which the advocacy groups do not engage. So a desire to enforce that statute cannot supply the sufficiently important governmental interest necessary to probe into non-commercial, protected speech and association. Accordingly, “the subpoenas [McCuskey] issued severely and unconstitutionally burden the Plaintiffs’ First Amendment right to free association.”
All West Virginia lawyers are required to take continuing legal education courses to maintain their law license. Perhaps Attorney General McCuskey could profit from a course in which he can brush up on the First Amendment.

name: Kentucky Lantern
title: ‘Tragic case’ of deported mother, child to Guatemala continues to wind through courts
description: The Kentucky Attorney General and the Kentucky Press Association are asking the state’s highest court to unseal confidential files involving a controversial family court case in which a Louisville judge ordered a toddler returned to her mother just before she was deported to Guatemala. The 15-month-old girl, a U.S. citizen, was born in Louisville though […]
text:
Caleb Yeske holding the Guatemalan baby shortly after she was born. Yeske was the baby's foster father. (Photo provided)The Kentucky Attorney General and the Kentucky Press Association are asking the state’s highest court to unseal confidential files involving a controversial family court case in which a Louisville judge ordered a toddler returned to her mother just before she was deported to Guatemala.
The 15-month-old girl, a U.S. citizen, was born in Louisville though her mother was undocumented and targeted for deportation by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). Both mother, 20, and child were sent by ICE to Guatemala in September over objections of the foster family that had cared for the child since birth.
Meanwhile, reunification of the child and mother in Guatemala has faltered, according to the Louisville foster father, Caleb Yeske, who visited them in Guatemala in October at the mother’s request. Guatemalan child welfare officials took custody of the child while he was there and hospitalized her over concerns about her health.
Yeske said he knows little about the girl’s status or plans for her care except that she remains in custody of the child welfare agency. He continues to try to monitor the case and offer any help he can.
“I want to be sure this child is safe and well-cared for,” he said.
Yeske said he faults the hasty reunification of the child with the mother as she was about to be deported. Typically, reunification occurs under the supervision of state social workers to ensure it goes smoothly and a parent is capable of taking over custody.
In this case, the mother—who had been in jail for the past year—and her child, were reunited just hours before ICE deported the mother, he said.
He also wonders if ICE’s current drive to deport immigrants worsened matters. Had the mother been allowed to remain in the United States at least long enough to get to know her child and learn parenting skills, the outcome might have been different, Yeske said.
“She was robbed of that,” he said.
In separate motions with the state Supreme Court, lawyers for Attorney General Russell Coleman and lawyer Michael Abate, representing the press association, argue that state law permits opening confidential child welfare files when warranted. They also argue the public has an interest in determining whether the case—which drew extensive media attention – was handled properly.
“The public has a substantial interest in this case,” said the attorney general’s motion. “The child at the heart of this case was born in Kentucky, and she spent the first year of her life here, cared for by foster parents. The child is every bit a Kentuckian.”
Abate’s motion said the case raises “substantial questions about how public officials — including judges — carried out their duties when ordering that an infant be hurriedly reunited with its mother . . . so the child could be deported with a mother it never knew.” 
‘She was born here’
Yeske, the foster father who cared for the girl from birth, said the child’s mother began trying to arrange her return to his care in the United States soon after she was deported, and he was willing to do so.
“This is a 15-month-old American citizen,” Yeske said. “She was born here, raised here and spent almost her entire life in Kentucky custody.”
Yeske said that in late October, the child’s mother contacted him and asked if he could resume caring for the girl and take her back to the United States to live. She told him she wasn’t ready to raise a child and also needed to work, but lacked child care.
So he flew to Guatemala to meet with her and to try to make legal arrangements. Yeske, who speaks Spanish, said he was able to communicate with the mother and locate a local lawyer to help.
The mother traveled with the child from a remote village where she lives to meet Yeske in Guatemala City, he said.
She executed legal documents to authorize the arrangement and Yeske was trying to obtain a U.S. passport for the girl through the U.S. Embassy when Guatemalan child welfare officials intervened and took custody of the child. She was hospitalized for a health evaluation and remains in the hospital as far as he knows, said Yeske, who had returned to the United States at that point.
Yeske said the U.S. embassy in Guatemala has thus far not intervened in the case and is leaving it to the discretion of the Procuraduria General de la Nacion, the child welfare agency.
An embassy spokesperson did not immediately respond to a request for comment emailed to the press office.
Lawyers for the child’s mother and with the Jefferson County Attorney’s office, which represents the state in family court, have filed motions objecting to unsealing the records in the Kentucky case.
The mother’s lawyers, John H. Helmers Jr. and Melina Hettiaratchi objected largely on technical grounds, saying there was no pending case before the Supreme Court and therefore the motions to unseal should be dismissed.
Lawyers for Jefferson County Attorney Michael O’Connell agreed the case should be dismissed on those grounds. But it added that “privacy interests” of the mother and child should be considered and that should the case be unsealed, personal or sensitive information should be redacted.
A ‘tragic’ case
The case first attracted public attention in September when the foster parents spoke out in opposition to a decision by Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson to reunite the child with the mother, who was in ICE custody and about to be deported.
Jefferson Family Court Judge Angela Johnson who is overseeing the child support case of former Gov. Matt Bevin, is also involved in the case of a child from Guatemala. (Pool photo by Michael Clevenger, Courier Journal, March 20, 2026)
Coleman’s motion to unseal the file acknowledges the case has a sad and complicated history.
“The facts in this matter are tragic all the way through,” it said.
The child was born in August 2025 and taken to the hospital by the mother, who spoke no English and reported giving birth alone at home, according to public court records. Court records say the pregnancy was the result of a sexual assault.
The infant had several lacerations and, suspecting abuse, child welfare officials, placed her in the custody of the state Cabinet for Health and Family Services, which then placed her in foster care.
The mother was initially charged with attempted murder and assault and remained in jail. In July she pleaded guilty to a reduced charge of wanton endangerment, was sentenced to time served and released from jail. But she was detained by ICE, which planned to deport her, according to court records.
In August, Johnson, the family court judge, agreed to proceed with plans to reunify the mother and child prior to deportation, prompting the foster parents to object and Jen Mortenson, an advocate on their behalf, to speak publicly about the case.
Mortenson told the Kentucky Lantern that Johnson at a hearing reminded those involved in the case that family court matters are confidential and that spreading “false information” about the case could result in jail time.
The foster parents attempted to appeal the judge’s decision to return the child to the mother.
But Appeals Court Judge Sara Walter Combs ruled against them, finding the law does not give foster parents standing, or legal grounds to pursue such a challenge. The state Supreme Court declined to overrule Combs.
A ‘gag order?’
Combs also said in her order that the facts in the confidential case “have been misrepresented by unwarranted publication in social media or otherwise.” The order said anyone who violates the confidentiality order “may be subject to sanctions or contempt proceedings.”
Abate, in the motion to open the case, compared any effort to silence those who wish to speak about it to a “gag order.”
While court records are confidential in child abuse and neglect cases, that doesn’t mean parties are forbidden from commenting on a case, his motion said.
“That is not the law,” his motion said. “This court has long recognized that a statute or order sealing a case file does not mean that parties are prohibited from discussing the subject matter of a case.”
Unsealing the files should answer questions about how the case was handled, it said.
“Only by bringing full transparency to this situation can this court ensure the public’s confidence in the judiciary—and particularly, the workings of its notoriously secretive family law system.”

name: Virginia Mercury
title: In Hanover County, environmental groups rally for statewide data center moratorium
description: A united front of environmental groups representing all corners of the commonwealth on Wednesday in Hanover urged the state government to implement a statewide pause on all new data center permit approvals and connections to the grid until stricter regulations for water use, energy infrastructure, and siting are enacted. Representatives from over a dozen org[...]
text:
A data center under construction in the town of Ashland in Hanover County, Va., Nov. 11, 2026. (Photo by Shannon Heckt/Virginia Mercury)A united front of environmental groups representing all corners of the commonwealth on Wednesday in Hanover urged the state government to implement a statewide pause on all new data center permit approvals and connections to the grid until stricter regulations for water use, energy infrastructure, and siting are enacted.
Representatives from over a dozen organizations stood outside the Hanover Humane Society where a few hundred feet away, through a thin smattering of trees, a hyperscale data center was being built. The facility was permitted by-right, meaning there were no public hearings or votes before supervisors gave it the green light.
“Here in Ashland, Big Tech swoops in, pulls the wool over our eyes and breaks ground before we’re able to fight back,” Blair St. Leger Olson with the League of Conservation Voters said.
The groups called for more transparency concerning the construction and operation of data centers in the area, stronger protections for any ill effects from the facilities for residents living near them, and for ratepayers to be shielded from shouldering the cost of energy infrastructure built for data centers.
They also pushed for these facilities to use clean energy, and for drinking water sources and private land to be protected.
Virginia is the home to over 400 data centers already in operation with about 280 planned and proposed.
Nate Benforado with the Southern Environmental Law Center emphasized that some regulatory changes for utilities are in the works, such as the new GS5 rate class for large load customers under Dominion Energy, and an effort to levy more transmission line costs onto those customers, as well.
“There are some utility reforms underway at our utility commission. But I’ll tell you from being in that courtroom, it is slow and it is incomplete,” Benforado said.
Some of the organizations at Wednesday’s demonstration stood beside Gov. Abigail Spanberger just a month ago when she unveiled her data center accountability framework. It’s a plan to rein in data center growth and address rampant public concerns about how data centers impact the environment. 
The groups’ requests on Wednesday overlap with the governor’s plan in key areas, including a proposed ban on nondisclosure agreements and enhanced air and water protections. 
Several leading environmental groups criticized the governor’s plan because it  doesn’t call for a full moratorium while lawmakers consider the legislative package.
Allowing new data centers to continue through the process without new checks and balances would leave too many Virginians and resources at risk, representatives of the group insisted.
“We don’t have six months, we don’t have a year,” Elena Schlossberg, with the Coalition to Protect Prince William County, said. “The pause needs to happen now. Not one more hookup if it means another Virginian loses their property, if it means they’re gonna breathe in more diesel generator fumes. Enough is enough.”
Some of the groups have been fighting to slow down the data center industry’s development in the state for years, including the Sierra Club and Schlossberg’s advocacy organization
New groups are now joining the chorus asking the state to create a moratorium. 
The Chesapeake Bay Foundation, which has been raising awareness about water availability within the Chesapeake Bay Watershed in a landmark drought year, is one of those new opposing voices. The growing concerns about the industry widened the scope of their priorities, representatives said Wednesday. 
“Last General Assembly, we did not support a moratory,” said Jay Ford, the Chesapeake Bay Foundation’s Virginia Policy Manager. “But I think that is really representative of how this issue has moved and something that we hope that the governor and her team are taking note of.”
Currently, the Department of Environmental Quality is studying areas east of Interstate-95 that are to be deemed “water scarcity areas,” which would limit data center development for facilities that use evaporative cooling systems. These systems can use hundreds of millions of gallons of water annually. 
That report is scheduled to be released this month.
DEQ is also tasked with developing noise regulations for data centers. The agency is looking into how quietly data centers are able to operate, with the goal to apply that as standard across the board.
Spanberger has proposed an idea for legislation that would expedite that process. The governor’s plan also requires new data centers to invest in cleaner backup generators.
Additionally, Spanberger’s plan outlines methods to direct more of the costs of energy infrastructure needed solely for data centers to the industry.
Several data center moratorium bills have already been filed for the 2027 General Assembly session that is set to begin in January. 
Sen. Russet Perry, D-Loudoun, has proposed a three-year pause on approving any new data centers. The senator said it would give the state time to develop more data center regulations and policies that would protect communities and ratepayers.
The data center industry remains adamantly against a data center moratorium.
“We join the many local governments, economic developers, business leaders, and labor unions who believe a top-down, statewide moratorium is the wrong approach to regulating this economically impactful industry,” Nicole Riley with the Data Center Coalition said. “States and communities that signal that they are closed for business and investment risk relinquishing substantial long-term economic investment, high-wage jobs, and critical tax revenue to neighboring areas or other states.”
The regular session for the General Assembly begins on Jan. 13.

name: Virginia Mercury
title: Newport News to create $9.5 million seafood market, revamp industrial park
description: Drive to the eastern end of Jefferson Avenue in Newport News and you’ll mainly find warehouses, industrial buildings and parking lots before the roadway terminates at the James River. But in a few years, this area will play host to a revamped waterside seafood market, where citizens can eat the catch of the day as […]
text:
A rendering of the revitalized Seafood Industrial Park in Newport News, which will be a public market for retail seafood sales, with vendor stalls for food-based businesses, an area for food trucks, and a section of pier where recreational boats will be able to dock. (Image courtesy of The City of Newport News)Drive to the eastern end of Jefferson Avenue in Newport News and you’ll mainly find warehouses, industrial buildings and parking lots before the roadway terminates at the James River.
But in a few years, this area will play host to a revamped waterside seafood market, where citizens can eat the catch of the day as commercial fishing vessels sail by, if all goes according to plan. 
Construction is underway to revamp the city’s Seafood Industrial Park (SIP) to include a public market for retail seafood sales, vendor stalls for food-based businesses, an area for food trucks, and a section of pier where recreational boats will be able to dock.
It is estimated to cost roughly $9.5 million to complete the market, which is slated to include 7,600 square feet of indoor space as well as 3,000 square feet of outdoor seating.
“Folks can come and have some food and look at the boats on the working waterfront,” said Derek Perry, Newport News’ interim director of development. “It will really be a gem and a jewel for this part of the community.”
Located near the northern entrance to the Monitor-Merrimack Memorial Bridge-Tunnel, the Seafood Industrial Park was established by the city in 1979 to host seafood and other water-dependent companies. But this port, which is Virginia’s largest commercial seafood port in terms of seafood landed value, has been closed to the public up until now. 
As part of the revitalization, the industrial park’s two commercial piers have been demolished, as well as two older finger piers at the end of the harbor that had reached the end of their service lives. 
A rendering of the revitalized Seafood Industrial Park in Newport News, which will be a public market for retail seafood sales, with vendor stalls for food-based businesses, an area for food trucks, and a section of pier where recreational boats will be able to dock. (Image courtesy of The City of Newport News)
The city also recently dredged to add depth to the harbor. The new docks, which will include moorings for recreational boats and space for roughly a dozen commercial vessels, should be completed by late spring 2027. The awarded contract for the dredging and the new dock come to $6.9 million.
“We’re creating more than a seafood market,” said Newport News Councilman John R. Eley III, who represents the South District where the industrial park is located. “We’re creating a waterfront destination, and it’s going to be a place where residents, families, boaters and businesses from across Hampton Roads can come together.”
The Seafood Industrial Park is located in the city’s East End, a historically Black community that has supported nearby Newport News Shipyard and counts jazz icons Ella Fitzgerald and Pearl Bailey and Norfolk State University head football coach Michael Vick as some of its famous former residents. 
The area — sometimes referred to as Southeast — experienced crime waves and gun violence in past decades and recent months, although these trends have waned citywide in the past year, police reported this summer.
Yugonda Sample-Jones, CEO of the East End Civic Association, expressed hope that the market would create entrepreneurial opportunities for the neighborhood. 
“We recognize that we need an economic driver in the East End, so this seafood market is just that,” Sample-Jones told WTKR in September. “I have some people right now that are wonderful cooks and I’m looking forward to helping them become franchisees or actually get a spot in the seafood market to sell their goods.”
The idea to revitalize the harbor came about after the city and the Newport News Redevelopment and Housing Authority (NNRHA) received a $500,000 Choice Neighborhoods Initiative planning grant from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development in 2016. 
The grant, which aims to redevelop severely distressed HUD housing and spur investment in the surrounding neighborhood, supported the Marshall-Ridley neighborhood in East End. 
In 2019, the city and NNRHA received a $30 million implementation grant. During the community engagement process that was part of rolling out the Choice Neighborhoods Initiative, citizens asked to access the catch – primarily Atlantic sea scallops, James River oysters and blue crabs – brought in through the port. That seafood would likely be sold at the new market.
“For a long time, we have talked about bringing meaningful investment and economic development in the Southeast community, and now we’re seeing that vision become a reality,” Eley said. “Citizens have been really excited about the opportunity that it’s going to create for local entrepreneurs, especially people right here in our community who want to start and grow a business.”
The seafood market is not funded by HUD, but will be paid for by the U.S. Economic Development Administration, the Virginia Department of Housing and Community Development, and the city.
The dock revamp and the dredging project are supported by $1 million in funding that U.S. Rep.  Bobby Scott, D-Newport News, secured through Congress’ Consolidated Appropriations Act for fiscal year 2024. The industrial park’s previous incarnation was “not the best use of the property,” Scott said.
“We’re looking forward to it (going) from, really, an eyesore, to a place where people will enjoy coming,” Scott said. “We’ll develop that area with the investments and improvements in the harbor and docks to support businesses and create a very exciting industrial park with good restaurants.”
Scott hopes that the revitalization will galvanize economic growth in the area.
“The seafood park will obviously create a lot of jobs, a lot of excitement, economic development, because you’ll have restaurants and other economic activity,” Scott said.
While market vendors have yet to be selected, the city has put out a bid for construction that is due at the end of October. Eley says that he has heard from startup businesses who would like to be vendors. 
Newport News City Council recently approved transforming a long-vacant building off nearby 34th Street into a commercial kitchen that could be used by such businesses, he added. 
The market, which will have its own kitchen for vendors, will operate year-round and has an estimated completion date of mid-2028.
City Council members are  considering how to unite the city’s waterways, including bringing watersports and water-focused activities to nearby King-Lincoln Park, which currently has a saltwater fishing pier. 
The city has also been working with Newport News Public Schools to invest $141 million to create a roughly 17-acre Southeast Community Resource Area that will include a new middle school, football field, recreation center, library, and community center with an indoor pool. That project is 60-70% complete, the Daily Press reported. 
Additionally, the Navy broke ground on a $450 million military housing development in downtown Newport News on Tuesday as part of a $1.7 billion effort to modernize housing for sailors across Hampton Roads.
Scott, who has an office near the seafood market site, says he’s excited to eat lunch by the waterside.
“It will be a nice place to visit,” he said. “I’m looking forward to being a customer.”

name: Maryland Matters
title: Commentary: An abuse finding disqualifies Maryland foster parents — unless they’re kin
description: Maryland has managed to place about half of the children in its foster care system in kinship care, but Sarah Font and Emily Putnam-Hornstein write that it has been able to do so only by severely relaxing security checks on those it regards as kin.
text:
Maryland has managed to place about half of the children in its foster care system in kinship care, but Sarah Font and Emily Putnam-Hornstein write that it has done so by severely relaxing security checks on those it regards as kin. (Stock.adobe.com photo by Fizkes)Gov. Wes Moore and Maryland’s Department of Human Services (DHS) are celebrating what they describe as a historic milestone: Half of children aged 10 and under in the state’s foster care system are currently placed in “kinship care,” up from 34% just two years ago.
How did they accomplish this?
Until recently, Maryland had a single set of licensing requirements for foster parents – kin and non-kin – with uniform rules about what was disqualifying and how exceptions could be made.
But in 2024, Maryland passed a law seeking to increase kin placements through two strategies.
First, the law expands the definition of kin. A third cousin who has never met the child qualifies as kin. As does a “person identified by the child’s parent”; no blood, legal, or relational bond to the child is required. There are often good reasons to consider, or give preference to, individuals who do not meet strict definitions of relative (such as a godparent or coach).
But the second change Maryland made was to systematically remove safeguards for this broad group of individuals now designated as kin. The law directed DHS to create a separate licensing track because, as Angelique Salizan, chief of staff for the state’s Social Services Administration, explained, licensure was previously a “big barrier for kin.”




Your opinion matters
Maryland Matters welcomes guest commentary submissions at editor@marylandmatters.org.
We suggest a 750-word limit and reserve the right to edit or reject submissions. We do not accept columns that are endorsements of candidates, and no longer accept submissions from public officials, elected officials or political candidates.
Opinion pieces must be signed by at least one individual using their real name. We do not accept columns signed by an organization. Commentary writers must include a short bio and a photo for their bylines.
Views of writers are their own.




Maryland has now removed a long list of standard licensure requirements, under the premise they constitute unreasonable barriers for kin. These include disqualification on the basis of confirmed child abuse, medical and mental health screenings, training, a complete home study and requirements that caregivers be able to meet their own material needs without taking the child’s foster care stipend for themselves.
On the traditional licensing track, a foster home is disqualified if either the foster parent or another adult household member “has been indicated for child abuse or neglect.” Exceptions can be made, in writing, by local directors.
Kin-specific licensing regulations only require the agency to “review” child protection records. A history of known child abuse is not itself disqualifying. And the agency must affirmatively demonstrate that any concerns – including a prospective kinship caregiver’s prior abuse and neglect, criminal history, or drug use – compromise the child’s safety before licensure can be denied.
That means a grandmother known to have abused her own daughter can now be approved, and paid over $1,000 per month to care for her granddaughter. So can a man the child’s mother identifies as a friend, even if he has never met the child and has a known substance use problem.
If the agency wants to deny placement with the grandmother, it must go through a secondary review process to prove to the state that she is likely to commit abuse again, rather than requiring the grandmother to prove that she is able to provide a safe home today. To deny the mother’s friend, the agency must provide “facts substantiated by objective evidence” that he cannot provide for the child because of  “substance or alcohol misuse.”
On the traditional licensing track an applicant is denied a license if their substance use “creates reasonable doubt” as to their capacity. But for kin caregivers, the agency is prohibited from relying on any general knowledge or common sense about how historical behavior predicts future behavior or the role of substance use in child harm – both of which are considered “stereotypes” and “generalizations.”
The safety shortcuts run through just about every licensing requirement. The agency is not only lowering the approval standards for kin, they are no longer collecting information that would inform whether the placement is appropriate.
Prospective kinship caregivers receive no home study – just a single visit. Agencies are not checking for concerns about other children already residing with the kinship caregiver, assessing financial stability, or verifying basic health status via medical examination. There is also no limit on the number of children placed in kin-licensed homes.
And, although the state purports to provide “trauma-informed environments” for children who have often experienced severe or chronic abuse or neglect, kinship caregivers – again, including people who have never met the child – will undergo no required training.
If Maryland believes that its traditional licensing requirements are unnecessary, why hasn’t it simply dropped them for all foster parents?
Maryland hasn’t and won’t, because it knows we are not talking about bureaucratic red tape – this is a blanket waiver of safety standards. Half of Maryland’s youngest children are now placed in foster homes approved under these lower standards. That is a milestone. But is it one that should be celebrated?

name: Honolulu Civil Beat
title: Hawaiʻi’s Green Party Finally Lodges Big Win After Decades
description:
Nick Nikhilananda has been a member of the Green Party of Hawaiʻi for nearly 35 years. His history is so deep that he played a role in getting the party on Hawaiʻi’s ballot for the first time, way back in 1992. That was accomplished along with people like the late Ira Rohter, a University of […]
The post Hawaiʻi’s Green Party Finally Lodges Big Win After Dec[...]
text:
Nick Nikhilananda has been a member of the Green Party of Hawaiʻi for nearly 35 years.
His history is so deep that he played a role in getting the party on Hawaiʻi’s ballot for the first time, way back in 1992. That was accomplished along with people like the late Ira Rohter, a University of Hawaiʻi political science professor who helped found and co-chair the group.
The Green Party has fielded dozens of candidates over the years, including Nikhilananda himself. It saw a couple of them elected in the 1990s to the Hawaiʻi County Council, which today is nonpartisan like all county offices.
But Greens have not succeeded in getting more members elected since. The state is too dominated by Democrats with Republicans comprising a weak yet vocal minority.
On Nov. 3, that all changed, at least for one seat in the 76-member Legislature. Pāʻele Kiakona, a Green, defeated Democrat Sne Patel and Republican Elle Cochran in House District 14 representing the Lahaina area.
It’s the first time in Hawaiʻi’s history that a Green has won office to the Legislature and one of only a half-dozen times any Green has been elected to a legislature nationwide.

Nick Nikhilananda, a member of the Green Party of Hawaiʻi for nearly 35 years.

“It was unbelievable,” Nikhilananda said in a interview Tuesday, who described his overall mood as “ecstatic.”
He had to wait for the good news, though, because he could only access the first online printout from the Hawaiʻi Office of Elections on election night.
“That’s all I could get from my computer,” said Nikhilananda, who lives in remote Huelo on the North Shore of Maui. “So I went to bed with him close but behind. And then I woke up and I saw some online comments that he’s in the lead by 107 votes.”
That lead increased to 119 this Tuesday when the Elections Office completed its curing of ballot signatures.
(Nov. 23 is the last day to file any objections to the 2026 elections.)
Nikhilananda is confidant that Kiakona will live up to the Green Party’s values (more on that in a moment) and be a voice to reckon with at the Legislature.
“He’s so humble,” said Nikhilananda. “He knows people at the Legislature. He’s not attached to the Democrats hating the Republicans, Republicans hating the Democrats. He says he’s going to work with both. He’s a community activist. He’s someone who cares.”
Nikhilananda and other Greens hope Kiakona’s unexpected win will also open paths to grow the party.
Susan Roberts-Emery, the party’s co-chair, said she and others have received lots of inquiries since the election expressing interest in helping the party spread its message.
“I just got off the Zoom with you and another person has reached out to the GPH that wants to run as a Green next round,” she said in an email Tuesday following my interview with her.
“We are seeing the reactions of the people who are ready for a better Hawai’i, one that puts the ʻāina, wai (water) and the future generations ahead of the almighty dollar.”
Four Pillars
The word “green” in Hawaiʻi evokes Gov. Josh Green, of course; the “green fee” — the nation’s first climate impact fee, established this year — and perhaps the Green New Deal pushed, thus far unsuccessfully, by progressive Democrats like Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez and Sen. Ed Markey in the U.S. Congress.
It’s likely many Hawaiʻi voters are unaware of the Green Party platform, even though two other Greens ran this year for Hawaiʻi’s 1st Congressional District (Jordan Conley, who lost to Democrat Rep. Ed Case) and House District 50 in Kailua and part of Kāneʻohe Bay (Jesse Fitzgerald, who lost to Democrat Rep. Mike Lee).
Green Party of Hawaiʻi co-chair Susan Roberts-Emery at a party convention in June presenting the party’s statement in support of Hawaiian sovereignty.  (Courtesy Jackie Keefe)
The Green Party also ran a ticket in the 2018 gubernatorial election, finishing third behind incumbents Gov. David Ige and Lt. Gov. Josh Green and the GOP ticket.
The party is based primarily on four pillars, according to a press release from the local Greens issued Wednesday:

Grassroots Democracy: “We champion direct democracy, transparent governance, public election financing, and Ranked Choice Voting so local communities hold the real power.”
Environmental Wisdom: “Hawaiʻi must live within its natural limits. We support sustainable land and water management, transitioning off fossil fuels, opposing LNG, and rejecting Data Centers.”
Social Justice: “We promote fairness, human rights, self-determination, inclusion, and economic security, ensuring safe housing, clean water, and healthcare as human rights.”
Peace: “We advocate for demilitarization, nonviolent conflict resolution, and addressing the heavy military footprint in Hawaiʻi. Land back and ‘cease the leases’ remain vital priorities.”

The platform reflects a degree of flexibility in the party depending on local priorities. Liquified natural gas, data centers and ranked choice voting, for example, are recent topics influencing public discourse.
But climate change, renewable energy, government reform and demilitarization are, if you will, evergreen issues that have their origins with the Green Party’s rise that began on the political fringe in the early 1970s in Australia, New Zealand and the United Kingdom before going mainstream in the 1980s in West Germany.
In the United States, the Green Party has struggled nationwide, according to the national party: No green-party member has been elected to any federal office and its best performance in a presidential election was Ralph Nader’s 2.7% of the popular vote in 2000.
“However, they have wielded influence in other ways,” reported a 2022 article from the Council on Foreign Relations. “As of November 2021, Greens held 133 state and local elected offices nationwide, and they were early proponents of a Green New Deal, which became popular among Democrats.” 
Going Green
While not in all states, the Green Party has a presence in blue states — California, Colorado, Connecticut, Delaware — and red — Florida, Georgia, Kansas and Texas and dozens of others. (Three of those red states turned pretty purple Nov. 3.)
Mike Feinstein, a Green Party member and former mayor and City Council member in Santa Monica, California, emailed me after the election to say that since the first Greens ran in the U.S. in 1985, members have been elected to public office approximately 1,750 times. At least 53 were elected to a local government office this year, with some results still being counted.
Pāʻele Kiakona (center) moderates a panel with community leader Kekai Keahi (at left) and Maui County Councilwoman Keani Rawlins Fernandez (at right) at the 2026 Green Party convention on Maui.  (Courtesy: Jackie Keefe)
As for Hawaiʻi, said Feinstein — he happens to also be the elections database manager for the Green Party of the United States — Greens have run for office 87 times since the party first qualified for the ballot in 1992.
In spite of the diversity of membership and various views, this statement on the national Green Party’s website captures its current broad vision: “Green political parties reflect a broader social movement seeking to reorient civilization in what supporters say are more sustainable and humane directions. Their environmental concerns began with opposition to nuclear power but have expanded to include climate change, pollution, and industrial agriculture.”
Aloha, ʻĀina
Kiakona’s Green candidacy almost didn’t happen. Jackie Keefe, who was considering running for the Lahaina House seat, heard about Kiakona’s interest. He was already well known for his work in the community activist group Lahaina Strong.
She said Kiakona was considering running as an independent but was persuaded by her and others to join the Green Party. Keefe also became his campaign manager.
Roberts-Emery said Kiakona was drawn to the party’s four pillars and participated in the party’s convention in June on Maui.
“That’s what attracted him to the party,” she said. “And this isn’t a movement about one man. Lahaina is the microcosm of what’s happening across Hawaiʻi, and Maui directly reflects what’s happening on all the islands.”
Reached by phone Wednesday, Kiakona confirmed that he was drawn to the party’s platform. But he had to be convinced, as many of his friends urged him to run as a Democrat.
“They were like, ‘You should just run as a Democrat and just get in, because if you don’t get in, then it’s all for nothing’,’ he said. “And I said, ‘Well, if anybody can do it, it’s myself right now. There’s nobody out there. There’s no other candidate that has been so like visible.’ And also, I basically spent three years campaigning. I didn’t think I was going to run for office, but those last three years of recovery was in itself a campaign to get more name recognition.”
Kiakona said he was frustrated that the incumbent, Cochran, missed a lot of floor sessions in 2025 and 2026. He was worried how a lack of a voice for Lahaina might affect funding for recovery and rebuilding as a result of the 2023 wildfires.
But he also started to do a little homework and found that the Greens resembled another third party, one that was formed for the 2020 election but has since disbanded. Their platform included a focus on economic diversification, renewable energy, sustainable agriculture and investment in the health care system
“As I started digging into the Green Party, I was like, ‘Wait, this is like the Aloha Aina Party or very similar, all of the same values.’ And at the end of the day, when you look at it, all of the Green Party values align with the Democratic values, but not all Democratic values align with Green Party.”
“I was like, ‘Okay, all of the good parts of the Dem Party are in the Green Party. Therefore, I’m gonna go here’.”
Running as a Green also had an advantage not afforded to nonpartisan candidates. Greens and Libertarians automatically advance from the primary to the general election, unlike other independent candidates, which must earn 10% of the total votes to move from the primary to the general, or earn a vote equal to or greater than the lowest vote received by the partisan candidates (that is, Democrats, Republicans, Greens and Libertarians).
It is too soon, obviously, to know if Kiakona and the Greens might have influence in state governance come January when the new session begins. Freshman orientation was Monday, but Kiakona doesn’t yet have an office as the Capitol undergoes repairs during the interim.
But he has met with House Speaker Nadine Nakamura and Vice Speaker Linda Ichiyama.
“I am willing to caucus with whoever, because all of this means nothing if I get in the building and I’m just shoved to the side and I can’t get any work done for the community,” he said. “I’m trying to look at this as an opportunity for for everybody.”
For Green Party co-chair Dave Mulinix, change can’t come soon enough.

Green Party of Hawaiʻi co-chair David Mulinix in a Zoom chat Tuesday with Civil Beat.  (Screenshot/2026)

“Susan and I have been doing this way before we had white hair, and that’s how long we’ve been working for peace and justice,” he said in the same Zoom interview with Emery Roberts. 
“And every year in the Legislature, it’s really disheartening. I’m not sure exactly what to call it, but it’s an old boys’ network. It is not a democratic system in any way, shape, or form. You’ve got one or two guys at the top who decide what’s going to get passed and what isn’t, and doesn’t matter how many people come forward and testify on what is important.”
Kiakona, predicted Mulinix, will not be a flash in the pan.
“For an Indigenous person, there’s certain things you’re not going to give away,” he said. “He’s not going to give away clean water, the clean ocean, protecting the human rights and civil rights of the people. It will be impossible to get him to move off of being what’s stitched into his DNA, who he is as a human being… I’m sure we’re going to hear some incredible speeches that are going to blow people out of the water.”

title: Computer Science Is In More Hawaiʻi Schools. Not All Kids Are Taking It
description:
Nearly all Hawaiʻi public schools are now offering computer science after the Legislature passed a law in 2021 requiring instruction on every campus. But not all students are benefitting equally from these courses.  Around 98% of schools offered at least one computer science course last year, up from roughly 54% three years prior. The course […]
The post Com[...]
text:
Nearly all Hawaiʻi public schools are now offering computer science after the Legislature passed a law in 2021 requiring instruction on every campus. But not all students are benefitting equally from these courses. 
Around 98% of schools offered at least one computer science course last year, up from roughly 54% three years prior. The course with the greatest enrollment was an introductory computer science class for third graders, which served more than 11,300 kids across the state, according to the education department’s recent report to the Legislature. At least 89% of students in grades kindergarten through five took a class last year.


But participation rates in computer science tended to peak in elementary school. Enrollment fell as students entered middle and high school, with ninth graders recording the lowest participation rate of 8% last year. 
Enrollment also varied based by geography. The Leilehua-Mililani-Waialua complex area on Oʻahu had the highest participation rates, with 69% of all students taking a computer science class last year. The Castle-Kahuku complex area reported the lowest enrollment rate of 39%, followed by the Kailua-Kalaheo complex area with a 45% enrollment rate. 
The racial and gender makeup of Hawaiʻi’s computer science classes reflected the overall demographics of public schools last year. Girls made up 47% of those enrolled in computer science classes. 
But enrollment rates were slightly lower among low-income students qualifying for free or reduced lunch. Low-income students made up roughly 42% of the state’s computer science enrollment last year, compared to 58% of the overall population in public schools. 


Around a dozen states currently require students to take computer science to graduate from high school. Local advocates have urged Hawaiʻi to follow suit, arguing that a mandate would ensure that all students have the opportunity to learn key technology skills and prepare for high-paying careers. But some educators and administrators have questioned if schools have the resources and staffing needed to add a new graduation requirement.
A 2024 report from the University of Hawaiʻi Economic Research Organization listed computer science as one of the most lucrative college majors in the state, with a projected mid-career income of $95,755. 
The education department is currently in the process of revising its computer science standards for the first time in nearly a decade. The proposed standards, which state leaders will present to the Board of Education on Thursday, include updated guidelines around artificial intelligence, cybersecurity and data science. 
For example, students would learn more about data privacy and common types of cyberattacks in middle school. Under the new standards, high schoolers would be tasked with evaluating the accuracy of AI-generated code and creating data visualizations.

title: He Was Rebuilding His Life. Then The Unthinkable Happened
description:
The lights came on in the rearview mirror: red then blue then red again on a Wednesday in Kailua-Kona, and the thump of his heart could be felt throughout his whole body before his foot found the brake.  Under the seat was a loaded handgun and unspent rounds. In a bag was 15.7 grams of […]
The post He Was Rebuilding His Life. Then The Unthinkable Happened ap[...]
text:
The lights came on in the rearview mirror: red then blue then red again on a Wednesday in Kailua-Kona, and the thump of his heart could be felt throughout his whole body before his foot found the brake. 
Under the seat was a loaded handgun and unspent rounds. In a bag was 15.7 grams of crystal, weighed and packaged the way you package something meant to be sold rather than used alone. He was 36 years old and he already had a criminal record to his name, which meant none of what happened next would be treated as a first mistake. It would be treated as confirmation.
The police searched the car on the spot. By the time the search was over, he was looking at a felony count for promoting a dangerous drug, a meth trafficking charge, possession of paraphernalia, and eighteen separate firearms offenses stacked on top of each other, the heaviest of them being a felon caught holding a gun he was never allowed to touch again. Bail came back at $593,000, a number designed to make sure he did not walk out the same day.
He did not know it yet, sitting in a holding cell doing the math on 18 charges, but this was not rock bottom. It was the first drop. The real one was still six years away, and it would not be his fault at all.
I met Danny Campogan in 2023 at Ocean’s bar in Kona. It was the kind of conversation that starts as small talk between strangers and ends with one of you setting your drink down because you have stopped being able to drink and listen at the same time. I already knew part of his story before he told me any of it. 
Danny Campogan, left, owner of Coconut Tree Trimmer Kona, shakes hands with his youngest employee, MJ Moses, at a job site in Kona on Hawaiʻi island. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Mikey Kaho’okaulana, employee and friend of Danny Campogan, shows his Kona Town knuckle tattoos. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Everyone on this island who was paying attention in November of 2019 remembers a head-on collision on Queen Ka‘ahumanu Highway, a stretch of road that produces these crashes with grim regularity. Unlike O‘ahu’s freeways, this part of the highway has no concrete median. Cars traveling at full speed pass in opposite directions, separated only by a painted line, with ‘a‘ā (jagged lava rock) on either shoulder. 

Highway 19 going toward the Kona Airport. (Cory Lum/Civil Beat)

A twenty-five-year-old motorist crossed into oncoming traffic trying to pass. He hit a Honda Pilot carrying a woman and her daughters. The woman did not survive.
I did not know, sitting across from Danny with a beer turning lukewarm, that the man telling me this story and the father in that headline were the same person, and that the woman who did not make it that day was the mother of his children, Cassandra.
Danny Campogan looks makai at Cassandra Lynn Ellis on Queen Kaʻahumanu Highway. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
By 2019, Danny was already out. He had served his time, and by his own account he was already climbing when the highway took the ground out from under him a second time, in a way that had nothing to do with anything he had done. That distinction matters. This is not a story about a man who built a business to outrun his grief. He was already building before the grief arrived. Grief just showed up uninvited in the middle of it and asked him to keep going anyway.
What struck me later wasn’t simply that Danny rebuilt his life. He never had the option of the safe road. The rest of us like to believe there is one, a paved and reasonable route where you take the steady job, sign the mortgage, lease the two cars because that is what qualifies as responsible now, and put something small away every month for a college fund you hope your kids will use someday. 




Ideas showcases stories, opinion and analysis about Hawaiʻi, from the state’s sharpest thinkers, to stretch our collective thinking about a problem or an issue. Email  news@civilbeat.org to submit an idea or an essay.


Read More

It looks like safety. It is sold as safety. But watch that road long enough and you start noticing how many people on it are barely breathing, working overtime to cover payments on things that were supposed to make their lives easier, watching a marriage strain under the particular pressure of money that is always spoken for before it ever arrives. Everything that comes in has already gone back out. 
That is not security. That is a hamster wheel and most people stay on it because the alternative feels like falling.
What happens to a man like that when he gets out is not usually a landscaping company and home ownership. It is usually nothing. He moved between family and friends’ couches, worked kitchens for cash under the table because that was the only work that would have him, and did all of it while raising three daughters. He needed something that did not require anyone’s permission.
What he had was a compact Kia and an idea. He bought a small trailer, hitched it to the back of the car, and started driving through Kona neighborhoods looking for green waste, the branches and cuttings and yard debris that homeowners pay to have hauled away. $100 a load to the dump. 
Danny Campogan, owner of Coconut Tree Trimmer Kona, fixes his hat as he prepares to go out to work at a job site, Oct. 30, in Kona. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Danny Campogan, middle, shares a laugh with two of his employees, Kenny Ken, left, and Michael Jally, right, at a job site last month in Kona. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Fifteen employees now. A house with his name on the title, paid for by hauling other people’s green waste one trailer load at a time until it turned into something else entirely.
He is 49 now and does not look it. There is a kind of fitness that comes from real labor, from climbing and hauling and running a crew, that no gym membership replicates, and Danny has it. He has a girlfriend who works the business alongside him. From the outside it reads like a comeback story, clean and inspiring, the kind of thing that gets a headline of its own.


Danny Campogan, right, owner of Coconut Tree Trimmer Kona, goes through cutting equipment with one of his lead employees, Michael Jolly, at a job site in Kona last month on Hawaiʻi island. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


Danny Campogan exits his truck before heading out to work.  (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)


He told me he would not stop for the day until he had made $500, however many trips that took. He did this every day until there was enough saved to buy a lawn mower. Then he was cutting lawns. Then there was a riding mower, and after that an actual truck, and after that a second truck and a couple of guys working for him instead of just him working alone. Then climbing bands, so the company could take on tree trimming. 
Danny Campogan, second from left, leads a pule with employees and friends Mikey Kaho’okaulana, left, Kassidy Ferris, second from right, and George Anderson at the memorial for Cassandra Lynn Ellis on Queen Kaʻahumanu Highway, Oct. 30, in Kona. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
Danny Campogan, left, embraces his girlfriend Kassidy Ferris at the memorial for Cassandra Lynn Ellis on Queen Kaʻahumanu Highway in Kona last month on Hawaiʻi island. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
But I do not think Danny would call it clean, and I do not think he would trade the true weight of it for the headline version. There was no ladder waiting for a felon with his history. He had to build his own out of scrap, one green waste run at a time, and the ladder he built happened to go higher than the one most people are handed. That is not the same as saying it was worth it. I believe that he would return the house and the trucks and the fifteen employees tomorrow for his daughters to have their mother back.
The markets have to move down before they can move up, falling below what everyone thinks is safe to locate the fuel that powers the resurrection. Lives, sometimes, do the same. Nobody chooses the down part.
I don’t see Danny as often as I would like, but do occasionally see his updates on social media. That is going to change. I’m going to take him up on his offer to go spearfishing. And maybe dinner again with his new girlfriend. 
We will go into the Hawaiian ocean when the conditions allow it, and afterward trade stories the way men do when neither of them is performing for the other anymore. What stays with me about Danny is the plainness with which he tells the worst parts. No self-pity, no polish. Just a man who hit the actual bottom, found daughters waiting for him when he climbed out, and decided that was reason enough to keep climbing.
Danny Campogan, owner of Coconut Tree Trimmer Kona LLC, puts a hand on his company logo as he prepares to go out to work at a job site in October in Kona. (Jamm Aquino/Civil Beat/2026)
