name: Indiana Capital Chronicle
title: Indiana Economic Development Corp. says 2025 audit’s issues ‘addressed’ while new one launched
description: The Braun administration says it is dealing with all oversight issues raised in last year’s Indiana Economic Development Corp. audit — and that officials are cooperating with a new review from the state attorney general’s office.
text:
Rep. Ed DeLaney parses through a portion of the 127-page IEDC audit before talking to reporters on Oct. 3, 2025. (Whitney Downard/Indiana Capital Chronicle)The Braun administration says it has dealt with all oversight issues raised in last year’s Indiana Economic Development Corp. audit — and that officials are cooperating with a new review from the state attorney general’s office.
The agency and its affiliated Indiana Economic Development Foundation have continued to face scrutiny since the audit ordered by Gov. Mike Braun found many instances of lax adherence to ethics policies and questionable spending on overseas travel.
IEDC forensic analysis highlights lackluster oversight and questionable spending

During a State Budget Committee meeting on Tuesday, Democratic Sen. Fady Qaddoura asked Braun’s commerce secretary, Chuck Goodrich, whether all the issues identified had been resolved.
“We have studied the audit,” Goodrich said. “I know that we have corrected, I think, every item on the audit.”
The audit was released in October 2025. It covered “findings” such as failures by the IEDC to investigate undisclosed conflicts of interest involving agency executives and “observations” of issues including the lack of a conflict of interest policy on companies giving money to the foundation.
Clinton Bohm, the IEDC’s chief financial officer, told the committee that the “actual findings have all been addressed.”
“The observations, we’re working on policies to put into place so that we can operate in a way that would alleviate those,” Bohm said.
Braun administration officials had said last year the Indiana Economic Development Foundation was “moving toward wind-down” after the audit found that over a five-year period about $11 million of its $13 million in spending was for travel, meals and entertainment. 
The foundation, however, continues to operate with additional transparency policies.
“We actually built a business plan for the foundation that’s very specific on where the money is raised and why we raise it,” Goodrich said.
New audit launched by attorney general
Those steps are occurring while state Attorney General Todd Rokita’s office has hired the same national consulting firm that did last year’s IEDC audit to specifically review the foundation’s travel and entertainment spending.
The attorney general’s office signed a contract in August with FTI Consulting for the review costing up to $275,000. 
The contract, which wasn’t announced publicly by the office, is for FTI to review a “risk-based sample selection” of 100 travel and entertainment expenses paid for by the foundation between Jan. 1, 2022, and June 30 of this year. That covers part of former Gov. Eric Holcomb’s tenure and Braun.
“Contractor will evaluate whether T&E expenditures were reasonable, properly documented, and consistent with the IEDF’s stated mission and the intended purposes of IEDF funding,” according to the contract.
Provisions of the contract say the attorney general’s office might broaden the review’s scope to include “whether recipient organizations failed to execute their stated missions, failed to use IEDC funds for their intended purposes, or were established or operated for fraudulent or improper purposes.”
FTI contract Aug 2026
FTI was paid $800,000 for last year’s audit, according to state records. That audit report was forwarded to the state’s Office of Inspector General, but no actions against any person or entity have been disclosed.
Rokita’s office did not reply to a request for comment this week about why it is pursuing the additional audit.
Braun spokesman Griffin Reid told the Capital Chronicle that the administration would work with the auditors.
“Since Governor Braun launched the investigation and audit of the IEDC/IEDF in April of 2025, both entities have been under a clear directive to cooperate with all state agencies seeking information, including the OIG and the OAG,” Reid said.

name: Wisconsin Examiner
title: In La Crosse and Eau Claire, citizen committees will tackle rising healthcare costs
description: The cost of healthcare was front and center across Wisconsin in last week’s election — and in western Wisconsin, the story was no different. “It’s really bad,” says Shawn Phetteplace of Main Street Alliance, which counts some 400 western Wisconsin small business owners among its members. They’ve been distressed by a spike in the cost […]
text:
A campaign poster urging people to vote for a referendum to create a citizens committee to study healthcare issues in La Crosse hangs in a store window. (Photo courtesy of Nick Padesky)The cost of healthcare was front and center across Wisconsin in last week’s election — and in western Wisconsin, the story was no different.
“It’s really bad,” says Shawn Phetteplace of Main Street Alliance, which counts some 400 western Wisconsin small business owners among its members.
They’ve been distressed by a spike in the cost of health insurance for people who buy coverage on the federal healthcare marketplace, Phetteplace says. He adds that “a disturbing number of people” have dropped coverage entirely.
Now two western Wisconsin cities, Eau Claire and La Crosse, are preparing to appoint teams of local citizens to dig into the issue. Voters in each city approved ballot measures on Nov. 3 to create healthcare action task forces.
Eau Claire voters approved the proposal 55% to 45%, while in La Crosse, the vote was 67% in favor to 33% opposed.
“It’s a novel approach, but I think it’s an exciting opportunity for people who are feeling directly the impact of healthcare costs skyrocketing, small business owners  and people interested in seeing city government taking a bigger role,” says Nick Padesky, who worked as a full-time time organizer for the campaign to pass the measures.
“In many ways it’s an expression of frustration with the federal and state governments for doing so little on managing healthcare costs,” says William Garcia, who led organizing for the La Crosse vote.
Sam Roecker, a Madison political strategist and a member of the team that pulled  the task force campaign together, says the proposals grew out of conversations among advocates in the spring of 2026.
People who joined the campaign were frustrated about steep Medicaid cuts that will start in 2027 from the massive tax-cut and spending bill passed by Republican members of Congress and signed by President Donald Trump in 2025, Roecker says. The bill is expected to carve almost $1 trillion out of Medicaid over the next 10 years.
Roecker says people have already been seeing how the end to enhanced subsidies for health plans sold at HealthCare.gov has sent premiums soaring for people buying  their own coverage. GOP lawmakers in Congress rebuffed repeated attempts to extend the subsidies, which expired at the end of 2025.
While the healthcare task force campaign was officially nonpartisan, Roecker has worked on Democratic campaigns in Wisconsin and elsewhere. Local Democratic groups promoted the ballot measures, and the reelection campaign of U.S. Rep. Derrick Van Orden in Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District was also a backdrop.
“Van Orden was still out there trying to frame that he in no way cut Medicaid,” says Roecker.
Van Orden, a Republican, voted for the 2025 GOP law while rejecting the characterization that the measure had imposed Medicaid cuts. He lost on Election Day to Democrat Rebecca Cooke.
Garcia chairs the 3rd Congressional District Democratic Party, but says that for the task force campaign, “I signed on not as a Democrat but as a citizen of La Crosse.”
Members of Main Street Alliance got involved in advocating for the ballot measures, Phetteplace says. Health professionals who belong to the advocacy group Committee to Protect Health Care did as well, says that group’s spokesperson, Annika Isaguirre.
The measures were introduced as direct legislation, provided for in the Wisconsin statutes for residents of a municipality to introduce local ordinances on their own. The state law requires that the municipality’s board or council vote on the measure or submit it to voters in a referendum.
Organizers in La Crosse submitted more than 5,000 signatures and in Eau Claire more than 8,000 signatures. While they could have left the issue just in the hands of the city councils, “We asked them specifically to send it to referendum,” Garcia said. “We wanted the community to have a say that this was a good idea.”
The ballot measures in each city asked voters whether the city should create a citizens advisory healthcare action committee. Each was tied to a lengthier ordinance that prescribes the number of members for the committee (seven), how they’re selected and what their duties and responsibilities are. Each committee is to produce a report every two years.
“They’re tasked with analyzing the state of healthcare in the cities,” says Padesky — what premiums residents are paying for their health insurance, how many small businesses have health insurance plans for their employees, the presence and demographics of population groups with less access to healthcare and other facts and trends.
The committees’ recommendations could include advocacy as well as possible strategies — “what do we need from state and federal policymakers to what direct actions can the cities of La Crosse and Eau Claire take to make healthcare more accessible and affordable with everyone in the cities,” Padesky says.
In structuring the proposals, the organizers sought to keep the committees open-ended, Roecker says, avoiding prescribing specific solutions.
Organizers say they didn’t encounter a concerted campaign against the ballot measures in either city. In Eau Claire, the local chamber of commerce issued a statement the Friday before Election Day that raised objections to the proposal, but stopped short of calling for a vote against it.
“Our concern is not with the goal of the proposal, but with whether the committee’s structure, authority, and resource requirements would meaningfully advance that goal,” the chamber statement said.
The organizers acknowledge that many of the problems relating to healthcare costs are due to state and federal policies.
“When I talked to people individually about it, the only concern that anybody expressed was the fact that, in many ways, the city does not have a lot of leeway in terms of what happens with healthcare costs,” Garcia says.
“Everyone acknowledges that most healthcare policy is decided at the federal and state level,” he says. “But that doesn’t mean local governments are completely useless in the matter.”

name: Pennsylvania Capital Star
title: Pa. DCNR unveils new climate action plan
description: Pennsylvania’s Department of Conservation and Natural Resources is unveiling a new climate action plan for the state, with varying deadlines for goals between 2030 and 2050. Several DCNR officials spoke Tuesday at the Mira Lloyd Dock Resource Conservation Center in Spring Mills, Centre County.  Formerly known as Penn Nursery and Woodshop, the state-run tree [...]
text:
Staff from Pennsylvania's Department of Natural Conservation and Natural Resources, along with other local and state agencies, unveiled the state's new climate action plan on Nov. 10, 2026 at the Mira Lloyd Dock Resource Conservation Center in Spring Mills. (Sydney Roach/WPSU)Pennsylvania’s Department of Conservation and Natural Resources is unveiling a new climate action plan for the state, with varying deadlines for goals between 2030 and 2050.
Several DCNR officials spoke Tuesday at the Mira Lloyd Dock Resource Conservation Center in Spring Mills, Centre County.  Formerly known as Penn Nursery and Woodshop, the state-run tree nursery conducts seed tests and has sent millions of trees to be planted across the state.
“We have to have a vibrant seedling nursery because we have to be planting the trees of the future,” said Pennsylvania DCNR Secretary Cindy Dunn.
Dunn said one of the goals in the climate action plan is to plant more trees across Pennsylvania to mitigate flood risk and provide more shade. Another goal is to reduce carbon emissions created by the DCNR by switching 80% of their vehicles and certain equipment to electric or hybrid.
Dunn said the state is already seeing the effects of climate change.
“In the heavy deluge storms and early warm ups, followed by deep frost and flooding patterns. More extreme heat days creating danger in the urban areas, particularly,” Dunn said.
Meredith Seltzer, the agency’s climate and sustainability director, said she worries how climate change will impact her 3-year-old son’s future. Seltzer pointed to severe weather over this year’s 4th of July weekend.
“Over 260,000 Pennsylvanians were without power, and widespread wind damage occurred after extreme storms and flooding swept through 64 of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties,” Seltzer said. “Then, dangerously unhealthy air quality forced everybody indoors in mid-July from Canadian wildfire smoke that came down into Pennsylvania.”
Seltzer said DCNR is also planning ways to keep staff and visitors safe on state lands.
“The Bureau of State Parks has committed to updating all park emergency manuals by 2030, in anticipation of more frequent major storms impacting our recreational resources,” Seltzer said.
DCNR published its first climate action plan in 2018. State officials said they did complete or make progress on many of those goals, such as completing the agency’s first greenhouse gas inventory.

name: Michigan Advance
title: Michigan’s Black voters sent a message to candidates in midterms: ‘You’ve got to earn it’
description: Autumn Butler, deputy executive director of Michigan United, said that on Election Day, she saw lines of people waiting to cast their ballots in cities across Michigan — driving what she expects to be significantly higher voter turnout among Michigan’s Black voters than the last midterm election in 2022. “Everywhere we went, people were coming out. […]
text:
DETROIT, MICHIGAN - NOVEMBER 03: People vote at a polling location on November 03, 2026 in Detroit, Michigan. Americans go to the polls in consequential midterm elections, where control of the House and the Senate is at stake for the remainder of President Donald Trump's second term in office. (Photo by Spencer Platt/Getty Images)Autumn Butler, deputy executive director of Michigan United, said that on Election Day, she saw lines of people waiting to cast their ballots in cities across Michigan — driving what she expects to be significantly higher voter turnout among Michigan’s Black voters than the last midterm election in 2022.
“Everywhere we went, people were coming out. They were excited. They were ready,” she said. “Anecdotally, just looking at the Black cities throughout the state of Michigan, I definitely saw a great enthusiasm for people to turn out.”
As the election results are certified and more detailed voter turnout data emerges, the main takeaway that James Johnson, the political director of Detroit Action, had for candidates in the future seeking to court Black voters is that “The overall lesson is you’ve got to earn it.”
“I think it shows that Black people will turn out and they will vote when you speak to them and speak to their issues. But you can’t do the wash, rinse, repeat of the traditional campaigning, or just dump a bunch of mail and commercials in here,” he continued. 
Johnson said candidates need to be “on the ground” and “touch some grass” to actually talk to Black voters and earn their vote.
“It is not something that you can just put in your back pocket and bank on. However, if you do earn it, we will show up, and we will show up for you,” he said.
James Johnson is the Political Director of Detroit Action.
Tameka Ramsey, executive director and convener of the Michigan Coalition on Black Civic Participation and Black Women’s Roundtable, similarly emphasized, “Everybody needs the Black vote. We’ve seen it across this country.”
As for what actually drove that higher turnout that Butler witnessed, she said that the cost of living, including healthcare costs, was a driving factor for many.  SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Struggling with gas, struggling with groceries, and this war has touched a lot of people who have been hearing that the government has enough money for wars, but it doesn’t have enough money for safety net programs here in the country,” Ramsey said.
An exit poll from the National Coalition on Black Civic Participation noted that over 36% of Black voters surveyed nationwide listed inflation as the top issue threatening voters and their families, and over 18% listed housing.
That drive to the polls stemming from the issues, Johnson said, also showed that turnout was not driven by a “cult of personality” — Black voters were largely not turning out specifically to vote for Gov.-elect Jocelyn Benson or Sen.-elect Abdul El-Sayed, but instead because they believed change needed to come on issues like housing and healthcare.
He did, however, call the results of the U.S. Senate race “a repudiation of the ideas of Mike Rogers as much as it was an acceptance of Abdul El-Sayed being the person who was carrying those ideas.”
Voters wait in line outside the Department of Elections in Detroit on Nov. 3, 2026. (Photo by Janelle D. James/Michigan Advance)
The highly contentious Senate election led to significant conversation about whether or not El-Sayed could mobilize Black voters, especially after he lost Wayne County in the primary to U.S. Rep. Haley Stevens. 
But Stevens herself turned off many Black voters just days before the midterms when she went with Rogers to the Perfecting Church in Detroit to announce her endorsement of his Senate campaign, despite having previously endorsed El-Sayed, a move that Ramsey said led some members of that church to feel “used.”
“When you talk about specifically anti-Blackness, you brought someone to a place of Black power whose entire career was based on diminishing Black power, and that is motivating because now I know that this person is attacking me in my home, at the home base,” Johnson said about Stevens’ decision not only to make her endorsement of Rogers, but to do so in what he called “the organizing base of Black political power in this country since its inception.”
U.S. Rep. Jim Clyburn (D-South Carolina), center left, speaks during a press conference supporting U.S. Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed, center right, on Sunday, Nov. 1, 2026 at North End Church of God in Christ in Detroit, Mich. (Photo by Ben Solis/Michigan Advance)
Johnson noted historical friction between Black and Arab communities in metro Detroit — but reminded, “We’re not a monolith, and we also don’t think in such tribalistic terms.”
El-Sayed’s presence in Detroit throughout the campaign, and his background as the health director for the city and for Wayne County, was also helpful in developing his trust among Detroit’s Black voters, Ramsey said. 
“Abdul has worked in Detroit. He has worked around Black people. He has worked with Black people, and he understands,” she explained. “Abdul has worked in Detroit to decrease the health inequalities in Detroit. I mean, getting little kids glasses that were considered problematic in school. So there can be race problems between groups, but I don’t think with Abdul it was as bad as they thought.”
Tameka Ramsey
Johnson also highlighted another candidate who he said did a good job engaging with Black voters in his own district, Rep.-elect Will Lawrence, whose district includes Lansing and East Lansing as well as more rural areas including in Eaton, Livingston and Shiawassee counties.
“A lot of the failure that I saw from candidates was based on the fact that they came into a lot of Black spaces and saying, ‘This is what I’m going to do to fix the community, and this is what Black people need.’ And you’re not a Black member of this community,” he said. “So I saw great successes with people like Will Lawrence who walked in the room and sat down and said, ‘I’m not Black. I’m here to listen. Tell me what’s going on and how we should be trying to help this community,’ because again, the Black community is not a monolith.”
Considering all of that, the lesson that Butler said she believes candidates in 2028 — including those running for president — must learn is that the results that they are able to deliver in the next two years are crucially important in convincing voters.
“If you want to get reelected, you better show us and be able to show us that you have passed policy that has made life in the Black community better. We need tangible, real things that we can talk about. We don’t need anything esoteric or theoretical,” she said. “If you want to win in 2028, you better start showing us in 2026 and 2027. And I think too, it needs to be early conversations with African Americans to truly listen to what they’re saying and put into action in real time. Don’t wait until three months before the election.”
Both Butler and Ramsey also noted that those tangible impacts in the next two years must be long-term positive changes in the Black community — “policies that are going to impact us generationally,” Butler described, such as promoting policies that allow small Black-owned businesses to thrive. 
And for any candidate seeking office in Michigan going forward, Johnson said that he believes that “the Black voter in Michigan is and has always been a game changer.”
“I think it is now a much more activated base, and it has to be recognized by any politician, any political party, anyone who’s seeking office and seeking to represent this state at any level, they’re going to have to speak directly to the issues facing the community,” he said.

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Commentary: Amidst election noise, some good news for the First Amendment
description: Slammed with unprecedented advertising and mudslinging, Ohioans across the political spectrum were relieved that the midterm election is over.  Spending in Ohio’s U.S. Senate race topped half a billion dollars and many experts have described the Ohio governor’s race as among the ugliest nationwide. But amidst the election noise, there was a bit of good news [...]
text:
First Amendment of the US Constitution. (Stock photo Getty Images)Slammed with unprecedented advertising and mudslinging, Ohioans across the political spectrum were relieved that the midterm election is over. 
Spending in Ohio’s U.S. Senate race topped half a billion dollars and many experts have described the Ohio governor’s race as among the ugliest nationwide.
But amidst the election noise, there was a bit of good news for the First Amendment right of free speech that undergirds our Republic in times of stress.
On the Saturday before the Nov. 3 election, a federal judge dismissed President Trump’s defamation lawsuit against The Wall Street Journal.
Importantly, the court’s decision affirmed a landmark U.S. Supreme Court ruling that protects freedom of the press and safeguards against public officials abusing libel and defamation claims to chill robust debate.
U.S. District Court Judge Darrin P. Gayles cited the legal standard established in New York Times v. Sullivan in 1964. The unanimous Sullivan ruling was intended to prevent public officials from using libel lawsuits as weapons to bankrupt the press and stifle criticism of public officials.
To prevail in libel claims, the Sullivan case said, public officials must prove that the press published false stories with “actual malice,” that is, reckless disregard for the truth. 
In the Trump v. Dow Jones case, the court said Trump failed to meet that standard, granting the Wall Street Journal’s motion to dismiss. 
Background
President Trump was displeased when the Wall Street Journal published articles linking him to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein, specifically a birthday greeting when Epstein turned 50.
Trump denied writing the letter, calling it “a fake thing.”
In dismissing Trump’s lawsuit, the judge said, “In effect, President Trump argues that once he declared the letter a ‘fake,’ Defendants should have disregarded everything else they learned in their investigation and not published the story.”
“But that is not what the actual malice standard requires and runs afoul of the First Amendment,” Gayles said. “Indeed, were that the law, any time a public figure or his team denies an accusation, journalists would be immediately blocked from publishing negative or contradictory press…”
Well said.
As the president continues to attack the press, insults journalists who question him, and sues media, we should remember the history of the Sullivan ruling more than 60 years ago. In Alabama, a police commissioner named L.B. Sullivan sued The New York Times because an ad criticized law enforcement’s brutal treatment of civil rights protesters. 
Sullivan’s libel claim was part of a pattern of exploiting libel law to harm the press and silence criticism. The U.S. Supreme Court ruled against Sullivan, saying that public officials should be held to a strict standard to win libel claims and that robust debate is a bedrock of American freedom.
America is not perfect and neither are its public officials. But the First Amendment right to question and to debate has served our nation well and the Sullivan ruling is a safeguard that buttresses that freedom.

name: Georgia Recorder
title: Democratic wins revive Medicaid expansion push in Georgia, but new hurdles await
description: Three days after Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s seat, Ryan Loke faced a crowd of Georgia health advocates, some giddy at the possibility of the state finally expanding Medicaid. Loke understood. In 2019, as health policy adviser to newly elected Gov. Brian Kemp, Loke had helped form the Georgia Pathways to Coverage program and […]
text:
Governor-elect Keisha Lance Bottoms speaks at the state Capitol about her transition into office on Nov. 6, 2026. Ross Williams/Georgia RecorderThree days after Keisha Lance Bottoms won the governor’s seat, Ryan Loke faced a crowd of Georgia health advocates, some giddy at the possibility of the state finally expanding Medicaid. Loke understood. In 2019, as health policy adviser to newly elected Gov. Brian Kemp, Loke had helped form the Georgia Pathways to Coverage program and knew its struggles well. He has long been a convert to full expansion.
Ryan Loke, senior vice president and chief health policy officer at Grady Health System, speaks at a gathering of the Atlanta Regional Collaborative for Health Improvement on Nov. 6, 2026. (Photo courtesy of ARCHI)
“I’m fully confident that the General Assembly is going to expand Medicaid in the 2027 session. Like, 100% confident,” Loke told the crowd. “No matter the Senate makeup, House makeup” – his words then drowned out by applause.
But he was actually delivering a warning.
“Medicaid expansion in this state under the provisions of H.R. 1 as it’s in effect right now – versus as if H.R. 1 were not in effect?” he said. “Massively different scenarios.”
Loke was referring to President Donald Trump’s One Big, Beautiful Bill law passed last summer that is packed with nearly $1 trillion in Medicaid cuts in the coming years. And knowing the issue intimately, now from inside the system as a senior vice president and chief health policy officer at Grady Health System, Loke wanted the people in the audience to know there was still more to do to make Medicaid expansion work. The coverage of large numbers of Georgians could depend on it.
A system ‘built on Windows 97′
If nothing changes to simplify eligibility on the federal level, Georgians who are eligible for Medicaid expansion will continue to fall through cracks in the state’s bureaucracy, said Jen Wagner, director of Medicaid eligibility and enrollment at the Washington-based Center on Budget and Policy Priorities.  
Wagner’s organization this year released a study using 2024 data, and it suggested that 347,000 uninsured Georgians might be eligible for insurance under full Medicaid expansion – but that doesn’t include those who would be culled by the work requirements, much less those who could meet them but can’t make it through the state’s rickety, glitch-prone, understaffed Medicaid enrollment system.

“To get closer to that number of eligible people, there’s a number of changes that Georgia would need to make, in making their application more friendly, their online system more accessible, their verification processes – and all of those things,” Wagner said.
“The Medicaid eligibility system in this state is built on Windows 97,” Loke said. “It takes 45 to 60 clicks to get somebody enrolled. I can buy a Tesla in the next five minutes and have it delivered to my house tomorrow quicker than I can get somebody enrolled in Medicaid. 
“We have to address that,” he added.
At this point, changing the work requirements – and the accompanying twice-a-year paperwork reporting that will be required by federal law – would take a change in the law and rules from Congress and the Trump administration. And fixing Georgia’s computer system would take an investment of state money.  
U.S. Sen. Raphael Warnock, a Democrat, is among those pushing to postpone the start of new federal Medicaid work requirements.  Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
Moreover, the One Big, Beautiful Bill Act cuts Medicaid in yet another way that discourages Medicaid expansion, reducing a particular funding stream for hospitals in states that expand.
In Washington, where Democrats now are set to control both the U.S. House and Senate, Sen. Raphael Warnock, a Georgia Democrat, has joined others in pushing for a two-year delay of the work reporting requirements.
“No state that has attempted work reporting requirements in Medicaid has ever meaningfully increased workforce participation. Instead, every state that has done so has either seen or predicted significant coverage loss for people who continue to be eligible for Medicaid but lose coverage because they can’t navigate all the red tape,” their letter read.
The politics
Last week’s Democratic wins are driving the conversation. Democrats such as Bottoms have long held full insurance for the poor and low-income as a goal. They now will take the governor’s seat and the Georgia House of Representatives too. But Republicans still hold the state Senate, so they hold some cards.
Patient advocacy groups like some of those that were in the room where Loke spoke Friday are working, researching and talking in a frenzy to put together a coherent recommendation to Democratic leaders on what will have the most impact.
There’s still a big reward for states that expand Medicaid under the Affordable Care Act: The federal government pays 90% of the cost. That’s a big carrot worth billions of dollars to Georgia, which normally has to pay one-third of the cost. And when more people are covered, struggling hospitals are more likely to stay afloat.
But there are now sticks for hospitals alongside that carrot. 
There’s that Medicaid funding stream for hospitals that will decrease after a state expands Medicaid. It will decrease for all states, but it will decrease slightly more for states that expand.
In addition, hospitals will have to take a lower fee for treating patients who got Medicaid through the expansion than if those patients were on Affordable Care Act plans. And there’s a huge group of patients – perhaps 500,000, hospital advocates say – who are currently insured on the ACA exchange but could have to switch to Medicaid if the state expanded Medicaid.
For those patients, getting Medicaid may be an improvement, studies show. But for the hospitals that treat them and lose the private insurance money, it may not be.
Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin, the lieutenant governor-elect, and Senate Minority Leader Harold Jones answer questions at a press conference at the state Capitol in Atlanta on Nov. 4, 2026. Republicans have a two-seat majority in the state Senate. Alander Rocha/Georgia Recorder
The Georgia Hospital Association has a powerpoint on the new complexities of Medicaid expansion. It doesn’t take a position on expansion; it says there would be “gains” and “losses.”  It also says there may be a third option. Or more.
“I’m very much looking forward to hearing what our hospital community and advocates are coming up with,” said Sandy Springs Democratic state Sen. Josh McLaurin, the incoming lieutenant governor.
Those calculations can shake out differently for different hospitals. If a hospital will lose more money through those federal funding cuts than it will gain for newly insured patients, is it worth it for them? In fact, does the new federal law pit patients against hospitals in that situation?
Georgia Hospital Association CEO Caylee Noggle acknowledged the issue but hopes to help negotiate changes. 
“My goal is to remain a partner at the table to find a solution where that’s not even an issue,” she said.
When it comes down to the Senate, the Georgia Recorder reached out to a handful of Georgia senators. None of them wrote off the idea of the Senate passing Medicaid expansion. 
“My answer is, ‘I don’t know,’” said Sen. Kay Kirkpatrick, a Marietta Republican and a physician who serves among Senate majority leaders as the Republican caucus secretary.
Sen. Russ Goodman speaks to the state Senate during the 2024 legislative session. Ross Williams/Georgia Recorder
Senate President Pro Tem Larry Walker referred questions to his press team, but didn’t say no.
Sen. Russ Goodman, a Cogdell Republican who is one of the senators who has signed on to support Medicaid expansion before, said he was listening. “You can’t commit to anything until you see it,” Goodman said. “I’d be a fool to do that. But I mean, I’ve been open to the idea all along.”
The Georgia Republican Party’s new post-election playbook, however, says part of their strategy going forward will be to focus on two sticking points: “negotiate any wider coverage on Georgia terms: work requirements and private plans.”
The patient
Michael Cortes, a lobbyist in Georgia for the American Cancer Society Cancer Action Network, said to remember what’s at stake. 
“Having access to quality health insurance is a top predictor of whether or not someone will survive their cancer,” Cortes said. 
That applies, he said, to not just through fancy treatments but through regular screenings that find cancers early.  
“We want everyone to be able to have access to those colonoscopies or breast cancer screenings and what have you,” Cortes said. 
He’s not a fan of work requirements but will take what he can get.
“The overriding emotion from Tuesday is hope,” Cortes said, referring to the midterm election results. “We’re feeling hopeful that over 300,000 Georgians are going to have a real chance for their concerns to be heard in the Legislature this upcoming year. 
“We’ve been working on this for years with both parties, and I think we’re looking forward to having those serious discussions again now with new leaders in the state.”

name: Ohio Capital Journal
title: Ohio Republican speaker considering reforms to executive offices before Democrats take over
description: Lawmakers are hurrying to pass their bills before the end of the year, but House leadership has been focusing on the balance of power in the capital. The lame duck period, in between a major election and the end of the legislative term, is when lawmakers make a mad dash to get policy passed. But […]
text:
Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, R-Lima. (Photo by Graham Stokes for Ohio Capital Journal. Republish photo only with original article.)Lawmakers are hurrying to pass their bills before the end of the year, but House leadership has been focusing on the balance of power in the capital.
The lame duck period, in between a major election and the end of the legislative term, is when lawmakers make a mad dash to get policy passed. But the Republicans in leadership are not being super clear about their priorities.
“I struggle to think about what exactly those things are,” Ohio House Speaker Matt Huffman, R-Lima, said. “But, you know, it’s going to appear.”
What Huffman is focused on is the election results and how to move forward.
As change approaches for the governor’s office, the General Assembly faces changes as well. Democrats flipped about a dozen legislative seats, breaking the Republican supermajority in the Ohio House. The GOP can no longer override a governor’s veto.
“I think the people spoke pretty clearly last week that they want a government that actually works on their behalf, a government that works for the people, not the other way around,” House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn, D-Cincinnati, said.
Despite Isaacsohn saying that this election should shape a more bipartisan legislature, some Republicans have expressed interest in limiting the powers of the governor before Acton takes office.
“There are a number of reforms; some of them have nothing to do with a new governor, but there’s a number of those things,” Huffman said. “But we’re sort of gathering those and deciding what is constitutional.”
One proposal would expand the General Assembly’s ability to rescind state Department of Health orders, which Huffman said was a “good thought.”
Last week, Gov. Mike DeWine said he would veto any proposals limiting any member of the executive branch’s power.
When Huffman was asked if the move was a negotiating tool with the Democrats, Huffman denied that, saying that was assuming “a fact not in evidence.”


“What we’re having is discussions about how we can reform government in lame duck, not just regarding the governor,” Huffman said.
He referenced legislation that would revise the Ohio Controlling Board’s notification process.
“If you or someone else says that’s limiting executive branch power, so be it,” Huffman said.
Others, like state Rep. Ron Ferguson, R-Wintersville, have proposed more drastic options. He is introducing a resolution that would reduce the veto override threshold from 60 to 50 votes. Both Huffman and Republican Senate President Rob McColley raised concerns about it, pouring cold water on the idea.
There is growing frustration among Republicans since Huffman lost 10 seats.
“The majority of the people are upset that the sitting speaker of the House actively worked against incumbent members, and was not able to actually help members in November,” Ferguson, an avid-Huffman opponent, said.
Huffman and the Republicans’ leadership team backed Ferguson’s and state Rep. Jason Stephens’ opponents in their primaries.
Ferguson was asked who the speaker of the House should be.
“Anybody but the guy that is now,” he replied.
But Huffman wants to retain speakership, and if he promises the Democrats not to infringe on Acton, they could make a deal to support him.
“I’ll be the nominee of the majority party, and I hope to get support from the minority party also,” Huffman said.
Or, the Dems could support another candidate who is more in line with their priorities, which Isaacsohn seems open to — but refused to answer when asked.
“Our job here is to make life better for the people we represent and serve,” he said. “The legislature has not been doing that for way too long, and we have an incredible opportunity to move in that direction starting next year.”
The House speakership vote takes place next week, and all policy has to be passed by mid-December.
Follow WEWS Statehouse reporter Morgan Trau on X and Facebook.

title: Ohio House advances measure allowing firearm suppressors and short barreled rifles
description: Ohio House lawmakers approved a measure Tuesday eliminating long-standing restrictions on firearm suppressors and short-barreled rifles. Currently, gun owners who knowingly acquire either could be subject to a fifth-degree felony under state law. Ohio Senate Bill 214 alters the definition of dangerous ordnance, which comes from the federal National Firearms [...]
text:
Firearms for sale are displayed at the Centennial Gun Club in Centennial, Colo., in June 2026. (Photo by Sara Wilson/Colorado Newsline)Ohio House lawmakers approved a measure Tuesday eliminating long-standing restrictions on firearm suppressors and short-barreled rifles. Currently, gun owners who knowingly acquire either could be subject to a fifth-degree felony under state law.
Ohio Senate Bill 214 alters the definition of dangerous ordnance, which comes from the federal National Firearms Act. Under federal law it’s illegal to own dangerous ordnance like explosives and automatic rifles without registration.
But after the Trump administration eliminated the fee as part of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, a Texas judge tossed the restrictions themselves. That ruling only applied to parties in the case, and the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives chose not to appeal. The agency later issued guidance stating it would no longer enforce the rules.
The problem, Ohio gun rights advocates contend, is that Ohio’s laws reflect the previous footing, under which owning a silencer or a short-barreled rifle constitutes a fifth-degree felony. And more to the point, Grant Balzer from Gun Owners of America told committee members, the path ahead for changing Ohio’s laws suddenly looks a bit less certain.
“Upcoming changes in our state government will likely make it far more difficult to secure the attention and votes needed to advance and finalize this legislation,” he said. “If this committee does not act before the session adjourns, these essential corrections could be delayed for months, if not years.”
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.The bill passed the state Senate 31-1 but it only addressed the issue of silencers. A last-minute committee amendment Tuesday added short-barreled rifles and shotguns to the bill.
The measure passed out of committee easily, but not without objections from Ohio state Rep. Darnell Brewer, D-Cleveland. Gun violence claims hundreds of lives a year, he said, holding up a sheet of paper with the pictures of nine different people.
“There’s just one bill that you guys are trying to push, but this same vigor is not given to the bills that will help save the lives of Ohioans,” he said. “I had a young man just literally get shot steps from my house — steps from my house. And we are here today talking about this bill. We need to save lives in Ohio.”
Before the proposal made its way to the floor, Republican House Speaker Matt Huffman said given the court rulings, “I don’t think (the penalties are) legal in the state of Ohio, or at least it’s not clear enough that they are.”
House Minority Leader Dani Isaacsohn, D-Cincinnati, echoed his frustration before the measure went to the House floor, saying pushing measures like this and not priorities like affordability could be “why Republicans lost so badly last week.”
“So, what did they do one week after the people of Ohio said, ‘please do something different’? They come back with a culture war gun bill,” he said. “You have to be so out of touch, your head has to be so deep in the sand, to think that is what the people of Ohio want right now.”
Floor debate
Ohio state Reps. Tex Fischer, R-Boardman, and Kellie Deeter, R-Norwalk, co-sponsored an S.B. 214 companion bill and urged their colleagues to support the Senate proposal.
“This is a win for gun owners. This is a win for public safety advocates. This is in no way, shape, or form anything that is going to make Ohio streets less safe,” Fischer insisted.
Deeter said her district has a rich tradition of hunting and shooting sports.
“For many of my constituents, these are not abstract legal classifications,” she said. “They have practical implications for how they exercise their Second Amendment rights.”
Deeter argued suppressors don’t actually silence firearms, but by reducing sound, they can help protect gunowners’ hearing. She also criticized the way current definitions classify firearms. With a few accessories, Deeter said, a pistol can become a short-barreled rifle under federal definitions.
“Same ammunition, same firing mechanism, different legal classification,” she said.
Brewer was the only lawmaker to debate against the measure. He questioned the lawmakers’ priorities, and recited a handful of stalled bipartisan proposals aimed at improving gun safety, through education or tax breaks on safety devices.
“I am tired of watching the General Assembly find urgency for political battles while Ohio families are waiting for solutions,” he said, “Our children cannot wait.”
The proposal passed the House 68-27. Because of the changes in committee, the proposal now returns to the Ohio Senate.

title: The midterms energized a powerful political constituency: abuse survivors
description: This story was originally reported by Amanda Becker of The 19th. Meet Amanda and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy. When Leanna Rocheleau saw the ad that Ohio gubernatorial hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy created, weaponizing his opponent Dr. Amy Acton’s childhood sexual abuse, the Columbus-area mother and small business owner felt “trigger[...]
text:
Dr. Amy Acton became the first Democrat in 20 years to lead Ohio after winning the governor’s race Tuesday, Nov. 3, at a rally in Cleveland. (Photo by Nick Evans/Ohio Capital Journal)
This story was originally reported by Amanda Becker of The 19th.  Meet Amanda and read more of their reporting on gender, politics and policy.
When Leanna Rocheleau saw the ad that Ohio gubernatorial hopeful Vivek Ramaswamy created, weaponizing his opponent Dr. Amy Acton’s childhood sexual abuse, the Columbus-area mother and small business owner felt “triggered.”
Rocheleau, like nearly half of all U.S. women, is a survivor of sexual violence, and the ad hit at a gut level. In it, Acton’s long-estranged mother suggested her daughter had lied about the well-documented abuse and neglect that Acton had discussed during her campaign. Court records confirmed Acton’s account. Ramaswamy spent $4 million airing the ad anyway. Then Acton, a Democrat, won by 8 points in a state where her party hasn’t been elected to the governor’s mansion in nearly 20 years.
“I was disturbed by the ad — but also fueled to jump back into the fight,” said Rocheleau, who has become an activist at the Ohio Statehouse pushing for legislation to protect survivors.
“Being able to have a woman survivor as governor of Ohio? I have high hopes that we’re going to be able to move some of this legislation into law,” she added.
Rocheleau has been in the fight for about five years now, since her own sexual assault by a massage therapist and the series of obstacles she confronted as she sought justice. She reported the alleged assault to the owners of the facility where it occurred — nothing happened. She went to the local police department — it took them a year to take her official report. A prosecutor told her they would not bring charges due to lack of evidence. She went to the state medical board. Attorneys advised her to wait for the medical board’s findings to bring a civil lawsuit. By the time the board’s investigation concluded, the statute of limitations had run out. The massage therapist received a six-month suspension after the board’s investigation.
“I needed somewhere to put that energy and anger, so I started talking to [state] legislators about changing all of the barriers that I faced,” she said.
Rocheleau started talking about her assault during Statehouse hearings and in meetings with lawmakers, urging them to pass legislation protecting survivors. Along the way, she met Chris Graham, a survivor of childhood sexual abuse who has become a well-known advocate in the halls of the Ohio Capitol, organizing fellow survivors and coaching them on how to engage in citizen advocacy.
Graham and Rocheleau are part of a growing movement of survivors of sexual abuse and gender-based violence who are showing up at statehouses, lobbying the U.S. Congress, and coming forward to share their experiences with political candidates — and they’re getting results. Sheerine Alemzadeh, the founder of Healing to Action, a grassroots organization focused on ending gender-based violence through survivor leadership, said she thinks of the movement as “a political constituency.” She has a book on the subject out next month.
In Ohio, Ramaswamy’s ad was seen largely as a desperate attempt to regain momentum in the waning days of a losing campaign. In northern Ohio, U.S. Rep. Max Miller lost a seat that Republicans have held since World War II amid allegations of spousal abuse during a contentious divorce.
Nationally, Graham Platner, a Democratic U.S. Senate candidate in Maine, was pushed out of the race after an ex-girlfriend accused him of rape. U.S. Rep. Jimmy Gomez, a four-term Democrat in California, lost to a Democratic challenger amid a House investigation into potential sexual misconduct. In Arizona, Democrat Bernadette Greene-Placentia, who said she was raped during her House campaign, was trailing her opponent by less than 3 points on Thursday in a district Republicans won by 13 points in 2024. Survivors of the late convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein toured the country this year calling for the release of investigatory files related to the disgraced financier and urging voters to demand accountability.
In a Wednesday morning note, Liz Roberts, the chief executive of Safe Horizon, the country’s largest nonprofit services agency for survivors of abuse and violent crime, called the midterms results “a win for survivors, period.”
“We saw candidates accused of sexual assault and abuse withdraw from their campaigns, we saw candidates accused of violence lose their race. A survivor of child abuse, who speaks openly and without shame about her experiences, was called a liar by her opponent in a message backed by millions of dollars and still won. She was believed, not just by the survivor community, but by her constituents, voters, and the public across the nation,” Roberts wrote.
Graham, who was raped by a priest when he was 14, said the Ramaswamy ad was particularly disturbing because it used Acton’s mother against her. Many children who experience sexual abuse do not tell their parents due to fear or shame.
“Amy Acton faced that monster in a way that a lot of people in Ohio, and across the world right now, are thinking to themselves: ‘The plan was to never tell anybody about what happened to me but what if I did the opposite? What would that look like?’ And they’re inspired,” Graham said.
At least 1 in 4 girls and 1 in 20 boys is a survivor of childhood sexual abuse, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. The average age that adults disclose childhood sexual abuse is 52, according to CHILD USA, a national nonprofit think tank that advocates for children’s civil rights.
“There are millions of Ohioans who share this type of background, and it was not only abundantly clear in these election results but on the last leg of that campaign trail,” said Jessica Miranda, a Democratic county auditor who served three terms in the Ohio House, from 2019 to 2024.
Miranda worked with Graham on survivor-supportive legislation when she was in the Statehouse after learning that Ohio had some of the most outdated laws related to protecting survivors. In the process of that work, she ended up telling her own story of surviving childhood sexual abuse by an older relative, then being raped when she was 15.
“Being a powerful storyteller is oftentimes what moves the needle in terms of policy change,” Miranda said of sharing her experiences.
During her time in the legislature, Miranda co-sponsored a bill 25 years in the making that banned all forms of spousal rape and another that suspended the statute of limitations for former Boy Scouts to seek civil damages for their abuse in a multi-billion dollar bankruptcy. Both were bipartisan, and signed into law by Republican Gov. Mike DeWine. She also identified a loophole in a Republican bill that created a new misdemeanor criminal charge for sexually grooming a child. “There are certain ramifications of policies that [survivors] will consider more than anyone who hasn’t had this type of experience,” she said.
Next up, Graham said, is legislation to address the broader issue of statutes of limitations on childhood sexual abuse — Ohio is one of just six states where survivors face a deadline to pursue criminal charges and lawsuits. The bicameral bipartisan bill from state Sen. Bill Blessing, a Republican, and state Rep. Rachel Baker, a Democrat, could drop as early as this week.
And now, a survivor governor could be signing it.
“Amy’s nightmare became her origin story, every hero has got one,” Graham said.

text:
The Ohio burgee waving along with the national flag of the United States of America. (Stock photo from Getty Images.)Every morning in the Ohio Capital Journal’s free newsletter, The Eye-Opener, we round up the news and commentary from across Ohio and around the country and world that is catching our attention. We call this feature Catching Our Eye, republished here.
Please subscribe to our free daily newsletter to get all the Ohio news you need to know right to your inbox every weekday morning.
If you already subscribe, please share with your family and friends so they know about the Ohio Capital Journal too: https://ohiocapitaljournal.com/subscribe/

 Catching Our Eye

• The salt mines. Ideastream’s Sofia Helena Dambros da Silva is reporting, “Could water intrusion destabilize Fairport Harbor’s salt mine? Geologist explains the risks.”
Water entering Morton Salt’s Fairport Harbor mine could weaken its underground structural support, according to an expert.
Morton Salt announced on Oct. 26 that it was ceasing operations at its Fairport Harbor salt mine after discovering a significant inflow of water Oct. 22. All employees were safely evacuated, according to Morton.
Two days later, the company informed the state of Ohio of its plans to lay off 77 workers at the Fairport Harbor location.
• Capital punishment. The Springfield News-Sun’s Jen Balduf is reporting, “Ohio prosecutors oppose DeWine’s efforts to commute death sentences.”
The Ohio Prosecuting Attorneys Association has denounced apparent plans by Gov. Mike DeWine to commute multiple death sentences in the final days of his administration.
“Using the executive clemency process this way completely undermines the decisions of the prosecutors who brought these cases, the juries who sat and listened to horrific facts, considered the evidence and voted to recommend a death sentence, and the judges who imposed these sentences,” Warren County Prosecutor David Fornshell, president of the association, said in a release issued Monday, Nov. 9. “Even worse is the renewed pain that this is going to cause the families of these victims and over the holidays to boot. It is just wrong for him to do this on his way out the door with zero accountability to the communities and families that it affects.
• Data centers. WTOL’s Anna Miller is reporting, “‘They were very happy to sign’: Rossford petition targets data center size.”
A petition that could eventually give Rossford voters a say on future data center development has been submitted to the city.
The petition, backed by Conserve Ohio, was turned in Monday and proposes a charter amendment related to future data center projects in Rossford.
The effort comes just weeks after news that a Florida company is seeking approval to build a data center in Rossford.

name: Maryland Matters
title: The author Wes Moore: Book on ‘healing a divided nation’ set for March release
description: For a guy who refuses to say he won't run for president in two years, Gov. Wes Moore sure seems to be checking all the right boxes. Traveling the country, making national media appearances and, now, publishing a book about how to heal a divided nation.
text:
Gov. Wes Moore (D) will release a new book in March. He joins a number of other Democrats listed as potential candidates for President in 2028 who have also released books. (File photo Bryan P. Sears/Maryland Matters)Fresh off a second thumping of Republican Dan Cox to win reelection to a second term as governor a week ago, Gov. Wes Moore (D) turned his attention this week to fixing the nation.
At least that’s the thrust of the book he touted Wednesday, “Repair: Healing A Divided Nation.” Scheduled for a March 2027 release, Moore’s book is billed “as a bold interrogation of where America falls short, what we still do right, and how we can fix our broken systems together,” he said in a statement from his publisher.
For a guy who refuses to say he won’t run for president in two years, Moore sure seems to be checking all the right boxes — just in case.
In the announcement from publisher Henry Holt & Co., Moore describes his latest book as “an invitation … into a broader conversation about what makes our country great, where we’ve fallen short, and how we build a better future, together.”
He said the book will tell the stories of “what happens when good people do hard things, even in the face of unimaginable odds.”
Gov. Wes Moore rolls to easy reelection win in rematch with Republican challenger Dan Cox

Moore, who became the first Black governor of Maryland when he was elected in 2022, said those stories will be interspersed with “memories of service from my life inside and outside of politics.” But the book, he said, is not a “personal political memoir.”
Moore has been coy about his plans and if they include a 2028 presidential run. Even so, Moore has spent a great deal of time in his first term traveling the country fundraising and building political relationships as well as being a regular on national news programs.
Moore’s latest release joins those of other Democrats mentioned as potential 2028 presidential candidates: Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear’s “Go and Do Likewise: How We Heal a Broken Country”: Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro’s “Where We Keep the Light: Stories from a Life of Service”: and “Young Man in a Hurry: A Memoir of Discovery,”
by California Gov. Gavin Newsom, among others. All three were published this year.
This is not Moore’s first book. He has written a number of others including the New York Times bestseller, “The Other Wes Moore,” as well as “Five Days” and “The Work.”
And Moore is not the only Maryland governor to write a book.
Larry Hogan released his book — “Still Standing” — in 2020. It was two years into his second term in office (the first for a Republican governor since Theodore McKeldin). It also came at a time when he was teasing the possibility of a run for president.
Martin O’Malley, a Democrat who also had presidential aspirations, published a book after he left office focused on governing in the information age. Robert Ehrlich, who became the first Republican since Spiro Agnew to be elected governor, has written more than a half dozen books. Most recently, “Trump 2.0: Revolution, Redemption, Revival” in 2025.
In addition to O’Malley and Hogan, another Maryland politician with presidential aspirations got briefly into the publishing business. Former Rep. John Delaney (D-6th) released “The Right Answer: How We Can Divide Our Divided Nation” in 2018, a year after he announced his 2020 presidential campaign, which subsequently fizzzled.
Moore said his new book is meant “to pose hard questions and spark honest dialogue. This book is about how we can rediscover our common humanity and relearn our common purpose. I offer my thoughts, with an invitation for readers to lend theirs. In the work of repair, every fingerprint matters.”
