name: Connecticut Mirror
title: Matt Ritter won’t seek UConn presidency; to remain House speaker
description: House Speaker Matt Ritter said he will remain in his legislative post and hinted that Radenka Maric will continue as UConn's president.
text:
House Speaker Matt Ritter announced Wednesday he will remain in his legislative leadership post for a fourth term.
And the speaker, who had been weighing a stint as the University of Connecticut’s interim president, strongly hinted that UConn President Radenka Maric’s contract with the state’s flagship university would be extended beyond next June.
“My understanding is there won’t be a vacancy, so there’s nothing to consider,” Ritter told The Connecticut Mirror Wednesday evening.
The Hartford Democrat, who has held the top post in the state House of Representatives for the past six years, is expected to be reelected unanimously as speaker for another two years when the regular 2027 session convenes Jan. 6. Democrats captured 116 out of 151 seats in the chamber during last week’s elections.
“There’s a bit of relief, because I really wanted a fourth term,” Ritter said, adding that “I love UConn and really wish everybody all the best over there.”
The speaker confirmed in late October that he was considering taking UConn’s interim presidency if the post became vacant next year. Maric’s contract expires next June 30, and The Hartford Courant reported last week that she was a finalist to become chancellor of the University of Wisconsin’s main campus in Madison and was under consideration for posts at two other universities.
A UConn spokesman confirmed Wednesday only that Maric remains UConn’s president but did not discuss any possible moves.
Any extension of Maric’s contract at UConn would have to be approved by its Board of Trustees. But Gov. Ned Lamont controls most appointments to that group, and any top leadership decision would be made in consultation with his office.
“The governor has had a great relationship with President Maric, who has accomplished a lot for the university,” Lamont’s communications director, Cathryn Vaulman, said Wednesday.
And though she did not discuss Maric’s future, Vaulman added that “the governor trusts the Board of Trustees to make a decision in the best interest of the university as they fulfill their duties.”
Meanwhile, Ritter said he looks forward to tackling the many important issues awaiting Connecticut’s next legislature.
Lawmakers and Lamont are expected to overhaul the system of budget caps that have dominated state finances over the past decade. These controls have helped officials eliminate $11 billion in pension debt. But many legislators say it is time for Connecticut to invest more in affordable childcare, health, education and property tax relief.
“I’m excited for the opportunity to lead the largest House Democratic Caucus in a generation,” Ritter said. “It remains my dream job.”
CT Mirror reporter Theo Peck-Suzuki contributed to this story.

name: Mississippi Today
title: Colom wins: Mississippi picks another senator
description: Democratic U.S. Senate candidate Scott Colom speaks to supporters on election night in Jackson on Tuesday, Nov. 3, 2026.
text:
Audio articles are automated for accessibility. Humans wrote and edited the story; however, this audio has not been reviewed for accuracy and may contain errors. Read more about how we use AI to increase access to our reporting.
Democrat Scott Colom has won a hard-fought U.S. Senate race in Mississippi, breaking Republicans’ dominance of statewide offices, ousting one of the state’s sitting senators for the first time since the 1940s and becoming the state’s first Black senator since Reconstruction.
Colom, a district attorney in north Mississippi, defeated Republican Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith and independent Ty Pinkins. Colom on Wednesday secured a come-from-behind triumph that has stunned pollsters, pundits and forecasters across the nation. Hyde-Smith has held the Senate seat since 2018. Mississippi has elected only Republican senators for the last 40 years.
The Democratic victory is an extraordinary upset in a state that President Donald Trump won by 23 points two years ago, and where Republicans have long maintained a stranglehold on state government and every statewide elected office. 
A source close to the Colom campaign said the Hyde-Smith had called him to concede on Wednesday evening. She also released a video on Wednesday night conceding the race and thanking her supporters. 


“While this is not the outcome we worked for or hoped for, I respect the decision of Mississippi voters,” Hyde-Smith said. “I want to congratulate Scott Colom and wish him well as he takes on the tremendous responsibility of representing our great state.” 
RESULTS: Mississippi 2026 midterm election results
Democratic leaders see Colom’s victory as a stinging rebuke of the Republican Party’s agenda under Trump, who visited the state in the election’s closing days and pleaded with voters to send Hyde-Smith back to the Senate to help advance his agenda.  
The Associated Press called the race with 99% of precincts reporting. Colom led 49.2% to Hyde-Smith’s 48.7%. He led Wednesday night by 4,645 votes. The AP called the race for Colom based on uncertified results. 
Colom will now be the 55th Democratic senator to join the chamber, with Alaska’s Senate election still too close to call. 
Colom’s long-awaited win caps more than a week of the nation waiting on Mississippi’s county election officials processing by hand thousands of affidavit ballots to determine the winner.

Credit: Vickie D. King/Mississippi Today
Colom, 43, will be the first Democrat elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since John Stennis in 1982. He is also the first Black person elected to the U.S. Senate from Mississippi since Reconstruction, when the state Legislature elected Hiram Revels in 1870 and Blanche Bruce in 1875. He is also the first Black person elected to any type of statewide office since Reconstruction. 
When asked about possibly becoming the first Black man in more than a century to win a U.S. Senate race in the state, Colom said he only wants to make sure he won’t “be the last.” 
Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith speaks during President Donald Trump’s rally at the Crossroads Arena in Corinth on Monday, Oct. 26, 2026. Credit: Eric Shelton/Mississippi Today
“I don’t want anybody to say that I did anything to hurt the next person that has the talent, the work ethic, the ability to be able to reach for their dreams,” Colom said. “That’s my focus.” 
Most forecasters rated the Mississippi Senate race as safe Republican. But on the issues defining the midterms, voters left little doubt the elections would be a referendum on soaring consumer prices exacerbated by tariffs and the president’s unpopular war in Iran.
A crowd watches as the Hinds County Election Commission finalizes the vote tally for Mississippi’s midterm election between Scott Colom and Cindy Hyde-Smith.
Colom believed his strategy of tying Hyde-Smith to the high cost of gasoline and consumer prices would be enough to pierce the Republicans’ dominance in the Magnolia State. He began to pick up steam rapidly in the campaign’s closing weeks, receiving endorsements and resources from national Democrats. 
Colom traversed the state from end to end and, in the election’s homestretch, engaged in a near-nonstop media blitz aimed at galvanizing any voters tuned into traditional cable news shows or following the race on social media.
In one viral ad, he mocked Hyde-Smith for suggesting voters upset over the rising price of beef should “pick another protein,” with Colom supporters saying they’d rather pick another senator. Another ad riffed off the Oscar-winning movie “Sinners,” which is set in Mississippi and his final ad before the election featured the home of slain civil rights hero Medgar Evers.
Colom mobilized the Democratic base through energetic rallies and appearances with high-profile national Democrats. He also tried to persuade skeptical Republicans. In one 24-hour span just over a week before Election Day, Colom roamed the line outside a Trump rally for Hyde-Smith in northeast Mississippi, spoke to some of the president’s supporters, then headed to the other end of the state for a rally with former U.S. Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg.
Dan Pffeifer, a political commentator and former senior adviser to President Barack Obama, said Colom “has run a campaign that is a model for Dems trying to flip very red states.”
And his strategy worked. Colom managed to crack the GOP’s iron grip on the state by turning out large numbers of Black voters, flipping several crucial swing counties blue and convincing Republicans to cross over and vote for him.
The most surprising feat was Colom winning DeSoto County, a reliably Republican stronghold in a Memphis suburb, by seven percentage points, something Democrats would have viewed as unthinkable last year. 
Colom also tempered his losses in Harrison County, a populous coastal county that has swamped statewide Democratic candidates over the last decade and become a red firewall for the state GOP.  He also flipped Lafayette and Madison counties, two majority-white, affluent areas of the state that have become swing areas in recent elections. 
As Colom’s profile rose and Democratic enthusiasm spiked, Hyde-Smith struggled to keep up. She refused to debate Colom or hold open town-hall forums for constituents. She rarely spoke to reporters for longer than a few minutes, often with great hesitation. In the U.S. Capitol, Hyde-Smith avoids hallway interviews that are customary for most members of Congress, and that standoffishness produced awkward encounters that gave Colom ammunition.
Democratic aligned super PACs, such as American Bridge 21st Century, saw an opportunity and injected millions of dollars into the race, claiming Hyde-Smith is “one of the most hated GOP senators in Congress.”
In a joint statement, Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer and Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee Chair Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand said Colom’s victory was historic and vowed to work with him “to fight for Mississippians’ health care, costs, and future in the 120th Congress.”
“Scott is a seventh-generation Mississippian, proud husband and father of two, and District Attorney who has dedicated his life to keeping communities safe,” Schumer and Gillibrand said. “He has never stopped fighting for his neighbors, because Mississippi Matters – and he’ll continue to be a champion for Mississippi in Washington.”
For many pioneering Black officials in Mississippi, Colom’s victory is the culmination of decades of organizing, campaigning and civil rights activism. It’s a moment that many never thought they would see in their lifetimes.
Mike Espy, the first Black person to represent Mississippi in the U.S. House since Reconstruction and the first Black person to become U.S. agriculture secretary, unsuccessfully ran against Hyde-Smith twice. 
The former cabinet secretary served as an advisor to Colom, handed over his donor and voter lists to the campaign and hoped his losses “paved the road” for the soon-to-be senator, he told Mississippi Today in an interview. 
“There is a time and place for everything,” Espy said. “This is Scott Colom’s time, and his place is in the U.S. Senate. I’m so pleased with the way he ran his campaign, and I was happy to support him.”
For Colom’s supporters, his victory brought a sense of poetic justice. Then-President Joe Biden in 2022 nominated Colom to a federal judgeship in northern Mississippi. A bipartisan coalition of Mississippi officials supported the nomination, but Hyde-Smith used her home-state “blue slip” privilege to oppose it.
Had Hyde-Smith not blocked Colom’s nomination, he likely would have served on the federal judiciary for the rest of his life and never run for the Senate.
But Colom decided to run and cast her as an out-of-touch politician who doesn’t represent Mississippi’s values. Hyde-Smith’s campaign called him a puppet of far-left national Democrats, with a spokesman calling Colom a stooge of Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer and to billionaire donor George Soros.
Hyde-Smith, a Brookhaven cattle farmer, was first appointed to the Senate in early 2018 by then-Gov. Phil Bryant to succeed longtime Republican Sen. Thad Cochran, who retired about halfway into the six-year term. She won two races against Espy, a special election in late 2018 to fill the end of the term Cochran started and a regular election in 2020, and hoped she would gain a third victory.
Hyde-Smith left little doubt that she hoped to stymie Colom’s future as a judge. But in the end, her decision to block him from the federal judiciary cost her a seat in the Senate.

name: Source New Mexico
title: New Mexico energy affordability council recommends 22 ratepayer protection, clean energy measures
description: As developers for energy-hungry projects such as data centers and advanced manufacturing hubs seek to build in New Mexico, the state’s utilities will face challenges in shielding ratepayers from increased costs and hitting the state’s clean energy goals, according to a new report.
text:
Power lines at the Algodones Electric Generating Station between Rio Rancho and Santa Fe. (Photo by Danielle Prokop for Source NM)As developers for energy-hungry projects such as data centers and advanced manufacturing hubs seek to build in New Mexico, the state’s utilities will face challenges in shielding ratepayers from increased costs and hitting the state’s clean energy goals, according to a new report.SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
The report, which Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham’s Energy Affordability and Grid Reliability Council announced on Tuesday, recommends 22 measures state leaders can take to protect residents from increased costs and boost grid reliability while meeting those clean energy goals.
Lujan Grisham established the 13-member Energy Affordability and Grid Reliability Council, which includes state cabinet secretaries, power company executives and energy experts, via executive order in April. She charged them with producing recommendations that could guide the Legislature’s work during the upcoming session that begins in January.
The report cites the contrast between the growing demand for New Mexico’s energy — particularly from data centers, advanced manufacturing facilities and increasingly electrified oil and gas operations — and the state’s goals of adopting carbon-free energy resources as the underlying challenges its recommendations seek to address.
Its 22 recommendations fit into four main categories: ratepayer protection; grid modernization and reliability; clean energy progress; and permitting efficiency.
Specifically, it recommends that the Legislature adopt legislation focused on large-scale development guardrails and ratepayer protections. It also recommends that the Public Regulation Commission support battery storage projects and that lawmakers expand the types of carbon-free energy sources utilities can use to comply with the state’s Energy Transition Act. And it recommends that the governor’s office establish a state-level infrastructure permitting council to streamline coordination among the various state agencies that issue permits for new developments.
“The future of energy is already here, and once again New Mexico is ready to lead,” Lujan Grisham said in a statement. “These recommendations give us a path to protect ratepayers, bring more power onto the grid and keep our energy clean, all at the same time.”
Don Tarry, president and CEO of PNM’s parent company, TXNM Energy Inc., who served as vice chair of the report’s council, in a statement said that “meeting growing demand requires careful planning and prudent investment.”
PNM is seeking to be acquired by private equity firm Blackstone Infrastructure. While the takeover has hit several speed bumps, including one in which state regulators deemed a financial transaction between the two parties to be illegal, Tarry and other PNM leaders have long maintained that a firm like Blackstone would give the utility the cash it needs for much-needed modernization.
During interim legislative committee hearings this year, lawmakers have often grappled with how to bolster New Mexico’s aging power grid. Protecting ratepayers has also been a key focus for utility regulators amid allegations that the state’s largest electric utility significantly overbilled rural customers during a meter reader shortage.
The report’s recommendations come as Lujan Grisham, who is term-limited, is set to leave office at the end of the year. Gov.-elect Deb Haaland, a fellow Democrat, will preside over the 2027 legislative session and has pledged to sign a statewide data center moratorium immediately upon taking office so lawmakers can craft bills with guardrails for the energy-intensive developments.
State Rep. Meredith Dixon (D-Albuquerque), who sat on the 13-member council, in a statement said the report gives lawmakers “a practical starting point” for the upcoming session.
“Families and small businesses need electricity they can afford and depend on,” she said.

name: VTDigger
title: ‘In memory of the greatest generation’: Rutland unveils new WWII memorial
description:
“The names on this memorial remind us that freedom is not free,” said the chaplain of Rutland’s Veterans of Foreign Wars chapter.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  ‘In memory of the greatest generation’: Rutland unveils new WWII memorial.
text:
World War II vet Bud Taggert kisses the hand of fellow vet Marion Wright during an unveiling of a WWII memorial in Rutland on Veterans Day, Wednesday, November 11, 2026. Photo by Glenn Russell/VTDigger
RUTLAND — A towering, tangible reminder of what one generation gave for the generations to come now stands in the city.  
Main Street Park hosted more than 300 neighbors, government officials, military service members and veterans Wednesday for the unveiling of a 10-foot granite monument honoring local World War II service members. 
The monument bears the names of 164 service members from Rutland County who died in the war, beneath an inscription reading “In memory of the greatest generation.”
“I feel the service of the World War II veterans that we recognize today, those that lost their lives, those that came back. We owe a dedication of our lives,” Rutland Mayor Tom Donahue said during the Veterans Day event. “My wife and I have five kids and 13 grandkids, all of them here in Rutland, and all of them free, and that is a testament to what this generation did for us.”
Donahue wore a World War II military uniform jacket that belonged to his father, who served in the war from 1942 to 1945. “I feel like he’s here with me right now,” Donahue said. 
The event was full of both solemn and hopeful remembrance. Several speakers noted veterans’ commitment to freedom, including Rutland High School student Ava Gallo. Gallo presented a biography of John “Jack” Hawkins, whom she profiled as part of a George Washington University program in which 15 high school students across the country learn about D-Day. The program culminates in trips to Washington, D.C., and Normandy in France. 
Hawkins, of Bomoseen, enlisted in the Army in 1943. He was killed in action 17 months later.  
“Jack was not just a soldier. He was a son, a student, an athlete, a writer and a young man with a promising future of living,” Gallo said. “His story reminds us that behind every casualty statistic is a real person with dreams, relationships and goals.”
Many Vermonters enlisted for the war from Rutland. That tally is 16,492 men and women, according to Ron Fredette, commander of the Rutland American Legion, who has and reviews documents from the era. One of those who enlisted was Gov. Phil Scott’s father, who lost both of his legs in service.
“It’s hard to put into words the amount of people that are here to honor our veterans, to have this memorial here to honor the World War II veterans,” Scott said in an interview after the event. “It’s especially important to me.”
During his remarks to the crowd, Scott spoke directly to World War II veteran Buddy Taggart, who was honored by President Donald Trump at this year’s State of the Union address for his role in liberating a Japanese internment camp in the Philippines. “You set an example for us that we should all learn. We’re fortunate to have you with us. We should all listen and learn from you,” Scott said.

The sun shone on Taggart, 100, and his fellow World War II veteran Mary Wright, 103, as they removed a covering from the monument after a prayer of remembrance from Wally Pratt, chaplain of the local Veterans of Foreign Wars chapter. 
“The names on this memorial remind us that freedom is not free,” Pratt said. “These brave Rutlanders paid the ultimate price for the freedom we enjoy today.”
The crowd sang along to “America the Beautiful” as Taggart and Wright posed alongside two other veterans in front of the just-revealed memorial. 
Taggart remained humble after the event. 
“Who’d ever expect it?” he said, reflecting on his modest childhood farming, logging and attending a one-room school in Castleton on Birdseye Mountain, and the honors he’s received since enlisting at age 17, including at Wednesday’s ceremony. “Oh, it was fantastic, fantastic, super.”
The monument’s story began in July 2025, when Rutland Cemetery Commissioner Tom Giffen told the city’s Board of Aldermen that he had received a call about a lack of World War II memorials in the city park, Giffen said in an interview Tuesday. 
The park holds memorials for most major wars, he said, adding that he was shocked to find that the city had never built a World War II veterans memorial. 
The Board of Aldermen then formed a committee in August 2025, composed of Giffen and members of the local VFW and the American Legion, Giffen said. Within 14 months, the committee had designed and received the 9,000-pound statue from Buttura & Gherardi Granite Artisans, a Barre granite manufacturer. More than $45,000 was raised from community donations for the monument, a nearby flagpole and upkeep, according to Giffen. 
Wednesday’s event concluded as the American Legion Post 31’s firing team gave the rifle salute: three blank shots apiece, representing duty, honor and sacrifice. As the Sons of the Union Veterans of the Civil War Honor Guard retired the colors, bagpipers played “Amazing Grace.”
Bob Snarski, who served on Wednesday’s firing team, as well as 22 years in the Army Reserves, said he was moved by the ceremony. 
“It may be the last time you’ll have live veterans from World War II, Korea, Desert Storm, Vietnam, right up to the present, all in one place together,” he said. “That just ran chills up my spine.”
Thanked for his service, Snarski simply replied, “It’s my honor.”

name: Alaska Beacon
title: Commentary: Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act compromises Alaska Native people’s rights
description: The words “bipartisan,” “American,” “affordability” and “jobs” altogether insinuate taking care of our communities. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act does anything but that.  BAAJA, under the pretext of a permitting reform package, undermines Tribal sovereignty and the rights of Alaska Native Corporations, weakens our environmental laws [...]
text:
The U.S. Capitol on the evening of Sept. 30, 2025. (Photo by Ashley Murray/States Newsroom)The words “bipartisan,” “American,” “affordability” and “jobs” altogether insinuate taking care of our communities. But the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act does anything but that. 
BAAJA, under the pretext of a permitting reform package, undermines Tribal sovereignty and the rights of Alaska Native Corporations, weakens our environmental laws and limits the public’s ability to both provide input and challenge decision-making. The bill’s Manager Amendment does not sufficiently address these impacts. And the bill is moving through Congress fast.
BAAJA was introduced in the U.S. Senate floor as S. 5653 on September 30, 2026, just before the Senate recessed. Leaders of the Senate Committee on Energy and Natural Resources and the Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works spearheaded the bill. Despite its significant implications for the Alaska Native community and Indian Country more broadly, the bill advanced without formal review by the Senate Committee on Indian Affairs. On Saturday, November 7, the bill’s sponsors released a substitute manager’s amendment. On Monday, November 9th, the Senate’s first day back in session, the Senate voted on cloture on the motion to proceed with a substitute amendment under H.R. 2347, taking a procedural shortcut to fast-track BAAJA.
Does the Chilkat Indian Village (Klukwan) Tribal Council want to see improved permitting across our state and the country? Absolutely. But this bill strips power from the Alaska Native community and the public in exchange for fast-tracking industry projects at agencies’ discretion, handing more decision-making to outside, extractive corporations. 
We could be building pathways for streamlined permitting and community-based consent while building new workforce opportunities in environmental stewardship and meeting our communities’ needs. But in Alaska, we trade these opportunities for empty promises from burgeoning outside industries that contribute little to our communities’ workforces and livelihoods. The promise of “development” for our future does not feed the people in Alaska today. 
BAAJA will depend on approval from the Alaska delegation who has a responsibility to consider the impact of their decisions on the more than 229 Tribal Nations across the State. Division B, Title III on Historic Preservation of BAAJA strips most of the protections afforded to our Tribal Nations and Alaska Native Corporations for consultation on sacred sites and cultural properties. These sites are spread across Alaska and encompass not only specific areas, but entire territories where we have depended on food for generations and our continued stewardship of these lands and waters are providing workforces for our tribal citizens. The Alliance of Sovereign Tribes of Southeast Alaska and its 19 federally-recognized participating Tribal Nations stand together in our opposition to Title III of BAAJA. 
U.S. Senators Lisa Murkowski and Dan Sullivan occupy positions of influence they could use to protect both Tribal Nations’ inherent sovereignty and the rights of Alaska Native Corporations in striking Division B, Title III of BAAJA or voting no on the bill to allow for stronger permitting reform language to be drafted that does not compromise the rights of the Alaska Native community or the public. Both Senator Murkowski and Senator Sullivan voted yes on cloture on the motion to proceed on Monday, November 9th. We hope they will stand with us moving forward.

title: Vermont Conversation: ‘Freedom in America is never guaranteed.’ Garrett Graff on America’s many revolutions
description:
“We are a country that gets better,” said Vermont historian and journalist Garrett Graff. “We are a country where we have the opportunity as each successive generation to expand the circle of who counts as an American.”
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Vermont Conversation: ‘Freedom in America is never guaranteed.’ Garrett Graff on America’s many revolution[...]
text:
The Vermont Conversation with David Goodman is a VTDigger podcast that features in-depth interviews on local and national issues. Listen and subscribe for free on Apple Podcasts, Spotify, YouTube or wherever you get podcasts.
Vermont author Garrett Graff explores the revolutions that remade America in his latest book, “America in 25 Revolutions.” Courtesy photo
The blue tsunami of Democratic victories in last week’s midterm elections included a number of notable firsts: the election of the first Black female governor, first female Native American governor and senator, the first openly gay male senator, the first Muslim senator, and the first Latina and Latino governors, respectively, for the country’s two most populous states, Texas and California.
These political milestones serve as an important corrective in the American story. When the country’s founders proclaimed that “all men were created equal,” they left out women, people of color and countless others. We have been fighting for a more inclusive democracy ever since.
“The beauty of the system that the founders left us is that we are a country that gets better,” said Vermont historian and journalist Garrett Graff. “We are a country where we have the opportunity as each successive generation to expand the circle of who counts as an American.”
Graff expands on this in his new book, “America in 25 Revolutions: The Story of Our Imperfect Nation’s 250-Year Quest to Become a More Perfect Union.”
The book includes 25 stories of “when the circle of who counted as ‘American’ was erased and made larger,” Graff writes. These include Reconstruction, women’s suffrage, LGBTQ rights, the civil rights movement, the environmental movement, disability rights, as well as the fight to end patronage in the civil service and the movement to end child labor.
Garrett Graff was a finalist for the Pulitzer Prize for his 2022 history of Watergate. He is the author of 10 books about history and national security, including “When the Sea Came Alive: An Oral History of D-Day,” “The Only Plane in the Sky: An Oral History of 9-11,” and “UFO: The Inside Story of the US Government’s Search for Alien Life Here ― and Out There.” Graff also shares his writing about current politics in his online newsletter, Doomsday Scenario.
As the United States marks its 250th anniversary, Graff argues that America’s defining story is not a single revolution, but a series of transformative movements that have repeatedly expanded democracy and civil rights.
“Freedom in America is never given, except grudgingly,” Graff said. “It is never guaranteed, and it’s not always linear.”
Graff characterized the MAGA movement as a reaction against profound demographic and cultural changes reshaping the country.
“I have always believed that MAGA, and particularly the white supremacist Christian nationalist wing of the MAGA movement, represented a last gasp rearguard action in an increasingly diversifying America,” he said.

READ MORE

According to Graff, anxieties about racial diversity, gender equality and LGBTQ rights are all part of a broader struggle over the nation’s future identity. “I think for a certain type of voter, for a certain type of American, they see all three of those revolutions as coming at their expense,” he said.
Yet Graff insists such conflicts are hardly unprecedented. The arc of American history, he argues, is marked by advances followed by backlash and retrenchment.
“We are living through one of those moments where we have seen progress and retrenchment across the last 20 years of American politics in a way that is actually very common from across American history,” he said.
A central theme of the book is that some of the country’s most important democratic advances are often overlooked. Alongside well-known movements such as Reconstruction and women’s suffrage, Graff examines reforms like the Americans with Disabilities Act and the battle against political patronage in the 19th century.
He points to Native American activist Sarah Winnemucca as one of the book’s unsung heroes. Her campaign against corruption in federal Indian affairs helped advance what Graff calls a “merit revolution” that established expectations of professional, competent government service.
“America deserved competent government administration,” he said of the reform movement. “We needed a nonpartisan civil service that was focused on professionalism and standards of quality.”
Despite his frequent warnings about democratic erosion in his newsletter Doomsday Scenario, Graff is optimistic. He believes the country’s progress toward a more representative democracy would astonish many of the nation’s founders.
“Look at just who was elected last Tuesday,” he said. “The extent to which America has actually achieved becoming a multi-gender, multiracial, multi-faith, multi-ethnic democracy is really astounding.”
For Graff, that achievement represents the true legacy of the American experiment: not perfection, but continuous expansion of rights and opportunity.
“The incredible thing about what the founders managed to do,” he said, “was build a system where a whole lot of people that the founders would not have considered citizens, either legally or morally, have been able to write themselves into the American story over the last 250 years.”

title: Elliot Russell sentenced to life in Ulysses Ivey murder
description:
Elliot Russell was sentenced to life in prison for the 2022 shooting death of Ulysses Ivey near Route 279 in Bennington. Russell maintained his innocence at sentencing.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Elliot Russell sentenced to life in Ulysses Ivey murder.
text:
The defense speaks with Russell’s sister and brother-in-law during the hearing. Photo by Jeff McRae/Bennington Banner

This story by Jeff McRae was first published in the Bennington Banner on Nov. 10, 2026.BENNINGTON — Elliot Russell, 50, will be spending the rest of his life behind bars for the pre-meditated shooting death of Ulysses Ivey, 39, of Bennington following a sentencing hearing on Monday afternoon.
At the hearing, Russell maintained his innocence and members of his family were allowed to play an extended version of the 911 phone call they say included at least one additional voice that they claim was omitted from the call tape submitted as evidence in the trial.
At sentencing, Russell’s defense attorney acknowledged that he had had a difference of opinion with Russell and Russell’s family as to the value of the extended call tape. Ultimately, Russell’s sister was allowed to play the tape following a brief discussion with the defense attorney and the attorney’s explanation to the court for the family’s agitation.
Following a second playing of the extended 911 call, the court acknowledged “I heard something at the end,” but did not characterize the sound.
The court emphasized that nothing presented at the sentencing would alter the outcome of the trial in which Russell was found guilty of murder by a jury of his peers.
Following a 35-minute recess, the court offered an explanation of the criteria they considered when coming to their conclusion, including: the nature and circumstances of the 2022 events; that the crime was committed when Russell was an adult; the luring of Ivey to a remote location, and Russell’s criminal history of increasing violence.
Given those factors, the court handed down the maximum sentence of life in prison without the possibility of parole.  
Russell, also known as “Face,” was charged in the Oct. 26, 2022 with first degree murder. Authorities say Ivey was lured to the area outside the Green Mountain power sub-station just before the exit ramp, west of Route 279 in Bennington, where he was killed.
A 911 call came from Ivey moments after he was shot. Prosecutors said during that call, Ivey identified the then-46-year-old Russell as the shooter. Rescue workers unsuccessfully attempted to save Ivey’s life.
Russell is no stranger to the Vermont and New York legal systems, with Vermont aggravated assault convictions in 2007 and 2009, and convictions in New York state in 1993 for robbery and for criminal possession of a loaded firearm in 1998. 
Most recently, he was convicted in 2007 of attempted murder after stabbing a man in front of a bar on Main Street in Bennington. Russell was sentenced to 13 to 15 years behind bars. He had been released from prison only three months prior to Ivey’s murder. 
During the recess, the prosecutor, Deputy State’s Attorney Jared Bianchi, declined to comment on the specifics of the Russell murder case. He said that generally when there’s been a conviction, there could be an appeal based on legal issues that arose during the trial or the sentencing, and that once a sentence is imposed, a person can file a petition for post-conviction relief (PCR). He said if, for instance, DNA is discovered that exculpates – or clears someone from guilt or blame – an individual would file a writ of habeas corpus, that, according to the Brennan Center for Justice, is “a civil lawsuit filed in court by or on behalf of a detained person to challenge the legality of their imprisonment or custody.”
In Vermont, “According to Rule 3(b) of the Vermont Rules of Appellate Procedure, any criminal case resulting in a sentence of life imprisonment triggers an automatic appeal to the Vermont Supreme Court,” as described by Justia Law.

title: Is your car ready for ski season? UDOT has a new way to help drivers prepare for traction laws
description: Ahead of the winter ski season, state transportation officials are urging drivers to make sure their vehicles are prepared to safely navigate winter canyon roads before heading to the slopes.
text:
The mouth of Little Cottonwood Canyon is pictured on Sunday, March 31, 2024. (Photo by Spenser Heaps for Utah News Dispatch)Ahead of the winter ski season, state transportation officials are urging drivers to make sure their vehicles are prepared to safely navigate winter canyon roads before heading to the slopes. 
The Utah Department of Transportation this week announced it has launched a new online quiz to help Utah motorists determine whether their vehicles meet winter traction requirements based on where they plan to drive and what type of vehicle they plan to use. 
“Nobody should have to be an expert on tires or traction laws to know whether they’re prepared for winter driving,” UDOT Traveler Information Director Becky Parker said in a prepared statement. “We’ve spent years helping Utahns understand these requirements, and this quiz takes that education a step further.”
The quiz helps Utah drivers be prepared for all state-owned roads in Utah. 
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
“Instead of searching through a list of rules to figure out which ones apply to their vehicle, drivers can now have that information presented directly to them,” Parker said. 
The new quiz comes as state transportation officials and local law enforcement agencies enter their second winter season of stricter traction laws for Big and Little Cottonwood canyons, where many of the state’s ski resorts draw long lines of traffic on snowy days. 
In 2025, the Utah Legislature passed HB196, which allows UDOT officials to enforce traction requirements up to 24 hours before a storm begins.
During severe winter driving conditions, the Utah Department of Transportation enforces a new administrative rule that requires vehicles to have specific traction abilities or devices, and the Cottonwood canyons have a “class 3 designation” with stricter requirements. 



When the beacons outside the canyons are flashing, vehicles driving up Big or Little Cottonwood canyons must have: 

At least 5/32 tire tread depth on all wheels if you’re relying on tires themselves and not traction devices like chains, cables, snow socks or tire studs. 
Tires rated for mud and snow, or snow, depending on whether the vehicle has two-wheel drive or all-wheel drive. 
All-wheel or four-wheel drive vehicles must have snow-rated tires on all wheels, or traction devices on at least two wheels. 
Two-wheel drive vehicles must have 3PMSF, or Three-Peak Mountain Snowflake-certified tires, on all wheels. Or, traction devices on at least the drive wheels are acceptable. 




Police may issue citations to those who violate the traction requirements.
“Preparing for winter travel includes more steps than just checking the forecast,” Parker said. “Drivers need to understand what equipment their vehicles require, what conditions to expect on the roads and what transportation options are available. We want to make it easier for people to find that information before they leave home, so they’re more prepared for the conditions ahead.” 
UDOT also has a Cottonwood Canyons Sticker Program that offers free tire inspections at more than 160 tire shops along the Wasatch Front. The voluntary program’s sixth season started this week and runs through Feb. 28, with the goal of improving safety and traffic flow in the canyons by encouraging drivers to make sure their vehicles are compliant. 
State transportation officials are urging Utah drivers to check their tires, slow down during winter conditions, and consider taking public transit or carpooling when heading up the canyons.
More information about traction requirements are available on UDOT’s website.

title: Iowa Board of Regents to take harder look at university athletics, continues efficiency work
description: Officials at Iowa’s public universities will be following up with the Iowa Board of Regents to provide more details of its fiscal year 2026 budgets and future financial planning as the board’s revenue and efficiencies study moves forward. Officials from the University of Iowa, Iowa State University and University of Northern Iowa presented their revenues […]
text:
The Iowa Board of Regents discusses its revenue enhancement and productivity study at its Nov. 11, 2026, meeting. (Photo by Brooklyn Draisey/Iowa Capital Dispatch)Officials at Iowa’s public universities will be following up with the Iowa Board of Regents to provide more details of its fiscal year 2026 budgets and future financial planning as the board’s revenue and efficiencies study moves forward.
Officials from the University of Iowa, Iowa State University and University of Northern Iowa presented their revenues and expenses for fiscal year 2026 to the board’s investment and finance committee during its Nov. 11 meeting, with calls from board members for further conversations and plan-setting for future budgeting needs.
Athletics department budgets were the main source of concern for Regent Christine Hensley and other board members, with Hensley saying UNI is operating with a budget deficit, ISU is borrowing from its reserve fund, and the UI is making minimum loan payments. Hensley said she’s received questions from Iowans about the state of collegiate athletics and it deserves a discussion at the board level.
SUBSCRIBE: GET THE MORNING HEADLINES DELIVERED TO YOUR INBOX.
Board President Robert Cramer agreed, saying he and President Pro Tem Kurt Tjaden are planning to meet with university leaders as soon as the coming days to discuss “looking forward” and the next steps in ensuring university athletics is in a strong budget position.
“We do need to take a look at all of it, and so we’ll come back to the board with a plan of how we’re going to address it … It’s a big deal,” Cramer said.
UI Chief Financial Officer and Treasurer Terry Johnson said the athletics department had a “very good year” altogether, with expenses and revenues exceeding the budget by more than $655,000. According to the fiscal year 2026 fiscal report, $2.5 million was budgeted for loan repayment and the university paid just under $2.43 million.
The athletics department saw increases in ticket sales for football, women’s and men’s basketball and wrestling, Johnson said, as well as from athletic conference distributions, royalty income, premium seats and fundraising.
“Similar to other Division One programs in the country, though, I mean, revenue share is real. It continues to be a stressor for our institution as well as probably all of the academic Division One programs in the country,” Johnson said. “But athletics is doing an excellent job to date of managing its resources, and I definitely anticipate that will continue in the future.”
Fiscal year 2026 was the first year of UNI’s three-year plan to balance its athletics budget after an audit of the department, UNI Senior Vice President for Finance and Operations Machael Hager said. The budget “contemplated a $2.2 million operating deficit” but the program ended up with a $5.3 million deficit, he said.
“The two largest budget-to-actual variances, foundation support under the income section and administrative in general under the expense section, are partially attributable to adjustments made to the balanced budget presented to the board rather than the operating contemplated by the three-year plan,” Hager said.
He said there were differences between “what was submitted for the requirement to have balance and what the operational plan was,” which expected a balanced budget, from an internal audit that allowed for the deficit. Regent Steve Lacy expressed confusion at how the budget turned out, saying he’d never heard of the internal audit, and Tjaden suggested regrouping to set a new baseline for next year and align projections accordingly.
Hensley also asked about potential loans and projecting budgets as much as five years out, saying it would be “extremely helpful,” which Tjaden said they should look at but could be too difficult, suggesting three years may be a better option.
ISU Senior Vice President for Operations and Finance Sean Reeder said the university’s exceeding of its budgeted revenues by $4.4 million was driven by “strong competitive performance gains” in football and both basketball teams, as well as from ticket sales, fundraising, premium seating, multimedia rights, licensing income and auxiliary revenues.
Overall, the athletics budget for fiscal year 2026 was balanced, he said.
“Stronger revenue performance reduced the need for cash reserves by $17 million compared with what our original budget was,” Reeder said.
Board receives REAPS update
The board of regents also received another update on its Revenue Enhancement and Productivity Study (REAPS), which board Chief Efficiency Officer Jake Nicholson said he is confident will be ready with a report for the board to consider at its February meeting.
Nicholson said the REAPS committee is over halfway through its review of potential opportunities for revenue enhancement or cost efficiency and it has held 12 meetings with different shared governance groups across the three university campuses. The study is still on–track with its timeline, he said, with meetings scheduled in December and January.
“I’m very confident that in February, REAPS will deliver vetted, validated, and actionable recommendations for the board,” Nicholson said.
Some of the opportunities the committee has looked over so far, without any final decisions made, include expanding opportunities for community college student transfers like the UNI@IACC program at the Cedar Falls university, reorienting bachelor’s degree completion programming, and aligning and centralizing information technology services.
“None of those are final recommendations,” Nicholson said. “These are all just exploratory opportunities that are building towards a combined and thoughtful portfolio that results in a roadmap for the board of regents to consider.”

title: With 274 trona workers facing January layoffs, WE Soda union opposes company’s pending $13M state grant
description:
The company, which plans to cut 350 jobs total over the next two years, should not receive state taxpayer dollars without conditions to reduce the job losses, the union says.
The post With 274 trona workers facing January layoffs, WE Soda union opposes company’s pending $13M state grant appeared first on WyoFile .
text:
The union representing workers at WE Soda’s trona and soda ash operations in southwest Wyoming, as well as some of their supporters, are calling on Gov. Mark Gordon to pump the brakes on a $13 million state taxpayer-funded grant request by the company.
The company says it will cut 350 jobs at its Westvaco operations over the next two years, beginning in January with 274 workers receiving pink slips, according to a notice WE Soda sent to state and local government officials.


How to comment
To comment on the WE Soda and other grant recommendations, send an email to the Wyoming Energy Authority at wea@wyo.gov. Click here to review the projects and to learn more about the Energy Dominance Fund. The deadline to submit a comment is Monday.


“I’m asking the State of Wyoming to FREEZE these funds until Wyoming Workers are assured they have a place to work at WE Soda!” Marshal Cummings, a WE Soda worker and United Steelworkers Local 13214 president, wrote in a recent social media post.
“If Wyoming can find nearly $13 million to support a corporation,” he added, “surely we can find a way to support the workers who made that corporation successful.”
London-based WE Soda announced Nov. 4 it would reduce its Wyoming workforce from about 850 to 500 over the next two years, primarily due to its plans to shift its Westvaco trona mine from underground mining to drill-and-pump solution mining. The initial 274 layoffs in January would impact positions throughout WE Soda’s Sweetwater County operations from an administrative assistant to engineers to miners, with 223 unionized workers slated to lose their jobs.
Prior to the announced layoffs, WE Soda applied for a $13 million grant from the state’s new Energy Dominance fund to build a “high-pressure natural gas supply connection from the Williams’ MountainWest Overthrust Pipeline system” to its Westvaco operations, according to the company’s project summary. The company’s contract for coal from the nearby Kemmerer coal mine will end this year, it explained, and it wants to shift to natural gas to fire boilers used in processing trona to soda ash — a global commodity used in glass manufacturing, in cleaning products and in water treatment, among other things.
This image depicts a trona mining operation in Wyoming. (The Center for Land Use Interpretation)
The natural gas connection that the proposed $13 million grant would support is not immediately integral to the planned conversion from underground to solution mining, according Cummings. Regardless, the state, if it chooses to approve the grant, should “tie those funds to protections for these workers,” he told WyoFile, adding that protection means maintaining jobs. “That would be the most ideal thing for us.”
The Wyoming Energy Authority, which administers the grant and loan program, recommended approving WE Soda’s request last month, kicking off a public comment period that ends Monday. The agency will forward its recommendation, along with public comments, to Gordon. 
The governor has sole discretion to deny the request, OK it, or approve with conditions.
Reached by WyoFile for comment, Gordon’s office said he would not comment on the grant request until after the public comment period. Gov.-elect Eric Barlow also declined to comment. Hours after WyoFile published a story about the layoffs, both men issued a joint-statement saying they are “especially concerned for the miners and their families in southwestern Wyoming and are working diligently to bring resources to address the impacts of these reductions.”
A trona miner stops to check in with fellow underground crew members on May 12, 2025. (Dustin Bleizeffer/WyoFile)
The Wyoming Democratic Party issued a statement Wednesday joining the union’s call to freeze any action on WE Soda’s grant “until workers are assured they have a place to work at WE Soda.”
The state’s Energy Dominance fund is “intended to create jobs and support economic growth,” the party said. 
“We are not only heartbroken, but extremely angry on behalf of the workers at WE Soda,” the party continued. “Our friends and neighbors in Sweetwater County are facing not only the devastating loss of hundreds of jobs, but a massive blow to the entire economy of their community. They deserve so much better than broken promises made by a company that prioritizes profits over people.”
WE Soda’s pending grant is among three recommended for approval by the Energy Authority, the first batch since the fund was created earlier this year. The three grants for a combined $48 million include $20 million to Canadian-headquartered Nucleon Fuel for its proposed Fort Union Uranium Conversion facility in Campbell County and $15 million to Tulsa, Oklahoma-based Williams Companies for its Flat Top Compressor Station project in Carbon County.
The Energy Dominance fund is intended to support projects “related to Wyoming’s energy needs,” to companies that “demonstrate established commitments for the dollar-for-dollar funding match” and projects that “provide a public benefit for Wyoming,” according to the Energy Authority’s description of the program. 
The Wyoming Legislature created the Energy Dominance Fund during the most recent legislative session, authorizing up to $105 million for loans and grants to support energy projects in the state. The pot of money is filled by severance tax revenue from energy extraction, like coal mining and oil and natural gas development.

name: VTDigger
title: Don’t blame immigrant students for rising education costs
description:
Vermont’s school costs are climbing because of health insurance and federal cuts, not because of the multicultural kids in Winooski’s classrooms.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Don’t blame immigrant students for rising education costs.
text:
This commentary is by Caitlin MacLeod-Bluver, a teacher at Winooski High School. She is the 2025 Vermont Teacher of the Year and the 2026 Vermont History Teacher of the Year. 
In the WCAX debate on Oct. 28, Gov. Phil Scott incorrectly claimed that the Winooski School District offers 17 languages, unlike smaller, more rural districts that may offer only one or two. 
This is false. Winooski offers one language, French. Elementary school students have no language opportunities, middle school students take French for one quarter, and high school students are offered French I or French II. 
When Scott claims that Winooski offers 17 languages, it is not just a curriculum mistake. It is a remark that serves to pit our rural, largely white communities against our more urban, more diverse communities.  
This misinformation fuels anti-immigrant, xenophobic thinking that hurts our students, our families and our communities. Collectively, our student body does speak at least 17 languages. At Winooski, we view their languages as our greatest asset. We honor students’ strengths, recognize the value of their languages and celebrate both their languages and cultural backgrounds, experiences and heritage. It is well documented that speaking more than one language has many benefits, from helping promote healthy aging to improved mental agility. Our students’ languages are their superpowers, and at Winooski, we actively celebrate this diversity. 
Scott’s comment distracts us from the underlying causes of our high education costs. Instead of thinking creatively about reducing healthcare costs for teachers — as S.190 would have done, which Scott vetoed — or moving mental healthcare funding out of the education budget to the Department of Mental Health, his comment implies that the funding problem in our state lies with our immigrant students. 
Nothing could be farther from the truth. 
But sadly, this rhetoric and mindset catch on quickly. Many districts across our state are facing dire financial realities this budget season. When the governor adds misinformation to an already difficult situation, it escalates tensions between communities and distracts people from the true causes of our financial woes. We will not be guilty of blaming our most vulnerable community rather than directing responsibility at our 10-year incumbent governor or lawmakers. Scott has often tried to distance himself from the MAGA right, but comments like this demonstrate that he is using the same playbook. 
In his response to the Winooski superintendent, Scott apologized, said he misspoke and added that he was not trying to pit communities against each other, but aiming to call attention to discrepancies in educational opportunities across our state. Governor, if you don’t want to pit communities against each other, I suggest not falsely calling out our only majority-minority district in the state, and if you aim to highlight different educational opportunities, do so with the correct information. 
Subsequently, in my civics class, we watched this segment of the debate. It is a reminder to the governor that our students are always listening and always watching. They deserve a public apology. 
Vermonters, we will not be fooled by this anti-immigrant language. We have real problems in how we fund our schools, but we will not blame our greatest asset: our students.

title: Shaftsbury man accused of driving into his friend denies manslaughter charge
description:
The charge stems from an incident early in the evening of May 31 that occurred in the driveway of the man who was killed in Dorset.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  Shaftsbury man accused of driving into his friend denies manslaughter charge .
text:
The Vermont Superior Court building in Bennington. Photo by Mike Dougherty/VTDigger

A Dorset man is facing a charge of involuntary manslaughter for allegedly losing control of his vehicle in his friend’s driveway, striking and killing him.
Arthur Coons, 67, of Shaftsbury, pleaded not guilty earlier this month to the felony charge and was released on conditions, including that he keep the court informed of his address and phone number.
Vermont State Police issued Coons a citation into court for the arraignment on the charge in late October following an investigation into the May 31 death of 39-year-old Philip Mecik of Dorset outside his Mecik’s home.
“It’s horrific because they were best friends,” Matthew Hart, Coons’ attorney, said this week. 
“We look forward to getting an explanation, if we can, as to why this accident happened,” Hart added. “It was definitely not an intentional act.”  
Bennington County Deputy State’s Attorney Jared Bianchi, reached this week, declined to comment.
Detective Sgt. Nicholas Grimes wrote in an affidavit filed in support of the charge that Mecik’s mother called 911 early in the evening on May 31 reporting that her son was pinned between their garage and a vehicle that had been driven by Coons. 
First responders pronounced Mecik dead at the scene, Grimes wrote. Investigators saw that the residence’s garage door was damaged and Coon’s vehicle, a 2019 Toyota 4-Runner, had heavy front-end damage, the affidavit stated. 
The two men had been working that day on a renovation project in the basement of Mecik’s home when in the early evening Mecik’s mother reported hearing “catastrophic” sound, “like a meteorite striking the residence,” Grimes wrote.
The mother reported that Coons told her he had hit a rock when backing up his vehicle in the driveway and that he was pressing the brake and trying to stop and that his transmission was not working properly, the affidavit stated. 
She then asked Coons where her son was before she began looking for him inside the residence, Grimes wrote.
When Mecik’s mother went back outside Coons had moved his vehicle and she saw her son lying on the ground near the damaged garage door, according to the affidavit. 
Coons, in an interview with investigators, called Mecik his best friend, and after finishing for the day working on the renovation project at Mecik’s home he packed his tools in his vehicle, waved goodbye to Mecik and started to back up, Grimes wrote. Coons reported that while backing up he struck a rock between a paved driveway and a gravel driveway, the affidavit stated.
“After striking the rock, Arthur put the vehicle into drive and the vehicle started rolling,” Grimes wrote. “Arthur claimed that when he put his foot on the brake, the vehicle ‘took off’ across the driveway.”
Coons reported that he saw that he hit the garage and started yelling for Mecik, who he couldn’t initially see or find. Then Coons discovered after backing up that he had struck Mecik, who did not have time to get out of the way, the affidavit stated. 
Information from the vehicle’s data recorder showed that Coons depressed the accelerator and failed to brake, the affidavit stated. 
“Being aware of Philip’s location in the driveway, Arthur continued to steer his vehicle in the direction of Philip while accelerating,” Grimes wrote. “Arthur failed to brake and failed to steer his vehicle in a direction to avoid colliding with Philip.”
The detective added, “Arthur operated his vehicle in a negligent manner, grossly deviating from the care that an ordinary person would have exercised, leading to a crash that resulted in death to a pedestrian.”
If convicted of the charge, Coons faces up to 15 years in jail.

title: I live in my barn so I can afford to stay in Vermont
description:
Not every short-term rental belongs to a wealthy out-of-stater. For some of us, it’s the only way to survive.
Read the story on VTDigger here:  I live in my barn so I can afford to stay in Vermont.
text:
Dear Editor,
I have one message for anyone in the Legislature talking about taxing second-home owners more. I am on the edge of having to sell up and move south because property taxes are almost as much as my mortgage.
I bought my home on 18 acres in 2007: a very simple ranch house, a run-down garage apartment and a small horse barn. After a breakup, I needed to buy my partner out, but I couldn’t afford to keep living in the house. So I took what was left in my 401(k), hired some cowboys to make the barn livable, and moved into it. I rented out my actual home and the little cottage so I could afford to stay in Vermont — barely. At times, I was literally surviving on potatoes from the garden and eggs from my hens.

READ MORE

I tried long-term rentals, but a couple of very bad tenant experiences left me with losses of $15,000 to $20,000 each time. When you’re already living on the financial edge, you simply cannot absorb that, and Vermont’s tenancy laws do not protect small landlords, while they encourage bad tenants.
Eventually, my choice was to sell and move south or find another way to stay. For me, that way was short-term renting through Airbnb. I had to refinance to do up the house, and my very kind ex-boyfriend co-signed for me because I didn’t meet the income requirements. Running an Airbnb is incredibly time-consuming and much harder work running than many people imagine. Between platform fees, Vermont taxes and fees, maintenance and running costs, even breaking even can be a struggle.
It has taken an enormous amount of blood, sweat and tears to stay here. I still live in the barn. It’s difficult to heat, and I don’t even heat my bedroom. I am hardly living high off the hog.
And I’m not alone. Other Vermonters are in similar circumstances, renting out their homes so they can afford to remain on their own properties and in their communities.
I understand the concern about housing. But please leave room in this discussion for people like me. For some of us, short-term renting is what has allowed us to keep our homes. Policies that overlook that distinction risk pricing us out.
Lou White
Hartland, Vt.

title: ‘The 120th Congress is coming’: Dems who flipped the US House pack freshman orientation
description: WASHINGTON — With a sweeping majority secured in the U.S. House next Congress, newly elected Democrats arrived in the nation’s capital this week vowing to act on their agenda of affordability and accountability.The dozens of Democrats who flipped the House majority are in Washington, D.C., for several days as part of new member orientation. The onboarding tr[...]
text: WASHINGTON — With a sweeping majority secured in the U.S. House next Congress, newly elected Democrats arrived in the nation’s capital this week vowing to act on their agenda of affordability and accountability.The dozens of Democrats who flipped the House majority are in Washington, D.C., for several days as part of new member orientation. The onboarding tradition for both parties features training sessions and programming, as well as a class photo on the U.S. Capitol steps and a room lottery to determine their office spaces. In early January, the new members will be sworn in, and Democrats will spend the next two years attempting to deliver on the issues they spent months campaigning on — ranging from lowering the high cost of healthcare to enacting anti-corruption efforts to trying to overturn the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law. Their introduction was overwhelming at times. Rep.-elect J.D. Ford, the Democrat who will represent Indiana’s 5th Congressional District, said orientation is “definitely like drinking from a fire hose, but I’m just trying to take it day by day.’’ Ford said he’s “really excited to make some relationships,” noting that “obviously this building is all about that, so this has been really good for us to not just meet members of my own party, but potential members I could work across the aisle with.” Rep.-elect Oliver G. Gilbert III, set to represent Florida’s historically Black-dominated 24th Congressional District, said “we have a lot to do, but I know we’re up to the task.“This country is 250 years old, and we’re the greatest country in the history of the world, but our greatness is always tomorrow, it’s not yesterday, so it’s what we make it, and so, we’re going to make it something better in this Congress,” he said.  “The 120th Congress is coming.” The blue tsunami During the programming, States Newsroom got a glimpse into the top priorities of several incoming Democratic members, who are riding on the heels of a blue tsunami that swept the country on Election Day and also flipped the U.S. Senate. At least 75 new House Democrats, excluding non-voting delegates, have been elected as of Wednesday afternoon, The Associated Press projected, with 12 races to be called. Democrats will control at least 255 seats in the House, according to the AP.House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries of New York — the likely speaker in the new Congress — would helm Democrats’ legislative agenda if elected by his peers. But with more than two years left in office, President Donald Trump is all but certain to veto many of Democrats’ measures, potentially making the party’s work more of a messaging exercise ahead of the 2028 presidential election.  Still, Democratic members-elect who made a new majority laid out the visions they are eager to deliver on in the next Congress, fueled by voters’ concerns in their districts:Florida Gilbert, set to represent the Sunshine State’s 24th Congressional District, wants to “make the American dream more accessible,” pointing to affordability and accountability as the avenue to those aims. “When I talk to people, it doesn’t matter whether you’re speaking Haitian Creole, you’re speaking Spanish, you’re speaking English, they’re all worried about the price of gas, the accessibility of healthcare, the lack of affordable, quality housing, how your kids are going to be educated, whether the American dream is still going to be accessible to them,” Gilbert said.Indiana Ford, who unseated incumbent Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz, said he heard “over and over again” from voters in the district that they were “really tired of seeing the grift from this administration.” He also cited healthcare accessibility and broader affordability as other major priorities. “Cost of utilities, groceries, you name it — people are actually talking about it at their kitchen dinner table, so I think moving forward, still trying to get my sea legs here, but we need to address those issues in this next Congress when we get back here in January,” Ford said. MarylandFor Rep.-elect Adrian Boafo of Maryland, addressing the Trump administration’s major downsizing of the federal workforce and its effects on constituents in his 5th Congressional District marks a priority for him heading into Congress. “Federal workers have been downright assaulted by this administration,” said Boafo, who is succeeding and previously served as an aide to retiring Democratic Rep. Steny Hoyer. “Frankly, we’ve got to find a pathway to not just rehire the people who, in my opinion, were illegally fired — we also have to provide some oversight as to what happened with DOGE,” Boafo added, pointing to an earlier initiative under the Trump administration that sought to drastically reduce federal government spending and resulted in mass firings across agencies, hitting Marylanders hard in particular. MichiganRep.-elect Donavan McKinney, set to represent Michigan’s 13th Congressional District, said overturning the GOP’s mega tax and spending cut law, known as the “One Big Beautiful Bill Act,” is top of mind for him heading into Congress. “What I’m hearing every single day from my residents, they’re getting letters in the mail as we speak ... that they’re going to get kicked off food assistance, their healthcare,” said McKinney, whose district is among the poorest in the country and includes parts of Detroit. NebraskaRep.-elect Denise Powell, who will represent Nebraska’s 2nd Congressional District, said “we need to get a farm bill passed as soon as humanly possible,” pointing to the long overdue agriculture aid and nutrition programs package that has stalled amid partisan disputes. Powell, who will be the first Latina to represent Nebraska in Congress after flipping the seat of retiring GOP Rep. Don Bacon, pointed to healthcare as another priority heading into Congress. For Powell, part of that includes wanting to reverse the Medicaid cuts baked into the tax and spending cut law, which axes roughly $1 trillion in program spending over 10 years.    WisconsinRep.-elect Mitchell Berman said his No. 1 priority is to deliver on the needs of constituents in his southeastern Wisconsin district, which includes “lowering costs of living, making sure that folks can afford to put food on the table, pay their rent and also healthcare.” As a registered nurse, Berman said with that background he wants to “make sure we can make healthcare affordable for folks.” Berman flipped Wisconsin’s 1st Congressional District after defeating incumbent GOP Rep. Bryan Steil. The district has not seen a Democrat hold the seat in more than three decades. Also in the Badger State, Rep.-elect Rebecca Cooke said she’s focused on fulfilling the campaign promises she ran on, including “lowering healthcare costs — making sure it’s affordable and accessible — combating corruption really on both sides of the aisle, delivering for our agricultural communities by ending the war in Iran, changing what we do with tariffs.” Cooke flipped Wisconsin’s 3rd Congressional District after beating incumbent GOP Rep. Derrick Van Orden in another upset for Republicans.
